title: Fixture-hash golden test is RED on the committed tree — daily-pull workflow gate is currently broken
evidence: Running `node tag28-tests.js` deterministically fails: `fixture-hash mismatch: stored=fd4a13856b18fc7b computed=e005f65977e02186` (reproduced on two consecutive runs; tests/fixture-hash.txt contains `fd4a13856b18fc7b`). Working tree is clean; the most recent commit is `ce8e33432 formel(quality): purity + correctness fixes (audit 2026-06-20)`, which altered method/aggregator output without re-baselining the hash. The test is wired into the pipeline at .github/workflows/daily-pull.yml:88: `node tag28-tests.js && echo "tag28 PASS" || { echo "tag28 FAIL"; exit 1; }`.
why_it_matters: tag28-tests.js gates the daily-pull workflow with exit 1. With the golden test failing, the entire ~14.6h pull/screen pipeline is blocked at the test step on every run. Either commit ce8e33432 introduced an unintended behavior change in score-aggregator/methods (a real regression), or it was an intentional formula change that nobody re-baselined. Both are pipeline-stopping. workflows/scripts are entrypoints, so this is not a dormant test — it is actively breaking CI now.
fix: Triage commit ce8e33432 against the projection in _computeFixtureHash (HG/QC pass+weight+computable+score). If the output change is the intended 'purity + correctness fix', regenerate the baseline with `ALLOW_FIXTURE_CHANGE=1 "C:\Program Files\nodejs\node.exe" tag28-tests.js` and commit tests/fixture-hash.txt in the SAME commit as the behavior change (the workflow comment at daily-pull.yml:423 documents this discipline). If the change was unintended, revert the offending method delta. Do not touch FTS_CACHE_VERSION. Add a CI assertion that fixture-hash.txt was modified in any commit that changes SCORE_WEIGHTS-bearing methods, so the baseline can never drift silently again.

_verdict.note:
CONFIRMED REAL — reproduced deterministically on the clean committed HEAD (ce8e33432). `node tag28-tests.js` fails the "fixture-hash: score-aggregator output is stable" test with the exact quoted mismatch (stored=fd4a13856b18fc7b computed=e005f65977e02186), prints "Passed: 183, Failed: 1", and exits 1 (verified raw exit code = 1; reproduced on two consecutive runs). tests/fixture-hash.txt at HEAD = `fd4a13856b18fc7b` (tracked, not gitignored). The gate at .github/workflows/daily-pull.yml:88 is `node tag28-tests.js && echo "tag28 PASS" || { echo "tag28 FAIL"; exit 1; }`, so the non-zero exit hits the FAIL branch and aborts the daily-pull job.

Root cause is unambiguous and self-documented: commit ce8e33432 ("formel(quality): purity + correctness fixes") changed four scoring methods (score-aggregator.js, altman-z-score.js, piotroski-f-score.js, quality-compounder-roic.js) that feed the _computeFixtureHash projection (HG/QC pass+weight+computable+score, tag28-tests.js:2770-2782). Its own commit message states "fixture-hash deliberately rebased fd4a13856b18fc7b -> e005f65977e02186" and "Gates: ... tag28 184/184" — but `git show --stat ce8e33432` lists only the 4 methods/*.js files; tests/fixture-hash.txt was NOT included in the commit. The prior ancestor commit 00d595b09 had set the baseline to fd4a...; ce8e33432 changed the output to e005... without re-committing the baseline. So the author intended e005... (the computed value the test now reports) but the baseline-file write was dropped from the commit. The behavior change appears intentional (quality/purity fix), so the correct remedy is to rebaseline, not revert.

Severity assessment: this is a hard, deterministic CI gate failure on the committed tree that blocks the daily-pull pipeline — critical is justified for the broken gate. (One nuance for triage: the fixture-hash test is RED, but it is one assertion among 184; the rest pass. The pipeline impact is real because the gate exits 1 on any failure.)

title: Anchor regression test passes VACUOUSLY when snapshots are absent (SKIP never fails the run)
evidence: evaluateAnchor: `if (!fs.existsSync(fp)) { return { ticker, status: 'SKIP', reason: 'snapshot-missing', modes: [] }; }`. main(): only `if (r.status === 'PASS') pass++; else if (r.status === 'FAIL') fail++; else skip++;` and the gate is `if (fail > 0) process.exit(1);`. snapshots/ is gitignored (`.gitignore`: `snapshots/` + `!snapshots/_manifest.json`) and 'regenerated fresh every run'. In this worktree `ls snapshots/` returns ONLY `_manifest.json` — all 10 anchors resolve to SKIP, so pass=0 fail=0 skip=10 and the test prints 'All anchors qualified.' and exits 0.
why_it_matters: This is the screener's only end-to-end guard that scoring/threshold/weight changes don't silently drop NVDA/MSFT/etc below their tier floor. On any fresh checkout or CI runner where snapshots haven't been pulled (the normal CI state — snapshots are not committed), the test is green while testing NOTHING. A real regression that drops every anchor to REJECT would not be caught. A 'green' test that cannot fail is worse than no test: it manufactures false confidence, which is exactly how the Tag 219c financialCurrency 30x-FX corruption survived for weeks.
fix: Treat SKIP as failure unless explicitly allowed. Add an assertion that at least N anchors were actually evaluated: after the loop, `if (pass + fail === 0) { console.error('No anchor snapshots found — test evaluated nothing'); process.exit(1); }`. Optionally require a minimum coverage (e.g. >=8 of 10 present) so a half-populated snapshots dir also fails. Do NOT hardcode any ticker skip-list.

title: 13F tests mutate the REAL on-disk cache (external-data/sec-13f-by-ticker.json) with non-atomic write + non-finally-safe restore against process kill
evidence: _writeCacheRaw uses `fs.writeFileSync(CACHE_PATH_13F, s)` (line 1861) directly on the production path `path.join(__dirname,'external-data','sec-13f-by-ticker.json')` (line 1852), which is a real 85KB data file on disk (verified: `-rw-r--r-- 85173 sec-13f-by-ticker.json`). Each test does `const orig = _readCacheRaw(); try { _stubCache(...) } finally { _restoreCache(orig) }`. The write is non-atomic (no temp+rename) and the only protection is a try/finally inside the test body.
why_it_matters: The test harness `test()` (line 10-13) only catches thrown Errors per-test, but a hard crash, SIGINT, OOM, or a throw inside _restoreCache itself between unlink and write leaves the user's real 13F cache truncated or deleted. Because institutional-ownership-13f reads this exact file at runtime, a clobbered cache silently degrades every subsequent screen for that signal (institutionsHolding drops to incomputable) with no alarm. Tests should never write to production data paths.
fix: Point the 13F tests at a temp fixture path instead of the production cache: have the method accept an injectable cache path (mirror the already-existing injectable pattern used by insider-conviction-score `_evaluateWithTxns`, lines 2418-2452), or set CACHE_PATH_13F to `path.join(os.tmpdir(), 'test-13f-'+process.pid+'.json')`. If the on-disk round-trip must stay, route writes through lib/atomic-write.js (the same writeFileAtomic used by walk-forward-perf.js:24) so an interrupted write can't truncate the real file.

_verdict.note: Confirmed with source evidence. tag28-tests.js:1852 sets CACHE_PATH_13F = path.join(__dirname,'external-data','sec-13f-by-ticker.json') — the PRODUCTION path read by methods/institutional-ownership-13f.js (CACHE_PATH at line 58, loaded in _load13F). _writeCacheRaw (line 1861) does a non-atomic fs.writeFileSync on it, and _stubCache/_restoreCache run for 3 tests (lines 1873-1926) guarded only by a try/finally in the test body. Verified the on-disk file is real (85173 bytes) AND git-tracked (git ls-files --error-unmatch => TRACKED), so an interrupted/crashed write (SIGINT between stub-write and finally-restore) can truncate or delete a versioned 85KB data file — a genuine data-integrity hazard, not just a transient test artifact. The auditor's claim that a cleaner injectable pattern already exists is also correct: insider-conviction-score._evaluateWithTxns (tag28-tests.js:2418-2452) injects test data directly and never touches the on-disk cache. lib/atomic-write.js (exports writeFileAtomic, used by ~10 production scripts) likewise exists, so the alternative atomic-write fix is viable. Minor inaccuracy in the PROPOSED FIX only: the cited 'walk-forward-perf.js:24' file does not exist under that name (actual writeFileAtomic consumers are generate-screener.js, pull-historical-prices.js, sector-medians-compute.js, etc.) — this does not affect the validity of the finding. severity=high is appropriate because the affected file is git-tracked.

title: listing-age QC multiplier treats annual-history DEPTH as company AGE — penalizes long-history compounders whose snapshot stores few annual entries
evidence: Line 382: `var ageMultiplier = Math.min(1.0, ageRes.value / 5);` then `auditMultiplier *= ageMultiplier`. But listing-age.value is `cleanYears` = count of consecutive non-null annualRev entries (listing-age.js:56-61, `value: cleanYears`), NOT calendar age. listing-age.js header itself states: 'the actual decision factor ... is the data length, not the calendar age.' The aggregator nonetheless divides by 5 as if it were years since listing.
why_it_matters: Yahoo frequently stores only 4 annual revenue rows. A 20-year compounder (MSFT/COST/V — the exact QC anchors) with 4 stored annual entries gets cleanYears=4 → multiplier 4/5 = 0.80, silently shaving 20% off the score of the highest-quality names, pushing A-tier (>=80) to B. This is LIVE: daily-pull.yml runs the dashboard + score-history steps with AUDIT_SCORE_MULTIPLIERS=1 (lines 395/407/413), so the multiplied score is what Karl sees and what is persisted to score-history. The cap is invisible (no flag, no red-flag) and systematically biases against durable compounders — the opposite of QC intent.
fix: Drive the multiplier from a true age signal, not data depth: use components.ipoAgeYears (already computed at listing-age.js:69) when finite, falling back to cleanYears only when ipoYear is absent; clamp to [0,1]. Comment: 'prevents history-depth being mistaken for company age — Yahoo stores ~4 annual rows even for 20y compounders, which falsely pro-rated QC anchors below A-tier.' Do not hardcode tickers.

_verdict.note: CONFIRMED real. score-aggregator.js:382 does `ageMultiplier = Math.min(1.0, ageRes.value/5)` where ageRes.value is listing-age.value = cleanYears = count of consecutive non-null annualRev entries (listing-age.js:56-61,74), i.e. DATA DEPTH, not calendar age. The method header (lines 14-18) itself states the factor "is the data length, not the calendar age." The pipeline structurally caps that depth: pull-yahoo.js:1030 sets the FTS window to period1 = now - 5*365 days, and the legacy incomeStatementHistory path returns ~4 annual periods. Empirical proof from the live universe (methods-history/2026-06-12.json, 4737 stocks): value=4 for 4619 stocks (97.5%) and ZERO stocks reach value>=5. So value/5 tops out at 4/5=0.80 for essentially every stock — a 20y compounder and a 4-years-of-data company get the identical 0.80 multiplier. The "100% credit at 5y+" branch described in the defensive comment (score-aggregator.js:379-381) is unreachable dead logic; the comment misdescribes reality (it assumes cleanYears can hit 5). Production impact is live: .github/workflows/daily-pull.yml:395 sets AUDIT_SCORE_MULTIPLIERS='1' on the dashboard step, so this flat ~20% QC penalty applies to all quality compounders and can push anchors below A-tier. The fix's input exists: listing-age.js:69 computes components.ipoAgeYears = NOW_YEAR - ipoYear, and ipoYear is populated from a genuine first-trade date (pull-yahoo.js:1691, firstTradeDateMilliseconds).

title: Ohlson SIZE term uses raw-dollar TotalAssets with GNP index = 1.0, biasing O downward by ~5-9 points and effectively disabling the DATAGUARD hard-gate
evidence: Line 80: `const GNP_PRICE_INDEX = 1.0;` and lines 173-175: `const sizeRatio = ta_t / GNP_PRICE_INDEX; ... const size = -0.407 * Math.log(sizeRatio);`. With ta_t in raw USD (~1e9-3e12 in the snapshots) the size term is -0.407*log(1e9..3e12) = -8.4 to -11.7. Ohlson (1980) expresses TA in deflated $thousands (values O(10-1e4), size term ~ -2 to -4). Verified numerically: TA=$50B -> size=-10.03 vs ~-2.8 if properly scaled; net offset ~ -5.6.
why_it_matters: Ohlson is a promoted DATAGUARD (header Tag 224b) whose pass gate is O < 0. The un-deflated size term injects a constant ~ -8 to -11 into O for every firm, so O is almost always far below 0 regardless of actual distress. The header's celebrated '7-sigma moat / every anchor O <= -7.05' is an artifact of this scaling error, not bankruptcy-distance. The hard-gate can essentially never fire (a genuinely distressed firm would need its other 8 terms to overcome an -8 offset), so a DATAGUARD that exists to catch FTX-style distress is silently inert. Tightening to Begley-1996 (O<-3.23), as the header muses, is meaningless while the offset stands.
fix: Deflate TotalAssets to the scale Ohlson calibrated on: divide ta_t by 1e6 (express in $millions) before the log, or introduce a documented SIZE_SCALE constant (e.g. GNP_PRICE_INDEX in $millions of 2010 dollars). Re-validate the O<0 boundary and anchor pass-rates after rescaling. Add comment: 'prevents failure mode: un-deflated size term makes the bankruptcy hard-gate permanently non-firing'. Do NOT add ticker exclusions; fix the size scale only.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed real. methods/ohlson-o-score.js:80 sets GNP_PRICE_INDEX=1.0 and lines 173-175 compute size = -0.407*log(ta_t/1.0). I verified via pull-yahoo.js (mapFTSToBalance / annualBalance, lines ~1169-1194) that totalAssets is stored in raw USD (only a currency `factor` is applied, never scaled to thousands/millions), so ta_t is ~1e9-3e12. Numerically the size term is -8.43 (TA=$1B) to -11.69 (TA=$3T); Ohlson 1980 calibrated TA in deflated $thousands, where the term sits around -2 to -4. The auditor's $50B example checks out exactly: size=-10.03 raw vs -4.40 at $millions scale.

This is not a harmless documented simplification. The header's claim (lines 38-42) that the bias is "<0.3 in O" is demonstrably false: it conflates the deflator's *time drift* (1.0 vs 0.5 -> only -0.407*log(2) approx -0.28) with the *absolute magnitude* of the size term (approx -8 to -12). The absolute term swamps every other sub-term.

Impact confirmed against the gate: method-types.js:92 classifies ohlson-o-score as DATAGUARD (line 124 group comment: "DATAGUARD - Disqualifiziert auf Fail"), so pass=false (O>0) hard-disqualifies a stock. I simulated a clearly insolvent $50B firm (TL>TA, consecutive losses -$8B/-$5B, negative OCF -$3B): O=-5.17, which is < 0, so it PASSES and the bankruptcy hard-gate does NOT fire. The size term (-10.03) single-handedly drags O negative, overwhelming the genuine distress signal (TL/TA term = +6.27). The registry reason text itself ("all anchors at O <= -7.05 ... ~7-sigma moat from O>0") is actually a fingerprint of this bug: the gate can essentially never fire for any large-cap regardless of distress. So the finding (size term biases O downward by ~5-9 points, effectively disabling the DATAGUARD hard-gate) is accurate. Severity high is appropriate: a DATAGUARD that silently never fires for its intended target (large distressed names) is a real safety-gate failure, though it is fail-open (lets names through) rather than wrongly disqualifying good names.

fix_safe=false: dividing ta_t by 1e6 shifts every computable O upward by +0.407*log(1e6) approx +5.62. That is intentionally NOT behavior-preserving for a DATAGUARD — it changes which stocks the gate disqualifies. The worst current anchor (MELI O=-7.05) survives (-1.43, still <0), but anchors nearer the boundary could flip and mid-distress names would newly hard-fail. The header and the proposed_fix both require re-validating the O<0 boundary and anchor pass-rates after rescaling, which is a human-review step. Auto-applying could newly disqualify legitimate holdings, so this needs human review.

title: Piotroski uses `!= null` (not isFinite) for balance fields, so a NaN balance value adds a phantom always-failing signal that corrupts both the F-score and the scaled threshold (0.15-weight TURNAROUND input)
evidence: `_balanceVal` (lines 33-37) returns `arr[idx] && arr[idx][field]` (raw, no finite guard). Signal guards use `!= null`, e.g. line 93: `if (debt0 != null && debt1 != null && ...)`. Since `NaN != null` is true, a NaN debt0 enters the signal: `lev0 = debt0/assets0 = NaN`, then line 96 `pass: lev0 < lev1` -> `NaN < x` -> false. Reproduced with `totalDebt:NaN`: delta_leverage AND delta_liquidity both INCLUDED and scored 0; F-score 5/8 instead of 5/6 (the two NaN signals should have been excluded), threshold still scaled against 8.
why_it_matters: Two effects compound: (1) phantom signals are counted as failed (depressing score), and (2) `signals.length` is inflated, so `scaledThreshold = round(6*length/8)` (line 130) demands more passes than the data supports — a stock with genuinely 6 computable signals can be judged against an 8-signal denominator. piotroski-f-score is 0.15 weight in TURNAROUND. NaN balance fields are plausible from partial Yahoo parses (pull-yahoo trims trailing nulls but mid-array bad values survive).
fix: Make `_balanceVal` finite-guarded (`Number.isFinite(v) ? v : null`) exactly like beneish/ohlson, and/or change every signal guard from `x != null` to `Number.isFinite(x)`. This both excludes non-finite inputs from `signals.length` and prevents the NaN-comparison-false trap. Comment: 'prevents failure mode: NaN balance field added as phantom failed signal, corrupting score and scaled threshold'.

_verdict.note: CONFIRMED by reproduction in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/methods/piotroski-f-score.js. _balanceVal (lines 33-37) returns `arr[idx] && arr[idx][field]` with NO finite guard, unlike the sibling forensic methods beneish-m-score.js (line 97: `return Number.isFinite(v) ? v : null;`) and ohlson-o-score.js (line 98: same). The signal guards use `!= null` (e.g. line 93 delta_leverage, line 100 delta_liquidity), and since `NaN != null` is true, a NaN balance field enters the signal. Reproduced exactly as claimed with totalDebt:NaN at idx 0: both delta_leverage and delta_liquidity were INCLUDED and scored 0 (NaN<x and NaN>x both false), giving F-score 5/8 with maxPossible:8 / scaledThreshold:6 / pass:false. The correct missing-data path (totalDebt absent rather than NaN) excludes both signals, giving 5/6 / scaledThreshold:5 / pass:true. So one phantom NaN field flips the verdict from PASS to FAIL — it corrupts both the numerator (extra always-failing signals) and the scaled-threshold denominator (signals.length stays 8 instead of 6). Severity high is justified: piotroski feeds the 0.15-weight TURNAROUND composite input, and NaN propagation from upstream parsing is exactly the failure mode the sibling methods already defend against.

title: Metric-divergence-guard is structurally blind on 'computed-margin' snapshots (annual margin is tautologically equal to TTM margin)
evidence: Guard: `const ttmMargin = H.metricValue(stock,'operatingMargin'); ... const annualMargin = oi0/rev0*100; const divergence = Math.abs(ttmMargin-annualMargin);` (lines 57,71-72). But pull-yahoo.js _deriveOpIncForFinancials() path 3 sets `annualOpInc[y] = annualRev[y] * operatingMargins_TTM` (pull-yahoo.js:589-596) and stamps `meta.opIncSource='computed-margin'` (pull-yahoo.js:848). For any such snapshot oi0/rev0 == operatingMargins_TTM, so annualMargin == ttmMargin and divergence == 0 ALWAYS. metricValue returns pp (pull-yahoo.js:895 multiplies by 100; header line 14 confirms 'pp'), oi0/rev0*100 is also pp — units match, so the cancellation is exact. The method never reads meta.opIncSource.
why_it_matters: This guard's whole purpose (header lines 4-9) is to catch financial/treasury entities like MSTR where TTM diverges from annual op income. Those are exactly the snapshots most likely to hit the Financial-Services-gated 'computed-margin' fallback, where annualOpInc is synthesized FROM the TTM margin — so the very names the guard targets get a guaranteed divergence of 0 and silently PASS. It is a DATAGUARD (method-types.js:74), so a false pass lets a data-anomalous stock into picks.
fix: Read `stock.meta.opIncSource`; when it is 'computed-margin' the annual-vs-TTM comparison is non-independent — return computable:false with reason 'annualOpInc derived from TTM margin (opIncSource=computed-margin) — divergence undefined'. Add comment: 'prevents tautological pass when annual op-income was back-derived from the TTM operating margin'.

_verdict.note: CONFIRMED real with full source evidence. Tautology chain verified: (1) guard computes annualMargin = oi0/rev0*100 (metric-divergence-guard.js:71) and ttmMargin = H.metricValue(stock,'operatingMargin') (line 57); (2) metricValue returns metrics.operatingMargin.value which is set to _y(fd,'operatingMargins')*100 in pp (pull-yahoo.js:895, _helpers.js metricValue:23-29); (3) for opIncSource=='computed-margin' snapshots, annualOpInc[y]=annualRev[y]*operatingMargins (pull-yahoo.js:589-596, and the post-FTS retry at 1973-1976 which uses _opMargFrac = operatingMargin.value/100 = same operatingMargins fraction). So annualMargin = (rev*operatingMargins)/rev*100 = operatingMargins*100 = ttmMargin EXACTLY -> divergence==0 -> always passes the <=1000pp gate. Units are both pp so cancellation is exact; FX conversion (pull-yahoo.js:1985) multiplies oi and rev by the same rate and cancels in the ratio, so it does not break the tautology. grep confirms NO method in methods/ reads meta.opIncSource — the guard (and siblings) are blind to the provenance flag that pull-yahoo.js:848/1976 deliberately stamps; the code's own comment (pull-yahoo.js:520-523) acknowledges path 3 'folds year-by-year volatility into a single TTM margin. Methods can flag this as derived via meta.opIncSource' — i.e. the hazard is documented but never wired up. NUANCE on the 'ALWAYS' wording: computed-margin is sector-gated (pull-yahoo.js:639, 1971-1972) — fires only for Financial Services tickers whose Yahoo native operatingIncome is null and the bank/insurance line-item paths failed. Within that subset the guard is structurally blind and rubber-stamps every value (pass, divergence=0). This is a real false-negative in a data-integrity DataGuard exactly for the anomaly class it exists to catch, so high is warranted. fix_safe=true: reading stock.meta.opIncSource and returning computable:false for 'computed-margin' is behavior-preserving for all other snapshots, only converts the meaningless tautological pass into computable:false, and matches the existing computable:false / H.buildResult pattern already used at lines 52 and 64. Low risk to auto-apply.

line: 12-19 (and identical in high-proximity-52w.js:12-19, drawdown-52w.js:12-19, volatility-annualized.js:12-19, price-momentum-12-1.js:78-89)
title: Five price methods each JSON.parse the 70MB prices/history.json into a separate module-level cache — up to 5x parse + 5 resident copies per process
evidence: prices/history.json measured at 73,523,579 bytes (17,183 tickers, 1.54M rows). above-200d-ma, high-proximity-52w, drawdown-52w, volatility-annualized each have their own `let _cache=null; function _loadPrices(){ ... _cache=JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(PRICES_HISTORY,'utf8')); }`; price-momentum-12-1 has its own `_loadHistory()`. No shared loader.
why_it_matters: On first stock evaluated, every one of these methods parses the full 70MB file independently, holding 5 deserialized copies (~hundreds of MB) for the whole pull. This is concrete wasted recompute/memory in the per-stock scoring hot path and contributes to the 14.6h pull / memory pressure.
fix: Extract a single shared price-history loader (e.g. methods/_price-history.js with one memoized parse) and have all five methods require it. Keeps FTS_CACHE_VERSION untouched and methods/index.js unmodified. Comment in each method: // prevents: redundant 70MB JSON parse — shares the single memoized price-history loader.

_verdict.note: Confirmed against source. C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/prices/history.json is 73,523,579 bytes (~70MB). Five method files each parse it into a separate module-level cache with no shared loader: above-200d-ma.js:12-19, high-proximity-52w.js:12-19, drawdown-52w.js:12-19, volatility-annualized.js:12-19 each have `let _cache=null; function _loadPrices(){... _cache=JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(PRICES_HISTORY,'utf8'));}`, and price-momentum-12-1.js:78-89 has its own `_historyCache`/`_loadHistory()`. All five are registered in methods/index.js (lines 39,95,96,97,183) and `require`d into one process by methods/runner.js (_loadAllMethods, line 11-40), so they coexist and each parses once on first call -> up to 5x parse + 5 resident parsed copies in a single process (parsed JS objects of a 70MB JSON are well over 70MB each, so a multi-hundred-MB RSS hit). grep confirms exactly these 5 files reference PRICES_HISTORY and no methods/_price-history.js shared loader exists. The claim is accurate; one nuance: memoization means parse-once-per-method, not per-stock, so it is 5x (bounded), not Nx.\n\nfix_safe=false: the extract-shared-loader fix is not a mechanically behavior-preserving change. The four MA/vol/drawdown methods set `_cache={}` on missing/parse-error, but price-momentum-12-1 sets `_historyCache=false` and guards with `if (cache && typeof cache==='object')` in its Priority-3 branch (_getSeries, line 145-153), and exposes `_resetCacheForTests` (line 286) that resets the per-module cache. A shared loader must preserve both cache-miss conventions and keep the test-reset hook pointed at the now-shared cache, otherwise price-momentum's source-priority logic or its tests change. This crosses two different cache semantics + a test hook across 5 files and needs human review, not auto-apply.

title: Asymmetric component fallback inflates RPO/deferred-revenue YoY when current/noncurrent coverage differs between years
evidence: Latest: `rpoLatest = (cr ? cr.val : 0) + (nr ? nr.val : 0)` (line 376). Prior, computed independently: `rpoPrior = ((crP || nrP)) ? ((crP ? crP.val : 0) + (nrP ? nrP.val : 0)) : null` (line 379). Identical pattern for DeferredRevenue split (line 407-410).
why_it_matters: If the latest 10-K reports both Current+Noncurrent contract liability but the prior year's filing (or the stale-cutoff filter at line 154-164) only yields the Current component, `rpoLatest` is a 2-part sum while `rpoPrior` is a 1-part sum. `rpoGrowthYoY` (line 429) then reports a fabricated jump that is purely a coverage artifact, not real growth. Net debt / RPO-growth signals feeding the screener get a phantom acceleration. The treat-missing-as-zero on a *sum of two balance-sheet lines* is the core defect.
fix: Require symmetric components: only compute YoY when the SAME set of components is non-null in both years (e.g. compute `rpoLatest`/`rpoPrior` only from components present in both, or set `rpoPrior=null` unless every component used in `rpoLatest` also resolved for the prior period). Comment: '// prevents phantom YoY from asymmetric Curr/Noncurr coverage'.

_verdict.note: CONFIRMED REAL. File C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/scripts/extract-ma-rpo.js. The CCL fallback (lines 369-381) and DeferredRevenue-split fallback (lines 400-412) each compute rpoLatest and rpoPrior independently, summing whichever components are present and coercing a missing component to 0 ((cr?cr.val:0)+(nr?nr.val:0)). The `(crP||nrP) ? ... : null` guard (lines 379,410) only prevents a 0/0 / false-zero prior when BOTH prior components are null; it does NOT enforce that the same set of components is used in both years. Concrete failure: a firm tags both ContractWithCustomerLiabilityCurrent + Noncurrent in the latest 10-K but only Current in the prior-year filing -> rpoLatest = curr+noncurr (2 components), rpoPrior = currP+0 (noncurrent silently treated as 0). rpoGrowthYoY (line 429 = (rpoLatest-rpoPrior)/rpoPrior) then reports phantom inflated growth from the structural mismatch, with no flag. pickBestAnnual/pickPriorAnnual (lines 150-193) resolve each component series independently, so nothing upstream enforces symmetry. The bad value flows into the output record's rpoGrowthYoY (line 454) consumed by the screener. Mitigating: only fires on firms lacking the preferred RevenueRemainingPerformanceObligation concept (the first tier, lines 356-365, is unaffected), and most filers tag current/noncurrent consistently YoY, so the asymmetric case is real but not the common path. Severity high is defensible because the wrong YoY is silent and directly feeds a growth screen. fix_safe=false: the proposed symmetric-component guard is the right direction but is a behavior change (it suppresses rpoGrowthYoY in cases that currently emit a number, and must also be applied to rpoLatest's 0-coercion and mirrored across both the CCL and DeferredRevenue tiers) -- not a behavior-preserving mechanical edit, so it needs human review.

title: Annual-backfill emits Q4-only labels (YYYY-Q4) that interleave with live quarterly TTM entries under string sort, corrupting the 'last 4 quarters' R40 durability gate
evidence: backfill writes `quarter = year + '-Q4'` for years CURRENT_YEAR-1..-4 (lines 109-111). snapshot-r40rx-history writes the live calendar quarter e.g. `2026-Q2`. Both histories are merged/sorted by quarter STRING ascending (backfill:189, snapshot:77). generate-screener.js:721-723 then does `const last4 = hist.slice(-4); ... e.r40 >= 40 ... qPass>=3 -> r40Durable=true; tabs.R40.push(r)`.
why_it_matters: `slice(-4)` is documented/intended as 'R40 >=40 in >=3 of the last 4 QUARTERS' (a within-year durability signal that McKinsey-style only ~16% of firms sustain). But after backfill the tail is dominated by ANNUAL points one year apart (…2023-Q4, 2024-Q4, 2025-Q4) plus maybe one live quarter. The gate therefore measures durability across 3-4 YEARS, not 4 quarters, and mixes two different FCF-margin definitions (annual-backfill vs TTM, tagged fcfMarginSource). A stock that printed R40>=40 in three separate annual snapshots wrongly earns r40Durable and enters the trusted R40 tab (which is exported to findash via r40-latest.json). This is a look-ahead/semantics defect feeding a live screening gate.
fix: Make the durability gate quarter-aware instead of position-aware: in generate-screener.js filter `hist` to entries whose fcfMarginSource==='TTM' (exclude 'annual-backfill') before `slice(-4)`, OR require the 4 entries to be 4 CONSECUTIVE calendar quarters (parse YYYY-Qn, assert no gaps). Backfill entries should populate the long-range chart but not the consecutive-quarter durability decision. Each gate change carries a comment naming the failure mode: 'prevents annual-approximation rows from satisfying the consecutive-quarter R40 durability gate (look-ahead/semantics mismatch)'.

_verdict.note:
CONFIRMED real with source + empirical evidence. Chain verified end-to-end (note: generate-screener.js is at repo ROOT, not scripts/; the cited line numbers match exactly):

1. backfill-r40rx-history.js:109-111 writes `quarter = (CURRENT_YEAR-1-i)+'-Q4'` for the last 4 completed years (e.g. 2022-Q4..2025-Q4) tagged `fcfMarginSource:'annual-backfill'` (line 120).
2. snapshot-r40rx-history.js writes the live calendar quarter (e.g. 2026-Q2) tagged TTM (computeEntry:100, isoToQuarter:35-39).
3. Both histories merged and sorted by quarter STRING ascending (backfill:188-189; snapshot appendAndPrune:77). generate-screener readR40rxHistory loads entries.slice(-12) preserving that order (line 444); no chronological re-sort anywhere.
4. The R40-tab durability gate at generate-screener.js:720-734 does `last4 = hist.slice(-4)` then `qPass = last4.filter(e=>e.r40>=40).length; if(qPass>=3){ r.r40Durable=true; tabs.R40.push(r) }` — with NO filter on fcfMarginSource. Annual-backfill rows count toward the durability decision identically to real quarters.

Empirical proof from the worktree's r40rx-history/ (5153 files): most files currently hold 3 annual-backfill Q4 entries + at most 1 TTM entry. NVDA.json = [2023-Q4 170.3 backfill, 2024-Q4 160.8 backfill, 2025-Q4 110.3 backfill, 2026-Q2 103.5 TTM] → qPass=4 → r40Durable=true, a 'durable across last 4 quarters' verdict driven by 3 annual approximations spanning ~3 years (adjacent points a full YEAR apart, not a quarter). The stated intent (comment 704-710: 'R40>=40 in >=3 of the last 4 quarters') is violated; the gate is satisfied by annual-approximation rows. The R40 tab + r40-latest.json are exported as a 'trusted' array to findash (comment 711-714), so this silently mislabels a headline quality signal. The minor imprecision in the title's word 'interleave' (YYYY-Q4 strings sort before later-year TTM quarters rather than literally between them) does not change the substance — the durability decision is corrupted.

fix_safe=FALSE. The proposed fix is NOT behavior-preserving and needs human review. Option (a) filter to fcfMarginSource==='TTM' before slice(-4): because the snapshot job started recently, nearly every stock has <4 TTM entries today, so `last4.length>=4` would become almost universally false — every R40 row would flip into the else-branch (r40InsufficientHistory=true) and rows currently flagged r40Durable (e.g. NVDA) would lose that flag; the R40_DURABLE tab would also empty out. That materially changes tab membership and durability flags across the dashboard. Option (b) consecutive-calendar-quarter parsing is a larger logic change. Either is a real semantic decision Karl should see in the output/diff, not an auto-apply. Recommend human-reviewed change (and the same source-filter should be applied consistently to the R40_DURABLE block at 739-758, which currently only records provenance for display).

title: court-buckets.json is read but produced by NO script in the repo — score step (and the whole regression gate) has a missing, undeclared dependency
evidence: Line 21-22: `const CAND = ... 'court-candidates.json'; const BUCK = path.join(ROOT, 'outputs', 'court-buckets.json');`  Line 131-133: `const buckDoc = readJson(BUCK); const cls = Array.isArray(buckDoc) ? buckDoc : (buckDoc.classifications || []); const bucketOf = new Map(cls.map(c => [c.t, c.bucket]));`  A repo-wide grep `grep -rl court-buckets --include=*.js` returns ONLY court-score.js — nothing writes it. court-screen.js writes court-candidates.json but never court-buckets.json. The classifier output (the thing that decides which bucket each ticker lands in — the most consequential input to the cross-sectional score) is an untracked, unreproducible artefact. _verdict.note: CONFIRMED. court-score.js:131 reads BUCK=outputs/court-buckets.json with NO try/catch and NO env override (unlike CAND line 21 and OUT line 23, which both have process.env overrides). title: classify() conflates true delisting with mere series-end staleness, and accepts a stale-but-within-7-days close as a valid exit — survivorship attrition is mislabelled
evidence: `const p1 = _priceAtCanonical(map, exitDate); if (p1 === null || p1 === undefined) { return { status: 'delisted', ret: null }; }` (lines 39-42). _priceAtCanonical (walk-forward-perf.js:257-268) only walks BACKWARD up to PRICE_MAX_STALE_DAYS=7. So: (a) a name whose series simply ends a few days early but is otherwise alive is labelled 'delisted'; (b) a name with a real last trade 1-7 days before exitDate (suspension/illiquid foreign) returns a valid 'ok' ret computed against a stale close, with no flag. There is no symmetric forward check and no distinction between 'series ran out' and 'company delisted'.
why_it_matters: The entire naive-vs-conservative survivorship lever (the stated primary value of this harness, freeze-full-baseline.js:92-95) depends on 'delisted' meaning a name actually died (conservative assigns it -1.0 / -100%). Mislabelling end-of-history names as delisted means the conservative variant punishes alive-but-untracked foreign/illiquid names with a fabricated -100% return, biasing conservative IC and cohortSpread downward by an unknown amount. Conversely, accepting a 7-day-stale close as 'ok' injects stale-price returns into the naive variant. Both corrupt the headline survivorship-bias quantification.
fix: Split the status: distinguish 'delisted' (series has dates AFTER exitDate region but a gap, OR an explicit delist flag) from 'no_exit_price'/'series_ended' (newest date for that ticker < exitDate - stale window). Only the former should map to -1.0 in the conservative variant; series-ended-but-universe-still-running names should be dropped from both. Record the staleness gap (days between chosen close and exitDate) and flag exits beyond a tighter threshold. Comment the failure mode: '// prevents alive-but-untracked foreign names being booked as -100% delistings'.

_verdict.note:
CONFIRMED real (core claim a). Verified the full data path in worktree C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening:

1. forward-returns.js:39-42 — `const p1 = _priceAtCanonical(map, exitDate); if (p1 === null || p1 === undefined) { return { status: 'delisted', ret: null }; }`. The 'delisted' label is assigned PURELY because no close was found at/near exitDate. No delist flag is consulted (the price records are plain {date, close} — no delist field exists in the data), no forward check, no distinction between true delisting and a series that merely ends early while the company is alive.

2. _priceAtCanonical (walk-forward-perf.js:257-268) only walks BACKWARD up to PRICE_MAX_STALE_DAYS=7, never forward. Confirmed exactly as the auditor states. So any ticker whose newest date < exitDate − 7 calendar days → 'delisted'.

3. Caller fitness/measure.js:130-132 — in the conservative variant, status==='delisted' maps to returnByTickerConservative[ticker] = -1.0 (booked as −100%). These feed rankIC / cohortSpread / hitRate / quintileMonotonicity for the conservative metric set (measure.js:154-158).

4. The only freshness gate (measure.js:92 isHorizonPending) uses maxPriceDate (walk-forward-perf.js:52-61), which is the GLOBAL max date across ALL tickers — it does NOT guarantee each ticker's series reaches exitDate. So a still-alive but untracked/illiquid name with an early-ending series, in a universe that is otherwise fresh, gets a fabricated −100% in the conservative variant. This silently biases the conservative survivorship-adjusted metrics downward. The measure.test.js DELISTED fixture (lines 161-197) confirms this exact mechanism is intended/tested as-is.

Sub-claim (b) — a stale-but-within-7-days close accepted as 'ok' with no recorded staleness gap — is also technically true (the 7-day backward window is by design to bridge weekends/holidays, but the gap is neither tightened nor flagged). This sub-point is low impact; the load-bearing problem is (a).

Severity: high is right (borderline medium). The naive variant is unaffected (drops these names) and both variants are reported side-by-side, so a careful reader sees the gap; impact magnitude depends on how many universe names have early-ending series. Not critical.

fix_safe=false: the proposed fix is NOT behavior-preserving and needs human review. It (i) changes the status taxonomy and which names map to −1.0, altering the entire conservative-variant return distribution and all conservative metrics; (ii) changes the output schema (survivorshipCounts keys) consumed downstream; (iii) requires a delist flag the price data does not carry, or a forward-looking heuristic that does not exist today; (iv) breaks the existing measure.test.js 'delisted' assertion. This is a semantic/schema change, not a safe auto-apply.

title: measure.js anchors entry at frozenAt 00:00:00Z and bypasses getEntryDate's pre-market next-day shift — reintroduces the same-day look-ahead walk-forward-perf.js was hardened against
evidence: `const t0Iso = frozenAt + 'T00:00:00Z';` (line 80) and `const exitTarget = addDaysIso(frozenAt, horizon);` (line 89). resolveWindow→computeBenchmarkReturn is called with this raw t0, while walk-forward-perf.js deliberately routes every vintage through getEntryDate(asOfRaw) (walk-forward-perf.js:164-184, 417) to push pre-close snapshots to the next trading day 'so we don't include the intraday move the screener couldn't have transacted at' (look-ahead guard, F-BT-001/F-BT-007). measure.js never imports or calls getEntryDate.
why_it_matters: If the picks-history vintage was generated from a pre-close (pre-21:00 UTC) snapshot, measure.js's entry window opens on the SAME calendar day the screener ran, capturing intraday price movement the strategy could not have traded at — a classic backtest look-ahead bias that inflates measured IC and cohortSpread. The harness exists specifically to be the 'honest signal' (freeze-full-baseline.js:5-7); silently using a more optimistic entry convention than the production walk-forward scorer makes the two non-comparable and over-states fitness.
fix: Import getEntryDate from walk-forward-perf.js and derive the entry from the vintage's asOf timestamp (read picks-history asOf, not just the date) before anchoring: `const entryDate = getEntryDate(vintage.asOf)`. Thread that through resolveWindow. Failing that, document loudly that measure.js entries are date-only and may include same-day look-ahead, and gate the metric. Comment: '// prevents same-day look-ahead: mirror walk-forward getEntryDate pre-close shift'. (Note: requires reading asOf from the baseline; baselines currently only store frozenAt — see A-fitness-08.)

_verdict.note: CONFIRMED real. measure.js anchors entry at frozenAt (date-only) and never applies getEntryDate's pre-close shift. Evidence: (1) measure.js:18 imports only {buildPriceIndex, addDaysIso, maxPriceDate, businessDaysSince} from walk-forward-perf.js — getEntryDate is NOT imported/called. (2) measure.js:80 `t0Iso = frozenAt + 'T00:00:00Z'`; line 104 resolveWindow(priceIndex, t0Iso, horizon) -> forward-returns.js:58-59 slices t0 to YYYY-MM-DD and feeds it raw to computeBenchmarkReturn as asOfDate. (3) The walk-forward pipeline deliberately routes asOf through getEntryDate (walk-forward-perf.js:417) then passes the SHIFTED entryDate into computeBenchmarkReturn (line 450) and addDaysIso (line 468) — the F-BT-001/F-BT-007 look-ahead guard ("use next day's price for pre-close snapshots", threshold 21:00 UTC market close, lines 161-184). measure.js bypasses this entirely. (4) Baseline schema confirms the loss: all baselines store only date-level frozenAt (e.g. "2026-05-14"), no asOf field — freeze-full-baseline.js:54/58 sets frozenAt from the picks-history FILENAME (YYYY-MM-DD) and never reads vintage.asOf, even though picks-history vintages carry real intraday asOf timestamps. (5) Quantified on the real baseline vintage: picks-history/2026-05-14.json has asOf=2026-05-14T18:29:27Z = 18:29 UTC = PRE-close, so getEntryDate shifts entry to 2026-05-15. measure.js anchors at 2026-05-14 instead. computeBenchmarkReturn resolves: measure.js -> entry 2026-05-14 / exit 2026-06-11 / SPY ret -1.39%; hardened walk-forward -> entry 2026-05-15 / exit 2026-06-12 / SPY ret +0.35%. The entire window is offset one day and pulls in the 2026-05-14 intraday close the screener could not have transacted at — the alpha sign flips. All three full-*-2026-05-14 baselines are affected. The proposed_fix's own caveat is correct: it requires reading asOf into the baseline (schema change, cross-refs A-fitness-08).

title: Candidate pull bypasses USD/FX normalization — apples-to-oranges scoring vs the watchlist
evidence: pullStock() builds the stock object directly and NEVER calls _convertSnapshotToUSD (pull-yahoo.js:275). Revenue is hardcoded USD regardless of issuer currency: `const rev = ftsArr(annualFin,'totalRevenue').map(v => ({ value: v, currency: 'USD' }))` (line 49). marketCap is taken raw: `marketCap: pr.marketCap ? { value: pr.marketCap } : null` (line 74) — Yahoo returns price.marketCap in the issuer's TRADING currency for foreign listings. The result is then scored with the same engine the normalized snapshots use: `const r = Runner.evaluateStock(stock)` (line 117).
why_it_matters: pull-yahoo.js:271-318 exists precisely because leaving annual/quarterly series in reporting-currency while marketCap is USD 'silently corrupts every ratio (fcf-yield, ev/ebitda, etc.) for non-USD stocks' (its own comment). This script re-introduces that exact defect for every candidate: a Japanese/Korean/EU name is scored with JPY/KRW/EUR revenue magnitudes against USD-calibrated method thresholds, so mcap-gated and absolute-magnitude methods pass/fail essentially at random. Since universe-candidates can contain foreign tickers (live watchlist already holds e.g. 000270.KS), the '≥N/17 pass' suggestions for non-USD names are not comparable to the watchlist members they are meant to augment. This is a direct cap on the screener's discovery quality.
fix: Reuse the real puller instead of the divergent minimal copy: import pull-yahoo's mapper + _convertSnapshotToUSD (or refactor that mapper into a shared lib) and run candidates through the identical normalization path before Runner.evaluateStock. At minimum, stop hardcoding currency:'USD' — read pr.financialCurrency / pr.currency, look up FX_TO_USD, and multiply series + marketCap to USD. Comment the failure mode: 'prevents non-USD candidates being scored on un-normalized magnitudes (mirrors pull-yahoo _convertSnapshotToUSD; see Tag 134 mixed-currency corruption)'.

_verdict.note: CONFIRMED REAL. suggest-watchlist-additions.js pullStock() (lines 31-93) is a divergent minimal copy of the puller that bypasses ALL USD/FX normalization: hardcodes currency:'USD' on revenue (line 49), takes pr.marketCap raw (line 74, trading-ccy for foreign listings), pulls annual.*/metrics.* straight from Yahoo, sets no meta.reportingCurrency, and never calls _convertSnapshotToUSD. The real puller (pull-yahoo.js:1985) calls _convertSnapshotToUSD(canonical) before scoring; that fn (lines 275-469) FX-scales marketCap, metrics.*, and all annual.* series, and the mapper (793-829) resolves financialCurrency->reportingCurrency. The un-normalized snapshot is then fed to the SAME engine: Runner.evaluateStock (line 117). Cross-currency corruption is concrete: buffett-criteria.js:433-436 computes ni(reporting-ccy)/mcap(trading-ccy); fcf-yield.js does fcfAdj(reporting-ccy)/mcap(trading-ccy); ev-ebitda.js:45 adds balance-sheet debt/cash (reporting-ccy) to mcap (trading-ccy). For ADRs/foreign listings these ratios are off by the FX factor -- the exact Tag 204/232 failure mode the main pipeline was hardened against. Bug is SILENT: the caller's Object.values(r)/.computable/.pass iteration works (verified _helpers.js:58-62 builds computable), so it emits plausible-but-wrong pass counts rather than crashing. USD-domiciled candidates unaffected; non-USD candidates get apples-to-oranges scoring vs the normalized watchlist.

title: Vintage-sector preference (F-GC-010) is permanently dead — methods-history has no inputs.sector field
evidence: Line 47-48: `const vintageSector = info && info.inputs && info.inputs.sector; const sec = vintageSector || tickerToSector[ticker] || 'Unknown';`  But probing methods-history/2026-05-13.json shows each per-stock `info` has keys EXACTLY `['results','computable','passing']` — there is NO `inputs` key. `info.inputs` is always undefined, so `vintageSector` is always falsy and the code ALWAYS falls through to today's `tickerToSector` mapping.
why_it_matters: The Tag 185 comment claims the report now uses each vintage's own sector (recorded at snapshot time) to avoid mixing re-sectorized tickers across history. In reality every historical run is retroactively re-labelled with TODAY's sector. A ticker that Yahoo re-classifies (or that changes GICS sector) silently corrupts the entire historical sector-trend table — the exact bug the comment says it fixed. The fix was never wired to a real field; either snapshot-methods-history.js must start recording inputs.sector, or the misleading comment+dead branch must be removed so nobody trusts a guarantee that does not hold.
fix: Decide one of: (a) make snapshot-methods-history.js persist `inputs.sector` per ticker per vintage, then this branch becomes live; or (b) delete the dead `vintageSector` branch and the F-GC-010 comment and document honestly that sector is today's mapping. Do NOT leave a comment asserting a guarantee the data shape cannot deliver.

title: Start/end price lookup uses string '>=' fallback that silently substitutes the wrong day and inflates/deflates returns
evidence: Line 76-77: `const startEntry = series.find(e => e.date === date) || series.find(e => e.date >= date); const endEntry = series.find(e => e.date === targetDate) || series.find(e => e.date >= targetDate);` Probe confirms prices/history.json series are ascending by date with sparse calendar days (e.g. CRDO first two entries 2025-05-12, 2025-05-13). `Array.find` returns the FIRST element with `date >= target`, i.e. the next available trading day after a weekend/holiday — fine for start, but there is no upper bound: if the snapshot `date` predates the price series start, the start fallback returns the very first bar of the whole 1-year series (a year-early price), producing an absurd return.
why_it_matters: methods-history dates can predate a ticker's price coverage (newly added universe entrants, late IPOs). When `date` is earlier than `series[0].date`, `series.find(e => e.date >= date)` returns the oldest available bar (could be 6-12 months off), so `ret = (end-start)/start` measures a multi-month move mislabelled as a 30/90-day horizon. This directly corrupts the pass-vs-fail alpha that the whole script exists to compute — a core 'is the screener working' signal. The horizon-overshoot on the end side (endEntry far past targetDate when the exact day is missing) compounds it.
fix: Bound both lookups to a tolerance window (e.g. accept the matched bar only if `|matched.date - target| <= ~7 days`, mirroring findClosestPrice in backtest-10-weeks.js), and skip the ticker otherwise. Reuse one shared nearest-trading-day helper across all three backtest scripts so the boundary semantics are identical.

title: wasComputable inferred from prev.value != null mis-fires for methods whose legitimate computable value is 0
evidence: Line 199: `const wasComputable = prev && prev.value != null;` and line 203 gates all PASS_LOST/GAINED events on `wasComputable && isComputable`. A method whose stored value is exactly `0` survives `!= null`, so 0 is fine here — but the deeper problem: `wasComputable` is reconstructed from the stored *value* rather than a stored computable flag. The METHOD_INCOMPUTABLE branch (line 232) writes `{value:null, pass:false, wasComputable:true}`; on the NEXT run `prev.value` is null so `wasComputable` (line 199) is false even though the prior observation WAS a real (incomputable) record. The code patches this with the sticky `prev.wasComputable` marker (lines 262, 303-305), but the base inference remains value-derived and fragile.
why_it_matters: The whole event taxonomy (PASS_LOST=WARNING, RECOVERED/INCOMPUTABLE) hinges on correctly distinguishing 'method was computable' from 'method had a truthy value'. Deriving it from value!=null conflates 'no prior observation', 'incomputable', and 'value happened to be null' into one state, which is exactly the class of bug the Tag 229c/NEW-6 comments keep re-patching branch-by-branch. Every new code path that writes state must remember to also set the sticky marker or the recovery signal is lost again (it has regressed at least twice per the comments).
fix: Store an explicit boolean `computable` in newState alongside value (e.g. `newState[id] = {value, pass, computable: isComputable, lastChanged}`) and read `wasComputable = prev && prev.computable === true`. This removes the value-derived inference and the need for the sticky-marker patches entirely. Add a comment: 'prevents the value-null-vs-incomputable conflation that silently dropped METHOD_RECOVERED across multi-run gaps.'

title: RUN_DATE_UTC freeze is bypassed by pull-yahoo.js — the snapshots themselves still get a wall-clock asOf, so the cross-midnight bug the Freeze step claims to fix is only half-fixed
evidence: Workflow Freeze step (line 51-55): `RUN_DATE_UTC=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%d) ... >> $GITHUB_ENV`, with the comment (line 50) 'Downstream snapshot-* scripts respect RUN_DATE_UTC over Date.now().' But the snapshot WRITER, pull-yahoo.js:1682, stamps every snapshot with `const asOf = new Date().toISOString();` and pull-yahoo.js contains NO reference to RUN_DATE_UTC (grep returns nothing). The downstream snapshot-picks.js:203/220, snapshot-methods-history.js:53, detect-changes.js:351 DO honor RUN_DATE_UTC. So the per-ticker snapshot `asOf`/`fetchedAt` (written by pull-yahoo across a 2.5h pull that the comment itself says can cross UTC midnight) uses real wall-clock, while picks-history/methods-history filenames+asOf use the frozen date. The exact divergence the comment warns about (picks-history/2026-05-17 vs snapshot asOf 2026-05-18) is still possible — just relocated to snapshot-vs-history instead of history-vs-history.
why_it_matters: The Freeze step is presented as the fix for vintage-continuity gaps (pick-diff findMethodFile + method-effectiveness vintage cache). Because pull-yahoo never reads RUN_DATE_UTC, snapshots written after 00:00 UTC carry the NEXT day's asOf while the picks/methods history that indexes them carries the FROZEN (previous) day. The freshness gate (line 264) reads `asOf` from the snapshot (wall-clock) and walk-forward joins picks-history (frozen) to snapshot asOf — a 1-day skew silently corrupts forward-return alignment exactly on month boundaries and long pulls. The mitigation gives false confidence that the class of bug is closed.
fix: Pass RUN_DATE_UTC into the Run Yahoo Pull step env (it is in GITHUB_ENV so it is already visible — confirm pull-yahoo consumes it) and make pull-yahoo.js:1682 prefer `process.env.RUN_DATE_UTC ? RUN_DATE_UTC + 'T00:00:00.000Z' : new Date().toISOString()` for the snapshot asOf/fetchedAt, mirroring snapshot-picks.js:220. This unifies every artifact in a run on a single frozen date.

title: gh-pages `if: success()` deploys reports even when the Yahoo Pull (and every report step) silently failed, because continue-on-error steps are treated as successful by success()
evidence: Run Yahoo Pull (line 210) is `continue-on-error: true`. Generate Modes-Report (384), Generate Screener Dashboard (397), Generate Dashboard (540), etc. are ALL `continue-on-error: true`. The Deploy step (line 660-661) gates on `if: success()`. GitHub Actions semantics: a step that fails but has continue-on-error:true reports `conclusion: failure` yet does NOT flip the job's `success()` status — `success()` only becomes false if a step WITHOUT continue-on-error fails. The only hard-fail gates between pull and deploy are Verify Snapshot Freshness (282, the one non-continue step) and Verify Pull Coverage (357) and the commit step. If those pass on partial data (coverage floor is only max(2500,13%)), the deploy proceeds even though modes-report.html generation crashed and `cp ... || true` (line 666-677) silently copies yesterday's stale HTML.
why_it_matters: The whole point of Tag 153's `if: success()` (line 658-659: 'only deploy when data commit succeeded — otherwise gh-pages would show picks that never landed in main'). But success() does not detect report-generation failure, and the `cp || true` swallows missing files. The live gh-pages site can show a green-looking deploy of stale or partially-broken reports while modes-report/screener silently failed — exactly the 'silently publishing yesterday's HTML' failure Tag 134 (line 378) tried to prevent, reintroduced via the continue-on-error retrofit.
fix: Add an explicit artifact-freshness assertion before Deploy: a step (NOT continue-on-error) that checks the mtime/content-date of modes-report.html, screener.html, dashboard.html against RUN_DATE_UTC and fails if any is stale. Remove the blanket `cp ... 2>/dev/null || true` swallowing — at minimum warn loudly per missing artifact. Do not rely on success() to detect report breakage when upstream is continue-on-error.

title: Four of five test files are wired into NO CI workflow and NO npm script — they are orphaned
evidence: Repo-wide grep for the five test basenames across .github/**, package.json, and *.js finds exactly ONE reference: `.github/workflows/monthly-sec-xbrl.yml:56  run: node tests/sec-user-agent-test.js`. package.json `scripts` has only `pull`, `pull:fast`, `pull:single` — no `test` script. daily-pull.yml invokes no test. So 13f-test.js, integration-anchor-test.js, sec-form4-test.js, and yahoo-schema-canary.js are never executed by any automation.
why_it_matters: A regression test that nothing runs cannot catch a regression. The yahoo-schema-canary explicitly exists because 'NO test fired' for the financialCurrency drift — yet the canary itself is unwired (its own header even admits 'Wiring is INTENTIONALLY left out of daily-pull.yml'). The 13f and form4 smoke tests guard the SEC parsers but never run. This is the single biggest structural reason the test harness underdelivers: the coverage exists on disk but is inert.
fix: Add a `test` script to package.json that runs the offline-safe suite (13f-test, sec-form4-test, sec-user-agent-test) and a separate `test:canary` for the network ones. Add a lightweight CI job (a `tests.yml` or a step in daily-pull) that runs the offline suite on every push, and schedule yahoo-schema-canary as the daily WARN-only canary its docstring describes. Gate integration-anchor-test behind a snapshot-present check (see A-tests-01) so it can run post-pull.

title: SEC User-Agent guard misses two live SEC-pulling scripts (false 'all compliant' assurance)
evidence: SEC_SCRIPTS = ['pull-sec-xbrl.js', scripts/pull-insider-form4.js, scripts/pull-13f-institutional.js]. But grep for 'sec.gov' across the repo finds two MORE programmatic pullers not in the list: `scripts/backfill-form345.js` (https.get to www.sec.gov/files/.../form345.zip, USER_AGENT at line 61) and `scripts/pull-insider-form4-daily.js` (https.get to www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/daily-index, USER_AGENT at line 59). The test's own header says 'Add new SEC pullers here.'
why_it_matters: The test's entire purpose is to make the contactless-UA-403 regression class 'loud and fast' across ALL SEC scripts. Two daily/backfill pullers sit outside the net. If an edit drops the email from backfill-form345.js or pull-insider-form4-daily.js, the test stays green and the script silently 403-storms (the exact failure pull-sec-xbrl suffered until 2026-06). Both currently happen to be compliant, so the gap is invisible today — that is precisely why it is dangerous.
