Better: discover SEC scripts dynamically — scan *.js + scripts/*.js for a `sec.gov` literal and assert each declares a contact-bearing USER_AGENT — so future pullers are auto-covered instead of relying on someone remembering to edit the list.

title: Form-4 lookback assertion uses hardcoded 2026 dates against live Date.now() — test self-rots
evidence: fakeSub.filingDate = ['2026-05-10','2026-01-01','2024-01-01','2026-04-20']; assertion `form4Recent.length === 2` where form4Recent filters `r.form==='4' && _withinLookback(r.filingDate,180)`. _withinLookback computes `(Date.now() - Date.parse(...)) <= 180*86400000`. The two in-window form-4s are 2026-05-10 and 2026-04-20. Verified: with clock=2026-06-20 the 180d cutoff is 2025-12-22, so both pass and the assertion holds. But once wall-clock passes ~2026-11-06, 2026-05-10 falls outside 180d → form4Recent.length becomes 1 → assertion `=== 2` FAILS.
why_it_matters: A test pinned to absolute dates but measured against the real clock will flip from pass to fail purely with the passage of time, with no code change. When this test finally gets wired into CI (A-tests-02), it becomes a time-bomb that breaks the build on a calendar date unrelated to any commit, training the team to ignore red. It also makes the test non-reproducible across machines with skewed clocks.
fix: Make dates relative to a fixed reference clock. Inject 'now' (e.g. accept an optional `nowMs` param into a testable `_withinLookback`, or generate fixture dates as `new Date(Date.now() - 10*86400000).toISOString()` for in-window and `Date.now() - 800*86400000` for out-of-window). Then the windowing invariant is asserted, not a frozen calendar coincidence.

title: Catch-and-swallow everywhere: bad snapshots, DQ failures, history parse errors, and FX/field gaps are silently dropped with no run-level error budget
evidence: main() per-stock: `catch(e){ ...console.warn('skip '+tk); }` (L4284-4288) — a parse/throw drops the entire stock. DQ.gradeSnapshot wrapped in `catch(e){ /* skip */ }` leaving dqGrade null (L403-407). readScoreHistory `catch(e){ /* swallow — null */ }` (L173), readR40rxHistory `catch(e){ /* swallow */ }` (L189). loadStocks per-file `catch(e){ return null; }` then filtered out (L97-100). r40-latest prior read `catch(_){ }` (L4396). Twemoji font `catch(e){ ...return ''; }` (L138-141).
why_it_matters: There is no aggregate guardrail: if a snapshot schema change or a corrupt write makes 30% of files JSON.parse-fail, loadStocks silently returns the surviving 70%, buildRow silently skips more, and the run still 'succeeds' (exit 0) with a quietly decimated universe. Combined with the r40-latest 60-day merge (finding 04), a day where most snapshots fail to parse produces a screener that looks normal but is mostly stale carry-over. Silent attrition is exactly the asymmetric-survivorship failure mode the audit brief calls out.
fix: Add a run-level sanity gate in main(): count loaded vs skipped vs parse-failed; if skipped/parse-fail exceeds a threshold (e.g. >5% of files, or loaded count drops >20% vs the prior run's logged count) exit non-zero so CI fails loudly instead of shipping a thinned universe. Keep the per-item swallow for resilience but tally and report it; never let a mass failure pass as exit 0.

_verdict.note:
CONFIRMED real. Verified all cited sites in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/generate-screener.js. loadStocks (L94-100): per-file try/catch returns null on read/parse failure, nulls filtered out (L100) — a corrupt snapshot silently disappears from the universe. main() per-stock loop (L4281-4288): catch only console.warn's and drops the stock; no tally. DQ.gradeSnapshot wrapped in catch{/*skip*/} (L403-407) leaving dqGrade=null. readScoreHistory L173 / readR40rxHistory L189 / r40-latest prior read L4396 / Twemoji L138-141 all swallow as described. The top-level handler (L4415 `main().catch(... process.exit(1))`) only fires on a thrown FATAL — none of the per-item swallows ever reach it, so a mass parse/read failure ships a thinned universe at exit 0. The console.log counts ('loaded N stocks', 'built N rows') are printed but never compared to anything, and no prior-run count is persisted to compare against. No run-level error budget exists anywhere in main(). Auditor's claim is accurate.

Notable genuine sub-bug the auditor flagged via the dqGrade-null path: a stock whose DQ.gradeSnapshot() THROWS gets dqGrade=null, and the hard-gate at L4347-4349 only blocks dqGrade==='D'||'C' — null is NOT blocked. So an ungraded stock silently bypasses the DQ gate and can enter both the R40 tab and the 'trusted' r40-latest.json export. This is the strongest concrete data-integrity consequence and corroborates the finding.

Severity medium is fair: no crash, no per-stock wrong numbers, but a silent universe-thinning + ungraded-passthrough that CI cannot detect. Not high because it needs multiple snapshots to fail, and the r40-latest merge (L4386-4402) keeps prior entries for 60d, blunting total loss there.

fix_safe=false: the proposed run-level gate is NOT behavior-preserving — it changes exit codes and would make CI fail where it currently passes. The suggested thresholds (>5% files, or loaded drops >20% vs prior run) must be calibrated against the codebase's own documented daily rotation (comment at L4368-4375: ~3.3k of ~24k tickers rotate per day, universe size varies run-to-run), and there is currently no persisted prior-run count to diff against — adding that persistence + a mis-tuned threshold could break every CI run. Needs human review and threshold tuning before auto-applying. The tally-and-report half (count loaded/skipped/parse-failed, log it) is safe; the exit-non-zero half is not.

title: Quarterly net-income FTS extraction uses raw r.netIncome — misses NetIncome / netIncomeContinuousOperations casing, unlike the annual path
evidence: ftsQuarterlyNI = (fts.quarterlyFin || []).slice().reverse().map(r => r && r.netIncome != null ? r.netIncome : null);  // vs annual path line 1102: const ni = _ftsValue(r, 'netIncome', 'NetIncome', 'netIncomeContinuousOperations');
why_it_matters: Yahoo FTS rows for many tickers emit PascalCase ('NetIncome') or the GAAP-continuous variant ('netIncomeContinuousOperations') instead of camelCase 'netIncome' (the file itself documents this drift at lines 1054-1064 and 1099-1102). This map() bypasses the _ftsValue helper, so for every such ticker the entire quarterly-NI series reads all-null. That silently disables the 8-quarter earnings-stability method (Tag-90) — exactly the kind of method that should separate the screener's '20% of potential' from its full power. The bug is masked because nulls look like 'Yahoo didn't provide it' rather than 'we read the wrong key'.
fix: Route through the existing helper: `.map(r => { const v = (r != null) ? _ftsValue(r, 'netIncome', 'NetIncome', 'netIncomeContinuousOperations') : null; return v != null ? v : null; });`. No FTS_CACHE_VERSION bump needed (read-shape change only; affects freshly-parsed rows). Comment the failure mode: 'prevents all-null quarterly-NI when Yahoo FTS emits PascalCase/continuous-ops netIncome key'.

_verdict.note: Confirmed real inconsistency. pull-yahoo.js:1836-1837 extracts quarterly NI with raw `r.netIncome` only (single camelCase key, no fallback), while the annual path at line 1102 uses `_ftsValue(r, 'netIncome', 'NetIncome', 'netIncomeContinuousOperations')`. Both consume the SAME raw FTS rows: `fts.quarterlyFin` is also fed to mapFTSToQuarterly (line 1810), which at lines 1216-1220 uses `_ftsValue(r, 'totalRevenue', 'TotalRevenue')` etc. — proving the codebase itself treats quarterly FTS rows as PascalCase-prone. So the quarterly NI path uniquely fails to handle PascalCase/continuous-ops casing AND skips the snake_case fallback `_ftsValue` provides (line 1062). Downstream impact: canonical.timeseries.netIncomeQ (line 1931) → quarterly-earnings-stability.js and earnings-surprise-momentum, plus the data-quality gate `timeseries.netIncomeQ>=4` (data-quality.js:73). Severity downgraded to medium: this only bites when Yahoo emits the non-camelCase key for quarterly rows (an edge case, not the dominant path — camelCase `netIncome` is the normal emission, same as `totalRevenue` being the primary tried key). When it does bite, it degrades gracefully to all-null (no corruption, no positional misalignment), costing only a 0.5-weight data-quality point and disabling two quarterly methods for that ticker.

title: Schema-stale + currency-stale probes each do a full readFileSync+JSON.parse of every young snapshot — two full parses per ticker on the 80%-hit fast path
evidence: _existingSnapshotMissingTag211lFields: `const raw = fs.readFileSync(fp,'utf8'); const s = JSON.parse(raw);` AND _existingSnapshotMissingCurrencyNormalization: `const raw = fs.readFileSync(fp,'utf8'); const s = JSON.parse(raw);` — both called back-to-back in processOne (lines 1657-1663) for every youngEnough ticker, then _priceOnlyUpdate parses a THIRD time (line 1535).
why_it_matters: For a ~15-20k universe where ~80% hit the young path, that is up to 3 full JSON.parse of a ~50KB snapshot per ticker per run (~45-60k parses), the file's own comment (line 1438) already flags one parse as a cost concern but two more were added by Tag 226a-2/230a. This is wasted recompute on the hottest path and a direct contributor to the long pull window. The two probes read the same file; they can share one parse.
fix: Read+parse the snapshot ONCE in processOne (or in a combined probe) and pass the parsed object to both checks plus _priceOnlyUpdate. Refactor the two `_existingSnapshot*` functions to accept an already-parsed object. No semantic change. Comment: 'single parse shared across schema/currency probes + price-only — was 3× parse per fast-path ticker'.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed at source. On the ~80% price-only fast path, the same snapshot file is fully read + JSON.parse'd three times per youngEnough ticker:
- _existingSnapshotMissingTag211lFields: fs.readFileSync(fp,'utf8') + JSON.parse(raw) at lines 1455-1456
- _existingSnapshotMissingCurrencyNormalization: same at lines 1506-1507
- _priceOnlyUpdate: JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(fp,'utf8')) at line 1535
processOne (lines 1657-1663) calls both probes back-to-back gated only by youngEnough, then enters _priceOnlyUpdate when !staleSchema && !staleCurrency (line 1664-1666). The code comment at line 1438 even claims "one ~50KB JSON.parse per ticker" — actual is 3x. Note: _getExistingSnapshotAge (line 1416) is NOT a redundant full parse — it reads only the first 500 bytes (Buffer.alloc(500)) and regex-matches asOf, so the redundancy is exactly the 3 full parses, not 4. No existing shared-parse helper exists. The finding's facts, line numbers, and call-graph are all accurate.

Severity medium is fair: real, bounded inefficiency (3 parses of ~50KB instead of 1) on the dominant fast path; not a correctness issue and no unbounded growth. Could arguably be low given the pipeline is network/Yahoo-bound, but the parse count + file size justify medium.

fix_safe=false: the refactor is behavior-preserving in principle but NOT low-risk to auto-apply. The three functions have non-uniform error handling: both probes catch all errors and return false (treat as not-stale), while _priceOnlyUpdate THROWS on a missing/corrupt file (line 1534-1535), and that throw is deliberately caught by the caller (line 1670-1672) to fall through to a full pull. A shared single-parse must preserve: (a) probes returning false on read/parse failure, (b) _priceOnlyUpdate's throw-and-fall-through on missing-or-corrupt snapshot, and (c) the existsSync guards in all three. Consolidating these distinct failure semantics across three functions plus a caller needs human review, not auto-apply.

title: Schema-validation failures on international tickers are reclassified as 'not-found' and the snapshot is marked delisted — silent survivorship attrition of valid non-US names
evidence: else if (/Failed Yahoo Schema validation|schema validation/i.test(msg)) errClass = 'not-found';  ... if (errClass === 'not-found') { existing.meta.delisted = true; existing.meta.delistedAt = ...; }
why_it_matters: The comment (lines 2106-2119) acknowledges the risk: a multi-module quoteSummary that fails the library's strict-shape validator gets classified not-found and the existing snapshot is permanently flagged delisted. For genuinely-listed Korean/Taiwanese/Japanese/HK/Chinese names that merely returned a partially-populated (but valid) payload, this is asymmetric survivorship attrition — the international leg of the universe quietly shrinks and never gets retried (delisted flag suppresses future attempts). This is precisely the 'silently swallowed errors → mark dead' and 'asymmetric survivorship attrition' pattern from the prompt, and it structurally caps international coverage.
fix: Do NOT mark delisted on schema-validation failures — only on literal 404/'no data'/'invalid symbol'. Split errClass: keep a distinct 'schema-fail' class (counted, monitored via pull-stats-check as the comment intends) that does NOT set meta.delisted, so the ticker is retried next run. Reserve the delisted flag for the unambiguous not-found regex (line 2102). Comment: 'prevents valid international tickers with partial-but-valid payloads from being permanently marked delisted (survivorship attrition)'.

_verdict.note: CONFIRMED via source. pull-yahoo.js:2119 maps /Failed Yahoo Schema validation|schema validation/i to errClass='not-found'; lines 2123-2133 then set existing.meta.delisted=true on the snapshot. scripts/prune-watchlist.js:82 (deadReason) returns 'delisted' for any snap with meta.delisted===true, and main() (lines 188-191) drops those entries from watchlist.json. The CI job .github/workflows/daily-pull.yml:124-127 runs prune-watchlist.js automatically every day (continue-on-error:true); the only guard is a coarse "size >= 200" floor (line 148) against a ~15,734-name universe, so losing the ~637 international tickers the Tag-215h comment itself reports from run #107 never trips the alarm. Once pruned from the watchlist the ticker is never iterated again by pull-yahoo's worker pool, so the success-path overwrite at line 2075 (which writes a fresh canonical with no delisted field) can never clear the flag — it is a one-way ratchet. This is exactly the silent survivorship attrition of valid non-US names the finding describes. Two things strengthen the finding over the author's defense: (1) the Tag-215h comment (lines 2106-2118) acknowledges the risk and says it is mitigated because "pull-stats-check should monitor the schema-vs-not-found ratio" — but there is NO pull-stats-check file or reference anywhere in the repo, so the claimed sentinel was never built; the tradeoff is unmonitored, not monitored. (2) A multi-module quoteSummary returning a partial-but-valid payload that fails the library's strict-shape validator is not equivalent to Yahoo's literal "Quote not found"/"No fundamentals data found" (the genuine not-found regex at line 2102), so treating it as definitively delisted is an over-reach. Severity medium is right: it biases the screener universe against non-US names but does not corrupt US results and is bounded. fix_safe=false: the proposed split (new 'schema-fail' class that skips delisting) is a deliberate behavior REVERSAL of the documented Tag-215h decision (which intentionally stopped daily retries hitting the same wall) and relies on the non-existent pull-stats-check for its safety story; it needs a human to decide retry policy and to actually build the monitoring before flipping. Not behavior-preserving, not safe to auto-apply.

title: FTS-vs-quoteSummary merge logic is a 80-line tangle of per-field non-null-count comparisons duplicated 7× — the structural source of the year-alignment bug class
evidence: Repeated pattern: `const _ftsXNonNull = (ftsA.x||[]).filter(...).length; const _qsXNonNull = (canonical...x||[]).filter(...).length; if (_ftsXNonNull > _qsXNonNull) canonical...x = ftsA.x;` for annualRev, annualOpInc, annualNetIncome, annualGP(unconditional), annualFCF(length-only), annualOCF(length-only), revenueQ-triplet. Each uses a SLIGHTLY different filter predicate and a different override condition (count vs length vs unconditional).
why_it_matters: The inconsistency between `> non-null count` (rev/opinc/ni), bare `.length > 0` (GP/FCF/OCF lines 1932/1936/1937), and unconditional triplet replacement (revenueQ siblings) is exactly what spawned the long parade of F-DP-030/031/F-002/F-010 alignment fixes documented inline. annualGP at line 1932 uses `ftsAnnual.annualGP.length > 0` — a length test, so a 4-entry all-null FTS GP array (placeholders) would overwrite a populated QS GP array, reintroducing the very drift the count-based guards elsewhere prevent. This god-merge block is the single biggest structural cap on data correctness in the file.
fix: Extract one helper `mergePreferRicher(qsArr, ftsArr, {mode:'count'|'length'})` and a single `mergeQuarterTriplet(...)` that moves rev/opInc/gp as a unit, then call them uniformly. Fix annualGP (line 1932) to use the non-null-count predicate like its siblings, not `.length>0`. Pure refactor preserving the count-based semantics. Comment each call with the failure mode (year-index drift) it prevents.

_verdict.note: Confirmed against source in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/pull-yahoo.js. The structural claim holds: lines 1859-1952 are a ~80-line sequence of per-field FTS-vs-quoteSummary merge decisions with three distinct override predicates — non-null COUNT (annualRev 1861, annualOpInc 1870, annualBalance 1898, annualRnD 1912, annualNetIncome 1935, revenueQ-triplet 1948-1951), bare `.length>0` (annualSGA/Depreciation/Shares 1921-1925, annualGP 1932, annualFCF 1936, annualOCF 1937), and unconditional-additive (annualSBC/Capex 1900-1902). The load-bearing concrete defect is REAL: mapFTSToAnnual (line 1107) pushes the identical `{value}|null` shape for annualGP as for annualRev/annualOpInc/annualNetIncome, yet line 1932 gates the GP override on `ftsAnnual.annualGP.length > 0` while its structurally identical siblings use the non-null-COUNT predicate. A company with revenue but no reported grossProfit yields annualGP=[null,null,...] (length>0, line 1104 only skips fully-empty rows), which then UNCONDITIONALLY overwrites a richer quoteSummary-derived annualGP. This is exactly the richer-data-overwrite / year-alignment failure mode the adjacent Tag-203/206f comments (1862-1882) were written to fix for annualOpInc; GP was simply never given the same treatment. annualGP feeds margin-quality, piotroski-f-score, beneish-m-score, gross-profitability — so the downgrade is silently consumed downstream. Caveat: the broader 'this is a tangle, refactor it' half is architecture/maintainability opinion, not a behavioral bug; my is_real=true is anchored on the GP predicate inconsistency, which is the verifiable defect. Live incidence is likely low (Yahoo usually omits GP for whole companies, not single mid-window years).

title: DCF + owner-earnings claim 'not in SCORE_WEIGHTS / fixture-hash safe by construction' but BOTH are weighted in the BUFFETT mode (0.30 / 0.20)
evidence: dcf-intrinsic-value.js index entry (methods/index.js:256-261): "DIAGNOSTIC: not in SCORE_WEIGHTS; fixture-hash safe by construction." owner-earnings.js index entry (index.js:249-254): "DIAGNOSTIC: not in SCORE_WEIGHTS". But score-aggregator.js:68-72: `BUFFETT: { 'buffett-criteria': 0.50, 'owner-earnings': 0.20, 'dcf-intrinsic-value': 0.30 }`. Both methods ARE first-class scored inputs of the BUFFETT mode.
why_it_matters: The 'fixture-hash safe by construction' guarantee is false: any change to DCF or owner-earnings math directly moves the BUFFETT-mode score. If the fixture-hash test exercises BUFFETT mode, every edit to these files silently drifts the hash and breaks the pre-pull gate (the exact failure class documented in _helpers.js:155-175 for medians). If the test does NOT exercise BUFFETT mode, then real scoring regressions in two 0.20/0.30-weight methods go completely untested. Either way the safety claim that protects edits to these files is wrong and misleads future maintainers into editing them freely.
fix: Decide and make consistent: either (a) confirm BUFFETT mode is covered by the fixture-hash test and DELETE the 'not in SCORE_WEIGHTS / fixture-hash safe' comments from both files + index.js entries (replacing with 'WEIGHTED in BUFFETT mode — edits move the score'), or (b) if BUFFETT is intentionally excluded from the hash fixture, add an explicit BUFFETT-mode case to the fixture so these weights are regression-tested. Do not change SCORE_WEIGHTS values. Each touched method comment must name the failure mode (silent BUFFETT-score drift / untested scoring path).

_verdict.note:
CONFIRMED REAL. Both methods ARE weighted scoring inputs in BUFFETT mode, and the "fixture-hash safe / not in SCORE_WEIGHTS" comments are factually false.

Evidence:
- score-aggregator.js:32-72 — SCORE_WEIGHTS.BUFFETT = { 'buffett-criteria':0.50, 'owner-earnings':0.20, 'dcf-intrinsic-value':0.30 }. So both owner-earnings and dcf-intrinsic-value ARE in SCORE_WEIGHTS (under the BUFFETT key).
- score-aggregator.js:216-296 — computeScore(allResults, modeId,...) does `weights = SCORE_WEIGHTS[modeId]` and builds a normalized weighted score; for modeId='BUFFETT' the 0.20/0.30 weights directly move the score. strategy-modes.js:126 defines the BUFFETT mode and :274 calls computeScore for it. So these two methods genuinely drive the BUFFETT score.
- The index.js claims are at index.js:253 (owner-earnings: "DIAGNOSTIC: not in SCORE_WEIGHTS ... Fixture-hash safe.") and index.js:260 (dcf-intrinsic-value: "DIAGNOSTIC: not in SCORE_WEIGHTS; fixture-hash safe by construction."). buffett-criteria at index.js:267 is more careful ("not in HG/QC/TURN SCORE_WEIGHTS") but the other two are unqualified and wrong.
- The fixture-hash golden test (tag28-tests.js:2752-2786, _computeFixtureHash) only evaluates HYPERGROWTH (:2766) and QUALITY_COMPOUNDER (:2767) and projects only { HG, QC } (:2781). BUFFETT is never evaluated. Therefore edits to owner-earnings/dcf-intrinsic-value CAN silently change BUFFETT scores without tripping the hash — the "safe by construction" claim is the exact opposite of true for BUFFETT.

Caveats on the auditor's line refs: the cited dcf-intrinsic-value.js:260-261 and 425-435 do NOT contain the misleading comment — :425-435 is the module.exports block and there is no such comment in the method file body (grep for SCORE_WEIGHTS/fixture-hash in both method files returns no matches). The false claims live ONLY in methods/index.js:253 and :260. The substance of the finding holds; the file/line attribution to the method bodies is slightly off.

Severity revised high -> medium: this is a latent regression-safety / false-documentation gap, not an active miscalculation. No wrong output ships today; the risk is a future editor trusting the 'hash-safe' comment and silently drifting the BUFFETT score. Real and worth fixing, but not high-impact in the running pipeline.

fix_safe=false: the proposed fix asks the human to DECIDE between (a) correcting/deleting the comments (pure docs, behavior-preserving) and (b) adding a BUFFETT case to the fixture hash (changes the golden test contract, requires the BUFFETT fixture to be computable and a human-blessed regen of tests/fixture-hash.txt with ALLOW_FIXTURE_CHANGE=1). The decision itself plus option (b)'s test-contract change need human review. Option (a) alone would be auto-safe, but the finding does not commit to it.

title: EV/EBITDA accepts Yahoo's enterpriseToEbitda whenever it is >0, silently ignoring negative-EBITDA firms that Yahoo encodes as a negative ratio
evidence: Line 27: `if (yahooRatio != null && yahooRatio > 0) { ... pass: yahooRatio <= THRESHOLD ... }`. When a firm has negative EBITDA, Yahoo's enterpriseToEbitda comes back NEGATIVE (EV>0 / EBITDA<0). The `> 0` filter drops straight through to the manual fallback — but the fallback's own EBITDA guard is `opInc*1.2` and `if (ebitda <= 0) return computable:false`. So negative-EBITDA names end up non-computable, which is correct ONLY by luck of the fallback. The real defect: a firm with a tiny POSITIVE EBITDA and huge EV yields a Yahoo ratio like 850 — that is correctly failed. But a firm whose Yahoo ratio is a small negative number (e.g. -2, near-zero negative EBITDA) is treated as 'use fallback', and if the fallback's opInc happens to be positive it can PASS at a low EV/EBITDA while the company is actually unprofitable on an EBITDA basis.
why_it_matters: EV/EBITDA is a `lte` valuation gate; the whole point is to reject expensive names. A near-breakeven company can flip between 'Yahoo negative ratio → ignored' and 'fallback opInc*1.2 positive → cheap PASS', producing a valuation verdict that contradicts the native ratio. The branch silently prefers the heuristic over Yahoo's own (more accurate) number for exactly the marginal-profitability names where the answer matters most.
fix: Treat a non-null Yahoo ratio as authoritative regardless of sign: when `yahooRatio != null` and `yahooRatio <= 0`, return computable:false with reason 'negative/zero EBITDA per Yahoo native ratio — EV/EBITDA not meaningful' instead of falling through to the heuristic. Only fall back when `yahooRatio == null`. Add comment naming the failure mode: 'prevents heuristic opInc*1.2 PASS overriding Yahoo's negative-EBITDA signal'.

_verdict.note: Confirmed against source. methods/ev-ebitda.js:27 is exactly `if (yahooRatio != null && yahooRatio > 0)`, so a NEGATIVE Yahoo enterpriseToEbitda falls through to the manual fallback. pull-yahoo.js:910 passes Yahoo's `enterpriseToEbitda` through raw (`_metric(_y(ks,'enterpriseToEbitda'),...)`) with no sign filtering, so a negative ratio (EV>0 / negative TTM-EBITDA) is real input. The key point: the fallback uses a DIFFERENT metric and period than Yahoo's ratio — `opInc = latestAnnual('annualOpInc')` (most recent full fiscal-year operating income, pull-yahoo.js:1100/1106), while Yahoo's ratio uses TTM EBITDA from financialData. So a name that has slipped to negative TTM EBITDA but still had a positive last-FY operating income passes the fallback's `ebitda = opInc*1.2 > 0` guard (line 67) and can emit a PASS at a low EV/EBITDA. The auditor's evidence is self-contradictory in spots (it concedes the clean co-negative case IS caught by the fallback "by luck") — but the divergence case is genuine and not caught. Downstream this matters: generate-methods-report.js:246 only excludes a stock when `computable===true && pass===false`; a false PASS keeps the stock with a valuation endorsement, whereas computable:false would be neutral. So the bug turns a should-be-neutral, EBITDA-negative name into a passing valuation gate. NOT high though — it is a narrow TTM-vs-annual divergence window on one of many gates, neutral-vs-pass (not a hard wrong-exclusion or broad silent corruption); revised to medium. The proposed fix (treat non-null yahooRatio <= 0 as computable:false) is consistent with the file's own existing `ev <= 0` (line 59) and `ebitda <= 0` (line 67) non-computable guards and with the Tag 219 "Yahoo native ratio is authoritative" design intent.

title: ΔOI/ΔRev reads fixed indices [0] and [3] with no contiguity/null-position guard — interior nulls or a short clean window corrupt the 3y leverage
evidence: `const rev0 = _unwrap(revArr[0]); const rev3 = _unwrap(revArr[3]); const oi0 = _unwrap(oiArr[0]); const oi3 = _unwrap(oiArr[3]);` then `const dOI = oi0 - oi3; const value = dOI / dRev;`. The only gate is `revArr.length < 4`. If revArr = [v, null, v, v] (interior null at the year-1 slot, a documented schema shape), [0] and [3] still unwrap fine and the method silently computes a 3-fiscal-year span that may actually cover 4 calendar years with a gap, or pairs OI from one year against Rev from a misaligned year if the two arrays have nulls in different slots.
why_it_matters: annualOpInc and annualRev are built in separate loops in mapFTSToAnnual (pull-yahoo 1098-1108) and a missing operatingIncome in a year writes null to annualOpInc but a real value to annualRev — so oiArr and revArr can have nulls in DIFFERENT positions. Indexing [0]/[3] blindly then divides a real ΔRev by a phantom/misaligned ΔOI. operating-leverage is defaultActive and surfaces in the dashboard as a quality signal; a corrupted value can flip pass at the 0.25 boundary.
fix: Collect aligned finite (rev,oi) tuples (like operating-leverage-margin-accel.js does at lines 96-101), require >=4, and take the newest and the 4th-newest of the ALIGNED set. Confirm the two endpoints are 3 fiscal years apart. Add comment naming the misaligned-interior-null failure mode.

_verdict.note:
CONFIRMED (primary claim), with one sub-claim overreached. operating-leverage.js evaluate() reads fixed indices revArr[0]/[3] and oiArr[0]/[3], gated ONLY by `revArr.length < 4 || oiArr.length < 4` (line 44). The null-check at line 57 catches a null landing EXACTLY on [0] or [3] (verified: rev[3]=null -> computable:false), but does NOT catch an interior null at index [1] or [2]. pull-yahoo.js provably emits such interior nulls: mapFTSToAnnual (lines 1104-1108) pushes null placeholders for any year missing rev/oi while another field is present, and the surrounding comments (Bug #26, F-004, F-DP-030/031) document that interior nulls are deliberately preserved for positional alignment. Simulation confirms the corruption: for annualRev=[200,null,150,110,80], evaluate returns computable:true with revStart=110(idx3)/revEnd=200(idx0), i.e. a window spanning FY-now..FY-3-back where the interior FY is MISSING, so the labeled "3Y" incremental-margin and revGrowth3y (0.82 here) are computed over a window that is not 3 contiguous fiscal years. operating-leverage-margin-accel.js (lines 96-101) handles the identical data correctly by collecting aligned finite tuples first.

OVERREACH: the auditor's secondary claim that it "pairs OI from one year against Rev from a misaligned year if the two arrays have nulls in different slots" is FALSE. annualRev and annualOpInc are built in lockstep in the same loop at the same index (pull-yahoo.js 1105-1106), so rev[i] and oi[i] are ALWAYS the same fiscal year. There is no cross-array OI/Rev mispairing; the real defect is purely the within-array window-span distortion.

Cited lines accurate. File: C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/methods/operating-leverage.js (evaluate at lines 44, 52-55, 57, 68-86). Reference impl: C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/methods/operating-leverage-margin-accel.js lines 93-101.

title: gmEnd/gmStart and medians derived from positionally-compacted gms[] can mix non-adjacent years and misalign GM vs OpM windows
evidence: `const len = Math.min(5, rawRevs.length, rawGps.length, rawOpIncs.length); for (i...) { if (finite rev>0 && finite gp) gms.push(gps/rev); if (finite rev>0 && finite opInc) opMs.push(opInc/rev); }` then `const gmEnd = gms[0]; const gmStart = gms[gms.length - 1];` and `gmDeclineFail = (gmEnd <= gmStart) && (gmTTM < gmMedian - 0.05)`.
why_it_matters: gms and opMs are pushed independently, so if year 2 has gp=null but opInc present, gms skips it while opMs keeps it: gms[k] and opMs[k] then refer to different fiscal years, and gms.length != opMs.length. gmStart (oldest GM) may be 3 years back while opMargMedian spans 5 — the asymmetric GM-Decline test then compares a TTM to a start year that isn't the window boundary it assumes. Since this gates QC MUST-3, a misaligned decline test can wrongly fail/pass a quality compounder.
fix: Build a single aligned per-year record {rev,gp,opInc} keeping only rows where all needed fields are finite (or track per-metric year indices), so gmStart/gmEnd/medians all reference the same contiguous window. Comment the failure mode.

_verdict.note: Confirmed real against source. The loop at methods/margin-quality.js:72-75 conditionally push()es into gms[] and opMs[] only when each metric is finite for that year, which positionally COMPACTS the arrays. The data pipeline (pull-yahoo.js mapFTSToAnnual ~1094-1108, mapFTSToBalance, _ftsExtractByYear, quoteSummary path) establishes a hard invariant — repeatedly fixed under F-004, F-DP-003, F-DP-030/031, F-002, F-010, Bug #26 — that annualRev/annualGP/annualOpInc are positionally year-aligned with null placeholders for missing years, AND that annualGP is overwritten independently of annualOpInc (line 1932) so a year can legitimately have {rev:x, opInc:y, gp:null}. The min-data gate (validGps>=4, gms.length>=3) lets such a stock through. Consequences I verified by simulation: (1) gmEnd = gms[0] (line 85) and gmTTM = gmEnd (line 122-123) are documented as the NEWEST year, but if the newest fiscal year has gp=null while rev/opInc present, gms[0] is silently the 2nd-newest year's GM — yet assetTurnover (line 89-90) and the OpMargin window use the TRUE newest rawRevs[0]/rawOpIncs[0], so the GM-decline FAIL test (line 124) mixes a stale GM against current-year OpM. (2) When an interior/oldest year drops out of only one metric, gmMedian and opMargMedian are computed over different year-sets, and gmStart=gms[len-1] can reference a non-oldest year, so gmEnd<=gmStart compares non-adjacent endpoints. Because gmDeclineFail is a hard pass=false condition, this can wrongly reject a qualifying stock or mask a genuine margin decline. The runner (methods/runner.js) passes raw canonical arrays without re-normalizing, so the case is reachable in production. The line-51 comment claims it "preserves positional alignment" — it preserves alignment of the INPUT arrays but breaks it again via the conditional push. Medium severity is appropriate: requires a GP-only null year (real but not the majority case), and the worst impact (gmEnd/gmTTM stale) needs the null specifically in the newest year.

title: Pairs are formed over the COMPACTED years[] array, so a dropped (null/neg-rev) year silently makes a 'consecutive pair' span two fiscal years, inflating revGrowth and diluting the leverage average
evidence: years[] is built by finite-filtering and skipping rev<=0 rows (lines 96-101), then pairs use `const newer = years[i]; const older = years[i + 1]; const revGrowth = (newer.rev - older.rev) / older.rev;` with no check that years[i] and years[i+1] are calendar-adjacent.
why_it_matters: If a loss year (oi present) or a null-rev year sits between two retained years, the 'consecutive pair' actually spans 2 fiscal years. revGrowth across 2 years is roughly double a 1-year growth, so leverage = marginDelta/revGrowth is understated, and the averaged value can fall below the 0.05 pass floor for a genuinely high-leverage compounder (or the reverse). This is the more-robust sibling method but it inherited the contiguity blind spot; the header even claims it 'explicitly conditions on positive-growth years so contraction years don't pollute the average' — but dropping a contraction year still merges its neighbors into one inflated-growth pair.
fix: Track each retained year's source index and only form a pair when the two are adjacent in the original array (index diff == 1); skip pairs that straddle a dropped year. Comment the gap-merge failure mode.

_verdict.note:
CONFIRMED real. In methods/operating-leverage-margin-accel.js the years[] array is built by compaction: the loop at lines 96-101 does `continue` on any entry where rev/oi is null or rev<=0, so dropped years collapse the array. Pairs are then formed over that compacted array (lines 114-117: `newer=years[i]; older=years[i+1]; revGrowth=(newer.rev-older.rev)/older.rev`) with no check that the two retained years were calendar-adjacent. There is no fiscal-year/date field carried into years[] (no endDate/period tracking) to detect a gap.

The premise that mid-series nulls actually occur is independently confirmed by the data pipeline's own history: pull-yahoo.js documents F-004, F-DP-003, F-DP-030/031 and Bug #26, which deliberately preserve null placeholders inside annualRev/annualOpInc to keep positional alignment for bank/insurer gap years (JPM/BAC/NU/SOFI pattern, OpInc null for financials). mapFTSToAnnual pushes `oi != null ? {value:oi} : null` (lines 1105-1106), so annualOpInc legitimately contains mid-series nulls; _helpers.js does not compact. Thus a null-OpInc or rev<=0 year in the middle of the series makes years[i]/years[i+1] span two fiscal years, so revGrowth for that pair is a ~2-year growth misread as 1-year, and that distorted leverage value is folded into the unweighted arithmetic mean (line 139), diluting/biasing the average.

Strong corroborating evidence: the sibling method operating-margin-acceleration.js (Tag 199g), solving the same "consecutive years" requirement, does it the safe way — fixed positional indices 0..3 with an immediate `computable:false` on any null/rev<=0 position (lines 67-78), never compacting. The audited method diverges from that established convention.

Impact is bounded: header comment (line 57) states this method is NOT in SCORE_WEIGHTS -> DIAGNOSTIC-only -> fixture-hash safe by construction, so it does not affect pass/fail scoring or screener ranking; only the displayed diagnostic value is wrong, and only for the gap-year subset (mostly financials). medium is defensible but at the low end of medium due to diagnostic-only scope.

title: Exported threshold/thresholdOp (0.35/gte) misrepresent the method: pass is a multi-branch composite, not value>=0.35
evidence: module.exports sets `threshold: 0.35, thresholdOp: 'gte'` while `value: gmMedian` and `pass` is computed from up to four independent sub-tests (GM hard-fail, GM floor by tier, OpMargin floor, asymmetric GM-decline). A stock can have gmMedian=0.30 (< 0.35) yet pass via retail-tier, or gmMedian=0.50 (>= 0.35) yet fail on OpMargin/decline.

Because value=gmMedian but the real gate is composite, the confidence/NEAR_THRESHOLD flag and the report's 'pass if value>=0.35' description are wrong for any tier-overridden or OpMargin/decline-driven outcome. Not a scoring bug (runner trusts the method's own pass), but it corrupts the confidence/flag metadata and operator-facing report for a CORE gate.

CONFIRMED real, with a caveat on the evidence. margin-quality.js sets value=gmMedian (line 133) and exports module-level threshold:0.35/thresholdOp:'gte' (line 155), while `pass` is a composite of up to four independent sub-tests. evaluate() does NOT pass threshold into buildResult, so result.threshold is undefined. title: Read/write fiscal-year asymmetry: median built from _firstNonNull (any year) but consumed against latestAnnual (strictly year 0)
evidence: Compute side picks `_firstNonNull(arr, getter)` which walks forward to the first non-null row (sector-medians-compute.js:79-87, used for ni/ta/cash/fcf at lines 94-102). The consuming method sector-relative-roic.js:_computeRoic uses `H.latestAnnual(stock,'annualNetIncome')` / `H.latestBalance(stock,'totalAssets')`, and _helpers.js:34 returns strictly `arr[0]` (returns null if position-0 is null).
why_it_matters: A stock whose latest fiscal year (index 0) has a null netIncome contributes an OLDER-year ROIC to the sector percentile distribution, but is itself ranked using the strictly-latest value (which is null → incomputable, so it drops out). The percentile distribution is therefore built from a mix of fiscal years while every ranked stock is forced to year 0. The Tag 232c-13 comment claims _firstNonNull fixes a survivorship bias, but it introduces a definitional read/write mismatch: the median a stock is compared against was computed on different-vintage data than the stock's own metric. sector-relative-roic's pass gate (rank>=75) becomes subtly miscalibrated.
fix: Make write and read agree. Either change the compute side to use position-0-only (matching latestAnnual/latestBalance) — accepting the survivorship trade-off the comment worried about — OR change sector-relative-roic._computeRoic (and roic.js) to also use a first-non-null walk. Pick one definition and route both through a shared helper. Add comment naming the failure mode: '// prevents read/write fiscal-year skew between sector median and the metric ranked against it'.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed real with source evidence. Write side: sector-medians-compute.js:79-87 _firstNonNull walks forward to the first non-null row (used for ni/ta/cash/fcf/sbc at lines 94-102). Read side: _helpers.js latestAnnual (lines 31-39) returns strictly arr[0] (null if position-0 is null), latestBalance (41-47) returns strictly arr[0][field]; consumed by sector-relative-roic.js:_computeRoic (85-87) and roic.js (10-12). The asymmetry is reachable because the live FTS pull path DELIBERATELY preserves leading/interior positional nulls so array index == fiscal year: mapFTSToAnnual (pull-yahoo.js:1105-1108) and mapFTSToBalance (1180) push null placeholders and only trim TRAILING nulls (1196-1199); _ftsExtractByYear (1076-1078) likewise. So a stock whose latest fiscal year is null for NetIncome/FCF/balance but populated in a prior year is INCLUDED in the sector median (via _firstNonNull) yet EXCLUDED from the ranked metric (latestAnnual returns null -> computable:false). This is a known-lineage issue: prior report audit-reports/2026-05-18.md:312 (F-DQ-007) and findings/data-quality.json:12 ("OPEN — null-positional read bias"). The Tag 232c-13 commit fixed only the WRITE side per that finding and never mirrored the read side, introducing exactly this skew.

Severity revised high->medium: the contaminated quantity is a sector-AGGREGATE threshold/percentile, not a per-stock value, so a single skewed stock barely moves a median/p75; live incidence is low (pull comments at lines 1119-1122 note Yahoo's missing year is "almost always the oldest", not position 0); and the most-affected consumer (sector-relative-roic) is DIAGNOSTIC and explicitly NOT in SCORE_WEIGHTS (its docstring lines 32-33) so it cannot move the aggregator score. roic.js is affected via effectiveThreshold but only at the threshold edge. Real directional survivorship bias, but bounded.

fix_safe=false: latestAnnual/latestBalance are shared by the entire method suite and are exactly what the fixture-hash invariant test (tag28-tests.js via effectiveThreshold) pins. Switching their position-0 semantics to a first-non-null walk would change computed value/pass for any stock with a leading null across multiple methods and break the fixture-hash gate; it also reverses a deliberate prior decision (Tag 206f / F-DP-101 comments: returning null on a position-0 null is intentional to avoid mixing fiscal years -> computable:false is "correct, not a wrong value from a misaligned year"). Routing both sides through one shared helper is the right direction but is a behavior-changing cross-cutting refactor needing human review + fixture-hash rebaseline.

title: Vacuous-pass: five 'fail-case' tests assert only !r.pass without guarding r.computable
evidence: ROIC fail (64-68): `const r = ...['roic']; if (r.pass) throw new Error('should fail (10% < 15%)');` — no `r.computable` check, no value check. Same shape at Net-Debt/EBITDA fail (84-88: `if (r.pass) throw new Error('should fail');`), Revenue-Growth-3Y fail (121-125), FCF-Yield fail (133-137), GM-Stability fail (149-156). Contrast the Rule-of-40 fail case (43-48) which is safe because line 47 also asserts `approx(r.value, 25)`, and every PASS-case which asserts `r.computable`.
why_it_matters: A result with computable:false carries pass:false (verified across the suite's contract). If a refactor accidentally makes any of these methods return incomputable for valid input (a missing-field guard regressing, an envelope-unwrap break, a thrown error swallowed to a default), the method is silently broken but these tests stay GREEN — they cannot distinguish 'correctly failed the gate' from 'never evaluated'. This is exactly the silent-method-drop failure class the suite elsewhere (line 160) tries to defend against.
fix: Add `if (!r.computable) throw new Error('should be computable')` before the `if (r.pass)` line in each of the five fail-case tests, OR add a positive value assertion (e.g. ROIC fail should also assert `approx(r.value, 0.10)`). Cheapest: insert the computable guard. This pins the fail-case to a real computed FAIL, not a vacuous incomputable.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed the structural weakness, but the "vacuous-pass" label overstates it. buildResult() in methods/_helpers.js (lines 58-68) forces pass:!!pass, and wrapEvaluate (lines 310-319) turns any thrown error into computable:false with pass:false — so a test that only asserts `if (r.pass) throw` does NOT fire when a method regresses to incomputable. That is a genuine missing-guard gap in all five cited fail-cases (tag28-tests.js: ROIC 64-68, Net-Debt/EBITDA 84-88, Revenue-Growth-3Y 121-125, FCF-Yield 133-137, GM-Stability 149-156). The contrast is also accurate: Rule-of-40 fail (line 47) additionally asserts approx(r.value,25), so it is regression-safe; every PASS-case asserts r.computable.

HOWEVER, none of the five tests is actually vacuous TODAY. I traced each input through its method and all five currently produce computable:true, pass:false (genuine computed FAILs): ROIC value=0.10 (10/100); Net-Debt/EBITDA value=50/12=4.17 (EBITDA=opInc*1.2=12); Rev-Growth-3Y CAGR≈9.1% (130 vs 100); FCF-Yield 0.02 (2e9/100e9, floored threshold 0.05); GM-Stability CoV≈0.29 (mean .45/sample-std .129). So the tests pass for the right reason now; the risk is a FUTURE silent regression to incomputable going uncaught — exactly the silent-method-drop class the suite guards elsewhere (line 160 test). That makes this a legitimate test-hardening item, but it is a latent test-robustness gap with zero current production or test-pass impact — medium, not high.

Fix is safe to auto-apply: inserting `if (!r.computable) throw new Error('should be computable')` before each `if (r.pass)` line is behavior-preserving (all five inputs compute today, so the new assertion passes immediately) and matches the existing idiom used throughout the file.

title: ROIC-trend pairs annualNetIncome[idx] with annualBalance[idx] assuming positional year-alignment that the quoteSummary path does not guarantee
evidence: Lines 49-53 read `niArr[yearIdx]` and `balArr[yearIdx]` by the SAME index and line 86 computes `deltaPp=(roic0-roic1)*100`. This assumes annualNetIncome[i] and annualBalance[i] describe the same fiscal year. But pull-yahoo.js `_arr` (line 493-499) builds annualNetIncome via `.map(...).filter(Boolean)` — it DROPS null years — while annualBalance (line 675-692) is built by a separate `.map(...).filter(Boolean)` over a different module (balanceSheetHistory) with its own null rows. The two arrays are compacted independently, so index i can reference different calendar years whenever either source has a hole.
why_it_matters: A one-year offset between NI and invested-capital silently computes ROIC from FY2023 NI over FY2022 balance, then reports a spurious YoY 'improvement' or 'decline'. roic-trend is a QC trajectory signal; a misalignment flips pass/fail (threshold is gt 0) on noisy data with zero error surfaced. The method header (lines 28-31) claims robustness to 2-3y balance coverage but never checks that NI and balance indices refer to the same year.
fix: Either (a) key both series by an explicit fiscalYear/period stamp and align on that, or (b) at minimum guard that niArr and balArr have equal length before index-pairing and bail to computable:false otherwise. Comment: '// prevents: NI/balance index drift from independent filter(Boolean) compaction misdating ROIC YoY delta'.

_verdict.note:
CONFIRMED REAL. roic-trend.js _roicAtYear (methods/roic-trend.js:48-68) reads niArr[yearIdx] and balArr[yearIdx] by the same positional index for yearIdx 0,1,2, and evaluate() computes deltaPp=(roic0-roic1)*100 at line 86. The only guard (line 51) checks niArr.length<=yearIdx || balArr.length<=yearIdx — a per-array length floor, NOT equal-length or year-alignment. The two arrays are built independently in pull-yahoo.js: annualNetIncome = _arr(isHist,'netIncome') (lines 620, 493-499) drops a row whenever netIncome is null; annualBalance (lines 675-692) drops a row only when cash AND totalDebt AND totalAssets are all null. They iterate DIFFERENT Yahoo modules (incomeStatementHistory vs balanceSheetHistory) with independent row counts and independent null patterns, so index i can reference different fiscal years whenever either source has a hole or the two modules differ in length. Worse: the FTS merge (pull-yahoo.js:1896-1898 for balance vs 1933-1935 for NI) selects each array's source independently by its own non-null count, so the final snapshot's annualNetIncome and annualBalance can even originate from entirely different sources/windows.

Why roic-trend is uniquely exposed: roic.js (methods/roic.js:10-12) and every other consumer use H.latestAnnual/H.latestBalance, which only ever read index 0 (_helpers.js:31-47) — immune to drift. roic-trend is the only method that cross-indexes NI and balance at idx 1 and 2, exactly where positional misalignment misdates the YoY delta and can flip the pass/fail sign. The codebase already treats this exact filter(Boolean)-compaction misalignment as a real recurring bug class and fixed it elsewhere with null-placeholder preservation (F-004, F-DP-003, F-DP-030/031, F-DP-101, F-NY-001, see comments at pull-yahoo.js:570-573, 1146-1153, 1871-1879), which corroborates the mechanism. The prior findings file (findings/methods-engine.json) only catalogues a DIFFERENT roic-trend issue (the IC-formula mismatch, since fixed per F-ME-001) — this index-drift claim is genuinely new and unaddressed.

fix_safe=false. Proposed (a) keying both series by an explicit fiscalYear/endDate stamp is the correct fix but a non-trivial refactor (the mapper does not currently persist per-row period stamps) — not behavior-preserving, needs human review. Proposed (b) equal-length guard is a behavior CHANGE (stocks currently scored go computable:false when lengths differ, altering screener output) AND is logically insufficient: equal length does not imply year alignment — both arrays can each drop a different single year yet end up the same length and still be misaligned. Either way a human should decide between the stopgap and the proper stamp-based alignment, so do not auto-apply.

Severity: revised to medium rather than high. The misdating is silent and can flip the sign of a YoY signal (data-integrity), but real-world incidence is bounded — Yahoo's missing annual year is almost always the oldest (noted pull-yahoo.js:1120), income-statement netIncome is rarely null when the matching balance row exists, and the affected method is a single DIAGNOSTIC trend signal, not a MUST-gate.

title: Volatility DATAGUARD hard-fails on a SINGLE -25% YoY anywhere in the window, including the OLDEST pre-IPO/ramp year — asymmetric survivorship attrition against early hypergrowth
evidence: `if (worstDecline && worstDecline.rate < SINGLE_YEAR_DECLINE_THRESHOLD) { ... pass:false, value:'VOLATILE' }` over ALL yoyRates with no recency weighting and no count requirement. A company with rev [1200,900,1100,300] (one -25% dip 2-3 years ago, now compounding) is permanently disqualified. As a DATAGUARD (method-types.js:137, type DATAGUARD defaultActive:true), pass:false + computable:true triggers isDisqualifiedByDataGuards → the stock is removed from the entire universe, not merely penalized.
why_it_matters: This is the dominant structural cap on the screener: a hygiene guard built for one pattern (SPHR) silently culls legitimate re-accelerating compounders that had a single down year (COVID air-pockets, divestitures, one weak fiscal year). Survivorship is asymmetric — only clean monotone histories survive — which is exactly the 'stuck at 20% of potential' symptom. Compounding bug A-methods-growth-09 means the same -25% guard ALSO reads non-USD magnitudes incorrectly via the post-conversion currency tag.
fix: Require the decline to be RECENT (e.g. only index 0 or 1) OR require >=2 decline years to fail, and exempt the oldest pair when the series is otherwise monotone-increasing toward the latest. Keep it a guard but stop hard-disqualifying on a single stale dip. Comment: 'prevents single stale-year dip from culling re-accelerating compounders (survivorship attrition)'.

_verdict.note: Mechanism CONFIRMED, but the finding overstates blast radius and its example is wrong. CONFIRMED: methods/revenue-volatility-guard.js:112-122 sets worstDecline = min rate over ALL yoyRates (no recency weighting, no count requirement) and hard-fails on a single YoY < -25% located ANYWHERE in the window, including the oldest pair. Reproduced: rev=[1500,1100,1000,1400] (newest-first; oldest pair (1000-1400)/1400 = -29%, recent trajectory 1000->1100->1500 cleanly re-accelerating) => pass:false, value:'VOLATILE'. It IS a DATAGUARD defaultActive:true (method-types.js:137) AND is listed in HYPERGROWTH mode dataGuards[] (strategy-modes.js:90), where any failed guard returns passed:false reason:'dataguard_fail' (strategy-modes.js:210-212). So one stale dip culls a re-accelerating compounder. OVERSTATED: the auditor's own example [1200,900,1100,300] does NOT fail (worst YoY only -18%); the -67% drop belongs to the original SPHR series [1220,574,1725,180]. Also the 'removed from the entire universe via isDisqualifiedByDataGuards' claim is incorrect for production: generate-screener.js uses the legacy Runner.evaluateStock (results-only) and does NOT call evaluateStockExtended/isDisqualifiedByDataGuards (those run only in tests/integration-anchor-test.js and scripts/regional-oos-test.js). The row-level hardGated chain (generate-screener.js:621) does NOT include revenue-volatility-guard. Real-world effect is HYPERGROWTH-TAB exclusion only — the stock stays visible in QUALITY_COMPOUNDER/BUFFETT/TURNAROUND/R40 (none list this guard). DESIGN-INTENT: the file header (lines 12-17) explicitly defines the strict rule ('kein -25%+ Decline-Jahr im 4-Jahres-Fenster'), so this is a deliberate strictness tradeoff for the HG lens, not an accidental coding bug.

title: PEG 'use earnings growth' fix is dead code — earningsGrowthYoY/epsGrowthYoY are never produced by the pipeline, so PEG ALWAYS uses revenue growth
evidence: peg.js:16-19 `const eg1 = H.metricValue(stock, 'earningsGrowthYoY'); const eg2 = H.metricValue(stock, 'epsGrowthYoY'); const earningsGrowth = eg1 != null ? eg1 : eg2; const growth = earningsGrowth != null ? earningsGrowth : H.metricValue(stock, 'revenueGrowthYoY');`. A repo-wide grep of pull-yahoo.js for `earningsGrowthYoY`/`epsGrowthYoY` returns ZERO producer sites — only `revenueGrowthYoY` is mapped (pull-yahoo.js:893, computed as `revenueGrowth*100` at :615). So `eg1` and `eg2` are always null and `growthSource` is always 'Rev'.
why_it_matters: Peter Lynch's PEG is BY DEFINITION P/E divided by EARNINGS growth. The method computes P/E divided by REVENUE growth and labels the result 'PEG (Lynch)'. For any company growing revenue faster than EPS (most hypergrowth SaaS, margin-dilutive scalers) the denominator is overstated, PEG is understated, and overvalued names pass the <=1.5 gate. The Tag-179 'Bug #4 / F-ME-009' fix that the comments celebrate has never once executed in production — it is permanently inert because the upstream field was never wired. This is a silent correctness hole masquerading as a fixed bug.
fix: Either (a) wire earningsGrowthYoY/epsGrowthYoY in pull-yahoo.js from Yahoo's earningsQuarterlyGrowth / financialData.earningsGrowth and keep the existing preference chain, or (b) until that field exists, rename the method/label/description to 'P/Rev-Growth' and stop claiming Lynch-PEG semantics. Add a method comment: 'failure mode prevented: mislabeling a revenue-growth ratio as earnings-PEG, which under-prices margin-dilutive growth.' Do not silently keep the inert branch.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed real by source reading. methods/peg.js:16-20 reads H.metricValue(stock,'earningsGrowthYoY') and 'epsGrowthYoY', but a full repo-wide grep shows these keys exist ONLY in peg.js — they are produced by NO file. The canonical mapper in pull-yahoo.js (mapYahooToCanonical, the sole source of stock.metrics.* consumed by methods) defines the complete metrics block at lines 891-928 and includes revenueGrowthYoY (line 893, = financialData.revenueGrowth*100 at :614-615) but NO earningsGrowthYoY / epsGrowthYoY. H.metricValue (methods/_helpers.js:23-29) only reads metrics.<key>, so both eg1 and eg2 are ALWAYS null, earningsGrowth is always null, growth always falls back to revenueGrowthYoY, and growthSource is permanently 'Rev'. The 'EPS' branch and reason-string variant are dead code. Net effect: a method labeled 'PEG (Lynch)' / description 'PEG (P/E / Growth) (Lynch)' computes P/E-over-REVENUE-growth and silently presents it as an earnings-based Lynch PEG — exactly the mislabeling the auditor describes. Note: Yahoo's financialData (the 'fd' object) IS pulled and does carry earningsGrowth / earningsQuarterlyGrowth, so option (a) is feasible, but the field is simply never mapped.

Severity: I revise high->medium. It is a genuine correctness/labeling defect in ONE diagnostic method (it changes how PEG should be interpreted and over-prices margin-dilutive growth), but it is not silent corruption of the wider snapshot — the fallback still yields a defined, finite ratio; only the label/semantics are wrong.

fix_safe=false: both proposed remedies change observable behavior or public contract. (a) Wiring earningsGrowth/earningsQuarterlyGrowth flips PEG values and pass/fail outcomes for every stock where Yahoo supplies earnings growth, and requires a human decision on unit/period mapping (fractional vs percent, quarterly-growth vs YoY) — earningsQuarterlyGrowth is a single-quarter YoY figure, not symmetric with revenueGrowth*100. (b) Renaming the id/label/description is a public-contract change touching downstream consumers and the fixture-hash test. Neither is behavior-preserving; needs human review.

title: marketCap envelope unwrap omits Number.isFinite guard, allowing NaN/Infinity marketCap to propagate into the yield and produce a NaN value that buildResult nulls silently
evidence: fcf-yield.js:23 `var mcap = stock && stock.marketCap && (typeof stock.marketCap === 'number' ? stock.marketCap : stock.marketCap.value);`. Unlike every other method's `_unwrap` (e.g. fcf-conversion-stability.js:90-95) this has no `Number.isFinite` check. If `stock.marketCap` is the number NaN, the truthy guard `stock.marketCap &&` makes `NaN` falsy → mcap becomes `NaN`(falsy)→ actually evaluates to NaN only via the .value path; if marketCap.value is NaN/Infinity it passes straight through. Then :33 `if (mcap <= 0)` is false for NaN, :51 `value = fcfAdj / mcap` = NaN, and H.buildResult (helpers.js:60) coerces non-finite value to null while still returning computable:true.
why_it_matters: A NaN/Infinity marketCap (FX-conversion edge, missing-data envelope with value:NaN) yields a result that is computable:true, pass:false (NaN>=thresh is false), value:null — i.e. the stock is silently marked as FAILING fcf-yield rather than incomputable. Because fcf-yield is a 'prefer' sort hint in QC core and was a scored weight historically, a NaN slips through as a real fail signal instead of a clean NO_DATA flag. Inconsistent with the isFinite discipline applied everywhere else (helpers.metricValue:28 explicitly returns null for non-finite for exactly this reason).
fix: Replace the inline unwrap with a finite-checked helper: `var mcap = _unwrap(stock && stock.marketCap);` using the same `_unwrap` shape as the sibling methods (return null unless Number.isFinite). Then the existing `mcap == null` branch (:26) correctly routes to computable:false. Add comment: 'failure mode prevented: NaN/Infinity marketCap propagating to a false-FAIL instead of clean incomputable.'

_verdict.note: Confirmed real against source. fcf-yield.js:23 unwraps marketCap inline WITHOUT a Number.isFinite guard, unlike the sibling _unwrap in fcf-conversion-stability.js:90-95 (which returns null for non-finite numbers/values). Traced the failure: (1) marketCap === number NaN -> `stock.marketCap && (...)` short-circuits to NaN; line 26 `mcap == null` is false (NaN==null is false), line 33 `mcap<=0` is false, line 51 value=fcfAdj/NaN=NaN; buildResult (_helpers.js:60) coerces non-finite to null but still returns computable:true, pass:false. (2) marketCap={value:NaN} -> .value path -> same NaN outcome. (3) marketCap={value:Infinity} -> value=fcf/Infinity=0, a clean numeric 0 yield -> pass:false. In all cases a corrupt marketCap becomes a silent FAIL / nulled value instead of the honest computable:false the `mcap==null` branch at line 26 is meant to produce. So the bug and its consequence are accurately described. Two caveats: the auditor's prose about the NaN mechanism is garbled ('truthy guard makes NaN falsy -> mcap becomes NaN') but the conclusion is correct; and real-world frequency is low since Yahoo marketCap is normally a clean positive number, so triggering requires upstream corruption. Medium severity is defensible given the file's explicit hardening intent, though arguably low-medium.

title: insider-net-buying nets TRANSACTION COUNTS, not share volume — defeats its own stated failure mode
evidence: Fallback path: `const buys = _num(act.buyCount90d); const sells = _num(act.sellCount90d); ... return { net: b - s, ... }` and the pass is `net > THRESHOLD` (THRESHOLD=0). The header docstring (L13-20) claims the method exists to catch 'A stock with 2 small buys and 15 large insider sells ... passes the cluster gate while screaming insiders are exiting.' But pull-yahoo.js:786-788 defines `buyCount90d` = total open-market buy *transactions* and `sellCount90d` = sell *transactions*, while `netShares90d` (the actual signed share volume) is ALSO present (pull-yahoo.js:788) and is read into components (L69, 93) but NEVER used for the pass decision.
why_it_matters: The exact scenario the method advertises catching — 2 small buys vs a few huge sells — still passes: 2 buy-transactions minus 1 sell-transaction = net +1 > 0 = PASS, even when the sells dwarf the buys in share count. It nets the wrong quantity. The correct signal (netShares90d) is sitting unused in the same object. The method gives a false 'insiders accumulating' verdict precisely when insiders are dumping in size.
fix: When using the insiderActivity fallback, base pass/value on signed share volume when available: prefer `act.netShares90d` (already computed by the puller) over the transaction-count delta. Keep the count delta only as a tiebreak/context. Add comment: '// prevents false-accumulate verdict when few large sells outweigh many tiny buys (transaction-count != share-volume).' Do not touch insiderActivity producer or FTS_CACHE_VERSION.

_verdict.note: Confirmed against source. Producer pull-yahoo.js:773-788 defines buyCount90d/sellCount90d as open-market *transaction counts* (buyCount++/sellCount++ per tx), while netShares90d is the signed *share volume* (netShares += shares / -= |shares|). The consuming method methods/insider-net-buying.js fallback (L63-68) sets net = buyCount90d - sellCount90d (a count delta) and the verdict is pass = net > 0 (L97). netShares90d is read (L69) and copied into components (L93) but NEVER used for value/pass. This dimensionally defeats the method's own docstring (L13-20), which says it exists to catch share-volume imbalance ("2 small buys vs 15 large sells"): a case of many tiny buys vs few huge sells nets a *positive count* and passes even though net shares are deeply negative. The signed-volume field needed to detect exactly this is present and ignored (the sibling insider-buy-cluster.js does surface netShares90d in its reason text). Note this fallback is the ONLY live path — Source-1 fields (netInsiderBuying/net6mShares/netShares180d) are documented "future fields" not populated by the producer, so the defect affects every ticker the method evaluates. Severity revised high->medium because the method is DIAGNOSTIC (defaultActive:true, not in SCORE_WEIGHTS per audit-reports/2026-05-16-tag201-cycle.md:57-59): a wrong verdict misleads a human reviewer but does not corrupt the screener score/ranking.

title: Yahoo fallback applies the curated-CIK threshold (>=3) to Yahoo's broad ~7,000-filer count → signal collapses to near-always-pass
evidence: THRESHOLD=3 is documented (L29-32, 56) as deliberately low BECAUSE the SEC bootstrap CIK list is only ~40 curated smart-money institutions. `_yahooFallback` then reuses that same threshold against `stock.meta.institutionsCount`: `const ic = stock.meta.institutionsCount; ... const pass = ic >= THRESHOLD;` where institutionsCount is the broad-based count across ~all 13F filers (per institutional-density.js header L7-9 and pull-yahoo.js:870).
why_it_matters: A '>=3 of ~40 curated smart-money names' bar is a meaningful conviction signal; a '>=3 of ~7,000 filers' bar is satisfied by essentially every non-microcap on earth, so the fallback turns a selective smart-money gate into a near-constant TRUE. Because the fallback fires whenever the SEC cache is missing or the ticker is absent (the common case until the curated cache is broadly populated), in practice the method almost always reports the trivial pass while masquerading (same id/threshold) as the concentrated 13F signal. components.source flags the regime but the binary pass is corrupted.
fix: Use a regime-specific threshold in `_yahooFallback` (e.g. broad institutionsCount needs a much higher floor, or compare institutionsPercentHeld instead) rather than reusing the curated THRESHOLD. Add comment naming the failure mode: '// prevents broad ~7k-filer count from trivially clearing a bar calibrated for a ~40-name curated CIK list.' Do not hardcode ticker exclusions.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed by source. THRESHOLD=3 is documented (institutional-ownership-13f.js L29-31, L56) as deliberately low BECAUSE the SEC bootstrap CIK list is only ~40 curated smart-money institutions. _yahooFallback (L109-128) reuses that same THRESHOLD: `const ic = stock.meta.institutionsCount; ... const pass = ic >= THRESHOLD;` (L110, L113). meta.institutionsCount is the BROAD ~7,000-filer count — verified via pull-yahoo.js L868 comment ("broad-based, ~7k institutions, Form 13F-aggregated"), institutional-density.js L7-9 ("ALL Form-13F filers (~7,000 institutions)"), and the schema-audit example value institutionsCount=7487 (audit-reports/2026-05-17-tag219c-yahoo-schema-audit.md:162). So in the Yahoo fallback regime any stock with institutional data clears a >=3 bar trivially → near-always-pass. The header itself half-acknowledges this (L40-41: "passes are easier than from SEC source") but understates that it's effectively guaranteed. Logic/calibration defect is real.

Severity downgraded high→medium: this module is DIAGNOSTIC-only. It is NOT referenced in methods/score-aggregator.js (SCORE_WEIGHTS) nor methods/strategy-modes.js (eligibility) — grep returned no matches (header L48 + README L83 confirm). So the collapsed signal cannot move any score, tier, or eligibility gate; impact is limited to the detail/diagnostic UI verdict, and components.source='yahoo.majorHoldersBreakdown' (L121) lets careful consumers distinguish the regime. Real defect, but no scoring impact → medium, not high.

fix_safe=false: the proposed fix changes pass/fail semantics of the fallback branch (flips many stocks pass→fail), and the suggested values are non-determined ("e.g." a higher floor OR switching to institutionsPercentHeld). Choosing the metric/threshold is a calibration/design decision — and comparing institutionsPercentHeld overlaps with the separate institutional-density.js module (already gates pct>=0.50). It is fixture-hash safe (diagnostic), but the fallback smoke tests in tag28-tests.js (~L1886-1921) may assert current pass behavior and need updating. Behavior-changing + needs a judgment call → human review required.

title: Altman coalesces NaN/garbage totalDebt and totalCash to 0 via `|| 0`, producing a false-SAFE Z-score on a 0.20-weight TURNAROUND gate
evidence: Lines 50-51: `const cashVal = cash || 0; const debtVal = totalDebt || 0;` where `cash`/`totalDebt` come from `_balanceVal` (line 34-38) which returns `arr[idx] && arr[idx][field]` with NO isFinite guard. A NaN or envelope value survives, then `NaN || 0` -> 0. Reproduced: balance `{totalAssets:1e9, totalDebt:NaN, totalCash:5e8}`, no CA/CL -> debtVal=0 -> X1=0.50, the X4 heuristic (line 110, `debtVal + 0.4*...`) also uses 0 -> X4=4.00 -> Z=9.61 'SAFE', pass=true.
why_it_matters: `|| 0` cannot distinguish a real zero (debt-free firm) from NaN/missing/corrupt data, and silently treats missing debt as 'no leverage' — the most favorable possible assumption for a solvency model. altman-z-score carries 0.20 weight in TURNAROUND SCORE_WEIGHTS (score-aggregator.js:63), so a single bad balance field flips a distressed turnaround candidate to a clean SAFE pass and lets it score 1.0 on a fifth of the mode weight. This is the exact '|| 0 falsy bug' class.
fix: Replace `_balanceVal` with the finite-guarded variant used in beneish/ohlson/penman (`return Number.isFinite(v) ? v : null;`). Then derive `cashVal`/`debtVal` with explicit presence checks: only coalesce to 0 when the field is present-but-genuinely-zero or the firm is independently confirmed debt-free; otherwise return computable:false('totalDebt/totalCash non-finite'). Comment: 'prevents failure mode: NaN debt masked to zero inflates X1/X4 into false SAFE'.

_verdict.note: CONFIRMED with source + runtime evidence. methods/altman-z-score.js `_balanceVal` (line 34-38) returns `arr[idx] && arr[idx][field]` with NO isFinite guard, unlike the sibling `_balField` in ohlson-o-score.js:97, beneish-m-score.js:97, penman-nissim:134 which all `return Number.isFinite(v) ? v : null`. Lines 50-51 then `cash || 0` / `totalDebt || 0`. Reproduced the cited fixture {totalAssets:1e9, totalDebt:NaN, totalCash:5e8}, no CA/CL: debtVal coalesces to 0 -> X1=0.50, X4 capped at 4.00 -> Z″=8.54 'SAFE', pass=true (auditor's 9.61 differs only because NI inputs weren't pinned; failure mode identical). Gate confirmed: altman-z-score is `required:true, weight:'must'` in TURNAROUND (strategy-modes.js:154) — a hard solvency must-gate, so a false-SAFE lets an insolvent turnaround through the exact bankruptcy screen. Two qualifications: (1) the auditor's 'envelope value survives' is WRONG — an object value yields Z=null and pass=false (fails safe), not false-SAFE; only NaN/null/undefined debt trigger it. (2) The title's '0.20-weight' is imprecise (it's weight:'must', not a numeric 0.20). Severity: the impact is real but the live blast radius is narrower than 'garbage->false SAFE' implies — pull-yahoo.js:687 writes totalDebt=null ONLY when BOTH debt components are genuinely absent, and F-NY-002 (pull-yahoo.js:681-686) deliberately keeps absence-as-zero; for a truly debt-free firm debt=0 is correct. The genuine gaps are: NaN/Infinity is unhandled, and altman ignores the `_debtPartial` signal that net-debt-ebitda already surfaces. high is slightly aggressive given that; medium-high is fair.

title: WC-anomaly guard silently passes any firm whose current-year WC proxy is negative — the growth ratio sign-flips and trivially satisfies `<= 1.3`
evidence: wcProxy (line 24) = `a - d - c` can be negative for cash-rich firms (cash > assets-debt). The guard at line 45 only rejects `wcT1 <= 0` (prior year), never `wcT <= 0` (current). Then line 50 `wcGrowth = wcT / wcT1` with wcT<0,wcT1>0 -> negative; line 57 `value = wcGrowth/salesGrowth` negative; line 60 `pass: value <= THRESHOLD(1.3)` -> true. Reproduced: balance flips +5e8 -> -1e8 with falling sales -> value=-0.25, pass=true, reason 'WC growth -120% vs Sales -20% -> ratio=-0.25'.
why_it_matters: working-capital-anomaly is a SoftGuard (score-aggregator.js:205, penalty 6). pass=true means the penalty is NEVER applied, and in graduated lte scoring a negative value would even earn 0.99 (score-aggregator.js:159). So precisely the firms most likely to be manipulating working capital while sitting on a large cash/deferred-revenue balance escape the detector entirely. The negative-ratio reason string ('WC growth -120%') is also nonsense reported to the dashboard.
fix: After computing wcT/wcT1, require BOTH to be positive for a meaningful growth ratio; if wcT<=0 (or sign differs between years) return computable:false with reason 'WC proxy non-positive / sign-flip — growth ratio undefined' rather than a misleading pass. Comment: 'prevents failure mode: negative current WC proxy flips growth ratio negative and trivially passes the <=1.3 manipulation gate'.

_verdict.note:
CONFIRMED real. methods/working-capital-anomaly.js wcProxy (line 24) = totalAssets - totalDebt - totalCash can legitimately be negative for net-cash firms (cash+debt > assets). The guard at line 45 only rejects wcT1<=0 (prior year) and revT1<=0; it never checks wcT (current year). With wcT1>0, wcT<0, and positive salesGrowth (line 52 only rejects salesGrowth<=0), line 50 wcGrowth<0, line 57 value=wcGrowth/salesGrowth<0, and line 60 pass:value<=1.3 is trivially true. Reproduction holds exactly: wcT1=+5e8, wcT=-1e8, sales 0.8x -> wcGrowth=-0.2, value=-0.25, pass=true, with the misleading reason 'WC growth -120% vs Sales -20% -> ratio=-0.25'.

Downstream impact verified: working-capital-anomaly is a TURNAROUND/QUALITY soft-guard (strategy-modes.js:118; method-types.js:65 DIAGNOSTIC; score-aggregator.js:205 penalty=6). A soft-guard is only flagged as failed when r.computable===true && r.pass===false (strategy-modes.js:219). It is NOT in SCORE_WEIGHTS, so a missed flag only forgoes a 6-point penalty -- it cannot by itself admit a stock or compute a wrong score, hence severity revised high->medium (degraded detection, bounded affected population, not a hard-gate/correctness failure).
