But returning computable:false instead of pass:false is a semantic choice for a guard: computable:false adds the NO_DATA flag and zeroes confidence via _helpers.js _autoFlags/_inferConfidence, and it still does NOT add the stock to failedSoftGuards (which needs pass===false), so it neither penalizes nor flags. Whether the desired remediation is computable:false vs an explicit pass:false (which WOULD apply the 6-pt penalty) is a judgment call about guard semantics that needs a human to decide -- so not auto-apply.

title: Sloan ratio uses FCF (NI - FCF) instead of operating cash flow (NI - CFO), so capex is wrongly counted as an accrual — overstating |Sloan| for capex-heavy firms
evidence: Line 35-36 pull `annual.annualNetIncome` and `annual.annualFCF`; line 58 computes `(ni - fcf)/ta`. The canonical Sloan accrual is (NI - CFO)/avg-assets. FCF = CFO - capex, so NI - FCF = NI - CFO + capex = true-accruals + capex. annualOCF exists in the snapshot (~86% coverage per piotroski.js:54 and is required by beneish/ohlson) but is not used here.
why_it_matters: Capex is an investing outflow, not an earnings accrual. Adding it inflates the Sloan magnitude for reinvestment-heavy firms (the TURNAROUND/hypergrowth archetype), pushing them toward the WARNING/REVIEW/EXTREME bands and toward the red-flag rule `val > 0.20` (score-aggregator.js:90-98). A capex-heavy but honestly-accounted recovery can be flagged as accrual-manipulation purely because it is investing. The asymmetric posV logic (lines 79-99) does not fix this — it only changes sign handling, not the capex contamination.
fix: Compute accruals as (NI - OCF)/totalAssets, preferring annualOCF and falling back to annualFCF only when OCF is absent (mirror piotroski.js:54-55 `cfo0 = ocf0 != null ? ocf0 : fcf0`). Ideally scale by average totalAssets ((ta_t+ta_{t-1})/2) per the canonical definition. Comment: 'prevents failure mode: capex miscounted as accrual inflates |Sloan| for reinvesting firms'.

_verdict.note: Confirmed real via source. methods/sloan-ratio.js line 36 pulls annual.annualFCF and line 58 computes (ni - fcf) / ta. Canonical Sloan accrual = (NI - CFO)/assets; since FCF = CFO - Capex, NI - FCF = NI - CFO + Capex, so capex is wrongly added into the accrual. The escalation logic acts only on the positive direction (posV = Math.max(0,v), lines 79/94-99), so this systematically inflates Sloan upward for capex-heavy reinvesting firms and can spuriously trigger WARNING/REVIEW/EXTREME flags — a genuine false-positive cohort bias. The SAME bug was already identified and fixed in the sibling method: piotroski-f-score.js lines 50-55 carry an explicit 'BUG-fix (audit 2026-06-20): Piotroski CFO/accrual signals are defined on OPERATING cash flow, not FCF. Using FCF (= OCF - capex) systematically docks capex-heavy reinvesting recoveries' with the OCF-preferred-FCF-fallback pattern (cfo0 = ocf0 != null ? ocf0 : fcf0). annualOCF is confirmed present (~86% coverage) and consumed by beneish-m-score.js:123, ohlson-o-score.js:131, reinvestment-rate.js:82, premium-compounder-proof.js:52, operating-cashflow-coverage.js:85 — sloan-ratio.js just never got the same treatment. Minor citation nit: the auditor wrote 'piotroski.js:54' but the file is actually piotroski-f-score.js:54; the cited code exists exactly as described, so the substance holds. _helpers.js:286 confirms sloan-ratio is a live scored method (threshold=0.20, lte_abs).

title: Index-pairing of NI/OpInc/GP with Rev and balance assumes year-aligned arrays, but the quoteSummary mapper compresses each series independently via _arr().filter(Boolean)
evidence: buffett pairs by raw index: T1 `const ni = rawNI[i]; const row = rawBal[i]; ... roes.push(ni / eq)` (line 154-159); T7 `if (...rawRev[i] > 0) margins.push(rawOpInc[i] / rawRev[i])` (line 383-384); Q2 same with rawGP/rawRev (line 574). But pull-yahoo.js `_arr` ends with `.map(...).filter(Boolean)` (line 499) — null years are DROPPED, compressing each array. annualRev, annualOpInc, annualNetIncome, annualGP are each built by a SEPARATE _arr call (pull-yahoo lines 618-621) and annualBalance by a separate `.filter(Boolean)` map (line 692). A company missing OpInc in FY-2 but not Rev gets annualOpInc[2]=FY-3 while annualRev[2]=FY-2.
why_it_matters: ROE, ROIC, operating margin, gross margin and EPS are all computed by dividing two values the code believes are the SAME fiscal year but which can be different years. The repeated 'F-004'/'F-DP-003' comments in pull-yahoo (lines 570-573, 593-594) explicitly acknowledge this exact alignment hazard and claim null placeholders fix it — but that fix lives only in the FTS path (line 1095+) and the financials-derived path; the PRIMARY quoteSummary _arr path still filters. Silent cross-year division corrupts the headline 14-point composite for any name with a gap year (banks/insurers/fintech are named offenders).
fix: Do not rely on positional alignment across independently-compressed arrays. Either (a) consume year-keyed objects (pair by fiscalYear), or (b) within each method build a single aligned table from arrays that share null placeholders. As a method-local guard, only compute a ratio when both arrays still carry the same length AND neither was compressed — but the real fix is upstream consistency. Add comment: `// prevents cross-fiscal-year ratio (NI[i]/equity[i] where i is not the same year)`.

_verdict.note:
Real but overstated latent data-integrity bug, not critical. Mechanism confirmed: pull-yahoo.js _arr() ends in .filter(Boolean) (line 499) and the four income series are separate _arr(isHist,...) calls (lines 618-621) with annualBalance a separate .filter(Boolean) map (line 692), so an interior null year in one field shifts indices independently. buffett-criteria.js does pair by raw index: T1 rawNI[i]/rawBal[i] (154-159), T7 rawOpInc[i]/rawRev[i] (383), Q2 rawGP[i]/rawRev[i] (574), and these read the merged annual.* canonical. So cross-fiscal-year ratios are mechanically possible.

But the finding is materially overstated and partly imprecise: (1) The DOMINANT data path is FTS (mapFTSToAnnual/mapFTSToBalance, lines 1083-1201), which deliberately pushes NULL PLACEHOLDERS to keep annualOpInc[i]/annualRev[i]/annualNetIncome[i]/annualGP[i]/annualBalance[i] year-aligned, and the merge prefers FTS by non-null count (1859-1898). The desync is only reachable on the residual quoteSummary-only path. (2) The financials OpInc fallback (Tag 203, lines 502-597) ALSO null-preserves, so the OpInc-vs-Rev example the finding leads with is largely already defended for the bank/insurer case it cites. (3) Yahoo's missing year is documented as 'almost always the oldest' with '~0 live incidence' (line 1120); a trailing-null compaction does not shift surviving indices, so only rare INTERIOR gaps actually misalign. (4) T3 (cited 222-231) only uses index 0 (latest year), where desync is essentially impossible — a weak citation. The genuinely fragile sites are T1 (NI from isHist vs balance from bsHist — two independent sources) and T7/Q2 on quoteSummary-only tickers with interior gaps. This is a recognized class in the repo (F-DP-004 in fixes-for-pull-yahoo.md; F-DP-030/031, F-DP-003, F-DP-101, F-004/Tag 206f comments) that was fixed elsewhere but not at the quoteSummary income-array build sites (618-621) nor guarded in buffett. Note buffett-criteria is DIAGNOSTIC, not in HG/QC/TURN SCORE_WEIGHTS (header line 25), though it is a BUFFETT-mode MUST-gate.

title: DCF Margin-of-Safety is a HARD pass requirement, but any dcf-intrinsic-value load/throw is swallowed and silently demoted to 'MoS not met' rather than 'not computable'
evidence: `try { const DCF = require('./dcf-intrinsic-value.js'); dcfResult = DCF.evaluate(stock); } catch (e) { /* dcf load/eval failed */ }` (lines 717-720) leaves dcfResult=null. Then `mosMet = !!(dcfResult && dcfResult.computable && ... marginOfSafetyMet)` (line 744) → false, and `pass = industryOk && mosOk && rateOk` (line 761) → hard fail with reason 'DCF Margin-of-Safety not met (HARD requirement)' (line 777). The whole evaluate still returns computable:true (line 785).
why_it_matters: A transient require error, a throw inside DCF, or a DCF that is merely not-computable for lack of data all collapse to the same verdict as a real valuation failure: the stock is reported as a genuine Buffett FAIL on valuation grounds. There is no distinction between 'expensive' and 'we could not value it'. In BUFFETT strategy mode this method is a MUST, so swallowed DCF errors quietly remove qualifying names with a misleading reason. This is the classic catch->degrade-silently data-integrity pattern.
fix: When dcfResult is null OR not computable, set the overall result computable:false (or carry an explicit `mosUnknown` flag and a distinct reason), instead of treating absent DCF identically to MoS-fail. Add comment: `// prevents swallowed DCF error from masquerading as a valuation FAIL`.

_verdict.note:
Mechanism confirmed in methods/buffett-criteria.js. A throw from DCF.evaluate or its require() is swallowed at lines 717-720, leaving dcfResult=null; mosMet then computes false (line 744), pass=false (line 761), reason="DCF Margin-of-Safety not met (HARD requirement)" (line 777), yet the overall result still returns computable:true (line 785). So a genuine DCF error IS conflated with a valuation FAIL — that part of the claim is accurate.

But the framing/severity is overstated. The catch block only fires on a true require/runtime throw, which is rare. The dominant route to "absent DCF -> mosMet=false" is dcf-intrinsic-value.js DELIBERATELY returning computable:false for legitimate, expected reasons: non-USD snapshot not FX-converted (lines 249-255), <5y owner-earnings prerequisite (208-214), non-positive intrinsic value (299-305), missing/zero mcap (270-276), discountRate<=terminalGrowth (220-226). None of these throw — they are normal "cannot value this stock" outcomes. For a hard-MoS strategy, "no margin of safety can be established" is a defensible FAIL (don't buy what you can't value), not necessarily an "unknown."

The proposed_fix conflates the two: it sets overall computable:false whenever dcfResult is null OR not computable. That lumps the rare true error in with the common legitimate not-valuable case. The test at tag28-tests.js:2406-2411 (genuine MoS fail, DCF IS computable) is unaffected by the fix, so the fix wouldn't break it — but the impact elsewhere is broad.

Severity is closer to medium than high: it is a data-integrity/observability conflation (a swallowed error looks like a valuation fail), not silent numeric corruption, and the practical blast radius is small (only genuine DCF throws).

title: Insufficient-data guard uses AND not OR: a stock with 4y net income but zero balance years (or vice versa) is treated as computable and scored on half-missing data
evidence: `if (niValid < MIN_YEARS_REQUIRED && balValid < MIN_YEARS_REQUIRED)` returns not-computable (line 696). MIN_YEARS_REQUIRED=4. The `&&` means the guard only trips when BOTH series are short. A name with niValid=8 and balValid=0 passes the guard, then T1/T2/T3/Q1/Q3 all silently degrade (ROE/ROIC/debt need balance rows; they return their own 'need >=3' sub-fails), dragging passRate down on absent data rather than declaring the composite incomputable.
why_it_matters: The whole premise (comment line 698-699: 'Buffett rules require multi-year track record') is that you need BOTH earnings and balance history. The AND lets through half-blind evaluations that then produce a confident-looking 0-100 score and pass/fail. The insufficientDataReason text even says 'both annualNetIncome AND annualBalance < 5y' — but it is checked against MIN_YEARS_REQUIRED=4, not 5, so the message is also wrong.
fix: Use OR for the hard gate (`niValid < MIN || balValid < MIN`) since balance data is required by the majority of tests, and fix the 5y/4y wording. Add comment: `// prevents scoring the 14-pt composite when one required series (NI or balance) is absent`.

title: parseFloat(...) || DEFAULT pattern for treasury yield and pass threshold: a legitimate env value of '0' silently falls back to the default (falsy-zero bug)
evidence: `const treasuryYield = parseFloat(process.env.BUFFETT_TREASURY_YIELD_10Y) || TREASURY_YIELD_DEFAULT;` (line 423) and `const threshold = parseFloat(process.env.BUFFETT_PASS_THRESHOLD) || PASS_THRESHOLD_DEFAULT;` (line 755). If an operator sets BUFFETT_TREASURY_YIELD_10Y=0 (zero-rate scenario / test) or BUFFETT_PASS_THRESHOLD=0 (accept-all), parseFloat returns 0 which is falsy, so the default (0.045 / 0.85) is used instead.
why_it_matters: This is the '|| 0'-class falsy bug inverted: 0 is a legitimately valid configured value that gets discarded. For the threshold, an intended 0 (diagnostic / let-everything-through run) silently becomes 0.85. NaN from a malformed env string also falls back (acceptable) but masks misconfiguration without warning.
fix: Parse then explicitly check Number.isFinite: `const t = parseFloat(env); treasuryYield = Number.isFinite(t) ? t : DEFAULT;`. Add comment: `// prevents env value 0 from being discarded by falsy || default`.

_verdict.note: Confirmed against source in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/methods/buffett-criteria.js. Both cited lines match exactly: line 423 `const treasuryYield = parseFloat(process.env.BUFFETT_TREASURY_YIELD_10Y) || TREASURY_YIELD_DEFAULT;` and line 755 `const threshold = parseFloat(process.env.BUFFETT_PASS_THRESHOLD) || PASS_THRESHOLD_DEFAULT;`. Defaults are nonzero (line 35 PASS_THRESHOLD_DEFAULT=0.85, line 36 TREASURY_YIELD_DEFAULT=0.045), so a legitimate env value of exactly '0' yields parseFloat('0')===0 (falsy) and is silently discarded in favor of the default — a genuine falsy-zero bug. Behavioral impact verified: treasuryYield feeds the T8 earnings-yield-vs-Treasury comparison (line 447 `pass = pretaxEY > treasuryYield`), and threshold gates the overall pass at line 760 (`passRate >= threshold`). Setting BUFFETT_PASS_THRESHOLD=0 (intended accept-all) would silently re-impose the 85% gate; BUFFETT_TREASURY_YIELD_10Y=0 (zero-rate test) would silently use 4.5%. These are the only two references to these env vars in the worktree (grep-confirmed), so no other parse layer mitigates it. Real but edge-triggered: it only manifests when an operator explicitly sets the var to 0; normal unset/valid use is unaffected. Severity medium is reasonable (accept-all=0 misconfig is a plausible operator footgun, no silent corruption in default operation).

title: Soft-error pulls (404 / no-13f / parse-fail) are written with a fresh `fetchedAt` and cached for the full 100-day TTL
evidence: pullInstitution13f returns an object with `error` but no throw for the common failure cases: line 324 `if (subRes.notFound) return { positions: [], error: 'submissions-404' };`, line 334 `return { positions: [], name, error: 'no-13f-hr-filings' };`, line 329 submissions-parse, line 346 no-information-table, line 368 info-table-404. None of these throw, so the main loop's catch (the Tag-211j failedAt path, line 648) is NEVER reached. Instead line 626-629 writes `byInstitution[cik] = { ... fetchedAt: new Date().toISOString(), positions: [], error: r.error }`. The freshness gate at line 618 keys ONLY on `fetchedAt`, so the entry is treated as fresh and skipped for 100 days.
why_it_matters: A transient SEC 404/rate-limit, a temporarily missing info-table, or a wrong/placeholder CIK is cached as a successful empty pull. The institution silently contributes 0 positions to the by-ticker view for a full quarter, with no retry. This is exactly the 'errored-pull written as fresh' failure the Tag-211j pattern was meant to prevent — but the pattern only fires on thrown exceptions, and these paths return instead of throwing. Asymmetric survivorship: big/healthy filers refresh, transiently-failing ones rot.
fix: Treat a returned `r.error` the same as a thrown error for cache-freshness: when `r.error` is set, write `failedAt` (NOT `fetchedAt`) while preserving any prior successful `positions`/`fetchedAt`, mirroring the catch block at line 648. Distinguish permanent (no-13f-hr-filings for a genuine non-13F CIK) from transient by allowing a short retry TTL. Comment must name the failure mode: 'prevents soft-error (return-not-throw) pulls being cached fresh and starving the by-ticker view for a quarter'.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed against source. pullInstitution13f RETURNS (does not throw) {error:...} for the common soft-failure cases: submissions-404 (L324-325), submissions-parse (L329), no-13f-hr-filings (L335), no-accession-number (L342), no-information-table-found (L347-353), info-table-fetch (L359-365), info-table-404 (L369-375). In main() the success path at L626-636 then writes byInstitution[cik] with fetchedAt=new Date().toISOString() and error:r.error||null. The freshness gate at L618-619 keys ONLY on prev.fetchedAt, so a soft-errored entry (positions:[]) is treated as fresh and skipped for the full TTL (default 100 days, DEFAULT_MAX_AGE_DAYS). The catch block at L643-658 — the Tag 211j failedAt-not-fetchedAt retry path that preserves prior data — is genuinely unreachable for these return-not-throw cases. So a transient soft failure (e.g. info-table-404, submissions-parse) on a real tracked institution caches it empty for a quarter, dropping it from the aggregated buildByTickerView output. The auditor's evidence is accurate; this also mirrors the identical latent gap in the sibling pull-insider-form4.js (L460-475 success path writes fetchedAt even when result.error is set).

Severity revised high->medium. Mitigating context: (1) the script is manual-only — verified NOT referenced in .github workflows, matching the header comment 'NOT wired into daily-pull.yml'; no automation silently propagates the stale cache. (2) The sole consumer methods/institutional-ownership-13f.js is DIAGNOSTIC-only (its header states 'NOT in SCORE_WEIGHTS -> DIAGNOSTIC-only'), so it does not affect screener pass/fail scoring. (3) Aggregation across ~40 institutions with a low threshold (>=3 holders) means losing one institution degrades but does not corrupt the signal; a Yahoo fallback exists (though it only triggers on ticker-ABSENT, not present-but-understated). Net: real correctness bug, real quarter-long staleness, but bounded blast radius on a diagnostic signal run by hand.

fix_safe=false: the proposed fix is not behavior-preserving. It re-routes r.error through the failedAt path (changing cache-freshness semantics), and explicitly asks to add a short retry TTL plus a permanent-vs-transient classification (e.g. cache no-13f-hr-filings long while retrying info-table-404 soon). That classification is a design decision, touches the resumable-cache invariant, and should mirror Tag 211j deliberately — needs human review, not auto-apply.

title: Form-4 soft-error returns (submissions-404 / submissions-parse) cached with fresh `fetchedAt`, suppressing retry for 24h and masking the failure as '0 transactions'
evidence: pullTickerForm4 returns instead of throwing on the two most common failures: line 354 `if (subRes.notFound) return { transactions: [], error: 'submissions-404' };` and line 359 `catch (e) { return { transactions: [], error: 'submissions-parse: ' + e.message }; }`. Back in main, the success path (line 462) runs because nothing threw: `byTicker[ticker] = { ... fetchedAt: new Date().toISOString(), transactions: [], error: result.error || null }`. The freshness gate (line 454) checks only `prev.fetchedAt`, so a 404'd ticker is skipped for CACHE_TTL_MS (24h). The elaborate Tag-211j failedAt block (line 484) only runs on a thrown exception.
why_it_matters: Form-4 consumer insider-conviction-score.js is in the live registry (methods/index.js:113). A ticker whose CIK 404s (stale map entry, delisting, share-class mismatch) is cached as a clean empty pull, so the method sees `transactions: []`, returns computable-but-empty, and the INSIDER_BUYING gate silently fails closed. No alarm, no retry next run. The header advertises 'failedAt (NOT fetchedAt) so the next run retries' (lines 478-491) but that guarantee does not hold for the return-path errors, which are the common ones.
fix: Have main inspect `result.error`: if set, write `failedAt` (not `fetchedAt`) and preserve prior good data, identical to the catch path. Alternatively make pullTickerForm4 THROW on submissions-404/parse so the existing catch handles it. Add comment: 'prevents return-path soft errors being cached fresh, which hides 404/parse failures as empty insider history and blocks retry for 24h'.

_verdict.note:
CONFIRMED as a real logic inconsistency in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/scripts/pull-insider-form4.js. All cited line facts check out: line 354-355 `if (subRes.notFound) return { transactions: [], error: 'submissions-404' };` and line 357-359 `catch (e) { return { transactions: [], error: 'submissions-parse: ...' }; }` both RETURN (not throw). Back in main(), since nothing threw, the success path (line 462-470) runs and writes `fetchedAt: new Date().toISOString()` with `transactions: []` and `error: result.error || null`. The freshness gate (line 454-455) checks ONLY `prev.fetchedAt < CACHE_TTL_MS`, so a soft-errored ticker is skipped for 24h. The Tag-211j `failedAt`/preserve-prior-data block (line 476-492) lives in the `catch` and only fires on a THROWN exception — these two return-path errors bypass it. main() never inspects `result.error` (line 469 only stores it, line 475 only logs it). Downstream consumer methods/insider-conviction-score.js line 437 accepts an empty `transactions` array as valid, so it returns computable:true / pass:false ('no P-buy in 90d') instead of the graceful computable:false ('not in cache') — i.e. a fetch failure is masked as a legit 'no insider buying' result, and any prior good data for that ticker is overwritten with []. The author's own Tag-211j comment (line 478-483) shows the failedAt path is the intended handling, so this is a genuine gap.

Severity revised high -> MEDIUM. Two mitigations cap the blast radius: (1) this script is explicitly NOT wired into daily-pull.yml (header lines 46-48) — manual-only tool; (2) insider-conviction-score.js is flagged DIAGNOSTIC ONLY, NOT in any SCORE_WEIGHTS, fixture-hash safe (line 50) — it gates only the INSIDER_BUYING display tab, not scoring/ranking. Also note `submissions-404` is arguably benign: selectUsTickers (line 420) only emits tickers with a valid CIK from the SEC map, and a 404 on a valid CIK's submissions file generally means a CIK with no filings (genuinely empty), so caching [] is defensible there. The clearly-wrong case is `submissions-parse` (truncated/garbled response = transient) being cached fresh and blocking retry for 24h. Net: real but display-only, transient-masking — medium.

fix_safe=false: the proposed fix is the right direction but is NOT behavior-preserving. Routing return-path errors to the failedAt branch makes those tickers retry every run instead of being cached 24h — that is a deliberate behavior change (more SEC requests, including for permanently-404 CIKs on every run). Needs human review, not blind auto-apply. If applied, prefer THROWing on submissions-parse only (clearly transient) while leaving the 404 case to decide explicitly.

title: Latest-filing picker can select a 13F-HR/A amendment that partially restates holdings, silently dropping most positions
evidence: Line 333 includes amendments in the candidate set: `const f13s = all.filter(f => f.form === '13F-HR' || f.form === '13F-HR/A');`. Line 338 sorts purely by filingDate desc and line 339 takes `f13s[0]`. A 13F-HR/A is frequently filed AFTER the original 13F-HR to correct or add a SINGLE position (SEC allows 'amendment type: RESTATEMENT' vs 'NEW HOLDINGS'). A restatement-amendment's information_table can legitimately contain only the changed rows, not the full book.
why_it_matters: If the most recent filing by date is a narrow /A, the puller replaces the full ~5000-position book with the handful of amended rows. The institution then appears to hold only those names, corrupting the by-ticker view and the institutions-holding count for every other name it actually owns. Berkshire/BlackRock-class filers amend regularly, so this hits the highest-signal institutions hardest.
fix: Prefer the latest 13F-HR (original); only use a /A when it is the newest AND its position count is within a sane ratio of the prior 13F-HR (e.g. >= 50% of it), otherwise merge the /A onto the base filing's positions. At minimum, when picking a /A, record `amendmentOf` + `form` and flag low-position-count amendments. Comment: 'prevents a partial 13F-HR/A restatement from replacing the full holdings book'.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed real at the source level. scripts/pull-13f-institutional.js line 333 includes both '13F-HR' and '13F-HR/A' in the candidate set; lines 338-339 sort by filingDate desc and take f13s[0]. A 13F-HR/A filed after the original outsorts it and is selected. SEC EDGAR amendments come in two types — RESTATEMENT (full book) and NEW HOLDINGS (only the added/changed rows). The code captures NO amendment-type metadata: _normalizeSubmissions (lines 260-273) pulls only form/filingDate/accessionNumber/primaryDocument, and the amendmentType lives in primary_doc.xml, never fetched. So a partial NEW-HOLDINGS /A would be parsed at face value and undercount that institution's positions. The bug is genuine.

Severity downgraded high->medium because the blast radius is contained: (1) the puller is explicitly manual-only, NOT wired into daily-pull.yml (header line 43); (2) its only consumer, methods/institutional-ownership-13f.js, is DIAGNOSTIC-only and NOT in any SCORE_WEIGHTS — fixture-hash safe by construction (method header line 48; methods/index.js line 174), so it cannot change screening pass/fail or scores; (3) the diagnostic aggregates distinct institutionCik across ~40 tracked institutions per ticker with a low >=3 threshold plus a Yahoo majorHoldersBreakdown fallback, so one institution's partial amendment dilutes into a count, not a verdict. Real data-integrity defect, low real-world impact.

fix_safe=false: the proposed fix is not behavior-preserving. The 50%-ratio acceptance gate is an arbitrary heuristic, and the 'merge the /A onto the base filing' path is materially risky — merging position lists across two separate filings can double-count or mix quarters and needs human design + tests. The minimal sub-fix (record form/amendmentOf, flag low-position-count /A filings) would be safe, but the picker/merge change as proposed requires human review.

title: isTenB5One footnote regex tests only the FIRST <footnotes> block and matches over-broadly; 10b5-1 sells may be mis-flagged or missed
evidence: Lines 231-233: `const isTenB5One = /<aff10b5One>\s*(1|true)\b/i.test(xml) || /10b5-?\s?1/i.test(_extractFirst(xml, 'footnotes') || '');`. `_extractFirst(xml,'footnotes')` returns only the first footnotes block. The flag is then attached to EVERY transaction in the filing (lines 276, used by the consumer at insider-conviction-score.js:267 to EXCLUDE 10b5-1 sells from the net-buying gate).

A filing with a 10b5-1 plan noted in a later/second footnote block is not flagged → a programmatic sale is counted against net-buying (gate3 fails spuriously, suppressing a real INSIDER_BUYING signal). Conversely the loose `10b5-?\s?1` substring can match footnote prose like 'rule 10b5-1(c)... NOT pursuant to a plan' and over-suppress. Either way the load-bearing net-buying gate is driven by a fragile filing-wide heuristic.

The consumer methods/insider-conviction-score.js:267 excludes any sell with isTenB5One===true from aggSellValue, which feeds netValue (273) and gate3 `netValue>0` (278). I ran the parser on a filing containing one 10b5-1 sell (footnote F1) plus one discretionary sell with no plan: BOTH got isTenB5One:true. So a genuine discretionary sell in the same filing as a plan sell is wrongly excluded from the net-buying gate, biasing the conviction gate toward passing (sells under-counted). No per-transaction footnoteId resolution exists anywhere (grep of scripts/ + methods/), confirming the flag is purely filing-wide. The regex IS over-broad: `10b5-?\s?1` matched `10b51`, `10b5-100` (substring), and bare legal references like `section 10b5-1 of the Act` in my tests.

title: byQuality buckets only know A/B/C/D — the dominant 'A+' grade (88% of universe) is silently dropped from every quality split
evidence: Buckets are hardcoded: `byQuality: { A: {...}, B: {...}, C: {...}, D: {...} }` (line 195-199). Both the cache-replay and fresh-load paths gate on membership: `if (quality && bucket.byQuality[quality]) { const q = bucket.byQuality[quality]; ... }` (lines 242 and 350). But the real grade in methods-history is 'A+': probe of 2026-06-12.json gives quality distribution {"A+":4180,"A":493,"B":53,"C":11} — 88% of stocks carry 'A+'. `bucket.byQuality['A+']` is undefined, so the entire A+ cohort is excluded from every per-quality `_evalGroup` (line 460), while still being counted in the overall bucket.
why_it_matters: The Phase-3.5 quality-split — the whole point of recording `_quality.grade` per vintage (snapshot-methods-history.js line 70-89) — is dead for the grade that covers ~9 of every 10 stocks. byQuality['A'] reports on the 493 plain-'A' stocks, NOT the 4180 'A+' ones, so any reader concluding 'method X works best on A-grade names' is reasoning from a 10% non-representative slice. This is exactly the kind of silent cap that holds the screener at '20% of potential': a built feature producing confidently-wrong sub-analysis.
fix: Normalize the grade to its bucket before lookup, e.g. derive a base grade `const qBase = quality ? quality.charAt(0) : null;` and key byQuality on qBase (so 'A+','A-','A' all fold into 'A'). Add buckets if finer grades are wanted, but folding is the minimal fix. Comment must name the failure mode: '// prevents: A+/A- grades silently excluded from quality split (byQuality only had A/B/C/D)'. Add a one-line guard that logs once if a grade fails to map to any bucket, so a future grade-scheme change is loud instead of silent.

_verdict.note: CONFIRMED. The byQuality buckets are hardcoded to A/B/C/D only (lines 195-199), and both lookup sites gate on direct membership: `if (quality && bucket.byQuality[quality])` at line 242 (cache-replay) and line 350 (fresh-load). The grade is read raw at line 341 with no normalization anywhere in the file (grepped charAt/qBase/byQuality — none). Across ALL 28 vintages (2026-05-10 -> 2026-06-12) the union of grades is {A+:74528, A:10831, B:2566, C:937, D:915}; A+ is the ONLY grade outside A/B/C/D and accounts for 74528/89777 = 83% of all non-null graded contributions, every one of which is silently skipped from the per-quality split while still being correctly counted in the overall bucket (lines 238/346). Confirmed downstream impact: methodology-report.js (lines 156-168) renders a "Method-Effectiveness by Data-Quality Grade" table whose stated purpose is to detect alpha concentrated in high-quality stocks; its "α A-grade" column is computed over only the ~12% bare-A minority, not the dominant A+ cohort, making that diagnostic structurally wrong/misleading. title: degenerateZero gate kills any method whose pass- or fail-median is exactly 0.0 — a legitimate median, conflated with the manufactured-zero signature
evidence: `const degenerateZero = (failMed === 0 && group.fail.length >= MIN_SAMPLES_PER_GROUP) || (passMed === 0 && group.pass.length >= MIN_SAMPLES_PER_GROUP);` then `: degenerateZero ? 'degenerate-zero-returns'` sets the evidenceGate to non-ok, nulling alpha and CI. The 0-day-window manufactured zeros are ALREADY dropped at resolution (lines 321 & 327 set p0=p1=null when entry===exit), so this is a defensive double-guard. But `=== 0` is exact float equality on a *median of real returns*: with an even-sized fail group, the median is `(sorted[m-1]+sorted[m])/2`, which is exactly 0 whenever the two central returns are equal-and-opposite (e.g. -1.2% and +1.2%) or both 0 from flat closes. A real median can also land on exactly 0.0 for an odd group when the central pick was flat over the window.
why_it_matters: A method with genuinely neutral central tendency (median≈0) is the MOST common honest outcome for a weak signal, yet it gets stamped 'degenerate-zero-returns' and suppressed entirely — alpha=null, no CI, excluded from methodology-report's significant/neutral tables. This systematically erases true negatives/neutrals from the effectiveness ranking, biasing the surviving set toward methods that happen to have non-zero medians. Combined with the resolution-level 0-day guard already in place, this second guard now does more harm than good.
fix: Since the manufactured-zero source is already eliminated at resolution time (entry===exit drops), tighten this defensive gate so it only fires on the manufactured signature, not on legitimate zeros: require BOTH a zero median AND evidence the cohort is artificial (e.g. canonicalFrac extremely low, or a high fraction of exactly-0 raw returns in group.fail). Or drop the median-equality gate and instead gate on 'fraction of exactly-0.0 raw returns > threshold'. Comment: '// prevents: legitimate median==0 (weak/neutral signal) being misclassified as a 0-day-window manufactured zero'.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed real via source + numeric check. scripts/method-effectiveness.js:408-409 computes `degenerateZero = (failMed === 0 && n>=10) || (passMed === 0 && n>=10)` using exact float equality on `median()` (lines 69-74) of real returns from `WF.returnPct` (walk-forward-perf.js:150-153, `(p1-p0)/p0*100`). When true it sets evidenceGate='degenerate-zero-returns' (line 418), which nulls alpha (line 430) and the bootstrap CI (lines 426-429), and methodology-report.js:114 routes the method into the "insufficient-evidence" bucket instead of the neutral/weak table.

The manufactured-zero source the gate targets (0-day window, entry===exit) is ALREADY dropped upstream at resolution time — lines 321 and 327 set p0=p1=null so returnPct returns null and the contribution is dropped (lines 331-338). By construction, then, any median that still equals exactly 0.0 at this gate is a LEGITIMATE zero, not the manufactured artifact. Verified mechanisms (node check): (1) a flat close on a NON-zero-day window — p1===p0 with entryDate!==exitDate — yields returnPct exactly 0 (Object.is(...,0)===true), a real 0% return for an illiquid/halted name that the 321/327 guard does NOT drop; these ret=0 values are pushed into buckets (lines 238, 346) and persisted/replayed via cache (line 233). A cluster of such flats straddling the median index makes failMed===0. (2) Even-sized group: (sorted[m-1]+sorted[m])/2 is exactly 0 for equal-and-opposite central returns e.g. -1.2/+1.2 (confirmed exact). So a genuinely neutral/weak method (median forward-return ~0 — exactly what this report exists to surface) gets its alpha+CI silently suppressed. This is a data-integrity false-negative; not a misread.

Severity: downgraded high->medium. The harm (a real method's evidence silently nulled) is squarely the data-integrity concern, but the trigger is narrow — it needs the median to land on EXACTLY 0.0, which realistically requires a mass of exact-0.0 flat-close returns at the median or exact even-split cancellation; ordinary near-zero medians (e.g. 0.03%) do NOT trip it. Failure mode is conservative (over-suppress) rather than fabricating positive alpha.

fix_safe=false: the proposed fix changes gate semantics — it would let some median===0 cohorts through to evidenceGate='ok', emitting alpha+CI where they were previously null, and requires picking new thresholds (canonicalFrac level, "fraction of exactly-0.0 raw returns") and judgment about the data distribution. Not behavior-preserving; needs human review and ideally a fixture test.

title: MIN_SAMPLES gate uses pickReturns count `n` for alphaVsBenchmark/alphaVsFrozenVintage, but the benchmark/frozen leg may itself have <MIN_SAMPLES — alpha published on a thin benchmark
evidence: `const n = pickReturns.length;` then all three alphas gate only on the PICK count: `alphaVsBenchmark = (n >= MIN_SAMPLES && pickMed != null && benchRet != null) ? pickMed - benchRet : null;`. universeMed comes from univResult.n and frozenVintage.median from frozenVintage.n, but those counts are never checked against MIN_SAMPLES. benchRet is a single-ticker (SPY) return so 'n samples' is meaningless for it, but frozenVintageMedianReturn can be computed from as few as 1-2 tickers in an early vintage and still be subtracted to form a headline alpha.
why_it_matters: A frozen-vintage benchmark median built from 2 tickers, or a universe median from a handful, is statistically meaningless, yet alphaVsFrozenVintage / alphaVsUniverse are published whenever the PICK side clears 10. The per-vintage value then flows into the summary medians (the F-BT-004 vintage-count gate only protects the cross-vintage aggregate, not the per-vintage value that pick-diff/dashboard may read). This is the same false-confidence failure the MIN_SAMPLES gate exists to prevent, applied to the wrong leg.
fix: Gate each alpha on BOTH legs: e.g. `alphaVsFrozenVintage = (n >= MIN_SAMPLES && frozenVintage.n >= MIN_SAMPLES && ...)`. For universe similarly check univResult.n. Benchmark is a single instrument so document that its 'n' is the pick n only. Comment naming the failure mode on each guarded line.

_verdict.note: Confirmed real against source in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/scripts/walk-forward-perf.js. MIN_SAMPLES=10 (line 33). At line 511 `n = pickReturns.length` is the PICK count. Lines 516-517: `alphaVsFrozenVintage` gates only on `n >= MIN_SAMPLES && pickMed != null && frozenVintage.median != null` — it never checks `frozenVintage.n`. computeFrozenVintageMedianReturn (lines 304-331) returns `{median, n: returns.length}` over `tickersAtVintage`, which in an early/sparse vintage can be 1-9 tickers. median() (lines 84-89) returns a finite number for any array with >=1 element and null only for empty, so `frozenVintage.median != null` passes on a 1-ticker baseline. Net: alphaVsFrozenVintage (and its legacy alias at line 558) is published even though the comparison baseline has far fewer than MIN_SAMPLES — an asymmetry vs the pick leg which the author explicitly gated. The same applies to alphaVsUniverse (lines 514/523/537/557): it gates on the pick `n`, never `univResult.n` (univResult.n comes from evaluatedTickers, usually large, so lower real exposure, but still ungated). The auditor correctly concedes the benchmark leg (line 519) is a single SPY/QQQ/IWM instrument where a sample-count gate is meaningless. Mitigating context the finding omits: frozenVintageN (line 547) and universeN (line 541) ARE exposed in output, so a careful downstream reader can detect and discard the thin-baseline case — the bad alpha is recoverable, not silently unrecoverable. Conclusion: real statistical-validity bug, severity medium holds (leaning low-medium given the exposed N fields and that it does not affect early-exit/too-early paths).

title: Non-atomic fs.writeFileSync into fundamentals-cache bypasses the repo's writeFileAtomic — SIGKILL/CI-timeout mid-write truncates a court-screen input file
evidence: Line 175 `const j = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(cacheFile, 'utf8'));` then line 180 `fs.writeFileSync(cacheFile, JSON.stringify(j));`. This is a read-modify-write on a committed-state file with a plain writeFileSync. The other three scripts in this batch all import and use `const { writeFileAtomic } = require('../lib/atomic-write.js')` precisely because (per lib/atomic-write.js header) plain writeFileSync left ≥9 state files truncatable: 'A SIGKILL / CI timeout mid-write truncated the file; downstream ... then aborted on parse-error or worse, silently loaded a {} shape and regenerated everything from scratch'. enrich-q-revenue.js does NOT import atomic-write at all.
why_it_matters: fundamentals-cache/{TICKER}.json is consumed by court-screen.js (durability v3, confirmed: grep revQYoYsec → court-screen.js). A crash between the open-for-write truncation and full flush leaves the WHOLE fundamentals payload (not just revQYoYsec) as a half-written/zero-byte file. The next court-screen run then JSON.parse-throws or silently loses every fundamental for that ticker. Worse than the form4 scripts because here the truncation destroys pre-existing data the script only meant to augment.
fix: Import writeFileAtomic from ../lib/atomic-write.js (same one-line require the sibling scripts use) and replace `fs.writeFileSync(cacheFile, JSON.stringify(j))` with `writeFileAtomic(cacheFile, JSON.stringify(j))`. No FTS_CACHE_VERSION touched; this is a scripts/ file, not methods/index.js.

_verdict.note: Confirmed at scripts/enrich-q-revenue.js:175-180: a read-modify-write (read line 175, mutate j.payload.ftsQuarterly lines 177-179, write line 180) uses plain fs.writeFileSync(cacheFile, JSON.stringify(j)), and the script never imports lib/atomic-write.js. The sibling-convention claim holds: ~25 scripts under scripts/ import { writeFileAtomic } from ../lib/atomic-write.js, and the lib header (lines 2-23) documents exactly the SIGKILL/CI-timeout mid-write truncation hazard. The downstream-consumer claim also holds: court-screen.js:134 reads payload.ftsQuarterly.revQYoYsec to compute the durability metric, so a truncated/empty file would silently degrade that input. So the defect is genuine and matches a real, repo-recognized pattern. BUT the finding's framing overstates the blast radius: it calls the target a 'committed-state file', whereas fundamentals-cache/ is gitignored (.gitignore:16-18 — '28-day local cache; not needed in git history, rebuilt on each runner'). The file is a rebuildable local cache, not committed state; the script is deterministic and idempotent (re-run rebuilds from SEC companyfacts.zip), and the cache regenerates on each runner. A mid-write truncation is recoverable by re-running, unlike the truly-committed state files atomic-write was built for. That justifies downgrading high -> medium.

title: adjclose backfill silently REWRITES historical closes (fetched wins on collision) — injects retroactive split/dividend restatement into the series backtests read, a look-ahead bias
evidence: Line 138 `const closeVal = q.adjclose ?? q.close;` combined with the merge at line 152 `for (const e of fetched) merged.set(e.date, e.close); // fetched overwrites`. The fetched value (adjusted close as of TODAY) overwrites any existing close already stored for that date. prices/history.json is read by backtest-from-history.js, backtest-pass-vs-fail.js, fitness/measure.js and 5 methods (above-200d-ma, drawdown-52w, high-proximity-52w, price-momentum-12-1, volatility-annualized).
why_it_matters: adjclose is recomputed by Yahoo every time a split or dividend occurs, so re-running backfill silently rewrites the price a stock 'had' on a past date to its today-adjusted value. A backtest that later reads history.json sees prices that embed information (future splits/dividends) not knowable on that date — textbook look-ahead bias — and historical close values silently change between runs, making backtest results non-reproducible. pull-historical-prices.js is cited as the 'same pattern' but the OVERWRITE-on-collision policy is what makes a backfill (vs an append) corrupt the past.
fix: Decide and document one consistent price basis. Either (a) store raw `close` only (drop adjclose) so historical values are immutable, or (b) keep adjclose but make EXISTING entries win on collision (swap the two merge loops so `for (const e of fetched)` runs first, then `for (const e of existing)`), preserving the value originally recorded for each past date. Add a comment naming the failure mode: 'prevents retroactive split/dividend restatement (look-ahead bias) in prices/history.json consumed by backtests'.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed the mechanism in source. backfill-prices.js line 137 stores adjclose-as-close, and the merge at lines 150-152 seeds the Map with `existing` then lets `fetched` overwrite on date collision (`for (const e of fetched) merged.set(e.date, e.close)`). So a re-run rewrites already-stored closes for past dates with today's freshly-fetched adjclose.

This DIVERGES from the production puller. pull-historical-prices.js (the script actually wired into .github/workflows/daily-pull.yml) is deliberately append-only: lines 119-128 only push the latest quote if its date isn't already the last entry, and NEVER rewrite an existing past entry. Two writers to the same prices/history.json with opposite collision policies is a genuine data-integrity inconsistency.

prices/history.json IS consumed by return/MA/momentum calculations: backtest-from-history.js:30 computes (endQ.close-startQ.close)/startQ.close; methods/price-momentum-12-1.js reads priceLastMonth/priceOneYearAgo; above-200d-ma.js / volatility-annualized / drawdown-52w / high-proximity-52w all read the series. So mutated past closes do feed real outputs.

Caveats that temper the auditor's framing:
1. The "look-ahead bias" label is defensible but overstated. Yahoo adjclose IS recomputed retroactively on splits/dividends, so overwriting does mutate history — but a fully as-of-today adjusted series is the STANDARD correct basis for split-adjusted returns. The real defect is that backfill produces a MIXED series (daily-appended bars frozen at their original pull-date adjustment vs. backfilled bars at today's adjustment), corrupting returns across any split boundary — in either direction.
2. backfill-prices.js is a MANUALLY-invoked CLI tool. grep shows zero callers outside its own header comment; it is NOT in daily-pull.yml. So it does not corrupt the production series on every scheduled run — only when an operator manually runs it, and only for tickers with a split/dividend in the window. This is why I revise high -> medium.

title: Daily index regex /^4\s+/ silently drops Form 4/A amendments — daily cache diverges from quarterly backfill, which keeps them
evidence: Line 212 `const re = /^4\s+.+?\s+(\d+)\s+(\d{8})\s+(edgar\/data\/\d+\/([0-9-]+)\.txt)\s*$/;` plus the line guard `if (line.charAt(0) !== '4') continue;`. Verified by executing the regex against real SEC daily form.idx row shapes: a plain '4' row matches, but '4/A' (amendment), '40-APP/A', '424B5' all FAIL the `\s` immediately after the 4. backfill-form345.js by contrast filters NONDERIV_TRANS purely on ISSUERTRADINGSYMBOL (line 237) and never inspects form type, so it ingests 4/A amendments.
why_it_matters: Form 4/A is the correction/late-filing amendment. A late or corrected insider purchase that arrives as a 4/A is invisible to the daily puller (the cache insider-conviction-score.js reads via methods/index.js), but present in the quarterly history cache — so the two caches that feed the same scorer disagree, and conviction scores shift when the quarterly backfill later fills in an amendment the daily run missed. Genuinely amended buys (e.g. corrected share counts) never reach the live screener.
fix: Broaden the FormType match to accept the amendment suffix: anchor on `/^4(\/A)?\s+/` in both the `line.charAt(0)` fast-path (keep it, it's a cheap prefilter) and the full regex. Carry a comment: 'prevents silent loss of Form 4/A amendments that the quarterly backfill keeps (daily-vs-history cache divergence)'.

_verdict.note:
CONFIRMED real data-integrity divergence. At pull-insider-form4-daily.js:212 the regex /^4\s+.../ requires whitespace immediately after the '4', so a plain Form 4 row matches but a Form 4/A amendment row does NOT (the '/' fails the \s). Verified empirically against real SEC daily form.idx column shapes: '4' MATCHES; '4/A', '40-APP/A', '424B5', '40-F' all NOMATCH. The line.charAt(0)!=='4' guard at line 214 is only a cheap prefilter and lets '4/A' through to the regex, which then rejects it. By contrast backfill-form345.js:237-238 filters NONDERIV_TRANS purely on ISSUERTRADINGSYMBOL and never inspects form type, so the quarterly backfill ingests 4/A amendment transactions. Both scripts write the same byTicker cache (FORM4_CACHE_PATH); txnKey dedupes on accessionNumber+date+code+shares, and amendments carry a distinct accession, so a 4/A is a legitimately distinct entry that the daily path silently never fetches/parses/merges. Net effect: the daily-incremental cache diverges from a quarterly backfill of the same period by dropping Form 4/A amendments.

fix_safe=false: the proposed_fix as WRITTEN is unsafe to auto-apply. It says to anchor on /^4(\/A)?\s+/ but does NOT mention renumbering the capture references at lines 218-221, which read m[1]=cik, m[2]=dateFiled, m[3]=fileName, m[4]=accession. Adding a CAPTURING group (\/A)? shifts every index by one: I verified that with the literal fix cik becomes undefined, dateFiled reads the CIK, fileName reads the date, accession reads the file path — breaking the parser for ALL rows, not just amendments. The correct surgical fix is a NON-CAPTURING group: /^4(?:\/A)?\s+.../ which preserves m[1]..m[4] (verified: cik=1234567, date=20260115, file/acc correct). It still correctly rejects 40-APP/A, 424B5, 40-F. The charAt(0) prefilter can stay as-is (it already passes '4/A'). Recommend a human apply the non-capturing variant rather than the verbatim capturing-group fix.

title: txnKey omits price/owner → two real same-day same-share buys at different prices (multi-lot) collapse to one; identical key in backfill-form345 means the bug is repo-wide
evidence: Line 229 `return [t.accessionNumber, t.transactionDate, t.transactionCode, t.transactionShares].join('|');` (identical in backfill-form345.js line 169). Verified by execution: two txns {acc:X, date, code:P, shares:100} priced 10 vs 12 both yield key `X|...|P|100` (collision=true). Also a single Form 4 can carry multiple reporting owners or multiple non-deriv lines; this key has no owner/price/line discriminator.
why_it_matters: Insiders routinely split one filing into several transaction lines at different prices on the same day. The dedupe in mergeTransactions (line 251-259) and backfill-form345 (line 307-311) drops every line after the first with the same share count, understating aggBuyValue (Σ shares*price) in insider-conviction-score.js line 257. Conviction/value gates (MIN_BUY_VALUE) and the topBuy selection are computed on incomplete data.
fix: Add the price (and for the history cache, rptOwnerCik) to the key: `[t.accessionNumber, t.transactionDate, t.transactionCode, t.transactionShares, t.transactionPricePerShare].join('|')`. _verdict.note: CONFIRMED. txnKey at pull-insider-form4-daily.js:229 and backfill-form345.js:169 are byte-identical and omit price/owner/line discriminators. Collision reproduced by execution: two txns {acc:X, date:2026-05-01, code:P, shares:100} at price 10 vs 12 both yield key "X|2026-05-01|P|100" (collision=true). Multiple non-derivative lines per filing are real — parseForm4Xml (pull-insider-form4.js:250) loops over _extractAll(xml,'nonDerivativeTransaction'), so one accession legitimately produces many txns; backfill iterates all NONDERIV_TRANS rows. Downstream impact is concrete and not theoretical: mergeTransactions (lines 251-260) does `if (seen.has(k)) continue;` and silently drops the second colliding lot — it is never pushed. The deduped cache feeds methods/insider-conviction-score.js, which at lines 255-258 computes aggBuyValue += shares*price against a HARD GATE of Σ(shares*price) >= $25,000 (documented line 36) and also picks the top buyer by $ value. So collapsing two distinct same-day same-share buys at different prices into one understates aggregate buy value and can flip both the $25k gate and the conviction score. One correction to the auditor: in the DAILY path the proposed rptOwnerCik addition is a no-op — daily txn objects never carry rptOwnerCik (parseForm4Xml attaches only the first reportingOwner's NAME, not CIK); only backfill txns have rptOwnerCik. The price field is the load-bearing discriminator and applies symmetrically to both files.

title: Q4 discrete-quarter revenue is systematically missing (duration heuristic excludes the ~365-day 10-K YTD figure) → YoY series has an annual hole, thinning the durability metric this script exists to thicken

Then rewrite the tag28 fixtures so surprisePercent matches epsDifference/epsEstimate (e.g. 0.04 not 4) — the fixture is currently the thing certifying the bug as correct. title: Closed-end-trust S3: revenue-volatility sub-clause is dead code (fully subsumed by hasNonPositive)
evidence: `s3 = hasNonPositive || (revVolRatio != null && revVolRatio > REV_VOL_RATIO_MAX && hasNonPositive);` (line 155). The right operand is ANDed with `hasNonPositive`, so whenever it could contribute, the left operand `hasNonPositive` has already made s3 true. The entire `revVolRatio > REV_VOL_RATIO_MAX` test (and REV_VOL_RATIO_MAX=3.0, line 103) can never change the result. The docstring (lines 38-40) describes S3 as 'negative year, OR max(|rev|)/min(|rev|) across 4y > 3x AND any year <= 0' — implemented redundantly.
why_it_matters: The documented intent was almost certainly a lumpy-revenue detector that fires on extreme peak/trough swings; as written, S3 collapses to 'any rev year <= 0'. Trusts with wildly volatile but never-quite-negative reported 'revenue' (gain years + near-zero years, ratio >3x) do not get the S3 signal, so they may stay below the 2-of-N fail count and leak into the R40 tab — the exact noise this DATAGUARD exists to remove.
fix: Make volatility fire independently of the negative-year test, e.g. `s3 = hasNonPositive || (revVolRatio != null && revVolRatio > REV_VOL_RATIO_MAX && hasZeroOrCollapse)` where hasZeroOrCollapse detects a near-zero/collapsing year — or, if the negative-year coupling is truly intended, delete revVolRatio/REV_VOL_RATIO_MAX as dead code. Comment the chosen branch with the failure mode (lumpy gain/loss revenue without a strictly negative print).

_verdict.note: Confirmed real dead code via boolean algebra. Line 155: `s3 = hasNonPositive || (revVolRatio != null && revVolRatio > REV_VOL_RATIO_MAX && hasNonPositive)` has the form `A || (B && C && A)` with A=hasNonPositive. By the absorption law this is identically equal to A, so the `revVolRatio > REV_VOL_RATIO_MAX` comparison and the `REV_VOL_RATIO_MAX = 3.0` constant (line 103) can NEVER change s3's value. The right operand can only become true when hasNonPositive is already true, at which point the left operand has already short-circuited s3 to true. Verified the comparison/constant appear nowhere else (only line 155); the only other use of `revVolRatio` is as an emitted diagnostic in components (line 196), so the variable itself is not fully dead — the auditor's evidence (right operand + constant) is precise. The tests (tag28-tests.js:749-801) never exercise the volatility path: SMT.L already trips hasNonPositive on its negative years, and the positive-rev anchors never reach the dead clause. Notably the docstring's documented intent (lines 37-40: '>3x AND any year <=0') is ALSO logically equal to hasNonPositive, so this is a latent intent bug — the volatility ratio was meant to add discrimination (lumpy gain/loss revenue without a strictly-negative print) but contributes nothing as both coded and documented. No runtime misbehavior today; it's a guard-logic gap / dead code. Severity medium is reasonable (slightly generous; low-medium also defensible).

title: R&D-cut guard is blind to the most extreme real-EM case: R&D slashed to zero
evidence: `if (!Number.isFinite(rd_t) || rd_t <= 0) missing.push('annualRnD[0]');` (line 90) and the same `rd_p <= 0` guard on line 91, with `if (missing.length>0) return computable:false` (lines 97-104). A company that cuts R&D from a positive prior year to exactly 0 (rd_t=0) trips `rd_t <= 0` → flagged missing → computable:false → never flags. rdYoY would be -100% (the strongest possible signal) but is never computed.
why_it_matters: Zeroing the R&D line while op-margin expands >2pp is the textbook Roychowdhury (2006) real-earnings-management pattern the method exists to catch (header lines 5-9). The guard self-disables on precisely its most severe trigger. It also can't distinguish 'R&D genuinely absent from data' from 'R&D deliberately cut to zero'.
fix: Require only rd_p > 0 (a valid prior baseline) and accept rd_t >= 0 (allow zero), computing rdYoY = (rd_t - rd_p)/rd_p which is well-defined for rd_t=0. Keep the rd_p>0 guard for the denominator. Comment: 'allow rd_t==0 so a full R&D elimination (the strongest real-EM signal) is detected rather than silently dropped as missing data'.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed against source. methods/rd-cut-guard.js line 90: `if (!Number.isFinite(rd_t) || rd_t <= 0) missing.push('annualRnD[0]');` plus the `if (missing.length>0) return computable:false` short-circuit (lines 97-104) means a company that cuts R&D from a positive prior (rd_p>0) to exactly 0 (rd_t===0) trips `rd_t <= 0`, is dropped as "missing data", and is never evaluated. The would-be signal rdYoY = (0 - rd_p)/rd_p = -1.0 (-100%, the strongest possible R&D cut) is never computed — a true false-negative in a detector whose entire purpose (Roychowdhury 2006 real-EM) is to catch exactly this pattern.

Refutation attempts all fail: (1) rd_t===0 is reachable — pull-yahoo.js maps absent R&D to null (not 0), so a reported 0 is a distinct, real state (a firm that genuinely zeroed its R&D line), rare but legitimate. (2) No division-by-zero: the proposed fix keeps the rd_p>0 denominator guard; rdYoY and rdRevRatio_t=rd_t/rev_t are both well-defined at rd_t=0. (3) No scoring/fixture-hash impact: rd-cut-guard is DIAGNOSTIC, not in SCORE_WEIGHTS (confirmed methods/index.js line 141-143 comment and tag28-tests.js line 1555). No existing test asserts rd_t===0 must be computable:false (the NOT-COMPUTABLE test at line 1607 uses a positive rd_t with only 1 year), so the fix won't break current tests.

fix_safe=false: the fix is sound and low-risk, but it is NOT behavior-preserving — it intentionally flips output (computable false→true, and a possible new flag) for affected stocks and changes a guard predicate. It should also still reject rd_t<0 (nonsensical negative R&D) rather than the literal `rd_t >= 0` wording, and a regression test for the rd_t===0 path should accompany it. That warrants human review before auto-applying.

title: Asset-growth-divergence compares revenue and asset CAGRs over potentially different fiscal-year spans (positional [0]/[2] across two independently-built arrays)
evidence: `_cagr2y` uses `latest=toNum(arr[0]); oldest=toNum(arr[2])` (lines 29-30) and is called separately on revArr (raw `stock.annual.annualRev`) and assetArrClean (derived from annualBalance). pull-yahoo builds annualRev and annualBalance independently and BOTH may contain interior null placeholders to preserve year alignment within their own series (annualBalance: pull-yahoo.js:1180 pushes null; annualRev similar). There is no check that revArr[2] and assetArrClean[2] refer to the same fiscal year — only that each array has length>=3 and the asset triple is non-null (lines 39-52,57).
why_it_matters: If revenue has a gap year that balance does not (or vice-versa), index [2] points to different fiscal years in the two series, so `spread = assetCAGR - revCAGR` (line 84) subtracts CAGRs measured over mismatched windows. The M&A-divergence DATAGUARD/softGuard (8-point QC penalty, score-aggregator.js:204) then fires or clears on a miscomputed spread — a silent false signal with no diagnostic that the periods didn't line up.
fix: Align on a shared fiscal-year index (e.g. carry period labels from the snapshot and intersect, or require both annualRev[i] and annualBalance[i] non-null for the same i before using that i for the CAGR endpoints). At minimum, only use indices where both series are non-null and identical years. Comment: 'prevents CAGR spread computed across mismatched fiscal windows when one series has a gap year the other lacks'.

_verdict.note:
CONFIRMED real. In methods/asset-growth-divergence.js, _cagr2y (lines 26-33) reads bare positional arr[0]=latest, arr[2]=2y-ago and is called independently on revArr (line 65, from stock.annual.annualRev) and assetArrClean (line 66, derived from stock.annual.annualBalance). Nothing checks that revArr[2] and assetArrClean[2] are the same fiscal year — guards only verify length>=3 (lines 39,46) and that the first 3 totalAssets are non-null/>0 (line 57). The two source arrays genuinely can diverge by fiscal year:
- pull-yahoo.js:1038 vs 1048: annualFin (income statement) and annualBs (balance sheet) are SEPARATE Yahoo fundamentalsTimeSeries API modules with independent try/catch, so each can report a different fiscal-year set.
- pull-yahoo.js:1104: mapFTSToAnnual uses `continue` to DROP fully-empty income rows (array compaction), while mapFTSToBalance:1180 pushes a null PLACEHOLDER (different skip semantics) — so even from one FTS payload the two arrays' indices can desync when one statement has a year the other lacks.
- pull-yahoo.js:1861 vs 1898: canonical.annual.annualRev and canonical.annual.annualBalance are each independently overridden QS->FTS by their own non-null counts, so the final two arrays can come from different providers with different year coverage.
- Entries carry NO period/endDate label ({value:n} and {totalAssets,...} only) — positional index is the ONLY alignment, and the in-code comment at pull-yahoo.js:1147-1148 merely ASSERTS annualBalance[i] aligns with annualRev[i] without enforcing it across the two independent modules.
Realistic trigger: Yahoo updating income vs balance statements at different times during earnings season -> annualRev[0]=FY2025 while annualBalance[0]=FY2024, offsetting BOTH CAGR endpoints. Effect is bounded: the method is registered (methods/index.js, used by strategy-modes/score-aggregator) and feeds RED_FLAG_RULES weight 8 (score-aggregator.js:204), so a mismatched-window spread can raise a spurious M&A red-flag penalty or miss a real one — a wrong value, not a crash or silent composite corruption.

title: Forecast-contamination uses null-compressed annualRev[0], so 'latest annual' may be a stale prior year when Yahoo returns a leading null
evidence: `var annualRev = _arrVals(stock,'annual.annualRev');` (line 43) where `_arrVals` (lines 25-29) does `.filter(function(v){return Number.isFinite(v);})` — it strips nulls AND compresses the array. Then `var annualLatest = annualRev[0];` (line 54). If Yahoo returns annualRev as [null, 5.0e9, ...] (latest fiscal year not yet reported), the compression makes annualRev[0] the PRIOR year. The quarterly side deliberately uses _rawArrVals to preserve calendar alignment (lines 33-37,45) — the annual side does not get the same treatment.
why_it_matters: The guard's ratio annualLatest/q4Sum (line 73) is meant to compare the most recent annual figure against the last four quarters. A leading-null on annualRev silently shifts annualLatest to an older, smaller year, deflating the ratio and masking genuine forecast-contamination (the look-ahead bias this DATAGUARD exists to catch, header lines 4-12). Inconsistent with the same file's own F-ME-006 alignment fix applied only to the quarterly array.
fix: Use a raw (non-compressed) extractor for annualRev and take the first finite leading entry while recording its index, OR require annualRev[0] (raw) to be finite (return computable:false on a leading null). Comment: 'prevents using a stale prior-year annual revenue as annualLatest when Yahoo has not yet populated the most recent fiscal year (leading-null compression)'.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed real. In methods/forecast-contamination-guard.js, line 43 uses `_arrVals(stock,'annual.annualRev')` whose helper (lines 25-29) does `.filter(Number.isFinite)`, which strips AND compresses leading nulls; line 54 then takes `annualRev[0]` as `annualLatest`. The quarterly side deliberately uses the non-compressing `_rawArrVals` (lines 33-37, 45) and adds an explicit leading/positional-null guard (lines 55-63) to keep calendar coherence — the annual side gets neither. So the asymmetry the auditor describes is exactly present in source.

The data model genuinely permits a leading null in `annual.annualRev`: the FTS producer `mapFTSToAnnual` in pull-yahoo.js (lines 1083-1136) preserves nulls and only skips/`continue`s rows where rev AND oi AND gp AND ni are all null (line 1104) — a row with rev=null but oi/gp/ni present pushes `null` into `annualRev` at index 0 (latest-first). There is NO leading-null trim anywhere (grep confirmed). The wholesale override at line 1861 (`if (_ftsRevNonNull > _qsRevNonNull) canonical.annual.annualRev = ftsAnnual.annualRev`) can install such an FTS array verbatim into the canonical snapshot. (Note: the legacy quoteSummary `_arr` at lines 493-500 does `.filter(Boolean)`, so the QS-only path never carries the leading null — only the FTS-override path does.)

Impact: when the latest fiscal year's annual revenue is not yet populated, the compression makes `annualLatest` the PRIOR year's annual revenue, which is then divided by the current calendar-coherent TTM q4Sum. The ratio compares mismatched periods → the guard's contamination verdict is unreliable for that ticker (false-negative for growers, possible false-positive otherwise). This is a global MUST-gate (protects Hypergrowth + Quality-Compounder per the header), so a wrong verdict matters, but the triggering condition (leading-null annualRev with non-null oi/gp/ni) is a narrow Yahoo schema gap, not a mainstream path. Medium severity is fair (not high — no silent mainstream corruption, niche data condition; not low — it's a real semantic bug in an all-modes guard). No existing test exercises the leading-null case (tag28-tests builds annualRev with finite leading entries).

title: Health gate covers only 4 snapshot scripts; the entire reporting/diagnostic tier fails silently
evidence: EXPECTED_SCRIPTS = [ snapshot-picks, snapshot-methods-history, generate-modes-report, snapshot-score-history ]. The breach filter is `const breached = reports.filter(r => r.failure_rate > THRESHOLD);`. None of picks-regression-check, pick-diff, methodology-report, compute-method-drift, data-quality-report, walk-forward-perf or method-effectiveness emit a pipeline-health/*.json report, and every one of those steps runs `continue-on-error: true` in .github/workflows/daily-pull.yml (lines 442, 490, 496, 502, 508, 525, 530).

The dashboard/methodology/pick-diff artifacts can silently freeze at yesterday's content for weeks. This is the structural cap on the diagnostic tier's trustworthiness.

Have each script write a tiny pipeline-health/<script>.json {script, n_total, n_ok, n_failed, failure_rate} in its finally/exit path (even the catch->exit 0 path) so the missing-report=100%-failure rule (lines 49-63) can catch a hard crash.

_verdict.note:
Core mechanism CONFIRMED. EXPECTED_SCRIPTS (pipeline-health-check.js:19-27) has exactly 4 entries (snapshot-picks, snapshot-methods-history, generate-modes-report, snapshot-score-history); all 4 verified to write pipeline-health/*.json. The missing-report->100%-failure rule (lines 49-63) and breach filter (line 65) only cover those 4. A repo-wide grep for "pipeline-health" finds writes only in those 4 emitters (+ snapshot-r40rx, which is NOT in EXPECTED). The named diagnostic scripts do NOT emit any health report and all run continue-on-error:true in daily-pull.yml (picks-regression-check:442, walk-forward-perf:490, method-effectiveness:496, methodology-report:502, pick-diff:508, compute-method-drift:530 — cited lines verified). BUT the auditor overstates it on three counts: (1) data-quality-report.js exists but is NOT wired into daily-pull.yml at all (no invocation) — it cannot "fail silently each run" because it never runs; listing it is a factual error. (2) "fails silently" is only fully true for methodology-report, pick-diff, compute-method-drift (catch -> process.exit(0), confirmed at lines 187/212/135). walk-forward-perf (line 857) and method-effectiveness (line 536) instead do catch -> console.error('::error::...') + process.exit(1), so a crash DOES emit a GitHub Actions error annotation — not silent, just non-gating. (3) These are diagnostic/reporting artifacts (markdown reports, pick-diff JSON, drift sparklines), not the core picks data path, which IS gated. title: Discipline audit only catches top-level `const NAME = <number>` changes — misses object-property and exported thresholds, the dominant pattern
evidence: findNumericChanges regexes `^-(\s*const\s+\w+\s*=\s*)(<number>)` paired with the next `+` line. But many method thresholds are object properties or live in the exports block, e.g. price-momentum-12-1.js exports `threshold: THRESHOLD` and other methods use patterns like `{ threshold: 0.10 }` or `module.exports = { ..., threshold: 0.12 }`. A change to `threshold: 0.10` -> `threshold: 0.15` does not match `const NAME = ...` and is silently exempt from the discipline check.
why_it_matters: This script enforces docs/threshold-discipline.md — the guardrail against single-ticker threshold tuning, which is precisely the failure mode that caps a screener's robustness. If the most common threshold-definition shape isn't matched, the audit reports 'clean' while undisciplined tunes slip through. False sense of governance.
fix: Broaden the matcher to also catch `(\w+)\s*:\s*<number>` property assignments and `const NAME = <number>` regardless of indentation, and/or compare the parsed numeric tokens on changed lines within methods/*.js hunks generally. Add a unit case for the `threshold:` property form.

_verdict.note: Core bug CONFIRMED with source + empirical evidence. findNumericChanges (threshold-audit.js:55-68) only matches diff line-pairs of the form `const NAME = <number>`. I ran the exported function on a synthetic unified=0 diff: it catches `const THRESHOLD = 0.10 -> 0.15` but returns ZERO changes for `threshold: 0.35 -> 0.40`. Real scored methods define their gate threshold as an inline numeric literal in the module.exports object property, not a const: margin-quality.js:155 (`threshold: 0.35`) and earnings-stability.js:152 (`threshold: 0.50`). Both are SCORED with weight 0.20 in methods/score-aggregator.js (lines 43-44), so a silent tune to these would change screener output AND evade the discipline/CI gate. margin-quality.js also has gate values as inline comparison literals (lines 93/102: `at >= 3.0`, `opMargMedian >= 0.035`, `gmMedian < 0.20`) — also missed. No unit test exists for the audit script. \n\nTWO auditor errors lower confidence in the framing: (1) The cited example is WRONG — price-momentum-12-1.js exports `threshold: THRESHOLD` (a const REFERENCE, line 282), and its real value is `const THRESHOLD = 0.10` (line 65) which the regex DOES catch; that file is fully handled. (2) The 'dominant pattern' claim is FALSE — `const NAME = <number>` occurs ~201x across 80 method files vs only 5 inline `threshold:` literals across 4 files (margin-quality, earnings-stability, deceleration-guard [where threshold:10 is metadata; real logic uses other literals], premium-compounder-proof). So the gap is a real minority pattern, not the dominant one. (Side note: the code comment says 'top-level const' but the regex actually allows any indentation via `\s*` — minor doc inaccuracy.)

title: Two scripts write the SAME prices/history.json with DIFFERENT price adjustment bases (raw close vs adjclose) — split-contaminated momentum
evidence: pull-historical-prices.js:100 `const quotes = (result.quotes || []).filter(q => (q.adjclose ?? q.close) != null);` and :103 `const latestClose = latestQuote.adjclose ?? latestQuote.close;` store SPLIT/DIVIDEND-ADJUSTED prices. pull-prices-bulk.js:61-64 stores RAW close: `.filter(q => q.close != null).map(q => ({ date: ..., close: q.close }))`. Both target `prices/history.json` (bulk HISTORY_PATH:10 `'./prices/history.json'`; historical histPath:67 `path.join(args.out,'history.json')` with default out='./prices'). scripts/backfill-prices.js:137 uses `q.adjclose ?? q.close` (adjusted). So the same per-ticker series can contain a mix of adjusted and raw closes depending on which puller last touched that ticker.
why_it_matters: price-momentum-12-1.js:206-209 computes `priceLastMonth / priceOneYearAgo - 1` across that single series, and walk-forward-perf.js:106/150 computes returns over it. A stock that split 2:1 in the window will have a ~100% phantom return at the raw/adjusted boundary, or a real split silently erased — directly corrupting the momentum factor and every backtest return that reads this file. This is exactly the kind of silent data corruption that caps the screener's reliability.

Standardize ALL writers on `q.adjclose ?? q.close` (pull-prices-bulk.js:61-64 must change `close: q.close` -> `close: q.adjclose ?? q.close`). Add a one-line provenance/version key per ticker series or a top-level `{ priceBasis: 'adjclose' }` marker so a future writer mismatch fails loud. Each touched method/consumer change must carry a comment naming the failure mode (split-contaminated mixed-basis series).

_verdict.note:
CONFIRMED at source. pull-prices-bulk.js:61-64 stores RAW close (`close: q.close`); pull-historical-prices.js:100/103/127 and its SPY backfill (:177) store ADJUSTED (`q.adjclose ?? q.close`); scripts/backfill-prices.js:137 also uses adjclose and comments it does so "to match pull-historical-prices.js". Consumers (e.g. methods/price-momentum-12-1.js reads ../prices/history.json as one untagged series) cannot tell raw from adjusted, so a ticker touched by both writers across a split/dividend gets a phantom price step — a real data-integrity hazard.

Severity tempered to MEDIUM (not critical): pull-prices-bulk.js is NOT in any workflow — the only automated daily step is pull-historical-prices.js (.github/workflows/daily-pull.yml:476); there is no package.json script and no CI reference for the bulk script. The repo's own follow-up audit already logged this as NEW-8 LOW "Manual CLI only". MEDIUM is the fair middle.

fix_safe=false: the one-liner (close: q.close -> q.adjclose ?? q.close) on its own is behavior-aligning and low-risk, but the proposed fix also bundles a top-level `{priceBasis:'adjclose'}` / per-ticker provenance schema marker that no consumer reads and could break a strict reader — that schema change needs human review, so the fix as proposed is not safe to auto-apply wholesale.

title: ABSOLUTE_FLOOR (50%) drift alert fires on cold start and for legitimately-sparse fields, re-creating the alert-fatigue this file's comments say it fixed
evidence: detectDrift() at :161-175 raises a HIGH 'below-50pct-floor' alert for ANY tracked field whose current coverage < 0.50, 'independent of baseline ... even on cold start when baseline is unavailable' (:154-155, :160). But many TRACKED_FIELDS are structurally sparse across the ~25k universe: `metrics.forwardPE.value`, `metrics.targetMeanPrice.value`, `metrics.insidersOwnership.value`, `annual.annualSBC` etc. are simply absent for most non-US / small-cap / non-covered names. The file's OWN header (:19-24) documents that a mis-named field firing the below-50% floor 'triggered the below-50%-floor HIGH alert every workflow run, contributed to alert fatigue.'
why_it_matters: A HIGH alert that fires every run for fields that are correctly below 50% trains Karl to ignore the drift detector — so when Yahoo actually drops a field (the whole point of this module, per the Nov-2024 incident in :8-9) it is lost in the noise. This structurally caps the screener: silent Yahoo schema regressions are the dominant cause of bad scores, and the detector meant to catch them is desensitized.
fix: Make the floor relative to each field's own established baseline, not an absolute 50%: only fire the floor alert when a field that HISTORICALLY sat above the floor drops below it (requires baseline[field] >= ABSOLUTE_FLOOR AND cur < ABSOLUTE_FLOOR). For cold start (no baseline), suppress the floor alert or emit it at INFO, not HIGH. Optionally give each field its own expected-coverage floor. This is a non-method file so no method-comment constraint applies.

_verdict.note: Confirmed real, but severity is medium not high, and the auditor overstated the "HIGH alert" part. CONFIRMED: detectDrift (field-coverage.js:161-175) fires a `below-50pct-floor` drift for ANY tracked field with current coverage <0.50, independent of baseline, explicitly including cold start (baseline {} -> baseline/drop emitted as null). The caller detect-changes.js:487-499 runs computeCoverage over allStocks = the entire snapshot universe (loaded at :430-463, ~3.5k-19k+ tickers per the perf comment), so the floor evaluates against the whole universe. Several TRACKED_FIELDS are structurally sparse there — metrics.forwardPE.value, metrics.targetMeanPrice.value, metrics.insidersOwnership.value, annual.annualSBC — exactly the analyst/covered-name fields Yahoo omits for most non-US/small-cap names. The file's own header (:19-24) documents this same floor mechanism caused "the below-50%-floor HIGH alert every workflow run, contributed to alert fatigue" for a mis-named field, so the failure mode is acknowledged. NUANCE the auditor got wrong: the `severity:'HIGH'` set at :170 is discarded by the only caller — detect-changes.js:497 hardcodes severity:'WARNING' for every FIELD_DRIFT event regardless of d.severity, and the Discord path labels all warnings "METHOD_PASS_LOST". So operators see noisy WARNING-level events, not HIGH/critical ones. No data corruption and no effect on screener results — impact is signal degradation / alert noise in the drift stream — hence medium, not high. Secondary cosmetic bug: on cold-start floor drifts d.baseline/d.drop are null, and the caller's template (d.baseline*100).toFixed(0) coerces null->0, printing a misleading "baseline 0%, drop 0pp". FIX_SAFE=false: the proposed relative-floor fix (only fire when baseline[field]>=ABSOLUTE_FLOOR && cur<ABSOLUTE_FLOOR, suppress/INFO on cold start) is a deliberate reversal of the documented F-DQ-005 design intent ("even on cold start when baseline is unavailable", :154-155). It changes detection semantics — a field genuinely broken/empty from day one would no longer be flagged on cold start — which is a policy tradeoff needing human sign-off. It also interacts with existing test `detectDrift: missing baseline field skipped` (tag22-tests.js:126) and the optional per-field-floor adds new config. Not behavior-preserving; do not auto-apply. Note: no per-stock snapshot fixtures exist in the worktree (only snapshots/_manifest.json), so the universe-sparsity numbers couldn't be measured empirically, but the claim is well-grounded in the file's own comments and the field semantics.

title: 'FCF Margin' columns silently report R40's 3y-annual-median fallback value, not TTM FCF margin
evidence: fcfMarginFromRo40 is taken from ro40.components.fcfMargin (line 138). The methods-report 'FCF Margin' leaderboard (line 510-512), the Metric Deep-Dive 'FCF Margin' column (line 275), the Top-Picks 'FCF Margin' cell (line 397/399) and 'Rev Growth'/'FCF' all read fcfMarginFromRo40 / growthYoYFromRo40 with no indication that the source switched.
