title: Annual fallback path yields REAL_HYPERGROWTH_ACCELERATING from a 1-factor model — spike-concentration (Faktor 3) is silently skipped
evidence: Header promises '3-Faktor-Klassifikation'. Faktor 3 (spikeShare) is computed only `if (revQ.length >= 4)` (line 128). The annual breadth branch (line 87, breadthSource='y') runs when revQ<8 but annualRev>=4, so spikeShare stays null → isSpikeConc false. Verified: a stock with revQ:[] and 4 annual pairs all >50% returns REAL_HYPERGROWTH_ACCELERATING / pass:true with breadthSource:'y'.
why_it_matters: Annual YoY is far coarser than quarterly breadth and cannot detect a single-quarter spike (the core fake-hypergrowth signal). A name passing on annual data alone gets the same top rank (5) and 0.20-weight credit as one validated on 4 strong quarters with no spike — diluting the very discrimination the method exists to provide.

_verdict.note: Confirmed by reproduction. File C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/methods/hypergrowth-quality-class.js. Ran evaluate() with revQ:[] + annualRev:[500M,300M,180M,100M,60M] (all YoY >50%), revenueTTM 500M, annualOpInc profitable -> returns value:5, class:REAL_HYPERGROWTH_ACCELERATING, pass:true, breadthSource:'y', spikeShare:null. The mechanism is exactly as described: Faktor 3 (spikeShare, line 127-135) is gated on revQ.length>=4, so the annual-breadth branch (line 87-106, reached when revQ<8 but >=4 annual pairs) never populates spikeShare; isSpikeConc (line 150) is therefore false, and the annual path can reach the top ACCELERATING rank via lines 164-166 having satisfied only 2 of the 3 promised factors. Note the spike-concentration factor is intrinsically a quarterly metric (largest-Q share of trailing 4Q) and cannot be derived from annual data at all — so it's a structural gap, not a fixable in-branch oversight. I checked whether the companion hard-gate compensates: it does not. q-spike-dataguard.js also gates its spike check on revQ.length>=4 (line 212), so an annual-only stock even at YoY=150% returns CLEAN (verified) — neither method applies any spike protection on annual-only data. The path is reachable in production: revenueQ is sourced from Yahoo quarterly history (pull-yahoo.js line 695), which is sparse/short for recent IPOs and newly-listed names, exactly where annual fallback kicks in. title: Degraded path reports value=position-in-range [0,1] against threshold=0.10 (a return), unit mismatch latent if ever promoted to scoring

Confirmed real (latent unit mismatch), verified against source + runtime repro. Degraded branch (methods/price-momentum-12-1.js:253-278) emits value=pos (positional fraction in [0,1]) but keeps threshold=0.10 / thresholdOp='gte' — the 12-1 RETURN floor used by the proper path (line 211/231). Reproduced the auditor's example exactly: a 100-bar rising stock takes the degraded path (len 100 < 252 LOOKBACK_FULL, >= 84 MIN_HISTORY) and returns value:1, pass:true, threshold:0.1.

Two nuances the auditor got right and one it understated:
1) pass is NOT wrong: it's computed in the method body as pos>=DEGRADED_RANGE_PASS (0.6) on line 254, independent of the emitted threshold. So no current pass/fail corruption.
2) Scoring is unaffected today: price-momentum-12-1 is DIAGNOSTIC-only (method-types.js:101) and absent from every SCORE_WEIGHTS bucket (score-aggregator.js:32-73); moreover normalizeMethodScore short-circuits to 1.0 on pass===true (line 112) and only reaches the value/threshold graduated math on pass===false. So 'latent if ever promoted to scoring' is accurate.
3) UNDERSTATED: there IS a present-day consumer. _helpers.js wrapEvaluate -> _inferConfidence (lines 282-293) and _autoFlags (lines 300-306) compute dist=|(value-threshold)/threshold| for EVERY method regardless of scoring. I reproduced a degraded-FAIL case with pos~0.105: it spuriously emits NEAR_THRESHOLD and drops confidence 0.7->0.6 — purely because a positional fraction near 0.10 is mistaken for being near the 10% return floor. Severity medium is fair (diagnostic-only, no scoring/fixture-hash impact, but real spurious flags/confidence). Fix direction (emit threshold=DEGRADED_RANGE_PASS=0.6 on the degraded branch so value and threshold share units; op stays 'gte') is correct and the constant already exists (line 76, also stored in components.thresholdsDegraded.rangePass line 271).

title: Look-ahead bias: magic-formula PASS/FAIL is computed from TODAY's market cap/EV, then matched to a PAST vintage's forward return
evidence: Header (line 10-15) justifies the design: 're-evaluate the three methods against TODAY's snapshots (these fundamental ratios change slowly)'. But magic-formula is NOT slow-moving: methods/magic-formula.js:160-168 computes earnings yield from `_unwrap(stock.metrics.enterpriseValue)` / `mcap = _unwrap(stock.marketCap)` (synthesized `ev = mcap + td - tc`). tag229b evaluates ONCE on today's snapshot (line 153 `m.mod.evaluate(stock)`) and reuses that pass flag for every vintage (line 186 `if (e.pass) passRets.push(ret)`), while `ret` is the forward return measured FROM the 2026-05-xx vintage date (line 184 `forwardReturn(priceIndex, t, asOf, FORWARD_DAYS)`).
why_it_matters: magic-formula's value leg depends on price, which moved materially between the vintage dates and 'today'. Using today's cheap/expensive classification to predict a return that already happened weeks earlier injects future information into the PASS bucket. The reported magic-formula spread is contaminated; only asset-growth-anomaly and penman-nissim (balance-sheet-only, confirmed reading `stock.annual.annualBalance`) honor the slow-moving assumption. A spurious 'PASS beats FAIL' for magic-formula could green-light a method that has no real edge — directly relevant to the '20% of potential' framing.
fix: Restrict the today's-snapshot shortcut to balance-sheet-only methods. For magic-formula, either (a) reconstruct EV at the vintage date from `prices/history.json` close * shares + net debt, or (b) exclude magic-formula from this smoke test and label it 'not testable without point-in-time EV'. Add a comment naming the failure mode: '// prevents look-ahead: price-derived EV must be as-of vintage, not today'.

_verdict.note:
CONFIRMED as a real methodological flaw, but severity overstated. Code reading is accurate: tag229b-new-method-backtest.js line 153 computes each method's PASS/FAIL once from TODAY's snapshot (m.mod.evaluate(stock)); line 186 reuses that flag for every vintage; line 184 measures the forward return FROM the vintage date. For magic-formula the pass flag depends on earningsYield = EBIT/EV (magic-formula.js:202), and EV is price-derived: metrics.enterpriseValue or synthesized mcap+td-tc (lines 160-168). marketCap/EV move 1:1 with the current price and are NOT slow-moving, so the header's blanket 'fundamental ratios change slowly' justification (lines 12-15) is false for the EY leg. The look-ahead channel (today's price -> pass flag -> partitions returns measured weeks earlier) is genuine. Verified vintages now span 2026-05-10..2026-06-12 (28 files) and prices run to 2026-06-15, so the >2-week gap the report itself warns about (report lines 32-33 'Beyond two weeks this assumption breaks') is actually exceeded by later vintages.

WHY NOT HIGH: (1) The script self-documents the exact limitation in its header AND in the audit report (report lines 26-33, 145-152: 'Pass flags inferred from today's snapshot, not the vintage-date snapshot'). (2) It is a DIAGNOSTIC-only research/smoke script (magic-formula.js:69 'NOT in SCORE_WEIGHTS' / fixture-hash invariant safe) — it does not feed production scoring; it writes a one-off report. (3) The magic-formula result the bias could corrupt is already discounted to near-worthless in the report: 13 PASS obs from ~10 unique tickers, 8% computability, labelled 'very low confidence / essentially noise'; the actionable conclusion ('recalibrate puller, don't trust the magnitude') is unaffected by the bias. A documented limitation in a non-production, self-caveated smoke test = medium, not high.

Caller verification: vintage files (methods-history/*.json) are used ONLY for the per-vintage ticker list (vintageTickers), never to evaluate the methods — the three methods didn't exist at vintage time so no point-in-time pass flag exists to fall back on; that absence is the actual reason for the today's-snapshot shortcut.

title: pickPriorAnnual independent fallback can pair Goodwill latest/prior from non-adjacent fiscal years, corrupting deltaGoodwillYoY
evidence: `pickBestAnnual` returns latest non-stale (line 162-165). `pickPriorAnnual` independently re-finds 'latest' then looks for an end-date 270-550 days earlier (line 183-189), but its final fallback `if (annuals[latestIdx + 1]) return ...` (line 191) takes the next record regardless of gap. `deltaGoodwillYoY = goodwillLatest - goodwillPrior` (line 302-303) assumes these are exactly one year apart.
why_it_matters: For companies with a fiscal-year change, a restatement (10-K/A), or a gap in filings, prior can be 2 years back or an amended duplicate of the same period. `deltaGoodwillYoY` and `headlineGrowth` (line 325-326) then measure the wrong interval. The fallback at line 191 has no day-gap guard at all, so it silently accepts any spacing.
fix: Drop the unconditional `annuals[latestIdx+1]` fallback, or constrain it to a max gap (e.g. <=550 days) and emit the actual gap in the record so downstream can reject mismatched pairs. Return null rather than a wrong-interval pair.

_verdict.note: Confirmed by source reading of C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/scripts/extract-ma-rpo.js. pickPriorAnnual (lines 169-193) first scans annuals[latestIdx+1..end] for a record with end-date gap in [270,550] days (lines 185-188). Only when NO record falls in that window does the unconditional fallback at line 191 fire: it returns annuals[latestIdx+1] (the immediately-preceding annual by end date) with no gap check. Since the in-window scan already failed for every candidate, this fallback is guaranteed to return an out-of-window pair when it runs. Two concrete mismatch cases: (A) gap too small — 10-K/A amendments are explicitly accepted (lines 157,174); a 10-K plus its same-fiscal-year 10-K/A share the same end date, so gap=0 fails the 270-day floor and the fallback returns the amendment as 'prior', yielding deltaGoodwillYoY≈0; (B) gap too large — a skipped/missing 10-K leaves the next available annual >550 days earlier, so deltaGoodwillYoY spans 2+ years but is labeled YoY. deltaGoodwillYoY = round(goodwillLatest - goodwillPrior) (lines 302-303) and its derivative deltaGoodwillPctRev (line 328) consume the pair at face value. The output record (lines 440-460) and committed data/ma-rpo-snapshot.json store no end dates or gap, so downstream cannot detect or reject a mismatched pair — matching the finding's evidence exactly. Caveat on severity: this is strictly a fallback path that only executes when the normal one-year window finds nothing; for the typical annual-filer the window scan succeeds and line 191 never runs. Impact is silent inaccuracy on a secondary M&A signal for a minority of tickers, not a primary screening gate — medium is fair, leaning low. Same unguarded-fallback pattern also affects RPO/DeferredRevenue priors via pickPriorAnnual at lines 377-378, 391, 408-409, 422 (not cited but identical risk).

title: snapshot-r40rx-history + backfill use raw `ticker + '.json'` while the READER uses safeSnapshotFilename() — write/read filename divergence for Windows-reserved & special-char tickers
evidence: snapshot-r40rx-history.js:61 `const file = path.join(outDir, ticker + '.json');` and :123 `writeFileAtomic(path.join(args.out, ticker + '.json'), ...)`. backfill-r40rx-history.js:59 same raw join. BUT the consumer generate-screener.js:184 reads via `path.join(R40RX_HISTORY_DIR, safeSnapshotFilename(ticker))`. snapshot-score-history.js already fixed this (lines 32,104,199 use safeSnapshotFilename). lib/snapshot-fs.js maps e.g. ticker `CON` -> `_CON.json`, and sanitises `[^A-Z0-9.-]` -> `_`.
why_it_matters: For any ticker whose safe filename differs from raw (Windows-reserved stems CON/PRN/AUX/NUL/COM1-9/LPT1-9, or tickers with characters outside [A-Z0-9.-]), the r40rx history is WRITTEN to one path and READ from another. The writer never updates the file the reader opens, so generate-screener silently gets stale/empty r40rx history for those tickers -> the multi-quarter R40 durability gate (generate-screener.js:721 `hist.slice(-4)`) sees <4 entries and routes the row through the weaker TTM-only fallback (r40InsufficientHistory). The audit note F-SM-004 / F-218b-01 documents this exact drift class as P1; score-history was fixed but the two r40rx writers were missed.
fix: Import `const { safeSnapshotFilename } = require('../lib/snapshot-fs.js');` in both snapshot-r40rx-history.js and backfill-r40rx-history.js and replace every `ticker + '.json'` (read in readHistoryFile, write in main) with `safeSnapshotFilename(ticker)`, exactly as snapshot-score-history.js does. No method/ files touched; FTS_CACHE_VERSION untouched.

_verdict.note:
CONFIRMED real write/read divergence. Verified against C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening:

WRITERS use raw `ticker + '.json'`:
- scripts/snapshot-r40rx-history.js:61 (read in readHistoryFile) and :123 (write in main) — `path.join(..., ticker + '.json')`.
- scripts/backfill-r40rx-history.js:59 (read) and :193 (write) — same raw join.

READER uses the safe helper:
- generate-screener.js:33 imports safeSnapshotFilename; readR40rxHistory at :184 reads `path.join(R40RX_HISTORY_DIR, safeSnapshotFilename(ticker))`.

lib/snapshot-fs.js:32-37 prefixes `_` when the pre-dot stem matches CON/PRN/AUX/NUL/COM[1-9]/LPT[1-9] and sanitises `[^A-Z0-9.-]`→`_`. So for a reserved/special ticker the writer's raw name and the reader's safe name diverge.

Blast radius measured against the ACTUAL universe (universe-list.txt + universe-candidates.txt, 1645 tickers): exactly ONE diverging ticker today — `CON.DE` (stem `CON` is reserved). Writer produces r40rx-history/CON.DE.json; reader looks for _CON.DE.json → silent miss, no R40/RX history shown for CON.DE. Confirmed Windows happily writes `CON.DE.json` (the device-name rule does not block it), so the file IS created under the wrong name rather than failing loudly — a true silent divergence, not a crash. The same was true for the snapshot producer side: pull-yahoo.js writes snapshots via safeSnapshotFilename (so CON.DE snapshot is _CON.DE.json) but keeps meta.ticker='CON.DE', which is what the history scripts key on — confirming the raw key flows through.

Precedent: scripts/snapshot-score-history.js already fixed this exact pattern (lines 32, 104, 199 route through safeSnapshotFilename, with comment F-SM-004). The proposed fix mirrors that.

Severity revised high→medium: impact is limited to the R40/RX history sub-table for the affected ticker(s) (a dashboard feature, not core screener filter results or data corruption), and only 1 ticker is currently affected. Real but narrow.

title: pbScore formula is a hand-copied fork of generate-screener.js — duplicated magic constants drift silently because nothing ties them together
evidence: snapshot-score-history.js:59-68 reproduces `(growthC/100*25)+(gmC/100*20)+(r40C/100*15)+gmaBonus+omaBonus+revAccelBonus` with gmaBonus 10/4/0, omaBonus 15/6/0, revAccelBonus min(15, delta/50*15). generate-screener.js:314-323 has the byte-identical formula. The file comment even says 'Mirror generate-screener.js' pbScore formula'. Same pattern for the _unwrap helper (lines 38-43) re-implemented locally.
why_it_matters: The script's own header warns that any drift between stored history and the dashboard 'produces a permanent fake score uplift today artifact'. Two independent copies of a 6-term weighted formula with eight hardcoded weights is exactly how that drift happens: a future tweak to the dashboard's omaBonus or the revAccel divisor will not be reflected here, and the score-history sparkline/ΔScore badge will diverge from the live pbScore with no test catching it. The formula is currently identical, so this is structural risk, not a present miscompute.
fix: Extract pbScore into a shared module (e.g. lib/pb-score.js exporting computePbScore(stock, allResults)) and require it from both generate-screener.js and snapshot-score-history.js. Do NOT touch methods/index.js. This collapses the fork to one source of truth and lets the existing fixture tests guard it.

_verdict.note: Confirmed real duplication. snapshot-score-history.js:59-68 reproduces the pbScore formula byte-for-byte against generate-screener.js:313-323 — identical weights (25/20/15), gmaBonus 10/4/0, omaBonus 15/6/0, revAccelBonus min(15, delta/50*15), and identical r40 cap logic. The local _unwrap (lines 38-43) is also byte-identical to generate-screener.js's unwrap (lines 73-78). The file header (lines 16-18, 36) self-documents the fork ("Mirror generate-screener.js' pbScore formula") and explicitly warns drift produces a permanent fake 'score uplift today' artifact in the dashboard. Drift risk is concrete: no automated test pins computed pbScore values (the only tag28-tests references are hardcoded entry literals feeding appendAndPrune, not formula assertions), so a retune in generate-screener.js would silently diverge. Severity medium is right: not a live correctness bug today (the copies currently agree), but a documented maintainability hazard with a real dashboard-corruption failure mode. fix_safe=false: the extraction is sound in principle but needs human review, not auto-apply — generate-screener.js's unwrap has many other call sites, and the two implementations derive growth/grossMargin/r40Value differently (inline at the generate call site vs. recomputed inside _computePbScore), so sharing one computePbScore(stock, allResults) signature rewires data flow at the generate-screener call site. The proposal itself leans on 'existing fixture tests' to guard the change, but no such pbScore-value test exists, so a pinning test must be added as part of the change.

title: Ticker injected into onclick JS-string context via fragile manual quote-escaping, not HTML-escaped — breakage + stored-XSS vector
evidence: Line 419: `parts.push('');` (same pattern line 448 for metric leaderboards). The argument is only run through `.replace(/'/g, "\\'")` — it escapes single quotes but NOT double-quotes, backslashes, `<`, `>`, `&`, or ``. Note the rest of the page religiously uses `escapeAttr`/`escapeHTML`; this one sink does not.
why_it_matters: ticker flows from picks-history / methods-history keys (`Object.keys(methodsHistory.stocks)`), which originate from the watchlist / Yahoo symbol list. A symbol containing a double-quote or `<` (foreign tickers, malformed Yahoo rows, or an attacker who can influence the watchlist) breaks out of the onclick attribute and injects arbitrary HTML/JS into the deployed GitHub-Pages dashboard. Even benign tickers with a backslash render a broken button (silent loss of the detail modal for that row). The whole point of the surrounding escaping was XSS-safety; this is the one hole.
fix: Stop building inline onclick with string concatenation. Render the ticker into a `data-ticker` attribute via `escapeAttr(...)` and attach a single delegated click listener (like the existing `#tabs` listener) that reads `e.target.closest('button[data-ticker]').dataset.ticker` and calls `openDetail`. This removes the JS-string context entirely. // failure mode: HTML/JS-attribute injection + modal breakage from un-escaped ticker symbols

_verdict.note: Confirmed in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/generate-dashboard.js lines 419 & 448. Verbatim: `<button onclick="openDetail(\''+p.ticker.replace(/'/g,"\\'")+'\')">`+escapeAttr(p.ticker)+`...`. The ticker is concatenated into a JS-string argument that lives inside a DOUBLE-quoted HTML onclick attribute, and is escaped ONLY via .replace(/'/g,"\\'") — it does NOT escape `"`, `\`, `<`, `>`, `&`. A `"` in the ticker breaks out of the onclick="..." attribute (HTML-attribute injection); a trailing `\` corrupts the manual \' escaping; `<`/`>`/`&` pass raw in the onclick portion. The auditor's observation that this is the lone sink bypassing the file's otherwise-consistent escapeAttr/escapeHTML discipline is accurate (escapeAttr defined L462, escapeHTML L161; both used everywhere else, incl. the visible button text on the very same line). The referenced delegated-listener pattern for the fix genuinely exists (L567: document.getElementById('tabs').addEventListener('click', e => e.target.closest('.tab')...)), so the proposed remediation is idiomatic and feasible. SEVERITY TEMPERED to medium: tickers are internal Yahoo-Finance symbols read from pipeline JSON (picks-history/latest.json, methods-history/*.json) — not end-user input. Real symbols use [A-Z0-9.\-^=] only, none of which are dangerous here, so live stored-XSS is very unlikely; existing char-sanitizers (lib/snapshot-fs.js, pull-yahoo.js, discovery/sec-tickers.js) are for filename/SEC-source paths and do NOT gate the ticker field consumed here, so the sink is genuinely unsanitized but the realistic blast radius is 'malformed ticker breaks the modal button / page markup' far more than active XSS. Real bug + latent low-likelihood injection vector = medium, not high.

title: Unguarded JSON.parse + latest.stocks access can throw on truncated/old-schema snapshot; workflow swallows it (continue-on-error) → stale diff-report.html silently deployed
evidence: Lines 41-42 do raw `JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(...))` with no try/catch (unlike the dashboard's `safeJSON`). Line 47 then does `Object.entries(latest.stocks)` with no guard that `stocks` exists. The workflow step is `continue-on-error: true` (daily-pull.yml:534-535), and the previous diff-report.html is committed and served by Pages.
why_it_matters: methods-history files are large (~14 MB per the workflow comments). A truncated file (CI cancellation mid-write of the upstream snapshot-methods-history.js) or a schema change where `stocks` is renamed/absent throws either a SyntaxError or `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'stocks')`. Because the step continues-on-error, the run goes green and GitHub Pages keeps serving the previous day's diff-report.html with no signal that the diff silently stopped updating — exactly the 'silently swallowed error' class in the audit scope.
fix: Wrap both parses in try/catch (reuse a safeJSON helper), and after parsing assert `latest && latest.stocks && previous && previous.stocks` are objects; if not, write the same 'need ≥2 snapshots' placeholder and `console.error` a distinct message so the failure is visible in logs rather than masked by continue-on-error.

_verdict.note: Confirmed against source in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening. generate-diff-report.js lines 41-42 do raw JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(...)) for both `latest` and `previous` with no try/catch. Line 47 `Object.entries(latest.stocks)` throws TypeError if `stocks` is missing/undefined, and line 48 `previous.stocks[ticker]` likewise. This is asymmetric vs generate-dashboard.js, which uses a safeJSON helper (line 58) AND guards `if (!methodsHistory || !methodsHistory.stocks) return []` (line 116) — the diff-report script has neither. The workflow step is confirmed continue-on-error:true (daily-pull.yml:534-535), so a thrown error is swallowed; the deploy step (line 667 `cp diff-report.html _site/`, gated `if: success()` which still passes because the diff step soft-fails) then ships the previously committed diff-report.html (present in the worktree). Net effect: a malformed/old-schema snapshot silently deploys a stale report with no visible failure signal. Severity tempered to medium (not high): the normal producer snapshot-methods-history.js:160 uses writeFileAtomic and always emits a {date,stocks:{}} shape, so a self-inflicted truncation in the current code path is unlikely — realistic triggers are pre-Tag-189 truncated files, legacy-schema snapshots, or external corruption (OneDrive/AV mid-write). Plausible but not a routine daily event.

title: NASDAQ-API marketCap hint is silently discarded for any ticker already discovered by an earlier source
evidence: nasdaq-api.js sets `marketCap: mcap` (line 181). But in refresh-universe.js the merge is `if (!allTickers.has(sym)) {...set marketCap...} else { /* only updates existing.source */ }` (lines 340-366). fetchNasdaqApiList() is index 5 (LAST) in `Promise.allSettled([fetchNasdaqAll, fetchSecTickers, fetchFinnhubUniverse, fetchWikipediaIndices, fetchOTCMarkets, fetchNasdaqApiList])` (refresh-universe.js:328-335). nasdaq-all (index 0) and sec (index 1) carry NO marketCap, so they populate the symbol first; when nasdaq-api reaches the same symbol the `else` branch runs and `existing.marketCap` stays null.
why_it_matters: marketCap is the SOLE ranking key for the universe hard-cap (refresh-universe.js:386-396: withMcap sorted desc, withoutMcap capped at 20% of MAX_UNIVERSE). The one source that provides a free mcap hint is the last to run, so virtually every US large-cap (already in nasdaq-all/sec) is treated as null-mcap and competes only for the 20% 'null bucket' instead of being ranked by its true size. This directly caps screener breadth — exactly the 'survivorship attrition' / silent-shrink failure mode. It also defeats the stated rationale of the module ('Provides company name, sector, and market cap hints').
fix: In the merge `else` branch of refresh-universe.js, backfill empty fields from the incoming source: `if (info.marketCap != null && (existing.marketCap == null)) existing.marketCap = info.marketCap;` and likewise for empty `name`/`sector`. (Do NOT edit nasdaq-api.js for this; the bug is in the aggregator contract, not the puller. Carry a comment naming the failure mode: 'prevents last-source mcap/sector hints being dropped for already-seen tickers'.) Reordering nasdaq-api earlier is NOT sufficient because nasdaq-all/sec would then overwrite-skip it later anyway given first-writer-wins semantics.

_verdict.note: Confirmed real by source reading. nasdaq-api.js:181 sets marketCap; nasdaq-all.js (records at lines 71/103) and sec-tickers.js (line 104) carry NO marketCap field. In refresh-universe.js the discovery merge (lines 336-368) processes Promise.allSettled in input order, and fetchNasdaqApiList is index 5/last (line 334). When nasdaq-all (idx0) or sec (idx1) first inserts a US symbol via the `if (!allTickers.has(sym))` branch, marketCap is set to `info.marketCap || null` = null (line 344). When nasdaq-api later hits the same symbol, the `else` branch (351-366) runs and ONLY updates existing.source — existing.marketCap/name/sector are never backfilled. Refutation checks all fail to clear it: (1) the Yahoo screener phase (lines 211-303) only retains tickers with mcap in [1e9,500e9], so any nasdaq-all/sec-discovered ticker NOT surfaced by a Yahoo bucket enters allTickers with null mcap first — exactly the population the bug drops; (2) fetchWithMcap (line 192) is defined but never called in main(), so there is no later enrichment that would backfill the lost mcap. Concrete downstream impact: the universe-cap logic (lines 382-402) segregates null-mcap tickers into a pool capped at 20% of MAX_UNIVERSE (line 393), so a ticker whose mcap WAS available from nasdaq-api is mis-bucketed as null-mcap and can be dropped; name/sector hints (written as sector_hint/name at lines 443-446) are also silently lost. The proposed_fix correctly locates the bug in the aggregator, not the puller, and correctly notes reordering would not help under first-writer-wins.

title: Class-share regex still rejects every class-share ticker the comment claims it fixes (BRK.B, BF.B, BRK-B)
evidence: Line 167: `if (!/^[A-Z][A-Z0-9]{0,4}([.\-][A-Z])?$/.test(rawSym)) continue;` runs AFTER line 163 `(row.symbol||...).trim().toUpperCase()`. The NASDAQ Screener API emits class shares with a slash or space ('BRK/B', 'BRK B') OR — for the download=true CSV-derived JSON — frequently as 'BRK.B'. The regex permits 'BRK.B'. BUT line 168 then applies `JUNK_SUFFIX_RE = /[WRU]$|.../` (line 37) which contains the alternative `[WRU]$` — matched against the WHOLE symbol with no anchor on the class part. A class share like 'BRK.U'-style is caught, but more importantly any legitimately valid ticker ENDING in U/R/W (e.g. 'BKU' BankUnited? no — ends U; 'NU' Nu Holdings ends U; 'EW'? ends W) is dropped.
why_it_matters: `/[WRU]$/` is unanchored to a suffix delimiter, so it nukes real common stocks whose ticker merely ends in W, R, or U — e.g. NU (Nu Holdings, ~$60B), BKU, RDW. These are large, liquid names silently excluded from the universe at discovery time. The same JUNK_SUFFIX_RE appears in nasdaq-all.js:25, nasdaq-api.js:37, and otc-markets.js:27 — a triplicated bug.
fix: Anchor the warrant/right/unit filter to a delimiter: replace `/[WRU]$|.../` with `/[.\-](WS|WT|WI|RT|UN|U|W|R)$/i` (only treat a trailing single letter as junk when it follows a dot/dash class delimiter, never a bare 'NU'/'EW'). Factor the corrected regex into one shared module imported by all three pullers to kill the triplication. Comment: 'prevents dropping real common stocks ending in W/R/U (NU, BKU, EW)'.

_verdict.note:
CONFIRMED real, but the finding's title/framing is partly garbled while the underlying bug is genuine. Two distinct filters run in sequence in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/discovery/nasdaq-api.js: line 167 `validRe = /^[A-Z][A-Z0-9]{0,4}([.\-][A-Z])?$/` (the Tag 217g class-share fix) and line 168 `JUNK_SUFFIX_RE = /[WRU]$|\.WS$|.../` (line 37).

The title is WRONG on the class-share part: I empirically verified the class-share regex does NOT reject BRK.B/BF.B/BRK-B — all three pass validRe and are kept (validRe test returns true, JUNK_SUFFIX_RE false). So the "rejects every class-share ticker" headline is a misread; the Tag 217g fix works as intended.

The REAL bug is the second one the finding also identifies: `[WRU]$` in JUNK_SUFFIX_RE is unanchored to any delimiter, so it matches the trailing letter of ANY symbol. Verified by running the actual regexes against real tickers: NU (Nu Holdings, large-cap NYSE), EW (Edwards Lifesciences, S&P 500), SNOW (Snowflake), FOUR (Shift4), ARW (Arrow Electronics), BKU (BankUnited) are all silently dropped (why:"junk-suffix"). This is genuine silent data loss in the nasdaq-api discovery source. The same buggy JUNK_SUFFIX_RE is duplicated in discovery/nasdaq-all.js line 25 (used at lines 70 and 97), so the same stocks are dropped there too — the triplication claim is partly right (this regex appears in 2 of the discovery files; sec-tickers.js uses a different `[\s\/\\]` reject, not this suffix filter). Net effect is mitigated because these symbols may be recovered via other discovery sources (sec-tickers, finnhub), but nasdaq-api/nasdaq-all themselves under-report.

Severity: I downgrade high→medium. It is real silent data loss, but (a) it only affects the subset of valid US tickers ending in bare W/R/U, (b) the union-of-sources discovery design means many of these are likely recovered elsewhere, and (c) it is not a crash/corruption.

title: Singapore exchange code mapped wrong: EXCHANGES key 'SP' with Yahoo suffix .SI, but Finnhub's Singapore code is 'SI' — the API call requests a non-existent exchange
evidence: Line 27: `'SP': '.SI',  // Singapore (Yahoo uses .SI)`. The key 'SP' is used as the Finnhub query param at line 74 `exchange=${exchange}` → `exchange=SP`. Finnhub's exchange code for Singapore (SGX) is 'SI', not 'SP'. 'SP' is not a valid Finnhub exchange and returns an empty/!Array response (handled at line 77-80 as 'unexpected response').
why_it_matters: The entire Singapore exchange yields zero tickers every run — a whole market silently missing from the global universe, masked as a benign 'unexpected response' log line. The comment confuses the Finnhub request code (left side, must be Finnhub's code) with the Yahoo suffix (right side).
fix: Change the key to Finnhub's real code: `'SI': '.SI'`. Verify each other key against Finnhub's /stock/symbol exchange list (several others — e.g. 'F' Frankfurt vs Finnhub 'F', 'SW' SIX) should be spot-checked the same way. Comment: 'Finnhub exchange code, not Yahoo suffix — prevents whole-exchange silent miss'.

_verdict.note: Confirmed real. In C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/discovery/finnhub.js the EXCHANGES map key (not the value) is used as the Finnhub API query param: line 72 iterates Object.entries(EXCHANGES) destructuring the key into `exchange`, and line 74 builds `...stock/symbol?exchange=${exchange}...`. So the key 'SP' (line 27) is sent as `exchange=SP`. The authoritative Finnhub exchange-codes list gives Singapore (SGX) the code 'SI' (symbols formatted like 500.SI), and 'SP' is not a valid Finnhub exchange — it returns a non-array/empty body that is caught at lines 77-80 as 'unexpected response', silently dropping the entire Singapore exchange whenever FINNHUB_API_KEY is set. I verified the auditor's spot-check candidates: 'F' (Frankfurt) and 'SW' (Switzerland) match Finnhub's real codes already, so this is isolated to the SP key, not a systemic mismapping. medium is the right severity: SGX is a smaller market, all other exchanges work, and the source is optional (skipped entirely without the API key), so impact is a bounded coverage gap, not pipeline corruption.

title: Finnhub only short-circuits on HTTP 401; any other persistent error (403/429/timeout) silently burns the full 16-exchange * (1.1s+30s) budget and discards all data
evidence: Lines 101-104 break ONLY on `/HTTP 401/i`. A 429 (rate-limit, very common on the 60 req/min free tier the header warns about, line 6) or 403 or repeated `timeout` (30s each, line 48) falls through to `await sleep(1100)` (line 106) and retries every remaining exchange. There is no retry/backoff on transient failure (unlike nasdaq-api.js:86 and otc-markets.js:72 which both added DELAYS backoff arrays).
why_it_matters: On a 429 storm, the loop wastes up to 16 * 31s ≈ 8 min doing nothing useful, and because each exchange independently fails, fetchFinnhubUniverse returns whatever partial Map it built (possibly empty) with no signal to the aggregator that Finnhub effectively contributed nothing. Inconsistent with the codebase's own Tag-215i retry hardening applied to the sibling pullers.
fix: Mirror the nasdaq-api/otc-markets Tag-215i pattern: add timeout/429 retry with exponential backoff, and broaden the early-bail to 403/429-on-first-call as well as 401. Comment naming failure mode: 'prevents 8-min wasted budget on rate-limit/auth storm and aligns retry policy with sibling pullers'.

_verdict.note: Confirmed against source. discovery/finnhub.js catch block (lines 94-105) breaks ONLY on /HTTP 401/i (line 101-103); any other persistent error falls through to `await sleep(1100)` (line 106) and the loop continues to the next exchange. get() rejects with bare `Error('HTTP ' + statusCode)` for any non-200/301/302 (line 41), so 403/429 produce 'HTTP 403'/'HTTP 429' messages that do NOT match the 401 regex and do NOT short-circuit. Timeouts reject with Error('timeout') after 30s (line 48), also no early-bail and NO retry. This is in direct contrast to the sibling pullers: nasdaq-api.js (lines 85-100) and otc-markets.js (lines 71-86) both implement the Tag-215i DELAYS exponential-backoff retry loop on timeout. finnhub.js has no retry path at all. Worst-case budget: the EXCHANGES map actually has 17 entries (report says 16 — minor off-by-one, does not change conclusion), so a persistent 429/403/timeout storm burns up to ~17 * (30s timeout + 1.1s sleep) ≈ 8.8 min and returns an empty Map (all data discarded). Caller refresh-universe.js:328-335 runs discovery via Promise.allSettled, so the wasted time does not serially add to other sources, BUT allSettled gates on the slowest promise — an 8-min Finnhub stall delays the entire discovery phase. medium is correct: degraded coverage + wasted wall-clock, not data corruption; the universe still builds from the other 5 sources.

title: nasdaq-api redirect handler does not drain the 3xx body and passes a possibly-relative Location straight to https.get — the exact failure mode sec-tickers.js was hardened against
evidence: Lines 52-54: `if (res.statusCode === 301 || res.statusCode === 302) { return get(res.headers.location).then(resolve).catch(reject); }`. Unlike sec-tickers.js (lines 48-62, Tag 229c-2) this branch: (a) does NOT call `res.resume()` to drain the socket, (b) passes a raw `res.headers.location` (may be relative) directly into `https.get(url,...)`, (c) has no redirect-depth cap, (d) ignores 307/308. nasdaq-all.js:35-37, otc-markets.js:40-43, finnhub.js:37-39, wikipedia-indices.js:27-29 share the same un-hardened pattern (only finnhub/nasdaq-all/otc/wiki call res.resume(), but still pass relative Location and lack depth cap / 307-308).
why_it_matters: api.nasdaq.com sits behind a CDN; a relative `Location: /api/...` redirect throws ERR_INVALID_URL, gets swallowed by the per-exchange try/catch (nasdaq-api.js:189), and that exchange contributes nothing — silent universe shrink. nasdaq-api.js additionally never drains the body (a), leaking a socket per redirect under keep-alive. This is the documented sec-tickers.js failure mode (a)/(b)/(c) replicated in 5 sibling files.
fix: Factor sec-tickers.js's hardened get() (URL-resolve via `new URL(loc, url)`, res.resume() drain, MAX_REDIRECTS cap, handle 307/308) into a shared http helper and use it in all six pullers. Comment: 'prevents relative-redirect ERR_INVALID_URL silently zeroing an exchange + socket leak'.

_verdict.note: CONFIRMED real. nasdaq-api.js:52-54 redirect branch verified against the hardened sec-tickers.js reference (Tag 229c-2, lines 38-75): the nasdaq-api branch (a) does NOT call res.resume() to drain the 3xx body -> socket leak with keep-alive (the other 4 pullers DO drain); (b) passes raw res.headers.location into get() -> https.get(url,{...}), so a relative Location throws TypeError[ERR_INVALID_URL], which is then swallowed by the per-exchange try/catch at lines 189-192 ("[NASDAQ-API] <label> failed") -> that exchange silently contributes 0 tickers while the run reports success; (c) has no redirect-depth cap (unbounded recursion on a redirect loop); (d) only handles 301/302, ignoring 307/308. The scope claim is also accurate: nasdaq-all.js:35-37, otc-markets.js:40-43, finnhub.js:37-39, wikipedia-indices.js:27-29 all DO call res.resume() but still pass a raw relative Location, lack a depth cap, and ignore 307/308 -- so all six share the relative-Location/no-cap/no-307-308 gap, and nasdaq-api.js is additionally the only one also missing the socket drain. Severity stays medium: the failure is latent because these CDN/API endpoints almost always issue ABSOLUTE redirects in practice (no evidence of an actual relative-redirect occurrence in the run logs), and the socket leak is bounded (few connections per run). fix_safe=false: the proposed fix is a cross-cutting refactor extracting a shared http helper across six files, and each get() carries load-bearing per-file specifics that must be preserved -- nasdaq-api needs its Referer + Accept-Language headers and 45000ms timeout plus its outer retry loop; sec-tickers/SEC needs its exact contact-email User-Agent (Tag 215g history: wrong UA -> HTTP 403); timeouts differ (30s vs 45s); Accept headers differ. A shared helper that flattens these risks regressing every discovery source feeding the universe, and adding 307/308 + relative-resolution changes live network behavior. Needs human review + a real run, not auto-apply. A minimal in-place hardening of nasdaq-api.js alone (mirror sec-tickers: res.resume(), new URL(loc,url), MAX_REDIRECTS cap, 307/308) is the lower-risk path but still warrants review of the most fragile network path. Files: C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/discovery/nasdaq-api.js (lines 41-66), discovery/sec-tickers.js (lines 38-76, reference), discovery/nasdaq-all.js, discovery/otc-markets.js, discovery/finnhub.js, discovery/wikipedia-indices.js.

title: OTC per-page catch breaks pagination on a single transient error, silently keeping only the pages fetched so far
evidence: Lines 182-186: `catch (e) { console.error(...); break; }` — comment 'Non-fatal: stop pagination for this batch but keep what we have'. fetchOTCPage already retries timeouts internally (lines 71-87), but a single JSON-parse error or HTTP 500 on, say, page 4 of 10 aborts the remaining pages 5-10 and returns a Map missing ~3000 tickers, with only a console.error as evidence.
why_it_matters: A mid-pagination hiccup truncates the OTC universe to whatever was fetched before the error, asymmetrically. Because the aggregator merges whatever Map it gets (refresh-universe.js:336-368) and there is no expected-count assertion, the shrink is invisible. This is the silently-swallowed-error / non-atomic-discovery failure class.
fix: Change `break` to `continue` for non-empty intermediate errors (skip the bad page, try the next), or retry the whole page once more before giving up. Track a pageErrors count and surface it to the aggregator so a partial OTC pull is detectable (mirror refresh-universe.js's F-DP-037 zero-quote alert). Comment: 'prevents one bad page truncating the entire OTC tail'.

_verdict.note: Confirmed real via source. discovery/otc-markets.js:182-186 — the page-loop catch does `console.error(...); break;`, so a single error on an intermediate page ends pagination and returns only the pages accumulated in `result` so far. The internal retry in fetchOTCPage (lines 74-86) ONLY retries timeouts: line 80-81 gates on `isTimeout` and re-throws non-timeout errors immediately. So an HTTP 500 (get() rejects at line 44-45) or a JSON-parse error (line 91-92) or unexpected-shape error (line 113) on page 4 of 10 propagates straight to the loop catch and truncates pages 5-10. Crucially the partial pull is invisible upstream: the caller refresh-universe.js:328-368 uses Promise.allSettled and merges the returned Map; because the error is swallowed inside the function and a (smaller) Map is returned, the promise is `fulfilled` with no error field and no count — only a console.error remains. This is exactly the silent-shrink scenario the same file already guards against for the custom exchange screener (F-DP-037, refresh-universe.js:254-318, which tracks pageErrors per exchange and emits a `[WARN] ... possible silent failure`); the OTC puller has no equivalent. The auditor's mechanism, line numbers, and F-DP-037 comparison are all accurate.

title: JUNK_SUFFIX_RE applied to whole symbol drops legitimate common stocks ending in W/R/U (shared triplicated bug)
evidence: Line 25 `const JUNK_SUFFIX_RE = /[WRU]$|\.WS$|\.WT$|\.WI$|\.RT$|\.UN$|\.U$/i;` then line 70 `if (JUNK_SUFFIX_RE.test(symbol)) continue;` (parseNasdaqListed) and line 97 (parseOtherListed). The leading alternative `[WRU]$` matches ANY symbol whose last character is W, R, or U with no delimiter — so NU, BKU, EW, ARW, etc. are rejected as 'junk'. The comment (lines 22-24) intends only warrant/right/unit suffixes.
why_it_matters: Direct loss of real, listed common stocks from the authoritative NASDAQ-Trader feed — the highest-confidence US source. Same root regex bug as A-discovery-02 (nasdaq-api) and otc-markets:27. Triplicated, so a fix must touch all three (or be centralized).
fix: Replace `[WRU]$` with delimiter-anchored alternatives only (e.g. require a preceding `.`/`-` or a known 5th-char pattern), or rely on the structured columns the file already parses: nasdaqlisted.txt has explicit ETF (parts[6]) and Test Issue (parts[3]) columns and NextShares; warrants/units are better filtered by Security Name containing 'Warrant'/'Unit'/'Right' than by a lossy suffix regex. Centralize into one shared filter. Comment: 'prevents NU/BKU/EW-class common stocks being filtered as warrants'.

_verdict.note: CONFIRMED real. Verified against source at C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/discovery/nasdaq-all.js. Line 25 defines JUNK_SUFFIX_RE = /[WRU]$|\.WS$|.../i and it is applied to the whole symbol at line 70 (parseNasdaqListed) and line 97 (parseOtherListed). The leading alternative [WRU]$ requires NO delimiter, so it matches any symbol whose last char is W/R/U. Empirically confirmed with node: UBER, SNOW, LOW, DOW, PLTR, NU, BKU, EW, SU, NEW, ARW, BW, TW, CCU are all DROPPED as "junk" — these are real, liquid NASDAQ/NYSE common stocks, directly contradicting the comment at lines 22-24 (intent was only warrant/right/unit suffixes). The bug is actually quadruplicated, not triplicated: the same regex/usage appears in nasdaq-api.js:37 and otc-markets.js:27 as well (the finding's "shared triplicated" count refers to the 3 usages across the 2 NASDAQ files). Caller refresh-universe.js:328-368 uses first-write-wins merge across sources; SEC/Finnhub do NOT apply this filter, so some dropped commons can be recovered via those sources — but Finnhub needs an API key and SEC has its own dot/hyphen rejection, so coverage is not guaranteed and the canonical exchange listings still lose these tickers. Real bug, real impact on universe completeness. Medium severity is appropriate (silent under-coverage, partially mitigated by source overlap; not data corruption or crash).

title: --top arg parsed with parseInt and no NaN/radix guard -> bad arg silently empties the entire report
evidence: Line 54: `else if (argv[i] === '--top' && argv[i+1]) args.topN = parseInt(argv[++i]);`  topN then flows to every `valid.slice(0, topN)` (topByScore l.169, blockedByOneMust l.185) and `Math.min(st.allMustPass, args.topN)` (l.1291). Verified in node: `parseInt('abc')` -> NaN, and `[1,2,3].slice(0, NaN)` -> `[]`.
why_it_matters: A typo or non-numeric --top value (e.g. `--top all`, `--top 200px`, or an env-substituted empty/garbled value in CI) makes topN=NaN. Every picks/near-miss list becomes empty, the report renders with zero cards, yet the script exits 0 and the workflow treats it as success. The pipeline-health failure-rate gate (l.1309) only counts per-stock evaluation throws, not an empty output, so a silently empty user-facing artifact ships. parseInt also lacks a radix (a leading-zero value like `--top 010` would historically be misread; minor vs the NaN issue).
fix: Parse defensively: `const n = Number.parseInt(argv[++i], 10); if (Number.isInteger(n) && n > 0) args.topN = n; else { console.error('invalid --top'); process.exit(1); }`. Add a comment naming the failure mode: 'prevents NaN topN -> slice(0,NaN) -> silently empty report'.

_verdict.note: Confirmed by source + runtime. Line 54: `else if (argv[i] === '--top' && argv[i+1]) args.topN = parseInt(argv[++i]);` — no radix, no NaN/validity guard, no default fallback on parse failure. There is NO validation anywhere between parse and use (grep for isNaN/isFinite/Number.isInteger on topN: none). args.topN flows unguarded into valid.slice(0, topN) at topByScore L169, topByMethod L263, topAllMust L285; items.slice(0, topN) at blockedByOneMust L185; and Math.min(st.allMustPass, args.topN) at L1291. Runtime confirmed in node: parseInt('abc')->NaN, [1,2,3].slice(0,NaN)->[], Math.min(5,NaN)->NaN. So `--top abc` (or empty/typo) silently yields an empty report (every mode's pick + near-miss lists empty) and NaN all-MUST-pass counts in the console log, with no error and exit 0 — silent data loss. Real defect. Severity downgraded high->medium: the CI daily-pull.yml (L383) invokes the script WITHOUT --top, so the production pipeline always uses the safe default topN:200 and never triggers this. Trigger is confined to manual operator invocation with a malformed --top value; serious effect but narrow likelihood and zero production-path exposure = medium.

title: Modal KPI mislabels latest annual revenue as 'Rev TTM'
evidence:
Line 1066 `var revA = arrVals(ann.annualRev).slice().reverse();` (now oldest->newest). Line 1074 `'
Rev TTM
' + fmtM(revA[revA.length-1]) + '
'` -> takes the last (newest) ANNUAL revenue figure but labels it 'Rev TTM' (trailing-twelve-months).
why_it_matters: The newest annual revenue is not TTM unless the fiscal year happens to be complete and current. For any company mid-fiscal-year, or where annualRev[0] is a stale prior FY, the headline number Karl reads in the click-through modal is wrong by up to a year. This is a decision-facing number on the primary artifact; mislabeling fundamentals undermines trust in the whole screener. (Snapshots store revenueGrowthYoY separately, confirming TTM and latest-annual are distinct concepts here.)
fix: Either relabel to 'Rev (FY, latest)' to match what is actually shown, or compute true TTM from `timeseries.revenueQ` (sum of last 4 quarters) and label it 'Rev TTM'. Whichever is chosen, the label must match the source series.

_verdict.note: CONFIRMED real mislabel. generate-modes-report.js:1066 `var revA = arrVals(ann.annualRev).slice().reverse()` then :1074 renders `fmtM(revA[revA.length-1])` under the label "Rev TTM". ann.annualRev is unambiguously annual (fiscal-year) revenue, not trailing-twelve-months: it is built in pull-yahoo.js from totalRevenue financial history (line 618 `_arr(isHist,'totalRevenue')`, line 1105 `annualRev.push(rev!=null?{value:rev}:null)`) and is treated as annual everywhere else, including the adjacent chart at line 1077 "Revenue (annual, 5y)" which consumes the SAME revA array. A genuine TTM value exists as a distinct field stock.metrics.revenueTTM (pull-yahoo.js:892, FX-scaled per Tag 204 tests) — reachable in the modal scope (line 1075 already reads stock.metrics.revenueGrowthYoY). So the newest fiscal-year revenue is being labeled "Rev TTM", which can differ materially from true TTM for any company partway through a fiscal year. Severity revised high->medium: this is display-only in a click-to-open detail modal — read-only, isolated, does not corrupt stored snapshots, and does not feed screening/filtering or any downstream computation. fix_safe=false: the proposed fix is a choice between two NON-equivalent remedies — (a) relabel to "Rev (FY, latest)" is trivially safe and behavior-preserving, but (b) compute true TTM from metrics.revenueTTM or sum of last 4 revenueQ changes the displayed value and needs source selection plus null/short-series handling. A human should pick the path; not a clean auto-apply.

title: Per-stock and per-mode failures are caught and silently turned into null/skip; snapshot parse errors return null with no diagnostics
evidence: loadStocks l.96-99 `catch (e) { return null; }` — a corrupt/unreadable snapshot is dropped with zero logging. evaluateAll modeEvals l.123-124 `catch (e) { modeEvals[mId] = null; }` — a mode evaluation throw becomes a null mode with no record. Only the OUTER per-stock catch (l.127-130) records {ticker,error} into _pipelineFailures. The inner mode-level and file-level swallows feed nothing into the 5% health gate (l.1296-1309).
why_it_matters: The health gate (the one safety net, l.1309 process.exit(1) at >5%) only sees outer per-stock throws. A systematic bug that makes, say, every QUALITY_COMPOUNDER evaluation throw would set modeEvals.QUALITY_COMPOUNDER=null for all stocks — QC silently shows zero/garbage picks, failure_rate stays 0%, gate passes, ships green. Likewise a batch of unparseable snapshots silently shrinks the universe with no count discrepancy surfaced. This is the 'silently swallowed errors' class: the screener can be badly degraded while every signal says healthy.
fix: Count and surface inner failures: increment a per-mode error counter in the l.123 catch and a parse-error counter in loadStocks, include both in the pipeline-health JSON (l.1305) and factor them into the threshold. At minimum console.warn each swallow with ticker+mode+message so CI logs show it.

_verdict.note:
CONFIRMED real. All three claims hold against source in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/generate-modes-report.js:

1) loadStocks l.96-99: `catch (e) { return null; }` — a file that fails readFile/JSON.parse returns null, is filtered out at l.102 (`if (p !== null && typeof p === 'object' ...)`), and never logs. Critically, n_total for the health gate is `stocks.length` (l.1296) = the POST-filter count, so a dropped/corrupt snapshot is not counted as a failure — it disappears from the denominator. A systematic snapshot-format break could silently shrink the universe while the gate reports ~0% failed on the survivors. No console.warn.

2) evaluateAll l.122-125: a per-mode throw becomes `modeEvals[mId] = null`. The stock is still pushed (l.126). Every downstream consumer guards null (l.166 `if (me && me.score != null)`, l.179 `if (!me ...) continue`, l.252/270/294, computeCrossProfileTags l.141), so a null mode silently drops the stock from that mode's eligibility/ranking with no record. Nothing reaches _pipelineFailures.

3) The outer per-stock catch (l.127-130) is the ONLY path that pushes into _pipelineFailures, and _pipelineFailures is the sole input to the 5% health gate (l.1297, l.1305, l.1309). So both inner swallows are invisible to the gate and produce zero diagnostics. Confirmed.

This is an observability / silent-degradation gap rather than active corruption — the outer gate still catches whole-stock failures. Medium is appropriate; the loadStocks denominator blind spot is the part that actually weakens the CI gate.

fix_safe=false: The fix bundles two things. The logging half (console.warn each swallow with ticker+mode+message; add parse-error + per-mode error counters into the health JSON at l.1305) is purely additive and behavior-preserving. But 'factor them into the threshold' (l.1309) changes the CI exit-code semantics of the 5% gate — runs that previously passed could newly fail, and these thresholds/accounting are hand-tuned (Tag 168 / F-ME-024 history). Changing what counts toward n_total / the gate needs human review, so the proposed fix as written is not safe to auto-apply. Recommend splitting: auto-apply the logging + JSON counters; defer any gate-math change to Karl.

title: res.json() on the 429 path runs with no timeout — a hung response body can block CI, the exact failure this module was built to prevent
evidence: const ctrl ... timer = setTimeout(() => ctrl.abort(), timeoutMs); ... } finally { clearTimeout(timer); }  inside _postOnce (line 57-67). Then in postDiscord: `try { const j = await res.json(); ... } catch (_) {}` at line 102. By the time res is returned, _postOnce's finally has already cleared the abort timer, so this body read has no timeout and the signal is no longer armed.
why_it_matters: The module's stated reason for existing (header lines 11-13) is 'a hung Discord webhook can't block CI'. The headers arrive (status 429) but a stalled/slow body stream on res.json() will hang indefinitely with the timer gone. Discord 429 bodies are tiny so this is rare, but it reopens precisely the hang vector the AbortController was added to close.
fix: Read the body under its own timeout, or skip the JSON body entirely and rely on the retry-after header (header is in seconds and already handled at line 99-100). Simplest: wrap the res.json() in Promise.race with a short timeout, or move the body read inside _postOnce before the timer is cleared. Comment: '// prevents CI hang — body read must stay under the same hard timeout as the request'.

_verdict.note: CONFIRMED real. File C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/lib/discord.js. _postOnce (lines 55-68) arms an AbortController timer (line 57) and clears it in finally (line 66) before returning res. Node's fetch (undici) resolves the promise on response HEADERS, leaving the body as a lazily-consumed stream. So when postDiscord reaches `await res.json()` on the 429 path (line 102), the abort timer has already been cleared and nothing remains to fire the signal — the body read runs with no timeout. A 429 whose body stalls (proxy/middlebox/Discord glitch) hangs postDiscord indefinitely. The sole caller pattern is bare `await postDiscord(msg)` (e.g. check-pull-stats.js:151, picks-regression-check.js:150/173) with no outer timeout, so nothing else bounds it. This is exactly the CI-hang failure mode the module documents as its reason for existing (lines 12-13, 36-37). Two minor caveats, neither of which refutes the finding: (1) the auditor's phrase "the signal is no longer armed" is slightly imprecise — in undici the signal WOULD still abort an in-flight body read if fired, but the timer that would fire it is cleared, so the net effect (unbounded body read) is exactly as claimed; (2) real-world probability is low because Discord normally returns a small JSON body promptly, which is why medium (not high) is correct. fix_safe=false: the proposed fixes are sensible but not strictly behavior-preserving — Promise.race with a short timeout could discard a legitimately slow-but-valid body (changing the computed wait), and the cleanest variant (reading the body inside _postOnce under the existing timer) alters the shared helper's contract. The body only ever raises waitMs via Math.max and the retry-after header (lines 99-100) is already handled, so a body-read timeout is safe in principle, but it should go through human review rather than auto-apply. No regression test currently covers the 429-then-retry body-read path (no discord*.test.js exists), so a test should accompany the fix.

title: AGE-NEUTRAL durability test is a tautology for the exact short-history regime the metric claims to fix
evidence: Line 159-161: `const base = [0.5,...,0.3]; // 12 newest-first` then `const olderTailDiffers = base.concat([9, 9, 9]);` and `assert(_durV3(base) === _durV3(olderTailDiffers), 'ältere Historie jenseits W=12 darf durV3 NICHT ändern')`. Because base already has 12 elements, `slice(0, _WCAP=12)` discards the appended tail unconditionally — the assertion is trivially true for ANY appended values. I reproduced this: with a 3-element base, `_durV3([0.5,0.4,0.3])`=0.6 but `_durV3([0.5,0.4,0.3,9,9,9])`=0.084 — durV3 IS history-coupled when the window is not yet full.
why_it_matters: The metric's headline claim is 'strikt alters-/längen-neutral' and the test file (line 12-15, 105-111) sells age-neutrality as the fix for the Youth-Bias that got v2 Court-DENIED. But young IPO leaders (ALAB has only 2 annual rows per the fixtures; CRDO 3) are precisely the names with <12 quarters, where durV3 falls back through `gYoYDur = (revQYoYsec.length >= 4 ? revQYoYsec : gSeriesA).slice(0, DUR_W)` to a short window — and there the metric is NOT length-neutral. The regression gate that is supposed to lock in the fix never tests that regime, so a real age/length leak for short-history names ships green. The companion LÄNGEN-NEUTRAL test (line 149-153) has the same blind spot (12-element `recent`).
fix: Add an assertion over a <12-element base, e.g. assert that durV3 of a 6-quarter young name is computed ONLY from those 6 quarters and document that names with winN<12 are NOT length-comparable (the code already lamps 'short-durability-window' at winN<12 in court-score.js:236 — the test should assert that lamp fires and that cross-sectional ranking treats short-window names as not-fully-comparable, rather than asserting a neutrality the metric does not have for them).

_verdict.note: Confirmed with source + numeric reproduction. court-score-tests.js:159-161: `base` has exactly 12 elements, so `base.concat([9,9,9])` then the slice(0,_WCAP=12) inside _durV3 discards the appended tail unconditionally — verified the assert `_durV3(base)===_durV3(olderTailDiffers)` holds for ANY tail ([9,9,9], [NaN,1e9], [-99] all slice-equal). The "AGE-NEUTRAL" assertion thus tests that Array.slice works, not age-neutrality. title: Unguarded fs.readdirSync(CACHE) throws raw ENOENT when fundamentals-cache is absent — no actionable error, and a partial/empty cache produces an empty candidate set with no alarm
evidence: Line 63: `const files = fs.readdirSync(CACHE).filter(...)`. Verified: with the cache dir absent, the process dies with `Error: ENOENT ... scandir '...\fundamentals-cache'` and a stack trace, which is what court-score-tests.js:38 surfaces as an opaque execSync failure. There is no check that `files.length > 0` or that `stats.passed > 0` before writing the output.
why_it_matters: Two failure modes: (1) missing cache -> cryptic ENOENT that the regression gate reports as a generic 'Command failed: node court-screen.js' with no hint that the cache is the problem (I hit exactly this). (2) Worse — a PARTIALLY pulled or empty cache (a real risk given the 14.6h pull can be interrupted) yields `candidates: []` and the script writes a valid-looking JSON with count 0 and exits 0. court-score then ranks an empty universe and the daily report shows nothing, with no error. Silent empty-output on a truncated upstream pull is a classic data-integrity hole for this pipeline.
fix: Wrap the readdir in a check: if (!fs.existsSync(CACHE)) throw new Error('fundamentals-cache missing — run the pull first'); and after the loop assert a sane floor (e.g. stats.parsed >= expectedMin or stats.passed > 0) before writeFileSync, exiting non-zero with a clear message otherwise. This converts a silent empty screen into a loud, gated failure. Comment: 'guards truncated/empty cache from producing a silent empty candidate set'.

CONFIRMED real in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening. Both claims verified against source + live run.

Claim 1 (unguarded readdir → raw ENOENT): TRUE. court-screen.js:63 `const files = fs.readdirSync(CACHE).filter(...)` has no existsSync guard. The cited caller court-score-tests.js:38 invokes it via `execSync('node court-screen.js', { stdio: 'ignore', env })`, so even the raw ENOENT text is swallowed and surfaces only as an opaque execSync throw — exactly as the auditor described.

Corroborating evidence the guard is the house pattern: the sibling production consumer of the SAME directory, generate-screener.js:86, does `if (!fs.existsSync(dir)) return [];` before its readdirSync (line 88). court-screen.js is the inconsistent omission.

Claim 2 (partial/empty cache → silent empty candidate set, no alarm): TRUE and the more material half. If CACHE exists but is empty/truncated, `files` is [], the loop yields zero candidates, and line 191 still `writeFileSync`s a well-formed output with `count: 0`/`stats.passed: 0` and exits 0. There is no `files.length > 0` / `stats.passed > 0` floor anywhere before the write. A genuine silent-data-integrity path.

Severity: medium is fair. The crash half is loud/self-correcting, but the silent-empty-output half is a real data-integrity gap (a downstream stage would consume an empty screen as if valid).

title: "top-decile" cohort is computed from universeSize (5657) but applied to the 81-pick ranking — silently collapses to "all picks"
evidence: `const cohortNDecile = Math.ceil(0.10 * universeSize);` (line 144) where universeSize=5657 → cohortNDecile=566. It is then passed as `cohortSpread(rankingEntries, returnByTickerNaive, { cohortN: cohortNDecile, label: 'top-decile' })` (line 149) but rankingEntries has only 81 entries (verified: full-hypergrowth-2026-05-14.json ranking.length=81, evaluatedTickers.length=5657). In cohortSpread the loop `if (cohortReturns.length >= cohortN) break;` never trips, so the 'decile' cohort = the entire pick list.
why_it_matters: cohortSpread_decile is reported as a distinct, more-robust metric next to cohortSpread_top8, but it is mathematically identical to 'mean of all picks minus universe median' for every real baseline (picks always << 10% of a 5657 universe). The dashboard/reader believes they are seeing a genuine top-decile concentration signal; they are seeing the whole cohort. A 10%-of-universe decile only makes sense against the universe's returns, not against an already-top-sliced 81-name pick list. This is exactly the kind of silently-degenerate metric that keeps the screener at '20% of potential' — a headline number that looks like signal but carries none.
fix: Decide what the decile is a decile OF and make it explicit. If the intent is top-10%-of-picks, use `Math.max(1, Math.ceil(0.10 * rankingEntries.length))`. If the intent is universe-decile, the metric must be a quantile of universe returns, not a cohortSpread over the 81 picks. Add a comment naming the failure mode: '// prevents decile cohort silently equalling the full pick list when picks << universe'. Also surface cohortN_used in the summary so a collapsed cohort is observable.

_verdict.note: CONFIRMED real via empirical run against the actual baselines in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening. The metric reported as `cohortSpread_decile` (labeled 'top-decile') is therefore NOT a decile of anything; it is "all picks vs universe median," mislabeled. Same collapse occurs for full-quality_compounder (23 picks, cohortNDecile=566) and full-turnaround (59 picks). Note: the `label:'top-decile'` arg is silently ignored — cohortSpread never reads opts.label. Two nuances that soften "high"→medium: (1) the collapse is only PARTIALLY silent — cohortN_used IS surfaced in the stored metric object and cohortDefinition.cohortNDecile=566 is also stored, so cohortN_used=81 vs 566 is observable to a careful reader; but no flag/warning fires and the console summary never prints the decile, so in a normal run it is effectively invisible. title: Baseline omits the vintage asOf timestamp and the per-universe scores, structurally preventing measure.js from ever fixing the entry-look-ahead (A-fitness-03) or computing universe-wide IC (A-fitness-04)
evidence: The baseline object (lines 78-99) stores frozenAt (date only), mode, ranking (top picks: rank/ticker/score) and evaluatedTickers (ticker strings only — no scores). why_it_matters: This is the structural cap behind two of the higher findings. Because the freeze step discards the asOf timestamp, measure.js cannot apply getEntryDate's pre-close shift (look-ahead, A-fitness-03). Because it discards universe scores, measure.js cannot compute selection-power IC over the full universe (A-fitness-04) — only within-cohort discrimination. The harness's own 'honest signal' ambition is bounded by what the freeze chooses to persist.
fix: Persist `asOf: vintage.asOf` and an `evaluatedScores` map (or include score on each evaluatedTicker entry) in the baseline. This is purely additive to the artifact (no scoring change, no FTS_CACHE_VERSION touch, measure.js still read-only). It unblocks A-fitness-03 and A-fitness-04 without violating any binding constraint.

_verdict.note:
CONFIRMED real, but the proposed fix is only half-safe. Verified against source in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening.

Facts confirmed:

Since asOf is ~18:29 UTC (post-session), entry on the frozenAt close is a look-ahead that downstream code cannot detect or correct without asOf. Correct.

Why fix_safe=false (the auditor's safety framing is wrong for half the fix):
- The asOf half (asOf: vintage.asOf) IS purely additive, trivial, behavior-preserving — fine to auto-apply.

Net: the finding is real (artifact structurally precludes both downstream fixes), severity medium is fair (it limits a read-only measurement artifact, not live screener output), but the proposed fix should not be auto-applied as written — only the asOf addition is safe; evaluatedScores cannot be populated additively.

title: cmdAdd never writes added_at → prune-watchlist's no-snapshot grace period can never fire
evidence: The stock object created in cmdAdd has only {isin, ticker, yahoo_symbol, name, track_hint} (lines 50-56) — no added_at/addedAt. cmdImport (lines 93-99) is the same. Cross-file: scripts/prune-watchlist.js:164-184 only prunes a no-snapshot ticker when `const addedAt = entry.added_at || entry.addedAt || null; if (addedAt) { ... ageDays > pruneNoDataDays ... }`. With addedAt null it falls straight through to `kept.push(entry)`. Live data confirms the blast radius: 4017 of 23748 watchlist entries currently have no added_at.
why_it_matters: F-DP-022 (the 'no-snapshot-after-Nd' prune rule) is dead for every ticker this CLI adds, because the timestamp it keys on is never set. Tickers that never produce a snapshot (bad symbol, delisted-on-arrival, Yahoo never returns data) accumulate forever unless --prune-orphans is run (which the workflow never passes, and which the code itself warns is irreversible mass-deletion). This is the upstream root cause of the orphan buildup the prune script's own comments lament ('audit found 12 207 orphans').
fix: In cmdAdd and cmdImport set `added_at: new Date().toISOString()` on the new stock object. This is the guard-side fix prune already expects — no hardcoded exclusions needed.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed by source. watchlist-cli.js cmdAdd (lines 50-56) builds {isin, ticker, yahoo_symbol, name, track_hint} and cmdImport (lines 93-99) builds {isin, ticker, yahoo_symbol, name, track_hint} — neither sets added_at/addedAt. In prune-watchlist.js the no-snapshot branch (lines 164-184) reads `const addedAt = entry.added_at || entry.addedAt || null; if (addedAt) {... ageDays > pruneNoDataDays ...}`; with addedAt null the F-DP-022 grace-period prune is skipped and, with pruneOrphans off (the default), the entry falls through to kept.push(entry). So a CLI-added no-snapshot ticker can never be pruned by the no-data grace period — exactly as claimed. Live data reproduced precisely: 4017 of 23748 watchlist entries currently lack added_at.

The design intent is corroborated: the OTHER watchlist writer, refresh-universe.js:446, already sets `added_at: new Date().toISOString()` on every auto-added ticker, and prune reads that field — so the CLI is the inconsistent path, not prune. This strengthens (does not refute) the finding.

Severity revised high -> medium: the effect is conservative — affected entries are KEPT forever rather than wrongly deleted (no data corruption, no crash, no wrong screener output). It is guard erosion / watchlist bloat, and only the no-snapshot+aged subset of the 4017 is actually affected (entries that later get a snapshot are handled by the deadReason path regardless of added_at). pruneOrphans (--prune-orphans) can still evict them in hard mode, so it is not strictly unremovable.

fix_safe true: setting `added_at: new Date().toISOString()` on the two new-stock object literals is purely additive and behavior-preserving — cmdExport ignores unknown fields, the field name matches what refresh-universe writes and prune reads, and no existing consumer breaks. Caveat (does not block auto-apply): the fix is forward-only; the 4017 pre-existing entries without added_at would still need a one-time backfill, which is out of scope for this guard-side change.

title: One corrupt/truncated methods-history file aborts the entire cleanup run (no per-file guard)

_verdict.note: Confirmed real. In C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/suggest-watchlist-cleanup.js lines 33-40, the loop does `const data = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(...))` and then `Object.entries(data.stocks)` with no try/catch and no existence check. main() has no surrounding catch, so one corrupt/truncated vintage throws SyntaxError (parse) or TypeError (Object.entries on undefined when `stocks` is absent) and aborts the entire cleanup scan. The truncation hazard is concrete, not hypothetical: snapshot-methods-history.js documents (Tag 217e, and Tag 232c-5 / F-SM-002) that pre-atomic-write a SIGKILL mid-write left truncated files; writeFileAtomic only protects FUTURE writes, not the older committed vintages already in methods-history/. Notably the sibling writer already uses exactly the defensive pattern proposed: loadFilesAsync in snapshot-methods-history.js wraps each JSON.parse in try/catch returning {data:null,error} and skips null entries — so per-file resilience is an established codebase convention that this script diverges from.

title: --threshold parses with no isFinite guard → bad input silently yields zero suggestions
evidence: `else if (argv[i] === '--threshold' && argv[i+1]) args.threshold = parseInt(argv[++i], 10);` (line 23). parseInt('abc',10) → NaN. Downstream `results.filter(r => r.pass >= args.threshold)` (line 124) is always false for NaN (verified: [{pass:12}].filter(r=>r.pass>=NaN) → []). The header even advertises `--threshold 10`.

No error, no signal. NaN-propagation with no isFinite guard is exactly the class flagged in the brief.

In C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/suggest-watchlist-additions.js line 23, `--threshold` is parsed via `parseInt(argv[++i], 10)` with no validation. parseInt('abc',10) -> NaN (verified in node). At line 124 `results.filter(r => r.pass >= args.threshold)` evaluates `12 >= NaN` as false for every row (verified: [{pass:12}].filter(r=>r.pass>=NaN) -> []), so bad input silently yields zero suggestions, prints 'Keine Kandidaten erfüllen die Schwelle.', and writes suggested-additions.json with threshold:null — no error raised. The same class of bug exists in suggest-watchlist-cleanup.js (lines 15-16): `--min-runs abc`/`--threshold-pct abc` -> NaN poisons the `files.length < NaN` (false), `slice(-NaN)` (returns full array), and `ratio*100 < NaN` (false) checks, also silently producing zero candidates. Severity medium is fair: these are interactive CLI dev tools (Tag 62/74 watchlist helpers), not the core scoring pipeline, so blast radius is limited, but the silent-wrong-result failure mode on a plausible typo is genuinely misleading.

title: Pipeline-health failure_rate understates eval failures 3x — denominator is stock×mode but eval failures counted once
evidence: Eval failures: `catch (e) { _pipelineFailures.push({ ticker, error: e.message }); }` (line 215, ONE push per stock). Denominator: `const n_total = stocks.length * 3;` (line 305, '3 modes × universe size'); `const n_failed = _pipelineFailures.length;` (line 306); `failure_rate = n_failed / n_total` (line 308); hard-fails at >0.05 (line 316).
why_it_matters: A stock that throws in Runner.evaluateStock contributes 1 to n_failed but 3 to n_total (it is skipped in all 3 mode loops via `if (!results) continue` at line 242, so it never adds the other 2). The 5% CI gate therefore divides apples (per-stock failures) by oranges (stock×mode slots), understating the true evaluation-failure rate by up to 3x. If 10% of the universe fails to evaluate, the reported rate is ~3.3% and the gate passes — masking a real Yahoo/engine breakage the gate exists to catch.
fix: Make numerator and denominator consistent. Simplest: count eval failures against a universe denominator (n_total = stocks.length) for the eval stage, and track per-mode pick failures separately; or multiply each eval failure by 3 when using the stock×mode denominator. Document which semantic the 5% threshold is calibrated to.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed real by source reading of C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/snapshot-picks.js. The single `_pipelineFailures` array is fed by TWO sites with different cardinalities: (a) eval stage, lines 209-217, loops once per stock and pushes at most ONE failure per stock on a Runner.evaluateStock throw; (b) pick stage, lines 236-249, runs inside the 3-mode loop and pushes up to ONE failure per stock×mode. The denominator at line 305 is `n_total = stocks.length * 3` (stock×mode pairs), and failure_rate = _pipelineFailures.length / n_total (line 308), hard-failing at >0.05 (line 316). An eval failure additionally suppresses the stock in all 3 modes (line 242 `if (!results) continue`), so it costs 3 pick-slots but is counted as 1 — i.e. eval failures are understated 3x against the stated denominator semantics. Direction matters: this makes the 5% gate LESS likely to fire, so a genuine systemic eval-failure event (e.g. ~4% of stocks crashing in evaluateStock, a real pipeline regression) records as ~1.33% and slips under the gate silently. That is exactly the data-integrity masking the category describes. Corroboration: the sibling script snapshot-methods-history.js implements the consistent pattern (n_total = fileList.length, exactly one push per stock at lines 100/107), and carries a prior audit-fix comment (Tag 228b-3 / F-227c-06) showing the project already treats pipeline-health denominator/numerator consistency as a tracked bug class. Severity medium (low end): no corrupted data reaches downstream consumers — only the health-gate sensitivity is weakened, and catastrophic (>15% eval-failure) events still trip the gate; the masking bites in the 5-15% degraded band the gate exists to catch.

fix_safe=false: the proposed fix is NOT behavior-preserving. It deliberately changes when the CI gate hard-fails (line 316/318 -> process.exit(1)), and the proposal itself offers three different semantics and explicitly says to 'document which semantic the 5% threshold is calibrated to.' Choosing among them affects whether real production runs start failing CI, so it needs human recalibration/review, not an auto-apply.

title: Marketplace OpInc-lag filter divides by rev[0]/rev[1] with no zero/finite guard; SaaS filter trusts _toNumber but gap math can mislead on huge magnitudes
evidence: Filter 4: `const oiMargin0 = oi[0] / rev[0] * 100; const oiMargin1 = oi[1] / rev[1] * 100;` (lines 154-155). Guard above is only `if (rev[1] <= 0) return null;` (line 147) and `if (rev.length < 2 || oi.length < 2) return null;` (line 146). rev[0] (the NEWEST year — confirmed via methods/rule-of-40.js where annualFCF[0] is 'the most recent annual FCF') is never checked for 0 or negative. _arrayValues filters out null/NaN but a legitimate 0 revenue survives.
why_it_matters: If the newest annual revenue rev[0] is exactly 0 (shell/early-stage marketplace, or a Yahoo zero-fill artifact), oiMargin0 = oi[0]/0 = ±Infinity, marginDelta = ±Infinity, and the `marginDelta < -5` test (line 159) either fires or not based on sign noise, emitting a garbage magnitude (-marginDelta = ∓Infinity) into the reasonCode detail. revGrowth at line 149 is guarded (rev[1]<=0 returns), but rev[0]=0 is not. The filter is INFO-only today so no score penalty, but the magnitude/detail string is surfaced to the user as evidence — an Infinity 'OpInc-Margin' flag is a credibility bug, and the Tag-9 plan to convert these to penalties would turn it into a scoring bug.
fix: Guard the newest year too before dividing: `if (!(rev[0] > 0) || !(rev[1] > 0)) return null;` and assert Number.isFinite(marginDelta) before building the result. Add the failure-mode comment required by the binding constraints, e.g. '// prevents Infinity OpInc-margin when newest annual revenue is 0 (Yahoo zero-fill / pre-revenue shell)'.
