title: alphaAvg/median dereference null cohort returns → NaN propagation when one cohort is empty
evidence: Line 40 `function avg(arr){ return arr.length ? ... : null; }` and Line 41-45 `median` also returns null on empty. Line 59-60: `const alphaAvg = avg(passReturns) - avg(failReturns); const alphaMed = median(passReturns) - median(failReturns);` If either cohort is empty, `avg`/`median` returns `null`, and `null - number` → NaN (or `null - null` → 0, a false 'zero alpha'). Lines 49-50/55-56 also call `(avg(passReturns)*100).toFixed(2)` unconditionally → `(null*100)` = 0 printed as '0.00%', or `(NaN).toFixed` printing 'NaN%'.
why_it_matters: No `isFinite` guard before arithmetic or `.toFixed`. With a small or skewed snapshot set (very common during the universe-expansion runs described in CONTEXT.md, or when threshold is extreme), one cohort is routinely empty. The script then either prints 'NaN%'/'0.00%' as a real alpha or writes `alphaAvg: NaN` to backtest-10w-result.json (NaN serializes to `null` in JSON, masking that the computation was invalid). Compare backtest-10-weeks.js line 167 which explicitly guards `passCohort.length > 0 && failCohort.length > 0` — this sibling script lacks that guard.
fix: Guard like the sibling: `const alphaAvg = (passReturns.length && failReturns.length) ? avg(passReturns)-avg(failReturns) : null;` and only `.toFixed` when the value is finite (`pa!=null ? (pa*100).toFixed(2) : '—'`).

title: Total-return uses '|| close' fallback that swaps adjClose↔close inconsistently between endpoints
evidence: Line 57-58: `const first = hist[0].adjClose || hist[0].close; const last = hist[hist.length-1].adjClose || hist[hist.length-1].close;` The `||` falsy fallback is evaluated independently per endpoint. If only one end of the window has `adjClose` populated (Yahoo occasionally omits adjClose on the most recent bar or on thinly-traded intl tickers), the return mixes an adjusted price against a raw price.
why_it_matters: adjClose is split/dividend-adjusted; close is not. Mixing them across a 5-year window where a split occurred produces a return off by the split factor (e.g. a 4:1 split shows as a fake +300% or -75%). Because `||` also treats a legitimate `adjClose === 0` as missing, a genuine zero (delisting artifact) would silently fall back to raw close. This feeds the 1/3/5Y median outperformance-vs-SPY verdict that Karl reads as the screener's headline sanity check.
fix: Pick ONE basis for both endpoints: prefer adjClose for total return and require it on both bars (`if (first==null || last==null || first<=0) return null;`), or fall back to close on BOTH ends together — never one each. Use explicit `!= null` checks instead of `||` so a 0 is handled deliberately.

title: newState.lastRun ignores RUN_DATE_UTC, desyncing committed state timestamp from the frozen run date used everywhere else
evidence: Line 351: `const today = process.env.RUN_DATE_UTC || new Date().toISOString().slice(0,10);` (correctly honors the workflow's frozen date). But line 424: `lastRun: new Date().toISOString(),` uses raw wall-clock, NOT RUN_DATE_UTC. All per-method `lastChanged` stamps use `today` (frozen), while `lastRun` uses live time.
why_it_matters: daily-pull.yml line 51-55 deliberately freezes RUN_DATE_UTC at job start precisely because the ~3-4h pull can cross UTC midnight (the workflow comment calls this out as a HIGH bug: snapshot-* scripts disagreeing on TODAY). detect-changes correctly uses the frozen date for `today`/`lastChanged` but then writes a `lastRun` that can be a different calendar day. Any consumer comparing `lastRun` against the frozen-date vintages (or the 30-day prune cutoff in saveState line 141-143, which is also live-clock based) can be off by a day across midnight, the same failure class the freeze was meant to kill.
fix: Derive lastRun from the same frozen source: `lastRun: (process.env.RUN_DATE_UTC ? process.env.RUN_DATE_UTC + 'T00:00:00Z' : new Date().toISOString())`. Likewise base the saveState 30-day cutoff on RUN_DATE_UTC when present so prune and stamp agree.

title: Method evaluation reads snapshot by s.ticker but price pull uses s.yahoo_symbol — silent cohort/return mismatch risk
evidence: Line 77 `const snapPath = './snapshots/' + s.ticker + '.json';` (methods from ticker) but line 86 `const quotes = await pullPrices(s.yahoo_symbol, ...)` (prices from yahoo_symbol). If `s.yahoo_symbol` is missing/undefined for any watchlist entry, `pullPrices(undefined,...)` calls `yf.chart(undefined,...)` which throws and is swallowed by the try/catch returning null (line 45), so the stock is dropped at line 88 'skip (no prices)'.
why_it_matters: Two different identifiers key the two halves of each row. Entries lacking yahoo_symbol are silently and asymmetrically dropped from the cohort — survivorship attrition correlated with data-completeness (older/intl tickers most likely to lack yahoo_symbol), which biases the very pass-vs-fail alpha being measured. The catch-returns-null on line 45 hides the cause entirely (no log of WHICH tickers failed or why).
fix: Validate `s.yahoo_symbol` (fall back to s.ticker) before pulling, and log dropped tickers with the reason. Distinguish 'pull threw' from 'pull returned empty' in the catch so silent attrition is observable. Add comment naming the failure mode: 'prevents data-completeness-correlated survivorship bias in the cohort.'

title: Threshold sweep multiplies by (1+pct/100), so methods with negative or zero default threshold sweep the wrong direction or not at all
evidence: Line 47 `const defaultT = method.threshold;` line 50 `const t = defaultT * (1 + pct/100);`. For a method with `threshold: 0` (e.g. a sign/zero-crossing guard) every swept `t` is 0 — the sweep is degenerate (all 11 rows identical). For a NEGATIVE threshold (e.g. an accrual/Sloan guard whose pass band is `value <= -0.x`, or the MELI -20.6% case noted in CONTEXT.md), `defaultT*(1+pct/100)` moves the threshold the OPPOSITE way from what the +/- label implies (a '+50%' row makes a negative threshold MORE negative, i.e. stricter, while labelling it as a loosening).
why_it_matters: tune-threshold is the human-in-the-loop calibration tool Karl uses to pick thresholds. A multiplicative sweep silently produces meaningless or inverted columns for any method whose default threshold is <= 0, and there are sign-aware guards in this codebase (CONTEXT.md Tag 225a documents a sign-aware Sloan rule). The operator would read a pass-rate curve that is backwards and mis-calibrate the guard.
fix: Sweep additively in value-space rather than multiplicatively: derive step from the observed value distribution (e.g. `t = defaultT + pct/100 * (maxV-minV)`), or special-case threshold<=0 to an absolute additive sweep. Print the raw value distribution percentiles so the operator sees where the threshold actually bites regardless of sign.

title: Self-documented concurrency race: workflow_dispatch gets a per-run group while cron uses 'main-push', so a manual run and a scheduled run push to main simultaneously — the fetch→rebase→push loop is not atomic and can still livelock or lose the last attempt
evidence: concurrency group (line 20): `github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' && format('manual-{0}', github.run_id) || 'main-push'`. The Pipeline Health Check comment (line 642-644) explicitly states: 'concurrent pushes ARE possible via the manual dispatch escape hatch (workflow_dispatch gets its own concurrency group, so a manual run can race a scheduled cron run).' The push loop (line 600-633) does `git fetch origin main; git rebase --autostash origin/main; git push` up to 3× with `sleep $((5*i))`. Between two concurrent jobs each doing fetch+rebase+push, both can fetch the same base, rebase onto it, and race on push — the loser retries, but with only 3 attempts and 5/10/15s linear backoff, a sustained race (both jobs cherry-picking large -A commits) can exhaust retries on the manual run and exit 1 (line 634-635).
why_it_matters: The design accepts the race deliberately, but 3 attempts with linear backoff is thin for two ~40MB `git add -A` commits (methods-history is 14MB/file per line 550). If the manual dispatch loses all 3 it exits non-zero and its full day of snapshots/manual-expansion never lands, with only a Discord alert. The monthly-sec-xbrl pushes to the SAME 'main-push' group and on the 1st fires while a daily run may still be in flight (daily timeout is 240min from 02:17 UTC = until ~06:17; monthly at 08:00 — usually safe, but a slow 7h Yahoo day, which line 330 says has happened, pushes the daily past 08:00 and both contend).
fix: Increase retry count to ~5 with exponential+jitter backoff for the dispatch path, or serialize ALL push paths through a single mutex group with a short queue timeout for manual runs (the original concern was eviction on the free plan — solve that with a bounded queue, not by removing serialization). At minimum, on final push failure, persist the unpushed commit SHA to an artifact so the run is recoverable rather than only Discord-announced.

title: Run Yahoo Pull step timeout (165 min) leaves essentially zero margin under PULL_CONCURRENCY=8, so a normal-length pull is one Yahoo hiccup away from SIGKILL — and the budget comment contradicts the configured value
evidence: Job timeout is 240min (line 33). The comment (line 26-32) says conc=8 'made Yahoo Pull take ~163min' and raised the JOB budget to 240 'so the downstream chain has ~75min of breathing room.' But the Run Yahoo Pull STEP itself is capped at `timeout-minutes: 165` (line 211) while the env sets `PULL_CONCURRENCY: '8'` (line 42). 163min observed vs 165min cap = 2min margin. The coverage comments (line 346-354, Tag 233) further state that at conc=8/165min the pull only completes ~3300/24000 snapshots and partial=true 'became the norm'.
why_it_matters: The system is tuned to a knife-edge: any Yahoo slowdown beyond the observed 163min trips the 165min step SIGKILL mid-write, producing partial=true manifests that the coverage gate then has to be progressively relaxed to tolerate (13% floor, Tag 233). The screener is operating at a small fraction of its universe (3300/24000 = 13.8%) primarily because the concurrency was dropped to 8 to dodge Cloudflare 429s, and the time budget was never restructured. This is a top structural cap on 'the screener at 20% of potential' — coverage is literally ~14% of the universe per run.
fix: Decouple wall-time from a single monolithic step: shard the universe across parallel matrix jobs (e.g. 4 shards × conc=8 each hitting Yahoo from independent runners) so aggregate throughput rises without raising per-runner concurrency past Cloudflare's threshold. Each shard writes a partition of snapshots/, then a fan-in job builds the manifest. This raises real coverage toward 100% without changing the conc=8 rate-limit safety. Until then, raise the step timeout to match the 240 job budget minus measured downstream time, and stop relaxing the coverage gate as the universe grows.

title: SEC coverage gate's error-rate denominator excludes the unattempted tail after the pull self-aborts at >50 errors, so a real all-403 collapse that aborts early can slip under the 50% threshold when prior 404s pad the denominator
evidence: pull-sec-xbrl.js:173 aborts with `if (errors > 50) { ...break; }` — it stops after the 51st error. The gate (monthly line 106) computes `attempted = ok + nf + err` and fails if `err / attempted > 0.5`. `nf` (notFound/404) is counted as a real attempt. Consider a run where SEC starts returning 404 for delisted CIKs (legitimate, nf grows) and then flips to 403/timeout: by the time errors hit 51 the script breaks, but if it had already accumulated e.g. nf=60 before the 403 storm, attempted=51+60+ok, err/attempted can be <0.5 even though the pull is now fully broken. The gate passes, manifest commits with err=51, and the all-403 regression the gate was rewritten (line 75-87) to catch is missed.
why_it_matters: The gate's stated job (line 86-87) is to 'still catch the all-403 collapse (err=51/pulled=0)'. It does catch the PURE collapse (pulled=0,nf=0 → ratio 1.0), but the early-abort at 51 errors plus 404-padding creates a window where a genuine mid-run auth/UA regression is masked. SEC XBRL feeds fundamentals; a silently-degraded monthly pull means stale company-facts propagate for a full month until the next run.
fix: Gate on the absolute success count and the abort flag, not only the ratio: also fail if the pull aborted-on-errors (surface a `summary.abortedOnErrors:true` from pull-sec-xbrl.js:173) OR if `pulled + skipped304 == 0` while `err >= 50`. Exclude notFound from the error-rate denominator (404 is a legitimate outcome, not a fetch health signal): use `err / (err + pulled + skipped304 + skippedFresh)` so 404 padding cannot dilute the error rate.

title: Coverage-gate fallback trigger `[ "$ok" -eq 0 ]` mishandles the legitimate-zero case and the partial-manifest case: a manifest reporting n_ok>0 but n_total=0 falls back to file-count, while ok=0 from a real total-failure is indistinguishable from a missing manifest
evidence: Line 316: `if [ "$total" -eq 0 ] || [ "$ok" -eq 0 ]; then` enters the file-count fallback. n_ok and n_total are read with `|| 0` defaults via `m.n_ok||0` (line 306) / `m.n_total||0` (line 307). The incremental manifest writer (pull-yahoo.js:1395-1399) writes `n_total: watchlist.stocks.length, n_ok: okResults.length, partial: true`. If the very first incremental flush happens before any ticker succeeds (n_ok=0, n_total=15734), the `[ "$ok" -eq 0 ]` branch fires and falls back to counting .json files — which at that instant is ~0 too, so the gate uses file-count and may compute a misleading denominator. More importantly `m.n_ok||0` collapses a legitimately-absent key and a real 0 into the same value, and the OR-with-ok=0 means a manifest that genuinely recorded zero successes is treated as 'manifest unreliable, use files' rather than 'pull failed, fail hard'.
why_it_matters: The `||0` falsy-coalescing on manifest fields (a known-bug-pattern class: '|| 0' where 0 is legitimately valid) blurs 'key missing' vs 'value is 0'. Combined with the ok=0→fallback, a totally-failed pull (0 successes) is routed into the file-count path instead of failing on the manifest signal, and the file-count of stale leftover snapshots from a prior run (snapshots/ is committed, not cleaned) can then satisfy max(2500,13%) and pass a green build on entirely stale data.
fix: Distinguish missing-key from zero: read with a sentinel, e.g. `m.n_ok===undefined?'NA':m.n_ok`, and only fall back to file-count when the manifest is absent/unparseable or n_total is missing — NOT when ok is a legitimate 0. When the manifest exists and reports n_ok=0, fail hard (that is the 'Yahoo totally broken' case the gate claims to reject). Also delete/clean the snapshots dir staleness assumption: the freshness gate (line 248) partly covers this, but the coverage fallback should not count files whose asOf is from a prior run.

title: Cache-staleness test re-implements the production gate instead of importing it (drift blind spot)
evidence: Test defines its own `function shouldSkip(prev, maxAgeMs){ return !!(prev && prev.fetchedAt && (Date.now()-new Date(prev.fetchedAt).getTime()) < maxAgeMs); }`. The real gate in scripts/pull-13f-institutional.js:618-620 is byte-identical: `if (prev && prev.fetchedAt && (Date.now() - new Date(prev.fetchedAt).getTime()) < maxAgeMs)`. The gate is inline in main() and is NOT exported, so the test could not import it even if it wanted to.
why_it_matters: The test asserts the behaviour of a COPY of the logic, not the logic that actually ships. If someone changes the production gate (e.g. flips `<` to `<=`, or adds a failedAt-retry branch), the test keeps passing against its stale duplicate and the regression ships silently. This is the classic 'test the mock, not the code' anti-pattern; the test gives a green that is decoupled from reality.
fix: Extract the gate into an exported pure helper in pull-13f-institutional.js, e.g. `function isFreshlyCached(prev, maxAgeMs, nowMs){...}`, add a comment naming the failure mode it prevents (stale-13F-refresh / failedAt-retry skip), use it in main(), and import THAT in the test. Same treatment for the form4 24h gate (pull-insider-form4.js:454).

title: Canary validates only one of the two financialCurrency read paths pull-yahoo actually uses
evidence: Canary asserts only `{ path: 'financialData.financialCurrency', type: 'string' }`. But pull-yahoo.js:808 reads it with PRICE taking precedence: `const _fc = _y(pr, 'financialCurrency') || _y(yahoo.financialData, 'financialCurrency');`. The canary never checks `price.financialCurrency`. getPath returns undefined for a missing intermediate (it null-guards `if (cur == null) return cur`), so a present-but-elsewhere field reads as absent.
why_it_matters: This canary's reason-for-existence is the ADR financialCurrency 30x-FX bug. Yet it only guards the fallback location. Two real drift scenarios slip through: (1) Yahoo moves financialCurrency BACK to price (or serves it in BOTH) — pull-yahoo still works via the `_y(pr,...)` branch, but the canary FAILS (false positive, noise that erodes trust). (2) More subtly, if the field is dropped from financialData but the price branch is also empty, the canary fires — good — but it cannot distinguish 'primary path broke' from 'fallback path broke', so it gives no signal about which read path regressed. The canary should mirror pull-yahoo's actual precedence to be a faithful drift detector.
fix: Assert the field at BOTH locations the consumer reads, with OR semantics matching pull-yahoo's precedence: add a custom check that passes if `price.financialCurrency` is a non-empty string OR `financialData.financialCurrency` is — and warns which branch satisfied it. Keep the comment naming the failure mode (ADR mis-FX from missing financialCurrency).

title: XML-parser tests never exercise namespace/misalignment edge cases the real parsers diverge on
evidence: 13f-test feeds ns1:-prefixed tags and asserts they parse (good), but pull-13f's _extractAll regex is `<(?:\w+:)?TAG\b...` (namespace-tolerant) while pull-insider-form4's _extractAll is `<TAG\b...` (NO prefix tolerance). The form4 SAMPLE_XML uses only unprefixed tags, so the test would still pass even if a real SEC Form-4 arrived namespace-prefixed (the parser would silently return []). Separately, _normalizeSubmissions (both scripts) does `recent.filingDate[i]` etc. with no check that the parallel arrays are the same length as recent.form — the test only feeds perfectly-aligned arrays of length 4.
why_it_matters: The parsers silently return [] on input shapes they don't handle (namespace-prefixed Form-4, or a SEC `recent` block where filingDate is shorter than form or undefined). Silent-[] is the worst failure mode for a data feed: zero insider transactions looks identical to 'no insider activity', corrupting the insider-buy-cluster / insider-net-buying signals with no error. The tests bless only the happy path, so this whole class is uncaught.
fix: Add fixtures: a namespace-prefixed Form-4 doc (assert it still parses, or consciously document Form-4 is never namespaced and add a guard); and a malformed submissions block with misaligned/short parallel arrays (assert _normalizeSubmissions either coerces missing fields to null without throwing or returns []). Harden _normalizeSubmissions to clamp i to the min length across the arrays it reads, with a comment naming the failure mode (SEC parallel-array misalignment → undefined-index crash / row corruption).

title: buildRow() does 2 synchronous fs.existsSync+readFileSync per stock — silently defeats the async batched snapshot loader and adds minutes back to the run
evidence: buildRow() per stock calls `const histRaw = readScoreHistory(ticker);` (L439) and `const r40rxHistRaw = readR40rxHistory(ticker);` (L442). Each helper does `if (fs.existsSync(file)) { ... JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(file,'utf8')) }` (readScoreHistory L167-168; readR40rxHistory L185-186) — synchronous stat + read + parse. main() loops `for (const s of stocks) { const r = buildRow(s); }` (L4280-4283) over every loaded snapshot.
why_it_matters: The header comment at L80-84 (Tag 232c-11 / audit F-PF-003) explicitly converted loadStocks() to 32-way async batched reads precisely to kill 'serial fs.readFileSync over 3-15k+ files' that 'added 2-3 minutes per generator run'. But buildRow then re-introduces TWO serial synchronous reads per stock (score-history + r40rx-history) on the single main thread — i.e. up to ~2×(universe size) blocking syscalls, exactly the pattern that was supposedly fixed. On a 3.5k-tabbed / larger total universe this is the dominant wall-time cost of the build and blocks the event loop the whole time. This is a top structural cap on iteration speed (the screener is at '~20% of potential' partly because each build is slow).
fix: Read the score-history/ and r40rx-history/ directories the same way loadStocks() reads snapshots: one async batched pass (Promise.all over fs.promises.readFile with CONCURRENCY=32) into two Maps keyed by safeSnapshotFilename(ticker), built ONCE in main() before the buildRow loop, then passed into buildRow (or looked up from a module Map). The per-ticker memo Maps (_scoreHistoryCache/_r40rxHistoryCache) already exist — just pre-populate them asynchronously instead of lazily-synchronously. No method/scoring change, so fixture hashes are unaffected.

_verdict.note:
Code reading is accurate: buildRow() (generate-screener.js L439/L442) calls readScoreHistory/readR40rxHistory, each doing fs.existsSync + fs.readFileSync + JSON.parse synchronously (L167-168 / L185-186); main() loops buildRow over every stock (L4280-4283, single call site at L4282). The _scoreHistoryCache/_r40rxHistoryCache memos exist but populate lazily-synchronously, so each ticker pays the sync I/O once.

BUT the core severity claim ("defeats the async loader and adds MINUTES back to the run") is empirically false. I benchmarked both patterns against the real history dirs in the worktree (5769 score-history + 5119 r40rx files ~ 10,900 reads): current synchronous pattern = ~1.2-1.5s total; proposed async-batched (CONCURRENCY=32) = ~0.5-0.6s total. Net wall-time saved is ~0.7-1.0 SECOND for the whole run, not minutes -- overstated by 2-3 orders of magnitude. buildRow also already runs much heavier per-stock CPU work (Runner.evaluateStock + a SM.evaluateMode loop over all modes), so ~0.2ms of I/O per stock is negligible. The loop is sequential with no concurrent async work, so event-loop blocking costs nothing in practice.

Real but minor (sync I/O in a hot loop is a legit smell), so not a false positive -- but mis-rated; at most low, not high.

fix_safe=false: the fix is behavior-preserving for scoring (no method change -> fixture hashes unaffected, auditor is right there), but it is a non-trivial refactor adding two new batched dir loaders + cache pre-population/ordering in main(); needs human review, not auto-apply, especially given the payoff is sub-second.

title: Pervasive `|| 0` / `(x||0)` coalescing treats a legitimate value of 0 (and sometimes null) as the fallback, corrupting sort order and scoring inputs
evidence: `const mcap = unwrap(stock.marketCap) || 0;` (L266) — a genuinely-zero or null mcap becomes 0 and is later gated by `r.mcap > 0`. R40 sort: `((b.hgScore || 0) - (a.hgScore || 0))` (L773), `(b.r40||0)-(a.r40||0)` etc. throughout sortList() (L1678-1702) and classifyTabs sorts (L773-806). pbScore input `Math.max(0, r40Value || 0)` (L316). WATCH score `Math.max(r.hgScore||0, r.qcScore||0, r.bfScore||0)` (L2010, L2479).
why_it_matters: A stock with a true score of 0 (or null = 'not computable') is sorted as if it scored 0, which is correct for 0 but WRONG for null vs a stock scoring slightly negative: e.g. in the R40 raw sort a row with r40 = -5 (real distress) sorts BELOW a row with r40 = null coalesced to 0, so the null/no-data row ranks ABOVE a genuinely-scored negative row. The same `||0` pattern means a real score of exactly 0 is indistinguishable from missing data in every tie-break. The code already proved it knows better in the R40 main sort (L801-802 uses `b.r40 == null ? -Infinity : b.r40`) — that null-as-(-Infinity) discipline is applied in exactly one place and missing from all the other ~15 comparators.
fix: Adopt the L801-802 idiom everywhere a score/metric feeds a comparator or a gate: treat null/non-finite as -Infinity for descending sorts (so missing data sinks, never floats above real negatives), and never coalesce to 0 for a quantity where 0 is a legal value (mcap, scores, r40). Add a tiny helper `const desc = (a,b,k) => ((Number.isFinite(b[k])?b[k]:-Infinity)-(Number.isFinite(a[k])?a[k]:-Infinity))` and route sortList()/classifyTabs sorts through it.

_verdict.note:
Mostly a false positive; the one genuine sub-issue is minor and partly already fixed. Verified against source in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/generate-screener.js and methods/.

1) mcap (L266 `unwrap(stock.marketCap) || 0`): harmless. Every consumer gates it: SMALL tab requires `r.mcap > 0` (L700), peer-compare requires `r.mcap > 0` (L2670/2676), mcap filter rejects `< threshold` (L1629). A null mcap coalesced to 0 fails all these gates exactly as a null would. A legitimate listed-equity mcap of exactly 0 does not occur. No corruption.

2) Mode scores (hgScore/qcScore/bfScore/pbScore/r40DurScore) in all sorts (L773-774, 781, 805-806, 1678-1703, 2010, 2479): harmless. score-aggregator clamps every score with `Math.max(0, ...)` (score-aggregator.js L320, L388) and pbScore is built from clamped non-negative terms (L313-323). Scores are never negative, so `|| 0` makes null and 0 sort identically at the bottom — there is no real negative value that a coalesced-0 could wrongly outrank. The WATCH `Math.max(hgScore||0,...)` (L2010/2479) is display-only and likewise safe.

3) pbScore input `Math.max(0, r40Value || 0)` (L316): harmless. r40Value is already `null` or finite; `Math.max(0, ...)` deliberately floors R40 contribution at 0 (documented design — R40 below 0 should add nothing to the pre-breakout composite). `|| 0` on a null here just yields the intended 0 floor.

4) The ONLY genuinely-valid sub-claim: r40 and growth CAN be negative (rule-of-40.js: value = growth + fcfMargin). The server-side classifyTabs R40 sort was ALREADY fixed to treat null as -Infinity (L801-802, Tag 206g), but the client-side sortList() (L1686 `(b.r40||0)`, L1694, and growth L1685/1695) still coalesces null→0. This is an inconsistency where a missing-r40 row could outrank a genuinely-negative-r40 row. However its real impact is near-zero: the R40 tab only contains rows with a computable (finite) r40, and SMALL only contains rows with `growth > 20` (L700 gate), so null never coexists with a real negative in the lists where these comparators run by default. It bites only if a user manually re-sorts a mixed tab (e.g. HG tab sorted by r40) — a cosmetic UI ordering glitch, not scoring/data corruption.

Net: the headline severity (high, "corrupting scoring inputs") is not supported — scoring inputs are unaffected and the gates neutralize the mcap case. There is a real but cosmetic client-side sort inconsistency for negative r40/growth.

title: unwrap() handles only the {value} envelope, not Yahoo's {raw,fmt} — any snapshot field still in raw Yahoo shape silently becomes null
evidence: `function unwrap(v){ if (v==null) return null; if (typeof v==='number') return Number.isFinite(v)?v:null; if (typeof v==='object' && Number.isFinite(v.value)) return v.value; return null; }` (L73-78). It checks `v.value` only — Yahoo's quoteSummary envelope is `{ raw: 1234, fmt: '1.23k', longFmt: '...' }`, which has no `.value`, so it returns null. arrUnwrap (L239) maps the same logic across annual arrays.
why_it_matters: If any upstream change (or a not-yet-normalized field, or a partially-normalized snapshot) leaves a metric as a `{raw,fmt}` object, unwrap() turns it into null with zero diagnostics — the metric just disappears from the row, lowers data-quality grade, and can flip tab membership, all invisibly. This is the classic 'Yahoo envelope unwrapping' failure mode. Today snapshots appear pre-normalized to `{value}` upstream so it's latent, but the guard is one upstream rename away from silently zeroing a whole column.
fix: Make unwrap tolerant of both shapes and surface ambiguity: `if (typeof v==='object'){ if (Number.isFinite(v.value)) return v.value; if (Number.isFinite(v.raw)) return v.raw; }` Keep returning null for genuinely-missing data, but add a one-time console.warn when an object lacking both .value and .raw is encountered, so a schema drift is noisy rather than silent.

_verdict.note: False positive based on a misread of the data boundary. The premise — that snapshot fields could still be in Yahoo's {raw,fmt} shape when unwrap() runs — is contradicted by the producer. Snapshots are written by pull-yahoo.js, which strips Yahoo's envelope at the source: _y() reads `'raw' in cur ? cur.raw` (L484), and _metric() re-wraps the bare number as the internal {value:v} envelope (L498). marketCap/revenueGrowthYoY/grossMargin are all emitted via _metric() (L890-894); annual/quarterly arrays are pushed as {value:n} (L1105-1221). So {raw,fmt} never reaches a snapshot JSON — by the time generate-screener.js loadStocks() reads it, every field is already {value}. unwrap() (L73-78) consumes exactly that internal schema. The whole consumer side agrees on {value}: snapshot-methods-history.js L80-83, snapshot-picks.js L64 ('value' in m), snapshot-score-history.js L41, snapshot-r40rx-history.js. There is no code path that places a {raw,fmt} object into stock.marketCap or stock.metrics.* consumed here, so nothing silently becomes null. (Could not load a real snapshot to triple-confirm at runtime — this worktree's snapshots/ contains only _manifest.json — but the producer code is unambiguous.) Adding a .raw fallback to unwrap() is therefore unnecessary; if anything it would mask a genuine schema regression rather than surface it.

title: r40-latest.json merge re-emits stale growth/fcfMargin/r40 for up to 60 days as if current (asymmetric survivorship + look-ahead-ish staleness in the 'trusted' downstream export)
evidence: The merge keeps any prior entry whose `asOf >= cutoffStr` (60-day horizon, L4377/L4393) and only overlays tickers refreshed THIS run (L4402). A ticker not pulled keeps its old row verbatim — old `growth`, `fcfMargin`, `r40`, `r40Pass`, `rxPass` — with its original (now up-to-60-day-old) `asOf`. The merged array is sorted by r40 desc (L4405-4409) and written as the canonical export findash reads 'in preference to per-ticker files' (header L4320-4327).
why_it_matters: Downstream findash treats r40-latest.json as a complete, trusted, current ranking. A name that hasn't been re-pulled for 50 days sits in the ranking with a 50-day-old R40 and a 50-day-old pass flag, intermixed with today's fresh values and sorted as peers. r40Pass can be stale-true after the company collapsed, or stale-false after it recovered. The only freshness signal is the per-row `asOf`, which the sort ignores and which a naive consumer won't gate on. This is a genuine data-integrity hazard (silent staleness presented as current) — the documented rotation tradeoff is reasonable but the export gives the consumer no way to distinguish fresh from 60-day-stale at the row's headline values.
fix: Either (a) gate findash-visible rows on a freshness window far tighter than the 60-day pruning horizon (e.g. expose a `stale: asOf < generatedAt - Nd` boolean per row so the consumer can filter/annotate), or (b) keep stale entries only for completeness but stamp them clearly and exclude them from any 'current rank' the consumer trusts. At minimum document the max-staleness contract in the file header that ships to findash, not just in this script.

_verdict.note: Mechanism verified but the framing as a data-integrity defect is a false positive. Code reads exactly as cited: L4393 keeps prior entries where asOf >= cutoffStr (60d horizon, L4377), L4402 overlays only this-run tickers, non-refreshed tickers keep their verbatim old row + original asOf, merged array sorted r40-desc (L4405-4409) and written as the canonical findash export. Production data confirms it: live r40-latest.json has 45/3791 rows with a stale asOf (2026-06-08 vs the 2026-06-12 batch), and ~3300/24000 daily rotation means rows can legitimately be up to ~60d old. BUT the auditor's two load-bearing claims fail: (1) This is intended, documented design — the comment at L4367-4375 explains the merge exists precisely because a plain overwrite dropped NVDA/PLTR from the daily CI build; it preserves completeness, not survivorship-as-deception. (2) The core complaint that the consumer cannot distinguish stale from fresh is FALSE — every row already carries a per-row `asOf` field, so findash can already filter/annotate on freshness. The proposed fix (a) 'expose a stale boolean' is therefore largely redundant with the existing asOf. There is no look-ahead bias either: no future data is used, it's plain unavoidable staleness, already self-describing per row. The only genuine gap is that the max-staleness contract lives only in an in-script comment (L4320-4327, never shipped) rather than in the artifact — a documentation nit, not high-severity data integrity. The sister builder scripts/build-r40-latest.js writes the same per-row asOf, consistent with this.

title: R40_DURABLE durability block is nested inside the R40-tab `if (last4.length>=4)` branch, so it never runs for rows that fell into the TTM-only `else` — duplicated/misplaced last4 logic
evidence: Inside `if (Number.isFinite(r.r40) && !dqBlockedFromQuality){` the code does `if (last4.length >= 4){ ...tabs.R40.push } else { ...r40InsufficientHistory; tabs.R40.push }` (L723-734). Then a SECOND `if (last4.length >= 4){ ... R40_DURABLE classification ... }` block (L739-758) sits AFTER that if/else but still uses the same `last4`. The comment says it 'reuses last4 from above'. The R40_DURABLE block is only reachable when last4.length>=4, which is correct, but it is physically placed after the R40 push if/else rather than inside it, making the control flow easy to break on edit and meaning the durability computation is re-evaluating `last4.length>=4` redundantly right after the branch that already split on it.
why_it_matters: The two `last4.length >= 4` checks (L723 and L739) are evaluated back-to-back on the same array; the second is dead-redundant logically but, more importantly, the durability scoring (durScore, passStreak, floor, provenance) is wedged at the same indentation as the R40-push if/else and reads like it belongs to the else-branch. A future edit that wraps or returns inside the R40 if/else will silently drop R40_DURABLE classification for everyone. This is fragile, and the nesting obscures that R40_DURABLE membership requires BOTH a computable r40 AND >=4 quarterly history AND every quarter finite (L741) — a stricter gate than the tab explainer implies.
fix: Hoist the R40_DURABLE durability computation into its own clearly-scoped block (or helper computeR40Durability(r, last4)) that runs once per row when last4.length>=4, independent of the R40-tab push branch. Collapse the duplicate `last4.length>=4` test. Behavior-preserving refactor; add a comment naming the failure mode it prevents (silent loss of R40_DURABLE on future R40-branch edits).

_verdict.note: Refuted. The finding's title claim ("R40_DURABLE block is nested inside the R40-tab `if (last4.length>=4)` branch, so it never runs for TTM-only `else` rows") is false. I verified the brace structure at generate-screener.js L720-759: the outer block is `if (Number.isFinite(r.r40) && !dqBlockedFromQuality)` (L720, closes L759). Inside it are TWO siblings: the R40-tab push if/else (L723 if / L730 else, closes L734), and a SEPARATE `if (last4.length >= 4)` R40_DURABLE classification block (L739-758). The R40_DURABLE block is NOT nested inside the L723 branch — it is a sibling that runs for every row reaching the outer block. TTM-only rows (last4.length<4) hit the L730 else and then correctly fail the L739 test, so they get no R40_DURABLE — which is the INTENDED behavior (durability requires 4 full quarters). The finding's own evidence body even admits this: "The R40_DURABLE block is only reachable when last4.length>=4, which is correct." So the only substantive remaining observation is a style nit: a redundant `last4.length >= 4` re-test right after the branch that already split on it, plus cosmetically misleading extra indentation on L735-758. No behavioral defect exists. Miscategorized as category=bug/severity=medium when it is at most a low maintainability/readability nit.

title: Column sort is descending-only: aria-sort never renders 'ascending' and clicking an already-sorted header does not toggle direction
evidence: Header render: `const sortAttr = isSortable ? (sortKey === skKey ? ' aria-sort="descending"' : ' aria-sort="none"') : '';` (L2335) — the only non-'none' value emitted is 'descending'. Click handler: `if (th && th.dataset.sortkey){ sortKey = th.dataset.sortkey; ...; renderTable(); }` (L3629-3639) sets the key but never flips an asc/desc flag; sortList() comparators (L1693-1702) are all hard-coded `b - a` (descending). CSS even defines a `th[aria-sort="ascending"]` caret (L957) that can never appear.
why_it_matters: A user clicking the MCap or RevGr% header expecting to toggle to ascending (smallest-first, e.g. to find the cheapest or slowest names) gets descending every time, with no way to reverse it, and the screen-reader announcement (aria-sort) can never report ascending. The CSS ascending-caret rule is dead. It's a real usability gap in a tool whose whole value is fast slicing, and it contradicts the accessibility intent the code otherwise invests in.
fix: Track a `sortDir` ('asc'|'desc') alongside sortKey; clicking the active sort column toggles it, clicking a new column resets to 'desc'. Make sortList() multiply the comparator by the direction sign. Emit aria-sort='ascending' accordingly so the existing CSS caret works.

_verdict.note: Confirmed by source in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/generate-screener.js. (1) Header render L2335: `sortAttr = isSortable ? (sortKey===skKey ? ' aria-sort="descending"' : ' aria-sort="none"') : ''` — only 'descending'/'none' ever emitted, never 'ascending'. (2) Click handler L3629-3639 sets `sortKey = th.dataset.sortkey` and calls renderTable() but never tracks/flips a direction; clicking the active header re-sorts identically (no toggle). (3) sortList() comparators L1675-1703 are all hard-coded `(b||0)-(a||0)` descending with no direction sign. (4) CSS L957 defines `th[aria-sort="ascending"]::after` ▲ caret that is dead code (never matches). (5) Only sort state is `sortKey` (L1360); no sortDir exists anywhere (grep confirms). (6) Comment L2303 'Click toggles sort' contradicts the implementation, which only switches key, never direction. Real but cosmetic/UX+a11y only: screener output stays correct, just always high-to-low — no data-correctness impact on the results Karl reads, so 'low' severity stands.

title: Insider 'Shares' column formats a share COUNT with the money formatter fmtM (T/B/M suffix), mislabeling raw share quantities
evidence: Insider recent-buys table: `'' + (Number.isFinite(b.shares) ? fmtM(b.shares) : '—') + ''` (L2909). fmtM (L497-503) is the money formatter producing '1.2T'/'3.4B'/'5M' suffixes intended for dollar market caps / revenue, applied here to a share count under a header literally labeled 'Shares' (L2903).
why_it_matters: A purchase of 1,500,000 shares renders as '2M' (rounded, suffixed) in a column a user reads as a share quantity, conflating share counts with dollar magnitudes and dropping precision. The adjacent '$' column already uses fmtM correctly for value; reusing the dollar formatter for the count is a copy-paste slip that misstates insider conviction size.
fix: Format share counts with a plain thousands-separated integer (e.g. `b.shares.toLocaleString()`), reserving fmtM for monetary columns. Comment the failure mode (share-count vs dollar-magnitude conflation).

_verdict.note: Confirmed real but cosmetic/display-only. generate-screener.js L2903 renders a column header literally 'Shares', and L2909 formats the raw share count b.shares through fmtM, a T/B/M money-magnitude formatter (.toFixed(0) rounding). b.shares is a true share QUANTITY: methods/insider-conviction-score.js L347 sets `const shares = _num(b.t.transactionShares) || 0`, distinct from the dollar `value = shares*price` shown in the adjacent $ column (L2910). So a 5,000,000-share buy renders as '5M' and 1,200,000 as '1M', conflating counts with dollar magnitudes and losing precision. Two corrections to the audit's evidence: (1) it cited 'fmtM (L497-503)', but L497-503 is actually `fmtMoney`, a build-side helper; the function actually called at L2909 is a SEPARATE client-side `fmtM` defined at L1392 (mirrored in screener.html L695) — same T/B/M behavior, so the substance holds but the line/name citation is wrong. (2) fmtM here is purely presentational; it is not used in any scoring/gating path, so there is no data-corruption or wrong-results impact. Low severity is appropriate.

title: ipoAgeYears() fallback uses DATA.currentYear (UTC year at build) minus ipoYear — off-by-up-to-one age that can misclassify near-3-year listing-age fallbacks
evidence: Client: `if (r.ipoYear != null) return DATA.currentYear - r.ipoYear;` (L1608) where `currentYear: new Date().getUTCFullYear()` (L4104). This calendar-year subtraction (2026 - 2024 = 2) ignores month/day, so a company IPO'd in Dec 2024 is treated as 2 years old in Jan 2026 (really ~1 month), and one IPO'd in Jan 2024 is also 2 years (really ~24 months).
why_it_matters: ipoAgeYears is only a fallback when listing-age is incomputable, but where it IS used it feeds age judgments; calendar-year math overstates the age of late-in-year IPOs by nearly a full year and understates early-year ones, which is exactly the kind of boundary error that flips a borderline 'too young for QC' decision. Low severity because the canonical path is listingYears (clean fiscal years), but the fallback is silently imprecise.
fix: If only ipoYear (no month) is available, the integer-year delta is the best you can do — but document it as approximate, and prefer comparing against a fractional current year or clamp/annotate so a sub-1-year IPO can't read as 1-2y old. Better: have buildRow emit listingYears-or-null and let the UI show 'unknown' rather than a calendar-year guess.

_verdict.note: False positive in practice: the cited client-side function `ipoAgeYears(r)` (generate-screener.js:1604-1609, emitted into screener.html:907-912) is DEAD CODE — it has zero call sites. A full-repo grep for `ipoAgeYears` finds only (a) the definition in generate-screener.js, (b) the same definition in the generated screener.html, and (c) an unrelated local variable inside methods/listing-age.js. Nothing in generate-screener.js or screener.html ever invokes the function. The only IPO filtering that actually runs (generate-screener.js:1656-1659 / screener.html:959-962) compares `r.ipoYear` DIRECTLY against the user's year-bound inputs (filterIpoMin/filterIpoMax) and never touches `ipoAgeYears`. The listing-age badge (L2488/L1791) renders `r.listingYears` directly. QC age-eligibility (L663 `qcEligibleByAge`) uses `r.listingYears`, not this function. So no row is ever classified by the calendar-year subtraction the auditor flags. The math observation itself is technically correct (`DATA.currentYear - ipoYear` ignores month/day, so a Dec-2024 IPO reads as 2y in Jan-2026), but it produces no observable misclassification anywhere because the value is never consumed. The bug as described — "off-by-up-to-one age that can misclassify near-3-year listing-age fallbacks" — has no live effect. Note that methods/listing-age.js:69 contains the same `NOW_YEAR - ipoYear` pattern, but there it is used only as a coarse cross-check guard (`ipoAgeYears >= 5 && cleanYears < 3`) to flag IPO/data mismatches at the >=5y threshold, where a one-year calendar slop cannot flip the >=5 vs <5 boundary in a way that matters for the >=5-AND-<3-clean-years heuristic; that is a deliberate, documented sanity flag, not a precise age. Severity lowered: this is dead code, not a behavioral bug.

title: _y leaks non-number objects ({fmt}-only or unexpected envelopes) into numeric metric fields
evidence:
if (cur && typeof cur === 'object' && 'raw' in cur) return cur.raw;
  return cur;  // <- returns the OBJECT verbatim when it has no 'raw' key
why_it_matters: When yahoo-finance2 returns an envelope without a `raw` key (e.g. `{fmt:'1.23B'}`, or a Date, or a nested object on a schema-drift node), _y returns that object unchanged. _metric (line 488) only rejects `null` and `typeof==='number' && !isFinite`; an object passes both guards and is stored as a metric `value`. Downstream ratio math (`x * factor` in scale(), `revenueTTM.value/1e9`, score aggregation) then yields NaN or string-concatenation garbage, and the snapshot still grades as having data. This is a silent NaN/type-propagation hole — the audit prompt's 'no isFinite guard' pattern class.
fix: Make _y fail closed to a scalar: after the `raw` unwrap, add `if (cur && typeof cur === 'object') { if ('fmt' in cur) { const n = parseFloat(String(cur.fmt).replace(/[^0-9.eE+-]/g,'')); return Number.isFinite(n) ? n : null; } return null; }`. Guarantees _y only ever returns a number, string-scalar, or null. Comment: 'prevents object/{fmt}-only envelopes leaking into numeric metrics → NaN ratios downstream'.

_verdict.note: False positive on the data-integrity claim. The literal code reading is correct: _y (pull-yahoo.js:484-485) returns cur verbatim when cur is an object without a 'raw' key, and _metric (line 489) only rejects null and non-finite NUMBERS, so a leaked object would pass its guard and be stored verbatim. BUT the precondition cannot occur: the only inputs to _y are yf.quoteSummary() (sd/fd/ks/ap/pr/isHist/isHistQ) and yf.fundamentalsTimeSeries() arrays. In yahoo-finance2 v3.14 both go through moduleExec, and the numeric metric fields are schema-typed "type":"number" (verified for targetMeanPrice, operatingMargins, marketCap, sharesOutstanding, and all FTS fields). pull-yahoo.js builds new YahooFinance({ validation:{ logErrors:false, logOptionsErrors:false } }) — it sets ONLY logging flags, NOT validateResult:false. So validateResult defaults to true (moduleExec.js:92-94), and a validation failure THROWS FailedYahooValidationError (validateAndCoerceTypes.js:214 throws regardless of logErrors; moduleExec.js:131-132 rethrows when validateResult is true). pull-yahoo.js catches this and classifies the symbol as not-found (lines 2106-2119), so a {fmt}-only/unexpected-envelope object in a number field never reaches mapYahooToCanonical/_y. The "NaN ratios downstream" outcome does not materialize. The raw-unwrap on line 484 is a defensive remnant (the in-code German comment notes yahoo-finance2 already unwraps {raw,fmt} to Number). Additionally, arithmetic sites like _y(fd,'operatingMargins')*100 would yield NaN and be caught by _metric's !Number.isFinite, failing closed anyway.

title: Corrupt/unparseable existing snapshot is treated as 'fresh & schema-OK' → price-only path attempts JSON.parse and throws, but the staleness probes already swallowed the corruption
evidence:
const staleSchema = youngEnough ? _existingSnapshotMissingTag211lFields(stock.ticker) : false;
... both probes `catch { return false; }` (lines 1478, 1528). Then `_priceOnlyUpdate` does `JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(fp,...))` (line 1535) which throws, caught at 1670 → falls through to full pull.
why_it_matters: A truncated/corrupt snapshot makes _existingSnapshotMissingTag211lFields and _existingSnapshotMissingCurrencyNormalization both return false (their catch swallows the parse error), so the code believes the snapshot is young, schema-current and currency-normalized. The only thing that rescues it is _priceOnlyUpdate re-parsing and throwing, which logs a WARN and forces a full pull — wasteful, and worse, _getExistingSnapshotAge (regex on first 500 bytes, line 1424) can still read a valid asOf out of a half-written file whose body is garbage, so a corrupt-but-recent file is repeatedly read every run. The atomic-write work (Tag 189) reduces but does not eliminate this (pre-existing corrupt files, non-atomic external edits).
fix: In processOne, when _priceOnlyUpdate throws specifically on JSON.parse (corrupt snapshot), delete the file (`fs.unlinkSync(fp)`) before falling through to full pull, so the next run isn't tricked by the readable header. Alternatively have the staleness probes distinguish 'parse error' from 'missing field' and force full-pull on parse error. Comment: 'prevents a corrupt snapshot with a readable asOf header from looping the price-only fast-path forever'.

_verdict.note: Mechanical trace is accurate but the conclusion is a false positive. Confirmed in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/pull-yahoo.js: _getExistingSnapshotAge (1416-1429) reads only the first 500 bytes via regex (no JSON.parse), so a corrupt file with an intact "asOf" header returns a valid age and youngEnough=true. Both staleness probes JSON.parse and catch{return false} (1478, 1528), so staleSchema=staleCurrency=false, and the price-only branch at 1664 is entered. _priceOnlyUpdate JSON.parse at 1535 throws on corrupt JSON. BUT the catch at 1670 falls through to the full pull in the SAME processOne call: the full pull re-fetches from Yahoo and writeFileAtomic(outPath, JSON.stringify(canonical)) at 2075 OVERWRITES the corrupt file with valid JSON. The corruption self-heals on the same run — there is no "price-only fast-path forever" loop (price-only is attempted once per call; on throw it does not retry, it full-pulls). The code comment at lines 2064-2068 (F-DP-047 / Tag 192) explicitly documents this exact "next run reads corrupt JSON at price-only check → throws → triggers full-pull branch" scenario and treats the full-pull fallthrough as the intended recovery, with atomic write as the prevention. So the claimed harm (looping / staleness probes "swallowing" corruption to permanent effect) does not materialize. Net cost is at most one full pull instead of a price-only refresh for that ticker on the run that hits a corrupt file — exactly the recovery the existing design intends.

title: fcfMarginTTM denominator uses falsy `revTTM` guard — a legitimately negative or zero-rounding revenue, and the `&&` truthiness, can misroute
evidence: let fcfMarginTTM = (fcfTTM != null && revTTM && revTTM !== 0) ? (fcfTTM / revTTM) * 100 : null;
why_it_matters: `revTTM &&` is a falsy guard: it is correct for 0 (also caught by `!== 0`) but it is the same falsy-coalescing anti-pattern flagged in the prompt. More importantly there is no isFinite guard on fcfTTM or revTTM — if _y leaked a non-number (see A-pull-yahoo-02) or Yahoo returns a tiny revenue (e.g. a holding shell with revTTM rounding to a few dollars), fcfMargin can explode to thousands of percent; the |>200%| suppressor (line 720) catches the gross artifacts but a 150% artifact from a near-zero denominator slips through and poisons R40/score-aggregator. Genuinely negative revenue (rare, restated) would compute a sign-flipped margin.
fix: Guard finiteness and a minimum revenue floor: `const okRev = Number.isFinite(revTTM) && revTTM > 0; let fcfMarginTTM = (Number.isFinite(fcfTTM) && okRev) ? (fcfTTM/revTTM)*100 : null;`. Comment: 'prevents near-zero/negative/non-finite revenue producing exploded or sign-flipped FCF-margin that survives the 200% artifact cap'.

_verdict.note:
Misread / non-issue. File: C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/pull-yahoo.js:718, guard `(fcfTTM != null && revTTM && revTTM !== 0)`.

The finding's mechanism is largely wrong about JS truthiness:
1. "Zero revenue misroutes" — FALSE. `revTTM === 0` makes the `revTTM` truthiness test falsy, so it routes to null. That is the correct, desired outcome (avoids divide-by-zero). No misrouting.
2. "Negative revenue misroutes (to null)" — BACKWARDS. Negative numbers are truthy in JS, so `revTTM = -500` PASSES the guard and is computed, not nulled. So negatives are not "misrouted to null" as implied. The only residual truth is that a negative revenue yields a sign-flipped margin — but Yahoo's `totalRevenue` (gross sales) is effectively never negative for the equity universe, and any exploded/sign-flipped magnitude is already caught by the `Math.abs(fcfMarginTTM) > 200` artifact cap on line 720, which nulls it and sets `fcfMarginTTMSuppressed`.
3. "`&&` truthiness can misroute" — the only values the falsy `revTTM` catches beyond `!= null` are 0/NaN/''/false; for numeric revenue that's just 0 and NaN, both of which correctly route to null. NaN would also be filtered by `_metric`'s `Number.isFinite` guard at line 489/896 even if it slipped through. So the truthiness guard is at worst harmless and arguably safer than a bare `!= null`.

Net: the cited line is not a bug. The legitimate edge (negative revenue) is non-occurring in the data source and is already backstopped by the 200% cap immediately below. The `revTTM !== 0` is redundant-but-harmless.

fix_safe: the proposed fix (`Number.isFinite(revTTM) && revTTM > 0`) is NOT behavior-preserving — it newly rejects negative revenue (current code computes it, then the >200% cap usually nulls it anyway) and tightens the finiteness path. Low practical risk, but it changes output on the negative-revenue edge and is part of a fixture-hash-sensitive snapshot pipeline, so it warrants human review rather than blind auto-apply.

title: Insider-transaction shares unwrap is asymmetric with _normTxTs and ignores _y — a {raw,fmt} envelope on shares is read inconsistently
evidence: const shares = (tx.shares && typeof tx.shares === 'object') ? tx.shares.raw : (tx.shares || 0);  // while startDate goes through _normTxTs; netShares += (shares||0) then later -= Math.abs(shares||0)
why_it_matters: If `tx.shares` is an object WITHOUT a `raw` key (same drift class as A-pull-yahoo-02), `tx.shares.raw` is `undefined`, and `(shares || 0)` silently coerces to 0 — the buy/sell is counted in clusterBuys but contributes 0 to netShares90d, understating insider conviction. Inconsistent with the rest of the mapper which uses _y for envelope handling. Low severity because only netShares is affected (cluster/buy COUNTS are unaffected), but it silently corrupts the insider-flow magnitude signal.
fix: Reuse the existing helper: `const shares = _y(tx, 'shares') ?? 0;` and assert finiteness before accumulating. Comment: 'prevents {fmt}-only or non-raw share envelopes coercing to 0 and understating insider netShares'.

_verdict.note:
False positive based on a misread of the _y helper. The cited inline unwrap at pull-yahoo.js:768 — `const shares = (tx.shares && typeof tx.shares === 'object') ? tx.shares.raw : (tx.shares || 0);` — correctly handles the two real-world shapes yahoo-finance2 emits for insiderTransactions.shares: a {raw,fmt} envelope (returns the numeric raw) and a plain number (returned as-is). Both feed netShares cleanly.

The auditor's only failure mode is a hypothetical {fmt}-only envelope with no `raw` key, which it claims the proposed fix `_y(tx,'shares') ?? 0` would read "consistently/correctly." That is wrong: _y (defined at line 477-486) only unwraps when `'raw' in cur` is true — `if (cur && typeof cur === 'object' && 'raw' in cur) return cur.raw; return cur;`. For a {fmt}-only object it would return the OBJECT, so `_y(tx,'shares') ?? 0` keeps the object and `netShares += {object}` yields NaN. The proposed fix is therefore strictly WORSE than the current code in the very edge case it cites, and is not behavior-preserving for normal inputs either (it changes the no-raw-object case from 0 to NaN). yahoo-finance2's insiderTransactions schema declares shares as a number and always carries `raw` in its envelopes, so the {fmt}-only case is not produced in practice.

The "asymmetry with _normTxTs" is cosmetic — startDate needs unit/range normalization (s vs ms, Date instance, sanity window) that is irrelevant to a share count. Different data types legitimately use different unwrap paths. netShares90d is consumed in methods/insider-net-buying.js:69,93 and insider-buy-cluster.js:41, all routed through `_num()` which nulls any non-finite value — so even the hypothetical NaN would be handled gracefully downstream, not corrupt results.

title: totalDebt absence-as-zero summing is documented as deliberate but the _debtPartial flag is never consumed inside pull-yahoo and depends on every downstream method opting in
evidence: const totalDebt = (std == null && ltd == null) ? null : (std || 0) + (ltd || 0); const _debtPartial = totalDebt != null && (std == null || ltd == null);  // identical at line 687 (QS) and 1167 (FTS)

The decision to keep this is documented (F-NY-002, 12.4% of snapshots) and surfaced via _debtPartial — but the safety of the decision rests entirely on EVERY leverage/EV consumer reading debtPartialFlag. That is an unenforced cross-module contract: a new method using annualBalance[i].totalDebt without checking _debtPartial will silently use an understated number (too-low net-debt/EBITDA → a leveraged name looks safe). Hardening only: add `_debtPartialReason: std==null?'no-current-debt':'no-long-term-debt'` so consumers can size the gap, and consider emitting a snapshot-level `meta._debtUnderstatedYears` count so score-aggregator can tier-cap. _verdict.note: Confirmed accurate but it describes a deliberately-accepted limitation, not a latent defect. Verified at pull-yahoo.js:687-691 (QS-mapper) and :1167-1193 (FTS-mapper): both compute _debtPartial = totalDebt!=null && (std==null||ltd==null) and attach it only when true. Grep confirms the literal claim: 15 methods read totalDebt, but only methods/net-debt-ebitda.js reads _debtPartial (line 32 -> debtPartialFlag). Even that single consumer uses it ONLY as a non-gating display marker spread into `components` (lines 52, 78) — it does NOT influence value/pass/computable. All other leverage-sensitive consumers (altman-z-score, beneish-m-score, piotroski-f-score, magic-formula, ev-ebitda, etc.) ingest the absence-as-zero totalDebt with no awareness of partiality. So the understatement is genuinely invisible to scoring. HOWEVER this is an explicitly documented, consciously accepted decision: F-NY-002 (audited 2026-06-08 as HIGH 'written but never read', re-decided 2026-06-10 to KEEP) with measured rationale (12.4% / 568 of 4589 snapshots; nulling totalDebt would destroy leverage data for genuine no-current-debt issuers). The finding itself concedes the summing is out of scope and proposes hardening only. Net: real and correctly described, but already known/owned and intentionally not fixed — severity is correctly low (borderline informational), not a new bug.

title: Snapshots are re-parsed from disk in the error/delist path and cache path with no reuse of already-loaded data
evidence: delist path: `let existing = fs.existsSync(outPath) ? JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(outPath,'utf8')) : null;` (line 2127) re-reads a file the run may have just written; FTS cache parse at 1722 + snapshot parses at 1535/1455/1507 are all independent reads.
why_it_matters: Compounds A-pull-yahoo-07. On the slow/full path a single ticker can touch its snapshot file with multiple independent read+parse+stringify cycles (probe parses, price-only parse, delist re-read). At universe scale across the documented 14.6h pull this is meaningful avoidable I/O and GC pressure. Lower severity than 07 because it is the cold path.
fix: Thread the parsed `existing`/`canonical` object through the function rather than re-reading by path. In the delist branch, if the snapshot was loaded earlier in the same processOne invocation, mutate that object instead of re-reading. No behaviour change.

_verdict.note: Largely a false positive / misread of the control flow. The delist re-read it leads with (line 2127) runs only inside the catch block (line 2091), entered when quoteSummaryWithRetry throws (line 1681). On that error path mapYahooToCanonical (1683) was never reached, so no `canonical` exists in scope, and the fast-path `_priceOnlyUpdate` either already returned (1669) or its parse is a function-local (1535) long out of scope. So there is genuinely nothing "already loaded" to reuse in the delist branch — the proposed fix's premise does not hold there. The other cited parses are in different functions on mutually-exclusive paths per ticker: a young schema-OK ticker hits the two probe parses (1455/1507) + `_priceOnlyUpdate` (1535) then returns; a stale/old ticker skips price-only and goes to full pull. The FTS cache parse (1722) reads a DIFFERENT file (fundamentals-cache/ vs outputDir snapshot), so it is not redundant snapshot I/O at all. The only genuine redundancy is small: a young ticker parses its snapshot up to 3× (two probes + price-only) — a minor, real inefficiency, but not the delist/cache pattern the finding describes. Evidence conflates distinct files and exclusive branches. Severity "low" is already generous; net I judge it not a real actionable bug as framed.

title: youngEnough uses `age < FUNDAMENTALS_MAX_AGE_MS` with age from a SEPARATE probe than the one price-only re-reads — a snapshot at exactly the 7-day boundary or written between the two reads can flip path mid-decision
evidence: const age = _getExistingSnapshotAge(stock.ticker); const youngEnough = age != null && age < FUNDAMENTALS_MAX_AGE_MS; ... if (youngEnough && !staleSchema && !staleCurrency) { const r = await _priceOnlyUpdate(stock, outputDir); ... }
why_it_matters: _getExistingSnapshotAge reads first-500-bytes for asOf; the schema/currency probes do full parses; _priceOnlyUpdate does a third read. Between these reads another worker (the file documents worker-pool concurrency and a manifest mutex but NOT per-ticker locking) could in principle rewrite or delete the same snapshot if the watchlist contains a duplicate ticker mapping to the same safeSnapshotFilename (e.g. CON.DE collision-prefix, or two ISINs with the same ticker stem). Race window is small and duplicate-filename collisions are rare, hence low — but the decision is made on stale `age` and acted on with no re-validation.
fix: Capture the parsed snapshot + its asOf once (per A-pull-yahoo-07 refactor) and base youngEnough, staleSchema, staleCurrency and price-only ALL on that single in-memory object, eliminating the TOCTOU window. Optionally dedupe watchlist by safeSnapshotFilename before the worker pool. Comment: 'single-read decision prevents path flip / TOCTOU on duplicate-filename tickers'.

_verdict.note: Multi-read structure is accurately described: processOne reads the snapshot file up to 4 times via independent helpers (_getExistingSnapshotAge reads 500 bytes -> youngEnough at L1655-1656; _existingSnapshotMissingTag211lFields full parse at L1455; _existingSnapshotMissingCurrencyNormalization full parse at L1506; _priceOnlyUpdate full parse at L1535). So a literal TOCTOU window exists. BUT it produces no wrong result, for concrete reasons: (1) The worker pool (runWorkerPool L2152-2172) dispenses each watchlist stock to exactly one worker and awaits processOne fully, so no two workers race the same file unless two watchlist entries collapse to the same safeSnapshotFilename -- a pre-existing duplicate-data problem, not introduced here. (2) A flip exactly at the 7-day boundary is harmless: both branches yield fresh, correct data (price-only refresh vs full pull); the full pull is the strictly safer fallback. (3) staleSchema/staleCurrency only ever FORCE a full pull (safe direction) -- they never authorize a price-only. (4) _priceOnlyUpdate operates on its OWN fresh re-read and independently re-validates: non-USD/fxApplied guard (L1560), MIN_MCAP floor (L1602); any throw falls through to full pull (L1670-1673). So even a stale youngEnough cannot persist bad data. The claim 'can flip path mid-decision' is technically true but the implied consequence (incorrect output) does not materialize -- every branch converges on fresh, validated data. This is a theoretical micro-inefficiency, not a defect; 'low' is generous, closer to informational.

title: DEFAULT_DISCOUNT_RATE (0.045) is permanently inert — Math.max with the 0.09 floor always wins under default config
evidence: Line 45: `const DEFAULT_DISCOUNT_RATE = 0.045; // base: ~10y UST yield proxy`. Lines 64-67: `const base = _envNum('DCF_DISCOUNT_RATE', DEFAULT_DISCOUNT_RATE); const floor = _envNum('DCF_DISCOUNT_RATE_FLOOR', DEFAULT_DISCOUNT_RATE_FLOOR); return { discountRate: Math.max(base, floor) ... }`. With defaults Math.max(0.045, 0.09) === 0.09 always. The 4.5% 'UST yield proxy' base never influences the model unless an operator sets DCF_DISCOUNT_RATE above 9%, at which point the floor is pointless.
why_it_matters: A future maintainer tuning the '10y UST proxy' base downward (e.g. to track falling rates) will see zero effect and may waste time, or wrongly conclude rates flow through. The discount rate — the single most sensitive DCF input — is effectively a hardcoded 9% constant dressed up as a configurable base+floor.
fix: Either document that the base is intentionally a no-op under normal rate regimes (rename constant to DCF_DISCOUNT_RATE_BASE_FOR_HIGH_RATE_OVERRIDE and add a comment), or change the model so base is the operative rate and the floor only clamps the lower bound when base is supplied below it (current code already does that — so the real fix is the comment: 'base is inert below 9%; floor dominates by design'). No SCORE_WEIGHTS / fixture change.

_verdict.note: False positive. The factual observation is correct — under default config `Math.max(base=0.045, floor=0.09) === 0.09`, so the 4.5% base never moves the result, and no caller sets DCF_DISCOUNT_RATE / DCF_DISCOUNT_RATE_FLOOR (verified by grep: both env keys are referenced only inside dcf-intrinsic-value.js lines 64-65). But this is intentional, working clamp logic, not dead code: (1) DEFAULT_DISCOUNT_RATE is the live fallback for the DCF_DISCOUNT_RATE env override — a real configuration surface, not an unused constant; (2) the Math.max guard does work whenever an operator raises the discount rate above 9%; (3) the module header (lines 20-21) explicitly documents the 9% floor as the operative Buffett hurdle, so 4.5% being shadowed by default is by design, not a defect. There is no wrong output, no unreachable branch, no SCORE_WEIGHTS/fixture impact. The auditor itself concedes in proposed_fix that 'current code already does that — so the real fix is the comment,' i.e. a self-admitted non-defect / documentation nit. Severity stays at the floor 'low', but substantively this is below the bug bar.

title: Decimal-vs-percent unit guard rejects legitimately small-but-percent inputs (|growth|<=1 AND |fcfMargin|<=1) as 'unit error'
evidence: rule-of-40.js:89 `if (Math.abs(growth) <= 1 && Math.abs(fcfMargin) <= 1) { return computable:false, reason: 'unit error...appear to be decimals' }`. Identical in rule-of-x.js:30. Inputs are confirmed already in PERCENT units (pull-yahoo.js:615 `revGrowthYoY = revGrowth * 100`, line 718 `fcfMarginTTM = (fcfTTM/revTTM)*100`). A real mature company with revenue growth of +0.8% and FCF margin of +0.5% (e.g. a low-growth utility/value name) has BOTH terms in [-1,1] as legitimate percents, and is wrongly declared a unit error and marked non-computable.
why_it_matters: The guard cannot distinguish a true 'someone passed 0.38 instead of 38' bug from a genuine near-flat company whose percent values happen to both be < 1.0. Such names are silently dropped from the R40 universe (the most permissive tab) — a survivorship/attrition bias against low-growth-but-positive names, and the data-integrity class flagged in the brief (0/small values legitimately valid). Because the pipeline already guarantees percent units upstream, the guard defends against an input shape that cannot occur on the real path while creating false negatives on the path that does.
fix: Tighten the heuristic so it only fires on the actual corruption signature: require BOTH |growth|<=1 AND |fcfMargin|<=1 AND at least one of them be non-zero-and-fractional in a way percents are not — e.g. only treat as unit error when the SUM |growth|+|fcfMargin| <= 1 AND both are non-integer-ish, or better, drop the heuristic and rely on the upstream percent guarantee. Minimum safe change: gate on `Math.abs(growth) < 1 && Math.abs(fcfMargin) < 1 && (growth !== 0 || fcfMargin !== 0)` is NOT enough; prefer requiring the combined R40 value < 2 to flag. Add comment: 'prevents false unit-error rejection of genuinely near-flat percent inputs'. Verify against fixture (growth=38/fcfMargin=22) which is unaffected.

_verdict.note: CONFIRMED real, severity downgraded to low. Code reads as cited: rule-of-40.js:89 and rule-of-x.js:30 both reject when Math.abs(growth) <= 1 && Math.abs(fcfMargin) <= 1 with reason 'unit error...appear to be decimals'. Inputs are verified to be in PERCENT units upstream: pull-yahoo.js revGrowthYoY = revGrowth * 100, and fcfMarginTTM = (fcfTTM/revTTM)*100 (both confirmed by reading mapYahooToCanonical). metricValue() in methods/_helpers.js passes the value through unchanged. So a genuinely near-flat percent stock (e.g. revenue growth +0.8% and FCF margin +0.5%, both legitimately in [-1,1]) is wrongly declared a unit error and marked computable:false. R40 is a core method run unconditionally for every stock (methods/index.js registry, no hypergrowth-only gate at evaluate-level), so such names do reach the guard. Downstream effects are real but narrow: (1) the stock is misreported as NO_DATA instead of a clean R40 FAIL; (2) it distorts computableCount in generate-methods-report.js and the correlation analysis; (3) detect-changes.js:222 can emit METHOD_INCOMPUTABLE alert churn when a borderline stock drifts in/out of the band week-to-week. Crucially it does NOT cause false positives/picks: any stock in that band has R40 value near 0, far below the threshold of 40, so it would FAIL anyway — no spurious PASS. That caps real impact at low. Also note the band requires BOTH metrics simultaneously in [-1%,+1%], which is uncommon (though plausible for a flat-year low-margin distributor/utility), further limiting frequency. The auditor's medium rating overstates impact since no selection/picks corruption results. Fixture-safety claim holds: engine-fixtures.js R40 inputs are all well above 1 (e.g. 38/8, 33/22, 15/28, 22/33), so any reasonable tightening leaves the fixture hash unchanged.

title: R40 fcfMargin annual-median fallback can flip FAIL->PASS using a different-period FCF margin added to a TTM growth term (period mismatch + selective inflation)
evidence: Lines 71-79: when `fcfMargin < 0 && fcfMargin > -20`, fcfMargin is replaced by `_annualFcfMarginMedian(stock)` (3y annual median, line 75 requires `annualMedian > 5` and latest annual FCF > 0). Line 96: `value = growth + fcfMargin` where `growth` is still `revenueGrowthYoY` (TTM YoY). So the composite becomes (TTM revenue growth) + (3-year median FCF margin). The fallback only ever RAISES the score (negative TTM replaced by a >+5 median), never lowers it, and only fires for the failing side.
why_it_matters: Mixing a TTM growth term with a 3-year-median margin term breaks the period coherence that makes Rule-of-40 a single-period efficiency metric, and the substitution is one-directional (it can only rescue FAILs into PASSes, never demote). The documented MELI rationale is plausible, but the rule applies to the WHOLE universe pattern-blind: any company with a transiently negative TTM FCF margin in (-20, 0) and a positive 3y median gets an upward-only adjustment, systematically inflating the R40 universe's pass rate for names with deteriorating-but-recently-positive FCF. The -20pp cliff (line 71) is also a hard discontinuity: -19.9% TTM gets rescued by a +33% median (swing of ~53 R40 points) while -20.1% does not.
fix: Make the adjustment symmetric and period-consistent or label it clearly: at minimum, when the fallback fires, ALSO recompute/annualize the growth term to the same annual basis (use 3y revenue CAGR from annualRev, already available in _annualFcfMarginMedian's revArr) so both terms share a period; and surface fcfMarginSource in components (already done) AND set a flag so downstream can see the value is a blended estimate, not a clean TTM R40. If symmetric repair is out of scope, soften the -20 cliff to a linear taper. Comment must name the failure mode: 'prevents one-directional TTM-growth + annual-margin period-mismatch inflation of the R40 universe'. Confirm fixture (fcfMarginTTM=22, positive) still never triggers the fallback.

_verdict.note:
Code facts are accurate but the "bug" is an intentional, documented heuristic, not a defect. Verified in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/methods/rule-of-40.js: line 71 guard `fcfMargin < 0 && fcfMargin > -20`; lines 72-78 replace fcfMargin with `_annualFcfMarginMedian(stock)` only when `annualMedian > 5` AND `latestAnnualFcf > 0`; line 96 `value = growth + fcfMargin` with growth still = revenueGrowthYoY (TTM, line 55, never recomputed). So the composite can indeed become (TTM rev growth) + (3y median FCF margin), and the substitution only ever raises a failing score. All true.

But this is the explicitly-designed "Tag 201c anchor-repair" path (header comment lines 2-10; rationale lines 59-70 citing F-ME-003 and F-06). It exists to fix a known false-FAIL (MELI: TTM fcfMargin -12.9% from a working-capital build masking ~33% structural FCF). It is heavily fenced (negative-only, capped at -20pp so structurally-negative FCF still fails, requires latest annual FCF > 0 and 3y median > 5) and it is NOT silent: `fcfMarginSource: '3y-annual-median'` is surfaced in `components` (line 99) and the reason string appends `[3y-annual-median]` (lines 100-101). The proposed_fix even concedes "fcfMarginSource ... already done". So downstream CAN distinguish a blended estimate from a clean TTM R40 — the central harm ("selective inflation" hidden in the universe) does not hold. The period mismatch is a legitimate methodology critique for a non-quant heuristic, but it is a deliberate, traceable tradeoff, not a coding bug, and there is no crash / NaN / silent corruption.

Fixture safety confirmed: fixture has fcfMarginTTM=22 (positive) at tag28-tests.js:2729, so the `fcfMargin < 0` guard is never entered; the dedicated test 'TTM positive — fallback NOT triggered' (lines 847-854) asserts source stays 'TTM'. Fallback test (835-845) confirms it only fires on the negative-TTM MELI pattern. So the fallback is fixture-hash-safe as designed.

Severity is overstated at medium; at most a low methodology-transparency nit.

title: R40-sanity F1 (revGrowth>150% spike) silently no-ops when annualOpInc[0] is missing — the ONDS/BEAM artifact class escapes the guard whenever OpInc data is absent
evidence: Line 99: `const f1 = (revGrowth != null && oi0 != null && revGrowth > REV_GROWTH_CAP && oi0 < 0);`. oi0 comes from `_unwrap(oiArr[0])` (line 82) where `oiArr = stock.annual.annualOpInc || []`. Confirm fixture (growth=38) and CRDO (OpInc>0) are unaffected — both have data so the new null-branch never touches them.

_verdict.note:
Code reads as cited: methods/r40-sanity-cap.js:99 `f1 = (revGrowth != null && oi0 != null && revGrowth > REV_GROWTH_CAP && oi0 < 0)` — when oi0 (annualOpInc[0]) is null, F1 cannot fire. So the literal "F1 no-ops when OpInc missing" observation is accurate. But the headline claim ("the ONDS/BEAM artifact class escapes the guard") is FALSE, which is why I mark is_real=false.

Refutation via the caller (generate-screener.js): R40 admission is gated by a 10-way OR defense-in-depth chain at line 621: `hardGated = qSpikeFail || lossMagFail || metricDivFail || niVolFail || preCommFail || cetFail || r40SanityFail || revShockFail || dqGrade==='D' || hgClassFail`. The finding is also internally inconsistent: loss-magnitude-guard.js:57-62 returns computable:false on missing oi0 (same hole), and pre-commerciality-megacap-guard.js (Tag 201b) was added specifically to plug the "annualOpInc/annualRev empty" bypass route (its header names this the Agent-5 'smoking gun'). A genuine escape would require a very narrow intersection: finite r40 (needs revGrowth + an FCF/margin input, so not data-empty), OpInc absent, fcfMargin/opMargin present-but-modest (else F2/F3 fire), no >55% quarterly spike (else qSpike), mcap<$1B (else preComm), and dqGrade not C/D (a name missing OpInc + quarterly data almost always grades C/D, which itself blocks R40 at line 720).
