title: forward-pe trusts Yahoo forwardPE blindly — no upper-bound sanity cap and no envelope/raw guard beyond H.metricValue, so a stale/garbage huge PE just fails silently while an absurdly low one passes
evidence: Lines 9-31: only guards are `fpe == null` (line 11) and `fpe <= 0` (line 17). Any positive number is accepted: `pass: fpe <= THRESHOLD` (line 25, THRESHOLD=40). There is no upper-bound implausibility check (Yahoo occasionally returns forwardPE in the thousands from a near-zero forward EPS estimate) and no cross-check against trailing PE or price. A forwardPE of 0.4 (from a corrupt/blown-up forward EPS) passes the <=40 gate as 'cheap'.
why_it_matters: forward-pe is a valuation sanity gate. A near-zero forward EPS estimate (denominator → 0) produces an explosively large forwardPE that correctly fails, but the symmetric corruption — a sign-flipped or unit-wrong forward EPS yielding a tiny positive PE — sails through as a false 'cheap' PASS. Other methods in this set (ev-ebitda Bug #11 net-cash, r40-sanity) have explicit implausibility caps; forward-pe has none, making it the weakest link of the valuation gates.
fix: Add a documented upper implausibility bound (e.g. forwardPE > 500 -> computable:false 'implausible forward PE, likely near-zero forward EPS') and optionally a lower bound (forwardPE < 1 with positive price -> flag for review). Comment naming the failure mode: 'prevents corrupt near-zero-forward-EPS PE from registering as cheap PASS / blown-up PE polluting computable set'. No SCORE_WEIGHTS dependency (forward-pe is not in SCORE_WEIGHTS, confirmed).

_verdict.note:
Largely a false positive built on a self-contradictory mechanism + overstated harm. Code confirmed at methods/forward-pe.js:9-31: guards are only fpe==null and fpe<=0, then pass: fpe<=40.

Refutation of each claimed harm:
1) "Huge stale/garbage PE fails silently / pollutes computable set." A forwardPE of e.g. 3000 evaluates 3000<=40 => pass:false, i.e. it correctly FAILS the cheapness gate. That is the intended screening outcome, not a defect. The auditor's named root cause ("near-zero forward EPS") actually PRODUCES this harmless huge-PE case, since Yahoo forwardPE = price/forwardEPS (near-zero positive EPS -> huge PE, not tiny). 
2) "Polluting the computable/median set." Verified this mechanism does not exist here: methods/sector-medians-compute.js gatherBySubProfile only buckets two metrics, 'roic' and 'fcf-yield' (lines 115/127). forward-pe is never gathered into any median, so no outlier can skew a threshold. effectiveThreshold() therefore always falls through to the static default 40 for forward-pe. 
3) Scoring impact: confirmed forward-pe is NOT in SCORE_WEIGHTS (methods/score-aggregator.js has no reference) and is classified type:DIAGNOSTIC, defaultActive:false in methods/method-types.js:119 ("Forward estimate, not a hard signal"). So even a false PASS/FAIL changes no composite score or pick ranking and isn't active by default.

The only real kernel: an absurdly LOW positive forwardPE (e.g. 0.4 from a corrupt blown-up forward EPS) passes 0.4<=40 as "cheap" with no lower implausibility guard. But (a) that requires forwardEPS ~2.5x price, the opposite of the "near-zero EPS" the finding cites, and is essentially never emitted by Yahoo for forwardPE; (b) zero scoring impact (DIAGNOSTIC, not weighted, default-inactive); (c) sibling valuation methods peg.js and ev-ebitda.js use the identical >0-only guard with no implausibility cap, so no codebase convention is violated. This is a low-value defensive-hardening suggestion, not a defect with demonstrable wrong output. Severity stays low.

fix_safe=false: the proposed fix adds two new computable:false branches (>500 and <1) with arbitrary magic thresholds. It flips affected stocks from computable:true (current PASS/FAIL) to computable:false, changing report output and the computable-set semantics. Behavior-changing (even if fixture-hash-neutral since not in SCORE_WEIGHTS) -> needs human review, not auto-apply.

title: Exported _compute() trusts annualOwnerEarnings.length (nulls counted) and is reachable by any external caller without the evaluate()-path yearsWithData>=4 validation
evidence: Line 208: `oeComponents.annualOwnerEarnings.length < MIN_OE_YEARS` uses raw array length. owner-earnings.js pushes `null` for missing years (owner-earnings.js:203-206, 214-218), so `annualOwnerEarnings` can be `[oe0, null, null, null]` — length 4, passing the gate with only 1 real datapoint. _compute is exported (line 434 `_compute`) 'for buffett-criteria composite to avoid redundant Runner call' (lines 192-203). The public evaluate() path is safe because it requires `oeResult.computable` (which enforces yearsWithData>=4 valid in owner-earnings.js:242), but a direct _compute caller bypasses that.
why_it_matters: Currently buffett-criteria uses DCF.evaluate (verified buffett-criteria.js:718-719), so no live caller hits the hole — but _compute is a public export explicitly advertised for direct use. The next caller that follows that advice and passes raw owner-earnings components will run a 12-year DCF off a single non-null OE datapoint with growth1 defaulting to 8% (cagrOE5y null), producing a confident-looking intrinsic value built on one year of data. Latent footgun on a BUFFETT-weighted method.
fix: In _compute, validate the count of FINITE entries, not raw length: `const validOE = oeComponents.annualOwnerEarnings.filter(v => Number.isFinite(v)); if (validOE.length < MIN_OE_YEARS) return computable:false`. Comment: 'prevents null-padded OE arrays from passing the length gate on the exported direct-call path'. No SCORE_WEIGHTS / fixture change (evaluate-path behavior unchanged since it already requires computable OE).

_verdict.note:
False positive as a bug. The finding's central evidence is a misread: it claims _compute() is "reachable by any external caller" and cites buffett-criteria as a direct _compute() caller. It is not. buffett-criteria.js:718-719 calls DCF.evaluate(stock), NOT DCF._compute(). I grepped the entire worktree: the ONLY invocation of _compute is the internal call at dcf-intrinsic-value.js:419 inside evaluate(), which is guarded by the oeResult.computable check at lines 411-417. There is no external direct caller anywhere — not in buffett-criteria.js, not in tag28-tests.js (which requires DCF but only uses evaluate via composite tests), not in scripts. The docstring at lines 192-203 saying _compute is "exposed so the buffett-criteria composite can call it directly" is stale — post-Tag-232e buffett-criteria delegates via evaluate(), not _compute().

Even on the hypothetical direct-call path the asserted harm does not materialize. _compute() only consumes annualOwnerEarnings[0] (line 229), which is immediately guarded by `!Number.isFinite(oe0) || oe0 <= 0` (line 230). Growth comes from the separate scalar oeComponents.cagrOE5y with a clamped GROWTH1_DEFAULT fallback (lines 261-264). _computeDCF never iterates the array, so a [oe0, null, null, null] input produces identical output to any 4-element array with the same oe0 — the null padding in indices 1..3 is never read. The MIN_OE_YEARS length check at line 208 is a soft prerequisite signal, not a data-integrity gate feeding the math. So "passing the gate with only 1 real datapoint" causes no wrong DCF value. On the real evaluate() path, owner-earnings returns computable:false (with cagrOE5y:null) whenever yearsWithData < 4 valid entries (owner-earnings.js:242-258), so a null-padded array can never reach _compute() via the public path anyway.

Net: this is at most a latent defensive-hardening nit on a dead/equivalent code path, and its primary justification (the buffett-criteria direct-call) is factually incorrect.

title: Quarterly path bails to annual (or incomputable) on a single interior null — drops the faster pre-breakout signal it exists for
evidence: _computeMargins iterates the first n entries and returns null on the FIRST gap: `for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) { const r = _unwrap(revArr[i]); const g = _unwrap(gpArr[i]); if (r == null || g == null || r <= 0) return null; ...}`. Caller: `if (revQ.length >= PERIODS_REQUIRED && gpQ.length >= PERIODS_REQUIRED) { margins = _computeMargins(revQ, gpQ, PERIODS_REQUIRED); if (margins) periodsUsed = 'quarterly'; }`.
why_it_matters: pull-yahoo.js mapFTSToQuarterly (lines 1208-1221) DELIBERATELY pushes `null` placeholders into the INTERIOR of revenueQ/grossProfitQ to preserve calendar alignment, and the comment states 'consumers finite-check each entry'. This method instead reads only the first 4 slots and returns null if any one is a placeholder. A single missing recent quarter (very common in Yahoo FTS) silently demotes the whole method from its quarterly raison-d'etre to the slower annual fallback, or to incomputable. The method header explicitly sells 'Quarterly preferred (faster signal)' — exactly the signal that gets thrown away. This is the documented Bug #26 / F-DP-003 interior-null class re-introduced.
fix: Compact valid (rev,gp) quarterly pairs scanning from index 0 and take the most-recent 4 finite pairs, instead of requiring slots [0..3] to all be finite. Add comment: '// prevents: interior-null placeholder in revenueQ/grossProfitQ (pull-yahoo mapFTSToQuarterly) silently dropping the quarterly signal'. Keep the annual fallback only when fewer than 4 finite quarterly pairs exist.

_verdict.note:
Mechanism is correctly observed but mischaracterized as a bug. _computeMargins (methods/gross-margin-acceleration.js:41-50) does bail on the first interior null in revenueQ[0..3], sending the method to the annual fallback. And interior nulls are genuinely possible: pull-yahoo.js mapFTSToQuarterly (lines 1203-1232) deliberately pushes null placeholders to preserve calendar alignment (F-002) and trims only TRAILING all-null quarters. So far the evidence checks out.

But the bail-on-first-gap is the deliberate, repeatedly-encoded codebase convention, not a defect. Same-era sibling single-quarter-dependency.js (Tag 199) uses the identical pattern: iterate revQ[0..3], return incomputable on the first v==null/<0 (lines 73-83), no compacting. More decisively, deceleration-guard.js (BUG-11, lines 37-47) and revenue-shock-guard.js (F-ME-005 line 61-68, F-ME-025 line 39-58) carry explicit comments that compacting/filtering ACROSS null gaps is itself a bug they fixed, because filter() reindexes non-consecutive quarters and breaks period/calendar alignment.

The proposed fix ('compact valid pairs, take most-recent 4 finite') is exactly that filter-then-reindex anti-pattern. GM deltas here are period-over-period (margins[0]-margins[1], etc.), so compacting across an interior null would compute a delta between NON-adjacent quarters (e.g. Q0 vs Q-2 when Q-1 is null) and label it a single-period improvement — a misleading acceleration signal. That is the BUG-11 failure mode, i.e. a regression. The current annual fallback is the safer, intended behavior. No test pins either behavior, and the only realistic interior-null position (latest quarter, mid-quarter gap per F-ME-025) is one the design intentionally declines to guess at.

Verdict: intentional conservative trade-off, not a high-severity bug — false positive on the 'bug' framing. Could not measure live incidence (no stock corpus in this worktree, only data/ma-rpo-snapshot.json which has no stock array), but incidence affects only severity, not validity.

title: Period-over-period deltas assume contiguous calendar periods; interior nulls in annual path mean deltas can span non-adjacent years
evidence: deltas are built positionally `margins[0] - margins[1]`, `margins[1] - margins[2]`, `margins[2] - margins[3]` directly from `_computeMargins(revY, gpY, PERIODS_REQUIRED)`. The annual path uses the same _computeMargins which returns null on any interior null, so in practice the annual path also aborts. But where the same compaction fix from A-01 is applied, naive positional deltas would treat e.g. FY2025 vs FY2023 (with FY2024 missing) as 'one period', mislabeling the trend.
why_it_matters: '3 consecutive period-over-period improvements' is the entire semantic of the method (trend = accelerating). If a fiscal year is missing mid-window and the array is compacted, the delta silently spans 2 years and the 'consecutive' claim is false, producing false accelerating/decelerating classifications that flow into the dashboard.
fix: When compacting (per A-01 fix), record each retained period's index/fiscal-date and only form a delta between periods that are calendar-adjacent; otherwise mark incomputable with reason 'non-contiguous periods'. Comment the failure mode.

_verdict.note: False positive / hypothetical. In the CURRENT code (methods/gross-margin-acceleration.js), _computeMargins (lines 41-50) is NOT compacting: it reads positions 0..n-1 (n=4) positionally and returns null the instant any position has a null rev/gp or r<=0 (line 46) — no .filter(), no index-skip. So when margins is non-null (the line-78 guard passed), margins[0..3] are the 4 stored array positions in original order, and the deltas at lines 89-93 are between ADJACENT stored positions. An interior null yields computable:false ("need 4 consecutive rev+gp points", lines 78-85), never a mislabeled trend. The finding's own evidence concedes this ("returns null on any interior null, so in practice the annual path also aborts") and only claims a bug "where the same compaction fix from A-01 is applied" — i.e. it is conditional on a future edit. That prerequisite does not exist: grep found no A-01 finding adding compaction to this file (it appears only in findings/methods-engine.json files_examined), and the whole pipeline trend is the OPPOSITE — pull-yahoo.js mapFTSToAnnual/_ftsExtractByYear (lines 1068-1136) plus F-DP-030/031, F-DP-101, F-ME-006, Bug #26 deliberately PRESERVE null placeholders for positional alignment and null-check by position. So the claim is speculation about a refactor that contradicts the codebase's direction. fix_safe=false: the proposed fix adds fiscal-date tracking + a new 'non-contiguous periods' incomputable branch, which changes outputs/reason strings and is not behavior-preserving — and it guards a condition that cannot currently occur.

title: Returns incomputable on the FIRST interior null instead of finite-filtering — and positional deltas assume contiguity
evidence: Gate is only `revArr.length < PERIODS_REQUIRED`. Loop: `for (let i = 0; i < PERIODS_REQUIRED; i++) { const r = _unwrap(revArr[i]); const o = _unwrap(oiArr[i]); if (r == null || o == null || r <= 0) { return H.buildResult({ computable: false, reason: 'period ' + i + ...}); } margins.push(o / r * 100); }`
why_it_matters: Identical interior-null class as A-01: any single null in the first 4 slots of annualRev/annualOpInc (common when Yahoo omits one operatingIncome year) makes the method incomputable even though 4+ valid years exist deeper in the array. Sister method operating-leverage-margin-accel.js already does the correct finite-filter-then-window approach (lines 96-101), proving the codebase knows the pattern — this one diverges. Net effect: a defaultActive operating-leverage signal silently goes dark on exactly the names with patchy fundamentals.
fix: Mirror operating-leverage-margin-accel.js: build an aligned finite-only `years[]` array, require >=4, then compute the 3 most-recent contiguous deltas. Comment the interior-null failure mode.

_verdict.note:
The code description is accurate but the conclusion is wrong — this is not a bug, and the proposed fix would introduce incorrect behavior. Verified against source in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening.

Facts confirmed:
1. operating-margin-acceleration.js gates only on revArr.length/oiArr.length >= 4 (line 57), then the loop (lines 67-78) returns computable:false on the first null/non-positive in positions 0-3. Interior/recent nulls ARE a real data shape: pull-yahoo.js deliberately preserves null placeholders in annualRev/annualOpInc to keep fiscal-year positional alignment (documented as F-004 line ~570, F-DP-003, Bug #26 fix at mapFTSToAnnual lines 1105-1106; banks/insurers like JPM/BAC/NU/SOFI are the canonical case). wrapEvaluate (_helpers.js line 313) passes the raw arrays through with no null-stripping, so the method does see interior nulls.

Why it is NOT a bug:
2. This is the "N consecutive period-over-period improvements" method family. Its direct sibling gross-margin-acceleration.js (Tag 195 — explicitly named as the parallel in this file's own header at lines 6-7) uses the IDENTICAL positional-slot logic and the identical null-on-any-entry guard (_computeMargins, lines 41-50). Positional deltas are required to be CORRECT here: "3 consecutive OpM improvements" is only meaningful across adjacent fiscal years, and because the pipeline keeps arrays positionally aligned, margins[i]-margins[i+1] is guaranteed to be an adjacent-year delta. Returning incomputable when a recent slot is null is the conservative, correct answer.
3. The proposed fix (mirror operating-leverage-margin-accel.js: finite-filter into years[] then take 3 contiguous deltas) would compute deltas ACROSS fiscal-year gaps and falsely label non-consecutive years as "3 consecutive improvements." That is semantically wrong for an acceleration signal. operating-leverage-margin-accel.js can finite-filter only because it averages over positive-growth PAIRS (gap-tolerant by construction), a different computation — not because positional logic is an error.

Impact bound:
4. The method is DIAGNOSTIC-only (method-types.js line 75; not in SCORE_WEIGHTS). generate-screener.js (lines 293-296) and snapshot-score-history.js null-guard omaTrend/omaChange, so incomputable degrades to "no pre-breakout signal," never a wrong score or corrupted data. The only real behavioral difference is that a ticker whose MOST-RECENT OpInc year is null (but with 4 valid older years) yields no signal where finite-filtering would — and "no signal" is the correct output for this metric anyway.

Net: filed as category=bug / severity=high; it is a false positive. At most a low consistency note, and the suggested remediation is itself incorrect.

title: CoV window is hard-capped at the first 4 array slots; interior nulls shrink the usable sample and can pull in non-adjacent years
evidence: Gate `if (revs.length < 4 || gps.length < 4)`, then `for (let i = 0; i < 4; i++) { ... if (r == null || g == null || r <= 0) continue; margins.push(g / r); }` and later `if (margins.length < 3)`. Only the first 4 slots are ever considered.
why_it_matters: If slot 1 or 2 is an interior null (documented schema shape), the method computes CoV over only 3 of the first 4 years and never looks at year 5+, even when more clean data exists. Worse, the surviving margins may be FY2025/FY2023/FY2022 (a gap), so the 'over 4 years' dispersion claim in the description is violated and CoV is computed across a non-contiguous span. Feeds the CORE gross-margin-stability signal (it is CORE/defaultActive per method-types.js line 17).
fix: Scan the whole array, finite-filter to the newest N (e.g. up to 5) contiguous valid margin points, require >=4 for the advertised 4y window (or relax the description). Document why a fixed [0..3] window is unsafe given interior nulls.

_verdict.note: Refuted as a false positive based on a misread. The method computes a coefficient-of-variation (mean/stdev) over gross-margin points — an order-INDEPENDENT dispersion metric. The loadbearing claim "can pull in non-adjacent years" does not apply: the loop is `for (i=0;i<4;i++)` (methods/gross-margin-stability.js:38), so it never looks past index 3; it stays strictly within the 4-most-recent-year window. Skipping an interior null within [0..3] yields points from non-contiguous slots (e.g. {0,2,3}), but contiguity is irrelevant to a CoV — there is no arr[i] vs arr[i+1] comparison here (unlike the YoY-acceleration methods, which genuinely break on holes). The "shrink the usable sample" part is true but intentional and harmless: a null drops a point and the `if (margins.length < 3)` gate (line 44) handles it — exactly the documented "need 3 of 4 years" design ("über 4 Jahre", line 72). This null-skip-then-min-count pattern is identical to the two sibling stability methods: fcf-stability.js (WINDOW=4, MIN_PAIRS=3, lines 88-103) and earnings-power-stability.js (WINDOW=5, MIN_YEARS=4, lines 96-112), both of which are treated as canonical and correct (this file's _unwrap comment even cites earnings-power-stability as the canonical reference). The only real difference is cosmetic: this file hard-codes `4` instead of `Math.min(4, revs.length, gps.length)` — but the preceding gate `revs.length < 4 || gps.length < 4` (line 30) already guarantees both arrays have >=4 elements, so `Math.min(4, len, len) === 4`. Functionally equivalent, no out-of-bounds, no different year pulled in. Interior nulls DO occur in this codebase (pull-yahoo.js preserves null placeholders for fiscal-year alignment: bank/insurer gap years JPM/BAC/NU/SOFI, F-004/F-DP-003), so the data premise is real — but the consequence the auditor draws is wrong for a CoV.

title: _rawVals strips Number.isFinite guard on envelope shape; NaN/Infinity .value flows into median, margins, and asset-turnover
evidence: `return arr.map(v => v == null ? null : (typeof v === 'number' ? v : v.value));` — for an object entry it returns `v.value` UNCONDITIONALLY (no Number.isFinite). The downstream guards use `Number.isFinite(rawRevs[i])` for the loop (lines 73-74) which catches it there, BUT `const latestRev = rawRevs[0]; const at = (Number.isFinite(latestRev) && latestRev > 0 && totalAssets) ? latestRev / totalAssets : null;` relies on that guard, and `_median` (line 40-45) sorts whatever gms/opMs contain. gms is push-guarded so it is safe, but the broader pattern of returning unguarded `.value` is the same NaN-propagation class _helpers.js F-ME-015 was created to kill.
why_it_matters: The whole codebase standardized on a Number.isFinite-checked `_unwrap` (see gross-margin-stability, margin-decay, all Tag-212+ methods). margin-quality is a CORE QC MUST-3 gate (method-types.js line 25) yet uses a weaker local `_rawVals` that can emit raw `undefined`/NaN from a malformed envelope `{value:'N/A'}` or `{}`. If totalAssets path or any future consumer reads _rawVals output without an isFinite re-check, a NaN silently makes comparisons false (NaN < 0.20 is false) — flipping a hard-fail into a pass.
fix: Make _rawVals return `Number.isFinite(x) ? x : null` for both number and envelope branches, matching the canonical _unwrap. Comment: '// prevents NaN/undefined envelope .value silently passing the GM/OpM floors (NaN<x === false)'.

_verdict.note: False positive as a live bug. _rawVals (line 37) does return v.value without a Number.isFinite guard, but EVERY downstream consumer of its output is independently guarded, so no NaN/Infinity can actually propagate into median, margins, or asset-turnover. Verified all four sinks in methods/margin-quality.js: (1) min-data count lines 58-60 use .filter(v => Number.isFinite(v)); (2) gms/opMs lines 73-74 are push-guarded — both rawRevs[i] AND rawGps[i]/rawOpIncs[i] must pass Number.isFinite before any value enters the arrays; (3) _median (lines 83-84) only ever receives the push-guarded gms/opMs, never raw arrays; (4) asset-turnover line 90 reads `const at = (Number.isFinite(latestRev) && latestRev > 0 && totalAssets) ? latestRev/totalAssets : null` — the Number.isFinite(latestRev) guard catches any unguarded .value before division. The finding's own evidence concedes each of these ("gms is push-guarded so it is safe", "The downstream guards use Number.isFinite(rawRevs[i])"), then falls back to a "broader pattern of returning unguarded .value is the same class as F-ME-015" argument — i.e. a consistency/hardening observation, not a demonstrated unguarded sink. There is no execution path where the missing guard changes a result. Grep confirms lines 52-90 are the only uses of the raw arrays and all are guarded.

title: 3y OCF/NI coverage window can silently span non-contiguous years due to interior nulls / sign skips, contradicting the '3 consecutive fiscal years' contract
evidence: `const maxYears = Math.min(WINDOW, ocfArr.length, niArr.length); for (let i = 0; i < maxYears; i++) { const ocf = _unwrap(ocfArr[i]); const ni = _unwrap(niArr[i]); if (ocf == null || ni == null) {skip} if (ocf <= 0 || ni <= 0) {skip} ratios.push(ocf / ni); }`. The window is the first 3 slots only.
why_it_matters: Header claims 'last 3 fiscal years'. Because only slots [0..2] are scanned and nulls/sign-mismatches are skipped, a name with a null OCF in year 1 yields a 2-point mean drawn from year0+year2 (a gap year), still passing MIN_PAIRS=2. annualOCF is built null-preservingly (pull-yahoo F-DP-101, line 1124) precisely so a mid-window OCF gap doesn't shift alignment — but this method then averages across the gap as if contiguous. Less severe than the indexing bugs (it is DIAGNOSTIC), but the displayed 'OCF/NI mean (3y)' is misleading and the n=2 across a 3-year gap is a weak quality signal presented as a 3y average.
fix: Either widen the scan to find the newest 3 CONTIGUOUS valid (OCF,NI) years, or relabel reason/components to report the actual span (e.g. 'n=2 across FY2025,FY2023'). Comment the gap-span failure mode.

_verdict.note: Refuted as a defect — the "3 consecutive fiscal years contract" it claims to violate does not exist. The method's documented contract (methods/operating-cashflow-coverage.js header lines 27-36, 47: "For each of the last 3 fiscal years where BOTH ... are positive", "3y mean coverage", "need at least 2 of 3 valid years") and its smoke tests (tag28-tests.js:998-1021) define the window as the FIRST 3 slots ("last 3 fiscal years"), averaging whichever same-sign-positive pairs are valid, requiring n>=2. Skips are an EXPECTED, designed-for case — sign mismatch is explicitly excluded as "non-informative" (lines 29-33) and the skipped count is surfaced, not silent: both components.skippedYears and the reason string ("skipped=N") report it. So the mechanical observation is accurate (an interior null/sign-skip at slot 0 or 1 does not make the loop reach slot 3+; the mean can span non-contiguous years among the first 3), but the framing that this contradicts a contiguity contract is a misread of the source. Materiality is negligible: (1) the method is DIAGNOSTIC-only — NOT in SCORE_WEIGHTS (line 60) — so it cannot move rankings or the fixture hash; (2) interior nulls only arise on the FTS construction path (pull-yahoo.js:1123-1137, written null-preservingly per F-DP-101; canonical write at 1935/1937), and that path's own comment (lines 1119-1122) documents ~0 live incidence because the missing year is almost always the OLDEST (array tail, outside the first-3 window), not interior. The only genuine residual is a labeling nicety (not naming WHICH fiscal years were averaged), which is the proposed fix's second/relabel branch — an enhancement, not a bug. Sibling sloan-ratio.js does track year indices and breaks on gaps (line 84), so there is prior art for richer labeling, but its purpose there is a true consecutive-year hard-fail rule, not a mean.

title: Capex ratio compares fixed [0] vs [3] with no contiguity guard and Math.abs masks sign — a misaligned/short window produces a spurious cash-burn pass/fail
evidence: Gate only `capexArr.length < 4 || revArr.length < 4`. Then `capexT = abs(_unwrap(capexArr[0]))`, `capexT3 = abs(_unwrap(capexArr[3]))`, `revT=_unwrap(revArr[0])`, `revT3=_unwrap(revArr[3])`, `value = (capexT/revT)/(capexT3/revT3)`.
why_it_matters: annualCapex is built by a different extractor than annualRev (pull-yahoo notes _ftsExtractByYear builds capex null-preservingly while rev/oi/gp come from mapFTSToAnnual). Their interior nulls need not align, so capexArr[3] and revArr[3] can be different fiscal years. Math.abs further hides that some Yahoo capex rows are stored positive vs negative; if sign convention flips between year0 and year3 the ratio is still 'fixed' by abs but the underlying years may be misaligned. Result: a Capex/Rev growth multiplier that doesn't correspond to a clean 3-year span, feeding the cash-burn early-warning. The F-ME-001 comment fixed the null->abs(null)=0 false-pass but did NOT fix the [0]/[3] positional-alignment assumption.
fix: Build aligned finite (capex,rev) tuples, require 4 contiguous years, pick the newest and 3-years-older from the aligned set; verify the two cross-arrays reference the same fiscal year before dividing. Comment the cross-array misalignment failure mode.

_verdict.note:

title: 3y SG&A slope built from positionally-compacted ratios then reversed — interior nulls make the regression x-axis non-uniform (treats gap years as adjacent)
evidence: `const maxYears = Math.min(WINDOW, sgaArr.length, revArr.length); for (i<maxYears) { if (sga==null||rev==null||rev<=0) continue; sgaRatios.push(sga/rev); }` then `const chrono = sgaRatios.slice().reverse(); const slope = _slope(chrono);` where _slope uses x=[0..n-1] uniformly.
why_it_matters: _slope assumes equal 1-year spacing (x = index). If year 1 SG&A is an interior null, sgaRatios = [FY2025ratio, FY2023ratio] (a 2-year gap) but _slope treats them as 1 year apart, doubling the apparent pp/yr slope and potentially flipping the pass at the tight 0.005 (+0.5pp/yr) threshold. Also MIN_YEARS=3 can fail spuriously when 3 clean years exist beyond slot 2. annualSGA is from the Tag-211l null-preserving path, so interior nulls are expected.
fix: Carry each retained ratio's fiscal-year index and regress ratio against actual year offset, or restrict to contiguous years; reject windows with internal gaps. Comment that uniform-x regression over gapped years biases the slope.

_verdict.note:
REFUTED. The auditor correctly read that the loop positionally compacts ratios (skips interior null/invalid years via `continue`) and that `_slope` regresses against a uniform x=[0..n-1]. But the claimed bug — gap years being treated as adjacent, biasing the slope — is structurally unreachable because WINDOW === MIN_YEARS === 3 (both module constants, no override path).

Mechanism: `maxYears = Math.min(WINDOW=3, sgaArr.length, revArr.length)` caps the loop at the first 3 latest-first positions. To reach `sgaRatios.length >= MIN_YEARS (3)`, ALL of positions 0,1,2 must be valid (non-null SGA, non-null Rev, Rev>0). If any of those three years has an interior gap, the surviving count drops to <=2 and the `sgaRatios.length < MIN_YEARS` guard (line 108) returns computable:false — no regression runs. The method never looks past position 2, so a gap at position 3+ is simply ignored, not interpolated.

Therefore the only way a slope is ever computed is from 3 contiguous fiscal years (positions 0,1,2), which are uniformly spaced by construction — exactly what uniform-x regression assumes. There is no input that produces a 3-element regression over non-adjacent years.

Verified empirically in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening: a mid-window gap (SGA=[16,null,12], Rev=[100,100,100]) returns "only 2 valid (SGA,Rev>0) years (need >= 3)"; the same gap in longer arrays behaves identically; and 3 clean leading years with a gap at position 3 compute a clean uniform slope ignoring the gap.

Context confirming interior nulls DO exist (so the auditor's premise about gapped arrays is genuine, just non-triggering here): pull-yahoo.js _ftsExtractByYear (builds annualSGA) and mapFTSToAnnual (builds annualRev) both deliberately push null placeholders to preserve cross-array year alignment. The bug pattern (compaction + uniform-x) WOULD bite a method with WINDOW > MIN_YEARS — but this method has them equal, which closes the gap.

title: GMI compares revs[0]/gps[0] vs revs[1]/gps[1] assuming both arrays are aligned at slot 1 — cross-array interior null at the prior year misaligns the yoy comparison
evidence: `const revT = _unwrap(revs[0]); const revT1 = _unwrap(revs[1]); const gpT = _unwrap(gps[0]); const gpT1 = _unwrap(gps[1]);` with only `revs.length < 2 || gps.length < 2` gating. value = gmT1/gmT.
why_it_matters: annualRev and annualGP are pushed in the same mapFTSToAnnual loop so they are usually co-aligned, but a year where grossProfit is null writes null to annualGP[k] while annualRev[k] is a real value (line 1105-1107). If slot 1 is such a year, gpT1 is null -> incomputable (acceptable), but if slot 0 has gp=null and a row was skipped earlier, the [0]/[1] pair can straddle a gap, computing a 2-year GM decay as if 1-year. Less likely than the capex/sga cross-extractor cases since GP and Rev share a loop, hence medium. margin-decay is DIAGNOSTIC (not defaultActive), limiting blast radius.
fix: Use aligned finite (rev,gp) tuples and take the two newest contiguous years; confirm they are adjacent fiscal years before computing GMI. Comment the failure mode.

_verdict.note: False positive / misread. margin-decay.js:29-32 reads revs[0]/gps[0] (year T) and revs[1]/gps[1] (year T-1), then the guard at line 33 (`revT1 == null || gpT1 == null`) returns computable:false on ANY null at slot 1. There is NO compaction/.filter(Boolean)/"skip-null-and-take-next" anywhere in this method, so an interior null at the prior year cannot "misalign" the comparison — the method just bails cleanly (correct conservative behavior). The auditor's described failure mode does not exist in the code. Furthermore, the pipeline GUARANTEES positional fiscal-year alignment by deliberately preserving interior null placeholders (pull-yahoo.js mapFTSToAnnual lines 1104-1108, _ftsExtractByYear 1070-1082, and the F-DP-030/031 / Tag 206f comments at 1871-1880 explicitly state annualRev[i]/annualGP[i] reference the SAME fiscal year, with only trailing pure-null rows trimmed). So revs[1] and gps[1] are the same year T-1, and slots 0/1 are adjacent fiscal years whenever both are non-null. The method receives raw aligned arrays; the only compaction (arrUnwrap in generate-screener.js:416-418) is a separate UI-sparkline path, not the evaluate path. The proposed fix is actively harmful: "take the two newest contiguous finite years" would, when T-1 is null, silently compare (T, T-2) and label a 2-year change as a 1-year GMI — changing behavior and producing a wrong decay magnitude rather than the current honest computable:false. Note: a genuinely different (uncited) hazard exists — annualRev override is gated by non-null count (line 1861) while annualGP override is gated only by length>0 (line 1932), so rev and gp could come from different sources with different offsets — but that is a pull-yahoo merge issue affecting all GP/Rev methods, not the slot-1-interior-null mechanism this finding describes.

title: Same fixed [0]/[1] yoy assumption as margin-decay; can compare non-adjacent years on interior null
evidence: `const revT = _unwrap(revs[0]); const revT1 = _unwrap(revs[1]); const oiT = _unwrap(ois[0]); const oiT1 = _unwrap(ois[1]);` gated only by length>=2. value = omT/omT1, pass when <=1.5.

Refuted — the finding is self-contradictory and based on a misread of the cited sibling. But methods/margin-decay.js (lines 29-32) uses the EXACT same pattern as opinc-margin-spike.js (lines 31-34): fixed indices revs[0]/revs[1], gps[0]/gps[1], gated only by length>=2, with the same _unwrap helper. Concrete evidence:

title: GP[0] and totalAssets[0] taken from index 0 of two independently-built arrays with no fiscal-year alignment check — mismatched-period GP/TA ratio
evidence: `const gpArr = (stock.annual && stock.annual.annualGP) || []; const balArr = (stock.annual && stock.annual.annualBalance) || []; ... const gp = _unwrap(gpArr[0]); const bal = balArr[0]; const ta = (bal && Number.isFinite(bal.totalAssets)) ? bal.totalAssets : null; const ratio = gp / ta;`
why_it_matters: annualGP[0] comes from mapFTSToAnnual (income statement rows) and annualBalance[0] from mapFTSToBalance (balance rows); these are built from different Yahoo modules with independent trailing-null trims (pull-yahoo 1197-1199 vs 1109). If one module returns one more (or fewer) recent period than the other, gpArr[0] and balArr[0] are different fiscal years, so Novy-Marx GP/TA divides this year's gross profit by last year's assets (or vice versa). The anchor checks in the header (NVDA/MSFT/COST) only validate the happy path. Result: a quality floor (>=0.20) decided on mismatched-period inputs.
fix: Match GP and totalAssets by fiscal-year/date key (the balance entries carry a period) rather than by array index, or assert the two arrays' newest periods are equal before dividing; otherwise return incomputable. Comment the cross-module period-alignment failure mode.

_verdict.note: Confirmed real but lower-severity than claimed, and the auditor's proposed fix is partly based on a misread. gross-profitability.js:91-94 divides _unwrap(gpArr[0]) by balArr[0].totalAssets with no period-alignment check. annualGP and annualBalance are built from TWO independent sources/modules: in the QS path annualGP = _arr(isHist,'grossProfit') from incomeStatementHistory while annualBalance is mapped from balanceSheetHistory (bsHist) — both run independent .filter(Boolean) compaction (pull-yahoo.js:493-500 and :675-692). In the FTS merge the two arrays are overwritten under INDEPENDENT gates: annualGP only needs ftsAnnual.annualGP.length>0 (line 1932), but annualBalance is overwritten only if newBalanceUsable>oldBalanceUsable (line 1898). So GP can switch to FTS (newest FY=2025) while balance stays on QS (newest FY=2024) — index 0 then mixes fiscal years. The repo has heavily engineered WITHIN-array positional alignment (F-DP-101 / F-DP-003, lines 1111-1153) by replacing `continue` with null placeholders, but that only aligns arrays sharing one source iteration; it does NOT solve cross-module GP-vs-balance alignment, and the QS path still compacts. CAVEAT 1: the auditor's evidence is wrong that 'balance entries carry a period' — entries are {totalCash,totalDebt,totalAssets,...} with NO date/period key in either the QS path (line 691) or the FTS path (lines 1183-1194), so the method physically cannot match by fiscal year, and the proposed match-by-date fix is not implementable without first adding period fields to the pull layer. CAVEAT 2: live incidence is low — the code documents (lines 1119-1121) that Yahoo's missing year 'is almost always the oldest', so index-0 (newest) misalignment within a single source is rare; the realistic trigger is the cross-source newest-FY mismatch. CAVEAT 3: this method is DIAGNOSTIC-only (header lines 21-23: NOT in SCORE_WEIGHTS), so a mismatched ratio cannot move screener results or the fixture hash; it can only mislead in detail-modal/percentile views.

title: _classify and minDelta call Math.min(...deltas) — safe today but will throw/NaN if deltas array is ever empty after a contiguity fix

title: Positive-only sign filter on OCF/NI silently excludes the most informative low-quality cases (NI>0 while OCF<=0), biasing the coverage mean upward
evidence: `if (ocf <= 0 || ni <= 0) { skipped.push({ i, why: 'sign' }); continue; }` — a year with strong reported NI but negative operating cash flow (the exact earnings-quality red flag the method advertises) is dropped from the average instead of scoring near/below zero.
why_it_matters: Header states the failure mode it detects is 'NI persistently exceeds OCF' / 'reported earnings increasingly non-cash'. But the worst manifestation — positive NI, negative OCF — is filtered out as 'sign mismatch', so the 3y mean only averages the years where cash conversion was already positive. A serial accruals-inflator with one heavily negative-OCF year gets that year excluded and can still clear the 0.80 floor on its two good years. Self-defeating for a DIAGNOSTIC quality signal.
fix: Treat NI>0 with OCF<=0 as coverage 0 (or a small floor) and include it, rather than skipping; keep skipping only true non-informative cases (NI<=0). Comment that excluding NI>0/OCF<=0 would hide the primary failure mode.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed real, but minor. Code at C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/methods/operating-cashflow-coverage.js line 108 (`if (ocf <= 0 || ni <= 0) { skipped.push({ i, why: 'sign' }); continue; }`) does exactly what the finding says: it lumps two semantically different cases into one "sign" skip. The NI<=0 (loss-year) skip is legitimately justified in the header (lines 27-34). But the header's stated rationale only addresses the NI<0/OCF>0 direction ("a loss year with positive OCF is a recovery signal"); it never justifies dropping the auditor's case — NI>0 with OCF<=0 — which is precisely the earnings-quality failure mode the method advertises (strong reported earnings, no cash). Dropping that year from the mean instead of scoring it near/below zero does bias the coverage mean upward; in a 3y window it can flip a borderline name from FAIL to PASS, and worse, if dropping the bad year leaves fewer than MIN_PAIRS=2 valid years the whole signal silently goes incomputable (line 111) for exactly the worst-quality firms.

Severity correctly stays LOW: this method is DIAGNOSTIC-only, NOT in any SCORE_WEIGHTS (confirmed header line 60 + method-types.js registry line 87) and does not feed the fixture hash or gate/score stock selection — it is deep-dive context, so impact is a cosmetically optimistic indicator for a narrow class, not corrupted screener output.

fix_safe=false: the proposed fix changes the method's computed value and interacts with the MIN_PAIRS gate (a previously-skipped year now counts toward the pair count, flipping some incomputable cases to computable). It is a methodology judgment call (floor value? split the `||` so only NI<=0 is skipped while NI>0/OCF<=0 scores 0?) and needs the header rationale rewritten — not a behavior-preserving mechanical edit. The two existing smoke tests (tag28-tests.js lines 998-1021) cover only all-positive PASS/FAIL, so they would not catch a regression here; a new test for the NI>0/OCF<=0 case should accompany any fix. Recommend human review.

title: fcf-yield sector/region median mixes two FX bases for ADR-class stocks (reporting-ccy FCF / trading-ccy marketCap)
evidence: Line 120-121: `if (fcfAdj != null && mc != null && mc > 0) { globalBuckets[sp.id]['fcf-yield'].push(fcfAdj / mc); }` (and the identical regional push at 132-133). `fcfAdj` derives from `stock.annual.annualFCF[].value`, which pull-yahoo.js scales by the REPORTING factor (`snap.annual[key] = snap.annual[key].map(scale)`, pull-yahoo.js:454). `mc = stock.marketCap.value` is scaled by the TRADING factor (`snap.marketCap = scaleTrading(snap.marketCap)`, pull-yahoo.js:415). pull-yahoo.js:435-440 explicitly documents that for ADR-class tickers `tradingFactor !== factor`.
why_it_matters: For any ADR or dual-currency listing (trading currency differs from reporting currency), the fcf-yield ratio fed into the sector median is numerator-USD-via-factor divided by denominator-USD-via-tradingFactor — a silently wrong number. Because Tag 167 now computes medians PER REGION, a handful of mis-scaled ADRs can skew an entire EU/APAC/EM region bucket, and that median becomes the live pass-gate threshold via effectiveThreshold(). Foreign stocks then get systematically wrong fcf-yield gating. This is exactly the kind of FX-normalization bug that caps screener quality.
fix: When building the fcf-yield ratio, divide quantities scaled by the SAME factor. Either (a) reconstruct an FCF in trading currency, or (b) reconstruct marketCap in reporting currency using meta.fxRateApplied vs meta.tradingFxRateApplied, then take the ratio. Simplest robust option: skip the fcf-yield bucket push when `stock.meta.tradingFxRateApplied != null && stock.meta.tradingFxRateApplied !== stock.meta.fxRateApplied` (ADR mismatch), so the median is built only from currency-consistent stocks. Add comment: '// prevents FX-base-mismatch poisoning the fcf-yield median (reporting-ccy FCF / trading-ccy mcap for ADRs)'.

_verdict.note: False positive — the auditor confused "two different FX factors" with "two different result currencies". In _convertToUSD (pull-yahoo.js) every persisted snapshot is normalized to a COMMON USD base before it ever reaches sector-medians-compute.js: snap.annual.* (incl. annualFCF) is scaled by `factor` (reporting-ccy→USD, line 454) and snap.marketCap by `tradingFactor` (trading-ccy→USD, line 415). The two distinct factors exist precisely BECAUSE Yahoo returns financials in the reporting currency but marketCap/price in the trading currency for ADRs (documented lines 335-355); applying each leg's own factor RESOLVES that native mismatch rather than creating one. After conversion both legs are USD, so `fcfAdj / mc` (lines 120-121, 132-133) is a correct dimensionless yield for ADRs. Worked example TSM: FCF reported in TWD → factor=TWD→USD gives USD FCF; marketCap quoted in USD (NYSE) → tradingFactor=1 gives USD mcap; ratio is correct. The non-ADR case is `tradingFactor===factor`, which trivially cancels. Snapshots where conversion fails (meta.fxConversionFailed===true) are unlinked/skipped before persistence (pull-yahoo.js:1992-1997, :290-295), so no mixed-currency snapshot reaches gatherBySubProfile (which has no fx guards and needs none). The cited evidence describes pre-conversion Yahoo values, not the post-scale values the gather actually reads.

title: SoftGuard failures never surface as human-readable warnings in buildStory (e.g. HYPERGROWTH revenue-shock / deceleration / quarter-concentration)
evidence: buildStory() only iterates `mode.softWarnings` (line 338-345) and `mode.dataGuards` (line 348-355) when collecting warnings. It never iterates `mode.softGuards` nor `modeEval.failedSoftGuards`. Yet SOFT_WARNING_TEXT (lines 302-311) is keyed on the softGuard IDs ('revenue-shock-guard','q-spike-dataguard','deceleration-guard','quarter-concentration-guard','working-capital-anomaly','asset-growth-divergence'). All four modes have `softWarnings: []` (only QC declares it, empty; others omit it entirely). HYPERGROWTH softGuards = ['revenue-shock-guard','quarter-concentration-guard','deceleration-guard'] (line 92).
why_it_matters: Karl reads the candidate STORY, not the score internals. A HYPERGROWTH stock whose revenue jump looks like a one-off (revenue-shock-guard fail) still passes (soft guard, correctly non-blocking) and gets a score penalty — but the story shows NO warning, so Karl sees a clean candidate with a hidden landmine. The SOFT_WARNING_TEXT table is effectively dead: it can only ever be reached via mode.softWarnings, which is empty everywhere. The whole soft-warning UX is wired to the wrong array.
fix: In buildStory, after the dataGuards loop, iterate `modeEval.failedSoftGuards` (already returned by evaluateMode at line 293) and push `SOFT_WARNING_TEXT[sgId] || (sgId + ' auffaellig')` into warnings. Keep the score penalty as-is. Add comment: '// prevents silent soft-guard failures — Karl must see revenue-shock/deceleration warnings in the story, not just a hidden score penalty'.

_verdict.note:
Code reading is factually correct but severity is overstated and the proposed fix targets dead code. CONFIRMED: buildStory (strategy-modes.js:338-355) iterates only mode.softWarnings and mode.dataGuards, never mode.softGuards nor modeEval.failedSoftGuards. SOFT_WARNING_TEXT (302-311) is keyed on the softGuard IDs. HYPERGROWTH (line 92) has softGuards=[revenue-shock-guard, quarter-concentration-guard, deceleration-guard] and declares NO softWarnings, so the softWarnings branch is skipped and the human-readable text for those guards can never be emitted by buildStory. They are also absent from RED_FLAG_RULES (only HIGH_DEBT/net-debt-ebitda and EXTREME_SLOAN/sloan-ratio exist), so they don't surface via redFlags either.

TWO findings that lower impact: (1) buildStory is DEAD CODE — grep for `.buildStory`/`buildStory(` across the whole worktree returns ONLY its definition at strategy-modes.js:325; it has zero call sites. The production UI (generate-screener.js:584-593, 2589-2593) and generate-modes-report.js never call it. They render redFlags labels plus a generic `SoftGuard-Penalty: −N` line. So patching buildStory changes nothing the user sees. (2) The soft-guard failures are NOT fully silent: they apply a numeric score penalty (SOFT_GUARD_PENALTY in score-aggregator.js:197-205 — deceleration −10, q-spike −8, revenue-shock −7, quarter-concentration −6), surfaced as the `SoftGuard-Penalty: −N` line and capable of tier downgrade. What is genuinely missing is the per-guard human-readable WHY, but only through an uncalled function.

So the system-level concern (Karl never sees a labeled revenue-shock/deceleration warning) is real, but the located defect is in dead code and the proposed fix has no observable effect. A real remedy must wire SOFT_WARNING_TEXT[sgId] (mapped from best.failedSoftGuards / ev.failedSoftGuards) into the actually-rendered path in generate-screener.js, not buildStory.

title: POSITIVE_ONLY_METRICS filter keeps values down to -0.05, contradicting its own 'positive only' contract
evidence: Line 147: `const POSITIVE_ONLY_METRICS = new Set(['roic', 'roce']);` Line 159: `const thresholdArr = POSITIVE_ONLY_METRICS.has(mid) ? arr.filter(v => v > -0.05) : arr;`. The F-ME-008 comment (155-158) says 'only use positive values for the scoring threshold median' and 'Negative values ... would invert the above/below-median logic', but the filter admits values in (-0.05, 0], i.e. small negatives and zero.

In a loss-heavy sector (e.g. SAAS/biotech-tilted region buckets) a cluster of small-negative ROICs pulls the median down toward/under zero. sector-relative-roic._rankRoic returns null when `p50 <= 0` (sector-relative-roic.js:99), so the whole method silently goes incomputable for that sector instead of ranking — or, if p50 lands just above 0, the percentile gate becomes anti-signal exactly as the comment warns. The -0.05 floor partially defeats the F-ME-004 minN-positive guard right below it.
fix: Either make the filter match the contract (`v > 0`) or rename the constant/comment to reflect a deliberate small-loss tolerance and document WHY -0.05. Given _rankRoic already rejects p50<=0, `v > 0` is the consistent choice. Add comment naming the failure mode: '// prevents small-negative ROICs inverting the above/below-median percentile signal in loss-heavy sectors'.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed mismatch but mis-categorized as a "bug" and over-severe. CODE: line 159 `arr.filter(v => v > -0.05)` admits the band (-0.05, 0], contradicting the constant name POSITIVE_ONLY_METRICS (147) and the F-ME-008 comment (156-158) "only use positive values" / "negatives would invert the above/below-median logic." Any median dragged to <=0 by the admitted near-zero band is caught there and yields non-computable — the "inverted above/below logic" the comment warns about cannot reach scoring. Where the median stays positive, admitting (-0.05, 0] only nudges the threshold slightly lower (more lenient), which is a defensible calibration for the loss-heavy growth sectors Karl screens (keeps near-breakeven peers in-sample). Git blame: `-0.05` was written deliberately in the original Tag 169 F-ME-008 fix; it was never a loosened `> 0`. No test pins a `v > 0` contract. title: Rolling 12m median is an unweighted median-of-daily-medians; ignores per-day sample count n
evidence: Line 330: `const med = median(entry.values.map(v => v.median).filter(Number.isFinite));` — entry.values are per-day `{asOf, median, n}` records (line 329). The rolling figure is the median of those daily medians with no weighting by `n`, even though n is stored and varies (a day with n=8 stocks counts equally to a day with n=400).
why_it_matters: effectiveThreshold() prefers the rolling12mMedian over the live auto-median once >=12 weekly samples exist (_helpers.js:226-228), so this is the AUTHORITATIVE threshold for mature sub-profiles. A few low-n days (e.g. early in a sector's history, or a partial pull) carry the same weight as full-universe days, so the live pass-gate can drift toward a noisy small-sample estimate. Median-of-medians is also statistically biased vs pooling the underlying observations.
fix: Weight by n (e.g. n-weighted percentile of the daily medians) or, better, persist the raw per-day value arrays and pool them for the rolling computation. At minimum drop daily entries below a small n-floor before taking the rolling median. Add comment: '// prevents low-sample days from dragging the authoritative rolling threshold'.

_verdict.note:
Code reading is accurate but the finding is materially overstated; downgrade to low. CONFIRMED at sector-medians-compute.js:330: `median(entry.values.map(v => v.median).filter(Number.isFinite))` is an unweighted median-of-daily-medians; the stored per-day `n` (pushed at line 329) is never used in the rolling computation. So the literal claim ("n ignored") is true.

BUT the finding's premise and severity are wrong on the facts:

1) The "n=8 counts equally to n=400" disparity cannot occur. A daily median only enters the rolling history AFTER _computeFromBuckets gates on MIN_STOCKS_PER_SECTOR=5 (line 155: `if (arr.length >= minN)`), so no sub-5 day is ever appended. Empirically, in the live methods/sector-medians-rolling.json, across all 30 sub-profile x metric entries the MINIMUM daily n is 93 (max 569); 0 entries have any day below n=5; only 1 entry has nMax/nMin > 3x. The auditor's low-n-floor remedy targets a case the upstream gate already prevents.

2) Actual impact is negligible. I recomputed an n-weighted percentile-50 of the daily medians vs the current unweighted median on the real file: max relative difference is 2.56% (HARDWARE roce 0.0791 -> 0.0771), and 17 of 30 entries are bitwise identical. These are slow-moving smoothed thresholds with highly correlated consecutive daily snapshots, so weighting barely moves them. Downstream use (_helpers.js effectiveThreshold step 1, gated by ROLLING_MIN_WEEKS=12) feeds pass/fail gates, but a sub-3% threshold shift is well inside noise and for fcf-yield is additionally clamped by EFFECTIVE_THRESHOLD_FLOORS (0.05).

Net: a real but cosmetic methodological imprecision, not a data-integrity defect. Reasonable to leave as-is or add a one-line comment; not worth a behavior-changing rewrite.

title: getRegion ignores currency for ADRs/foreign-domiciled stocks on US exchanges, misrouting them into the US region bucket
evidence: Priority chain: meta.region (1) → exchange code (2, line 89-90) → currency (3, line 93-94). An ADR like a Chinese or European company listed on NMS/NYQ resolves at step 2 to 'US' regardless of its reporting currency. Currency (step 3) is only consulted when the exchange is unknown.
why_it_matters: Tag 167's entire premise (region-mapping.js:5-9) is that calibrating Japanese/European fundamentals against US SaaS thresholds produces false negatives. But every ADR (TSMC, Alibaba, SAP ADR, etc.) trading on a US exchange is bucketed as US, so its fundamentals are pooled into the US region median AND ranked against US thresholds — re-introducing exactly the miscalibration regionalization was meant to remove, and simultaneously polluting the US bucket with non-US accounting profiles. With MIN_STOCKS_PER_REGION_SECTOR=20, a non-US bucket may never populate while its stocks hide in US.
fix: When the exchange resolves to US but the reporting/trading currency is non-USD (and not CAD), prefer the currency-based region. Or add an explicit ADR/foreign-domicile signal (meta.country) ahead of exchange. Add comment: '// prevents ADRs/foreign issuers on US exchanges from polluting and being miscalibrated against the US region bucket'. (Honors the no-hardcoded-ticker constraint — this fixes the guard, not a ticker list.)

_verdict.note:
REFUTED as described — the cited mechanism cannot occur on real data. The finding claims an ADR "resolves at step 2 (exchange code, lines 89-90) to 'US' regardless of reporting currency." Three load-bearing checks against source:

1) Priority 2 reads stock.meta.exchange (region-mapping.js:89), but the mapper pull-yahoo.js (object literal lines 822-887) NEVER writes meta.exchange — it writes meta.exchangeName ("NasdaqGS" display string), meta.region, meta.tradingCurrency, meta.reportingCurrency. So EXCHANGE_TO_REGION[stock.meta.exchange] is always EXCHANGE_TO_REGION[undefined] => undefined on every real snapshot. Priority 2 is effectively dead code. This is independently corroborated by findings/data-quality.json ("pull-yahoo writes meta.exchangeName, never meta.exchange or meta.exchangeCode"). Only test fixtures (tag28-tests.js:1223,1295) set meta.exchange:'NMS', and they also set region:'US', so Priority 1 still wins there.

2) Priority 1 (meta.region) is ALWAYS populated: pull-yahoo.js:827 sets region: normalizeRegion(rcOriginal, exchangeName). For an ADR, rcOriginal is the financial/reporting currency (_fc preferred over trading ccy per Tag204/219, lines 808-810), so BABA => 'CN', TSM => 'TW', a Japanese issuer => 'JP'. getRegion receives meta.region='CN'/'TW'/etc.

3) Those granular codes are NOT in getRegion's 5-bucket allowlist (region-mapping.js:80, only US/EU/APAC/EM/OTHER) nor in DISPLAY_NAME_TO_REGION (:84), so they fall THROUGH (:85) to Priority 2 (dead) then Priority 3 currency (:93). Priority 3 reads stock.price.currency = the TRADING currency, which for a US-listed ADR is USD (pull-yahoo.js:830 tradingCurrency, :356-357) => CURRENCY_TO_REGION_FALLBACK['USD']='US'.

So an ADR CAN land in 'US', but via Priority 3 (trading USD), not Priority 2 (exchange) as claimed — the auditor inverted the path. Critically, the proposed fix ("when exchange resolves to US but trading currency is non-USD, prefer currency") would do NOTHING here because the trading currency IS USD. The fix targets a path (Priority-2 US resolution) that never fires and would not address the actual routing.

There is a genuine but DIFFERENT latent issue worth a separate low-severity note: normalizeRegion (pull-yahoo.js:242-268) emits country-granular codes (CN/TW/JP/HK/UK/CA/CH/SE/...) that getRegion's Priority-1 allowlist silently rejects, collapsing all non-bucket regions through to currency. That is a schema-vocabulary mismatch (consumer expects US/EU/APAC/EM, producer emits ~18 codes), not the ADR-via-exchange bug described.

fix_safe=false: the proposed change either guards a dead path (no-op) or reorders the priority chain by inserting meta.country ahead of exchange — a behavior change affecting Tag-167 regional median calibration that requires human review, not auto-apply. revised_severity=low: real impact is limited and the described severity-medium mechanism is not real.

title: Rolling-window cutoff uses local-time date slice while 'today' uses UTC date slice — boundary drift can mis-prune or duplicate entries
evidence: Line 289: `const today = new Date().toISOString().slice(0,10);` (UTC date). Line 291-292 cutoff: `const d = new Date(); d.setUTCDate(d.getUTCDate() - ROLLING_WINDOW_DAYS); return d.toISOString().slice(0,10);` (UTC). These are consistent UTC, OK — but line 328 dedup `v.asOf !== today` compares against the UTC `today`, while pre-existing entries may have been written on a prior run under a different machine TZ assumption. The real boundary issue: `entry.values.filter(v => v.asOf !== today && v.asOf >= cutoff)` keeps `asOf >= cutoff` as a STRING compare; an entry exactly ON the cutoff day is retained, making the window effectively 366 inclusive days, and a value written 365 days ago is dropped — an off-by-one in window length.
why_it_matters: Off-by-one in the rolling window length is minor in isolation, but combined with median-of-medians (finding 06) it shifts which historical days define the authoritative threshold. More importantly the string `>=` compare assumes every asOf is a clean YYYY-MM-DD; any legacy entry with a full ISO timestamp (older format) would mis-sort lexically and never be pruned, growing the file unbounded.
fix: Make window membership explicit and inclusive-exclusive by intent, and normalize asOf to YYYY-MM-DD on read before comparing. Document the intended window length (365 vs 366). Add comment: '// prevents off-by-one window drift and lexical mis-prune of legacy timestamp formats'.

_verdict.note: Headline claims refuted against source + data. (1) "Legacy timestamp format / TZ mismatch mis-prune": the ONLY writer of values[].asOf in sector-medians-compute.js is line 329 (asOf: today), where today = new Date().toISOString().slice(0,10) -> always zero-padded YYYY-MM-DD. Grep confirms no second writer of sector-medians-rolling.json; inspecting the actual file shows every stored asOf is clean YYYY-MM-DD (e.g. "2026-05-14"). Zero-padded ISO dates sort lexically == chronologically, so v.asOf >= cutoff (line 328) is correct; no legacy format exists to mis-prune. The auditor itself concedes today and cutoff are "consistent UTC, OK". The dedup v.asOf !== today correctly prevents same-day duplicates on re-run — no duplication/data-loss bug. (2) Off-by-one window: technically cutoff = today-365d and retained span [cutoff, today] is 366 inclusive calendar days while _windowDays:365 — a real but cosmetic ±1 discrepancy. "Rolling 12 months" June20->June20 is arguably the intended inclusive window, not a defect. In practice each rolling series holds only ~21-23 daily samples (history is weeks old, nowhere near 365d), so the cutoff boundary never fires on real data — zero current impact; even at maturity one boundary day in a 250+-sample median cannot flip a result. Net: not a medium bug, at most a doc/intent nit.

title: eligibleForMode duplicates the sector-exclude + dataGuard reject logic that evaluateMode already performs
evidence: eligibleForMode (generate-modes-report.js:236-241) re-runs `SM.isExcludedBySector(ev.stock, mode)` and the `for (guardId of mode.dataGuards) { ... pass===false → reject }` loop, which is identical to the early-return hygiene block inside strategy-modes.js evaluateMode (lines 181, 204-212). The modeEvals cache already encodes pass/fail.

Single-source-of-truth violations like this are how 'fixed in methods/ but still wrong in the report' bugs arise.
fix: Derive eligibility from the cached modeEval (e.g. reject when `me.reason` is one of the hygiene reasons, or expose an `eligible` boolean from evaluateMode) instead of re-deriving from raw guards/sector. Keep methods/strategy-modes.js as the single arbiter. (Respect the constraint: this edit is in generate-modes-report.js, not methods/index.js.)

_verdict.note: Confirmed the textual duplication: eligibleForMode (generate-modes-report.js:236-241) re-runs SM.isExcludedBySector + the dataGuards `computable && pass===false` reject loop, and evaluateMode (strategy-modes.js:181, 204-212) contains the same two checks as early-return hygiene gates; the modeEvals cache (evaluateAll line 122-123) already encodes them. So the smell is real but it is correctly classified as low / architecture-only. CAVEAT — the duplication is NOT fully redundant and the proposed fix is NOT behavior-preserving: (1) eligibleForMode checks only sector+dataGuards, whereas evaluateMode has an extra mcapFloor gate between them (lines 183-199), and QUALITY_COMPOUNDER sets mcapFloor:5e9 (strategy-modes.js:121). 'eligible' (line 577, drives sectorExcluded count line 591 + modeStats) is intentionally a broader set than 'passed' (used separately in topByMethod/topAllMust). (2) evaluateMode returns on the FIRST failing gate, so me.reason only records that first failure (sector → mcap → dataguard order). A QUALITY_COMPOUNDER stock that fails BOTH the mcap floor AND a dataguard gets reason='mcap_below_floor' and never reaches the dataguard loop; the auditor's suggested 'reject when me.reason is a hygiene reason' mapping would then KEEP it, while the current independent dataguard re-check REJECTS it — a real behavioral divergence. The truly safe fix (an explicit `eligible` boolean independent of gate ordering) requires editing strategy-modes.js, which the finding's own constraint forbids.

title: v1 legacy flat-schema branches in lookupMedian/lookupPercentile are unreachable from production loaders
evidence: Both production loaders normalize to v2 before calling these helpers: _helpers.js:_loadAutoMedians wraps old shape as `{ _version: 2, byRegion: { _GLOBAL: raw.medians } }` (lines 127-129) or `{}` (131); sector-relative-roic.js:_loadAutoMedians does the same (lines 72-75). _verdict.note: Confirmed. sector-median-lookup.js is imported by exactly two production files plus the test file (grep: _helpers.js:10, sector-relative-roic.js:53, tag28-tests.js). Both production loaders normalize to v2 before calling the helpers: _helpers.js:_loadAutoMedians (119-138) returns full v2, or wraps old shape as {_version:2, byRegion:{_GLOBAL: raw.medians}} (129), or {} (131); sector-relative-roic.js:_loadAutoMedians (65-81) does the identical normalization. So `medians` is always v2 or {}. The v1 flat-schema inner blocks (lines 57-62 in lookupMedian, 115-120 in lookupPercentile) only fire when `medians._version !== 2` AND `medians[subProfileId]` is a populated flat object — impossible from either loader (a {} object makes medians[subProfileId] undefined, so they immediately fall through to not-found). The _helpers.js call site is further gated by `if (autoMedians._version === 2)` at line 233. All four lookup tests in tag28-tests.js (1214-1262) also pass v2-shaped fixtures, so even tests do not exercise the v1 flat path. Minor correction to the auditor's line ranges: the final `return {value:null, source:'not-found'}` at lines 64 and 122 ARE reachable (e.g. medians={}); the genuinely dead code is only the inner if-blocks at 57-62 and 115-120. Substance of the finding holds: legacy v1 flat branches are unreachable from production. Classification dead-code / low is accurate — defensive legacy code, no functional impact.

title: ROIC bucket uses invested-capital = totalAssets - cash with no guard against cash > assets or near-zero IC blowups
evidence: Lines 117-119: `const ic = ta - (cash || 0); if (ic > 0) globalBuckets[sp.id].roic.push(ni / ic);` (mirrored at 129-131). The only guard is `ic > 0`. A cash-rich company with tiny non-cash assets yields a near-zero `ic`, so `ni / ic` explodes to a huge ROIC that survives (it's finite and >-0.05) and skews the upper percentiles (p75/p90) used by sector-relative-roic ranking.
why_it_matters: Net-cash software/biotech names (very common in the growth universe Karl targets) can produce ROIC of several hundred percent purely from a denominator artifact. Because p75/p90 drive the sector-relative top-quartile gate, a couple of these inflate the bar so legitimately-strong-but-not-absurd compounders fall below p75 and get filtered. Anti-signal in the high tail.
fix: Add a denominator sanity floor (e.g. require `ic >= some fraction of ta`, or cap |ni/ic| at a sane bound before pushing), consistent with however roic.js / sector-relative-roic.js intend to treat net-cash firms. Mirror the exact guard in both compute and the consuming method. Add comment: '// prevents near-zero invested-capital from producing artifact ROIC that inflates sector p75/p90'.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed real, low-severity. The push sites (sector-medians-compute.js:117-118 and 129-130) compute ic = ta - (cash||0) and guard only ic > 0. A net-cash firm with 0 < ta-cash << ta and positive ni yields an artifact ROIC (e.g. 10x-50x) that passes the only roic filter, arr.filter(v => v > -0.05) at line 159 (POSITIVE_ONLY_METRICS), and then feeds percentile() (lines 47-60, linear interpolation, no outlier cap). p75/p90 are genuinely pulled upward. p75 IS consumed: sector-relative-roic.js:131-132 reads _p75_roic via lookupPercentile and ranks against it (lines 100-104). Verified no upper bound exists anywhere: not at push site, not in percentile(), not in lookup (sector-median-lookup.js), and the effectiveThreshold floors (_helpers.js F-ME-202) apply only to fcf-yield and are floors not caps. So the mechanism is exactly as the auditor described — not a misread.

Severity stays LOW because the impact is benign and bounded: (1) an inflated p75 makes the top-quartile gate HARDER to clear (false negatives), not easier — conservative direction; (2) sector-relative-roic.js is DIAGNOSTIC and explicitly NOT in SCORE_WEIGHTS (its own header lines 32-34), so it cannot move the aggregator score or the fixture hash; (3) the median used by the absolute roic.js threshold is robust to a single outlier — only upper percentiles in the diagnostic method are exposed; (4) the minN guard (5 global / 20 regional) dilutes a lone outlier's pull on p75. Note the compute-side formula deliberately MIRRORS roic.js:22-23 and sector-relative-roic.js:89-91 (same ic = ta-cash, same ic>0 guard) — this consistency is intentional per the F-ME-203 'mirror exactly' comments, so the artifact is a known proxy weakness of assets-minus-cash invested capital, not an inconsistency bug.

fix_safe=false: the proposed fix (require ic >= fraction*ta, or cap |ni/ic|) CHANGES which stocks enter the percentile distribution and therefore CHANGES the persisted p25/p50/p75/p90 values in sector-medians-auto.json that downstream methods read. That is a behavior change to relied-on data and needs fixture-hash re-baselining. Worse, applying it only to the compute side would re-open the write/read definition divergence that F-ME-203 specifically closed; the guard must be mirrored across compute + roic.js + sector-relative-roic.js in one coordinated, human-reviewed change. Relevant files: C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/methods/sector-medians-compute.js (lines 116-119, 128-131, filter at 159, percentile at 47-60), methods/sector-relative-roic.js (p75 consumption 131-132, ranking 94-105), methods/roic.js (mirrored formula 22-30), methods/sector-median-lookup.js (lookupPercentile).

title: FX-conversion tests depend on the mutable live fx-rates.json — non-hermetic, can flip between live rate and stale fallback
evidence: The TWD test comment admits the coupling (lines 421-424): 'the live FX rate from fx-rates.json may differ from the hardcoded fallback (0.031)'. The assertion is a wide band `twdSnap.marketCap.value > 50e9 || < 10e9` (441-443) precisely to tolerate that. pull-yahoo.js loads fx-rates.json only when `<= 14d` fresh (line 130) else falls back to the hardcoded table (TWD: 0.031, line 142). Current fx-rates.json fetchedAt=2026-06-12 (8d old → live path today), but on day 15 the SAME test silently switches to the fallback rate. The metrics allow-list test (536-556) has the same dependency.

The wide band masks a real FX-normalization regression (e.g. a 2x scaling bug would still land inside [10e9,50e9] for some inputs). It also means a stale-FX state that production should alarm on is invisible to the test.

_verdict.note: Confirmed factually, but severity overstated. The tests at 418-454 and 536-556 do `require('./pull-yahoo.js')` (line 387), which loads the module-level FX table from the real fx-rates.json at load time; there is NO injection seam (module.exports line 2269 exposes _convertSnapshotToUSD but no FX setter, FX_TO_USD is a private `let`). HOWEVER this is a test-hygiene/hermeticity weakness, not a data-integrity bug and NOT even flaky in practice: the TWD band [10e9,50e9] (line 441) holds for BOTH 1000e9*0.0316=31.6e9 and 1000e9*0.031=31.0e9, and the ratio assertions (FCF-yield, rev/mcap, lines 444-453) are currency-invariant; the metrics allow-list test only asserts revenueTTM<5e11 (line 553) which passes under both JPY live=0.0062 and fallback=0.0067. I ran `node tag28-tests.js` — all FX tests pass on the live path. The genuine defect is that the loose band cannot catch a scaling regression (the auditor's own fix rationale), which is a low-severity test-robustness gap, not medium data-integrity. No production behavior is affected either way.

title: 'getMethods matches filesystem' guard relies on a hand-maintained NON_METHOD_FILES denylist that silently rots
evidence: The anti-drop test counts filesystem .js files minus a hardcoded Set: `const NON_METHOD_FILES = new Set(['runner.js','trend.js','method-types.js','score-aggregator.js','strategy-modes.js','sector-medians-compute.js','index.js','data-quality.js','region-mapping.js','sector-median-lookup.js'])` (170-176), then `assertEq(ids.length, fsCount, ...)`. Note `_helpers.js` is excluded only by the `!f.startsWith('_')` filter, not the Set. Verified counts today: runner loads 92 methods; 102 non-underscore .js files in methods/; 102-10=92 → passes. The comment history ('Tag 167: helper modules') shows the Set has already been patched reactively at least twice.

Compare runner's loaded id-set against files that export a method-shaped contract (e.g. have `module.exports.evaluate` and an `id`), or move helpers into a methods/_lib/ subfolder excluded by the existing `_`/dir filter so no denylist is needed. title: assertEq uses JSON.stringify equality (NaN/undefined/key-order pitfalls) and approx() has no isFinite guard
evidence: `function assertEq(a,b,m){ const aS=JSON.stringify(a), bS=JSON.stringify(b); if(aS!==bS) throw ... }` (14-16). JSON.stringify(NaN)==='null', JSON.stringify(undefined)===undefined (not a string), and object key order is significant — `{a:1,b:2}` !== `{b:2,a:1}`. `function approx(a,b,eps){ return Math.abs(a-b) <= (eps||0.001) }` (18): if a method regresses to return NaN, `Math.abs(NaN - 60) <= 0.001` is `false`, so `!approx(...)` is true and it throws the right way here — but many call sites are `if (!r.pass)`-style and a NaN value slipping through approx elsewhere gives confusing messages rather than an explicit isFinite failure.
why_it_matters: The suite's whole job is catching numeric regressions (NaN propagation is an explicitly named failure class for this codebase). assertEq comparing two `null` strings would treat a NaN result as equal to an expected null, and key-order sensitivity makes assertEq brittle for the components/object comparisons. These are latent false-greens/false-reds in the assertion primitives every test depends on.
fix: Harden the primitives: in approx, first `if (!Number.isFinite(a)) throw new Error('non-finite value: '+a)` before the tolerance check (names the NaN failure mode explicitly). For assertEq, guard against `undefined` stringify results and consider a structural deep-equal that is key-order independent, or document that callers must pass canonically-ordered objects.

_verdict.note:
False positive against a test-harness helper file (tag28-tests.js), not production/pipeline code. Both claimed pitfalls are unreachable with the actual arguments used:

(1) assertEq JSON.stringify pitfalls (NaN/undefined/key-order): there is exactly ONE call site, line 181: assertEq(ids.length, fsCount, ...), comparing two finite non-negative integers. No NaN, no undefined, no objects, no key-ordering can occur. The theoretical JSON.stringify edge cases never manifest.

(2) approx() lacking an isFinite guard: the auditor's OWN evidence concedes the safe behavior — Math.abs(NaN - x) is NaN, NaN <= eps is false, so !approx(...) is true and the test throws (fails) on a NaN regression. I verified all 20 approx call sites: every one is the safe `if (!approx(...)) throw` form; `grep 'if (approx('` returns NO matches. The auditor's speculated dangerous pattern ('many call sites are if(!r.pass)-style and a NaN slips through approx elsewhere') does not exist — `!r.pass` is an unrelated boolean check, and no NaN can silently slip past approx. The only residual is cosmetic: the thrown message reads 'value=NaN' rather than an explicit 'non-finite' message — a diagnostics nicety, not a correctness bug.

Net: no code path produces a wrong/silent result. This is defensive hardening of test primitives, not a defect.

title: Cyclical-Recovery positive-year counting breaks on a leading null (missing-data year), corrupting the state classification
evidence: Lines 51-55: `for (const v of arr) { if (v == null) break; if (v > 0) {...} else counting = false; }` — the loop BREAKS on the first null. If annualNetIncome[0] (latest year) is null but [1],[2],[3] are positive, positiveCount=0 and consecutiveFromY0=0. Then line 62 `olderPositive` and line 64 `positiveCount >= Math.ceil(yearsAvail/2)` both fail, so a genuinely-stable company drops out of the STABLE/RECENT branch entirely. Note `yearsAvail` on line 56 counts ALL non-null entries across the array (not just the leading run), so the two counts disagree about what 'available' means.
why_it_matters: On the quoteSummary income path, `_arr` in pull-yahoo.js (line 499) does `.filter(Boolean)` so nulls are compacted away there — but on the FTS path (`_ftsExtractByYear`, line 1078, and mapFTSToAnnual line 1089) nulls are deliberately PRESERVED for year-alignment. So a FTS-sourced stock with a missing latest NI year (e.g. delayed annual filing) is mis-classified: the `for...break` discards every subsequent positive year. This is a CORE method feeding the QC/aggregator score; a STABLE compounder can silently fall to RECENT/TURNAROUND and lose score weight.
fix: Do not `break` on null inside the counting loop. Iterate with an index, treat null as 'unknown' (skip it for positiveCount but stop the consecutive-from-Y0 run only on a confirmed non-positive value, OR bail to computable:false if arr[0] is null since 'latest state' is then unknowable). Comment must name the failure mode: '// prevents: leading-null FY (FTS null-preserved arrays) zeroing positiveCount and demoting STABLE compounders'.

_verdict.note:
REFUTED as written. The finding's central mechanism — "annualNetIncome[0] (latest year) is null, positiveCount=0, STABLE compounder drops out of branch" — is impossible. methods/profitability-state.js lines 37-38 (`const y0 = arr[0]; if (y0 == null) return null;`) return BEFORE the counting loop (51-55) is ever reached. The auditor reasoned about the break-on-null loop in isolation and missed the early-return guard four lines above. Verified by execution: input NI=[null,100,90,80] returns computable:false / reason:"cannot classify NI" (evaluate() line 116) — NOT a demotion to a wrong state. That is exactly the auditor's own proposed fallback ("bail to computable:false if arr[0] is null since latest state is unknowable"); the code already does it. So no STABLE company is misclassified on a leading null.

There IS a real-but-different, milder residual the finding does NOT describe: an INTERIOR null mid-window. e.g. NI=[100,90,null,80] classifies RECENT instead of STABLE (break stops consecutiveFromY0 at 2, never hitting >=3), and NI=[100,null,50,40] falls through to TURNAROUND instead of RECENT (positiveCount=1 fails the >=ceil(yearsAvail/2) test while yearsAvail=3 counts all non-nulls — the count-disagreement the auditor notes). But (a) the finding's title, evidence, line reasoning, and proposed comment text all name the LEADING-null / "latest year null" case, which is the false part; (b) pull-yahoo.js lines 1119-1122 document interior-null incidence as "Currently ~0 live incidence because Yahoo's missing year is almost always the oldest." Annual arrays are FTS null-preserved, latest-first, with only TRAILING pure-null rows trimmed (lines 1091-1109), so interior nulls are structurally possible but practically near-zero.

Key source evidence: profitability-state.js:37-38 (guard refuting the claim), :51-56 (loop + yearsAvail), :64 (branch); _helpers.js:12-21 (H.val); pull-yahoo.js:1093-1136 (array build, trailing-only trim), :1119-1122 (~0 interior-null incidence), :1933-1935 (FTS merge keeps null-preserved arrays).
