title: computable:false branch reports the wrong p75 (raw lookup) while the pass branch uses the degraded synthetic p75 — misleading diagnostics and a latent NaN in the reason string
evidence: After the degraded-mode block (lines 160-166) sets `p75 = p50`, the guard at line 168 `if (p50==null || p75==null)` reports `p75=' + p75Lookup.value` (line 174) and components `sectorP75: p75Lookup.value` (line 175) — i.e. the ORIGINAL null lookup value, not the local `p75` actually used downstream. Conversely the success path (line 219) prints `(p75*100)` using the synthetic value. The two code paths disagree about what 'p75' means.
why_it_matters: Operators reading the computable:false reason see 'p75=null' even though the method internally substituted p50; and when degraded mode is active the printed sector p75 is silently p50, overstating how much real distribution data exists. This is a DIAGNOSTIC (fixture-hash safe) so it cannot move the score, but it actively misleads the human triaging sector-relative rank — the whole point of the method.
fix: Use a single consistent variable in both the guard's reason/components and the success reason; print the real lookup value with an explicit '(synthetic=p50)' annotation when degraded. Comment: '// prevents: reason/components reporting raw p75=null while logic used synthetic p75=p50'.

_verdict.note:
False positive — based on a control-flow misread. The finding assumes the line-168 guard (`if (p50==null || p75==null)`) can fire while the degraded synthetic assignment `p75=p50` (lines 160-166) is in effect, so that the reason/components (which print `p75Lookup.value`) would diverge from the local `p75`. That state is unreachable.

The degraded block at line 160 runs ONLY when `p75==null && p50!=null && p50>0`; it then sets `p75=p50` (non-null). So after that block, `p75` is null ONLY if the block was skipped. For the guard at 168 to fire:
- via `p75==null`: the block was skipped (because `p50==null || p50<=0`), so no synthetic substitution happened and `p75 === p75Lookup.value === null`. Reason prints `p75=null`, local p75 is null — they AGREE.
- via `p50==null`: the block requires `p50!=null`, so it was skipped, hence `p75 === p75Lookup.value` — they AGREE.

In every reachable path that hits line 168, `degraded===false` and `p75 === p75Lookup.value`. There is no path where the degraded synthetic p75 coexists with the computable:false branch, so reason/components are never misleading there. The success branch (line 219 `p75*100`) is only reached when `p75!=null`. 

The 'latent NaN' claim is also wrong: line 173 does string concatenation (`'p75=' + p75Lookup.value`), which yields the literal "null", not NaN; arithmetic on p75 only happens on the success path where p75 is guaranteed non-null. The code was already hardened for exactly this scenario (Tag 211 fallback comments lines 144-156, and the Tag 211j/F-ME-206 degraded-rank cap at lines 187-192). No bug.

title: Coefficient-of-variation uses POPULATION stdev (÷n) on a 4-5 point sample, understating dispersion and letting borderline cyclicals pass the CoV<=0.30 gate
evidence: Line 127 `variance = sum((x-mean)^2)/n` (population, divides by n). With n=4 the sample stdev (÷(n-1)) is sqrt(4/3)=1.155x larger — ~15% higher. Note fcf-stability.js (the documented sibling, Tag 204) should be checked for the same divisor for consistency.

Line 127 of methods/earnings-power-stability.js does use population stdev (÷n); sample stdev (÷n-1) would be sqrt(n/(n-1))x larger = ~15.5% at n=4, ~11.8% at n=5, so the borderline-pass mechanism (true sample-CoV ~0.34 reads ~0.29 and passes the ≤0.30 gate at line 131) is directionally real. Switching to Bessel without re-tuning 0.30 doesn't make it "more correct," it just multiplies every stock's CoV by a constant and silently tightens the gate. title: Sign-flip 'turnaround' branch uses a fixed $1M absolute swing threshold, mis-scaling for both micro-caps and mega-caps

A mispaired opMargin median can wrongly satisfy or fail the OPMARGIN_RETAIL_GATE (0.035), flipping the CORE pass for exactly the retail-compounder class the tier was added to catch. fix: Guard `rawRevs.length === rawOpIncs.length` before the paired loop (mirror the alignment guard recommended for roic-trend), and skip the pair when either side is null rather than relying on Number.isFinite of a possibly-misaligned element. Comment: '// prevents: cross-year Rev/OpInc pairing inflating/deflating retail-tier opMargin median'.

_verdict.note:
PARTIALLY CONFIRMED as a real latent bug, but the finding's evidence is mischaracterized and its proposed fix is wrong/ineffective. Downgraded medium->low; fix NOT safe to auto-apply.

What's real: In the pure-quoteSummary path, mapYahooToCanonical (pull-yahoo.js:618-619) builds annualRev = _arr(isHist,'totalRevenue') and annualOpInc = _arr(isHist,'operatingIncome'). _arr (lines 493-499) does .map(...).filter(Boolean), and _y (477-486) returns null for a present row whose field value is null. So a fiscal-year row that carries revenue but a null operatingIncome (or vice versa) is dropped from one array but kept in the other -> the two arrays compact to different lengths AND shifted indices. quality-compounder-roic.js lines 119-128 then zip rawRevs[i]/rawOpIncs[i] positionally, yielding cross-year opMargins. This is the exact bug-class the codebase already fixed elsewhere (F-004 line 570-572, F-DP-030/031 line 1085-1090, F-DP-101 line 1111-1122). _rawVals (lines 45-49) faithfully reproduces whatever the stored arrays contain, so it inherits any upstream misalignment.

Where the auditor is wrong: (1) The claim that "annualRev vs annualOpInc come from different extraction paths (QS _arr-compacted vs FTS null-preserved)" is inaccurate. For any single snapshot BOTH arrays come from the SAME path. The FTS path (mapFTSToAnnual lines 1094-1108) builds both with null placeholders and is guaranteed equal-length/aligned; the merge (lines 1858-1882, Tag 206f) swaps the WHOLE annualOpInc array as a unit and never mixes QS-rev with FTS-opInc. The misalignment can ONLY occur within the pure-QS path where both are independently _arr-compacted. (2) The proposed fix is ineffective: by the time the arrays reach the method, _arr's .filter(Boolean) has ALREADY removed the nulls, so "skip the pair when either side is null" is a no-op (no nulls remain to skip), and a `rawRevs.length===rawOpIncs.length` guard merely suppresses the whole median computation (or gives a false skip when lengths differ legitimately) rather than realigning by year. The correct fix is upstream: make the QS extraction null-preserving (like mapFTSToAnnual already is) so years stay positionally aligned. Therefore fix_safe=false — applying the suggested guard would silently kill a working computation without fixing the root cause, and needs human review/upstream change.

Why severity low, not medium: opMarginMedian feeds ONLY the retail-tier override (lines 140-144, at>=3.0 AND opM-median>=3.5%), which only LOOSENS the ROIC floor 20%->15%; it can at most flip a borderline stock with AT>=3.0 and ROIC in [15%,20%). The pure-QS path almost always loses to FTS for exactly the high-revenue retail-compounder names that reach AT>=3.0 (the related F-DP-101 note explicitly records "~0 live incidence" because Yahoo's missing year is almost always the oldest). Genuine but low-probability and bounded blast radius.

title: Majority-vote tie-break uses Object.entries ordering and Math.min over source ranks, but a 1-1-1 three-way split is resolved 'conservatively' in a way that can contradict the documented hierarchy when only 2 sources exist
evidence: Lines 136-145: counts states, sorts by frequency desc, takes sorted[0] if its count>=2 else falls to `RANK_STATE[Math.min(...ranks)]`. With exactly 2 sources that disagree (e.g. NI=STABLE, OI=LOSS), no count reaches 2, so it takes Math.min(rank)=LOSS. That is the documented 'conservative' intent — but with 2 sources a single noisy OI/FCF year can veto a clean NI=STABLE down to LOSS even though NI (the primary source, no persistentLoss veto) says STABLE.
why_it_matters: For 2-source stocks (FCF missing — common), the conservative-min rule gives the secondary source full veto power over a healthy primary NI signal, demoting STABLE compounders to LOSS/TURNAROUND on one weak OI year. This is milder than finding 01 but compounds it. CORE method.
fix: When sources.length===2 and they disagree (and NI is not persistentLoss), prefer the NI-anchored state or emit the lower of {NI, other} only by at-most-one rank step rather than absolute min; or require >=2 sources to agree before allowing a demotion below NI's own state. Comment: '// prevents: single weak secondary source vetoing a clean NI=STABLE in 2-source stocks'.

_verdict.note: REFUTED — code mechanics are described correctly, but the characterization is wrong. With exactly 2 disagreeing sources (e.g. NI=STABLE, OI=LOSS, no FCF) the tie branch at lines 142-144 does fire and Math.min(...ranks) yields LOSS. However this is the EXPLICITLY DOCUMENTED intended behavior, not a bug: the file header (lines 8-11) states "Bei tie/disagree: konservativ (niedrigster State im Hierarchie LOSS<TURN<RECENT<STABLE)". The 2-source case follows that documented conservative-min rule identically to the 3-source tie case — it does NOT "contradict the documented hierarchy" as the title claims. NI is documented as primary ONLY for the persistentLoss veto (lines 11, 130-133), never as a tie-break anchor that should override the conservative-min rule; the finding invents an NI-primacy expectation that the documentation never makes. The auditor's own evidence concedes "That is the documented 'conservative' intent." So the report describes an intentional design preference (the screener deliberately demotes ambiguous profitability rather than over-promote on a single source) reframed as a defect. No deviation from spec, no inconsistency, no misordering. The premise of the title is false. File: C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/methods/profitability-state.js lines 135-145.

title: R&D/SG&A capitalization weights the NEWEST year fully and the oldest least, inverting Mauboussin straight-line amortization (older capitalized spend should retain LESS, but unconsumed asset of recent spend should retain MORE — the weighting double-counts in the same direction as decay)
evidence: Lines 105 `w=(windowYears-i)/windowYears` with i=0 newest → weight 1.0, i=4 oldest → 0.2. Header (lines 15-17) states this is intentional 'straight-line 5y amortization — newest year gets 5/5=1.0'. For a capitalized-and-amortized R&D ASSET, the unamortized book value of year-i spend after amortization is indeed (remaining life)/(total life): newest spend has ~full life remaining (correct ~1.0) and oldest ~1/5 remaining (correct 0.2). So the weighting is actually defensible — BUT the code treats any year with `v<=0` as skipped (line 104) AND counts only positive contributions in yearsUsed, so a year of zero/negative reported R&D silently shrinks the capitalized base with no flag, understating adjIC.
why_it_matters: A firm that reports R&D in 4 of 5 years (one null/zero) gets a quietly smaller capitalized intangible asset and thus a HIGHER adjIC-relative... no: smaller capRD lowers adjIC, raising adjROIC slightly — making the quality gate marginally LOOSER for spotty-R&D reporters, the opposite of the documented 'prefer false-negatives' stance (lines 36-37). DIAGNOSTIC, so no score impact, but the signal direction contradicts its own design note.
fix: Surface yearsUsed/window coverage in the pass decision or reason (already in components) and consider treating sparse-R&D coverage as reduced confidence rather than silently shrinking the base. At minimum add a comment naming the failure mode. Comment: '// prevents: sparse-R&D years silently shrinking capitalized base and loosening the quality gate'.

_verdict.note: False positive — self-refuting and based on a misread of intent. (1) The headline "inverted amortization" claim is explicitly conceded as wrong in the auditor's own title/evidence: weight w=(windowYears-i)/windowYears correctly gives newest spend ~full unamortized life (1.0) and oldest 1/5, which is exactly straight-line remaining book value. (2) The secondary "silent shrinking" claim fails on multiple grounds. R&D expense is never legitimately negative; a zero/missing year correctly contributes 0 (no spend = no capitalized asset that year) — that is correct accounting, not a shrink of an existing base. (3) Direction is backwards: smaller capRD → smaller adjIC → HIGHER adjROIC (adjROIC=NI/adjIC, line 169/182), which makes the >=0.15 gate EASIER to pass, the documented graceful degradation toward nominal ROIC (header lines 26-43), not an "understatement." (4) Not silent: coverage is surfaced via components rdYearsUsed/sgaYearsUsed/rdUsed/sgaUsed (lines 205-208) and the reason string explicitly emits "R&D Ny capitalized" / "NO intangibles capitalized (R&D+SG&A both missing)" (lines 189-191). (5) Inconsequential: confirmed DIAGNOSTIC and NOT in any SCORE_WEIGHTS (methods/method-types.js:93, methods/index.js:138), so it cannot loosen any output-gating quality decision. File: C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/methods/intangible-adjusted-roic.js.

title: Per-method module-local re-load/parse of sector-medians-auto.json duplicates the cache already maintained in _helpers.js, doubling JSON parse work and risking divergent cached copies
evidence: Lines 64-81 define a SECOND `_autoMediansCache` + `_loadAutoMedians()` inside sector-relative-roic.js, with the comment 'kept local so this method doesn't depend on _helpers internals' (lines 62-63). _helpers.js already has an identical `_loadAutoMedians` (helpers lines 119-138) and exposes effectiveThreshold. The file is parsed and cached twice per process.
why_it_matters: Over a full-universe pull (thousands of stocks) the parse is amortized by the module-local cache so runtime cost is small — but the two caches can diverge if the test hook `_setMediansForTest` (helpers lines 176-186) swaps the helpers cache for the fixture-hash test: sector-relative-roic's private cache is NOT reset, so under test it reads the real on-disk file while the rest of the pipeline reads the injected empty stub. That is a latent test-determinism hole adjacent to the FTS_CACHE_VERSION/fixture-hash discipline the codebase guards carefully.
fix: Share the loader/cache via a small exported accessor from _helpers.js (read-only) rather than a private duplicate, so the test hook resets all consumers atomically. Do NOT change FTS_CACHE_VERSION. Comment: '// prevents: private medians cache escaping _setMediansForTest and drifting from pipeline under fixture-hash test'.

_verdict.note: Code observation is accurate but both cited harms are non-issues. CONFIRMED: sector-relative-roic.js:64-81 defines a private _autoMediansCache + _loadAutoMedians() that duplicates _helpers.js:119-138 verbatim (same path.join(__dirname,'sector-medians-auto.json'), same v2/legacy wrap). REFUTED on impact: (1) Performance — both loaders memoize (if cache !== null return), so the "doubling" is exactly ONE extra readFileSync+JSON.parse per process lifetime of a small file, NOT per-stock. Negligible; 'low' severity is already generous and arguably it's not a perf finding at all. (2) "Divergent cached copies / fixture-hash drift" — the drift premise is FALSE for this method. _setMediansForTest({},{},{}) (tag28-tests.js:2762) resets only _helpers.js caches, true, but sector-relative-roic.js is a DIAGNOSTIC method (line 33: "NOT added to SCORE_WEIGHTS — fixture-hash invariant safe"). The fixture-hash projection (_computeFixtureHash, tag28-tests.js:2776) hashes only scoreBreakdown/scoring-method output; a diagnostic method's result cannot enter the hash. So the private cache does NOT cause hash drift today. The proposed_fix's prescribed comment ("prevents private medians cache escaping _setMediansForTest and drifting from pipeline under fixture-hash test") is factually incorrect. At most this is a minor DRY/maintainability nit, not a real performance or correctness bug.

title: Proportional 'needed' scaling via Math.round can demand more positives than the rounding of 4*obs/5 intends at the 3-year boundary
evidence: Lines 71-72 `oiNeeded = Math.round(4 * oiObservable / 5)`. For oiObservable=3 → round(2.4)=2 (ok), =4 → round(3.2)=3 (ok), =5 → 4 (ok). But the earlier gate (lines 47-52) already requires oiObs>=4 to be computable, so the 3y branch documented in the comment (lines 69-70 '3y→2') is UNREACHABLE — a 3-observable-year stock returns computable:false at line 47 before ever reaching the scaling. The comment advertises behavior the gate forbids.
why_it_matters: PLTR/CRDO-type 3-4y-history compounders the Tag 221 fix (lines 66-72) explicitly names as the motivation are still rejected at the >=4 observable gate for OpInc/FCF, so the proportional-scaling 'fix' does nothing for the 3y case it cites. Low severity (no wrong PASS), but it is dead/contradictory logic that masks an unmet requirement — a newly-listed quality compounder with exactly 3 clean years is dropped as incomputable.
fix: Decide the real minimum-history policy: if 3y compounders should be scored, lower the computable gate (lines 47) to >=3 and let the proportional needed handle it; otherwise delete the unreachable 3y branch from the comment. Do not hardcode tickers. Comment: '// prevents: contradictory >=4 gate vs 3y-needed scaling silently dropping 3y-history compounders'.

_verdict.note: Confirmed against source. methods/earnings-stability.js gate (lines 45-47) computes oiObs = opInc.filter(non-null) over the ENTIRE array and returns computable:false when oiObs<4. The scaling (line 64,71) computes oiObservable over the 5-year window opInc.slice(0,5) and applies oiNeeded=Math.round(4*oiObservable/5). Verified arithmetic via node: 3y->2, 4y->3, 5y->4. The data contract is a 5-element annual series ([0]=newest..[4]=oldest, lines 12-13), so the window equals the whole array and oiObservable==oiObs. Given the gate guarantees oiObs>=4, oiNeeded is only ever 3 or 4 — the documented '3y->2' branch (lines 69-70) and the Tag-217g '2 missing years -> needed 3' scenario (lines 60-61) are BOTH unreachable. So the claim is accurate: the comment advertises a path the gate forbids. BUT this is purely a stale/aspirational comment (dead documentation), not a behavioral bug — the branch never executes, no stock is mis-scored, no false pass/fail. Auditor's own 'low' severity is correct. (Theoretical exception: if arrays could exceed length 5 with nulls front-loaded, the 3y branch could fire and demand only 2-of-3 positives — but real Yahoo annual data is 5 elements, so not reachable.)

title: normalizeMethodScore reads thresholdOp ONLY from methodMeta, never from the per-result — graduation silently breaks for region/scaled-threshold methods
evidence: Line 118 prefers the per-RESULT threshold: `var threshold = methodResult.threshold != null ? methodResult.threshold : (methodMeta && methodMeta.threshold);` but line 132 takes the operator ONLY from meta: `var op = (methodMeta && methodMeta.thresholdOp) || 'gte';`. methodMeta comes from strategy-modes.js:19 `reg[m.id] = { threshold: m.threshold, thresholdOp: m.thresholdOp }` — i.e. the MODULE-LEVEL static op, while the per-call result may carry a different threshold (e.g. piotroski scaledThreshold at piotroski-f-score.js:137, net-debt distressed value=999).
why_it_matters: If any scored method ever emits a per-result threshold whose correct operator differs from its module-level thresholdOp (or if methodRegistry is ever null — strategy-modes.js:23 returns null on require failure, and computeScore is still called with it), the graduated score silently defaults op to 'gte'. A method that should be scored 'lte' (e.g. net-debt-ebitda, weight 0.10 in QC) would then be graduated upside-down: a low (good) leverage ratio of 0.5 against threshold 2.5 gives ratio=0.5/2.5=0.2 → ~0.04 points instead of ~0.99. With methodRegistry===null every method falls to 'gte' and the entire QC/HG/TURN score silently inverts for all lte methods. This directly caps and can invert the investment score the screener is built to produce.
fix: Mirror the threshold-precedence logic for the operator: `var op = (methodResult.thresholdOp != null ? methodResult.thresholdOp : (methodMeta && methodMeta.thresholdOp)) || 'gte';` and harden against a null methodRegistry by falling back to the result's own threshold/op. Comment must name the failure mode: 'prevents op/threshold desync — meta op applied to a per-result threshold inverts lte graduation (net-debt-ebitda QC weight 0.10)'.

_verdict.note: False positive. The claimed op/threshold desync cannot occur given the actual method contracts. The registry meta op comes from each method's MODULE export (strategy-modes.js:19 reads m.thresholdOp), and every buildResult call in every method file sets thresholdOp to the SAME constant/literal as that module export. Verified across all methods/*.js: no file emits more than one distinct literal thresholdOp value, and none computes the op conditionally. Therefore methodResult.thresholdOp is always either (a) identical to methodMeta.thresholdOp, or (b) absent (e.g. earnings-stability emits no per-result op; its buildResult calls at lines 48/132 omit thresholdOp, only the module export line 152 sets 'lte'). The two cited methods refute the finding directly: piotroski-f-score.js:138 emits thresholdOp: THRESHOLD_OP (it scales only the THRESHOLD via scaledThreshold, never the op), and net-debt-ebitda.js:55/82 emit thresholdOp: THRESHOLD_OP ('lte') on both the value=999 sentinel path and the normal path — same op as its registry entry (line 89). So for net-debt-ebitda the meta op IS 'lte', matching the per-result; no lte-graduation inversion happens. _helpers.buildResult (line 58-68) is a pure pass-through and never synthesizes a divergent op. The secondary 'null methodRegistry' concern is also moot in production: the only caller (strategy-modes.js:274) always passes _getMethodRegistry(), which returns null only if require('./runner.js') throws (a fatal module-load failure that breaks the whole pipeline regardless); in that degenerate case meta would be null for ALL methods, not just one, and threshold also falls back to the per-result — i.e. it is not a region/scaled-threshold-specific bug. The evidence's framing ('per-call result may carry a different threshold' true; 'different op' false) conflates threshold variance with op variance.

title: Audit multipliers env-gated ON for dashboard+score-history but OFF for picks-history/fixtures — three score bases coexist for one stock
evidence: computeScore gates q-spike + listing-age multipliers behind AUDIT_SCORE_MULTIPLIERS (line 343-345). daily-pull.yml sets it '1' for the dashboard and score-history steps (lines 395/407/413) but 'INTENTIONALLY does NOT' set it for picks-history (lines 422/448). The returned object exposes `score` (multiplied) and `baseScore` (unmultiplied) (lines 447-448) but downstream consumers pick whichever they read.
why_it_matters: The same stock has a different numeric score and potentially a different TIER depending on which pipeline step computed it. score-history (multiplied) vs picks-history (unmultiplied) diverge structurally; the design doc itself flags 'AUDIT_SCORE_MULTIPLIERS flag drift' as producing a permanent fake score-delta. Tier classification (lines 394-397) runs on the multiplied score, so a stock can be A-tier in picks but B-tier in the dashboard for the same snapshot. This is a correctness/reconciliation hazard that undermines trust in the score and makes backtests on stored history non-comparable to live display.
fix: Make the multiplier basis a single source of truth: compute and persist BOTH score variants in every step (already have baseScore), and have every consumer explicitly select the documented one, OR stamp the score object with `auditMultipliersApplied: _amEnabled` (currently only auditMultiplierApplied per-stock at line 338, not surfaced in the return) so downstream can detect mismatch. Add the CI parity assertion referenced in the design doc. Comment: 'prevents silent score-basis drift between multiplied (dashboard/history) and unmultiplied (picks/fixtures) paths.'

_verdict.note:
Refuted as a false positive built on two misreads.

(1) MISREAD OF baseScore. The auditor claims the return exposes `score` (multiplied) and `baseScore` (unmultiplied) so "downstream consumers pick whichever they read." That is wrong. In score-aggregator.js, `baseScore = Math.round(normScore)` (line 297) and `score = max(0, baseScore - softGuardPenalty)` (line 320), with audit multipliers applied to `score` only (line 388). `baseScore` is the score BEFORE the SoftGuard penalty (Tag 120b, line 448) — it is NOT an "unmultiplied" mirror of `score`. A grep for `baseScore` across all non-test .js files returns ZERO external consumers — nothing downstream reads it. So the alleged "three score bases coexist via field selection" mechanism does not exist.

(2) MISREAD OF THE CONSUMER MECHANISM. Every consumer reads the SAME field, `ev.score`: snapshot-picks.js:102, snapshot-score-history.js:143-144, generate-screener.js. The multiplied-vs-unmultiplied difference comes ENTIRELY from the per-process env var AUDIT_SCORE_MULTIPLIERS, not from consumers picking different fields. So "downstream consumers pick whichever they read" is false.

(3) THE ENV SPLIT IS INTENTIONAL, DOCUMENTED, AND SAFE. daily-pull.yml sets the flag for the dashboard (line 395), score-history (line 407) and r40rx-history (line 413), and explicitly does NOT set it for picks-history (lines 422-427) and methods-history (lines 448-451), each with a multi-line rationale (Tag 199/203/219a). Score-history is deliberately env-matched to the dashboard because that is the ONE place the two values are shown together (the detail-modal sparkline) — drift there would produce the "fake score uplift" artifact, which is precisely the case the design closes. Picks-history/methods-history persist unmultiplied scores for fixture-hash stability and as clean backtest inputs; they are NEVER compared against a multiplied dashboard score. I traced the only picks-history consumers (compute-picks-lookback.js, fitness/freeze-full-baseline.js): they attribute forward returns by comparing a frozen pick to its own later PRICE, self-consistently within the unmultiplied basis — no cross-basis score comparison exists. snapshot-score-history.js even stamps `auditScoreMultipliers` into _meta.json (line 212) so the basis is recorded.

There is no silent data-integrity drift. The two bases never meet in any comparison except the dashboard/score-history pair, which is explicitly kept in sync. The finding's evidence quotes real lines but draws an incorrect conclusion from them.

title: lte graduation awards 0.99 for any val<=0 when pass is not strictly false — masks genuinely missing/zero-data lte methods
evidence: Line 159: `if (val <= 0 && methodResult.pass !== false) return 0.99;`. The guard only blocks the credit when pass===false. A computable lte method that returns value:0 with pass===true|undefined|null (e.g. a method emitting 0 as a neutral/default rather than a real measured 0) receives near-full credit 0.99.
why_it_matters: 0 is a legitimate value but is also the default-ish output of several methods when a component is absent. For an lte-scored method (net-debt-ebitda is the live one at QC weight 0.10), a spurious 0 reads as 'best possible' and contributes 0.099 of the QC score to a stock that may simply have had no EBITDA/debt data folded into a 0. The asymmetric `pass !== false` gate (added per F-ME-201) only catches the explicit-fail case; the undefined/null verdict still over-credits.
fix: Require an affirmative pass for the val<=0 shortcut: `if (val <= 0 && methodResult.pass === true) return 0.99;` and let pass-unknown/zero fall through to a measured ratio or the 0.3 ambiguous-credit. Verify net-debt-ebitda still scores net-cash names correctly (it sets pass=true for net cash). Comment: 'prevents a neutral/absent 0 from an lte method scoring as best-possible — only an affirmed pass earns the net-cash shortcut.'

_verdict.note: False positive — the described bad path is unreachable. Line 159 `if (val <= 0 && methodResult.pass !== false) return 0.99;` can only be reached when `methodResult.pass` is falsy at line 112 (`if (methodResult.pass) return 1.0;` short-circuits every truthy/true pass before the lte block). The finding requires `pass` to be `true` or `undefined`/`null` at line 159, but: (1) `pass===true` returns 1.0 at line 112 and never reaches line 159; (2) `pass===undefined|null` is impossible — every method result is built by `H.buildResult` (methods/_helpers.js:61 `pass: !!pass`), which coerces pass to a strict boolean, and `wrapEvaluate` (_helpers.js:326) preserves it via Object.assign without re-introducing undefined. So the only value that can reach line 159 is `pass===false`, for which `pass !== false` is false → the 0.99 shortcut is skipped and control falls to line 160 `return 0.0`. I verified all three scored (in SCORE_WEIGHTS) lte methods: earnings-stability (methods/earnings-stability.js:152, value=maxDecline>=0, always explicit boolean pass — the existing F-ME-201 fix already covers its val=0+pass=false case), gross-margin-stability (gross-margin-stability.js:7, value=cov>=0, pass=cov<=THRESHOLD, and cov=0 passes→1.0 at line 112), and net-debt-ebitda (net-debt-ebitda.js:9/67, net-cash gives negative value with pass=true→1.0 at line 112). None can deliver val<=0 with a non-false pass to line 159. The evidence's premise ('a method emitting 0 as neutral with pass===true|undefined|null') does not match the codebase: there is no such pass value possible after buildResult's `!!pass`.

title: Confidence/age decay never reaches scored methods — wrapEvaluate is called without methodType-appropriate opts and effectiveThreshold/percentile are never wired in
evidence: runner.js:52 calls `H.wrapEvaluate(m, stock, { methodType })` — only methodType is passed. wrapEvaluate computes confidence (line 322) and sectorPercentile (line 331 reads opts.sectorPercentile, never supplied) but score-aggregator.normalizeMethodScore ignores result.confidence and result.dataAgeDays entirely (it only reads value/pass/threshold/computable). effectiveThreshold() (exported _helpers.js:336) is referenced by only 4 methods (roic, reinvestment-rate, fcf-yield, sector-relative-roic per grep) — never by the runner/wrapEvaluate, so the elaborate rolling/regional median priority is dark for every other CORE scored method.
why_it_matters: The screener computes per-result confidence and STALE_DATA/NEAR_THRESHOLD flags (lines 296-307) on every method, but the score aggregator throws all of it away. A method scored on 13-month-old data (confidence -0.3) contributes identically to one on fresh data. Combined with the region-aware effectiveThreshold being applied in only 4 of ~15 scored methods, the much-touted 'authoritative rolling/regional median' machinery influences a tiny slice of the score. This is a large part of why the engine sits at '~20% of potential': the confidence/recency/sector-relative signal is fully built but not consumed by the score.
fix: Either (a) fold confidence into normalizeMethodScore weighting (weight *= result.confidence) so stale/near-threshold inputs are down-weighted, or (b) explicitly document that confidence is display-only. For the threshold path, route effectiveThreshold() through wrapEvaluate or a runner pre-pass so all threshold-comparison methods get region/rolling medians uniformly. Each method change must name the failure mode it prevents (e.g. 'prevents stale-data inputs contributing full weight to the investment score').

_verdict.note:
Refuted as a bug — this is an architecture/enhancement observation, not a defect, and one key evidence claim is inaccurate.

VERIFIED FACTS (correct in the finding): runner.js:52 calls H.wrapEvaluate(m, stock, { methodType }) passing only methodType. wrapEvaluate (_helpers.js:310-334) computes confidence/dataAgeDays/flags and reads opts.sectorPercentile (line 331), which is never supplied, so sectorPercentile is always null. score-aggregator.normalizeMethodScore (lines 110-186) reads only computable/pass/value/threshold/thresholdOp — it never reads result.confidence or result.dataAgeDays. Confirmed via grep that nothing in the production scoring path consumes result.confidence/dataAgeDays for weighting (the only confidence reads are _inferConfidence's own input at _helpers.js:272-273 and an unrelated map in court-score.js).

INACCURATE EVIDENCE: the finding says effectiveThreshold() is "referenced by 4 methods (roic, reinvestment-rate, fcf-yield, sector-relative-roic)." Only TWO methods actually CALL H.effectiveThreshold(): roic.js:14 and fcf-yield.js:24 (grep on `H\.effectiveThreshold`). reinvestment-rate.js merely declares a LOCAL variable also named effectiveThreshold (line 195) fed by its own _sectorThresholdFor() sector-override logic — a name collision, not a call site. sector-relative-roic.js only mentions effectiveThreshold in a doc comment (line 12) and does its own peer-percentile computation. The auditor conflated a same-named local var and a comment with real usages.

WHY NOT A BUG: (1) confidence/dataAsOf/dataAgeDays/sectorPercentile/flags are deliberately DISPLAY/DIAGNOSTIC metadata surfaced in the methods report (generate-methods-report.js:342 explicitly calls these fields display-only; the tag220b report-generators audit lists them as report fields). No spec or comment anywhere states confidence is meant to weight the investment score. The finding's own fix option (b) — "explicitly document that confidence is display-only" — concedes the current behavior may be intentional. (2) effectiveThreshold is a per-method OPT-IN: each method that wants region/rolling medians calls it inside its own evaluate() and returns the resolved threshold on the result (roic, fcf-yield do this). Many CORE scored methods use absolute or scaled thresholds by design (piotroski scaledThreshold, profitability-state/-trend stringly thresholds, altman-z, rule-of-40) — there is no evidence they were intended to be sector-relative. "Dark for every other CORE method" assumes a uniformity the design never had. No wrong screener output, no crash, no silent corruption results from any of this.

title: Largest-weight CORE inputs are categorical (string thresholds) and can only score binary 0/1 — caps score discrimination on the dominant signals
evidence: profitability-state (HYPERGROWTH weight 0.20, TURNAROUND 0.25) exports THRESHOLD='TURNAROUND' (profitability-state.js:20, unit:'state'); hypergrowth-quality-class (HG 0.20) exports THRESHOLD='REAL_HYPERGROWTH_BUT_LOSSY'; profitability-trend (TURN 0.25) exports THRESHOLD='FLAT'. In normalizeMethodScore the non-numeric-threshold branch (line 128-130) returns exactly 1.0 (pass), 0.0 (explicit fail), or 0.3 (ambiguous) — no graduation. So ~0.40 of HG weight and ~0.50 of TURNAROUND weight is effectively binary.
why_it_matters: Half of the TURNAROUND score and 40% of HYPERGROWTH is a coin-flip 0/1 with no gradient, so two stocks with very different underlying profitability trajectories that land in the same state bucket get identical points. The graduated-scoring architecture (Tag 120's whole premise) is bypassed for the heaviest inputs, flattening A/B/NEAR_MISS discrimination precisely where it matters most — a structural cap on screener precision.
fix: Have the categorical methods additionally export a numeric ordinal in components (e.g. profitability-state: LOSS=0, TURNAROUND=1, RECENT=2, EMERGING=3, STABLE=4) and teach normalizeMethodScore to graduate on that ordinal vs an ordinal threshold when threshold is a known enum. Keep the binary path as fallback. Comment each touched method: 'prevents heavy categorical CORE inputs collapsing to binary 0/1, flattening score discrimination.'

_verdict.note:
Confirmed against source. The three named CORE methods do export string THRESHOLDs (profitability-state.js:20 'TURNAROUND', hypergrowth-quality-class.js:23 'REAL_HYPERGROWTH_BUT_LOSSY', profitability-trend.js:27 'FLAT'), and in normalizeMethodScore (score-aggregator.js:118,128-130) a string threshold short-circuits before the graduation/ratio logic (lines 148-185), returning exactly 1.0 (pass), 0.0 (explicit fail), or 0.3 (ambiguous). The weight math is accurate: profitability-state(0.20)+hypergrowth-quality-class(0.20)=0.40 of HG; profitability-state(0.25)+profitability-trend(0.25)=0.50 of TURNAROUND score binary. Discrimination loss is real: e.g. profitability-state pass=stateRank>=1, so RECENT(2)/STABLE(3) get the same 1.0 as a bare TURNAROUND(1); HG-quality HYPERGROWTH_REVIEW(3) gets the same 0.0 as Q_SPIKE_FAKE(0).

BUT three caveats temper this from a bug to a design characterization: (1) This is the DELIBERATE, documented result of a prior fix — Tag 206 MEDIUM-3 (audit-reports/2026-05-16-tag206-aggregator-modes-review.md:59-61) specifically flagged this branch and the Tag 152/206l comments at lines 119-130 show the 0.0/1.0/0.3 outcome was intentionally chosen (explicit fail forced to 0.0 to prevent NEAR_MISS leakage). (2) The proposed fix is partly based on a misread: the numeric ordinal ALREADY exists in methodResult.value (STATE_RANK 0-3 / RANK 0-5 / trendRank 0-2 via buildResult), so 'additionally export a numeric ordinal in components' is redundant — the real gap is that normalizeMethodScore never consults value when threshold is a string. (3) The dominant non-categorical inputs (rule-of-40 0.25, altman-z 0.20, piotroski, roic, etc.) still graduate, so scores are not actually binary overall. Net: a true but minor architectural limitation on granularity, not a correctness defect producing wrong tiers.

title: Methods loaded once at module-eval (good) but evaluateStock re-derives type/core/coverage sets per stock via repeated Object.keys().filter() over the universe
evidence: runner.js:61-62 recomputes `Object.keys(results).filter(id => MT.isCore(id))` and `.filter(id => MT.isCore(id) && results[id].pass)` on EVERY evaluateStock call. MT.getType (method-types.js:148) does a REGISTRY hash lookup each time, and evaluateStock loops all METHODS calling MT.getType(m.id) again at line 49 plus MT.isDefaultActive at 51. For ~4,739 OK stocks × ~70 methods, the per-stock re-classification and double key-scan is pure repeated work; the CORE-id set and per-method type are static for the process lifetime.

_verdict.note: Code description is accurate but severity is overstated; downgrade to low. CONFIRMED: runner.js:61-62 runs two Object.keys(results).filter(id => MT.isCore(id)) passes per stock, and line 49 calls MT.getType(m.id) per method per stock; each MT.isCore/getType is a REGISTRY[id] lookup (method-types.js:148-152). WHY IT'S OVERSTATED: the alleged "redundant work" is the cheapest possible V8 operation — a plain-object property read plus a string '===' compare (~210 such ops/stock). It sits directly beside METHODS.length (~70) calls to method.evaluate(stock) via _helpers.wrapEvaluate (line 52), each of which does the actual heavy lifting: annual revenue regressions, multi-year CoV / geomean, Beneish/Ohlson/Altman scores, plus per-call date parsing (_dataAsOfFromStock/_dataAgeDays), confidence inference, flag concat and an Object.assign allocation. The classification lookups are a vanishingly small fraction of per-stock cost — a micro-optimization, not a medium perf problem. Two factual nits: (1) line 51 MT.isDefaultActive is only reached when opts.onlyDefault is true, which the production buildRow path does NOT pass, so it is NOT in the prod hot path (overstated in evidence); (2) coreCount/coreCountPass (lines 61-62) are computed on every stock but consumed by NO caller anywhere in the repo (grep: only definitions, zero reads) — so this is redundant work producing dead output, which lowers the stakes further.

title: SOFT_GUARD penalty / score-weight only fire when the underlying method is actually evaluated — onlyDefault callers and disabled methods silently drop penalties and weight
evidence: method-types.js carries inline 'Bug #20' (line 63-65, working-capital-anomaly flipped defaultActive:true 'so the penalty is actually computable') and 'Bug #21' (line 116-118, above-200d-ma). But the pattern is general: strategy-modes.js:218 only pushes a failed soft-guard if `r && r.computable===true && r.pass===false`. If a soft-guard method is not in the evaluated set (filterType/onlyDefault path in runner.js:50-51) its result is absent → penalty silently 0. Likewise SCORE_WEIGHTS entries whose method is defaultActive:false would contribute 0 weight under onlyDefault but still inflate totalWeight only if present.
why_it_matters: The coupling between (a) SCORE_WEIGHTS / SOFT_GUARD_PENALTY registration and (b) whether the method is in the evaluated set is implicit and has already caused at least two logged bugs (#20, #21). Any future weight/penalty added without flipping defaultActive, or any caller using onlyDefault:true, silently zeroes that contribution with no error — the score quietly drifts. This is a recurring class, not a one-off.
fix: Add a startup invariant check (in runner or a test) asserting every id in SCORE_WEIGHTS[*] and SOFT_GUARD_PENALTY is both registered and isDefaultActive(); throw/log loudly on violation. This converts the silent-drop class into a loud failure, consistent with the index.js 'fail LOUDLY' philosophy. Comment: 'prevents a scored/penalized method silently contributing 0 because it was not in the evaluated set.'

_verdict.note:
Mechanism is real but currently LATENT, and the specific cited evidence is already fixed in this worktree. Verified the code paths: runner.js:51 skips non-isDefaultActive methods only when onlyDefault:true; strategy-modes.js:219 records a failed soft-guard only when allResults[sgId] exists with computable===true && pass===false, so an absent (skipped) soft-guard silently pushes no penalty; score-aggregator computeScore only adds weight for computable results. REFUTATION of live impact: I enumerated every id at runtime. All 7 SOFT_GUARD_PENALTY ids and all HYPERGROWTH/QC/TURNAROUND SCORE_WEIGHTS ids are registered AND defaultActive:true. The two cases the finding cites as evidence (Bug #20 working-capital-anomaly methods/method-types.js:63-65; Bug #21 above-200d-ma :116-118) are ALREADY FIXED here — both flipped to defaultActive:true with inline comments. No production caller passes onlyDefault:true (only docs/audit-reports/*.md mention it); runner defaults onlyDefault=false, so every method evaluates and every penalty/weight fires today. Net: no current miscalculation.

One real unhandled gap supporting the general thesis (not in the cited lines): SCORE_WEIGHTS.BUFFETT references buffett-criteria, owner-earnings, dcf-intrinsic-value — all three load as method modules but have NO method-types.js REGISTRY entry, so isDefaultActive() returns false for them. Under onlyDefault:true the whole BUFFETT score would collapse to null (computedWeight===0). Still latent (BUFFETT softGuards is empty; onlyDefault=false default evaluates them fine). This is a hardening/invariant gap, not a present defect.

title: metricValue unwraps {value} but does NOT unwrap Yahoo {raw,fmt} envelopes — fmt-only / raw-keyed metrics silently read null
evidence: metricValue (line 23-29) handles only two shapes: `(typeof m === 'object' && 'value' in m) ? m.value : (typeof m === 'number' ? m : null)`. Yahoo's quoteSummary modules return numbers wrapped as `{ raw: 123, fmt: '123.0', longFmt: '123' }`. An object with a `raw` key but no `value` key falls to the `typeof m === 'number'` test, fails it, and returns null.
why_it_matters: Any metric persisted in raw/fmt envelope form (a documented hazard in the prompt's bug classes) is silently treated as missing by every method that reads via metricValue, making those methods computable:false for no visible reason — invisible attrition of signal. Given the snapshot layer's job is to normalize Yahoo, anything that slips through un-normalized is dropped here with zero diagnostics.
fix: Extend the unwrap to cover the envelope: after the 'value' check, add `if (typeof m === 'object' && 'raw' in m) return Number.isFinite(m.raw) ? m.raw : null;`. Keep the Number.isFinite guard already at line 28. Comment: 'prevents Yahoo {raw,fmt} envelope metrics reading as null — F-ME envelope-unwrap.' Verify against a snapshot that actually stores raw-form metrics before shipping; if the snapshot layer guarantees normalization, downgrade to defensive.

_verdict.note: False positive based on misreading where Yahoo {raw,fmt} envelopes are unwrapped. metricValue (methods/_helpers.js:23-29) is a snapshot READER; it only ever sees the normalized {value,source,confidence,asOf} envelope, never a raw {raw,fmt} object. Evidence chain in pull-yahoo.js: stock.metrics.* is built EXCLUSIVELY via _metric(_y(...)) (lines 891-928). _y(obj,...keys) at line 484 strips the Yahoo envelope BEFORE return: `if (cur && typeof cur === 'object' && 'raw' in cur) return cur.raw;` — yielding a plain number. _metric (488-491) then wraps that number as {value,...} and returns null for non-finite. The only later mutation of metrics.* is scale()/scaleTrading() (lines 433/443), which both branch on `if ('value' in item)` and preserve the {value} shape (lines 377-381 / 397-401) — they never introduce a {raw} key. So a metrics.<key> is always null or {value:<number>,...}, which is exactly the `'value' in m` branch on line 26. The scenario described (a {raw}-keyed object with no value key reaching metricValue and silently reading null) cannot occur in this pipeline. The finding's own caveat applies: 'if the snapshot layer guarantees normalization, downgrade to defensive' — and it does (_y/_metric mapper). No caller passes raw Yahoo modules into metricValue; methods read from the persisted snapshot only (e.g. peg.js:10-19 calls H.metricValue(stock,'pe') on snapshot data).

title: dataAsOf candidate order can pick lastFiscalYearEnd over fetchedAt, mislabeling fresh pulls as stale (or vice-versa)
evidence: _dataAsOfFromStock (line 254-261) builds candidates [meta.dataAsOf, meta.fetchedAt, annual.lastFiscalYearEnd, meta.lastUpdate].filter(Boolean) and returns candidates[0]. If meta.dataAsOf is absent but annual.lastFiscalYearEnd is present, the function still prefers fetchedAt over fiscal-year-end (order is correct) — BUT when dataAsOf and fetchedAt are both absent, it falls to lastFiscalYearEnd, which for an annual filing can be 6-15 months old even on a fresh pull. That feeds _dataAgeDays → confidence decay (line 277-281) and STALE_DATA flag (line 298).
why_it_matters: A freshly pulled stock lacking meta.dataAsOf/fetchedAt is mislabeled with the age of its last fiscal year, dropping confidence by up to 0.3 and raising STALE_DATA — penalizing exactly the value-relevant signal. Conversely if lastFiscalYearEnd is missing but lastUpdate is a price-only refresh timestamp, a stale-fundamentals stock looks fresh. The semantic mixing of 'as-of fundamentals' vs 'fetched' vs 'fiscal-year-end' in one ordered list is fragile.
fix: Separate the two notions: use fetch/update timestamps for a 'data freshness' age and fiscal-year-end strictly for a distinct 'fundamentals vintage' age; never let fiscal-year-end stand in for fetch freshness. At minimum reorder so a fetch/update timestamp always wins and only fall to fiscal-year-end with an explicit components flag noting the substitution. Comment: 'prevents fiscal-year-end masquerading as fetch-freshness in confidence/STALE_DATA.'

_verdict.note: Refuted as a non-issue against current data shapes. _dataAsOfFromStock (methods/_helpers.js:254-262) builds candidates [meta.dataAsOf, meta.fetchedAt, annual.lastFiscalYearEnd, meta.lastUpdate].filter(Boolean) and returns candidates[0]. I traced where stock objects are constructed: the canonical producer is pull-yahoo.js. Its mapper (line 820-887) writes meta.fetchedAt (line 831) AND meta.asOf (line 840) on every snapshot, but NEVER meta.dataAsOf, meta.lastUpdate, or annual.lastFiscalYearEnd. The annual object (pull-yahoo.js:1013-1018) contains only annualRev/annualOpInc/annualNetIncome/annualGP/annualFCF/annualOCF/annualBalance/annualRnD — there is no lastFiscalYearEnd field. A whole-repo grep confirms 'lastFiscalYearEnd' appears in exactly ONE place: the candidate list itself (methods/_helpers.js:258) — it is never assigned anywhere, in pull-yahoo.js or pull-sec-xbrl.js or any snapshot loader. Likewise meta.dataAsOf and meta.lastUpdate are never written. Consequence: candidates[0] is always meta.fetchedAt in practice; the third candidate is always undefined and removed by .filter(Boolean), so it can never be selected. The finding's described harm — falling through to a 6-15-month-old fiscal-year-end on a fresh pull and tripping confidence decay / STALE_DATA — is unreachable. The auditor even concedes 'order is correct,' and the in-code comment at pull-yahoo.js:873-875 explicitly states _dataAsOfFromStock 'continues to prefer meta.fetchedAt for now; methods may opt in.' This is speculative defensive hygiene about a dormant fallback, not an active data-integrity defect. (Note: meta.fetchedAt reflects API call time, not filing time, but that is by design and orthogonal to this finding.)

title: Coverage gate divides by totalWeight which only sums weights of methods present in the loop — a SCORE_WEIGHTS id never returned by the runner is invisible to the coverage denominator
evidence: Line 239 `totalWeight += weight` runs for every id in the static SCORE_WEIGHTS map regardless of presence (good), so totalWeight is the full mode weight. But computedWeight (line 242) only counts isComputable. The minCoverage check (line 265) `computedWeight/totalWeight < minCoverage`. If a weighted method id is misspelled in SCORE_WEIGHTS or de-registered, allResults[methodId] is undefined → normalizeMethodScore returns 0, isComputable false, its weight still inflates totalWeight → coverage ratio is depressed by a phantom method, pushing borderline stocks to insufficient-coverage REJECT.
why_it_matters: A registry/weights typo doesn't fail loud here — it silently lowers every stock's coverage ratio in that mode, mass-REJECTing names near the 0.30/0.40 boundary. Given the heavy reliance on string-keyed weight maps and the history of registration drift (Bugs #20/#21, Tag 206d), this is a realistic silent-degradation path.
fix: Cross-check SCORE_WEIGHTS keys against the live method registry at startup (ties into finding -08's invariant) so an unmatched weight key throws rather than silently inflating totalWeight. Comment: 'prevents a typo'd/de-registered SCORE_WEIGHTS key silently depressing coverage and mass-rejecting borderline stocks.'

_verdict.note:
CONFIRMED REAL (latent). Mechanism verified in methods/score-aggregator.js: line 239 `totalWeight += weight` runs unconditionally for every id in SCORE_WEIGHTS[modeId], while computedWeight/weightedSum (lines 242-243) only accumulate when isComputable. allResults is built by iterating the live METHODS registry (runner.js:48), so a SCORE_WEIGHTS id with no matching registered/active method yields allResults[id]===undefined -> normalizeMethodScore returns 0 (line 111) -> isComputable false -> its weight inflates only the denominator. Coverage gate line 265 (computedWeight/totalWeight < minCoverage) is then depressed by the phantom weight, producing a silent insufficient-coverage REJECT of borderline stocks. Corroborated by the codebase's own history: method-types.js Tag 206d (3 TURNAROUND weight ids had no REGISTRY entry) and Tag 206h (rule-of-x weighted 0.10 but defaultActive:false 'silently zeroing 10% of the HG composite' under onlyDefault:true) document two prior real incidents of exactly this failure mode. No structural cross-check exists and no test guards it (grep of tag28-tests.js found nothing).

WHY LOW (not higher): currently dormant in the production path. generate-screener.js:259 calls Runner.evaluateStock(stock) WITHOUT onlyDefault, so ALL registered methods are evaluated regardless of defaultActive — I verified all 19 SCORE_WEIGHTS ids resolve to real result objects in the default path, so totalWeight is correct today. The trigger is a developer error (typo'd/de-registered id) or an onlyDefault:true evaluation. Notable live exposure: BUFFETT's three weighted methods (buffett-criteria 0.50, owner-earnings 0.20, dcf-intrinsic-value 0.30) are all DIAGNOSTIC + defaultActive:false, so any onlyDefault:true caller would zero the entire BUFFETT denominator (computedWeight=0 -> null at line 248). Low is appropriate; borderline low/medium given that BUFFETT exposure.

WHY fix_safe=false: the proposed fix THROWS at startup on an unmatched weight key. That is NOT behavior-preserving — a cross-check keyed on default-active status would throw immediately because the 3 BUFFETT methods are defaultActive:false today, crashing the whole pipeline. Even a presence-only registry check converts silent-degrade into a hard fail and requires human judgment on what 'registered' means and how to treat the onlyDefault paths. Needs human review, not auto-apply. Relevant files: C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/methods/score-aggregator.js (lines 225-272), methods/runner.js (lines 42-64), methods/method-types.js (lines 29-53), generate-screener.js (line 259).

title: Red-flag detection requires fr.value != null, so the net-debt distressed sentinel and any value:null-but-failed method never trigger their red flag
evidence: Line 407: `if (fr && fr.computable && fr.value != null && rule.condition(fr.value, fr))`. HIGH_DEBT keys on net-debt-ebitda. When net-debt-ebitda is computable but represents distress via components.distressedFlag with value=999 it fires (999>4). But any rule whose method signals a problem through components/pass while leaving value null (a common pattern for categorical guards) is skipped by the `fr.value != null` precondition before the condition even runs.
why_it_matters: Red-flag downgrade (line 413-415) is a key safety net (A/B → NEAR_MISS). Gating it on a non-null scalar value means problem-states expressed structurally (value null, pass false, distress in components) cannot raise a red flag. The current two rules happen to use scalar values, but the framework silently can't support component-based red flags — limiting the very safety layer the architecture relies on.
fix: Pass the full result to the condition unconditionally when computable (the condition already receives fr), and let each rule decide whether it needs value: change the guard to `if (fr && fr.computable && rule.condition(fr.value, fr))` and make value-based rules null-check internally. Comment: 'prevents component/pass-based red flags being suppressed by a value!=null precondition.'

_verdict.note:
False positive against the current codebase. Verified in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening.

(1) The distressed sentinel is NOT suppressed. methods/net-debt-ebitda.js lines 45-56 return `value: 999, pass: false, computable: true` with components.distressedFlag. At score-aggregator.js line 407 `999 != null` is true and HIGH_DEBT.condition(999, fr) returns `999 > 4.0` = true, so the red flag fires. The finding itself concedes this.

(2) No rule uses the hypothesized "components/pass-based, value:null" pattern. RED_FLAG_RULES (lines 76-102) has exactly two entries: HIGH_DEBT (line 83-86, `val > threshold`) and EXTREME_SLOAN (line 98, `val > 0.20`). Both are purely value-based — neither inspects pass/components while leaving value null.

(3) The hypothetical method doesn't exist either. sloan-ratio.js sets `value: v` only on the computable:true branch (lines 105/107); all other branches are computable:false. net-debt-ebitda's two computable branches both set a numeric value (real ratio or 999 sentinel). So there is no real method+rule combination where a problem is signaled via components/pass with value null. The `fr.value != null` precondition is currently dead-safe — it never suppresses any real red flag.

The finding is speculation about a "common pattern for categorical guards" that has no instance in this code today.

fix_safe=false: removing the `fr.value != null` guard is not behavior-preserving. The finding admits the existing value-based rules must be rewritten to null-check internally, and line 408 (`value: fr.value`) would then push `value: null` into the redFlags audit-trail payload that downstream UI/reports consume. Today both conditions happen to return false on null input (`null > N` is false), but the change alters the contract and the recorded payload — needs human review, not auto-apply.

title: latest/oldest unwrap uses `&&` short-circuit: legitimate revenue of 0 becomes falsy and falls through to NaN in the reason string / components
evidence: `const latestVal = typeof arr[0] === 'number' ? arr[0] : (arr[0] && arr[0].value);` and same for `arr[3]`. If arr[0] is the envelope `{value:0}`, `arr[0] && arr[0].value` returns 0 (ok), but if arr[0] is a plain number 0, `typeof===number` returns 0 — fine. The real hazard: `arr[0]` can be `null` (pull-yahoo pushes `null` placeholders to preserve positional alignment, see pull-yahoo.js _arr/null handling). `arr[0] && arr[0].value` then yields `null`, and the reason template does `(latestVal/1e9).toFixed(1)` → `(null/1e9)` = 0, silently mislabeling. More importantly cagr3y() already guards null/<=0 and returns null (handled), but the display path computes latestVal/oldestVal INDEPENDENTLY of the cagr guard, so a null arr[3] prints `0.0B` as the oldest base.
why_it_matters: revenue-growth-3y is CORE, weight 0.15 in HYPERGROWTH and 0.10 in TURNAROUND. The scoring uses `cagr` (guarded) so the score itself is safe, but the human-facing `reason`/`components.oldest` can render misleading 0.0B baselines on snapshots with a null in position 0 or 3, eroding trust in the dashboard the owner reads.
fix: Reuse the same `_unwrap` helper the sibling methods use (return null for null/NaN), and guard the reason template: only format `latestVal/oldestVal` when both are finite, else emit the cagr value alone. Add a comment naming the failure mode: 'prevents null-positional-placeholder rendering as 0.0B baseline'.

_verdict.note:
False positive — misreads the control flow and misattributes pull-yahoo's null-placeholder behavior. Refutation:

1) The display path (revenue-growth-3y.js:35-42) is NOT reached independently of the cagr guard. At lines 26-33 `cagr = H.cagr3y(arr)` runs FIRST and the function returns early (computable:false) when `cagr == null`. `cagr3y` (_helpers.js:49-56) uses the IDENTICAL unwrap on arr[0]/arr[3] (`x && (typeof x==='number'?x:x.value)`) and returns null when `latest==null || oldest==null || latest<=0 || oldest<=0` (line 54). So a null arr[3] (→ oldest==null) or a legit-zero base (→ oldest<=0) makes cagr3y return null → early return → lines 35-42 are never executed. The auditor's core assertion ("the display path computes latestVal/oldestVal INDEPENDENTLY of the cagr guard") is factually wrong: latestVal/oldestVal at lines 35-36 are computed with the same unwrap and are strictly downstream of, and gated by, the cagr guard. There is no reachable state where null/0 reaches `(latestVal/1e9).toFixed(1)`.

2) The premise that arr (annual.annualRev) contains null positional placeholders is also wrong. annualRev is built by `_arr(isHist,'totalRevenue')` (pull-yahoo.js:618). `_arr` (pull-yahoo.js:493-500) maps null→null then ends with `.filter(Boolean)`, stripping every null. The F-004 null-placeholder-preservation the auditor cites applies to the DERIVED annualOpInc / financials arrays (pull-yahoo.js:570-573, 593-594, 652-657), not annualRev. So annualRev never carries null placeholders in the first place.

Both the bug and the proposed fix's stated failure mode ("null-positional-placeholder rendering as 0.0B baseline") are non-issues. The proposed fix would add a redundant guard for an unreachable state; harmless but unnecessary, and not behavior-preserving in a meaningful sense (it changes a never-taken branch). Not safe to auto-apply without human review since it's premised on a misunderstanding. revised_severity low (cosmetic-only even hypothetically: it only ever touched the human-readable reason string, never `value`/`pass`/`components` correctness, since components mirror the same already-guarded values).

title: Deceleration DATAGUARD compares latest-quarter YoY (point-in-time) against revenueGrowthYoY (a TTM/annual metric) as if both are the same growth basis
evidence: `var ttmGrowth = H.metricValue(stock, 'revenueGrowthYoY');` then `var hardFail = ttmGrowth >= 25 && qYoY < 10 && qBelowAvg;`. pull-yahoo.js:614-615 sets `revenueGrowthYoY = revenueGrowth * 100` straight from Yahoo financialData.revenueGrowth, which is Yahoo's TTM-vs-prior-TTM figure, NOT an annual-fiscal figure and NOT the same window as qRev[0]/qRev[4]. The method header even calls it 'TTM-Growth' but the doc-comment and 'revenueGrowthYoY' naming conflate quarterly-YoY and TTM growth. When Yahoo's revenueGrowth lags (it updates on its own cadence) a stock mid-re-acceleration can show qYoY healthy but stale ttmGrowth high, or vice-versa.
why_it_matters: deceleration-guard is a DATAGUARD (method-types.js:136) AND carries the highest soft-guard penalty (score-aggregator.js:200, penalty 10). A basis mismatch produces both false HARD_DECEL disqualifications and spurious 10-point penalties. Because the comparison hinges on a Yahoo field whose refresh cadence differs from the persisted quarterly series, the verdict is non-deterministic across pulls.
fix: Compute TTM growth internally from the persisted quarterly series (sum(qRev[0..3]) vs sum(qRev[4..7])) so both sides of the inequality share one basis and one as-of date, instead of mixing a Yahoo-cadence metric with the snapshot's quarterly array. Comment: 'prevents quarterly-YoY vs Yahoo-TTM basis mismatch producing non-deterministic deceleration verdicts'.

_verdict.note:
The factual plumbing claims are accurate but the "bug" verdict is a misread of intent. Confirmed: deceleration-guard.js:32 reads metrics.revenueGrowthYoY, which pull-yahoo.js:614-615 (+ mapped at :893) sets from Yahoo financialData.revenueGrowth*100 (a TTM-vs-prior-TTM figure on Yahoo's own update cadence), while qRev[0]/qRev[4] is a point-in-time same-quarter YoY from timeseries.revenueQ. So the two sides do use different bases/as-of dates.

But that divergence is the method's deliberate design, not an accident. The header (lines 4-7) states the premise verbatim: "latestQuarterYoY << TTM-Growth = Wachstum operativ tot, TTM laggt" — the guard exists precisely to flag when the fast quarterly signal collapses while the slower lagging TTM metric is still high. The in-code variable is correctly named ttmGrowth and the soft-fail (line 56, qYoY < ttmGrowth-30) is explicitly a non-gating warning. The hard-fail (line 54) additionally requires qBelowAvg, an intra-series sanity check computed purely from qRev[0..3], so the exclude decision never rests on the cross-basis comparison alone.

The "non-deterministic verdicts" claim is wrong: both inputs are persisted in the snapshot, so output is fully deterministic per snapshot. The auditor is really describing lag — which is the signal the method consumes, not a defect. Prior audit (audit-reports/2026-05-19.md, findings/methods-engine.json) reviewed this exact method, treated revenueGrowthYoY as the legitimate "TTM growth" side, and its accepted fix is the ttmGrowth==null guard now at lines 50-52 — confirming maintainers intend this basis.

Only mild, non-bug nit: the field name revenueGrowthYoY is overloaded across methods (rule-of-40 treats it as the growth input), so the name conflates two notions — a documentation/naming smell, not a correctness bug here.

title: Single-Q-dependency collapse metric removes recent peak quarter but only flat-scales prior window by 0.75 — flags sustained-acceleration compounders as single-Q-dependent
evidence: `const ttmExMax = ttm - maxQ;` (3-quarter sum, peak removed) compared via `const priorScaled = priorTtm * 0.75;` (a flat average-3-quarter prior). `gEx=(ttmExMax-priorScaled)/priorScaled; collapsePct=(gFull-gEx)/gFull`. For a clean compounder whose largest quarter IS the latest (normal for sequential growth), removing the single biggest recent quarter drops ttmExMax sharply while prior only drops a flat 25%, so gEx can swing strongly negative and collapsePct exceeds the 0.50 gate → FAIL. The header even admits 'sustained acceleration ... doesn't collapse it by 50%' but the flat-0.75 scaling breaks that promise when growth is back-loaded.
why_it_matters: Mislabels exactly the back-loaded sequential-growth pattern the screener is hunting (the latest quarter being the biggest is the bullish case). It is DIAGNOSTIC-only (not in SCORE_WEIGHTS/SOFT_GUARD_PENALTY), so it cannot disqualify — but it pollutes the scorecard the owner reads and would become an active false-FAIL the moment it is wired into scoring.
fix: Remove the peer quarter by POSITION not by max (e.g. drop the same calendar quarter from both windows), or compare ttmExMax against the prior window with its own max removed (priorTtm - max(prior)) so the operation is symmetric. Comment: 'prevents back-loaded sequential growth (peak==latest) from reading as single-Q dependency'.

_verdict.note:
REFUTED — false positive built on two misreads of the math in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/methods/single-quarter-dependency.js (lines 106-124).

(1) The auditor calls `priorScaled = priorTtm * 0.75` a "flat 25% drop"/"damping" of the prior window. It is not. priorTtm is a 4-quarter SUM (revQ[4..7]); ttmExMax is a 3-quarter sum (recent minus its max). Multiplying the 4Q prior by 0.75 rebases it onto a 3-quarter basis so gEx is a true apples-to-apples 3Q-vs-3Q growth rate. This is exactly the correct normalization, not an arbitrary discount.

(2) The core premise — "a clean sequential compounder whose largest quarter is the latest gets flagged" — is empirically false. I simulated the actual code. For clean QoQ compounders the max recent quarter is only ~27-42% of recent TTM, so removing it drops ttmExMax by roughly the same fraction the 0.75 rebasing drops the prior; gEx tracks gFull closely and collapsePct stays far below the 0.50 gate:
  - 3% QoQ -> collapse 13.2% PASS
  - 5% QoQ -> 13.8% PASS
  - 10% QoQ -> 15.7% PASS
  - 20% QoQ -> 18.5% PASS
  - 30% QoQ -> 21.5% PASS
  - 40% QoQ -> 24.6% PASS
  - 50% QoQ (absurdly steep but still sequential, peak==latest, maxShare 41.6%) -> 27.5% PASS.
Even a smooth accelerating inflection passes (23.8%). The header promise ("sustained acceleration ... doesn't collapse it by 50%") is UPHELD by the code.

The only cases that FAIL are genuine single-Q dependency: a spike on a flat base (e.g. latest 200 on flat 50 -> 94%; latest +60% over a flat recent base -> 77.5%; any single quarter jump on a flat 4Q prior -> 100%). That is precisely what the guard targets. The distinguishing factor is growth DISTRIBUTION across the recent window vs CONCENTRATION in one quarter — not whether the peak is the latest quarter, which is what the auditor assumed. The crossover to FAIL only occurs around maxShare > ~50% of recent TTM (true spike territory), unreachable by sequential ramps.

fix_safe=false: the proposed fix (drop prior-max, or remove by calendar position) is NOT behavior-preserving — it changes the metric's semantics, would weaken detection of real spikes, and introduces calendar-alignment assumptions Yahoo data does not guarantee. It addresses a problem that does not exist and must not be auto-applied. No code change warranted; severity downgraded to low (documentation could note distribution-vs-recency, but the logic is correct).

title: CoV consistency signal returns incomputable (not a fail) for high-and-volatile growers because the MIN_MEAN_GROWTH gate fires before dispersion is assessed; also n=3 sample-stdev is statistically fragile
evidence: `if (mean < MIN_MEAN_GROWTH) { computable:false }` — but a company with growth rates like [+60%, -10%, +5%] has mean ~18% (passes the gate) while [+5%, -3%, +4%] (mean 2%) is dropped as incomputable. The deeper issue: CoV is computed from only 3 YoY points with sample stdev (n-1=2 denominator, line 51), so a single outlier year dominates std and the 0.30 threshold is essentially a coin-flip on 3 data points. The header sells this as a 'quality consistency' signal but 3 points cannot support a 0.30 CoV cut.
why_it_matters: revenue-quality is DIAGNOSTIC defaultActive:true but NOT in any SCORE_WEIGHTS or SOFT_GUARD_PENALTY (verified against score-aggregator.js and strategy-modes.js) — it is computed on every snapshot and consumed by nobody except the display. So this is wasted recompute plus a low-power signal masquerading as a quality gate.

_verdict.note: Refuted on the central claim and downgraded the rest to a doc nit. (1) The headline is a misread: the auditor says the signal "returns incomputable (not a fail) for high-and-volatile growers." It does the opposite. I executed the actual code path on the auditor's own example [+60%,-10%,+5%]: mean=18.3% passes the 5% gate, then CoV=2.01 >> 0.30 -> computable=true, pass=FALSE. The volatile grower is correctly flagged as inconsistent. The ONLY incomputable case is the low-mean steady example [+5%,-3%,+4%] (mean 2% < 5% gate), and that is documented design intent (revenue-quality.js header lines 26-27, 39: low-mean denominators inflate CoV misleadingly; near-zero growth is explicitly out of scope for a 'consistency' signal). (2) The n=3 / sample-stdev (n-1) fragility point is statistically valid in the abstract, but it cannot harm results: revenue-quality is a pure DIAGNOSTIC. (3) The proposed fix is actively unsafe: this worktree's own reports document the quarterly sibling revenue-quality-cov as DEAD on current data (audit-reports/2026-05-17-tag225d-method-effectiveness.md:27 — 0/10 anchors, needs >=8 quarters; pull-yahoo retains only 5). Promoting it to canonical and retiring the annual one would silently remove the only computable variant. Residual: at most a minor doc nit (the n=3 caveat isn't spelled out in the header), not a medium bug.
