evidence: method-types.js:67 `'quarterly-earnings-stability': { type:'DIAGNOSTIC', defaultActive:false, reason:'8Q earnings volatility' }`. No reference in score-aggregator.js or strategy-modes.js. Loaded at index.js:70. Also `const v = q && (typeof q === 'number' ? q : q.value);` then `if (v != null && v > 0)` — when q is a plain number 0 the `q &&` short-circuits to 0 (treated as not-positive, correct here) but a NEGATIVE plain number passes `q &&` and is correctly counted as non-positive; the subtle issue is q===0 → v=0 vs q={value:0} → v=0 both fine, so logic is ok, but the method is simply never run.
why_it_matters: Pure dead weight on the default path; maintenance surface with zero output consumer. Low severity because logic is otherwise correct.
fix: Flag for deletion (owner OK required) or wire into the QC earnings-consistency display if intended. No code change needed for correctness.

_verdict.note:
Headline claim ("computed by nobody in the default path / simply never run") is FALSE — based on a misread of the gating semantics. runner.js:48-52 evaluates EVERY loaded method and only skips non-default-active ones when a caller passes onlyDefault:true (line 51: `if (onlyDefault && !MT.isDefaultActive(m.id)) continue;`). The production report generators call Runner.evaluateStock(stock) with NO opts — generate-methods-report.js:103 and generate-modes-report.js:115 — so onlyDefault is falsy and quarterly-earnings-stability IS computed for every stock, with its result landing in the methods-report rows[].results (deep-dive tables / pass-count ranking). defaultActive:false only suppresses it in the separate onlyDefault-filtered path, not the default evaluation path.

The auditor's verifiable sub-facts are all individually correct: method-types.js:67 = DIAGNOSTIC/defaultActive:false (confirmed); no reference in score-aggregator.js (confirmed — not in SCORE_WEIGHTS, and NOT in SOFT_GUARD_PENALTY {q-spike, deceleration, revenue-shock, quarter-concentration, asset-growth-divergence, working-capital-anomaly, net-debt-ebitda}); no reference in strategy-modes.js (confirmed); loaded at index.js:70 (confirmed). The `const v = q && (typeof q === 'number' ? q : q.value)` logic is, as the auditor themselves concede, correct.

But the conclusion does not follow. This is a deliberately score-neutral DIAGNOSTIC method whose output is surfaced (not consumed by any weight/guard) — identical pattern to dozens of other DIAGNOSTIC entries in the registry (e.g. drawdown-52w, volatility-annualized, insider-ownership). Score-neutral != dead. It is not dead code, so the dead-code finding is a false positive.

title: Three growth DIAGNOSTICs (revenue-quality, revenue-quality-cov, revenue-acceleration-yoy, single-quarter-dependency, quarterly-revenue-acceleration) are defaultActive:true but feed no score and no gate — computed every run, consumed only by display
evidence: revenue-quality-cov header line 61: 'NOT in SCORE_WEIGHTS -> DIAGNOSTIC-only -> fixture-hash safe by construction.' Confirmed: none of revenue-quality / revenue-quality-cov / revenue-acceleration-yoy / single-quarter-dependency / quarterly-revenue-acceleration appear in score-aggregator.js SCORE_WEIGHTS (lines 32-73) or SOFT_GUARD_PENALTY (197-211) or strategy-modes.js. They are all defaultActive:true (method-types.js:70,76,72,99 + quarterly-revenue-acceleration:45), so they run on every snapshot in the ~4.7k-stock universe each pull.
why_it_matters: Performance + signal-dilution: five non-trivial array methods recomputed for every stock every pull (the multi-hour pull the brief flags) while contributing nothing to ranking. This is part of why high-quality signals are diluted — the screener computes a lot it never acts on. Several (revenue-quality-cov, single-quarter-dependency) are the BETTER versions of signals that are not scored, while weaker scored proxies remain.
fix: Decide per method: promote the strong ones (revenue-quality-cov, revenue-acceleration-yoy) into HYPERGROWTH SCORE_WEIGHTS or a soft-guard, and gate the rest behind an explicit on-demand/detail-modal flag so they are not recomputed for the whole universe. Do not change FTS_CACHE_VERSION or methods/index.js wiring as part of this; adjust method-types defaultActive + aggregator weights only.

_verdict.note:
Factual claims confirmed against source in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening. All five methods are registered DIAGNOSTIC + defaultActive:true: method-types.js:70 (revenue-quality), :72 (single-quarter-dependency), :76 (revenue-acceleration-yoy), :99 (revenue-quality-cov), :45 (quarterly-revenue-acceleration). None appear in score-aggregator.js SCORE_WEIGHTS (32-73) or SOFT_GUARD_PENALTY (197-211), and none appear in strategy-modes.js MODES core/dataGuards/softGuards (verified via grep: zero matches in both files). They are typed DIAGNOSTIC so isDisqualifiedByDataGuards skips them. runner.js evaluateStock runs every defaultActive method when no filter is passed, and generate-screener.js:259 calls Runner.evaluateStock(stock) with no opts -> all five compute on every snapshot of the full universe. So the mechanism the auditor describes is accurate: computed every run, consumed only by display.

HOWEVER this is a design observation, not a defect, and the 'dead-code' category is a misnomer. The DIAGNOSTIC tier exists by explicit design for 'Kontext fuer Deep-Dive' (method-types.js:47) -- context surfaced in the detail modal/reports, i.e. the output IS consumed (display), so it is not dead code. Dozens of other defaultActive DIAGNOSTICs (operating-leverage, roic-trend, beneish-m-score, gross-profitability, etc.) are identically unscored-and-computed; singling out these five is arbitrary. revenue-quality-cov's own header (line 61) documents the unscored status as a deliberate 'fixture-hash safe by construction' property, not an oversight. low severity is appropriate (at most a per-run CPU micro-cost on ~4.7k stocks for cheap arithmetic on already-loaded fields).

fix_safe=false: the proposed fix is explicitly behavior-changing and must not be auto-applied. (a) Promoting revenue-quality-cov / revenue-acceleration-yoy into HYPERGROWTH SCORE_WEIGHTS or a soft-guard alters the weighted composite, tier classification, and fixture hashes for the whole universe -- and breaks the documented 'NOT in SCORE_WEIGHTS -> fixture-hash safe' invariant. (b) Flipping defaultActive:false + gating behind an on-demand flag changes which methods run and what the detail modal displays. Both require human design decision, anchor re-verification, and fixture-hash regeneration. Not low-risk.

title: Acceleration gate requires r1>0 and r2>0 but not r0>0; a swing from negative revenue base is mishandled and a tiny denominator inflates delta without a magnitude floor
evidence: `if (r0 == null || r1 == null || r2 == null || r1 <= 0 || r2 <= 0)` — r0 (latest) is allowed to be <=0. Then `yoyT0=(r0-r1)/r1` with no guard that r1 is materially large; a near-zero r1 (e.g. a trough year) makes yoyT0 explode (e.g. r1=1, r0=200 → 19900%). delta is then a meaningless +pp spike that PASSES the >0 gate. No materiality floor on the revenue base, unlike the shock/volatility guards.
why_it_matters: DIAGNOSTIC-only today (not scored), so bounded, but it produces nonsense reason strings ('Δ=+19900pp') for trough-recovery names and would be actively misleading if promoted. The negative-r0 case yields a negative yoyT0 that can still beat an even-more-negative yoyT1 and falsely report 're-acceleration'.
fix: Add a base-materiality floor (skip when r1 or r2 below a revenue floor) and require r0>0; cap/flag delta when any denominator is a trough. Comment: 'prevents trough-base denominators from manufacturing fake re-acceleration'.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed against source. methods/revenue-acceleration-yoy.js:58 gates `r1 <= 0 || r2 <= 0` but NOT r0, and lines 66-68 compute yoyT0=(r0-r1)/r1 with no magnitude/materiality floor on the denominators. A genuine trough year (e.g. r1 small after a COVID-style revenue collapse, then recovery) makes yoyT0 explode and produces an inflated positive delta that PASSES the >0 gate. The math example (r1=1,r0=200 -> 19900%) is correct. The inconsistency-with-siblings claim checks out: revenue-shock-guard.js:31-37 and revenue-volatility-guard.js:30,80-85 both have explicit materiality/base floors that this method lacks.

Real-world impact confirmed via caller: generate-screener.js:298-323 reads revAccel.value (the delta) and converts it to revAccelBonus = min(15, delta/50*15), which feeds the Pre-Breakout composite pbScore. So an inflated trough-driven delta directly inflates pbScore. Bonus saturates at delta=50pp, so even a modest trough maxes it.

Two caveats that temper but do not refute the finding: (1) The method is DIAGNOSTIC, not a hard gate (method-types.js:76) — it cannot admit a stock by itself, only bias the score. (2) The companion DATAGUARD revenue-volatility-guard hard-fails material stocks (TTM>$100M USD) with any >25% single-year decline, which a trough-recovery pattern implies — a partial backstop for material stocks, but immaterial stocks (<$100M) are exempt and the acceleration method runs independently. The 'negative revenue base' framing in the title is the weakest part: the YoY denominators r1/r2 ARE guarded >0; only the numerator r0 is unguarded, and genuinely negative revenue is not a realistic input. The material defect is the missing trough-denominator floor, which is real. 'low' severity is appropriate given the DIAGNOSTIC status and partial guard backstop.

title: Concentration DATAGUARD fails any stock whose single largest of the last 4 quarters exceeds 50% of the 4Q sum, with no seasonality exemption — unlike q-spike-dataguard which has Q4-seasonal and launch-inflection suppression
evidence: `var concentration = maxQ / sum; var pass = concentration <= SPIKE_THRESHOLD (0.50);` with no _isSeasonalQ4Spike / _inLaunchInflection escape hatches (compare q-spike-dataguard.js:93-116 which has both). A retailer/e-commerce name with a structurally large Q4 (>50% of trailing 4Q during the ramp) is hard-disqualified by quarter-concentration-guard even though q-spike-dataguard would suppress it as seasonal. method-types.js:135 confirms DATAGUARD type → universe-wide disqualification.
why_it_matters: Two DATAGUARDs implement the same single-Q-concentration concept with DIFFERENT exemption logic (q-spike has YoY>100% trigger + seasonal/launch suppression; quarter-concentration has none and fires unconditionally at 50%). The stricter, exemption-free one wins (any DATAGUARD fail disqualifies), so q-spike's careful seasonal suppression is defeated by its blunt sibling — culling legitimate seasonal compounders and contributing to the survivorship narrowing.
fix: Either consolidate the two concentration guards into one (single source of truth, shared seasonal/launch suppression) or apply the same _isSeasonalQ4Spike/_inLaunchInflection suppression here before failing. Do not parallel-edit methods/index.js. Comment: 'prevents blunt 50% concentration cut from overriding q-spike seasonal/launch suppression'.

_verdict.note:
Code-level claims verified, but the severity-driving impact claim is overstated. CONFIRMED: quarter-concentration-guard.js:38 uses a blunt `concentration <= 0.50` with no _isSeasonalQ4Spike/_inLaunchInflection escape hatches, whereas q-spike-dataguard.js:93-116 + 219-228 has both seasonal-Q4 and launch-inflection suppression. method-types.js:135 types it DATAGUARD and isDisqualifiedByDataGuards (method-types.js:162-168) does treat any failing DATAGUARD as a disqualification.

REFUTED on impact: it does NOT hard-disqualify seasonal retailers universe-wide in production. The production screener generate-screener.js:259 calls Runner.evaluateStock = evaluateStockLegacy (runner.js:83-86), which returns ONLY out.results and DISCARDS the `disqualified`/`disqualifiedBy` flags. Production gating is per-mode via SM.evaluateMode, and in strategy-modes.js the HYPERGROWTH mode lists quarter-concentration-guard in softGuards (line 92, score penalty only via SOFT_GUARD_PENALTY) while q-spike-dataguard is the HARD dataGuard (line 90). So a seasonal/e-commerce name only takes a soft score penalty from quarter-concentration-guard, not a reject; the hard gate (q-spike) already has the seasonal exemption. The universe-wide DATAGUARD path (runner.js:55) is only reached by evaluateStockExtended, used solely in tests/scripts (integration-anchor-test.js, regional-oos-test.js), and even those gate on modeEval.passed and ignore the `disqualified` field.

Net: a genuine design inconsistency (two concentration checks, divergent thresholds 50% vs 55%, only one with seasonal/launch suppression) that matters for the evaluateStockExtended contract and any future caller, but not the medium data-integrity disqualification bug as framed. Better characterized as low-severity consistency debt.

title: OI-Severity branch only evaluates loss-EXPANSION; the else-if chain mislabels a profitable-to-loss flip ('flip-negative') without raising severity, so a company swinging from profit to large loss escapes the OI check
evidence: `if (y0<0 && y1<0 && Math.abs(y0)>Math.abs(y1)*1.5){ ...oiSeverity... }` else branches just set oiDir labels ('flip-negative' when y0<0 && y1>0) with no fail. A name that was solidly profitable (y1>0) and just printed a large operating loss (y0<<0) is labeled 'flip-negative' and contributes nothing to `fail`, even though a profit→deep-loss flip is at least as concerning as loss-expansion for a YoY>100% hypergrowth suspect.
why_it_matters: The guard's stated purpose (line 8) is catching operating-loss deterioration alongside revenue spikes; the profit→loss flip is a blind spot. Bounded because the spike-concentration check may still fire, but a 40-55% concentration (below the 55% hard cut) combined with a fresh deep loss passes clean.
fix: Add a flip-negative severity test (e.g. fail when y0<0 and |y0| exceeds a revenue-scaled floor regardless of prior sign) so profit→large-loss is treated as an OI red flag. Comment: 'prevents profit-to-deep-loss flip from bypassing the OI-severity check'.

_verdict.note:
False positive. The code reading is accurate (the `else if (y0<0 && y1>0)` branch sets oiDir='flip-negative' without fail=true at methods/q-spike-dataguard.js:246), but the "bug" conclusion is wrong on three counts.

1) Intended, documented design. The module header (lines 5-7) explicitly scopes the OI criterion as "(b) OI-Severity > 3.0 — Operating-Loss EXPANDIERT >3x" and calls the gate "schmal & spezifisch" — a deliberate loss-EXPANSION test, not a general profitability gate. The sibling methods/hypergrowth-quality-class.js documents the same taxonomy (header lines 8-9; isOIBad/isOIGood at lines 152-153): only 'loss-expanding' is bad, 'flip-negative' is neutral by design (Council + ChatGPT-Verdict Tag 113).

2) The exact concern is independently hard-gated. methods/loss-magnitude-guard.js (Tag 199) hard-fails any company whose latest annual operating loss exceeds 50% of revenue REGARDLESS of prior-year sign (pass = annualOpInc[0]/annualRev[0] >= -0.50). That is precisely the "profit→deep-loss flip" case the auditor claims "escapes." Both guards are registered active in methods/index.js (q-spike-dataguard line 43, loss-magnitude-guard line 75). A profit→large-loss hypergrowth name does NOT escape the pipeline — it fails loss-magnitude-guard. The auditor's premise that q-spike-dataguard is the sole defense is false.

3) Fix is unsafe/forbidden. The proposed "revenue-scaled floor" loss test duplicates loss-magnitude-guard's exact role and adds a new numeric threshold. docs/threshold-discipline.md (Tag 129) forbids new numeric thresholds without 3+ ticker or 2+ period evidence, which the finding does not supply.

title: QoQ-CoV skips pairs with non-positive baseline but keeps non-consecutive deltas after a skip, mixing non-adjacent quarters into a 'sequential' dispersion measure
evidence: `for (i=0..6){ if(newer==null||older==null||older<=0) continue; ... qoqDeltas.push(d); }`. When a middle quarter is null/<=0, the loop CONTINUES rather than breaking, so a later valid pair (i+2,i+3) is included in the same qoqDeltas array as earlier pairs — but the gap means the dispersion now blends two disjoint sub-series. The method advertises 'QoQ over the last 8 quarters' as a sequential smoothness measure; a gap silently changes it to a mixed-window measure (the same filter-then-use anti-pattern other methods here were hardened against, e.g. revenue-shock-guard F-ME-005 line 61-68 which BREAKs on gaps).
why_it_matters: Inconsistent with the suite's own positional-alignment doctrine. DIAGNOSTIC-only so bounded, but the signal is subtly wrong on any snapshot with an interior null quarter (mid-quarter Yahoo gaps), exactly when smoothness matters most.
fix: Mirror revenue-shock-guard's consecutive-run approach: stop at the first interior gap (break, not continue) or explicitly require the 8 quarters to be contiguous before computing CoV. Comment: 'prevents interior null gap from blending non-adjacent quarters into the sequential CoV'.

_verdict.note:
False positive based on a misread of the statistic. CoV here is a dispersion measure over a BAG of independent adjacent-pair QoQ ratios, not over a contiguous ordered series. Each delta pushed at line 116 is (vals[i]-vals[i+1])/vals[i+1] — a genuine quarter-over-quarter rate between two TRULY consecutive quarters. When an interior quarter is null/<=0, line 113 drops BOTH straddling pairs (older<=0 catches one, newer==null catches the other), so the loop never produces a delta spanning non-adjacent quarters. A gap merely removes deltas; every surviving delta is still a valid adjacent QoQ measurement. The auditor's "blends two disjoint sub-series into a sequential measure" is incorrect — CoV does not require the surviving deltas to be contiguous with each other; no ratio borrows data across the gap.

The revenue-shock-guard analogy is false. There (lines 61-68) the statistic is median/MAD over prior[], whose elements must all be PEERS of one reference quarter (latest); filter/reindex across a gap pulls a non-peer quarter into the peer window and corrupts median/MAD, so BREAK is load-bearing. Here contiguity between deltas is NOT load-bearing, so continue is correct.

Additionally the method is DIAGNOSTIC-only (methods/index.js line 170; not in any SCORE_WEIGHTS), so even a behavior change here cannot affect screener output or the fixture hash.

title: Composite leverage sub-check uses LEVERAGE_MAX=2.0 but net-debt-ebitda's distress sentinel and its own pass threshold are 2.5 — boundary stocks (2.0–2.5 ND/EBITDA) are scored as failing leverage by the composite while passing the standalone gate
evidence: capital-allocation-quality.js:97 `const LEVERAGE_MAX = 2.0;` and :141 `debtContribution = (debtR.value <= LEVERAGE_MAX) ? 25 : 0;`. The underlying net-debt-ebitda.js:8 defines `THRESHOLD = 2.5` and passes at `value <= 2.5` (net-debt-ebitda.js:67). The composite header comment (capital-allocation-quality.js:36) even states '+25 net-debt-ebitda <= 2.0 (prudent leverage)'.
why_it_matters: A stock at ND/EBITDA = 2.3 PASSES the standalone net-debt-ebitda gate (<=2.5) but the composite assigns it 0 of 25 leverage points, dropping its composite score by 25 and likely flipping it below the 75 pass line. The two methods disagree on what 'prudent leverage' means, producing internally contradictory diagnostics for the SAME stock. The discrepancy is undocumented as intentional beyond a terse 'tighter than underlying' note for SBC — but leverage's 2.0 vs 2.5 gap is not flagged as deliberate and reads like a transcription slip from the underlying 2.5. Given net-debt-ebitda also emits a 999 sentinel for distressed names, those correctly score 0; the silent harm is the 2.0–2.5 band.
fix: Decide deliberately and document it: if the composite intends an elite 2.0 ceiling, add a comment `// failure mode prevented: composite treats 2.0–2.5 leverage as elite-fail by design, intentionally stricter than net-debt-ebitda's 2.5 standalone gate` next to LEVERAGE_MAX. If it was meant to mirror the standalone gate, set LEVERAGE_MAX = 2.5. Do not leave it ambiguous — the current state cannot be distinguished from a typo.

_verdict.note: False positive (intentional design, not a bug). Facts cited are accurate: capital-allocation-quality.js:97 LEVERAGE_MAX=2.0, :141 gates debtContribution at <=2.0, while net-debt-ebitda.js:8/67 passes standalone at <=2.5. BUT the 2.0 ceiling is deliberate, not a typo: lines 94-95 carry an explicit comment "Composite-internal sub-thresholds (tighter than the underlying methods' own pass thresholds — we want ELITE allocation, not just 'not failing')". This is corroborated by an identical sibling pattern — composite SBC_MAX_FRAC=0.05 (5%) vs standalone sbc-revenue.js THRESHOLD=0.15 (15%), a 3x tightening. The header comment the auditor quotes (line 33, "<= 2.0") AGREES with the code, which refutes the typo hypothesis rather than supporting it. No correctness impact: the composite is DIAGNOSTIC-only and NOT in SCORE_WEIGHTS (method-types.js:90, capital-allocation-quality.js:63, confirmed across tag28-tests annotations), so it never gates or alters the aggregated screener score. A 2.0-2.5 stock correctly passes the standalone leverage gate AND correctly scores as non-elite on the composite's leverage dimension — two different questions, both answered as intended. At most this is a doc-clarity nit (the auditor's own primary fix is merely "add a comment"), not a high-severity bug.

title: Composite re-evaluates four sub-methods per stock instead of consuming already-computed runner results — duplicate work across the universe
evidence: capital-allocation-quality.js:84-87 require buyback-yield, net-debt-ebitda, capex-trend, sbc-revenue and :125-128 call `_safeEvaluate(buybackYield, stock)` etc., each of which re-runs the full evaluate() (re-unwrapping arrays, recomputing ratios). The runner already evaluates all four standalone methods for every stock (they are registered separately in index.js:36,61,62,83). The header comment at :80-83 acknowledges this ('without depending on a runner-level allResults plumbing change... re-requiring is cheap') but conflates module-cache cheapness with evaluate() cheapness — the require is cached, the evaluate() recompute is not.
why_it_matters: Across a multi-thousand-name universe each stock pays for 4 redundant sub-method evaluations (array unwrap + arithmetic) every run, on top of the standalone runs. Cheap per call, but it is exactly the 'per-method re-classify / wasted recompute over the universe' pattern that structurally caps throughput; capital-allocation-quality is also one of several composites (premium-compounder-proof, etc.) doing the same, so the pattern compounds. It also creates a correctness coupling risk: if the runner ever applies effectiveThreshold overrides or wrapEvaluate flags to the standalone results, the composite silently uses the RAW evaluate() output instead, diverging from what the dashboard shows.
fix: Plumb the runner's allResults map into composite methods (an optional second arg `evaluate(stock, allResults)`), and have the composite read `allResults['buyback-yield']` etc. when present, falling back to _safeEvaluate only when a dependency result is absent. This removes the recompute and guarantees the composite sees the same values the rest of the pipeline does. Add comment: 'failure mode prevented: composite diverging from standalone results + O(n) duplicate sub-evaluations across the universe.'

_verdict.note:
CONFIRMED but over-rated. The mechanism is real: methods/capital-allocation-quality.js:84-87 require the four sub-method modules, and :125-128 call _safeEvaluate(...) which invokes method.evaluate(stock) afresh (lines 103-114). Each sub-method's evaluate() does real work (array unwrap + ratio math), not just a cached require — buyback-yield.js:82-122, net-debt-ebitda.js:11-84, capex-trend.js:11-57, sbc-revenue.js:10-46. The runner (methods/runner.js:42-53) calls H.wrapEvaluate(m, stock) per registered method with NO allResults arg, and _helpers.js:310-334 confirms evaluate is invoked single-arg — so the allResults plumbing the audit proposes genuinely does not exist.

Two corrections that lower the severity:
1) Duplication is only PARTIAL. Per method-types.js, capex-trend (line 56) and sbc-revenue (line 57) are defaultActive:false — in a default/production run the runner does NOT evaluate them standalone, so the composite is their ONLY caller (zero duplication for those two). Only buyback-yield (defaultActive:true, line 79) and net-debt-ebitda (CORE/default, line 128) are actually evaluated twice per stock in a default run. So it is 2-of-4 duplicated dims, not 4.
2) The cost is trivial in-memory arithmetic over short arrays — no I/O, no network. O(n) over the universe of a handful of redundant ratio computations is a micro-optimization, not a meaningful perf problem.

Also: the proposed-fix rationale claims it prevents "composite diverging from standalone results." That divergence risk does NOT exist in current code — evaluate() is pure given the same stock object and the runner never mutates stock between calls, so the recompute yields byte-identical values. The only true benefit of the fix is removing the redundant compute, which is negligible here.

Net: real but LOW severity (micro-optimization, no correctness impact, half the claimed duplication doesn't occur in default runs).

title: Quarterly buyback fallback assumes index [4] is exactly 1 year prior without verifying the series is quarterly or contiguous — mixed-frequency or gap-filled sharesQ produces a wrong-horizon yield
evidence: buyback-yield.js:67-71 `const qArr = stock.timeseries && stock.timeseries.sharesQ; if (Array.isArray(qArr) && qArr.length >= 5) { const now = _unwrap(qArr[0]); const prior = _unwrap(qArr[4]); ...source:'sharesQ' }`. The [0] vs [4] = '1y diff' assumption (also stated in the header :34) is never validated — there is no check that the 5 entries are consecutive quarters, no date alignment, and the partial branch (:72-76) uses `qArr[qArr.length-1]` whose horizon is entirely unknown yet is still annualized-as-is.
why_it_matters: If sharesQ ever contains a missing quarter, a TTM duplicate, or semi-annual reporters (common for non-US names — and the screener pulls a global universe with FX normalization), qArr[4] is not 1 year back. The yield is then computed over the wrong horizon and reported as an annual buyback yield with no flag, feeding capital-allocation-quality's buyback dimension (>=1% gate) and the buyback diagnostic. Off-by-period error that silently mis-rates capital return for exactly the international names most likely to have irregular share series.
fix: Carry per-point dates in sharesQ and pick the entry closest to now-365d, or at minimum record the realized horizon (months between [0] and the chosen prior) in components and refuse to annualize when it deviates from ~12m by more than a quarter (return computable:false with reason). Add comment: 'failure mode prevented: assuming index[4] is 1y prior for non-quarterly / gapped share series → wrong-horizon buyback yield.'

_verdict.note: Code observation is literally accurate (lines 67-71 assume qArr[0] vs qArr[4] = 1y with no date/contiguity check; partial branch 72-76 annualizes an unknown horizon), but the branch is DEAD CODE, so the described wrong-horizon yield cannot occur in production. Evidence: `timeseries.sharesQ` is referenced ONLY inside methods/buyback-yield.js (grep across all .js files in the worktree finds zero other references). pull-yahoo.js builds timeseries as {revenueQ, opIncQ, grossProfitQ} (line 1010) and only additionally sets netIncomeQ (line 1931); it NEVER writes sharesQ. So at runtime qArr is always undefined, both Array.isArray(qArr) guards are false, and Source 2 is unreachable. The live source is Source 1 annual.annualShares (added Tag 219, pull-yahoo.js:1925), which uses correctly year-aligned [0] vs [1] annual entries — the path the auditor did NOT flag, and it is sound. The repo's own audit history confirms this: audit-reports/2026-05-16-tag209-bug-hunt.md:66-69 notes timeseries.sharesQ is not in the snapshot shape. Tests (tag28-tests.js) only ever feed annual.annualShares, never sharesQ. At most this is a latent/low trap if someone later wires up sharesQ without dates — not a medium bug today.

title: Negative-FCF years are floored to 0.01 BEFORE the geometric mean, which structurally caps how much a single cash-destroying year can hurt the 5y score and lets chronic cash-burners clear the 0.75 pass gate
evidence: fcf-conversion-stability.js:136-139 `const clamped = r <= 0 ? NEG_RATIO_FLOOR : r > POS_RATIO_CAP ? POS_RATIO_CAP : r;` with NEG_RATIO_FLOOR=0.01 (:87). Geomean over 5 entries (:154-155). Worked example: ratios [1.2, 1.2, 1.2, 1.2, 0.01] → geomean = exp((4*ln1.2 + ln0.01)/5) = exp((0.729 - 4.605)/5) = exp(-0.775) = 0.46 (fails). But [1.5,1.5,1.5,1.5,0.01] → exp((4*0.405-4.605)/5)=exp(-0.597)=0.55. Push the four good years to the 2.0 cap: [2.0,2.0,2.0,2.0,0.01] → exp((4*0.693-4.605)/5)=exp(-0.366)=0.69 — still fails, but a company with 4 years at FCF/NI≈2.0 and one catastrophic negative-FCF year sits just under the 0.75 line, where the floor (not the real magnitude of the burn) sets the score.
why_it_matters: A negative-FCF year means the company consumed cash against positive accounting earnings — the single strongest 'earnings are not cash' signal this method exists to catch. By flooring every such year to a fixed 0.01 regardless of how negative, the method discards the magnitude and makes the penalty constant. A firm that burned -$5B and one that burned -$50M get the identical 0.01 contribution. Combined with the 2.0 upper cap on good years, the dynamic range is compressed enough that the pass/fail outcome can hinge on the arbitrary floor constant rather than on actual cash conversion. The header sells this as 'a very strong fail signal' but the math shows it is a bounded, magnitude-blind one.
fix: Keep the floor only to keep the log defined, but additionally short-circuit: if any in-window year has FCF<=0 against NI>0 (rawRatios[i] <= 0), force pass:false regardless of geomean (the persistence claim is already violated), and surface a `negativeFcfYears` count in components. Document: 'failure mode prevented: a magnitude-blind 0.01 floor letting a chronic cash-burn year be out-voted by capped good years.' This preserves the geomean for the all-positive case while restoring the hard fail the header promises.

_verdict.note:
REFUTED. The headline claim ("lets chronic cash-burners clear the 0.75 pass gate") is mathematically false, and the finding's own worked example admits it. I exhaustively checked every combination of floored negative-FCF years with all good years pinned at the POS_RATIO_CAP=2.0 (the most favorable possible inputs), for window sizes n=3,4,5: the MAXIMUM achievable geomean when even ONE window year has FCF<=0 (floored to 0.01) is 0.6931 — strictly below the 0.75 gate. n=5/1neg=0.6931, n=4/1neg=0.5318, n=3/1neg=0.3420; all multi-neg cases far lower. So it is impossible for any company with a negative-FCF year in the window to PASS. The auditor's [2.0,2.0,2.0,2.0,0.01] example yields 0.69 and they themselves write "still fails." The title contradicts its own body.

The only genuine kernel is that the 0.01 floor is magnitude-blind (FCF/NI=-0.5 and -50 both clamp to 0.01). But this only affects the precise failing *value* among companies that already fail — it never flips a fail to a pass. So it has zero effect on the pass/fail outcome the finding claims to be about.

Additionally, the method is DIAGNOSTIC, not gating: methods/method-types.js:97 marks it type:'DIAGNOSTIC', the header (line 65) and test (tag28-tests.js:1693) both state it is NOT in any SCORE_WEIGHTS and is fixture-hash safe. Its `pass` does not gate screener output; it is deep-dive/detail-modal context. So even the imagined harm could not propagate to results.

fix_safe=false: the proposed fix adds a `negativeFcfYears` field to components. evaluateStock() flows through the fixture-hash invariant in tag28-tests.js; _helpers.js documents (lines 155-175) how repeatedly hash drift has broken pre-pull guards. Adding a component field changes the serialized result and would break the fixture-hash test, requiring a coordinated hash bump. It also introduces a new short-circuit branch. Not behavior-preserving; needs human review.

Relevant files: C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/methods/fcf-conversion-stability.js (lines 83-88, 130-139, 167); C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/methods/method-types.js:97; C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/methods/_helpers.js:58-68 (buildResult), 155-175; C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/tag28-tests.js:1692-1745.

title: R&D-year skip logic can drop a hard MUST-gate stock to incomputable when R&D coverage is partial, silently removing it from QC results instead of failing or passing it
evidence: reinvestment-rate.js:151-154 `if (rnd.length > 0 && (j >= rawRnd.length || !Number.isFinite(rawRnd[j]))) { rndSkippedYears++; continue; }` removes any year with a missing R&D point once the company has R&D in ANY year. Combined with the capex skip (:143) and OCF<=0 skip (:157), the surviving ratio count can fall below 3, triggering :161 `if (ratios.length < 3) return computable:false`. reinvestment-rate is a hard `must` gate in QC mode (strategy-modes.js:109) AND carries weight 0.15 in SCORE_WEIGHTS (score-aggregator.js:45).
why_it_matters: A Yahoo schema change that nulls R&D for 2 of 5 years (the exact scenario F-ME-008 cites as why the skip exists) can push an R&D-heavy quality compounder from a clear PASS to computable:false. In QC mode an incomputable MUST gate typically drops the stock from the qualified set entirely — survivorship attrition driven by data sparsity, not by the company's economics. The fix that prevents understating reinvestment (skip-not-zero) introduces the opposite failure: silent disqualification. There is no floor on how many years the skip can erode before the method gives up, and no flag distinguishing 'genuinely low reinvestment' from 'we threw away half the data'.
fix: When rndSkippedYears reduces usable ratios below MIN, fall back to capex-only ratios for the skipped years (R&D treated as 0 only for those years) rather than dropping them, OR emit computable:false with an explicit `DATA_SPARSE` flag so the aggregator can treat it as a data-quality issue distinct from a quality fail. Surface rndSkippedYears in the incomputable reason (it currently only appears in the computable branch components). Comment: 'failure mode prevented: partial-R&D-coverage silently disqualifying a MUST-gated compounder via attrition.'

_verdict.note: REFUTED on its central mechanism. The cited code lines exist exactly as quoted (reinvestment-rate.js:143/151/157 skips, :161 `ratios.length < 3 -> computable:false`), and the gate/weight facts are correct (reinvestment-rate is core weight:'must' required in strategy-modes.js QUALITY_COMPOUNDER, and 0.15 in SCORE_WEIGHTS). BUT the finding's key claim — that an incomputable result "silently removes the stock from QC results instead of failing or passing it" — is false. In strategy-modes.js evaluateMode (lines 231-266): an incomputable MUST is recorded as status:'incomputable' and does NOT increment mustPassCount; then allMustPass = (mustPassCount === mustChecks.length) is false, so the mode returns passed:false (line 279). That is a clean QC gate FAIL, identical in outcome to a quality fail — precisely the "fail it" behavior the finding proposes as the fix. The stock is not silently dropped. In the score path, score-aggregator.js:240-245 (F-ME-023) excludes the incomputable method's 0.15 weight from computedWeight and renormalizes over the remaining computable methods; a full REJECT only occurs below the 40% coverage floor (lines 264-272), which this finding does not trigger. So the attrition scenario, if it ever materializes (it needs >=3 of 5 years with missing/non-finite R&D while rnd.length>0 plus capex/OCF gaps — a narrow data edge case), produces a deterministic gate fail, not silent data corruption. Residual valid-but-minor points: (1) rndSkippedYears is indeed absent from the incomputable-branch reason at :161-167 (only present in the computable components at :212) — an observability nit, not a data-integrity bug; (2) a capex-only fallback is a methodology choice, not a defect.

title: components.latestRatio / reason 'latest=' report ratios[0] which is the first VALID year, not fiscal year 0 — mislabels the latest ratio whenever the most recent year was skipped
evidence: capex-vs-sbc-quality.js:89-97 builds `ratios` by pushing only years where both capex and SBC are non-zero (`if (acx === 0 || asbc === 0) continue;`). Then :115 reason `', latest=' + ratios[0].toFixed(2)` and :127 `latestRatio: ratios[0]`. If fiscal year 0 had SBC=0 (a firm that just stopped issuing stock) or capex=0, ratios[0] is actually year 1 or 2, but it is labeled 'latest'.
why_it_matters: The diagnostic claims to show the most-recent-year capex/SBC ratio but can silently show a 1–2 year stale value, misleading anyone drilling into the dashboard component. Low severity (display/diagnostic only, not in SCORE_WEIGHTS) but it is a correctness-of-evidence bug: the number a reviewer trusts as 'this year' may be two years old, and there is no indication the latest year was dropped.
fix: Track the source year index alongside each ratio (push {ratio, yearIndex}) and report latestRatio with its true yearIndex, or rename the field to firstValidRatio. Comment: 'failure mode prevented: labeling a skipped-year-adjusted ratio as latest-year.'

_verdict.note: Confirmed real but cosmetic. capex-vs-sbc-quality.js:89-97 builds `ratios` with `continue` on any year where capex or SBC is null/zero (acx===0 || asbc===0), so ratios[0] is the FIRST VALID year, not necessarily fiscal-year 0. The skip-at-index-0 case is achievable: pull-yahoo.js _ftsExtractByYear (1072-1081) and mapFTSToAnnual (1084-1093) deliberately preserve null placeholders for absent years INCLUDING the most recent one (latest-first arrays), and a firm that stopped issuing stock yields SBC=0 at index 0. In that case reason ', latest=' (line 115) and components.latestRatio (line 127) mislabel ratios[0] as the latest fiscal year when it is actually year 1 or 2. BUT the impact is confined to a human-readable reason string and a diagnostic component field. The numeric score/value/pass (line 111-112) are unaffected, and the method is DIAGNOSTIC + NOT in SCORE_WEIGHTS (header lines 43-44), so no screener result or scoring outcome changes. The live incidence is also low — pull-yahoo comment (line 1120) notes Yahoo's missing year is almost always the oldest. Severity 'low' is correct (arguably cosmetic). NOTE on fix_safe: both proposed variants mutate the public `components` contract — renaming latestRatio->firstValidRatio breaks any reader of components.latestRatio (e.g. tests/consumers), and pushing {ratio,yearIndex} changes the components.ratios shape from number[] to objects, which would break iterators like sector-medians-compute.js. Needs human review, not auto-apply. Safe minimal fix would be to relabel only the reason string text to 'firstValid=' while leaving component keys intact.

title: Coefficient-of-variation uses population stdev (divide by n) over only 3-4 samples, biasing dispersion downward and letting genuinely lumpy FCF margins pass the 0.40 CoV gate
evidence: fcf-stability.js:113 `const variance = margins.reduce((s, x) => s + (x - mean) * (x - mean), 0) / n;` divides by n (population), with n as small as MIN_PAIRS=3 (:62). Sample stdev would divide by (n-1). For n=3 the population stdev is sqrt(2/3)=0.816x the sample stdev — a ~18% downward bias in CoV.
why_it_matters: The method's entire purpose (header :31-37) is to flag lumpy/non-recurring FCF that fools quality screens. Using the population estimator over a 3-4 point sample systematically understates dispersion, so borderline-lumpy names (CoV ~0.45-0.49 on a sample basis) report ~0.37-0.40 and PASS. For a volatility-detection method the conservative (sample) estimator is the correct choice; the current bias works directly against the method's stated goal. Low severity because it is a calibration bias on a DIAGNOSTIC, but it is a real statistical defect.
fix: Use the sample estimator `/ (n - 1)` (Bessel's correction) since n>=3 is guaranteed, OR recalibrate the 0.40 threshold with documentation that it assumes the population estimator. Prefer the former — it matches how QMJ-style safety metrics are normally computed. Comment: 'failure mode prevented: population stdev over a 3-4y sample under-reporting CoV and passing lumpy FCF.'

_verdict.note: Arithmetic is correct but the "bug" framing is a false positive. Confirmed at C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/methods/fcf-stability.js:113 that variance divides by n (population stdev), with n in {3,4} (MIN_PAIRS=3 line 62, WINDOW=4 line 63); for n=3 population stdev is sqrt(2/3)=0.816x the sample stdev, so CoV runs ~18% lower than the Bessel-corrected value. That math checks out. But this is not a defect: (1) Population stdev is the standard textbook definition of CoV and is a deliberate codebase-wide convention — the two sibling CoV stability methods use the identical estimator (earnings-power-stability.js:127 and revenue-quality-cov.js:144 both `/ n`). (2) The 0.40 gate is explicitly described as empirically "calibrated" against anchor stocks (header lines 28-29, 50-52), i.e. calibrated to the population estimator that is actually computed — so there is no mismatch between estimator and threshold; the auditor's "letting lumpy FCF pass" claim assumes a sample-stdev calibration that was never used. (3) The method is DIAGNOSTIC-only, confirmed in method-types.js:86, NOT in SCORE_WEIGHTS, and the header marks it "fixture-hash safe" — it annotates a pass/fail flag in the detail view and does not affect the composite score or screener ranking. So real-world impact is negligible.

title: Inline envelope unwrap treats any truthy object as an envelope; an array or unexpected object at sbcArr[0]/revArr[0] yields undefined .value and is then mishandled vs the shared _unwrap pattern
evidence: sbc-revenue.js:25 `const sbcRaw = sbcArr[0] && typeof sbcArr[0] === 'object' ? sbcArr[0].value : sbcArr[0];` and :28 likewise for rev. This differs from the canonical `_unwrap` used in the sibling files (sbc-trend.js:48-53, sbc-growth-ratio.js:38-43) which guards `Number.isFinite(v.value)`. Here if sbcArr[0] is e.g. a nested array or an object without a numeric `.value`, sbcRaw becomes undefined; the subsequent `Number.isFinite(sbcRaw)` (:26) catches it for SBC, so it degrades to incomputable — but the divergence from the shared helper is the smell, and rev at :29 has the same shape.
why_it_matters: Functionally this one currently lands on incomputable (safe) because of the isFinite guards at :26 and :29, so the live blast radius is small. The risk is maintenance drift: five sibling methods unwrap the SAME annual.* fields, four use the shared `_unwrap` and this one hand-rolls a subtly different version. Any future contributor copying sbc-revenue's pattern (it is the one cited in F-ME-002 as the reference fix) inherits the weaker check. Consistency matters because these envelopes come from one source and should be unwrapped one way.
fix: Replace the two inline ternaries with the shared `_unwrap` helper already used by sbc-trend.js / sbc-growth-ratio.js (add it to this file or import a common one). Keep Math.abs on the SBC result. Comment: 'failure mode prevented: divergent envelope-unwrap implementations across the SBC method family.'

_verdict.note: Refuted as a behavioral bug; it is a style/consistency observation only. File: C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/methods/sbc-revenue.js lines 25-29. I exhaustively compared the inline ternary's RESULT against the canonical _unwrap (sbc-trend.js:48-53, sbc-growth-ratio.js:38-43) for every input the pipeline can produce. pull-yahoo.js (lines 1105, 1900-1902, mapFTSToAnnual) shows annual array elements are only ever {value:n} envelopes, bare numbers, or null placeholders. Case-by-case: (1) bare number -> both yield the number; (2) {value:n} -> both yield n; (3) null placeholder -> inline `null && ...` short-circuits to null, then line-26/29 `!= null` guard yields null == _unwrap returning null; (4) the finding's hypothetical object-without-numeric-.value (e.g. {value:undefined} or a nested array) -> inline sets sbcRaw=undefined, then the `Number.isFinite(sbcRaw)` guard at :26 (and the identical guard at :29 for rev) yields null -> line 30 returns computable:false. _unwrap returns null for the same input -> also computable:false. RESULT IS IDENTICAL in every case. The finding itself concedes the :26 guard 'catches it for SBC, so it degrades to incomputable', and admits 'the divergence from the shared helper is the smell' -- i.e. it is explicitly a smell, not a defect. The claim that the value 'is then mishandled' is unsupported: the value never reaches the division; it is short-circuited to computable:false exactly as _unwrap's null would be. No wrong numeric output, no silent pass/fail flip, no crash. fix_safe=false: the proposed consolidation is behavior-preserving ONLY if Math.abs is retained on the SBC path (a deliberate F-ME-002 fix that _unwrap does NOT replicate), so a naive swap to the shared helper would silently drop the sign-normalization and re-introduce the F-ME-002 dilution-hiding bug. That makes it a refactor needing human review, not an auto-applicable patch -- and it fixes nothing functional regardless. Severity low stands (cosmetic/maintainability).

title: Math.abs on SBC defeats the very sign-sanity check it was added for: a Yahoo payload that flips SBC sign for an off-setting reason (e.g. forfeiture reversal) is silently treated as positive expense, and capital-allocation-quality inherits this
evidence: sbc-revenue.js:26 `const sbc = sbcRaw != null && Number.isFinite(sbcRaw) ? Math.abs(sbcRaw) : null;` (F-ME-002, Tag 179). The same Math.abs pattern is repeated in sbc-trend.js:89-90, capex-vs-sbc-quality.js:93-94, and fcf-yield.js:48. capital-allocation-quality.js:128,149-150 then consumes sbc-revenue's value directly for its dilution dimension.
why_it_matters: Math.abs was introduced to handle Yahoo storing SBC as a negative number (expense-convention quirk), and for the dominant case it is correct. But it is applied unconditionally, so it ALSO masks the legitimate case where a negative SBC line genuinely means a net reversal/credit (large forfeitures, clawbacks) — that company gets charged a positive dilution expense it did not incur, failing the <=15% gate and the composite's <=5% sub-gate spuriously. More importantly, the abs is now copy-pasted across four methods with no single source of truth for SBC sign normalization; if Yahoo's convention shifts, four files must change in lockstep. The screener has no guard distinguishing 'negative because Yahoo flips sign' from 'negative because it was actually a credit'.
fix: Centralize SBC normalization in one helper (e.g. H.normalizedSBC(stock)) that documents the sign assumption and is the single place to change if Yahoo's convention changes, and have all four methods call it. If feasible, cross-check the sign against another always-positive field (e.g. SBC magnitude vs revenue plausibility) before abs-ing, so a genuine credit is not silently converted to an expense. Comment in the helper: 'failure mode prevented: four divergent SBC sign-normalizations + abs masking genuine SBC credits.'

_verdict.note:
Structural claims verified but the data-integrity thesis is a false positive. Confirmed: Math.abs is applied at sbc-revenue.js:26, sbc-trend.js:89-90, capex-vs-sbc-quality.js:93-94, fcf-yield.js:48 (and also rule-of-40-sbc-adjusted.js:68, which the auditor missed); no centralized helper exists in methods/_helpers.js (grep negative); capital-allocation-quality.js:128 calls sbcRevenue and consumes its .value at 149-150. So the duplication and consumer topology are accurate.

But the "silent corruption" mechanism is speculative and unsupported. The Math.abs was added deliberately (F-ME-002 / Tag 179, fcf-yield Bug #16 / Tag 174) to normalize a KNOWN Yahoo inconsistency: annualSBC for the SAME gross-expense quantity is sometimes stored negative, sometimes positive. SBC in cash-flow statements is a gross add-back — a near-universally one-signed magnitude. The auditor's failure scenario ("forfeiture reversal flips the sign to a genuine net credit") is invented with an unqualified "e.g." and no evidence it ever occurs in Yahoo's annualSBC field; an aggregate annual net-negative SBC is economically implausible for the growth/SaaS names this screener targets. So abs() normalizes vendor noise rather than masking a real signal — the documented lesser-evil, not a bug.

The only concrete, defensible point is DRY: four-to-five divergent copies of the sign-normalization. That is a maintainability smell, not a data-integrity defect, hence is_real=false for the finding as framed (category=data-integrity, severity=medium).

title: Upside ratio can mix currencies for ADR-class tickers: target is FX-converted to USD, current price is left in trading currency
evidence: `upside = (tgt / cur) - 1` where `tgt = H.metricValue(stock,'targetMedianPrice')` and `cur = stock.meta.regularMarketPrice || stock.price.regularMarketPrice`. In pull-yahoo.js:441-444 `targetMedianPrice` IS routed through `scaleTrading()` (trading-ccy → USD). But _convertSnapshotToUSD explicitly does NOT scale `snap.price` (pull-yahoo.js:411-413: 'We intentionally do NOT scale snap.price here ... price stays in trading currency by design'). So when a ticker's trading currency != USD and tradingFactor != 1, `tgt` is in USD while `cur` is in the raw trading currency.
why_it_matters: For any ADR-class / non-USD-quoted name where tradingFactor != 1, the numerator and denominator of the upside ratio are in different currencies, producing a wildly wrong upside (off by the FX factor) — either fabricating a huge pass or a huge fail and tripping the [-1,+5] sanity reject. For the common US-listed USD-quoted case tradingFactor==1 so it is a no-op, which is why it has gone unnoticed. The comment at pull-yahoo.js:439-440 even asserts 'the analyst-upside ratio vs currentPrice stays correct' — true only when tradingFactor==1.
fix: Compute the ratio in a single currency: either read the current price through the same trading-scaled path as the target, or divide target by an equivalently-scaled price. Guard explicitly when meta.tradingFxRateApplied != 1 and the price was not scaled. Add comment: '// prevents currency-mismatch upside (USD target vs trading-ccy price) on ADR-class tickers.'

_verdict.note:
Refuted — based on misread code. The finding assumes the current price stays in raw trading currency while targetMedianPrice is scaled to USD. Tracing the actual data flow shows the two price fields the method reads are never left half-converted relative to the target:

1) meta.regularMarketPrice (the method's PRIMARY source, _currentPrice line 58): never written anywhere in the repo. The full-pull mapper (pull-yahoo.js:820-887) builds meta with NO regularMarketPrice key, and grep over the whole worktree finds zero assignments to meta.regularMarketPrice (only reads in analyst-upside.js + prune-watchlist.js and doc comments). So this branch is effectively dead for puller-produced snapshots.

2) price.regularMarketPrice (the FALLBACK, line 61): written ONLY in the price-only fast path at pull-yahoo.js:1584 — `existing.price.regularMarketPrice = q.regularMarketPrice * tradingFactor`, where tradingFactor is derived from q.currency (the TRADING currency, lines 1565-1574). That is the exact same trading-ccy→USD conversion (tradingFactor, incl. GBp /100) that scaleTrading applies to targetMeanPrice/targetMedianPrice at lines 441-444. So whenever both fields coexist (only on price-only snapshots), they share the same trading-currency basis and the ratio is currency-consistent.

The evidence's cited comment 'We intentionally do NOT scale snap.price' (pull-yahoo.js:411-413) is about snap.price during the full-pull _convertSnapshotToUSD pass — but the full-pull mapper never builds snap.price at all (explicitly stated at lines 348-350: 'snap.price is ONLY present on the price-only fast-path'). On a full-pull snapshot there is neither meta.regularMarketPrice nor price.regularMarketPrice, so _currentPrice returns null and evaluate() returns computable:false at line 79 — no mismatched ratio is ever produced.

Net: there is no code path where tgt is USD-scaled while cur is left in raw trading currency. The ADR currency-mismatch the F-DQ-001 fix at lines 435-444 was designed to prevent is actually handled (target and the only-extant price both routed through tradingFactor).

title: Documented formula (percent) disagrees with emitted value (ratio); reason string and value use different units
evidence: Header L19 states the formula `composite = institutionsPercentHeld * 100 (just rescaled to %)`, but the code emits `value: Math.round(pct * 10000) / 10000` — i.e. the raw RATIO (0.50..1.0), not the percent. The reason string then re-multiplies for display: `(pct * 100).toFixed(1) + '% of float'`. So value is a ratio while the spec and human-readable text are in percent.
why_it_matters: Any downstream consumer that trusts the header / treats this method's `value` as the documented percent composite will be off by 100x. Even if no current consumer does, the in-file contradiction is a latent trap and makes the diagnostic table inconsistent with the method's own description (the same divergence that historically caused field-name/scaling regressions elsewhere in this codebase). Self-documenting code is load-bearing here because Karl reads results, not implementation.
fix: Make value and the docstring agree — either emit the percent (`pct*100`) to match the documented composite, or correct the header to say value is the ratio. Pick one and add a comment naming the unit explicitly to prevent the 100x consumer bug.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed as a real but purely DOCUMENTATION inconsistency, not a behavioral bug. The factual claim is accurate: header L19 states `composite = institutionsPercentHeld * 100 (rescaled to %)`, but code L86 emits `value: Math.round(pct*10000)/10000` = the raw RATIO (0.50..1.0), and the reason L94 re-multiplies `(pct*100).toFixed(1)+'% of float'` for display only. The word "composite" appears ONLY in the docstring — there is no `composite` variable; the L19 formula describes code that does not exist.

However the code is internally CONSISTENT and the warned "100x consumer bug" cannot occur: value (ratio) is paired with threshold=0.50 (ratio, L57), thresholdOp 'gte', and the module explicitly declares `unit: 'ratio'` (L105). `pass = pct >= 0.50` compares ratio-to-ratio correctly. I traced every consumer (scripts/_tag225d_effectiveness_probe.js, methods/method-types.js, methods/index.js, methods/_helpers.js): the probe quintiles each method's value within its own id and reports that method's own threshold alongside — there is NO cross-method numeric comparison that mixes percent vs ratio. _helpers _inferConfidence/_autoFlags use value/threshold in matching ratio units. So no runtime/scoring impact; the defect is a stale/incorrect header comment only.

Severity downgraded medium -> low: zero behavioral effect, cosmetic doc drift.

fix_safe=false: the proposed_fix offers two options and says "pick one." Only ONE is safe — correcting the header to say the value is the ratio (the established contract: unit:'ratio', threshold 0.50). The other listed option, emitting `pct*100`, would BREAK the contract (value 50..100 vs 0.50 threshold => every stock passes) — actively harmful. An auto-applier could pick the wrong branch, so this needs human review to scope it to a comment-only edit.

title: Filing-lag gate (gate4) has no lower bound — a filingDate before the transactionDate passes via negative lag
evidence: `const lagDays = (filingMs - mostRecentBuy.tMs) / DAY_MS; gate4 = lagDays <= MAX_FILING_LAG_DAYS;` There is an upper bound (<=90d) but no `lagDays >= 0` check. A corrupt or mis-parsed filingDate earlier than transactionDate yields a negative lagDays, which satisfies `<= 90` and passes the gate.
why_it_matters: SEC Form 4 must be filed AFTER the transaction (2-business-day rule); a filing-before-transaction is a data error, yet it silently satisfies the timeliness gate, letting a malformed record contribute to a pass on the load-bearing INSIDER_BUYING hard gate. Low severity because it requires bad cache data, but the gate exists precisely to validate data sanity.
fix: Require `lagDays >= 0 && lagDays <= MAX_FILING_LAG_DAYS`. Add comment: '// prevents filing-before-transaction (negative lag) data errors from clearing the timeliness gate.'

_verdict.note: Confirmed against source at methods/insider-conviction-score.js:285-291. The gate is exactly `gate4 = lagDays <= MAX_FILING_LAG_DAYS` (90) with no lower bound, where `lagDays = (filingMs - mostRecentBuy.tMs) / DAY_MS`. A filingDate earlier than the transactionDate yields negative lagDays, which satisfies `<= 90` and passes the timeliness gate. `_parseDate` (lines 111-115) does no ordering validation, and the txn partitioning (lines 237-246) filters only on transactionDate within the 90d window — nothing upstream enforces filingDate >= transactionDate, so the negative-lag path is reachable and not handled elsewhere. The bug is genuine but only triggers on corrupt/mis-parsed data: a real SEC Form 4 cannot be filed before the transaction occurs, so under valid data the gate behaves correctly. Failure mode is permissive (a garbage record clears the gate) rather than a crash, and the other three gates (buys exist, min buy value, net positive) still apply, so blast radius is small. Low severity is appropriate.

title: Duplicated institutional-ownership logic: 13f Yahoo-fallback and institutional-density both read the same meta.institutions* fields with divergent thresholds
evidence: Both methods now consume Yahoo majorHoldersBreakdown: institutional-density reads `meta.institutionsPercentHeld` (>=0.50) and `meta.institutionsCount`; institutional-ownership-13f's `_yahooFallback` reads `meta.institutionsCount` (>=3) and surfaces `institutionsPercentHeld` in components. The two compute overlapping verdicts from the same raw fields with two different, independently-maintained thresholds and unit conventions (count vs ratio).
why_it_matters: When the SEC 13F cache is sparse (the prevailing state per audit-reports/2026-05-17-tag225d), institutional-ownership-13f effectively becomes a second institutional-density driven off the same data but with a near-trivial >=3 bar — two methods voting on the same underlying signal, inflating its weight and confusing the dashboard about what is being measured. This is a structural cap on signal independence in the institutional dimension.
fix: Establish a single source of truth for broad institutional ownership (institutional-density) and have institutional-ownership-13f fall back to incomputable (not to the broad count) when the curated 13F cache lacks the ticker, OR clearly re-scope its fallback to a distinct, higher bar. Keep the curated-13F path as the only thing institutional-ownership-13f asserts a pass on. Do not parallel-edit methods/index.js.

_verdict.note: Refuted as a defect. The two methods read overlapping Yahoo fields but compute genuinely different signals, by deliberate, documented design — not accidental duplication with "divergent thresholds for the same verdict." institutional-density.js:84 thresholds institutionsPercentHeld >= 0.50 (a RATIO of float = "broad-density"); institutional-ownership-13f.js:_yahooFallback (lines 109-128) thresholds institutionsCount >= 3 (a COUNT of filers). Those are two different quantities (percent-of-float vs filer-count), so the auditor's "divergent thresholds and unit conventions (count vs ratio)" is intrinsic to measuring different things, not a conflict. The split is explicitly cross-referenced in both file headers and in methods/method-types.js:100/107 (Tag 213a concentrated ~40-CIK smart-money count vs Tag 223a broad ~7k-filer density). The 13F Yahoo fallback (Tag 220c, added per prior audit F-219c-F6 MEDIUM) intentionally uses the broad count when the curated SEC cache lacks the ticker, and flags it via components.source='yahoo.majorHoldersBreakdown'. Crucially there is NO correctness consequence: both methods are DIAGNOSTIC and NOT in SCORE_WEIGHTS (verified methods/score-aggregator.js:32-73 contains only HYPERGROWTH/QUALITY_COMPOUNDER/TURNAROUND/BUFFETT, neither id present), so no tier/score can be corrupted by the threshold difference — worst case is a cosmetic display where two distinct diagnostics disagree, which is expected. At most a minor clarity nit, not a medium architecture defect.

title: Period selection returns the FIRST period with present 4w fields and never aggregates or prefers larger coverage
evidence: `const periodKeys = ['0y', '+1y', '0q', '+1q']; for (const pk of periodKeys) { ... if (u4 != null && d4 != null) { return {...} } }` — the loop short-circuits on the first period whose upLast30Days/downLast30Days are both non-null, regardless of how thin that period's analyst cohort is, and ignores all later periods even if they carry far more revisions.
why_it_matters: If '0y' happens to carry a sparse up=0/down=0 (a real but uninformative reading), the method locks onto net4w=0 and never consults '+1y' which might hold the broad consensus the docstring (L104-109) explicitly says it wants ('Annual is the more durable / larger-N signal'). The selection heuristic can therefore pick the weakest available cohort, undercutting the very breadth-quality argument used to justify the period ordering.
fix: Either sum across the annual periods, or pick the period with the largest (up+down) sample rather than the first non-null one. Add comment naming the failure mode: '// prefer the largest-N cohort; first-non-null could lock onto a sparse 0/0 period.'

_verdict.note: False positive — the auditor misread a deliberate, documented design choice as an oversight. methods/analyst-revision-breadth.js:110-129 iterates periodKeys ['0y','+1y','0q','+1q'] and returns the first with both 4w fields non-null, but the Tag 215a comment directly above (lines 102-109) explains this ordering IS the larger-coverage preference: "favor annual ('0y','+1y') over quarterly ('0q','+1q'). Yahoo's quarterly estimate-revision counts include only the smaller subset of analysts who explicitly publish per-quarter; the annual numbers reflect the broader consensus... Annual is the more durable / larger-N signal so we prefer it." So the method already prefers the larger-N cohort, just via domain-informed period order rather than a runtime up+down max. The proposed fix would REGRESS this: picking max (up+down) could lock onto a transient quarterly spike the Tag 215a fix specifically moved away from; summing across 0y+1y would double-count analysts revising both fiscal years (a methodology error, not an improvement). The "add a comment naming the failure mode" suggestion is moot — that rationale comment already exists. Additional context: this is a DIAGNOSTIC method (line 35), not in SCORE_WEIGHTS, fixture-hash-safe, and per audit-reports/2026-05-17-tag225d-method-effectiveness.md it has ~0-1.5% live coverage, so zero blast radius on screener verdicts even if the heuristic were debatable. The premise "first-non-null could lock onto a sparse 0/0 period" is also weak: a 0/0 annual row yields net4w=0 which cleanly fails the >=3 gate — a legitimate no-net-revision signal, not corruption.

title: Conviction sub-score compares SEC Form-4 transaction price against (potentially) non-FX-normalized 52-week range
evidence: `const low52 = H.metricValue(stock,'fiftyTwoWeekLow'); const high52 = H.metricValue(stock,'fiftyTwoWeekHigh'); conviction = _convictionScore(_num(topBuy.t.transactionPricePerShare) ?? price, low52, high52)`. fiftyTwoWeekLow/High are not in the CCY_DENOMINATED_METRICS allow-list (pull-yahoo.js:423-444), so they are not FX-scaled, whereas SEC Form-4 transactionPricePerShare is a US-filing price in USD.
why_it_matters: For any non-US/ADR name (if ever present in the Form-4 cache) the price-location sub-score would compare a USD transaction price against a 52w range left in trading currency, mislocating the buy within the range and skewing the 0..20 conviction points. Currently low-risk because SEC Form 4 covers US issuers (USD), but the cross-source unit assumption is undocumented and brittle if coverage widens.
fix: Document the USD-only assumption explicitly, and/or guard that price and 52w-range share a currency basis before computing position. Add comment: '// assumes SEC Form-4 USD price and 52w range share currency basis (US issuers only).'

_verdict.note:
Refuted as a practical issue; at most a latent/theoretical concern. The cross-currency comparison the auditor flags never executes with live data. In pull-yahoo.js the metrics block (lines 891-928) populates NONE of the three keys the conviction sub-score reads: currentPrice, fiftyTwoWeekLow, fiftyTwoWeekHigh are absent. The repo's own schema audit (2026-05-17-tag219c, lines 338/345) lists fiftyTwoWeekHigh/Low explicitly under "Useful fields NOT extracted". A repo-wide grep confirms fiftyTwoWeekLow/High appear ONLY in this method, the test file (synthetic injection via icsStock), and audit-report markdown — never in the extraction pipeline. Therefore in production H.metricValue(stock,'fiftyTwoWeekLow'/'High') always returns null, and _convictionScore (insider-conviction-score.js:144-148) short-circuits on the `low52 == null || high52 == null` guard to {points:10, basis:'unavailable'} BEFORE ever comparing the USD Form-4 price against any 52w range. No FX mismatch can occur because the range operands do not exist.

Secondary points: (1) The auditor's evidence string misquotes the code — actual line 310-312 uses a ternary `_num(topBuy.t.transactionPricePerShare) != null ? topBuy.t.transactionPricePerShare : price`, not `?? price`, and the `price` fallback is itself currentPrice which is also never populated. (2) Even if the 52w fields were extracted later WITHOUT FX scaling, the issue is bounded: snap.price and summaryDetail-sourced 52w values are both in TRADING currency (pull-yahoo.js:409-414 intentionally leaves price unscaled), so price-vs-52w would actually be self-consistent in trading currency; the only genuine mismatch is the USD Form-4 transactionPricePerShare vs a trading-currency 52w range, which matters solely for non-US issuers. SEC Form 4 §16(a) applies to US-listed issuers, so the USD-only assumption largely holds. (3) The method is DIAGNOSTIC-only (method-types.js:44; header line 50 "NOT in any SCORE_WEIGHTS → fixture-hash safe"), and the conviction sub-score feeds only the displayed `value`, never the `pass` hard gate — so even a wrong conviction value cannot corrupt screener gating or fixture hashes. Real-world impact today: zero. Severity overstated even as a latent note.

title: WC-anomaly reads balance fields without unwrapping the {value} envelope (unlike its own revenue path), so any envelope-wrapped balance row yields NaN and silently drops to computable:false
evidence: Lines 30-35 define a correct `_unwrap` and apply it ONLY to revenues (lines 38-39). wcProxy (lines 23-27) reads `b.totalAssets, b.totalDebt, b.totalCash` raw, and `a == null` is the only guard. If a balance entry is ever shaped `{value:...}` (the shape used by every other annual.* array in the snapshot, confirmed in engine-fixtures: annualRev/annualNetIncome are `{value,currency,...}`), `a` is a truthy object, `a == null` is false, and `a - d - c` = NaN -> line 40 `wcT == null` is false (NaN != null) so it proceeds; ratio becomes NaN.
why_it_matters: Balance rows are currently raw numbers (pull-yahoo.js:691,1183), so this is latent today — but the codebase has an explicit, repeatedly-burned history of balance/annual shape drift (the F-ME-005 comment on line 28 documents the exact prior incident for revenues). The method already imports the fix for one array and forgot the other. A future mapper change that wraps balance rows would silently zero out this guard universe-wide with no warning.
fix: Route totalAssets/totalDebt/totalCash through the same `_unwrap` helper (or use the finite-guarded `_balField` pattern from beneish), and treat NaN as missing. Comment: 'prevents failure mode: envelope-wrapped balance row -> NaN -> guard silently disabled'. Quality-of-earnings guard must fail closed, not open.

_verdict.note: FALSE POSITIVE — premise misreads the data contract. The auditor conflates two distinct shapes: annualRev/annualNetIncome ARE {value,currency,...} envelopes, but annualBalance entries are plain objects whose FIELDS (totalAssets/totalDebt/totalCash) are RAW NUMBERS, never {value}-wrapped. Concrete evidence: (1) pull-yahoo.js QS builder line 691 returns `{ totalCash: cash, totalDebt, totalAssets }` where cash/totalAssets come from _y() which returns a raw Number (line 484: unwraps {raw,fmt}→Number, never produces {value}); totalDebt is `(std||0)+(ltd||0)`, a raw number. (2) FTS builder mapFTSToBalance lines 1183-1194 likewise pushes `{ totalCash: cash, totalDebt, totalAssets, ... }` with raw _ftsValue numbers. (3) The canonical reader beneish-m-score.js _balField (lines 91-98) does `row[field]` + `Number.isFinite(v)` with NO .value unwrap — proving the established contract is raw numbers; every other balance consumer (sloan-ratio, ohlson, altman) follows the same raw pattern. (4) engine-fixtures.js annualBalance rows are `{ totalEquity:100e9, longTermDebt:30e9, ... }` — raw numbers, while annualRev uses the annual() envelope helper. (5) tag28-tests.js:2356 explicitly reads `annualNetIncome[0].value` (envelope) yet assigns to `annualBalance[0].totalDebt` as a raw number — the two shapes side by side. Therefore inside wcProxy, b.totalAssets is a raw number or null; `a == null` is the correct guard for this shape and `a-d-c` is a finite number, never NaN-from-truthy-object. The proposed failure mode (envelope balance row → truthy object → NaN → guard silently disabled) cannot occur. Applying _unwrap only to revs (which IS envelope-shaped) is exactly consistent with the rest of the codebase, not an inconsistency bug. The auditor's claim 'every other annual.* array is {value}-shaped, confirmed in fixtures' is the misread: annualBalance is NOT shaped like annualRev.

title: Penman-Nissim treats missing totalDebt as 0 only for the D/E leg but the same 0 enters NOA/NFO, so a debt-data-absent firm gets the most favorable leverage classification by default
evidence: Lines 157-159: `const tdRaw = _balField(stock,0,'totalDebt'); const td = Number.isFinite(tdRaw) ? tdRaw : 0;`. The header (lines 63-64) justifies td=0 only for 'genuine net-debt-free firms (PLTR/CRDO)'. But `_balField` returns null for BOTH 'genuinely zero/absent' and 'field missing from this snapshot row' — they are indistinguishable. td=0 then flows into `de = td/cse` (line 202, always passes D/E<1.5), `noa = (ta-tc)-(tl-td)` (line 191), and `nfo = td-tc` (line 210).
why_it_matters: A firm whose balance row simply lacks the totalDebt field is scored as fully debt-free — it passes the D/E<1.5 leg unconditionally and gets an understated NOA (higher RNOA). This is DIAGNOSTIC (not in SCORE_WEIGHTS) so blast radius is the dashboard/quality view rather than tier scoring, but it produces a confidently-wrong 'durable, debt-free' label for data-incomplete names. The pattern is the same missing-vs-zero conflation as findings 02/03.
fix: Distinguish present-zero from absent: only coalesce td to 0 when the balance row is otherwise populated (totalAssets present) AND debt is genuinely null (the beneish.js:153-156 debt-free heuristic). If the row is sparse, return computable:false('totalDebt absent — cannot confirm debt-free'). Comment: 'prevents failure mode: missing debt field mislabeled as debt-free, free D/E pass + understated NOA'.

_verdict.note:
FALSE POSITIVE — misreads both the pipeline and the guard ordering.

(1) The claim "null totalDebt is indistinguishable between genuinely-zero and field-missing" is wrong. In pull-yahoo.js (line 687 and the FTS twin at 1167): `totalDebt = (std == null && ltd == null) ? null : (std||0)+(ltd||0)`. totalDebt is null ONLY when BOTH short- and long-term debt line items are absent. On a balance row that still carries totalAssets/totalLiabilities/totalCash, a null totalDebt IS the debt-free signature, not an ambiguous gap. (A partial-debt row — one component present, the other absent — yields a real number, not null, and is tracked separately as F-NY-002/F-DQ-001 with `_debtPartial`, explicitly decided as KEPT; that is out of scope here.)

(2) The td=0 default (line 159) is never USED until after three guards pass: line 161 requires ta finite and >0, line 167 requires tl finite, line 174 requires tc finite. So by lines 191/202/210 the row is fully populated except debt — i.e. the exact debt-free case. The "sparse row mislabeled as debt-free" scenario the finding describes returns computable:false at line 162 (no positive totalAssets) before td is ever consumed.

(3) The existing code therefore ALREADY implements the proposed fix in substance: coalesce debt to 0 only when the row is populated (totalAssets present). That is identical to the beneish-m-score.js:156 heuristic the auditor cites as the correct template (`if (ltd_t == null && _balField(stock,0,'totalAssets') != null) { ltd_t = 0; }`). The penman method achieves the same gating via its earlier ta/tl/tc guards.

fix_safe=false: applying the proposed change would add a redundant computable:false branch that risks regressing legitimate debt-free passers (PLTR/CRDO are in the validated anchor set, header lines 79-81) and would alter the documented anchor pass-rate — needs human review, not auto-apply. Severity revised medium→low (correctness is already sound; at most a doc/comment clarification that null⟺both-components-absent could be added).
