title: Sloan validity check is decoupled from per-year zipping: NI/FCF presence is validated globally but the consecutive-year fail rule reads positional indices that can mix non-aligned years
evidence: Lines 39-41 build `validNis/validFcfs` by FILTERING out nulls (collapsing positions), used only for the length check at line 42. The actual computation (lines 52-58) re-zips by raw index i across rawNis/rawFcfs/assetsArr and pushes `{year:i,value}` only when all three are finite. The consecutive-high loop (lines 83-87) then compares `sloans[k].year` deltas. This is internally consistent for gap-detection, BUT the `year:i` is the array index, not a fiscal year; if annualNetIncome and annualFCF arrays have different lengths or differing null patterns (which pull-yahoo's independent trailing-null trims at mapFTSToBalance vs mapFTSToAnnual can produce), index i may not denote the same fiscal year across the three arrays.
why_it_matters: pull-yahoo.js explicitly warns (comment near line 1147) that annualBalance[i] could reference a different fiscal year than annualRev[i] before the alignment fix; the Sloan code assumes positional alignment across annualNetIncome / annualFCF / annualBalance without verifying a shared fiscalYear key. A misalignment silently computes accruals from year t NI against year t-1 FCF/assets, and the 2-consecutive-year CHRONIC_FAIL gate (the only hard-fail, feeding the red-flag rule) can fire or not-fire on phantom adjacency.
fix: If the snapshot exposes a per-row fiscalYear/endDate, key the zip on it and assert equality across the three arrays per year; otherwise document and assert equal lengths + shared origin before positional zipping. Comment: 'prevents failure mode: cross-array positional zip mixes non-aligned fiscal years in accrual + consecutive-fail logic'.

_verdict.note: CONFIRMED real, severity overstated. Sloan (methods/sloan-ratio.js:54-58, 83-87) zips annual.annualNetIncome / annualFCF / annualBalance by raw index i and treats year:i (line 58) as a fiscal-year proxy for the 2-consecutive-year CHRONIC_FAIL hard-disqualifier (lines 91-93). The auditor's mechanism holds against source: (1) the three arrays are built from INDEPENDENT source arrays with INDEPENDENT null-handling, and the FTS-merge in pull-yahoo.js selects each array's source INDEPENDENTLY via different gates — annualBalance @1898 (newBalanceUsable>oldBalanceUsable), annualNetIncome @1935 (_ftsNiNonNull>_qsNiNonNull), annualFCF @1936 (ftsAnnual.annualFCF.length>0) — so the three can come from different producers on the same stock. (2) The quoteSummary path collapses nulls: _arr (pull-yahoo.js:493-500) and the inline .filter(Boolean) for annualFCF/annualBalance (661,675) drop missing years, so a mid-array gap shifts all older entries. (3) Even all-FTS is not cross-array aligned: mapFTSToAnnual's income loop `continue`s on all-empty rows (1104) compacting annualNetIncome, while its cash loop pushes a placeholder for every row (1126-1135) — NI and FCF can drift within one pull. The repo's own alignment comments (F-DP-030/031, F-DP-101, F-DP-003) only guarantee alignment WITHIN same-source-iteration groups, not across NI/FCF/Balance. No length/origin guard exists in Sloan; line 52 Math.min only tolerates differing lengths, it does not align years. Existing tests (tag28-tests.js:90-102) use pre-aligned equal-length null-free arrays and do not exercise misalignment. WHY medium->low: misalignment shifts the OLDER end of latest-first arrays; index 0 (the dominant single-year WARN/REVIEW/EXTREME signal via sloans[0]) stays the newest year in all three, so only the CHRONIC_FAIL 2-year rule is exposed, and only when a mid-window year is dropped in one array but not another — which the code notes is ~0 live incidence (Yahoo's missing year is almost always the oldest, trimmed/at the tail).

title: WC/Rev trend regresses on array index, not actual elapsed years, so a gap year (a skipped invalid year) silently compresses the time axis and distorts the slope
evidence: Lines 99-107 build wcRatios by `continue`-skipping any year missing CA/CL/Rev>0, then line 120-121 reverse and regress against `_slope` (lines 68-78) which uses x = loop index 0,1,2 (`sx += i`). If year index 1 is skipped (e.g. CL missing), the surviving ratios from fiscal years t, t-2, t-3 are treated as if equally spaced at x=0,1,2. The slope (pp/yr) then misattributes a 2-year jump to a 1-year step.
why_it_matters: The pass gate is slope <= +0.02 pp/yr (lines 56,131). Treating a 2-year gap as 1 year doubles the apparent annual slope, which can flip a holding cash-cycle to a 'degrading' FAIL (or vice-versa). DIAGNOSTIC only (not in SCORE_WEIGHTS), so impact is dashboard quality labeling rather than tiering, hence low severity — but the 'pp/yr' unit it reports is simply wrong when years are skipped.
fix: Carry the real year offset (fiscal-year delta or original array index) as the regression x-coordinate instead of the dense push-index, or refuse to compute when the surviving years are not contiguous. Comment: 'prevents failure mode: gap year compresses regression x-axis, distorting pp/yr slope and pass/fail'.

_verdict.note:
False positive — the gap-year compression is structurally unreachable in working-capital-trend.js. The loop is capped at WINDOW=3 (line 97: maxYears = min(WINDOW, balArr.length, revArr.length)), so it only ever examines indices 0,1,2. MIN_YEARS=3 (line 109) then requires all three of those to be valid. Any skipped/null year inside [0,1,2] yields at most 2 survivors -> the method returns computable:false rather than regressing. There is no path to reach index 3+ to backfill a third ratio, so you can NEVER have 3 surviving ratios with a gap among them. The slope is therefore only ever computed on a fully contiguous 3-year block where x=0,1,2 exactly equals the real fiscal-year offset — no distortion.

The auditor's evidence ('surviving ratios from fiscal years t, t-2, t-3 treated as equally spaced at x=0,1,2') requires 3 survivors drawn from a 4+-year span, which the WINDOW=3 cap forbids. The finding correctly describes a real anti-pattern in the abstract but misreads the gating constants. Notably, refusing to compute on non-contiguous survivors is itself one of the auditor's proposed fixes — and the code already does exactly that, just via the MIN_YEARS>=WINDOW guard.

Verified by runtime: a stock with a 4-entry balance array and a missing CL at index 1 returns computable:false ('only 2 valid years, need >= 3'); same for a null placeholder at index 1 (the actual shape pull-yahoo.js emits per the F-DP-003/Tag 233c null-alignment invariant, pull-yahoo.js:1146-1200). Only the contiguous-3y case is computable (slope correct). Data-model context confirms arrays are dense/index=fiscal-year-aligned with null placeholders, never sparse-compacted (pull-yahoo.js:1105, 1180; roic-trend.js reads annualBalance[yearIdx] by aligned index too).

Caveat: a prior report (audit-reports/2026-05-18.md F-ME-001) raised the same claim jointly for sga-revenue-trend.js AND working-capital-trend.js. The bug could be real for sga-revenue-trend.js if its scan window exceeds its MIN_YEARS — but that method is out of scope for this WC-trend-scoped finding.

title: Beneish debt-free coalescing is asymmetric between current and prior year and sets the provenance flag for only one side
evidence: Lines 156-157: `if (ltd_t == null && _balField(...,0,'totalAssets') != null) { ltd_t = 0; _ltdIsDebtFreeProxy = true; }` then `if (ltd_p == null && _balField(...,1,'totalAssets') != null) { ltd_p = 0; }`. The prior-year branch sets `ltd_p = 0` but does NOT record any debt-free provenance, and `_ltdIsDebtFreeProxy` reflects only year t. The LVGI term (line 244-249) uses both ltd_t and ltd_p.
why_it_matters: Functionally the LVGI math is correct (both default to 0), but the provenance/transparency flags are inconsistent: a firm that was debt-free in the prior year only is not surfaced, undermining the audit trail the method otherwise maintains in components. Minor because beneish is DIAGNOSTIC and (per its header) returns computable:false for ~all current snapshots anyway due to missing AR/PPE/SGA/Dep fields, so LVGI rarely actually computes. Flagged for completeness of the debt-free handling, not a scoring impact.
fix: Track debt-free provenance symmetrically (e.g. `_ltdIsDebtFreeProxyPrior`) and expose both in components, or collapse into a single helper applied to each year. Comment: 'prevents failure mode: asymmetric debt-free provenance obscures which year was inferred zero-debt'.

_verdict.note: Refuted as a behavioral bug. The factual asymmetry exists literally (line 156 sets _ltdIsDebtFreeProxy=true on the year-t branch; line 157 does not on the year-p branch), but it has ZERO observable effect. Both _ltdIsDebtFreeProxy and _ltdIsTotalDebtProxy are DEAD variables: a worktree-wide grep shows they are assigned at lines 153/155/156 and never read anywhere — not returned, not logged, and NOT in the components object (lines 279-290 expose only mScore/zone/DSRI/GMI/AQI/SGI/DEPI/SGAI/TATA/LVGI). The auditor's evidence that "_ltdIsDebtFreeProxy ... expose[d] in components" and "LVGI uses both ltd_t and ltd_p" is a misread of provenance vs. math: the LVGI numeric computation (lines 244-249) IS symmetric — ltd_t and ltd_p are both coalesced to 0 under identical guard conditions (totalAssets present), and lines 172-174 already require both years' totalAssets to be finite and positive before reaching here. So the M-Score output is correct and symmetric; only a dead boolean differs. No data corruption, no wrong screener result, no caller impact. Cosmetic dead-store inconsistency at most.

title: Altman X1 working-capital source can mix real current accounts with the cash-minus-debt proxy across firms, making X1 non-comparable and the proxy fallback systematically biased
evidence: Lines 63-69: when currentAssets/currentLiabilities are finite, X1 uses real (CA-CL); otherwise `workingCapital = cashVal - debtVal*0.3` (a proxy that, per the method's own comment lines 56-59, 'overstates working capital for cash-rich firms and understates it where short-term liabilities exceed 30% of total debt'). The chosen source is recorded in components.wcSource but the Z threshold (1.1) is identical for both regimes.

title: EV synthesis mixes trading-currency marketCap with reporting-currency totalDebt/totalCash; ROC denominator uses reporting-currency balance fields — currency mismatch for ADR-class tickers
evidence: magic-formula synthesizes `ev = mcap + (td||0) - tc` (line 168) using `_unwrap(stock.marketCap)` and `_balField(...,'totalDebt'/'totalCash')`. In pull-yahoo.js marketCap is scaled by the TRADING factor: `if (snap.marketCap) snap.marketCap = scaleTrading(snap.marketCap)` (line 415), while annual/balance series are scaled by the REPORTING factor: `snap.annual[key] = snap.annual[key].map(scale)` (line 454). The code itself documents `tradingFactor !== factor` for ADR-class tickers (lines 437-440). So mcap and totalDebt/totalCash are in different currencies when synthesizing EV.
why_it_matters: For every ADR / dual-listed name where trading currency != reporting currency, synthesized EV is arithmetically nonsense (USD mcap minus local-ccy cash), so EarningsYield = EBIT/EV is wrong and pass/fail flips silently. The comment 'No enterpriseValue ... → synthesize' (lines 16-17, 62-66) is hit precisely for the ASML/foreign shapes most likely to be ADRs. EBIT (from annual, reporting-ccy) over EV (mixed) further compounds it.
fix: Prefer metrics.enterpriseValue (already FX-handled consistently). When synthesizing, convert all three legs to one currency first, or only synthesize when meta.reportingCurrency === trading currency (non-ADR). Add comment: `// prevents EV synthesized from mixed trading-ccy mcap + reporting-ccy debt/cash (ADR mismatch)`.

_verdict.note:
False positive — the auditor inverted the FX logic. EV synthesis at magic-formula.js:168 reads a snapshot AFTER _fxConvert() in pull-yahoo.js has run, where ALL currency-denominated fields are normalized to USD. The two different scaling factors are applied precisely BECAUSE the source values start in different currencies, and they converge both legs to USD:

- ADR-class ticker (e.g. TSM: reports TWD, trades USD): Yahoo returns marketCap in the TRADING currency (USD), so it is scaled by tradingFactor=FX_TO_USD['USD']→USD. totalDebt/totalCash come from annual.annualBalance in the REPORTING currency (TWD), scaled by factor=TWD→USD. Both end up in USD. The trading-factor path (Tag 232c-8 / F-DP-005, lines 335-371, 415) is the FIX that prevents the ~32x mispricing that would occur if mcap were scaled by the reporting `factor`. The lines 437-440 comment the auditor cites as evidence is documentation of that fix, not of a remaining bug.
- USD-reporting ticker: origCurrency==='USD' early-returns at line 297-300 with no scaling — marketCap and balance are both already USD. The one genuinely risky case (ambiguous OTC issuer whose financials may be in a third currency, F-NY-004) is explicitly failed closed (fxConversionFailed=true, line 290-296), so the pull loop skips the ticker and magic-formula never sees a mixed snapshot.

Control-flow check: all early returns (lines 276, 278, 295, 300, 317) precede any scaling. Once execution reaches marketCap scaling (line 415) it always proceeds through annual scaling (line 454) to the final return (469). There is NO path where marketCap is scaled but annualBalance is not — they are normalized together in the same pass, and snap.meta.reportingCurrency is set to 'USD' (line 463). Hence mcap, totalDebt, totalCash at synthesis time are all USD; no currency mismatch exists.

Note: magic-formula is a DIAGNOSTIC method (not in SCORE_WEIGHTS, lines 69, 77-83), so even a hypothetical mismatch would not corrupt the composite score / fixture hash. metrics.enterpriseValue is already preferred when present (line 160); the synthesis fallback is the documented secondary path and is currency-consistent.

title: T8 earnings-yield fallback unwraps the wrong layer: _toNum(H.val(...) && H.val(...)[0]) double-evaluates and passes a {value} envelope's truthiness, not its number
evidence: `const ni = _toNum(H.val(stock, 'annual.annualNetIncome') && H.val(stock, 'annual.annualNetIncome')[0]);` (line 433). H.val returns the raw array; `arr && arr[0]` yields the element (which is `{value:N}` or a number). _toNum handles {value} so the number is recovered — BUT the `&&` operand evaluates H.val twice (wasteful) and, more importantly, when the array is the empty array `[]`, `[] && [][0]` evaluates to `[]` (truthy) then `[][0]`=undefined → _toNum(undefined)=null (ok by luck), while a present-but-all-null array yields _toNum({value:null})... _toNum reads v.value=null → Number.isFinite(null)=false → null (ok). It works only incidentally; the construct is fragile and re-reads the path.
why_it_matters: This is the Yahoo-envelope-unwrap + double-evaluation smell. It currently limps because _toNum is defensive, but it re-traverses the object path twice per call across the whole universe and is exactly the shape that breaks the next time someone changes annualNetIncome to be a sparse (null-placeholder) array, since [0] could be a null placeholder for the latest year while a later index holds the real latest NI.
fix: Compute once: `const niArr = _rawArr(stock,'annual.annualNetIncome'); const ni = niArr.length ? niArr[0] : null;` (_rawArr already maps through _toNum). Add comment: `// prevents double path-traversal and {value}-envelope truthiness confusion in E/P fallback`.

_verdict.note: False positive on the correctness claim; at most a cosmetic nit. Line 433 reads `_toNum(H.val(stock,'annual.annualNetIncome') && H.val(stock,'annual.annualNetIncome')[0])`. The auditor's headline ("unwraps the wrong layer", "passes a {value} envelope's truthiness, not its number") is a misread: `_toNum` is applied to `arr[0]` (the ELEMENT), not to the array. The `&&` only gates existence of the array; the value passed into `_toNum` is always the first element. Traced every case against the actual helpers (_helpers.js:12 `val` = plain path traversal; buffett-criteria.js:44 `_toNum` unwraps {value:N} and returns null for non-finite): missing path → null&&… → _toNum(null)=null; empty [] → []&&undefined → _toNum(undefined)=null; [{value:N}] → _toNum({value:N})=N; [null,…] → _toNum(null)=null; [N,…] → _toNum(N)=N. All correct. The auditor itself concedes "the number is recovered" and "it works." There is NO behavioral defect — category 'bug'/severity 'medium' is unjustified. The only real (minor) point is that H.val is evaluated twice, a trivial inefficiency on a pure cheap function with no side effects. So this is a readability/consistency nit, not a bug.

title: One-Dollar test misaligns dividends with net income: rawDiv is indexed positionally against ni5 even though the two series are independently filtered/compressed
evidence: ni5 = `_finite(rawNI.slice(0, window))` (line 489) — finite-filtered, so its indices no longer correspond to fiscal years. Then `const div = (rawDiv.length > i && Number.isFinite(rawDiv[i])) ? Math.abs(rawDiv[i]) : 0; retained5y += ni5[i] - div;` (lines 499-500). rawDiv is a separate _rawArr of annualDividends. ni5[i] (post-filter year) is subtracted by rawDiv[i] (pre-filter year i) — different fiscal years, and if rawNI had a null that ni5 dropped, every subsequent dividend is shifted by a year.
why_it_matters: retained5y (NI minus dividends) drives the capital-allocation pass/fail and the 'capital destruction' fail branch (line 521-524). Subtracting a dividend from the wrong year's earnings can flip retained5y sign for borderline payers, producing a false 'capital destruction' fail or a false pass.
fix: Build a single aligned [{ni,div}] table over the un-filtered arrays before summing, skipping years where NI is non-finite. Add comment: `// prevents subtracting dividend[year_k] from netIncome[year_j] after independent filtering`.

_verdict.note: Mechanically code-accurate but DORMANT. At buffett-criteria.js:489 ni5=_finite(rawNI.slice(0,5)) is index-compressed (drops null NI years), while rawDiv=_rawArr(stock,'annual.annualDividends') (line 484) is unfiltered. The loop at 498-501 subtracts rawDiv[i] from ni5[i], so once any NI year is null the two series reference different fiscal years — exactly the positional-drift anti-pattern the pipeline documents and guards against elsewhere (pull-yahoo.js:1869-1877 / F-DP-030/031 / Bug #26). However the impact is zero in production today: 'annual.annualDividends' is NEVER produced anywhere — grep across the whole worktree (pull-yahoo.js, fixtures, tests) shows the path is referenced ONLY at line 484, with the author's own comment '// may be empty'. So rawDiv is always [], 'rawDiv.length > i' is always false, div is always 0, and the misalignment can never fire. It is a latent landmine that would silently corrupt the One-Dollar test only if someone later wires up a dividend feed. Severity 'medium' overstates current impact; realistic is 'low'. Caller chain confirmed: _testT10_OneDollar reads only stock.annual.* which the pipeline canonical object never fills for dividends.

title: EV synthesis requires totalCash present but treats absent totalDebt as 0, understating EV for net-debt-laden firms whose balance row carries _debtPartial
evidence: `if (Number.isFinite(mcap) && mcap > 0 && Number.isFinite(tc)) { ev = mcap + (Number.isFinite(td) ? td : 0) - tc; }` (lines 166-169). td=null is silently treated as 0 (comment line 167 'net-debt-free firm'). But pull-yahoo builds totalDebt by summing components with absence-as-zero and flags _debtPartial when one leg is missing (pull-yahoo lines 1167-1168, 687-688) — 12.4% of snapshots. A firm with real long-term debt but a missing current-debt line still gets a (partial) totalDebt, yet a firm with BOTH legs missing gets td=null and is assumed debt-free.
why_it_matters: Assuming debt-free understates EV, inflating EarningsYield (EBIT/EV) and pushing leveraged names toward an undeserved PASS. magic-formula reads the _balField directly and never inspects the persisted _debtPartial flag that the rest of the codebase relies on to surface exactly this understatement.
fix: When td is null AND the firm is not credibly net-cash (e.g. row exists but totalDebt null), prefer not synthesizing (return not-computable) rather than assuming 0; or check row._debtPartial and lower confidence. Add comment: `// prevents EV understatement by assuming missing totalDebt == 0 for leveraged firms`.

_verdict.note:
Refuted. Code is read correctly (magic-formula.js:166-169 treats td=null as 0; pull-yahoo.js:687-688 and 1167-1168 build totalDebt with absence-as-zero and flag _debtPartial), but the finding mischaracterizes the impact and proposes a logically inapplicable fix.

(1) The proposed `row._debtPartial` check cannot catch this case. The td=null branch in magic-formula triggers ONLY when BOTH debt legs are absent (std==null && ltd==null). In exactly that case _debtPartial is NOT set — the flag is defined as `totalDebt != null && (std==null || ltd==null)`, i.e. it requires a non-null partial sum (one leg present). The auditor conflated two mutually exclusive populations: _debtPartial firms (one leg missing) get a non-null td and are handled correctly; td=null firms (both legs missing) never carry _debtPartial. So the suggested check would never fire here.

(2) The behavior is a deliberate, project-wide convention, not a bug. Both pull-yahoo mappers carry the F-NY-002 decision note (audited 2026-06-08, decided 2026-06-10): absence-as-zero debt summing is KEPT because absence almost always means a genuine 0, and nulling totalDebt would destroy leverage data for the 12.4% partial population. net-debt-ebitda.js follows the same `totalCash || 0` / accept-partial-totalDebt convention.

(3) The 12.4% figure is misapplied. That is the _debtPartial rate (one leg missing → non-null td → correctly handled), NOT the both-legs-missing td=null rate, which is a separate and smaller population; within it, firms with real debt but zero reported debt lines are rarer still.

(4) Directional impact is benign and self-limiting. Understating EV inflates EY (ebit/ev), making a stock look CHEAPER → more permissive, not a false reject. Magic Formula is a DIAGNOSTIC type, explicitly NOT in SCORE_WEIGHTS (magic-formula.js:69) and fixture-hash-invariant-safe — it does not feed the composite score. The synthesis path is a fallback used only when metrics.enterpriseValue is absent.

File: C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/methods/magic-formula.js:162-171; corroborating: pull-yahoo.js:687-688, 1167-1168; net-debt-ebitda.js:27-32.

title: T3 totalLiab fallback can go negative and tlRatio NaN-formats; liabTest passes when tlRatio is null, weakening the debt gate silently
evidence: `totalLiab = Number.isFinite(row.totalLiabilities) ? row.totalLiabilities : (totalAssets != null && _equityFromRow(row) != null ? totalAssets - _equityFromRow(row) : null)` (lines 240-241). The quoteSummary balance row has NO totalLiabilities and NO totalEquity (pull-yahoo line 691 returns only {totalCash,totalDebt,totalAssets}), so _equityFromRow returns null → totalLiab=null → `liabTest = tlRatio == null || tlRatio < 0.60` is TRUE by the null branch (line 251). The reason string at line 257 does `(tlRatio * 100).toFixed(0)` which would be NaN if reached with null, but the !liabTest branch can only run when tlRatio<0.60, so it is reachable only with a finite tlRatio — OK there; the real defect is the silent pass.
why_it_matters: For the entire quoteSummary-sourced universe (no equity/liabilities fields), the 'TotalLiab/Assets < 60%' leg is a no-op pass, so T3 collapses to just LTD/NI<5x. The method advertises a two-pronged conservative-debt test (lines 243-251) but one prong is dead for the majority data shape. Leverage that the second prong was meant to catch slips through.
fix: Derive totalLiab from totalAssets - totalEquity only when equity exists; otherwise mark the liab leg 'unknown' and require the LTD/NI leg to be stricter, or count the test as not-passed-but-not-failed explicitly. Add comment: `// prevents liab/assets leg becoming a silent always-pass when equity/liab fields absent`.

_verdict.note:
Core mechanism CONFIRMED in source: in methods/buffett-criteria.js _testT3_Debt, when totalLiab is null, tlRatio is null (line 250) and `liabTest = tlRatio == null || tlRatio < 0.60` (line 251) is TRUE via the null branch — the Liab/Assets leg silently passes. So T3 reduces to the LTD/NI leg alone whenever liabilities/equity are absent. Worse: ltd defaults to 0 when totalDebt is missing (line 238), so a data-poor row carrying only totalAssets passes BOTH legs and T3 returns pass:true with no real debt evidence.

BUT the auditor's data-shape evidence is partly WRONG/outdated. The claim that the balance row has NO totalLiabilities/totalEquity (citing pull-yahoo line 691) is true only for the LEGACY quoteSummary mapper (lines 675-691). The newer fundamentalsTimeSeries mapper (pull-yahoo.js lines 1155-1194) DOES populate both totalLiabilities (line 1175) and totalEquity (line 1176), and line 1898 overrides annual.annualBalance with the FTS version whenever FTS has more usable rows (the usual case). So _equityFromRow/totalLiab is usually finite at runtime; the null scenario is only reachable when the QS path wins (FTS thinner). The finding is therefore not a false positive, but it is not the universal silent-pass the evidence implies.

NaN-format sub-claim is self-refuted by the auditor and confirmed non-issue: line 257 `(tlRatio*100).toFixed(0)` is only reached in the !liabTest branch, which requires tlRatio<0.60 (finite), so NaN is unreachable.

Severity downgraded medium->low: the liab leg is an explicit secondary 'fallback' (comment line 248), the primary LTD/NI leg still gates in most cases, and the null path only triggers on data-poor rows where every screener leg is inherently weak — and only when the QS source wins over FTS.

fix_safe=false: the proposed remedy (require stricter LTD/NI when liab unknown, or mark the leg not-passed) changes which stocks clear T3, altering pass/passCount and downstream screen output. That is a semantic/behavior change needing human sign-off, not an auto-applyable behavior-preserving edit. A comment-only documentation of the intent would be safe, but the auditor's substantive fix is not.

title: Q1 moat returns inconsistent component key: 'industryMedianPlus5pp' on the insufficient-data path vs 'industryMedianPlus10pp' on the computed path
evidence: Insufficient-data return: `return { pass: false, avgROIC: null, industryMedianPlus5pp: null, reason: ... }` (line 544-545). Computed return: `return { pass, avgROIC, industryMedianPlus10pp, reason }` (line 560). The variable is named industryMedianPlus10pp and set to 0.20 (line 553).
why_it_matters: Any consumer (report generator, dashboard, downstream aggregator) that reads `q1.industryMedianPlus10pp` gets undefined when the test was insufficient-data, and one reading the legacy `industryMedianPlus5pp` key gets a value only on the failure path. Inconsistent component schemas across return paths are a quiet source of undefined/NaN in reports.
fix: Use the same key on both paths (industryMedianPlus10pp). Add comment: `// prevents component-key drift across return paths (undefined in downstream report)`.

_verdict.note: Confirmed real key-drift in methods/buffett-criteria.js _testQ1_Moat. Insufficient-data path (line 544-545) returns `industryMedianPlus5pp: null`, while the computed path (line 560) returns `industryMedianPlus10pp` (the variable declared at line 553 = 0.20). Same function, two return paths, different component key name — an inconsistency. The finding's factual evidence is accurate. However, its "undefined in downstream report" impact is overstated: the whole q1 object is spread into components.q1_moat (line 802), and a repo-wide grep shows NO consumer reads either key anywhere — aggregation at line 738-740 reads only `.pass`, and the reason string reads only `.reason`. So no logic breaks; the only real effect is an inconsistent serialized JSON shape between the two branches. Severity "low" is correct (cosmetic/report-shape, not a logic bug).

title: T2 ROIC 'not declining' compares latest vs a 5-element slice that, when fewer than 5 valid years exist, equals the full set including latest — making the test near-tautological
evidence: `const fiveSlice = valid.slice(0, 5); const fiveAvg = fiveSlice.reduce(...)/fiveSlice.length; const notDeclining = latestROIC >= fiveAvg;` (lines 201-205). With exactly 3 valid years (the minimum, line 192), fiveSlice = all 3 values INCLUDING latestROIC=valid[0]. notDeclining then asks 'is the newest >= average of {newest, mid, old}', which is satisfied whenever the newest is at or above the mean of the three — trivially true for any non-decreasing or flat-ish series and even for mildly declining ones.
why_it_matters: The 'not declining' guard is meant to reject deteriorating moats, but at the common Yahoo 3-4y depth the comparison includes the very year it is testing, biasing strongly toward pass. The method's own header (line 295-298) notes Yahoo FTS max is 4y, so this short-window degenerate case is the NORM, not an edge case.
fix: Exclude the latest year from the comparison baseline (compare valid[0] against mean of valid.slice(1, k)), and require a minimum baseline length before applying the trend leg. Add comment: `// prevents self-comparison: latest year must not be inside its own trend baseline`.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed against source (methods/buffett-criteria.js:200-205). `fiveSlice = valid.slice(0,5)` does include valid[0] (latest), and `notDeclining = latestROIC >= fiveAvg` compares the latest year against a mean that contains itself. So the structural defect the auditor points at is real: the latest year sits inside its own trend baseline, which systematically biases the "not declining" leg toward leniency (at every length, not just <5). The comment "latest year >= 5y average" and the reason string "5y-avg" also mislabel what's computed — at the 3-year minimum it's a 3-element average, never a true older-baseline.

HOWEVER the auditor's headline ("near-tautological", "trivially true for mildly declining series") is overstated and based on a math misread. With exactly 3 valid years, `latest >= mean(latest,mid,old)` reduces algebraically to `2*latest >= mid+old`, i.e. `latest >= (mid+old)/2` — latest vs. the average of the two OLDER years. That is a genuine, non-trivial trend check: it correctly FAILS a declining series (e.g. 10/15/20 -> 10 >= 17.5 is false -> flagged declining) and passes flat/rising. It is not satisfied for "mildly declining" series of any meaningful slope. So the test is weakened, not vacuous.

Only caller is the aggregate scorer at line 724; no test pins this behavior, so a fix wouldn't break the suite — but it would change real pass/fail outcomes.

Net: real but lower-impact than described; severity medium -> low.

title: T4 EPS acceleration window arithmetic can index out of bounds / build degenerate CAGR when valid.length is small, and nShort can equal nLong-? producing a misleading 'accelerating' verdict
evidence: `const nLong = Math.min(valid.length - 1, 7); const nShort = Math.min(3, nLong - 1);` then `oldestLong = valid[nLong]; oldestShort = valid[nShort]` (lines 297-303). With valid.length=4 (the minimum, line 290): nLong=3, oldestLong=valid[3] (ok, last element). nShort=min(3,2)=2, oldestShort=valid[2]. cagrShort uses nShort=2 periods over valid[0]->valid[2]; cagrLong uses 3 periods over valid[0]->valid[3]. These share the same latest and overlapping span, so 'cagrShort > cagrLong' (line 314) measures convexity of essentially the same 4 points, not a genuine recent-vs-historical acceleration. With only 4 datapoints the 'acceleration' signal is dominated by the single oldest point.
why_it_matters: T4 claims to detect EPS growth ACCELERATION (recent CAGR > long CAGR). At Yahoo's 4y depth the short and long windows overlap so heavily that the result is noise, yet it counts as a full 1/14 test toward the 85% gate. A single odd base-year value (valid[3]) can flip both the growth leg and the acceleration leg simultaneously.
fix: Require non-overlapping windows (short window must end before long window's start) or disable the acceleration leg below ~6 valid years (treat as N/A, as the code already does when cagrShort==null) instead of computing it from overlapping spans. Add comment: `// prevents acceleration verdict from overlapping short/long windows at shallow Yahoo depth`.

_verdict.note: Partly refuted. The two alarming claims in the title are false: (1) NO out-of-bounds is possible. valid.length>=4 is guaranteed (line 290 guard). nLong=min(valid.length-1,7) is always <= valid.length-1, so valid[nLong] is in bounds for every length; at length 4, nLong=3 (last element). nShort=min(3,nLong-1); at length 4 nShort=2 -> valid[2], in bounds. The auditor's own walkthrough concedes both accesses are "ok". (2) NO "degenerate CAGR": _cagr (lines 75-79) returns null unless both latest and oldest are >0, so values are well-defined finite CAGRs; the cagrLong==null branch (307-310) handles the degenerate base case. The ONLY substantive part — that with 4 datapoints the short (valid[0]->valid[2], 2 periods) and long (valid[0]->valid[3], 3 periods) windows overlap, sharing the latest point, so cagrShort>cagrLong is a convexity test dominated by the single oldest point rather than a clean recent-vs-historical comparison — is a fair quantitative observation, but it is NOT a bug: the comment at lines 295-296 explicitly documents this as the intended adaptive behavior at Yahoo's 4y depth ("With Yahoo's max 4y, nLong=3 periods and nShort=2 periods"). It produces correct, in-bounds, finite output and never throws/corrupts. Impact is muted: accelOk only gates when growthOk (CAGR>7%) is already true (lines 312-315), and T4 is 1 of 14 tests behind a passRate threshold plus two unrelated hard gates (x1 industry exclusion, dcf MoS, lines 738-761). This is a known/documented methodology limitation of shallow data, not a medium-severity bug.

title: _computeAnnualROIC recomputed twice per stock (T2 and Q1) — full balance-row iteration done redundantly across the whole universe
evidence: T2: `const roics = _computeAnnualROIC(stock);` (line 188). Q1: `const roics = _computeAnnualROIC(stock);` (line 539). _computeAnnualROIC (lines 109-137) re-reads annual.annualOpInc and annual.annualBalance and loops up to 10 rows recomputing equity/IC each call. Both calls happen unconditionally inside the same evaluate(stock).
why_it_matters: Per the brief, per-method re-classify / wasted recompute over the universe is a named performance dimension. Across ~19k stocks every Buffett evaluation does the ROIC array build twice. Minor per call, but it is pure duplicated work on the hot path and the kind of redundancy that compounds across 36+ methods × universe × the multi-hour pull.
fix: Compute the ROIC array once at the top of evaluate() and pass it into both _testT2_ROIC and _testQ1_Moat. Add comment: `// prevents double ROIC recompute per stock (T2 + Q1 shared input)`.

_verdict.note:
CONFIRMED. why_it_matters: The author explicitly built this to catch the survivorship/delisting bias that 'systematically biases alpha' (comment lines 281-291) — asymmetric exclusion of delisted tickers' returns from one side of the pass/fail cohort. But the signal only appears in CI logs on the single day a vintage is first processed, then disappears. An operator scanning recent logs sees nothing and assumes the cohorts are balanced. The bias itself still occurs (dropped tickers are simply absent from pass/fail arrays on replay too) — only the *visibility* is lost.
fix: Persist the per-vintage attrition counts into the cache entry header (e.g. `cache.vintageReturns[cacheKey]` could be `{ entries: [...], droppedPass, droppedFail, droppedTickers }`) and re-emit the imbalance warning on replay. Bump CACHE_SCHEMA_VERSION (allowed — that is not FTS_CACHE_VERSION) so old caches rebuild once. Alternatively aggregate attrition into the final report JSON so it is observable in the artifact, not just transient logs.

_verdict.note:
CONFIRMED via source. The asymmetric-attrition (delisting-bias) diagnostic runs only on the fresh-load branch and is invisible on every cache replay.

Evidence in scripts/method-effectiveness.js:
- Attrition accounting (droppedPassContribs/droppedFailContribs/droppedTickers, lines 292, 306-309, 334-337) and the IMBALANCE log (lines 366-372) live entirely inside the "Not in cache" branch (252-372).
- The cache entry stores only successful returns: line 356 pushes {ticker, methodId, ret, pass, quality, matured}; line 360 sets cache.vintageReturns[cacheKey] = cacheEntries. Nothing about dropped tickers is persisted.
- The replay branch (223-249) only re-buckets stored returns and never recomputes or re-emits attrition.

Lifecycle confirms "fresh exactly once": a vintage×horizon is skipped while immature (futureDate > today, line 219); the first run after it matures takes the fresh-load path (writes cache, emits warning); thereafter cachedDates.has(cacheKey) is true and it is always served from the replay branch. With CACHE_RETENTION_DAYS=90 (line 166) and the daily cron (daily-pull.yml `17 2 * * 2-6`, line 5; Method-Effectiveness step line 493-496), every vintage is fresh exactly once and replayed for the rest of its 90-day window.

The counts are not aggregated into the report JSON either (the out/report objects at 447-483 carry no attrition fields), and methodology-report.js has no reference to dropped/attrition/IMBALANCE (grep: no matches). So the warning lives only in transient CI stdout for one run.

Scope correction: this is an observability/diagnostics defect, not active data corruption. Dropped tickers are dropped identically on both paths (the cache never held them), so alpha/CI values are unchanged whether or not the warning fires. The cost is that the operator-facing signal for a real survivor/delisting bias vanishes after the first maturity run. "medium" severity is defensible; the data-integrity category label is generous (it is really diagnostic-coverage), so I down-rate to low.

title: Universe/frozen-vintage legacy (non-canonical) price path uses `map.get(date) || null`, converting a legitimate 0 close to null — and skips the staleness gate the pick path enforces
evidence: In the non-canonical branch: `p0 = map.get(entryDate) || null; p1 = map.get(exitDate) || null;` (lines 290-291, 325-326). `|| null` treats a close of exactly 0 as missing. More importantly, this branch does NOT apply the `_daysBetween(...) > PRICE_MAX_STALE_DAYS` symmetric staleness gate that the pick path applies in its own legacy branch (lines 495-496). nearestTradingDay can snap up to 5 calendar days; the universe/frozen medians then silently include returns anchored to closes up to 5 days off, while pick returns in the same vintage are gated at 7 — an asymmetric window between the numerator (picks) and the benchmark (universe/frozen) used to compute alpha.
why_it_matters: alpha = pickMed − universeMed (line 514). If the universe leg admits stale/loosely-snapped anchors that the pick leg rejects, the two legs are measured over subtly different windows for the long-tail thinly-traded names, biasing alpha sign and magnitude — the exact asymmetry the Tag 231a-2 canonical-date work was meant to remove, still live whenever the benchmark is absent/too-short (canonical==null). A 0 close (rare but real for halted/penny names) being coerced to null also drops that ticker asymmetrically. Note the canonical path (_priceAtCanonical) correctly uses `map.get()` without `|| null` and walks backward only — so the two paths disagree.
fix: In both legacy branches, replace `map.get(d) || null` with an explicit `map.has(d) ? map.get(d) : null` and apply the same symmetric `_daysBetween > PRICE_MAX_STALE_DAYS` gate used in the pick legacy path (lines 495-496) so picks and benchmark share one staleness rule. Comment: '// prevents: asymmetric snap-window between pick leg and universe/frozen leg (and 0-close coerced to null) biasing alpha when no benchmark anchors canonical dates'.

_verdict.note:
Refuted. Both sub-claims fail under the actual code.

ASYMMETRIC-STALENESS claim (the core of the finding): FALSE. All three legacy/non-canonical branches (pick 490-498, universe 287-291, frozen 320-326) snap dates with nearestTradingDay(), which is hard-capped at +/-5 calendar days (loop `for (offset=1; offset<=5; ...)`, lines 205-216) and returns null otherwise. The pick path's "extra" gate `_daysBetween(...) > PRICE_MAX_STALE_DAYS` at lines 495-496 compares against PRICE_MAX_STALE_DAYS=7 (line 95). Because the snap can never produce a date more than 5 days off (and the `|| entryDate` fallback at 492-493 yields a 0-day delta), `_daysBetween > 7` can NEVER be true. The gate is inert/dead code. So picks and universe/frozen already share the identical effective +/-5 snap window — there is no asymmetric 5-vs-7 window biasing alpha. The finding also describes the asymmetry backwards (a 7-day gate is MORE permissive than the benchmark's effective 5, not less).

Additional context that further weakens it: the legacy branch is reached only when canonicalDatesByHorizon[days] is null, and that single condition (no benchmark / benchmark series too short, lines 348-363, 452-454) is shared by all three paths via the SAME `canonical` value (computed once per horizon at 449-457). So either all three use canonical anchoring or all three use the legacy +/-5 snap together — never a mix.

0-CLOSE-TO-NULL claim: technically true at the line but immaterial. A 0 entry price is already rejected by returnPct's `p0 <= 0` guard (line 151), and `|| null` only changes behavior for an EXIT close of exactly 0.0 — which is a Yahoo data defect (delisting/bad tick), not a legitimate close; dropping it (vs recording a fabricated -100% return) is arguably more correct.

Cited lines verified: 270-297, 304-331, 490-498, 202-218, 150-153, 95-98, 448-457.

title: Exported `priceAt` (and its forward-walk staleness path) is referenced by no caller; method-effectiveness uses nearestTradingDay/_priceAtCanonical instead
evidence: `priceAt(priceIndex, ticker, targetDate)` is defined (115-131) and exported (837). Grepping the two audited files plus method-effectiveness.js shows the actual lookups go through `WF.nearestTradingDay`, `WF._priceAtCanonical`, and direct `map.get` — never `WF.priceAt`. walk-forward's own main loop uses _priceAtCanonical and nearestTradingDay. The comment at 111-114 says callers 'should migrate to buildPriceIndex + priceAt' but no caller ever did. priceAtLegacy (136-148) is only reached via priceAt's own backward-compat delegation (line 118), so if priceAt is dead, priceAtLegacy is reachable only through tests.
why_it_matters: Two divergent price-lookup implementations with different staleness semantics (priceAt walks FORWARD via setUTCDate(-i)? no — backward; but it lacks the symmetric gate logic of the canonical path) invite future drift: a maintainer 'fixing' lookups may edit priceAt believing it is live. Dead exported surface also enlarges the module's apparent contract for method-effectiveness, which imports WF.
fix: Confirm via repo-wide grep for `.priceAt(` and `priceAt,` across all callers/tests; if truly unused outside tests, remove priceAt + its export (and priceAtLegacy if it becomes unreachable), or collapse all lookups onto the canonical helper so there is one resolution path. Do not touch the FTS cache or methods/index.js. If kept for tests only, mark `@internal` and stop exporting from the public surface.

_verdict.note: Confirmed. Repo-wide grep for `priceAt\b` (excluding priceAtLegacy/_priceAtCanonical) finds priceAt referenced ONLY in its own definition/export (walk-forward-perf.js:115,837) and in tag28-tests.js:374-376 (WF.priceAt(hist,...)). No production caller. The main loop in walk-forward-perf.js uses _priceAtCanonical (285-286,318-319,488-489) and nearestTradingDay; method-effectiveness.js uses WF.nearestTradingDay, WF._priceAtCanonical, and direct map.get (lines 317-328). No dynamic WF[...] access exists. priceAtLegacy (136-148, exported 838) is reachable only via priceAt's backward-compat delegation at line 118 — and since the three priceAt test calls pass raw Arrays, they DO hit that delegation, so priceAtLegacy is exercised only transitively through tests; it has no direct caller. The migration comment (111-114, 135) never materialized. So priceAt is production-dead (test-only) and priceAtLegacy is reachable only through priceAt-via-tests. Accurate in every specific; correctly rated low (test-only dead code, zero impact on computed results).

title: Maturity pre-gate uses asOf+1 (conservativeEntry) but the actual entry can be asOf+0 when generatedAt is post-close — pre-gate can DROP a mature vintage (over-conservative), shrinking the corpus
evidence: Pre-load gate: `const conservativeEntry = WF.addDaysIso(asOf, 1); const futureDate = WF.addDaysIso(conservativeEntry, days); if (futureDate > today) continue;` (217-219). After load, the real entry is `WF.getEntryDate(file.generatedAt || asOf+'T00:00:00Z')` (262-263). Probe: generatedAt in 2026-06-12.json is 09:17 UTC → getEntryDate returns asOf+1 anyway, so today they agree. But getEntryDate returns asOf+0 for any vintage whose generatedAt is ≥21:00 UTC (post-close). For such a vintage the real exit is asOf+days, but the pre-gate demands asOf+1+days ≤ today — so on the single day when asOf+days==today, a genuinely-mature post-close vintage is skipped.
why_it_matters: The comment claims +1 is 'conservative ... so we never include vintages whose exit price isn't yet available' — true for excluding immature ones, but it ALSO excludes a mature vintage for one extra day, and because results are cached per (asOf,key) the first time they're processed, a vintage skipped on its eligibility day is simply processed one day later — minor. The real risk is the divergence between the two date computations: any future change to getEntryDate's threshold (already changed once, Tag 232c-28/F-BT-007 in walk-forward) silently desyncs the pre-gate from the actual maturity check, reintroducing look-ahead (pre-gate too loose) rather than just lag (too tight).
fix: Derive the pre-gate from the same getEntryDate logic, or read generatedAt before the horizon loop (one extra cheap stat/read) and gate on the real realFutureDate. At minimum add a comment cross-linking the +1 assumption to getEntryDate's post-close threshold so the two are changed together. Comment: '// prevents: pre-gate desyncing from getEntryDate threshold → look-ahead (too loose) or corpus shrink (too tight)'.

_verdict.note:
Mechanically correct but currently DORMANT. Confirmed in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/scripts/method-effectiveness.js: the pre-load gate (lines 217-219) hard-codes conservativeEntry = WF.addDaysIso(asOf, 1) then skips when asOf+1+days > today, while the post-load real entry (lines 262-264) uses WF.getEntryDate(generatedAt || asOf+'T00:00:00Z'). getEntryDate (walk-forward-perf.js:164-184) returns asOf+0 ONLY when generatedAt hour >= 21 UTC (post-close); otherwise asOf+1. So for a post-close vintage the real horizon ends at asOf+days, but the pre-gate demands asOf+1+days <= today, dropping a genuinely-mature vintage on the single day asOf+days == today. The pre-gate is the only maturity check; no post-load re-inclusion exists (lines 301-358 process the file unconditionally). I verified there is NO look-ahead risk — the desync only ever DROPS a mature vintage (over-conservative), and nearestTradingDay scans backward-first so even a today-dated exit resolves to an observable prior close.

Decisive empirical finding: across the entire 28-vintage corpus in methods-history/, ZERO vintages are post-close. 22 are pre-close (hour < 21 UTC, e.g. 2026-06-12 at 09:17 UTC as the auditor noted), 6 have no generatedAt (fall back to hour 0). All 28 yield getEntryDate == asOf+1, which exactly matches the pre-gate. So the bug cannot fire on any existing vintage. It is a latent desync that would only trigger if the screener cron ever moves to post-close runs (hour >= 21 UTC). Even then the impact is bounded to one vintage on one calendar day, statistically immaterial under MIN_VINTAGES gating.

Severity revised medium -> low: dormant (no trigger in current data), self-limiting (over-conservative, never look-ahead; one vintage, one day), immaterial to alpha. Line refs (217-219, 262-264) are accurate.

fix_safe=false: the documentary cross-link comment is safe, but the primary proposed fix (derive pre-gate from getEntryDate, OR read generatedAt before the horizon loop) is a behavior change — it would start admitting post-close vintages one day earlier (alters corpus inclusion) and the second variant removes the deliberate no-file-read optimization the pre-gate's own comment (lines 215-216) calls out. Needs human review; only the comment-only mitigation is auto-applyable.

title: canonicalFrac (unmatured gate) is computed from cache-replayed `matured` flags whose value depends on the benchmark series length AT THE TIME THE VINTAGE WAS FIRST PROCESSED, not now
evidence: `canonicalFrac = group.matured / group.total` (line 400); `unmatured = canonicalFrac < CANONICAL_FRAC_MIN` (0.80) gates the method (line 414). `matured` is set at fresh-load resolution (line 322 sets matured=true only when canonicalEntry/Exit exist AND are in the ticker map). It is then frozen into the cache (line 356) and replayed verbatim (line 233/241). If the benchmark was insufficient/absent on the day a vintage was first processed (computeBenchmarkReturn returned entryDate=null), every contribution for that vintage was stored matured=false permanently — even after prices/history.json later gains a full SPY series.
why_it_matters: A method can be permanently stuck in 'unmatured-nearest-day-snapped' (alpha+CI nulled) because of a transient benchmark gap on one historical processing day, with no way to recover short of a cache-schema bump. Conversely, the gate's protection is only as good as the benchmark availability on first-touch. This couples a *statistical-validity* gate to a *historical-IO-timing* artifact — fragile and non-reproducible across machines that first-processed vintages on different days.
fix: Either recompute `matured` on replay (cheap: re-derive canonical dates for the vintage and check map membership) or document that canonicalFrac reflects first-touch benchmark availability and bump CACHE_SCHEMA_VERSION whenever the benchmark series materially changes. Prefer recomputation so the gate is a pure function of current data.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed mechanism, but the "permanently" framing is overstated. CONFIRMED: `matured` is computed once at fresh-load (scripts/method-effectiveness.js:316-322), frozen into the cache via cacheEntries.push({...matured}) at line 356, and replayed verbatim from cache at lines 233/241 with NO recomputation. matured=true requires canonicalEntry && canonicalExit && map.has(both) && non-0-day window; canonicalEntry/Exit come from WF.computeBenchmarkReturn (walk-forward-perf.js:342-386), which returns entryDate=null when SPY/QQQ/IWM is absent (line 350) or the benchmark series is shorter than horizon+buffer (line 363). When canonical dates are null the per-ticker fallback runs and matured stays false. canonicalFrac = group.matured/group.total (line 400) drives unmatured = canonicalFrac < 0.80 (line 414), which sets evidenceGate='unmatured-nearest-day-snapped' and nulls alpha+CI. So the gate's value does reflect first-touch benchmark availability, not current data — the core claim is accurate.

MODERATING FACTS (why severity is lower than 'medium' and why the fix is not auto-safe): (1) The cache is pruned of every vintage older than CACHE_RETENTION_DAYS=90 (lines 166-179), and only vintages within the 84d horizon contribute live alpha data. A stale matured=false therefore self-heals: once the SPY series materializes, all newly-processed vintages get matured=true fresh, and stale cached vintages age out within <=90 days (after pruning they are no longer in cachedDates, so the still-in-horizon ones are recomputed). The finding's "permanently — even after prices/history.json later gains a full SPY series" is wrong; it is transient and bounded. (2) The trigger requires SPY AND QQQ AND IWM all missing/too-short at first-touch — an edge condition since these are core pipeline benchmarks. (3) There is already a documented partial mitigation: CACHE_SCHEMA_VERSION (line 53/155) can be bumped to force a clean rebuild, which the proposed_fix itself references.

title: Benchmark ENTRY date can still backward-snap before the post-close entryDate, anchoring entry to a close BEFORE the screener could have transacted
evidence: getEntryDate shifts a pre-close snapshot to T+1 (the realistic entry). Then computeBenchmarkReturn calls `nearestTradingDay(asOfDate /*=entryDate*/, map)` (line 366) which, on a non-trading entryDate (weekend/holiday), snaps BACKWARD first (lines 207-210). For a Monday-holiday entryDate it returns the prior Friday — a close that is one trading day BEFORE the intended post-screener entry. The canonical entry then anchors all pick/universe/frozen entries to that earlier Friday.
why_it_matters: Backward-first is correct for EXIT (use latest observable close ≤ horizon) and the comment (189-201) justifies backward-first specifically to avoid pulling T+2 into entry. But for ENTRY, snapping backward past the realistic entry day reintroduces a (small) look-ahead in the opposite direction: the trade is priced at a close that predates the moment the screener output existed. Magnitude is ≤1 trading day and only on holiday-adjacent vintages, hence low severity, but it is an asymmetry the canonical-anchoring comments claim to have eliminated.
fix: For ENTRY specifically, snap FORWARD (next available trading day ≥ entryDate) so entry is never before the screener existed; keep backward-first for EXIT. This requires nearestTradingDay to take a direction hint, or a dedicated nearestTradingDayForward for the entry leg. Comment: '// prevents: entry anchored to a close that predates the screener output (holiday-adjacent backward snap)'. Do NOT change FTS_CACHE_VERSION.

_verdict.note:
False positive. Verified scripts/walk-forward-perf.js in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening (nearestTradingDay lines 202-218; computeBenchmarkReturn line 366; caller evaluateVintage lines 411-458).

The backward-first snap for ENTRY is a DELIBERATE, documented fix (Tag 231a-1, comment lines 189-201), NOT a bug. Three reasons the finding does not hold:

1. Not look-ahead. Backward-snapping a non-trading entryDate to the prior Friday uses a close that is OBSERVABLE before the screener acted. The finding itself concedes the result is "one trading day BEFORE the intended entry" — that is a 1-day staleness, not a look-ahead. The proposed forward-snap is the look-ahead direction the codebase explicitly removed: the Tag 231a-1 comment states forward-first "pulled in T+2 returns, leaking up to one additional day of future price movement into the entry price." For the common weekend case (asOf snapshot Sat/Sun, entryDate lands on Sun → backward to Fri), the screener ran on Friday-close data, so Friday-close entry is exactly correct; forward-snapping to Monday would be the classic look-ahead bias.

2. Alpha is unbiased regardless of which trading day is chosen. Per Tag 231a-2, computeBenchmarkReturn returns a single canonical entry/exit pair that anchors ALL legs — pick (lines 487-489), universe (285-286), frozen-vintage (318-319). alphaVsBenchmark = pickMed - benchRet (line 519) is therefore measured over the SAME window for both sides. A 1-trading-day shift in the absolute entry close hits every leg identically and cancels in the relative alpha. The only residual effect is on absolute return magnitude, which is already surfaced via horizonActualDays (lines 371-385, 533-535).

3. The Monday-holiday case is the narrowest sub-case and its harm is overstated. The realistic earliest real execution after a Monday holiday is Tuesday's close; the choice is Friday (observable, 1-day stale, no look-ahead) vs Tuesday (look-ahead). Backward-first correctly picks the safe direction.

fix_safe=false: the proposed fix (forward-snap for entry) would REGRESS the previously fixed look-ahead bias (Tag 231a-1) and break the documented single-canonical-window invariant (Tag 231a-2) — it would also re-create the pick/benchmark window mismatch those tags eliminated. Must not be auto-applied.

title: Freshness + coverage business-day math ignores US market holidays, so the fail-loud staleness guard can be defeated by a long weekend / holiday cluster
evidence: businessDaysSince counts Mon-Fri only ('holidays not modelled', line 63). MAX_PRICE_STALENESS_BUSINESS_DAYS=3 (line 39). A pull that last succeeded before e.g. Thanksgiving or the late-Dec cluster can be 4-5 calendar-stale but only 2-3 weekday-stale, passing the guard. businessDaysBetween (coverage diagnostic, 232-244) shares the same blind spot, inflating expectedBusinessDays so missingPct reads artificially high around holidays — potentially tripping the 20% COVERAGE_MISSING_THRESHOLD warning on a perfectly healthy holiday week.
why_it_matters: The F-BT-001 guard is the fail-loud line of defense against 'every forward-return computed against stale prices is silently wrong'. Holidays create exactly the windows where a missed cron is most likely (reduced ops attention) and where weekday-counting under-estimates staleness. The coverage diagnostic's holiday over-count also cries wolf, training the operator to ignore the warning.
fix: Either widen MAX_PRICE_STALENESS_BUSINESS_DAYS to absorb a holiday (e.g. 4) with a comment, or fold a small US market-holiday calendar into both helpers. For coverage, subtract known holidays from expectedBusinessDays. Low severity because the upstream snapshot-freshness gate (daily-pull.yml 'Verify Snapshot Freshness', 36h asOf) provides a second net, but the two should agree.

_verdict.note:
Refuted on both sub-claims with source + numeric evidence in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/scripts/walk-forward-perf.js.

CLAIM 1 (staleness guard "defeated" by holidays) is logically inverted. businessDaysSince (L65-78) counts Mon-Fri; weekdays are a SUPERSET of NYSE trading days. Ignoring holidays means a closed holiday weekday is still COUNTED as a missed session, so priceStalenessBizDays is >= the true number of missed trading sessions, making the guard (>3, L590) strictly MORE eager to fire than a holiday-aware version, never more lenient. There is no holiday cluster that lets a genuinely failed/stale pull slip past when a holiday-aware guard would catch it. The finding's scenario ("4-5 calendar-stale, only 2-3 weekday-stale, passing the guard") is normal correct behavior: across a holiday fewer trading sessions occur, so fewer new prices are EXPECTED, and the 3-session tolerance correctly absorbs that. Verified empirically (Thanksgiving Nov 2025: Wed Nov 26 -> Tue Dec 2 = 4 bizDays => guard FIRES; late-Dec cluster behaves the same).

CLAIM 2 (businessDaysBetween inflates expectedBusinessDays and trips the 20% COVERAGE_MISSING_THRESHOLD on a healthy holiday week) is quantitatively wrong. businessDaysBetween (L232-244) over-counts by exactly the ~10 NYSE weekday holidays/year = ~3.85% over a full year (~4.35% even in a holiday-dense single month) vs a 20% threshold (L631) — ~5x too small to ever trip it alone. And the coverage diagnostic is non-fatal: it only emits a console.warn + an informational coverageWarning string in walk-forward.json (L632-660); it never aborts, never fails CI, never corrupts any alpha number.

Both helpers carry explicit "holidays not modelled" comments — a documented, intentional approximation that errs conservative for the guard and is in the noise for the diagnostic. The independent second net (daily-pull.yml "Verify Snapshot Freshness", 36h asOf, continue-on-error:false per Tag 218, L248-282) hard-fails on stale snapshots regardless. Callers method-effectiveness.js (L138-139) and fitness/measure.js (L82) share the same helper and inherit the same conservative behavior.

title: USD-only unit lookup silently yields zero YoY for foreign-currency filers; combined with the bare cf.units['USD'] access there is no diagnostic when a concept exists but in another currency
evidence: Line 164 `if (!cf || !cf.units || !cf.units['USD']) continue;` — only the 'USD' unit key is ever read. SEC companyfacts stores values under the reporting currency key (e.g. 'EUR', 'GBP', 'CNY', or 'USD/shares'). ARM is in DEFAULT_TICKERS (line 27) and is a UK filer; many fabless names report non-USD. There is no FX normalization and no log line distinguishing 'concept absent' from 'concept present in EUR'.
why_it_matters: For a non-USD filer every REV_CONCEPT is skipped, so qPts stays empty, newestFirst is empty, and line 171 logs the generic '[skip] no quarterly YoY' — indistinguishable from a genuinely dataless ticker. The durability axis silently has no SEC series for exactly the international fabless members the feature targets. (YoY is a ratio so FX cancels — the data is usable, it's just being discarded by the hard 'USD' key.)
fix: Iterate cf.units keys and accept the first non-share currency unit (`Object.keys(cf.units).find(k => !/share/i.test(k))`), since YoY = ratio is currency-invariant as long as the numerator and denominator share a unit. Record the unit in revQYoYsecMeta. Comment: 'prevents silently discarding non-USD foreign filers (YoY is FX-invariant)'.

_verdict.note: Code reading is accurate (enrich-q-revenue.js:163-164 reads only cf.units['USD'], and the court-screen.js:134-152 consumer silently falls back to the thin annual YoY series when <4 SEC quarterly points exist, with no log distinguishing 'concept absent' from 'present in another currency'). BUT the data-integrity harm is empirically false for this script's scope. I inspected the actual companyfacts.zip: all 8 DEFAULT_TICKERS report every REV_CONCEPTS value under the USD unit key only. The auditor's named smoking gun — ARM (UK filer) — reports revenue as RevenueFromContractWithCustomerExcludingAssessedTax:USD; its ONLY GBP-denominated us-gaap concept is DerivativeNotionalAmount, which the script never reads (ARM has no 'Revenues' concept at all). This is structural: the script reads only facts['us-gaap'] (line 156), and SEC us-gaap XBRL facts for SEC-form filers are USD-mandated. Non-USD currencies live in ifrs-full or in FX-disclosure concepts, neither of which this code touches. The 'USD/shares' example in the evidence is a per-share EPS unit, never on revenue concepts. So no foreign-currency filer is silently dropped in practice. The proposed fix is also NOT safe: 'grab the first non-share currency unit via Object.keys().find()' assumes the whole series shares one currency, but companyfacts can carry a concept across multiple currency keys by period; blindly selecting one key changes which array feeds extractQuarterlyPoints and could alter the freshness-winner at line 167 — a real correctness regression to chase a non-existent problem. A diagnostic log (absent vs. non-USD) would be a harmless observability add, but the behavioral fix needs human review.

title: loadTickerFile trusts JSON array contents verbatim — non-string/object elements flow into yf.chart() and history[ticker] keys, corrupting the store
evidence: Lines 52-59: `if (raw.startsWith('[')) return JSON.parse(raw);` returns the parsed array unmodified — no .map(String)/.trim()/.filter as the newline branch (line 58) does. Those values become `tickers`, then `yahooSymbol = wlSymbolMap[ticker] || ticker` (line 125) and the object key `history[ticker] = arr` (line 160).
why_it_matters: A ticker-file like `[{"ticker":"AAA"}, "BBB ", 123]` yields: an object key stringified to '[object Object]' in history.json, a ' BBB ' key with a trailing space that will never match the watchlist symbol later, and a numeric 123 passed to yf.chart. The newline-delimited path is hardened (trim+filter) but the JSON path is not, so the safety is inconsistent and a malformed ticker-file silently pollutes prices/history.json.
fix: Normalize both branches identically: after JSON.parse, `return arr.map(t => (typeof t === 'string' ? t : (t && t.ticker) || '').trim()).filter(Boolean);` so object-shaped and stray entries are coerced or dropped the same way as the newline path.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed the code reading. In loadTickerFile (C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/scripts/backfill-prices.js:52-59) the JSON branch `if (raw.startsWith('[')) return JSON.parse(raw);` (line 55-56) returns the parsed array verbatim, while the newline branch (line 58) applies `.map(l=>l.trim()).filter(Boolean)`. The asymmetry is genuine: a JSON array like `["AAA"," BBB ",""]` keeps untrimmed/empty entries, unlike the newline path. Non-string elements (numbers, objects, null) also pass through Set dedup (line 76) into yahooSymbol (line 125) and yf.chart() (line 130).

However, the severity claim ("corrupting the store") is overstated. The only path that writes `history[ticker]` (line 160) is a SUCCESSFUL fetch; empty/garbage symbols throw or return no bars and are caught into `failed` (lines 142-146, 168-171), not written. The genuinely real, low-noise defect is the trim/filter asymmetry between the two branches plus lack of String coercion — a robustness/consistency gap. The trust boundary is also weak: --ticker-file is an operator-supplied local file for a CLI maintenance script, not untrusted external input. Real but low severity, not medium.

title: AFF10B5One parsing double-tests and mis-handles whitespace: r.AFF10B5ONE==='1' is redundant with the regex, and the regex is not anchored-trimmed

_verdict.note:
Verified scripts/backfill-form345.js:243 and parseTsv (lines 133-150). Two sub-claims:

(1) Redundancy: TRUE but cosmetic. `r.AFF10B5ONE === '1'` is fully subsumed by the regex alternative `1` in /^(1|true|y)$/i — the disjunct is dead code. Pure hygiene, not a bug.

(2) Whitespace mishandling ('Y ' treated as not-10b5-1): the MECHANISM is correct — parseTsv (line 146) splits on \t and never trims cell values, so an anchored regex would reject a whitespace-padded cell. BUT the TRIGGER is hypothetical/invented. The SEC ownership dataset encodes SUBMISSION.tsv AFF10B5ONE as a numeric 0/1 flag, not Y/N — the 'Y '/'y'/'true' branches are defensive extras the real data never exercises, and SEC tab-delimited flag columns are not whitespace-padded. The finding offers no evidence (no sample row, no failing case) that real data ever contains '1 ' or 'Y '. The file is split on /\r?\n/ so trailing \r is already gone (the finding concedes this). So against the actual ingested data the code is correct; the bug is purely theoretical.

Impact even if it ever triggered is bounded and not corruption: isTenB5One only gates whether a SELL is excluded from the net-positive hard gate (insider-conviction-score.js:267). A mis-flagged 10b5-1 sell would be wrongly counted as a real sell, making the net gate slightly harder to pass — a signal-suppression edge case, low severity, not silent data corruption.

Net: this is a defensible hardening/hygiene suggestion (drop the redundant ===, trim defensively) but not a real defect against the data the script actually processes. Default is_real=false stands.

title: _seen Set is attached to byTicker entries and only stripped at the per-quarter write boundary — an exception mid-processQuarter before the strip can serialize a Set as {} into the history cache
evidence: Line 302 `entry._seen = new Set();` mutates the persisted object. The strip loop runs at lines 377 and 381 — AFTER processQuarter returns. But processQuarter pushes txns and sets _seen inline (lines 304-309) and the main loop's catch (line 372) swallows mid-quarter throws. If a throw occurs after some entries got _seen but the function still returns into the catch, the subsequent writeHistory (line 378) does run the strip first (377 is before 378), so the common path is safe — but writeHistory is ONLY called from the main loop; processQuarter itself never writes, so the window is narrow.
why_it_matters: JSON.stringify(new Set()) === '{}', so any _seen that survives to a write would persist a useless empty object and, on reload (line 305 `if (!entry._seen) entry._seen = new Set(entry.transactions.map(txnKey))`), the truthy '{}' object would be treated as an already-populated Set, disabling dedupe for that ticker on the next backfill run (silent duplicate transactions). The current strip-before-write ordering prevents it, but the design is fragile: the dedupe helper lives on the serialized object.
fix: Keep _seen out of the persisted object entirely: hold it in a side `Map<ticker, Set>` local to processQuarter/main rather than as `entry._seen`. Removes the strip loops (lines 377, 381) and the reload-rebuild guard, eliminating the empty-Set-disables-dedupe failure mode.

_verdict.note: False positive — the claimed failure mode cannot occur. _seen Sets are attached only inside processQuarter (lines 302/305/309), and processQuarter NEVER calls writeHistory. The only two writeHistory calls (lines 378, 382) are each immediately preceded by an UNCONDITIONAL strip loop `for (const t of Object.keys(byTicker)) delete byTicker[t]._seen;` (lines 377, 381). The main-loop catch at line 372 swallows any mid-quarter throw from processQuarter and falls THROUGH to that same strip-then-write at 377-378 — so a Set can never be serialized as {}. The auditor's own evidence concedes "the common path is safe" and that the only writer is the main loop after the strip; that observation actually closes the window entirely rather than narrowing it. There is no alternate write path: grep confirms writeHistory is defined and called only here, and the other grep hit (elliott-export.js) is unrelated first_seen_at substring noise. Self-rated low by the auditor and an empty cache file (worst plausible outcome of a crash mid-run) would simply contain stripped entries with intact transactions arrays, from which line 305 rebuilds _seen on next load. Not a real bug.

title: Watchlist-CIK intersection rebuilds no index but parseDailyForm4Rows materializes EVERY Form-4 row for the day before filtering — fine at daily scale, but allRows.filter is O(rows) on a list dominated by non-watchlist filings
evidence: Line 317 `const allRows = parseDailyForm4Rows(idxRes.body);` builds an array of all ~hundreds-to-thousands of Form-4 rows for the day, then line 319 `const hits = allRows.filter(r => watchlistCiks.has(r.cik));`. The only waste is allocating row objects for the ~99% of daily Form-4 filings that aren't on the watchlist. At one trading day's volume this is negligible; flagged only for completeness against the 'wasted recompute' dimension.
fix: Optional micro-optimization: push into rows inside parseDailyForm4Rows only when watchlistCiks.has(cik), by passing the Set in. Not worth changing unless DAYS is set very large; documenting as acceptable-as-is.

_verdict.note: Code at lines 317-319 matches the description exactly: parseDailyForm4Rows materializes all Form-4 rows for the day, then allRows.filter(r => watchlistCiks.has(r.cik)) selects watchlist hits. But this is a non-issue, and the auditor's own proposed_fix concedes as much ("Not worth changing unless DAYS is set very large; documenting as acceptable-as-is"). Concrete reasons it is not real: (1) Scale is tiny and bounded — one daily SEC form index lists at most a few thousand Form-4 rows for a single trading day; allocating a few thousand small plain objects and GC'ing them is microseconds. (2) The filter is O(rows) with O(1) Set lookups, which is optimal — you cannot do better than scanning each row once. (3) The real per-day cost is network I/O (one index fetch + one fetch per hit at 125ms throttle each, line 311/343), which dwarfs the in-memory filter by many orders of magnitude. (4) The DAYS knob only loops over MORE days sequentially (line 294); it never enlarges a single day's row count, so even DAYS=large does not change the per-iteration O(rows) the auditor worries about. (5) The proposed coupling (push the watchlistCiks Set into parseDailyForm4Rows) would harm the clean separation that makes parseDailyForm4Rows a pure, exported, unit-testable function (module.exports line 392), for zero measurable benefit. This is acceptable-as-is by design, not a defect.

title: Local _cagr() lacks the latest<=0 guard that _helpers.cagr3y() has — NaN possible if latest revenue is non-positive
evidence: Line 37-40: `function _cagr(latest, oldest, years){ if (oldest == null || oldest <= 0 || latest == null) return null; return Math.pow(latest / oldest, 1/years) - 1; }`. It guards `oldest <= 0` and the two nulls but NOT `latest <= 0`. Compare _helpers.js:54 `if (latest == null || oldest == null || latest <= 0 || oldest <= 0) return null;`. Caller guards only finiteness (line 72: `Number.isFinite(rawRevs[0]) && Number.isFinite(rawRevs[4])`), not sign.
why_it_matters: If a snapshot carries a negative latest 'revenue' (data-quality artifact: sign-flipped FTS row, or a non-revenue row mis-mapped to annualRev — the file's own comments warn FTS mapping has had alignment issues), `Math.pow(negative, 0.25)` = NaN. rev5yCagr becomes NaN; `NaN >= 0.15` is false so the check fails closed rather than throwing, but NaN then lands in components.checks[].val and the report. Low severity because revenue is rarely negative, but it is an unguarded NaN-propagation path inconsistent with the shared helper.
