Comment: '// prevents: NaN from fractional power of non-positive latest revenue (sign-flipped/mis-mapped FTS row)'. Pure internal helper, no index.js/fixture-hash concern unless a fixture currently relies on negative-revenue behavior (none do).

_verdict.note: Code discrepancy confirmed. premium-compounder-proof.js:37-40 `_cagr()` guards `oldest<=0` + nulls but NOT `latest<=0`, whereas _helpers.js:54 `cagr3y()` guards both. Caller (line 72-73) passes `_cagr(rawRevs[0], rawRevs[4], 4)` checking only Number.isFinite, not sign. Verified in node: with the caller's years=4, a negative latest yields NaN (fractional power 1/4 of a negative base); latest=0 yields -1. So the missing guard does produce NaN for sign-flipped/mis-mapped revenue. HOWEVER the realistic impact is near-zero, justifying the LOW severity (I'd even argue cosmetic): downstream at line 75, NaN flows to `computable: rev5yCagr != null` => TRUE and `pass: NaN >= 0.15` => FALSE. So the stock is not crashed and not spuriously passed — check #1 just fails instead of being marked N/A. A company with negative latest revenue can never be a premium compounder either way, so screening correctness is unaffected; the only difference is N/A (guarded) vs failed-check (current). `val:NaN` also serializes to null in JSON, so no output corruption. Requires abnormal/sign-flipped source data to trigger at all — no fixture in engine-fixtures.js uses negative revenue. Real defensive-consistency gap, negligible practical effect.

title: Exported value=passing counts ALL checks (incl. N/A) but threshold=6; graduated score in fail-case under-credits stocks with legitimate N/A checks
evidence: Line 184 returns `value: passing` where `passing = checks.filter(c => c.pass).length` (line 169) over all 6 checks. Module exports `threshold: 6, thresholdOp: 'gte'` (line 196). But the actual pass logic is `allEvaluablePass = evaluable.every(c => c.pass)` over computable checks only (line 180), explicitly treating N/A checks as not-failures (line 178-179). In score-aggregator.normalizeMethodScore, when pass=false the gte branch does `ratio = val/threshold = passing/6` (score-aggregator.js:149-150).
why_it_matters: A stock with, say, 4 computable checks of which it passes 3 and fails 1, plus 2 genuine N/A (OCF/RnD cache gap), reports value=3 -> ratio 3/6=0.5 -> low partial score, as if it failed 3 of 6. But it only failed 1 of 4 evaluable. The denominator should be evaluable.length, not the fixed 6. The pass=true path short-circuits to 1.0 so this only bites the partial-credit fail case, but premium-proof carries a (small) 0.05 QC weight, so it does feed the score and systematically under-rewards data-incomplete names — the opposite of the file's stated 'N/A is not an implicit failure' intent.
fix: Make value/threshold semantics align with the evaluable-only gate. Either export value as a fraction the aggregator can grade against threshold=1 (e.g. `value: evaluable.length ? passing_evaluable/evaluable.length : null`, thresholdOp 'gte', threshold computed to all-pass) or set `value: passingEvaluableCount` and pass a per-result `threshold: evaluable.length` via buildResult so normalizeMethodScore divides by the right denominator (it already prefers result.threshold over meta, score-aggregator.js:118). Comment the failure mode: '// prevents: N/A checks inflating the score denominator (passing/6) and under-crediting data-incomplete compounders'. Verify against tag28 premium-proof fixtures.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed the code chain. premium-compounder-proof.js line 184 returns `value: passing` where `passing = checks.filter(c => c.pass).length` (line 169) over ALL 6 checks, while the pass verdict is `allEvaluablePass = evaluable.every(c => c.pass)` over computable checks only (lines 168/180), with N/A checks explicitly excluded (comment lines 178-179). The module exports `threshold:6, thresholdOp:'gte'` (line 196) and evaluate() calls H.buildResult WITHOUT a per-result threshold, so methodResult.threshold is undefined and normalizeMethodScore falls back to methodMeta.threshold=6 (score-aggregator.js:118). On a fail (pass=false) the gte branch computes ratio = value/threshold = passing/6 (lines 149-150). premium-compounder-proof IS a scored CORE method (method-types.js:27) carrying 0.05 weight in QUALITY_COMPOUNDER (score-aggregator.js:47), so this path is live.

The denominator-inflation is genuine but only manifests in a narrow case: when at least one check is N/A AND the method fails. Worked example: 5 evaluable checks, 4 pass, 1 fails, check #6 N/A → value=4, ratio=4/6=0.667 (curve→sub-score ~0.267) instead of the consistency-correct 4/5=0.80 (curve→~0.50). When the method PASSES, normalizeMethodScore returns 1.0 at line 112 and value/threshold are never read, so passing stocks are unaffected. When all 6 are computable, passing/6 is already the correct denominator.

I am downgrading severity medium→low. The bug only affects the graduated partial-credit of an ALREADY-FAILING method (it can never flip a pass to a fail), the bias is conservative (under-credit, not over-credit), and the weight is just 0.05 with proportional renormalization (computedWeight~0.95) — worst-case net QC score impact is on the order of ~1 point out of 100. It is a real cross-component semantic inconsistency, not a tier-flipping defect.

fix_safe=false: the proposed fix mutates the returned `value` (to a fraction) and/or injects a per-result `threshold`. `value` is also serialized into breakdown[methodId].value (score-aggregator.js:236) for UI/reporting, and the evaluate() scoring path is covered by the tag28 fixture-hash invariant (see _helpers.js:155-175 _setMediansForTest rationale). Any change to value/threshold semantics shifts serialized output and the fixture hash, requiring human review and a deliberate hash rebaseline — not behavior-preserving, not auto-apply-safe.

title: EBITDA<=0 AND net-cash returns computable:false -> silently bypasses the QC must-gate and TURNAROUND soft-guard for loss-making firms with no debt-service buffer
evidence: Lines 45-63: when `ebitda <= 0`, if `netDebt > 0` it returns the value=999 distressed sentinel (good), but in the `else` it returns `computable: false` with reason 'EBITDA <= 0 but net-cash positive'. net-debt-ebitda is required:true weight:'must' in QUALITY_COMPOUNDER (strategy-modes.js:113) and the TURNAROUND softGuard (strategy-modes.js:161). In score-aggregator.normalizeMethodScore, `if (!methodResult.computable) return 0` (line 111) — a non-computable must-gate is typically treated as 'gate not applicable / not failed' by the strategy layer's missing-guard handling rather than a hard fail.

For TURNAROUND that is the exact population the soft-guard exists to scrutinize — a firm burning operating cash is the canonical turnaround risk, and 'net cash this snapshot' can flip fast. The comment frames net-cash as 'no debt service risk', but EBITDA<=0 with net cash still signals an unprofitable balance sheet the QC quality mandate cares about. Validate that tag28 fixtures for this branch still hash-stable or bump intentionally; do NOT add any hardcoded ticker handling — fix the branch logic only.

A profitless net-cash name therefore does NOT silently clear the must-gate; it fails via the incomputable path. For TURNAROUND, net-debt-ebitda is a softGuard (line 161); softGuards never block `passed` (lines 216-223, 278-298) — they only collect warnings/penalty, so there is no gate to bypass; computable:false just adds no penalty. The score-aggregator.js:111 quote (`if (!computable) return 0`) is real but is the soft 0-1 investment-SCORE layer, where 0 is the most conservative contribution and cannot help a stock pass. Business logic of the net-cash branch is also sound: netDebt<=0 means more cash than debt, so the "debt with no cash flow to service" concern genuinely does not exist, and the ratio is mathematically undefined (neg/neg). title: earningsHistory order is assumed oldest-first (slice(-WINDOW)) but pull-yahoo persists Yahoo order verbatim with no normalization or assertion
evidence: Method comment line 83 'Yahoo orders earningsHistory chronologically (oldest first)' and `const lastN = hist.slice(-WINDOW);` (line 85). pull-yahoo.js:994-1005 iterates `for (const q of hist)` and pushes in source order — no .reverse(), no sort, no date check (contrast: every annual/quarterly FTS path explicitly `.slice().reverse()` to force latest-first, e.g. pull-yahoo.js:1073,1093,1154,1204). There is no runtime guard that hist is actually ascending by `quarter`.

BUT components.lastFourSurprises and any future 'recency-weighted' or 'most recent quarter' logic silently take the wrong 4 quarters if Yahoo ever returns descending order (it has historically varied by endpoint/region). The code relies on an unasserted external ordering invariant while the rest of the puller never trusts Yahoo ordering and always re-sorts.
fix: Harden against ordering drift: sort by parsed `quarter` date in the method before slicing (`const sorted = hist.filter(r=>r&&r.quarter).sort((a,b)=>Date.parse(a.quarter)-Date.parse(b.quarter)); const lastN = sorted.slice(-WINDOW);`), falling back to original order when dates are unparseable. Comment: '// prevents: silently selecting the wrong 4 quarters if Yahoo earningsHistory order flips (rest of puller never trusts Yahoo order)'. No index.js edit; recheck tag28 fixtures (their quarters are already ascending so behavior is unchanged).

_verdict.note:
Factual claims check out but the framing is a non-issue / false-positive hardening suggestion, not a defect. Confirmed in worktree C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening:

- methods/earnings-surprise-momentum.js:83-88 does assume oldest-first via `hist.slice(-WINDOW)`, and the comment says so.
- pull-yahoo.js:982-1008 (the Tag 220c earningsHistory builder) iterates `for (const q of hist)` and pushes Yahoo's order verbatim — no .reverse(), no sort, no date assertion. There is no runtime ordering guard anywhere (tests/yahoo-schema-canary.js:99 only asserts `earningsHistory.history` is an array, not its order).

Why it is NOT a real bug:
1. The auditor's central evidence — that FTS paths explicitly `.slice().reverse()` (pull-yahoo.js:1073,1093,1154,1204) — is a FALSE ANALOGY. Those paths come from a DIFFERENT Yahoo API (fundamentalsTimeSeries), which returns oldest-first while the engine wants latest-first, so they reverse. earningsHistory comes from quoteSummary and its only consumer (earnings-surprise-momentum) wants oldest-first, so NOT reversing is correct and intentional. Producer and consumer agree on oldest-first; the missing .reverse() is not an oversight.
2. The residual risk is purely hypothetical ("if Yahoo flips order someday"). Yahoo's quoteSummary earningsHistory has empirically returned the 4 trailing quarters oldest-first (period -4q..-1q) for years; yahoo-finance2's type (quoteSummary-iface.d.ts:223, EarningsHistoryHistory with quarter:Date|null, period:string) documents no ordering contract but there is no evidence of drift. So even 'low' is generous — it is defensive hardening, not a live data-integrity bug.
3. Only one order-sensitive consumer exists (this method). data-quality.js:74 just checks meta.earningsHistory presence (order-irrelevant).
4. The tag28 fixtures (tag28-tests.js:2177-2200) are all ascending-by-quarter, so the claim 'behavior unchanged on fixtures' holds.

title: Loss-magnitude-guard tests TTM margin re-labelled as annual when opIncSource=='computed-margin'
evidence: `const oi0 = _unwrap(oiArr[0]); ... const ratio = oi0/rev0; const pass = ratio >= THRESHOLD;` (lines 55,74-75). When pull-yahoo synthesized annualOpInc via path 3 (pull-yahoo.js:589-596, meta.opIncSource='computed-margin'), oi0/rev0 reduces to operatingMargins_TTM. For financial-sector names that fell to the margin fallback the 'annual' figure is just the TTM margin — the guard is not measuring what its reason string and audit trail claim, weakening the SOUN/IONQ-style detection for that cohort and making the components.oi0 value misleading for downstream review.

_verdict.note:
CONFIRMED but severity overstated; downgraded medium->low. The guard (methods/loss-magnitude-guard.js:52-85) computes ratio = oi0/rev0 from annual.annualOpInc[0]/annualRev[0] and never reads stock.meta.opIncSource (verified: the file contains zero references to meta). When opIncSource==='computed-margin', annualOpInc is literally annualRev.map(r => r.value * operatingMarginsRaw) (pull-yahoo.js:589-596), where operatingMarginsRaw = _y(fd,'operatingMargins') = Yahoo financialData.operatingMargins, a TTM figure. The auditor's algebra is correct, and the codebase itself documents this exact flattening in findings/data-pipeline.json F-DP-006 ("Computed-margin applies a single TTM margin to all historical years, flattening year-by-year OpInc volatility").

WHY LOW, NOT MEDIUM: The computed-margin path is strictly sector-gated to Financial Services/Financials (pull-yahoo.js:638-639 and 1971-1972). For the financial-sector stocks where it does fire, banks/insurers have structurally positive operating margins, so ratio >= -0.50 passes and the TTM-vs-annual distinction almost never flips the sign across the -50% gate; a financial with TTM op-margin worse than -50% is genuinely distressed (a correct fail). So the pass/fail OUTCOME is essentially unaffected — the defect is a provenance/disclosure gap (the reason string + Deep-Dive modal don't disclose the figure is TTM-derived), not silent result corruption. Categorizing it as data-integrity is a stretch; it's really a transparency issue.

WHY fix_safe=false: The proposed fix is NOT behavior-preserving. Setting computable:false would actively remove a previously-active loss-magnitude signal for financial-sector stocks, changing screener output. Even the milder opIncDerived:true components flag, if it feeds the reason string or any downstream consumer, is a behavior change needing human review (and arguably belongs upstream/centralized, since several guards — ni-volatility-guard, metric-divergence-guard — share the same opIncSource provenance gap per the pull-yahoo comments at line 627). title: NI-volatility denominator rev0 and NI swing can reference different fiscal years (independent arrays, no alignment check)
evidence: `const niArr = stock.annual.annualNetIncome||[]; const revArr = stock.annual.annualRev||[];` (lines 67-68); rev0=_unwrap(revArr[0]) (line 76); the NI prefix is built by breaking at the first null (lines 85-90) and maxDelta is taken over that NI prefix (lines 99-104); ratio=maxDelta/rev0 (line 106). annualNetIncome and annualRev are built independently in the mapper and either may have a leading/interior null; there is no check that revArr[0] is the same fiscal year as nis[0].
why_it_matters: The ratio is interpreted as 'max single-year NI swing as a fraction of one year's revenue' (header lines 11-12). If revArr has a leading null (latest year unreported) while annualNetIncome does not, rev0 is a prior, smaller year, inflating the ratio toward the 1.0 hard-fail gate (DATAGUARD, method-types.js:82) and risking a false disqualification — or the reverse. Lower severity than the divergence/forecast cases because both Yahoo arrays usually populate together, but it is the same class of unguarded positional assumption.
fix: Require revArr[0] (raw, pre-compression) to be a finite latest-year value aligned with nis[0], or normalize the NI swing against the revenue of the same fiscal index that produced maxDelta. Comment: 'prevents dividing an NI swing by a revenue figure from a different fiscal year when the two annual arrays are misaligned'.

_verdict.note: Partially real but low-impact; consistent with deliberate codebase design. Confirmed: the guard reads rev0=_unwrap(revArr[0]) (line 76) and builds the NI prefix from a separate niArr (lines 85-90), with no per-call cross-array fiscal-year assertion. annualRev and annualNetIncome ARE built/merged independently in pull-yahoo.js: in mapYahooToCanonical both come from _arr(isHist,...) whose helper (lines 493-500) ends in .filter(Boolean), compacting each array on its own; in the FTS merge, annualRev (line 1861) and annualNetIncome (line 1935) are each swapped to the FTS source based on their own non-null count, so they can in principle end up from different sources. REFUTATION of severity: (1) The pipeline's documented invariant is positional alignment by index — the mapper preserves null placeholders precisely for this (F-004, F-DP-030/031, F-DP-101, Bug #26 comments throughout pull-yahoo.js), and array[0]=latest fiscal year is the convention every annual-array consumer relies on. The explicitly-complementary metric-divergence-guard.js does the IDENTICAL thing (oi0/rev0 over two independent annual arrays, lines 58-71) with no alignment check — so this guard is not an outlier; adding a check here would diverge from the established pattern. (2) Leading-index drift is a rare corner: it requires the latest income-statement row to have revenue-without-NI (or NI-without-rev), or cross-source FTS/QS mixing; Yahoo income-statement rows normally carry totalRevenue and netIncome together. (3) A leading null in NI is safely handled: the prefix loop breaks at the first null (line 89) → nis.length<2 → computable:false (lines 91-96), not silent misalignment. (4) Impact is bounded even when drift occurs: rev0 is only a scale denominator; a one-year offset moves it by the revenue growth rate (~10-50%), nowhere near enough to flip a verdict given the ~6x separation between the calibrated anchor cluster (≤0.32) and quarantine cluster (≥2.0) around threshold 1.0. tag28-tests.js (lines 678-693) constructs annualRev and netIncome independently and expects correct behavior, confirming the no-alignment-assertion design is intentional.

title: Missing/blank latest.asOf makes the prior-window filter exclude EVERY vintage -> regression check silently passes green
evidence: `const todayDate = (latest.asOf || '').slice(0, 10);` then `const priors = files.filter(f => f.replace('.json','') < todayDate).slice(-8)...`. If latest.asOf is absent or empty, todayDate === '' and the string compare `f < ''` is false for every real date filename, so priors === []. The collapse guard (totalPicks<5) still fires, but any non-collapse drift goes unseen.
fix: Fall back to the newest dated vintage filename (or new Date()) when latest.asOf is missing, and emit a ::warning when asOf is absent so the operator sees the degraded comparison: `const todayDate = (latest.asOf||'').slice(0,10) || (files.length ? files[files.length-1].replace('.json','') : new Date().toISOString().slice(0,10));`

_verdict.note: Mechanism is technically correct but the impact claim is overstated/false as framed, so I rate it not-real at the asserted severity. CONFIRMED MECHANICALLY: with blank asOf, todayDate==='' and `files.filter(f => f.replace('.json','') < '')` returns [] (verified empirically against the 29 real vintage files in picks-history/ — priors.length===0). So the drift comparison would be skipped. WHY THE FINDING IS WRONG AS STATED: (1) The evidence cites line 154 (MIN_HISTORY_RUNS early return) but OMITS the `totalPicks < 5` hard-fail guard at lines 146-152, which runs BEFORE line 154 by deliberate design (comment NEW-7, lines 140-145, added precisely so a drift-INDEPENDENT collapse is caught even when history is short). The exact catastrophic cases the auditor names — 'method bug / empty snapshots / universe-wide throw' — produce a 0/0/0 collapse that fires this guard => `return 1` + Discord HARD FAIL, NOT silent green. So the headline 'regression check silently passes green' is false for the dangerous scenarios. (2) The ONLY case that does silently skip is: asOf missing AND pick counts healthy (>=5). That is a genuine but minor degradation, identical in outcome to the already-accepted insufficient-history path (cold start / post-cleanup). (3) The trigger is effectively unreachable in normal operation: the sole writer of picks-history/latest.json is snapshot-picks.js line 285, copying `result` whose asOf (line 220) is ALWAYS a non-empty ISO string (`RUN_DATE_UTC+'T00:00:00.000Z'` or `new Date().toISOString()`). No code path emits a blank/missing asOf. Missing asOf requires external file corruption or a future writer regression. Net: at most LOW defensive hardening, not a HIGH data-integrity hole.

title: whyDropped only inspects methods present in the PRIOR vintage; a method newly added since prior that flips a pick out is never reported

title: Ticker / method-id values interpolated into HTML without escaping (stored-XSS / markup-corruption if a symbol contains < & ")
evidence: pick-diff.js line 185 `m.added.map(t => '' + t + '')` and line 192 `'' + r.ticker + ''` inject ticker strings raw; whyDropped strings (method ids) at line 192 likewise. compute-method-drift.js line 96 `${methodId}` injects method ids raw. _verdict.note: CONFIRMED real, low severity. Both raw interpolations exist as cited: pick-diff.js line 185 (`m.added.map(t => '' + t + '')`) and line 192 (`'' + r.ticker + ''`), plus compute-method-drift.js line 96 (`${methodId}`). Both HTML files land in outputs/*.html which daily-pull.yml lines 660-697 deploy to public GitHub Pages. Reachability of the TICKER vector is real, not purely operator-curated: refresh-universe.js (lines 218-229 and 277-283) ingests symbols from Yahoo's screener/exchange API and filters only `$`, `/`, `\`, whitespace, and length>12 — it does NOT strip `<`, `>`, `&`, `"`. A corrupt/crafted Yahoo symbol containing those chars (<=12, no $/slash/space) survives, enters the watchlist -> picks-history, and reaches pick-diff.html unescaped (added or removed table). So markup-corruption / reflected-from-data XSS is technically possible. Two mitigants keeping severity at low: (1) the symbol must survive the mcap filter ($1B-$500B) and actually become/leave a pick; (2) the methodId path in compute-method-drift.js line 96 is NOT externally controllable — method IDs are internal code-defined slugs (above-200d-ma, fcf-yield, etc.), so that part is defense-in-depth only, not a live vector. title: jaccard() doc-comment says 'Jaccard distance' but the function returns Jaccard SIMILARITY (intersection/union)
evidence: Line 41 comment: 'Jaccard distance = |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|. 1.0 = identical, 0.0 = no overlap.' That formula and the 1.0=identical semantics are the Jaccard *index/similarity*; Jaccard *distance* = 1 - that. The code (line 48 `inter / union`) correctly computes similarity, matching how it is consumed (line 172 `m.jaccard >= 0.7 ? 'jac-good'`), so behavior is fine — only the term 'distance' is wrong.
why_it_matters: Mislabeled metric in an audit doc invites a future 'fix' that inverts it (1 - x) to match the word 'distance', which would silently flip every stability threshold (0.7 good becomes 0.3 good). Terminology bugs in shared diagnostics are how downstream regressions get introduced.
fix: Change the comment to 'Jaccard similarity (index)' and keep the formula/behavior.

_verdict.note: Confirmed by source. scripts/pick-diff.js line 41 comment reads "Jaccard distance = |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|. 1.0 = identical, 0.0 = no overlap." The formula intersection/union and the "1.0=identical" semantics are the Jaccard similarity/index, NOT distance (distance = 1 - similarity, where 1.0 would mean no overlap). Code at line 48 returns inter/union (similarity) and line 44 returns 1.0 for empty/empty (identical) — both similarity semantics. Consumers agree: line 172 treats jaccard>=0.7 as 'jac-good' and line 167 documents "Jaccard ≥ 0.7 = healthy stability" (higher = more overlap = healthier). So behavior is correct; only the word "distance" in the doc-comment is wrong. Cosmetic doc inaccuracy, no functional impact. Severity low is correct.

title: sh() swallows all git errors and returns '' — a broken git invocation makes the audit report 'No commits' and pass green
evidence: Line 46-49 `function sh(cmd){ try{...execSync...}catch(e){ return ''; } }`. Line 71 `const commits = sh('git log ...').trim().split('\n').filter(Boolean);` — if git fails (not a repo, bad --since syntax, detached state), commits===[] and line 72-74 prints 'No commits touching methods/ since ...' and returns 0, including under --strict.

').filter(Boolean) === [], so commits.length===0 hits lines 72-75 ('No commits touching methods/ since ...' + return 0). title: computableCount counts any result with pass!=null, so a method that errored-but-recorded {error,pass:null} is correctly excluded — but a recorded {pass:false} from an incomputable-coerced result inflates computable
evidence: Lines 44-46: `if (r.pass != null) counters[methodId].computableCount++; if (r.pass === true) counters[methodId].passCount++;`. This treats pass===false as computable. That is correct ONLY if every method sets pass:false strictly when computable. Methods like price-momentum-12-1.js return `{computable:false, pass:false, ...}` on the not-computable branches (methods/price-momentum-12-1.js:179, 192, 247) — pass:false WITH computable:false. compute-method-drift never reads r.computable, so those incomputable-but-pass:false records are counted as computable and as failures.
why_it_matters: The drift sparkline's 'Computable %' column (line 93 last.computableCount/totalStocks) and the pass-count trend over-count coverage for every method that emits pass:false on its not-computable path. The frühwarn signal (a method's coverage quietly collapsing) is muted because incomputable rows masquerade as computable-fails.
fix: Gate on the result's computable flag, not pass: `const computable = r.computable === true || (r.computable == null && r.pass != null); if (computable) computableCount++; if (computable && r.pass === true) passCount++;` — or, better, have methods-history record an explicit computable flag and key off it consistently across compute-method-drift, pick-diff and the probe.

_verdict.note:
False positive — the auditor reasoned about the method's raw buildResult return shape but compute-method-drift never sees that shape; it reads methods-history snapshots, which are already coerced.

Chain of evidence:
1. methods/_helpers.js:58-68 buildResult always emits pass:!!pass and computable:!!computable, so price-momentum-12-1.js incomputable branches (lines 179/192/247) DO return {computable:false, pass:false} at the method level. Auditor correct so far.
2. BUT snapshot-methods-history.js:122 is the only writer of methods-history, and it stores a trimmed shape: `compact[mid] = { value: r.computable ? r.value : null, pass: r.computable ? r.pass : null }`. It already nulls pass whenever computable is false and drops the computable field entirely. So an incomputable method is persisted as {value:null, pass:null} — exactly the gating the auditor proposes, applied upstream.
3. compute-method-drift.js:24,36 reads those history JSONs (HIST_DIR = methods-history/), not raw method output.
4. Empirical scan of all 28 vintages / 8,311,196 records in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/methods-history: every record has exactly key-shape {pass,value}; 0 records carry a computable field; 2,396,682 records have pass===false; 0 of those have computable===false. So in the data drift actually reads, `pass != null` is a writer-enforced exact proxy for computable===true. The incomputable-but-pass:false records the finding worries about do not exist in methods-history.

Therefore computableCount (r.pass != null) and passCount (r.pass === true) at lines 45-46 are correct; nothing is inflated. The cited line 247 etc. records are coerced to pass:null before drift ever sees them.

fix_safe=false: the proposed fix references r.computable, which is never stored in history. On current data the new `r.computable === true` branch is always false so the `r.computable == null && r.pass != null` fallback makes it a no-op (behavior-preserving by accident), but the change is grounded in a misread of the data flow and should not be auto-applied. The only legitimate improvement here would be the auditor's secondary suggestion (persist an explicit computable flag in snapshot-methods-history.js and key all consumers off it) — that's a cross-file design change needing human review, not a low-risk drift-script tweak.

title: isPresent() counts all-null balance/SGA/depreciation arrays as present, blinding drift detection for object-row fields
evidence: isPresent() at :95-101: for arrays it returns true if any element passes, but the element test at :99 is `if (typeof x === 'object' && 'value' in x) return Number.isFinite(x.value);` followed by :99 fallthrough `return true; // balance-row objects etc. count`. Tracked fields `annual.annualBalance` (:47), `annual.annualSGA` (:55), `annual.annualDepreciation` (:56) are arrays of period objects that do NOT carry a top-level `value` key (they are balance rows like `{date, totalDebt, ...}`), so they hit the unconditional `return true`. An array of N objects that are all present-but-empty (every numeric field null) is therefore scored 'present'.
why_it_matters: The comment at :91-94 explicitly says the fix was to stop counting 'an array of all-null placeholders' as present, but that fix only applies to elements that are numbers or have a `value` key. For balance/SGA/depreciation rows the old blind-spot remains: Yahoo delivering empty balance objects (the Bug #26 positional-alignment artifact named at :92) still reads as 100% coverage, so altman-z / net-debt-ebitda / ohlson-o inputs can silently go empty with no drift alert.
fix: For object array elements without a `value` key, count present only if at least one own enumerable property is a finite number (e.g. `Object.values(x).some(Number.isFinite)`), rather than `return true`. Keep the 'value'-wrapper branch as-is.

_verdict.note: REFUTED — premise misreads the snapshot schema. The claim says annual.annualSGA and annual.annualDepreciation are "arrays of period objects without a top-level value key (balance rows like {date,totalDebt,...})". That is false: both are produced by _ftsExtractByYear (pull-yahoo.js:1072-1081), which pushes the raw scalar from _ftsValue (:1053-1066) or null — i.e. arrays of PLAIN NUMBERS like [12345,11000,null], not objects. In isPresent() they hit field-coverage.js:97 (typeof x==='number' -> Number.isFinite(x)), so an all-null SGA/Depreciation array correctly returns false. The :99 `return true` fallthrough is never reached for them. Only annual.annualBalance is genuinely an object-array without a `value` key, so it does reach the `return true` at :99 — but the claim's harmful scenario (an array of objects that are all "present-but-empty", every numeric field null, scored present) cannot occur: both balance constructors emit `null` (not an empty object) when every field is null — quoteSummary path returns null then .filter(Boolean) strips it (pull-yahoo.js:690-692); FTS path pushes null placeholder (pull-yahoo.js:1177-1182). Every object that actually reaches the array therefore has >=1 finite numeric field, and null entries short-circuit at field-coverage.js:96. The currency-conversion scale() (pull-yahoo.js:373-388) preserves structure and never fabricates all-null objects. So no realistic input blinds drift detection.

title: earningsDate Yahoo envelope only handles {raw}; a {fmt}-only or already-Date-array entry yields null and the earnings date is silently dropped
evidence: Line 33: `const iso = (first instanceof Date) ? first.toISOString() : (first && first.raw ? new Date(first.raw * 1000).toISOString() : null);`. yahoo-finance2 v3 returns calendarEvents.earnings.earningsDate as an array of Date objects in the typed path, but under `validation.logErrors:false` (configured :13-15) and schema drift it can fall back to raw envelope objects `{raw, fmt}`. If `first.raw` is 0/undefined but `first.fmt` is a date string, iso=null and the stock is skipped. The whole try/catch at :36 also swallows EVERY error with a bare `/* skip */` comment.
why_it_matters: earnings-calendar.json is consumed by earnings-cli.js and the dashboard; a stock whose earnings date comes back as fmt-only just vanishes from the calendar with zero diagnostic. Combined with the silent catch, a Yahoo schema shift could empty large swaths of the calendar and the run still prints '✓ Saved' (:48) with a low count nobody notices.
fix: Broaden the unwrap to handle all three shapes: Date -> toISOString; `{raw}` -> epoch*1000; `{fmt}` or string -> `new Date(first.fmt || first)`. Add a per-ticker skip counter and log a WARN summary at the end (`skipped N of M for parse/empty`) instead of a blind `/* skip */`, so silent attrition is visible.

_verdict.note:
False positive based on a misread of yahoo-finance2 v3's runtime coercion. I traced the actual library code in the worktree's node_modules (yahoo-finance2 ^3.14.0).

The schema (quoteSummary.schema.js:340) types each earningsDate item as {type:"string", format:"date-time"}. The date-time coercer (esm/src/lib/validate/types/string.js) runs on EVERY quoteSummary response and handles exactly these shapes: (a) Date -> kept as Date; (b) number -> new Date(n*1000); (c) {raw:number} envelope -> UNWRAPPED to new Date(raw*1000) at lines 43-46; (d) ISO/date string -> new Date(input); (e) {} -> null. ANYTHING ELSE (including a {fmt}-only object with no numeric raw) pushes a validation error (lines 55-62).

Consequences that refute the claim:
1. A {raw,fmt} envelope is converted to a Date INSIDE the library before reaching the caller. So at pull-earnings-dates.js:33, `first` is already a Date -> `first instanceof Date` is true -> iso is set correctly. The `first.raw` branch on line 33 is effectively dead code; it never sees a raw envelope. The claim that this unwrap is "too narrow" is moot.
2. A {fmt}-only / un-coercible entry does NOT silently reach line 33 and yield iso=null. It fails coercion, and validateAndCoerceTypes.js:214 THROWS FailedYahooValidationError for result-type validation. The throw happens regardless of logErrors:false — logErrors only gates the console logging (line 183), NOT the throw (confirmed: the throw at line 214 is outside the `if (options.logErrors)` block). So the claim's premise that logErrors:false lets raw/fmt envelopes "fall through to the caller" is factually wrong; the call at line 28 throws and is caught at line 36.

So the title's mechanism ("a {fmt}-only entry yields null on line 33 and is silently dropped") cannot occur. The proposed fix (broaden unwrap to handle {fmt}|string) would add dead code for a shape that never arrives.

The ONE legitimate residual point is the bare `catch (e) { /* skip */ }` (line 36): it does swallow all per-ticker errors with no counter/WARN summary, so attrition (including genuine schema-drift throws) is invisible at this script's level. That is a real observability/code-quality gap — but it is low severity, not the high-severity silent-parse-drop the finding describes, and the repo already has tests/yahoo-schema-canary.js independently monitoring schema drift on an anchor symbol.

title: todaysSnapshot stores asOf:`today` (UTC calendar date) even though the close is the last actual trading day — re-introduces the weekend phantom-date the history path was fixed for
evidence: Line 116: `todaysSnapshot[stock.ticker] = { close: latestClose, asOf: today, ... }` where `today` is UTC `new Date().toISOString().slice(0,10)` (:60). The very next block (:104-115) goes to great lengths via `latestQuoteDate` to store the REAL exchange date in history.json specifically because (per the Tag 231a-3 comment :104-112) using calendar `today` on a weekend mapped Saturday to Friday's close. But the per-day snapshot file `prices/${today}.json` (:193) still records `asOf: today`, not `latestQuoteDate`.
why_it_matters: Any consumer that reads the daily prices/<date>.json snapshot (rather than history.json) gets the same weekend/holiday phantom-date the history fix was meant to eliminate — asymmetric correctness between the two outputs of the same loop. It also makes the two files disagree about what date a price belongs to.
fix: Use `latestQuoteDate` for the snapshot's `asOf` as well (or add both `asOf: today` and `tradeDate: latestQuoteDate`). Carry a comment naming the failure mode: 'weekend phantom-date — snapshot asOf must be the exchange trade date, not UTC calendar today.'

_verdict.note:
Factual observation is accurate but the impact claim is a false positive. Line 116 does write `asOf: today` (UTC calendar) while the history path (lines 126-127) writes `latestQuoteDate`. BUT the Tag 231a-3 phantom-date bug was harmful only because history.json is a date-KEYED time series (`{date, close}` arrays) consumed by date-sensitive lookups (scripts/walk-forward-perf.js, scripts/macro-regime.js, fitness/measure.js, backtest-*.js) that map a date to a price — a `{date:Saturday, close:Friday-price}` row corrupts those lookups. That path is correctly fixed and is NOT touched by this finding.

The per-day snapshot `prices/YYYY-MM-DD.json` (line 193) is a different artifact: a flat ticker->{close, asOf, currency} map whose date identity is its FILENAME (`${today}.json`), not the inner `asOf`. I traced every consumer of the dated price files repo-wide: the only readers are (1) the writer itself, (2) scripts/archive-old-snapshots.js (line 171-180 — archives by filename date, explicitly commented "daily snapshots, not history.json"), and (3) scripts/backfill-prices.js (operates on history.json, never reads the dated snapshots). No date-sensitive code ever maps the snapshot's `asOf` to a price, so no phantom-date row and no date->price mismatch is produced. The snapshot-freshness gate (README:273) reads `asOf` from the separate snapshots/ fundamentals directory (scripts/tag229a-stale-snapshot-verify.js SNAP_DIR=snapshots, getExistingSnapshotAge), not these price files. As a "when was this snapshot taken" timestamp, `today` is arguably the more correct value (using Friday for a Saturday pull would make a fresh snapshot look staler). At worst this is a cosmetic asOf/filename redundancy, not a data-integrity defect.

fix_safe=false: the proposed change is not purely behavior-preserving — switching `asOf` to `latestQuoteDate` (or adding a `tradeDate` field) alters the value/schema of a written daily artifact for zero downstream benefit and could shift the meaning of a field other tooling may compare. Needs human review, not auto-apply.

title: Non-SPY tickers only ever get ONE day appended per run, so the 252-day momentum/backtest history takes a year of clean runs to build and any gap is never back-filled
evidence: In processOne() the history extension (:119-129) appends only the single latest quote: `if (arr.length===0 || arr[arr.length-1].date !== latestQuoteDate) arr.push({date, close})`. The full multi-hundred-day `quotes` array fetched at :96-100 is discarded except for its last element. Only SPY gets a real back-fill loop (:172-182). So for every normal ticker, history.json grows exactly one row per daily workflow run.
why_it_matters: price-momentum-12-1.js needs LOOKBACK_FULL_DAILY=252 entries for the proper path (:205-207) and 84 for even the degraded path; walk-forward-perf.js needs a year of dated points. Until ~252 successful consecutive daily runs accumulate, every non-benchmark stock is stuck on the degraded/incomputable path. Worse, any day the run fails or a ticker errors (:131-134) leaves a permanent hole that is never repaired (only backfill-prices.js, run manually, can fill it). This is a direct structural cap on the momentum factor and backtest coverage.
fix: Back-fill all fetched quotes for every ticker the same way SPY is handled (:172-182): build a Set of known dates and insert every missing dated quote, then sort+cap to 400. The data is already fetched — discarding it is pure waste. Carry a comment: 'prevents permanent history gaps / 252-day warm-up — back-fill all fetched bars, not just the latest.'

_verdict.note: Mechanism is accurate: in pull-historical-prices.js processOne() (lines 119-129) every non-SPY ticker appends only the single latest quote; the ~280-bar `quotes` array fetched at :96-100 is discarded except its last element. Only SPY back-fills (:172-182). So in steady state each history[ticker] grows by one row per run. BUT severity is overstated on three counts. (1) The daily cron runs every US trading day ('17 2 * * 2-6'), so one-append-per-run DOES accrue continuous daily coverage — the "year of warm-up" only applies to a brand-new empty ticker, and even then is seeded by the bulk tools below. It is NOT per-run data loss. (2) The named consumers are all DIAGNOSTIC-only: price-momentum-12-1.js is explicitly NOT in SCORE_WEIGHTS (line 57) and I confirmed the full SCORE_WEIGHTS table (score-aggregator.js:32-73) contains none of the six methods that read prices/history.json (momentum/above-200d/volatility/drawdown/high-proximity/insider-conviction). The scored, fixture-hash-gated picks are unaffected; momentum even has an explicit <252d degraded path (:35-42,237-278). (3) The "pure waste / gap never back-filled" claim ignores TWO dedicated scripts that write the SAME file with exactly the proposed merge-all logic: pull-prices-bulk.js (100d/ticker) and scripts/backfill-prices.js (~400d, fetched-wins-on-collision, sort, cap 400). The capability exists; it is just split out of the daily incremental puller by design. The one genuine continuous-coverage consumer (scripts/walk-forward-perf.js priceAt entry/exit lookups) is additionally guarded by the F-BT-001 freshness/coverage abort, so it fails loud rather than emitting silently-wrong returns. Real but minor robustness/cold-start gap, not a high data-integrity defect.

title: Universe membership keyed on ticker.toUpperCase() but merge stores yahoo_symbol = info.ticker (already upper) — case/suffix-normalized symbols can never match Yahoo and survivorship is asymmetric
evidence: existing-set built upper at :205 `wlRaw.stocks.map(s => s.ticker.toUpperCase())`; new entries pushed at :438-447 set both `ticker: info.ticker` and `yahoo_symbol: info.ticker` where info.ticker was upper-cased at discovery (:222 `q.symbol.toUpperCase()`, :279). For non-US venues Yahoo symbols are case- and suffix-sensitive (e.g. `7203.T`, `RoG.SW`, `nestle` vs `NESN.SW`). Forcing yahoo_symbol to the upper-cased bare symbol means pull-yahoo will query a symbol Yahoo doesn't recognize for many foreign listings.
why_it_matters: Foreign tickers (the REGIONS/EXCHANGE_CODES expansion at :86/:90-121 is the whole point of the multi-region pull) get added with a yahoo_symbol Yahoo rejects, so they silently fail every daily pull and never produce a snapshot — asymmetric survivorship that quietly biases the universe toward US names while the universe-size gate (daily-pull.yml) still counts them as 'present'. No hardcoded exclusion is needed — the guard itself is wrong.
fix: Preserve Yahoo's original-case symbol from the screener quote (`q.symbol`) as `yahoo_symbol`, and only upper-case the internal `ticker` dedupe key. Track exchange suffix where the discovery source provides it. Comment the failure mode: 'foreign-listing case/suffix loss — yahoo_symbol must keep Yahoo's exact casing.'

_verdict.note:
REFUTED on both core claims with source + empirical evidence.

(1) SUFFIX-LOSS claim is false. The finding asserts `yahoo_symbol` becomes "the upper-cased BARE symbol" with the exchange suffix lost. But `String.toUpperCase()` cannot strip a `.XX` suffix — it only changes letter case. Verified directly: `"7203.T".toUpperCase()` => `"7203.T"`, `"000270.KS".toUpperCase()` => `"000270.KS"`, `"BP.L"` => `"BP.L"`. Suffixes are intact. Upstream, discovery sources append the Yahoo suffix and use the SUFFIXED string as the map key, so `info.ticker` already carries it: finnhub.js toYahooSymbol() (lines 54-61) appends `.T/.HK/.SW/.SI` etc.; wikipedia-indices.js (lines 100-103) appends `.L/.DE`. The Yahoo screener endpoint itself returns suffixed symbols (e.g. `7203.T`). Ground truth: the worktree watchlist.json has 23,748 stocks of which 1,325 carry foreign suffixes (.KS=26, .HK=115, .T=221, .DE=119, .L=267, .SW=47, .PA=101, .AX=116, ...) and every one stores `yahoo_symbol` WITH the suffix (e.g. {ticker:"005930.KS", yahoo_symbol:"005930.KS"}, ABBN.SW, NESN-class .SW set). No suffix is being lost.

(2) CASE-SENSITIVITY claim is false. The finding says foreign Yahoo symbols are case-sensitive and uppercasing breaks them, citing `RoG.SW` and `nestle` vs `NESN.SW`. I tested the live yahoo-finance2 quote endpoint in the worktree: `yf.quote('nesn.sw')` and `yf.quote('NESN.SW')` BOTH return `NESN.SW` Nestlé S.A. — Yahoo's API is case-INSENSITIVE and normalizes the symbol back to canonical uppercase. So even a hypothetical mixed-case input would resolve correctly. Moreover the premise is wrong: Yahoo represents these tickers in uppercase (ROG.SW, NESN.SW), not mixed case; the cited `RoG.SW`/`nestle` forms do not occur. Confirmed: zero watchlist entries contain any lowercase letter, so no source ever emits a mixed-case Yahoo symbol that could be 'corrupted'.

Files inspected: C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/refresh-universe.js (lines 205, 218-239, 277-296, 438-448), discovery/finnhub.js, discovery/wikipedia-indices.js, discovery/sec-tickers.js, discovery/nasdaq-all.js, pull-yahoo.js (yahoo_symbol consumer at lines 1536/1681/1687/1800), watchlist.json. The asymmetric-survivorship angle also fails: both the existing-set key (:205) and the dedupe key (:220/:279) use the SAME toUpperCase() normalization, so membership is symmetric, not asymmetric.

title: Object.assign mutates the `existing` object in place and lets blank/garbage CSV rows overwrite good prior scores; no validation of score range
evidence: Line 38: `const merged = Object.assign(existing, data);` mutates `existing` (the parsed prior file) rather than merging into a fresh object — harmless for the single write here but a footgun. More importantly, parseFloat at :27 accepts out-of-range or malformed values: `parseFloat('8.5x')` -> 8.5, `parseFloat('500')` -> 500 (scores are documented 0-10 at :4). Any newly-imported ticker with a worse/garbage score unconditionally overwrites the prior good score (last-writer-wins with no recency or validity check). The header skip at :24 `line.toLowerCase().startsWith('ticker')` also silently drops any real ticker literally named 'TICKER'-prefixed only by coincidence (minor).
why_it_matters: external-data/aktienfinder.json feeds the scoring overlay; a bad export (truncated CSV, locale decimal comma turning '8,5' into NaN-skip or '8' partial) can silently degrade or wipe correct scores. Not wired into any workflow (manual CLI), so blast radius is bounded, but the data it writes is consumed by the scorer.
fix: Use `Object.assign({}, existing, data)` (don't mutate the source). Validate `score >= 0 && score <= 10` before accepting a row; warn-and-skip otherwise. Reject rows whose scoreStr isn't a clean numeric (`/^\d+(\.\d+)?$/` after trim, accounting for decimal comma). Consider keeping the higher/more-recent score on conflict instead of blind overwrite.

_verdict.note:
Mostly a false positive / non-issue, confirmed by reading the file and tracing consumers in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening.

DEAD OUTPUT — no impact: Nothing reads external-data/aktienfinder.json. The aktienfinder-quality method is listed in methods/method-types.js DISABLED ("Manueller CSV-Import skaliert nicht", since 2026-05-08) and its method file doesn't even exist (Glob methods/aktienfinder*.js = none). pull-yahoo.js:930 only carries a stale comment "// aktienfinderScore via Bookmarklet manuell synced" and never loads the JSON. So even a garbage/out-of-range score has zero pipeline effect today.

Per-claim:
1. Object.assign(existing,data) mutation (line 38): real but harmless. `existing` is a freshly parsed throwaway local (lines 34-37), written once via writeFileAtomic, then process exits at main()/line 43. Never reused. Auditor concedes "harmless for the single write here."
2. parseFloat range/garbage (line 27): technically true — parseFloat('8.5x')=8.5, parseFloat('500')=500, no 0-10 clamp. But the input is Karl's own manually-exported Aktienfinder bookmarklet CSV (single-user, trusted, hand-curated per the header doc), not untrusted data. Low realism.
3. last-writer-wins "overwrites good prior score": that is the intended, documented merge-on-reimport behavior, not a defect. A re-import is supposed to update.
4. header-skip dropping a 'TICKER'-prefixed symbol (line 24): no real ticker starts with the literal string "ticker"; auditor labels it "minor." Non-issue.

Note the earlier atomic-write concern from audit 2026-05-19 (state-management.json) is already fixed — the script uses writeFileAtomic.

title: Universe hard-cap drops tickers by mcap rank with no protection for already-in-watchlist names — established holdings can be evicted by newly-discovered larger caps
evidence: When allTickers.size > MAX_UNIVERSE (:382) the cap (:386-401) sorts purely by descending marketCap and slices, with the only carve-out being a 20% null-mcap quota (:393-396). The `existing` watchlist set (:205) is NOT given priority. allTickers is built from discovery sources and includes both new and re-discovered existing tickers; an existing tracked stock that this run re-discovers with a now-smaller mcap (or null mcap beyond the 20% quota) can be sliced out of `capped`, and since the merge at :409-413 only ADDS new tickers and never removes, the stock stays in the watchlist — but if a future run rebuilds from the capped set it is lost.
why_it_matters: Survivorship/attrition asymmetry: the universe can quietly shed mid-caps that drifted just under a rank threshold, biasing backtests upward (only survivors remain) — the classic look-ahead/survivorship trap the audit brief calls out. The cap is a blunt instrument applied before existing-membership is considered.
fix: Before the mcap slice, force-include every ticker already in `existing` (they're already being tracked; pin them). Apply the cap only to genuinely-new discoveries. Comment the failure mode: 'survivorship attrition — never evict an already-tracked ticker via the discovery mcap cap.'

_verdict.note: False positive. The finding's own evidence concedes the decisive fact: the merge at refresh-universe.js:438-448 only ADDS newTickers and never removes — existing watchlist entries are left untouched in wlRaw.stocks. The mcap cap (:382-402) operates solely on the in-memory allTickers Map, which is used only to compute newTickers (tickers NOT in `existing`, :411-412). An already-tracked ticker that falls out of `capped` is simply not re-added; it stays in the watchlist. The alleged harm rests entirely on a conditional that does not exist anywhere in the codebase: "if a future run rebuilds from the capped set it is lost." Verified: (1) refresh-universe.js never does `wlRaw.stocks = <capped>` (grep for `.stocks =` from capped set: no matches; it only .push()es and sorts); (2) the sole watchlist remover, scripts/prune-watchlist.js, prunes by snapshot delisted/no-data/orphan status, fully independent of the mcap cap, and never references allTickers; (3) the CI chain in .github/workflows/daily-pull.yml (refresh -> prune -> pull) has no rebuild-from-capped step; (4) suggest-watchlist-additions/cleanup do not rebuild from the capped universe. Furthermore MAX_UNIVERSE=25000 sits above the ~15.7k existing watchlist by design (Tag 227a comment, :374-379), so the cap rarely bites and cannot evict tracked names even when it does. No survivorship-attrition path is reachable in the current code.

title: Redundant Object.fromEntries(...)/Object.values round-trip over the SEC ticker map, and --max slices an arbitrary insertion-ordered subset (no determinism / no prioritization)
evidence: Line 124: `const entries = Object.values(Object.fromEntries(tickers));` — `tickers` is a Map (used as Map at :111 `tickers.size`); `Object.fromEntries(map)` then `Object.values` rebuilds an array that `[...tickers.values()]` would produce directly, and collapses any duplicate keys silently. Then :125 `const todo = entries.slice(0, args.max)` takes the first N in map-insertion order — so a partial `--max` run always re-pulls the same head of the list and may never reach the tail across runs.
why_it_matters: Minor perf/allocation waste, but the slice-by-insertion-order means `--max`-limited runs (or the >50-error/>200-429 abort gates at :165/:173) systematically under-serve tail tickers; combined with the 90-day stale skip (:131) the tail may rarely refresh. Low severity because the monthly full run normally has max=Infinity.
fix: Replace with `const entries = [...tickers.values()];`. If `--max` is used operationally, sort `todo` by oldest `fetchedAt` first (round-robin freshness) so partial runs make uniform progress instead of re-pulling the head.

_verdict.note: See structured note. fix_safe=false because the proposed_fix bundles a behavior-CHANGING step (sort todo by oldest fetchedAt) with the safe cosmetic refactor. Part 1 (`[...tickers.values()]`) alone is behavior-preserving and safe. Part 2 changes which tickers a bounded run pulls, requires joining against manifest.entries (keyed by CIK), and would be meaningless in the actual CI deployment where the cache is ephemeral and fetchedAt-based freshness ordering does not translate to coverage gains — so it needs human review, not auto-apply.

title: Benchmark ETFs are unshifted into the in-memory watchlist every run but the array is never the watchlist on disk — harmless here, but currency field for benchmarks/foreign stocks is stored without FX normalization
evidence: Lines 116/160 store `currency: result.meta && result.meta.currency` alongside an unadjusted-for-FX close. history.json (:127, :177) stores ONLY `{date, close}` and drops the currency entirely. So a London or Tokyo stock's close is recorded in GBp/JPY with no currency tag in history, while the daily snapshot keeps currency but the consumers (price-momentum, walk-forward) read history.json which has none.
why_it_matters: Returns are scale-invariant to a constant currency, so single-ticker momentum is unaffected — BUT cross-sectional comparisons and any alpha-vs-SPY computation in walk-forward (:10) implicitly assume comparable units; a foreign stock whose Yahoo currency silently switches (e.g. GBP vs GBp pence, a known Yahoo quirk) injects a 100x jump indistinguishable from a real move, with no currency context retained in history.json to detect it.
fix: Either normalize foreign closes to a single currency before storing in history.json (using fx-rates.json already present in the repo), or persist the per-entry currency so downstream can detect a unit switch. At minimum flag GBp/ZAc pence-vs-pound style currencies. Document the failure mode in the comment.

_verdict.note: False positive — the asserted harm does not exist. The two named consumers compute currency-UNIT-INVARIANT quantities within a single ticker's own series, so a missing currency tag in prices/history.json cannot corrupt them. price-momentum-12-1.js (methods/price-momentum-12-1.js:209,253) computes priceLastMonth/priceOneYearAgo-1 and (priceNow-lo)/(hi-lo) — pure within-series ratios; a London stock stored consistently in GBp yields the identical momentum as if stored in GBP/USD. walk-forward-perf.js (scripts/walk-forward-perf.js:150-153 returnPct = (p1-p0)/p0) likewise computes per-ticker returns; alpha is pickMedianReturn − benchmarkReturn, a difference of two already-unitless percentages (lines 514-520). The benchmark canonical-date anchoring (Tag 231a-2) aligns DATES, not currencies — no cross-currency level arithmetic exists anywhere in either consumer, nor in the other history.json readers (above-200d-ma, drawdown-52w, high-proximity-52w, volatility-annualized — all single-ticker ratios). Yahoo's yf.chart() returns one consistent currency per symbol across the whole series (pull-historical-prices.js:96-116), so there is no within-series unit mix. The only mode that WOULD matter, a mid-series currency redenomination, is exceptionally rare and the snapshot's currency field would NOT help walk-forward anyway since walk-forward reads only history.json. FX normalization in pull-yahoo.js (loadFx / _convertSnapshotToUSD, incl. the GBp ÷100 handling at :303-333) applies to the SNAPSHOT/financials path for cross-stock ratio comparability, not to the per-ticker return series. The title's first half ("benchmark ETFs unshifted into in-memory watchlist, array never written to disk") is true but the auditor itself labels it harmless — wl.stocks.unshift (line 58) mutates only the in-memory copy; wl is never persisted. Net: nothing for these consumers to gain from a per-entry currency tag.

title: Pass-Count filter silently leaves matrix rows ranked 201-300 visible (map holds only 200, matrix renders 300)
evidence: STOCK_DATA_MAP is built only from topPicksRanked = ranked.slice(0, TOP_PICKS_N) with TOP_PICKS_N=200 (line 337). The matrix renders matrixRanked = ...slice(0, TOP_MATRIX_N) with TOP_MATRIX_N=300 (line 432-437). applyPassCount iterates BOTH tables: `var allRows = document.querySelectorAll('#matrix tbody tr, #top-picks-tbody tr');` then `var data = STOCK_DATA_MAP[tr.dataset.ticker]; if (!data) return;` (lines 966-974). For the 100 matrix rows ranked 201-300 there is no map entry, so the callback returns BEFORE `tr.classList.toggle('pc-hidden', !show)` ever runs. Those rows stay visible at every threshold and are also excluded from the `total`/`visible` counters (lines 982-986).
why_it_matters: The Pass-Count >= N filter is the primary triage control on the matrix. 1/3 of the visible matrix rows (the lowest-ranked 100) ignore it entirely, so a stock with passCount=2 sitting at rank 250 stays on screen when Karl sets the filter to >=8. The on-screen 'X / Y >= N pass' count is also understated because those rows are never counted. The old per-row data-row blob (removed in Tag 221c) covered all rendered rows; the STOCK_DATA_MAP refactor narrowed coverage to 200 without shrinking the matrix to match.
fix: Make the rendered set and the data map share one source of truth. Cleanest: drive both the matrix slice and STOCK_DATA_MAP from the same N (e.g. include every ticker that appears in either table in stockDataMap), OR set TOP_MATRIX_N === TOP_PICKS_N. Minimal: when building stockDataMap, also add matrixRanked entries. Add a comment naming the failure mode: '// prevents pass-count filter no-op on matrix rows beyond TOP_PICKS_N (map/render set divergence)'.

_verdict.note:
CONFIRMED real via source. STOCK_DATA_MAP is built only from topPicksRanked = ranked.slice(0,200) (lines 336-373). The matrix renders matrixRanked = [...rows].sort(...).slice(0, TOP_MATRIX_N=300) (lines 432-438, 836). ranked (line 264-268) and matrixRanked (433-437) use the IDENTICAL comparator (passCount desc, computableCount desc, ticker asc) over the same `rows`, so the matrix's first 200 tickers equal the map's keys and rows 201-300 are 100 distinct tickers with no map entry. applyPassCount (lines 964-987) selects `#matrix tbody tr, #top-picks-tbody tr` (line 966 — `#matrix tbody tr` matches all 300 matrix rows), then `var data = STOCK_DATA_MAP[tr.dataset.ticker]; if (!data) return;` (lines 973-974) returns BEFORE `tr.classList.toggle('pc-hidden', !show)` (line 981) for those 100 rows. Result: pass-count filter is a no-op on matrix ranks 201-300 (they stay visible at every threshold) and they are also excluded from the total/visible counters (982-983). The author comment at 970-972 ("matrix rows without an entry skip silently (same as before)") shows they assumed harmlessness but missed that the matrix renders more rows (300) than the map holds (200).

Severity revised high->low: this is a UI-only interactive-filter correctness defect in a generated HTML report. The matrix lives inside a collapsed <details> and the pass-count filter is a browsing convenience; no data corruption, no wrong screener output, no pipeline/CI impact. Visible symptom is 100 stale-visible rows plus an undercounted "x / y >= min" badge — genuine but low-stakes/cosmetic.

fix_safe=false: NOT a safe auto-apply. (a) Setting TOP_MATRIX_N === TOP_PICKS_N drops 100 rendered matrix rows — a behavior change, not behavior-preserving. (b) Adding matrixRanked entries to stockDataMap enlarges the embedded JSON, directly fighting the heavily-documented size-reduction goal of prior audit fixes (Tag 221c/222b: slim the map, keep output <10MB / drop 267MB->5MB). Adding ~100 more full results+trends entries risks regressing the artifact-size constraint those commits exist to protect. Choosing which N to converge on, and accepting the size impact, is a human tradeoff call.

title: methodHistory fallback to alert-state only fires when sidecar yields ZERO keys; a stale/partial sidecar silently suppresses trend data
evidence: The sidecar method-history-state.json is read first (lines 50-58). The legacy fallback runs only `if (!Object.keys(methodHistory).length && fs.existsSync(args.state))` (line 59). So if the sidecar exists and parses to even one ticker, the alert-state fallback is skipped entirely. Both the sidecar read (line 57) and the legacy read (line 63) swallow parse errors with empty catch blocks, after which methodHistory may be `{}` and every trend silently becomes 'n/a' (Trend.computeTrend returns direction:'n/a' for empty history, methods/trend.js line 21-23).
why_it_matters: The trend arrows (↑/↓/·) are a core signal in the matrix and modal. A corrupted or partially-written sidecar (the file is ~55MB per the directory listing; a truncated write would still JSON.parse-fail into the empty catch, or parse to a subset) makes trends degrade to blank with no log line and no fallback to the older alert-state data. The failure is invisible — the report renders 'successfully' with a silently dead column.
fix: Log a warning in each catch (line 57, 63) instead of silent ignore, and merge sidecar+legacy rather than treating sidecar presence as exclusive: if the sidecar parsed but a given ticker is missing, fall back per-ticker. At minimum emit `console.warn` with the parse error and the count of tickers loaded so a regression is visible in CI logs. Comment: '// prevents silent trend-column blackout when the history sidecar is truncated/partial'.

_verdict.note:
Mechanism described is literally accurate but the impact is overstated and the "partial/stale sidecar silently suppresses trend data" premise is refuted by the writer side.

VERIFIED TRUE (mechanically): generate-methods-report.js reads the sidecar first (lines 50-58), the legacy alert-state fallback runs only `if (!Object.keys(methodHistory).length && fs.existsSync(args.state))` (line 59) so a sidecar yielding >=1 ticker skips it, both catch blocks (57, 63) are empty `/* ignore */`, and methods/trend.js computeTrend (lines 21-23) returns direction:'n/a' for empty history.

WHY IT IS NOT A REAL DATA-INTEGRITY BUG:
1) "Truncated/partial sidecar" is not a realistic on-disk state. detect-changes.js writes method-history-state.json via writeFileAtomic (line 95), which per Tag 230c-1/232a-1 carries Windows EPERM retry + parent-dir fsync precisely to prevent partial writes.
2) A corrupt sidecar never silently reaches the report. The sidecar reader in the producer, _loadMethodHistory (detect-changes.js lines 53-74), does NOT swallow errors: it backs up the file, logs ERROR, and process.exit(1) unless RESET_METHOD_HISTORY=1. The empty catch is only in the read-only downstream report generator.
3) The proposed "merge sidecar+legacy per ticker" is based on a misread of the post-F-SM-003 architecture. saveState (detect-changes.js lines 138-185) EXPLICITLY strips methodHistory out of alert-state.json and writes it only to the sidecar; the legacy fallback yields methodHistory={} for any current-era alert-state. So merging recovers nothing. _saveMethodHistory's liveTickers filter (F-SM-006, lines 76-97) keeps the two committed files in lock-step, so alert-state cannot hold a ticker the sidecar lacks.

WORST REALISTIC CASE: a manually/externally corrupted sidecar that still reaches this generator -> the HTML report's trend column shows all 'n/a'. title: Pass-count input parse uses `parseInt(value) || 0`; non-numeric input is silently coerced to 'show all' instead of being rejected
evidence: `var min = parseInt(pcInput.value) || 0;` (line 965). The input is type=number so the browser usually blocks letters, but pasted/locale content or a cleared field yields NaN; `NaN || 0` → 0, which means 'no filter'. There is no isFinite guard and no visual cue that the entered value was ignored. (The companion top-picks sort at line 1073 `parseInt(a.cells[3].textContent)` correctly extracts the leading passCount from '8 / 43' because parseInt stops at whitespace — that one is fine.)
why_it_matters: A user who fat-fingers the pass-count box gets a silent reset to 'show everything' rather than an error or a retained previous value — easy to misread as 'these are all the passing stocks'. Minor, but it is the classic `|| 0` falsy-coercion pattern called out in the audit scope where 0 is a legitimate value that should be distinguishable from 'invalid'.
fix: Use `var parsed = parseInt(pcInput.value, 10); var min = Number.isFinite(parsed) ? parsed : 0;` and optionally flag invalid input. Also pass radix 10 to parseInt throughout (line 965, 1073) to avoid legacy octal surprises.

_verdict.note:
Code reading confirms the literal description but the "bug" describes intended, benign behavior — not a real defect. File: C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/generate-methods-report.js.

Line 965: `var min = parseInt(pcInput.value) || 0;`. The bound input (line 685) is `<input type="number" id="passcount-filter" min="0" max="30" value="0">`. The only way to reach NaN is an empty/cleared field (parseInt("") = NaN → 0). Falling back to min=0 means "show all rows," which is precisely the correct neutral state for an empty pass-count filter — and applyPassCount() then clears the counter text via `min === 0 ? ''` (line 986). There is no data corruption, no crash, no wrong screener output; this is a client-side HTML-report UI convenience filter, not pipeline logic. The pasted-locale concern is weak: parseInt("3,5") = 3 (still filters), and genuine non-numeric paste into a number input is browser-rejected; even if it slipped through, defaulting to show-all is a reasonable failure mode.

Line 1073: `parseInt(a.cells[3].textContent) || 0` on "8 / 43" — the finding itself concedes this is correct (parseInt stops at whitespace → 8). Confirmed fine.

fix_safe=true: the proposed `Number.isFinite(parseInt(value,10)) ? parsed : 0` is behavior-preserving for every numeric input and merely keeps the degenerate empty/NaN case at 0 — identical observable behavior. Adding radix 10 is harmless (guards an octal case that cannot occur for 0–30 values). Safe to auto-apply, but it fixes a non-problem; treat as cosmetic hardening, not a bug fix.

title: Ordinal RANK value (0-5) scored against a STRING threshold collapses 4 distinct classes to 0.0 — graduated signal lost

The header also asserts 'NOT in SCORE_WEIGHTS' (line 57-ish analog) which is false — it IS weighted 0.20.

Comment in method: // prevents: ordinal class rank silently collapsing to binary 0/1 in score-aggregator.

_verdict.note:
Mechanically the trace is correct but the framing as a BUG is a false positive — this is documented, intended behavior, not a defect.

Confirmed facts (C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/methods/):
- hypergrowth-quality-class.js:23 THRESHOLD='REAL_HYPERGROWTH_BUT_LOSSY' (string), :186-187 value=RANK[cls] (0-5), pass=value>=4 (always an explicit boolean on the computable path).
- _helpers.js:58-68 buildResult passes threshold through verbatim and sets pass:!!pass.
- score-aggregator.js:128-130: for non-numeric threshold + pass===false → 0.0; pass undefined/null → 0.3. Since this method's pass is always an explicit boolean when computable, failing classes (Q_SPIKE_FAKE 0, NOT_HYPERGROWTH 1, LOW_BASE_EFFECT 2, HYPERGROWTH_REVIEW 3) all map to 0.0 and pass classes (4,5) to 1.0. The graduated ordinal signal is indeed not used. The method is wired in (HYPERGROWTH weight 0.20, line 39).

Why it is NOT a bug:
- The 0.0 collapse is a deliberate, documented decision. score-aggregator.js:122-130 (Tag 206l, "Bug-Hunt Agent F MEDIUM-3") explicitly REPLACED an earlier 0.3 partial-credit fallback with 0.0 specifically because, quote, "when threshold is non-numeric AND pass is EXPLICITLY false, the method has rendered a definitive negative verdict ... The previous 0.3 partial-credit fallback was too generous for such verdicts. Return 0.0 in that case." The auditor is essentially re-proposing the exact partial-credit path that a prior audit reviewed and intentionally removed.
- It is a consistent house pattern, not a one-off slip: profitability-state.js:20 (THRESHOLD='TURNAROUND') and profitability-trend.js:27 (THRESHOLD='FLAT') are also scored CORE methods that hit the same branch and resolve to binary 0.0/1.0 by the same design (Tag 152, lines 119-121). hypergrowth-quality-class behaves identically by design.
- HYPERGROWTH_REVIEW (rank 3) is by definition a failing class (pass=value>=4 is false); giving it 0.0 is the documented contract, not an error. Whether rank 3 *should* earn partial credit is a modeling judgment, not a correctness defect.

So at most this is a debatable design/quality-improvement suggestion (graduated partial credit for borderline classes), already considered and rejected upstream — it does not meet the bar for a real bug.

title: break-on-first-null walks latest-first annualRev, so one missing/late LATEST fiscal year zeros cleanYears for an established company
evidence: `for (const entry of revArr){ const v=_unwrap(entry); if (v==null) break; cleanYears++; }`. annualRev is latest-first (pull-yahoo.js:618 `_arr(isHist,'totalRevenue')`, latest=index 0 per line 694 'latest first → wir flippen NICHT'). At minimum, if revArr[0]==null but revArr[1..] are clean, start counting at the first non-null index. Comment: // prevents: a single missing latest-FY revenue zeroing the clean-year count for long-established names.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed real, but lower incidence than implied. The break-on-first-null loop (listing-age.js:57-61) does walk a latest-first array — annualRev is built latest-first (pull-yahoo.js:618 via _arr, comment line 617 "latest first"; FTS path comment line 1120 reiterates). A leading null at revArr[0] makes the loop break immediately → cleanYears=0, which (a) zeroes QC score in score-aggregator.js:382 (ageMultiplier = min(1, 0/5) = 0, applied at line 388) and (b) disqualifies the stock from QC classification in generate-screener.js:663 (qcEligibleByAge = listingYears==null || listingYears>=3; value 0 is not null and 0>=3 is false). REFUTATION ATTEMPT — partially succeeds on the mechanism's likelihood, not on its existence: The auditor's primary-source claim is imprecise. The quoteSummary path uses _arr (pull-yahoo.js:493-500), which does `.filter(Boolean)` — it STRIPS nulls entirely, so that path can NEVER produce a leading null (or any null). Net: is_real=true (the break-on-first-null on a latest-first array that CAN carry a leading null is a genuine defect), but severity should drop to low given the documented near-zero incidence and that it only affects a DIAGNOSTIC scaling/eligibility for QC (not a hard correctness gate on price/financials).

FIX NOT SAFE TO AUTO-APPLY: the proposed fix says 'reuse a shared warn helper' — but _warnMediansLoad is NOT exported from _helpers.js (module.exports lines 336-342 omit it). title: Weekly-frequency gate checks series[0].date && series[1].date (oldest end) but measures the gap on series[len-2]/series[len-1] (newest end)
evidence: `if (series.length>=2 && series[0].date && series[1].date){ const d0=Date.parse(series[series.length-2].date); const d1=Date.parse(series[series.length-1].date); ... }`. The presence-guard inspects indices 0 and 1; the values parsed are indices len-2 and len-1. If the head has dates but the tail does not (mixed legacy/backfilled rows), the guard passes but Date.parse(undefined) → NaN, falling back to daily silently.
why_it_matters: Currently benign because history.json has dates on every row (verified: 0 missing across 1.54M rows), but it is a latent frequency-misclassification: any future backfill that dates only the head would silently force daily lookbacks on weekly data, halving/doubling the effective window. The guard and the measurement must reference the same indices.

title: Forward horizon is calendar days, mislabeled as '5-trading-day' return
evidence: `const FORWARD_DAYS = 5; // 5-trading-day forward return` (line 32-33) and `console.log('Forward horizon: ' + FORWARD_DAYS + ' calendar days (5d)')` (line 118). `addDaysIso(asOf, days)` (line 53-57) advances 5 *calendar* days via `setUTCDate`. `nearestTradingDay` (line 66-79) then snaps to the closest stored date within ±7 days.
why_it_matters: 5 calendar days starting on a Thursday/Friday spans a weekend = ~3 trading days, while starting Monday = 5 trading days. The horizon silently varies per vintage, so per-vintage spreads are not comparable and the pooled median mixes 3-day and 5-day returns. The dataset here happens to carry daily (incl. weekend) entries so the snap is benign now, but on real trading-day price data the inconsistency is live.
fix: Either index forward returns by N entries in the sorted per-ticker price array (true trading days) or rename everywhere to 'calendar days' and document that horizon length varies. Comment the chosen invariant.

_verdict.note: Confirmed real labeling bug. In scripts/tag229b-new-method-backtest.js, FORWARD_DAYS=5 is applied via calendar-day arithmetic: addDaysIso (lines 53-57) does setUTCDate(getUTCDate()+5), and forwardReturn (lines 85-93) snaps both endpoints with nearestTradingDay (lines 66-79, +/-7 day window). So the horizon is 5 *calendar* days, not 5 trading days. Yet line 32-33 comments it as "5-trading-day forward return", the printed/JSON column headers are med_pass_5d/med_fail_5d (lines 227, 231), and the companion report audit-reports/2026-05-17-tag229b-new-method-backtest.md labels the scope "5-trading-day forward return" (lines 5, 28) while contradicting itself at line 35 ("5 calendar days"). I simulated the actual code against prices/history.json: realized spacing already drifts (asOf 2026-05-10 -> 5 trading days apart; 2026-05-13/14/15 -> 4 apart) even though this fixture is gap-light synthetic data (it contains Sat/Sun rows e.g. 2026-05-09, 2026-05-10, 2026-05-17). On real market data with weekends/holidays, 5 calendar days collapses to ~3 trading days and varies per vintage, plus nearestTradingDay's forward-biased snap can stretch the exit further. So the realized horizon both varies and is systematically shorter than the "5-trading-day" label implies. Counter-points that cap the severity: this is an explicitly self-described "directional smoke test, not a rigorous walk-forward" (header lines 13-15), it is not imported by any production code (only self-reference + its own report), and line 118 plus report line 35 already correctly say "calendar days" -- so the defect is a documentation/label inconsistency in a one-off diagnostic, not a screener-output bug. The computed numbers remain valid for the horizon actually measured; only the name is wrong.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed the factual claim. extract-ma-rpo.js:247 calls fetchSecTickers() from discovery/sec-tickers.js, which builds each entry's cik as String(cikRaw).padStart(10,'0') (line 94) and returns that map (line 110). However, impact is minimal and severity 'low' is appropriate (arguably it could even be cosmetic/info). It is a pure debug `console.warn('nearby keys:', ...)` diagnostic hint for a human; it does not feed into extraction, return values, control flow, or any data-correctness path. fix_safe assessment: The proposed change only alters the content of a console.warn diagnostic, so it cannot break extraction — low risk. But it is not strictly behavior-preserving (it changes what gets logged) and the two proposed variants have real tradeoffs: `k.includes(cik)` with the full padded CIK will likely match nothing (since the exact `CIK<cik>.json` was already shown absent), making the hint useless; `cik.replace(/^0+/,'')` (un-padded numeric) is the more sensible fuzzy match but is a semantic choice worth a human glance. Because it touches only a debug log and can't affect results, it's reasonable to auto-apply, but the 'best variant' is debatable — I mark fix_safe=true given the blast radius is confined to logging, with the note that the replace-leading-zeros variant is the better of the two.

title: Unguarded JSON.parse of prices/history.json in a live workflow step throws and fails the daily-pull job
evidence: `const history = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(args.history, 'utf8'));` (line 69) with no try/catch, and `main();` is called bare at line 114 (no .catch, no process.exit(0)). This script IS a workflow entrypoint: .github/workflows/daily-pull.yml:482 `run: node scripts/macro-regime.js`.
why_it_matters: A truncated/half-written prices/history.json (e.g. interrupted upstream write) makes macro-regime.js throw an uncaught exception → non-zero exit → the daily-pull workflow step fails. By contrast elliott-export.js (line 138-140) and check-pull-stats.js (line 158-161) wrap main and exit 0 on error precisely to avoid breaking the pipeline. macro-regime is the asymmetric outlier. Note it DOES gracefully handle the empty-series case (line 72-85) — only the parse itself is unguarded.

_verdict.note: Partially confirmed but severity-inflated. The unguarded parse IS real: scripts/macro-regime.js:69 `JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(args.history,'utf8'))` has no try/catch, and main() is called bare at line 114 (no .catch). On a CORRUPT prices/history.json it throws and exits non-zero. The step is non-blocking, so a crash does not fail the job. Also note the empty/missing-ticker case is ALREADY handled (lines 72-85: writes `error:'no_price_data'` fallback + process.exit(0)); only the malformed-JSON path is unguarded. Downstream consumer scripts/walk-forward-perf.js degrades gracefully on a missing/stale outputs/macro-regime.json (loadMacroRegimes()->loadJson() returns null on bad file; getRegimeAt() falls back to UNKNOWN/null, lines 388-409, 599-605), so even a skipped regime step does not corrupt or crash the pipeline. Net: legitimate hardening gap, not a job-failing data-integrity bug — downgrade medium->low. fix_safe=true: the proposed fix mirrors the existing empty-series fallback branch and the project-wide loadJson try/catch idiom (check-pull-stats.js:43, method-effectiveness.js:60, etc.), is behavior-preserving on the happy and already-handled paths, and only alters the currently-crashing corrupt-file path.
