title: 'Median-R40' picks middle of a descending-sorted list with no even-length handling
evidence: List is sorted descending by r40 (evaluateAll line 55 `out.sort((a,b)=>(b.r40||0)-(a.r40||0))`). Then `const med = list[Math.floor(list.length/2)].r40;` (line 80). For length 2 -> index 1 (the smaller of two), for length 4 -> index 2 (the lower-middle).
why_it_matters: Reported 'Median-R40' is the upper-middle element's value (because list is descending, index floor(n/2) is below center) and never averages the two middle values for even n. It is a single-element proxy, not a true median, biasing the regional comparison that the whole report exists to make. Low severity because it is a reporting stat, not a screener gate.
fix: Reuse the proper `median()` helper already written in check-pull-stats.js (line 44-49) / tag229b (line 47-52): `median(list.map(p=>p.r40))`. Consider extracting median to lib/ to stop re-implementing it.

_verdict.note: Confirmed by source. scripts/regional-oos-test.js line 55 sorts the result list descending by r40 (`out.sort((a,b)=>(b.r40||0)-(a.r40||0))`); byRegion grouping (line 67) preserves that order. Line 80 then does `list[Math.floor(list.length/2)].r40` and labels the column "Median-R40" (line 76/81). For even-length lists this is wrong: length 2 -> index 1 = the smaller value; length 4 -> index 2 = lower-middle (3rd largest), not the average of the two middle elements. A statistically correct median should average the two middle values on even length. The verifier's two concrete examples are accurate. The repo already has correct median() helpers (e.g. check-pull-stats.js:44-49, tag229b-new-method-backtest.js:47) that filter non-finite and average the two middle values on even length. Severity is genuinely low: the value feeds only a diagnostic markdown report cell (no pick selection, no thresholds, no pipeline decision), and on odd-length lists the result is already correct. No test asserts this behavior.

title: `b.r40 || 0` / `p.score?.toFixed` treat a legitimate r40 of 0 as missing in sort, and only score (not r40) is null-guarded in the table
evidence: Sort: `(b.r40 || 0) - (a.r40 || 0)` (line 55) coerces an r40 of exactly 0 to 0 (harmless for sort) but the row render `p.r40.toFixed(1)` (line 90) assumes r40 is always finite — it is guarded upstream by `r40.computable` check (line 48), so currently safe, but `(p.score?.toFixed(1) || '-')` guards score while r40 is unguarded, an inconsistency that will bite if the computable gate is ever relaxed.
why_it_matters: Defensive asymmetry: score may be null (handled) but r40 is assumed present. Today the `r40.computable` filter (line 48) protects it; the coupling is implicit and fragile. Flagged as low because no live crash.
fix: Guard r40 the same way as score in the table row, or assert finiteness at push time. Avoid `|| 0` if 0 is a valid r40 (it is — a company at exactly 40% combined can yield rule-of-40 value 0).

_verdict.note:
False positive by the auditor's own admission. Both cited claims are conceded non-issues in the evidence itself ("harmless for sort", "currently safe"), and code-reading confirms there is no present defect.

Claim 1 (line 55 sort, `(b.r40 || 0) - (a.r40 || 0)`): an r40 of exactly 0 coerces to 0, which is identical for a numeric subtraction sort — no behavior change. The finding admits this.

title: Drift detector compares today against a window that still includes today, weakening the alert
evidence: Line 124 `history.push(today)` then line 136 `detectStatsDrift(today, history.slice(0, -1), DRIFT_THRESHOLD)`. The intent of `slice(0,-1)` is to drop today. Combined with the dedupe at line 123 (`history.filter(h => h.asOf !== today.asOf)`) this is actually correct for the same-day case — BUT if the script runs twice in one day, the first run's `today` was already pushed and persisted to history.json (line 127), and on the second run the dedupe removes the stale same-date entry, so the median baseline silently shrinks by one run that day.
why_it_matters: The trailing-4 median is the drift baseline; on a re-run day it is computed from only the genuinely-prior distinct dates, which is the intended behavior — but the persisted history.json already contains today (written line 127 BEFORE drift is computed line 136), so a crash between the write and the alert leaves today permanently in history with no alert ever fired for it. The write-then-evaluate ordering means the alert is best-effort while the state mutation is committed first.
fix: Compute drift BEFORE persisting today to history.json, or pass the explicitly-deduped prior array to both the write and the detector. Reorder: collect -> detectDrift(prior) -> alert -> then writeFileAtomic(history+today).

So the baseline passed to the detector is exactly the loaded history minus every same-date entry. On run #2 of the same day, the only thing removed is run #1's own same-date today snapshot — which is NOT legitimate baseline data: comparing today against an earlier run of the same date is precisely the self/look-ahead comparison the dedupe is designed to prevent. The four genuinely-prior distinct-date runs (d1..d4) that feed median() via recent = history.slice(-MIN_HISTORY_RUNS) (line 97) remain fully intact on every run. Baseline size is unchanged. The auditor's evidence even concedes "this is actually correct for the same-day case," then asserts a shrink that the code does not produce. The verify block (lines 121-136) runs AFTER that synchronous rename returns, so it reads back complete, committed bytes.

The toWrite lines DO land at the tail deterministically, not by "luck": merged is seeded from existing file lines (lines 91-92), toWrite is exactly the dates NOT already in merged (line 95), and merged.set on those new keys (lines 107-109) appends them to the end of the Map by JS spec insertion-order guarantee. So the verify already parses exactly the just-written lines. The only true gap is that it parses them rather than asserting parsed.date === expected date, but the content was just built in-memory from toWrite and written atomically; there is no realistic path from a successful atomic rename to a synchronous read-back that yields parseable-but-wrong-date lines.

Confirmed at generate-dashboard.js:136-158. buildDetailIndex loops over the union of all picks.modes entries plus all metric-leaderboard entries and, for each ticker with methods-history, calls readQuarterly(ticker) (line 153) and readSnapshotMeta(ticker) (line 154). Both helpers (lines 73-99) independently call safeJSON(tickerToSnapshotPath(ticker)), and safeRead/safeJSON (lines 57-58) do an uncached fs.readFileSync + JSON.parse every call — so there is no memoization. The O(tickers) synchronous-read claim is real.

CORRECTION to the evidence: the "SAME snapshot file read up to twice per ticker" is overstated. Line 154 is `meta: nameMap[ticker] || readSnapshotMeta(ticker)`, so JS short-circuit means readSnapshotMeta only runs when nameMap[ticker] is falsy. nameMap is built by buildTickerNameMap (line 102) from every picks.modes entry, so for mode-pick tickers readSnapshotMeta is SKIPPED (1 read via readQuarterly). The double read only occurs for tickers that appear solely in metric leaderboards (not in any mode pick). So it is "1 read per mode-pick ticker, 2 reads per leaderboard-only ticker", not "2 per ticker".

Severity low is appropriate: this is a one-shot build script (not a request hot path), the ticker set is bounded (all mode entries + 7 boards x <=25), and there is zero behavior impact — purely build-time speed.

title: picks (latest.json) and methods-history are loaded from independent sources with no date-consistency check — dashboard can blend today's picks with a stale methods snapshot
evidence: Line 587 `const picks = safeJSON(PICKS_LATEST);` (picks-history/latest.json, asOf 2026-06-12) and line 588-589 `methodsFile = latestMethodsHistoryFile(); methodsHistory = safeJSON(methodsFile)` (newest methods-history/YYYY-MM-DD.json). Nothing compares `picks.asOf` to `methodsHistory.date`. The metric leaderboards + detail modal (results, inputs, marketCapUsd) come entirely from methodsHistory, while mode picks + scores come from picks. The header 'Stand' shows only `picks.asOf` (line 186/317).
why_it_matters: If a run regenerates picks/latest.json but the methods-history snapshot for that date fails to write (the snapshot step can fail independently; the dashboard step is continue-on-error), the dashboard shows fresh mode picks dated today alongside metric leaderboards and detail values from an older methods snapshot — with the header asserting today's date. A pick can appear with a primaryMetric from picks but a contradictory ROIC/EV-EBITDA from a different day, and nothing flags the mismatch. This is asymmetric-staleness data integrity, masked by the single-date header.
fix: After loading both, compare `picks.asOf.slice(0,10)` to `methodsHistory.date`; if they differ, render a visible banner ('Mode-Picks Stand X · Kennzahlen Stand Y') and log a warning, rather than presenting one date as authoritative.

_verdict.note: Confirmed against source. Line 587 loads picks from picks-history/latest.json (asOf "2026-06-12T00:00:00.000Z"); lines 588-589 load methodsHistory from latestMethodsHistoryFile(), which returns the lexicographically newest methods-history/YYYY-MM-DD.json (currently 2026-06-12.json, which carries a top-level "date":"2026-06-12"). Grep across the file (.date / Stand / stale) confirms there is genuinely NO comparison of picks.asOf to methodsHistory.date anywhere. The header "Stand" at line 186/317 renders only picks.asOf, while every metric leaderboard (buildMetricLeaderboard) and the detail modal (buildDetailIndex: results/inputs/marketCapUsd) come exclusively from methodsHistory. So the structural claim is accurate: the two artifacts are loaded from independent sources, latestMethodsHistoryFile() always picks the newest methods file regardless of whether picks was regenerated, and one date is presented as authoritative for both. BUT severity is overstated. In normal pipeline runs both artifacts are written together and align (they do today: both 2026-06-12). Divergence only arises on a partial-failure path (e.g. picks write skipped while a newer methods snapshot lands). Impact is cosmetic/informational — a potentially misleading "Stand" label — not data corruption: leaderboards stay internally consistent (all methodsHistory), picks stay internally consistent (all picks); nothing is numerically mis-blended. The title's "blend today's picks with a stale methods snapshot" overstates it: rows are not cross-joined by date, only the displayed header date is single-sourced. Real but low-severity presentation gap, not data-integrity corruption.

title: marketCap field-name mismatch: picks carry `marketCap`, methods-history carries `inputs.marketCapUsd`; dashboard reads only marketCapUsd, so MCap is blank for tickers present only via mode picks
evidence: Live picks objects have `"marketCap": 62987276288` (no Usd suffix). buildMetricLeaderboard line 128 reads `data.inputs && data.inputs.marketCapUsd` (methods-history field), and the modal line 486 reads `inputs.marketCapUsd`. A ticker that is in picks.modes but absent from methodsHistory.stocks gets `inputs: null` (line 148) → modal shows no MCap even though picks carried `marketCap` for it.
why_it_matters: Field-name/case mismatch in the audit scope. Tickers that dropped out of the latest methods-history snapshot but survive in picks (survivorship-attrition asymmetry between the two files) lose their market-cap display in the modal despite the value being available on the pick object. Minor UX data loss, but it is a real cross-source field mismatch (`marketCap` vs `marketCapUsd`) that will keep biting as the two producers drift.
fix: In buildDetailIndex, when `inputs` is null but the ticker exists in nameMap/picks, fall back to the pick's `marketCap` (carry it into the detail meta). Pick the field deliberately and document the unit assumption (picks marketCap currency vs methods marketCapUsd).

_verdict.note: Code reads are accurate but the bug is latent and not observable in practice. Line 128 (buildMetricLeaderboard) reads data.inputs.marketCapUsd, which is the CORRECT methods-history field — this function iterates only methodsHistory.stocks, never picks, so no mismatch exists there (and the entry's marketCap field is never even rendered in the leaderboard row, lines 443-453). The modal at line 486 reads inputs.marketCapUsd from det.inputs, which is null (line 148) only when a pick ticker is absent from methodsHistory.stocks. That trigger does not occur: snapshot-picks.js and snapshot-methods-history.js both read the same ./snapshots dir in the same pipeline run, so picks (240 tickers) are a top-N subset of the full methods universe (4737). Live verification in the worktree: 0 of 240 pick tickers are missing from methods-history, all 240 have inputs.marketCapUsd populated, and picks asOf (2026-06-12) matches the methods file date (2026-06-12) — in sync. The only realistic trigger would be a stale-picks-vs-fresh-methods desync, which is not present. Even if triggered, the sole effect is one cosmetic '· MCap …' fragment missing from a modal subheading — no data corruption, wrong results, or crash. Marginally defensible as a low/info hardening note, but not a real observed bug.

title: methodValueDiffs is re-sorted inside the template render after passCountDiffs already sorted — redundant, and the .slice(0,50) sort mutates the source array
evidence: Line 74 sorts passCountDiffs. Line 111: `for (const d of methodValueDiffs.sort((a,b)=>Math.abs(b.deltaPct)-Math.abs(a.deltaPct)).slice(0,50))` sorts methodValueDiffs in place during the for-of header. The count rendered in the heading (line 106, `methodValueDiffs.length`) is computed before the slice, so the heading says e.g. '312' while only 50 rows render — heading/row mismatch.

fix: Sort + slice into a named const before building the heading, and render the heading as `top ${Math.min(50, methodValueDiffs.length)} of ${methodValueDiffs.length}` so the count matches what is shown.

_verdict.note: Partially confirmed, but the finding's framing is mostly wrong. VERIFIED at C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/generate-diff-report.js. (1) "redundant / re-sorted after passCountDiffs already sorted" is FALSE: line 74 sorts passCountDiffs, line 111 sorts methodValueDiffs — two distinct arrays. The methodValueDiffs sort is the only sort on that array, not redundant. (2) "sort mutates the source array" is technically true (Array.sort is in-place) but HARMLESS: after line 111, methodValueDiffs is only read again at line 122 via .length, which is order-independent. No observable bug from the mutation. (3) The ONLY genuine issue is the heading/row mismatch: line 106 renders the full `methodValueDiffs.length` in the <h2>, while line 111 caps the table at .slice(0,50). When >50 value-diffs exist, the heading says e.g. "312" but only 50 rows render with no "showing top 50" indicator — a real but cosmetic UX inconsistency in an internal HTML report. Note the category is mislabeled: this is a display/UX inconsistency, not performance (one sort of a bounded array is trivial). Downgrading framing accordingly; keeping is_real=true on the strength of the heading/row mismatch alone.

title: Tier thresholds (80/65/50) duplicated inline in two places and divergent from the server-side TIER_STYLE constant — single source of truth missing
evidence: The cutoff ladder `score >= 80 ? 'A' : score >= 65 ? 'B' : score >= 50 ? 'NEAR_MISS' : 'REJECT'` appears verbatim at line 416 (renderModes) and line 499 (openDetail). TIER_STYLE (line 49) defines the badge styling for these tiers but not the thresholds, so the numeric boundaries live only as duplicated inline ternaries.
why_it_matters: Duplicated business logic: if the screener's tier cutoffs change (and tier boundaries are exactly the kind of thing that gets retuned), one of the two copies will be missed and the leaderboard badge will disagree with the modal badge for the same stock. Also, these thresholds almost certainly should match whatever the upstream score-aggregator/methods use to assign tiers — embedding them in the view layer risks the dashboard inventing its own tiering that contradicts the pipeline.
fix: Define a single `function scoreToTier(score)` (server-side, injected into the client payload or duplicated once) and call it in both places; ideally source the thresholds from the same config the score-aggregator uses so the dashboard cannot drift from canonical tiering.

_verdict.note: Confirmed real. The cutoff ladder `score >= 80 ? 'A' : score >= 65 ? 'B' : score >= 50 ? 'NEAR_MISS' : 'REJECT'` appears verbatim at generate-dashboard.js:416 (renderModes) and :499 (openDetail). A canonical single source of truth genuinely exists and is NOT reused: methods/score-aggregator.js defines `TIER_THRESHOLDS = { A:80, B:65, NEAR_MISS:50 }` (lines 24-27), exports it (line 462), and applies it at lines 393-397. The dashboard hardcodes the same numbers independently, so it can silently drift from the aggregator. One nuance correcting the evidence: TIER_STYLE (line 49) is purely presentational (badge bg/fg/label) and rightly holds no thresholds — it is not the missing source of truth. The real canonical owner is the aggregator, which the proposed_fix's second clause correctly names. Severity low is appropriate: today all three numeric copies agree, so there is no user-visible defect — this is a maintainability/drift risk only. fix_safe=false: a naive `scoreToTier(score)` extraction that keeps the raw `>=80/65/50` ladder is behavior-preserving, BUT the proposed_fix explicitly suggests sourcing from the aggregator's tiering, and the aggregator's tier is NOT a pure score-cutoff — it additionally applies red-flag downgrades (line 413) and an env-gated data-quality tier-cap (line 417+). Wiring the dashboard to the aggregator's true `tier` would change displayed badges for some picks (those downgraded), which is a behavior change requiring human decision about which tier notion to show. Hence not safe to auto-apply.

title: OTC pagination completeness check uses PAGE_SIZE arithmetic that breaks the moment any page is filtered or short, terminating early and dropping tickers
evidence: Line 175: `const fetched = (page - 1) * PAGE_SIZE + rows.length;` then line 176 `if (totalRecords !== null && fetched >= totalRecords) break;`. `rows.length` is the RAW rows returned by the API, but the API may return fewer than PAGE_SIZE on intermediate pages, or `total` (totalRecords) is captured once on the first page that reports it (line 133 `if (total !== null && totalRecords === null)`). If page 1 does not include `totalRecords` (one of the documented response shapes at lines 98-110 has no total), `totalRecords` stays null and the ONLY stop condition becomes the empty-page check (line 138) capped by MAX_PAGES=10.
why_it_matters: Two opposite failures: (1) if totalRecords is reported, `(page-1)*PAGE_SIZE` assumes every prior page returned exactly 500 raw rows; any API hiccup returning a short-but-nonempty page makes `fetched` undercount and the loop keeps going past real end (benign) OR if the API returns MORE than PAGE_SIZE the count overshoots and stops early (drops data). (2) MAX_PAGES=10 * 500 = 5000 hard ceiling while the file's own header says 'Expert Market + OTCQX+OTCQB combined can exceed 5,000' (lines 9, 193-196). The warn at 193 fires but the data is already truncated — asymmetric survivorship attrition against OTC small-caps.
fix: Track fetched count from the actual cumulative rows consumed, not `(page-1)*PAGE_SIZE`: `cumulative += rows.length` across iterations. Keep the empty-page stop as the authoritative terminator. Raise MAX_PAGES (or make it `Math.ceil(totalRecords/PAGE_SIZE)` when known) so the documented >5000 case is actually fetched. Comment: 'prevents early pagination stop / 5000-ticker OTC ceiling silently truncating discovery'.

_verdict.note:
Partially real but heavily over-described and over-rated. File: C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/discovery/otc-markets.js lines 138, 172-179.

The ONE genuine defect: lines 175-176 use `fetched = (page-1)*PAGE_SIZE + rows.length`, which assumes every prior page was full. If a NON-FINAL page returns short AND totalRecords is known, `fetched` over-counts and the `fetched >= totalRecords` early-exit can fire before the tail pages are consumed. Concrete trace: raw page rows [300, 500, 200] with totalRecords=1000 -> after page 2, fetched = 500+500 = 1000 >= 1000 -> break, dropping page 3's 200 rows. The auditor's proposed `cumulative += rows.length` fix correctly removes this.

But most of the auditor's mechanism is wrong/misread:
1. "filtered" pages break it — FALSE. `rows.length` (line 175) is the RAW API row count, computed before the junk-suffix/regex filtering, which only affects the `added` counter (lines 143-167). Filtering has zero effect on the arithmetic.
2. "short ... terminating early" as a general claim — FALSE for the common cases. A short FINAL page is handled correctly: the authoritative terminator is the EMPTY-page check at line 138, and the comment at 172-174 explicitly documents that this code was rewritten to stop only on empty pages, not short ones. Over-counting from a prior short page makes the early-exit fire LATER (errs toward more fetching), never on the final short page.
3. "If page 1 has no totalRecords, the ONLY stop condition becomes the empty-page check capped by MAX_PAGES=10" — accurate as a description but NOT a bug: when totalRecords is unknown the empty-page check is the correct intended terminator. The MAX_PAGES=10 / 5000-ticker ceiling is a SEPARATE, already-audited item: Tag 227a finding F2 deliberately DEFERRED it, and Tag 218 already added the `HIT MAX_PAGES ... tickers truncated` warning (lines 189-196). Not a new finding.

Severity: this exact short-non-final-page mechanism was previously filed as F-DP-017 (findings/archive-2026-05-14/data-pipeline.json) and correctly rated LOW — standard pagination returns full pages until the last, so a short intermediate page is abnormal, and the loop is bounded by MAX_PAGES. OTC is a best-effort source (null-mcap tickers sit at the bottom of the marketCap-ranked cap in refresh-universe.js, merged via Promise.allSettled). Re-rating at 'high' is an over-escalation; downgraded to low.

fix_safe=false: the `cumulative` fix is behavior-preserving for the normal full-pages-until-empty path and only changes the buggy edge case, so it is low-risk in principle, but it edits a pagination terminator on a live discovery source and overlaps with the previously-deferred MAX_PAGES decision — it warrants a quick human glance rather than blind auto-apply.

title: toYahooSymbol skips suffix for ANY symbol containing a dot, mangling foreign class shares and US-style tickers on foreign exchanges
evidence: Line 59: `if (sym.includes('.')) return sym;` — comment says 'If symbol already contains the suffix (e.g. BP.L), don't append again'. But Finnhub `displaySymbol` for non-US exchanges often contains a dot that is NOT the Yahoo suffix (e.g. a London class share 'RDSA.L' is fine, but a symbol like 'BMW.DE'-style or a ticker with an internal dot 'BRK.B' fetched from US exchange would be returned without its needed exchange suffix). Worse: line 86 passes `s.displaySymbol || s.symbol` — Finnhub's `symbol` for .L stocks is frequently already suffixed while `displaySymbol` is the bare local code, so the dot-check fires inconsistently depending on which field is present.
why_it_matters: For the 16 non-US exchanges in EXCHANGES (lines 14-32), any symbol that legitimately contains a dot for a class/series but lacks the Yahoo exchange suffix is emitted WITHOUT the suffix (e.g. would yield 'ABC.A' instead of 'ABC.A.L'), producing a Yahoo ticker that 404s. These silently never resolve in pull-yahoo and vanish — foreign-universe attrition.
fix: Replace the blanket dot-check with a suffix-aware test: only skip appending when the symbol already ENDS with the exact target suffix, e.g. `if (suffix && sym.toUpperCase().endsWith(suffix.toUpperCase())) return sym;`. Otherwise append. Comment: 'prevents foreign class-share tickers losing their Yahoo exchange suffix'.

_verdict.note:
Refuted as a real bug; rests on a misread of the code and the Finnhub API contract.

(1) The headline US example is impossible. toYahooSymbol returns at line 57 `if (!suffix) return sym;` BEFORE the dot-check, and the US exchange maps to suffix '' (finnhub.js line 15). So `BRK.B` fetched from the US exchange is returned untouched as `BRK.B` — which is exactly the correct Yahoo symbol. The dot-check on line 59 never runs for US tickers, so the auditor's claim that BRK.B "would be returned without its needed exchange suffix" is wrong (US needs no suffix).

(2) For the 16 non-US exchanges in EXCHANGES, Finnhub's /stock/symbol returns both `symbol` and `displaySymbol` already carrying the local exchange suffix (e.g. LSE `BP.L`, Frankfurt `BMW.DE`). The dot-check correctly prevents double-suffixing in that real, dominant case. The auditor's secondary claim that `displaySymbol` is "frequently the bare local code" while `symbol` is suffixed is backwards: the code prefers displaySymbol (line 86), and even if displaySymbol were bare (e.g. `BP`), it contains no dot, so line 59 would NOT fire and the suffix WOULD be appended (`BP` -> `BP.L`). The dot-check only short-circuits when a dot is already present — i.e. when the suffix is already there.

(3) The only genuine gap is theoretical: a non-US symbol whose Finnhub field carries an internal dot but NOT the mapped exchange suffix. The auditor gives no concrete instance from any of the 16 configured exchanges (the cited RDSA.L is conceded to be "fine"), so there is no source evidence of actual corruption.

Downstream impact context: the produced string becomes the Yahoo ticker key merged into allTickers in refresh-universe.js (lines 339-350). A mangled key would surface as a no-data ticker downstream, not silent corruption.

fix_safe=false: the proposed endsWith(suffix) test is NOT behavior-preserving and can introduce NEW corruption. Finnhub's Frankfurt entries (mapped suffix '.F', finnhub.js line 19) commonly carry '.DE' suffixes; `BMW.DE` does not end with '.F', so the proposed fix would append and yield the corrupt `BMW.DE.F`. Similarly LSE class lines like `BT.A` would become `BT.A.L`. The change alters output for every dotted-but-non-matching symbol and needs human review with real fixtures, not an auto-apply.

title: Wikipedia ticker extraction is a brittle wikitext heuristic that conflates row-splitting and yields both false positives and missing constituents
evidence: Line 79 splits the whole article on `/\|\-/` (table row separator) then line 82 splits cells on `/\|+/`. Modern Wikipedia constituent tables are frequently rendered via templates / sortable wikitables whose ticker cell is `[[NYSE: AAPL|AAPL]]` or `{{NYSE|AAPL}}` — the regex at line 92 `/^[A-Z][A-Z0-9]{0,5}$/` only matches a BARE token after markup strip (lines 85-90). Any exchange-prefixed or templated symbol is missed. Conversely the NOT_TICKERS denylist (lines 46-61) and single-letter whitelist (lines 71-74) are hand-maintained — 'May 2026'/'verified against current NYSE listings' — guaranteeing drift.
why_it_matters: S&P 500 / FTSE 100 / DAX membership is the highest-signal source for index-quality names. A parser that depends on a frozen denylist and a specific wikitext table dialect will (a) miss real constituents whenever Wikipedia editors change table markup, and (b) admit garbage tokens that happen to match. The header claims to 'Cover S&P 500, FTSE 100, DAX 40' but correctness is unverifiable and decays over time. The single-letter whitelist also hardcodes a point-in-time NYSE snapshot that will silently exclude future single-letter listings.
fix: Stop scraping raw wikitext. Use the structured data: for S&P 500, parse the rendered HTML table via the action=parse&prop=text endpoint and select the Symbol column by header, or better pull from a structured source (the index provider, or Wikidata SPARQL). At minimum, locate the ticker COLUMN by its header rather than scanning every cell, eliminating the need for NOT_TICKERS/SINGLE_LETTER guesswork. Comment: 'prevents index-membership drift from wikitext dialect changes and frozen denylists'.

_verdict.note:
Real underlying brittleness but materially over-severe and partly misread. The denylist/whitelist drift is genuine: NOT_TICKERS (lines 46-61) and SINGLE_LETTER_TICKERS (lines 71-74, frozen "May 2026, verified against current NYSE listings") are hand-maintained and will drift. The {{NYSE|AAPL}} template form is stripped to empty by line 86 and would be missed. So it's not a pure false positive.

BUT three things deflate it to LOW, not medium data-integrity: (1) Impact is near-zero because Wikipedia is one of SIX discovery sources merged as a first-write-wins UNION (refresh-universe.js:328-335: nasdaqAll, sec, finnhub, wikipedia, otc, nasdaqApi). S&P 500 names like AAPL/MSFT and single-letter NYSE tickers also arrive from SEC EDGAR and NASDAQ — a constituent "missed" by the Wikipedia heuristic is not missing from the universe. There is no corruption of downstream data, only redundant-source under-yield. (2) The auditor's central "exchange-prefixed/templated symbol is missed" claim misreads line 87: the regex \[\[(?:[^\]|]*\|)?([^\]]*)\]\] keeps the display text, so [[NYSE: AAPL|AAPL]] -> AAPL which DOES match line 92. The three pages used (List_of_S%26P_500_companies, FTSE_100, DAX) put bare tickers in the symbol cell, which is exactly the case the regex handles. (3) This exact code was already audited and triaged as F-217a-10 LOW (audit-reports/2026-05-17-tag217a-discovery-pullers.md:87-90), and the single-letter whitelist is a deliberate documented response to that finding — this is a re-report of known, accepted debt, not a new defect.

Net: real engineering brittleness worth a backlog item, but not a medium data-integrity bug. revised_severity low to match the prior triage.

Relevant files (absolute): C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/discovery/wikipedia-indices.js (lines 76-108 extractor); C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/refresh-universe.js (lines 328-368 union merge); C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/audit-reports/2026-05-17-tag217a-discovery-pullers.md (lines 87-110 prior LOW triage).

title: OTC rawSym may be a non-string field, and .trim() will throw if symbol is numeric/null in one of the tolerated response shapes
evidence: Line 146 `const rawSym = row.symbol || row.ticker || row.Symbol || row.tickerSymbol || '';` then line 147 `const sym = rawSym.trim().toUpperCase();`. If the API ever returns a numeric symbol field (e.g. `symbol: 12345` for an Expert-Market numeric placeholder) the `|| ''` fallback does NOT trigger (a truthy number), and `(12345).trim` is not a function → throws → caught at line 182-186 → `break` → aborts ALL remaining pages (compounds A-discovery-09).
why_it_matters: A single numeric symbol cell in an Expert-Market page would crash the page handler and, via the break, truncate the whole OTC pull. Low likelihood but high blast radius because of the break-on-error pagination.
fix: Coerce defensively: `const rawSym = String(row.symbol ?? row.ticker ?? row.Symbol ?? row.tickerSymbol ?? '').trim().toUpperCase();`. Comment: 'prevents non-string symbol field crashing the page and truncating OTC pagination'.

_verdict.note: Confirmed against source at C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/discovery/otc-markets.js:146-147. The mechanism is correct: line 146 `const rawSym = row.symbol || row.ticker || row.Symbol || row.tickerSymbol || ''` short-circuits on any truthy non-string value (e.g. a number), because the `|| ''` fallback only triggers on falsy values. A truthy number like 12345 propagates, and line 147 `rawSym.trim()` then throws TypeError: rawSym.trim is not a function (numbers have no .trim). That throw is inside the per-row loop (144-168), which is inside the try block (130-181), so it is caught at 182-186, logged, and `break`s — aborting all remaining pages and truncating the OTC universe (genuinely compounds the pagination-abort concern the auditor cites). The same latent pattern exists in nasdaq-api.js:163; nasdaq-all.js (splits a CSV line, parts are always strings) and finnhub.js:55 (already wraps in `(rawSymbol||'')` from a string source) are not exposed. So the defensive-coercion gap is real and the blast radius is real. CAVEAT on realism: there is NO concrete evidence in the repo that the OTC Markets API ever returns a numeric symbol field — the 'Expert-Market numeric placeholder' is the auditor's speculation. Symbols are normally strings, so this is a low-probability hardening issue, not an observed crash. 'low' severity is appropriate.

title: parseMcap silently mis-scales any market cap expressed in plain dollars or with unexpected formatting, and never validates against a sane range
evidence: Lines 136-147: regex `/^([\d.]+)([BMT]?)$/i` — a NASDAQ API value like '1,234,567,890' (already stripped of commas at line 138) with NO suffix returns the raw number `1234567890` (treated as dollars, correct) but a value like '1.23' (meaning $1.23B in some download formats that drop the 'B') returns `1.23` (1.23 dollars). No isFinite guard beyond parseFloat, and no plausibility check. A garbled '12.3.4' fails the regex → null (fine), but a legitimately suffix-less billions figure is under-scaled by 1e9.
why_it_matters: marketCap feeds the universe ranking cap (refresh-universe.js:386-390 sorts by it). A mis-scaled mcap of 1.23 instead of 1.23e9 sorts a mega-cap to the bottom of withMcap and it gets cut. Because the value 'looks parseable', no error is logged. Compounds A-discovery-01.
fix: After parsing, guard with isFinite and a plausibility floor/ceiling (reject < 1e5 as obviously mis-scaled, log it). Prefer the API's numeric marketCap field over the formatted string when present. Comment: 'prevents suffix-less mcap strings being under-scaled and mis-ranking the universe cap'.

_verdict.note:
Refuted as a real defect. parseMcap (nasdaq-api.js:136-147) parses the `marketCap` field from api.nasdaq.com/api/screener/stocks?download=true. That endpoint returns marketCap as either an empty string or a PLAIN INTEGER dollar string (e.g. "2750000000000"), NOT abbreviated suffix-less values. The auditor's harm scenario — a value like "1.23" meaning $1.23B getting under-scaled by 1e9 — rests on a hypothesized "download format that drops the B" that this API does not actually emit. The B/M/T branches and the "$1.23B" docstring (line 133) are speculative tolerance; for the real input (suffix-less integer) the `return n` path is already CORRECT (raw dollars). So the central claim is based on an assumed-but-unobserved input format.

Impact is also overstated. The parsed value flows only into refresh-universe.js:344 (`marketCap: info.marketCap || null`) and is consumed solely by the Tag 147 universe-cap *ranking sort* (refresh-universe.js:386-398) to pick top-N discovery candidates. It is never displayed, never used as a screen threshold, and where Yahoo provides authoritative mcap (pull-yahoo.js, the source of the dollar figures in picks-history/latest.json) this hint is irrelevant. Note also F-217a-05 already documents that nasdaq-api's mcap is usually discarded entirely due to first-write-wins merge ordering, further shrinking any real-world effect. Worst case = marginal mis-ordering of a discovery hint near the cap boundary, not data corruption.

There is a small kernel of truth: no isFinite/plausibility guard, and the docstring advertises a B/M/T format that doesn't match the live integer payload. But this is cosmetic/informational, not a low-severity data-integrity bug as filed.

fix_safe=false: the proposed "reject < 1e5 as mis-scaled" floor is behavior-CHANGING and risky — it would silently null out any genuinely small marketCap (legit micro-caps, partial-integer values), and "prefer the API's numeric marketCap field" assumes a separate numeric field that is in fact the same string already being parsed. Needs human review, not auto-apply.

title: SEC ticker filter drops valid tickers containing a hyphen-class on one path while the regex allows it on another — and rejects dotted class shares present in SEC data as 'BRK-B' only
evidence: Line 96 `if (/[\s\/\\]/.test(ticker)) continue;` rejects whitespace/slash/backslash (fine). Line 103 regex `/^[A-Z][A-Z0-9]{0,4}([.\-][A-Z])?$/` allows exactly ONE single-letter class suffix after a dot or dash. But SEC's company_tickers.json uses the bare exchange ticker form (e.g. 'BRKB' or 'BRK-B' depending on vintage); two-letter class suffixes (e.g. preferred series like 'BAC-PB') and tickers >5 base chars (rare but exist, e.g. 'GOOGL' is 5 = ok, but some ADRs are 6) are rejected.
why_it_matters: The `{0,4}` base length caps the ticker at 5 characters total before the optional class group; legitimate 6-char symbols and multi-char preferred-series tickers from the authoritative SEC feed are dropped. Lower severity because SEC tickers are mostly <=5, but it is a silent exclusion of the long tail the screener is trying to expand into ('20% of potential').
fix: Loosen the base length to `{0,5}` (Yahoo supports 6-char roots) and allow an optional 1-2 char class/series group `([.\-][A-Z]{1,2})?`, OR — preferred — stop regex-validating SEC's authoritative feed at all and instead only reject on the whitespace/slash check (line 96), trusting SEC's own ticker field. Comment: 'prevents 6-char and multi-char-series tickers being dropped from the authoritative SEC feed'.

_verdict.note:
False positive — the headline claim misreads working, already-fixed code. File: C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/discovery/sec-tickers.js.

Claim refutation:
1) Title asserts an inconsistency between line 96 and line 103 ("drops hyphen-class on one path while the regex allows it on another"). Line 96 `if (/[\s\/\\]/.test(ticker)) continue;` only rejects whitespace, forward-slash, backslash — it does NOT touch hyphens or dots. So there is no conflicting path; the two lines do not disagree on class-share tickers. Misread.
2) Claim that the regex "rejects dotted class shares ... as 'BRK-B' only" is empirically wrong. Tested the live regex /^[A-Z][A-Z0-9]{0,4}([.\-][A-Z])?$/: BRK-B PASS, BRK.B PASS, BF-B PASS, BF.B PASS, BRKB PASS, GOOGL PASS. The Tag 217g fix (lines 97-103) already accepts both dot and dash single-letter class separators. The auditor is re-flagging the very bug that was already fixed.

Residual sub-claims (real-but-immaterial):
- Two-letter preferred series (BAC-PB, JPM-PA) are rejected by the regex (confirmed DROP), but SEC's company_tickers.json maps CIK -> primary common-stock ticker and does not enumerate preferred-series symbols as separate entries, so these are essentially absent from THIS feed. No concrete dropped SEC entry named.
- 6-char common-stock roots on US exchanges are vanishingly rare; the finding's own example (GOOGL) is 5 chars and passes. Speculative, no named case.

Impact is negligible regardless: refresh-universe.js (lines 328-368) unions SEC with five other sources (nasdaq-all, finnhub, wikipedia, otc-markets, nasdaq-api) — SEC is not the sole authority — then hard-caps at MAX_UNIVERSE=25000. The identical regex is intentionally shared across sec-tickers.js:103, nasdaq-api.js:167, otc-markets.js:152 as a consistent junk-symbol gate.

fix_safe=false: the "preferred" proposed fix (stop validating and trust SEC's field) would admit arbitrary junk and break the shared invariant across three modules; even the looser-regex variant changes a coordinated cross-module contract and could let unpriceable preferred-series tickers into the universe. Behavior-changing, needs human review, not safe to auto-apply.

title: finnhub get() leaks the API token into error messages and logs on non-200, exposing the secret in CI logs
evidence: Line 41 `if (res.statusCode !== 200) return reject(new Error('HTTP ' + res.statusCode));` is safe, but the redirect branch (line 39) `return get(res.headers.location)...` follows a Location that — for an auth-failed Finnhub request — can echo the full `?token=...` query string, and line 95 `console.error('[Finnhub] ' + exchange + ' failed: ' + e.message)` plus the timeout/connection errors can surface the URL (which contains `token=${token}`, line 74) in stack traces. The token is also embedded in the URL passed to https.get at line 74.
why_it_matters: FINNHUB_API_KEY is a secret. Any error path or redirect that includes the request URL risks printing the live token into Run logs / CI artifacts. Per the project's binding constraint, secrets must never be emitted. Low severity only because the common error messages here are sanitized, but the URL-in-redirect and any future logging of the URL is a latent leak.
fix: Pass the token via an `X-Finnhub-Token` request header instead of the query string (Finnhub supports the header), so it never appears in URLs, redirects, or error text. Scrub any URL before logging. Comment: 'prevents FINNHUB_API_KEY leaking into logs via request URL / redirect Location'.

_verdict.note: False positive based on misread code. The token IS in the request URL (finnhub.js:74 `token=${token}`), but no code path in this file logs that URL or the token. (1) Redirect branch (line 39) only calls `get(res.headers.location)` — it never logs the Location header; the claim that it "echoes ?token= into error text" is unfounded since Location is never interpolated into any log/error string. (2) The sole error log, line 95, prints `e.message` only (never `e.stack`, never the URL). The errors `get()` can reject with are deterministic and URL-free: `'HTTP '+statusCode` (line 41, e.g. "HTTP 401"), `'timeout'` (line 48), Node socket errors (lines 45/47), and JSON.parse SyntaxErrors (line 76). None contain the query string. (3) Empirically verified on this box: `https.get('...?token=SECRET123')` against a bad host yields `e.message` = "getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND <host>" — hostname only, secret absent. GitHub Actions masks registered secrets in logs anyway as a second layer. So there is no leak path; severity is effectively moot. fix_safe=false: moving to an X-Finnhub-Token header changes the wire protocol of every request and is NOT behavior-preserving — it needs live verification that Finnhub honors the header for stock/symbol on the free tier, and critically the existing recursive redirect handling `get(res.headers.location)` would DROP a custom header on the redirected call (whereas a query-string token travels inside the URL and survives the redirect), a subtle regression. Needs human review/testing, not auto-apply.

title: Fixed `parts.length < 7` guard silently skips every data row if NASDAQ-Trader changes column count, zeroing the entire US feed without error
evidence: Line 64 `if (parts.length < 7) continue;` (parseNasdaqListed expects 8 cols) and line 88 same in parseOtherListed. The trailing 'File Creation Time' footer line is handled (line 62), but if NASDAQ-Trader ever adds/removes a column (they have changed these files historically) every row fails the `< 7` check and the function returns an empty Map. The caller (lines 116-118) logs the count but does not assert it is non-zero, so the US backbone of the universe vanishes with only a benign '0 common stocks' log.
why_it_matters: nasdaqlisted/otherlisted are the primary US source (~7-8k stocks). A column-count change silently zeroes them; the screener would lose its entire US backbone and the only signal is a count that nobody asserts on. Silent-shrink / swallowed-schema-drift failure class.
fix: Parse by HEADER (split the header row, locate Symbol/ETF/Test Issue columns by name) instead of fixed positional indices; assert the returned Map size is within an expected band (e.g. > 3000) and throw/warn loudly otherwise so the aggregator's F-DP-037-style alerting can catch it. Comment: 'prevents silent zeroing of the US backbone on NASDAQ-Trader column drift'.

_verdict.note: Code cited accurately: discovery/nasdaq-all.js line 64 (parseNasdaqListed) and line 88 (parseOtherListed) both `if (parts.length < 7) continue;` on 8-column pipe-delimited NASDAQ-Trader files, and the caller (refresh-universe.js lines 111-131) logs counts without a non-zero assertion under Promise.allSettled. But the finding's impact claim is overstated and partly wrong, so I refute it as a real bug at the stated severity: (1) The "add/remove a column zeroes every row" premise is false for the common case — if NASDAQ-Trader ADDS a column, parts.length becomes >=8, the `<7` guard still passes, and existing positional indices keep working. Only a DROP of 2+ columns (≤6 fields) trips the guard, a narrow historically-rare event. (2) "US backbone vanishes" is incorrect: refresh-universe.js is purely ADDITIVE (lines 410-419 build newTickers = allTickers not in existing; 437-448 only push NEW entries; if newTickers.length===0 it returns "Universe unchanged"). An empty Map means "no new NASDAQ tickers this run," NOT deletion of the existing US universe. Existing US tickers persist, and SEC EDGAR/NASDAQ-API/Finnhub also supply US names — this is not the sole US source. (3) Not fully silent: Tag 228c (lines 421-435) logs per-source new-ticker attribution specifically so a zero-count for a known source is visible in the `new-ticker source attribution` log. Net: a minor defensive-hardening nice-to-have (fixed positional parse + no >0 assert), not a latent silent data-zeroing bug.

title: Sparkline assumes annualRev is newest-first; if any series is oldest-first the trend renders reversed
evidence: Line 313-314 `const a = (stock.annual && stock.annual.annualRev) || []; const vals = _arrVals(a).slice(0, 5).reverse();` The comment says 'oldest -> newest, max 5' but that only holds if annualRev is stored newest-first. The modal code (l.1066-1068) makes the SAME newest-first assumption (`arrVals(...).reverse()`), so the assumption is at least consistent across this file — but it is nowhere validated, and `_arrVals` (l.307-310) silently drops non-finite entries, which shifts which 5 elements survive the `slice(0,5)` taken BEFORE the filter is applied inside _arrVals.
why_it_matters: Order is load-bearing for a visual that Karl uses to eyeball growth direction. If a future Yahoo-envelope change, a method that pre-sorts, or a partially-null leading element flips/shifts the order, every sparkline silently lies about trend direction with no error. Because `_arrVals` filters nulls, `slice(0,5)` on the raw array can yield fewer than the 5 most-recent valid points (a leading null consumes a slot), making the spark omit the latest year.
fix: Filter to finite values first, THEN slice the most-recent 5: `const vals = _arrVals(a).slice(0,5).reverse()` -> change to `_arrVals(a)` first, take `.slice(0,5)`, reverse. Add an explicit order assertion or sort by the snapshot's period key if available. Comment: 'prevents reversed/short sparkline when leading annualRev entry is null or order changes'.

_verdict.note:
False positive based on misreading method-chain order. At line 314 the code is `_arrVals(a).slice(0,5).reverse()`. JS evaluates left-to-right, so `_arrVals(a)` (the finite-value filter, l.307-310) runs FIRST, producing finite values in original order; THEN `.slice(0,5)` takes the 5 newest of the already-filtered array; THEN `.reverse()` gives oldest->newest. The auditor's claim that "slice(0,5) is taken BEFORE the filter" is backwards. Consequently the proposed_fix ("_arrVals(a) first, then slice(0,5), reverse") is exactly the existing code -- a no-op.

The newest-first assumption is also NOT unvalidated: pull-yahoo.js l.617 explicitly comments "Annual-Arrays (latest first)" and builds annualRev via _arr(isHist,...) from Yahoo's incomeStatementHistory, which is newest-first by API contract. Every fixture in engine-fixtures.js and tag28-tests.js stores annualRev newest-first (descending). The assumption is a provable invariant, not a guess, and it is consistent across buildSparkline (l.314) and the modal (l.1066+1077: full .reverse() then .slice(-5)).

The only genuine slice-before-filter is the unrelated stash at l.364 (`((s.annual.annualRev)||[]).slice(0,5)`) feeding the modal -- but it slices the 5 NEWEST raw entries (newest-first preserved) and the modal filters afterward, so at worst the modal shows 4 points instead of 5 if a leading year is null. That is a minor cosmetic completeness nit, never a reversed trend, and it is not the line (313-314) the finding cites. Neither the cited line nor the proposed fix represents a real bug.

title: fcfMargin/revGrowth carry the string 'n/a' as a sentinel, then are passed through Number.isFinite and arithmetic comparisons
evidence: Lines 375-376 set `const fcfMargin = (... Number.isFinite(...)) ? r40.components.fcfMargin : 'n/a';` and likewise `revGrowth = ... : 'n/a'`. Later l.412 `(revGrowth != null && Number.isFinite(revGrowth)) ? ...` and l.416 `data-fcf-margin="${Number.isFinite(fcfMargin) ? fcfMargin.toFixed(1) : 'n/a'}"`. The variable holds EITHER a number OR the literal string 'n/a'. Number.isFinite('n/a') is false, so it mostly works, but it conflates 'no data' with a sentinel string and relies on Number.isFinite never being reached with a numeric-looking string.
why_it_matters: Mixing a string sentinel into a numeric field is fragile: any later code that does `fcfMargin >= x` or `+fcfMargin` would coerce 'n/a' to NaN and produce a silently-wrong comparison (the client-side applyFilters at l.1148-1149 explicitly works around this by string-comparing `card.dataset.fcfMargin === 'n/a'`, proving the sentinel leaks into the data layer). The 0-vs-missing ambiguity is exactly the falsy-bug class flagged for this audit: a legitimate fcfMargin of 0 is fine here (guarded by Number.isFinite) but the dual-type variable invites a future `|| 'n/a'` regression.
fix: Use `null` for missing internally and format to 'n/a' only at the HTML boundary: `const fcfMargin = (...finite) ? value : null;` then `data-fcf-margin="${fcfMargin == null ? 'n/a' : fcfMargin.toFixed(1)}"`. Keeps the numeric field strictly number|null.

_verdict.note: False positive (code-quality smell at most, not a bug). Traced the full data flow in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/generate-modes-report.js. Lines 375-376 set fcfMargin/revGrowth to EITHER a finite number (already gated by Number.isFinite(r40.components.*)) OR the exact literal string 'n/a'. There is no input path that produces a numeric-looking string like '42' — the only non-number value is the hardcoded 'n/a'. Therefore the auditor's stated risk ("relies on Number.isFinite never being reached with a numeric-looking string") cannot occur: Number.isFinite('n/a') is always false, and a real number always passes. Lines 412-413 and 416 all produce correct output on every reachable input; the auditor even concedes "it mostly works." Moreover the 'n/a' sentinel is an intentional, relied-upon contract: the client-side filter at lines 1148-1149 explicitly tests `card.dataset.fcfMargin === 'n/a'` / `=== 'n/a'` as an escape hatch, and parseFloat('n/a')=NaN is handled. So 'n/a' is a deliberate wire value, not an accidental sentinel. The `!= null` guards on 412-413 are redundant (value is never null) but harmless. No behavioral defect exists; "bug/medium" is overstated — this is at most a low/style observation.

title: IPO year rendered as 2-digit (ipoYear % 100) is century-ambiguous
evidence: Line 429: `${ipoYear ? "'" + (ipoYear % 100).toString().padStart(2, '0') : '...'}`. Verified: 1998 -> '98, 2003 -> '03. A 1998 IPO and a hypothetical 2098 (and the pre-1962 floor used elsewhere, l.454) all collapse to the same 2-digit label.
why_it_matters: The IPO slider min defaults to 1962 (l.454), so the universe legitimately spans >60 years. `'98` is read by most users as 1998, but old-economy names with pre-2000 IPOs sit next to post-2000 names showing `'05`, `'12` etc., and the apostrophe-2-digit convention silently loses the century. Low severity because the filterable data-ipo attribute (l.416) carries the full year; only the visible badge is ambiguous.
fix: Render the full 4-digit year, or only abbreviate within an unambiguous window. Simplest: `${ipoYear || '—'}` full year in the badge.

_verdict.note: Code on line 429 is described accurately (`'` + ipoYear % 100, zero-padded), but the "century-ambiguous bug" is a non-issue, and one of its three cited collisions is a misread. (1) This is a stock screener of currently-listed public companies; real IPO years span ~1962-2026, all of which map to DISTINCT 2-digit labels ('62-'26). The "1998 vs 2098 collision" is purely hypothetical — no 2098 IPO can exist for ~70 years. (2) The apostrophe-prefixed 2-digit year ('98) is a universally understood convention for recent decades; nobody reads '98 as 2098. (3) The cited "pre-1962 floor at l.454" is a MISREAD: line 454 (`ipoMin = ipos.length ? Math.min(...ipos) : 1962`) is the slider's fallback MINIMUM default when no IPO data exists — it is never stamped onto a card as an IPO year, so it cannot "collapse" with any badge. Functionally, all IPO filtering/sorting uses the full 4-digit year: data-ipo="${ipoYear||0}" (line 416) feeds card.dataset.ipo in the filter JS (lines 1135/1145), and the slider min/max (lines 539-540, ipoMin/ipoMax) are full years. The 2-digit label on 429 is purely cosmetic display with zero functional consequence. The proposed fix (full year, or '—' fallback) also CHANGES user-visible rendering (badge layout designed for compact 3-char output in a 9.5px monospace card-bottom slot) — it is a design/UX choice, not a behavior-preserving safe edit.

title: fmtValue is never called; topByMethod and topAllMust are exported but consumed by nobody (and unused internally)
evidence: `grep` over the file: `fmtValue` (defined l.71) has zero call sites. `topByMethod` (l.245) and `topAllMust` (l.266) appear only in their definitions, the module.exports line (l.1316 `module.exports = { eligibleForMode, topByMethod, topAllMust, evaluateAll, dedupeByCompany }`), and comments. Repo-wide grep for external requires found only generate-methods-report.js, snapshot-methods-history.js and scripts/pipeline-health-check.js — and in all three the matches are COMMENTS or a CLI invocation `node generate-modes-report.js ...` (daily-pull.yml l.383), never a `require('./generate-modes-report')`. So the exports are dead. Internally, only countAllMustPass (l.291) is used for stats; topAllMust survives only in comments (l.288-290, 1287-1288).
why_it_matters: Dead exports/functions are maintenance traps: the prior audit already deleted renderRow for the same reason (l.434-439 comment). fmtValue additionally hides a latent bug — `if (unit === 'ratio' && Math.abs(v) < 1)` (l.74) silently rescales any ratio in (-1,1) to a percent, which would be wrong if it were ever wired up. Carrying three unreferenced symbols (one buggy) inflates the file and misleads future readers into thinking topByMethod/topAllMust are part of a live code path.

Keep evaluateAll/dedupeByCompany only if a test or external caller actually needs them (none found — confirm before trimming).

_verdict.note: Confirmed real dead code on all three sub-claims, verified against C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/generate-modes-report.js. (1) fmtValue (defined l.71-77) has zero call sites in this file — grep `fmtValue(` returns only the definition. The other fmtValue with a call site (l.449) lives in a SEPARATE file, generate-methods-report.js, with its own definition (l.157); it is not this one. So the modes-report copy is dead. (2) topByMethod (l.245) and topAllMust (l.266) appear in this file ONLY as their definitions, the module.exports line (l.1316), and comments (l.288-290, 436, 1287-1288); grep for call sites `topByMethod(|topAllMust(` returns only definitions + comment lines, no invocations. The live stats path uses countAllMustPass (l.291) instead. (3) No external consumer: repo-wide grep for `require(...generate-modes-report...)` over *.js returns zero hits (the only string match is inside a comment in an archived findings JSON). The script is launched as a CLI (`node generate-modes-report.js`, daily-pull.yml), and `require.main === module` runs main() which never references the exported names — so the module.exports surface is consumed by nobody. title: dedupeByCompany decides 'US listing' purely by absence of a dot in the ticker — wrong for several US venues and ADRs
evidence: Lines 221-222: `const evIsUS = !/\./.test(ticker); const exIsUS = !/\./.test(existing.stock.meta.ticker);` Then l.223-226 prefer the 'US' listing over a foreign dup, else keep larger mcap. REGION_TO_COUNTRY (l.30-46) maps real US venues like 'OTC Markets OTCPK'/'OTCQX' and many non-US venues; the dot-heuristic ignores region entirely.
why_it_matters: When the same company appears as both a US listing and a foreign listing, the dedupe keeps the dotless one assuming it is the more-liquid US line. But dotless tickers are not exclusively US (and US OTC/ADR lines can carry suffixes), so the wrong listing can win — propagating that listing's mcap, FX-denominated fundamentals and region into every mode. This is asymmetric survivorship: which of two near-identical companies survives dedupe changes ranking and counts. Cross-listing collisions are exactly where FX/region correctness matters most.
fix: Use the already-available region/country signal instead of the dot heuristic: prefer the listing whose REGION_TO_COUNTRY[region] === 'USA' (or a primary-listing flag if the snapshot carries one), falling back to mcap. The instruction bans hardcoded ticker exclusions — this is a guard fix, not an exclusion.

_verdict.note:
Verified against generate-modes-report.js (dedupeByCompany l.191-230, call site l.1278) and pull-yahoo.js (the sole writer of meta.region). Two reasons the finding does not stand as written.

1) The proposed fix is broken — it misreads the data model. meta.region is written ONLY at pull-yahoo.js:827 via normalizeRegion(), which returns enum buckets ('US','EU','UK','JP','HK','CN','CA','AU','EM','OTHER',...). REGION_TO_COUNTRY (l.30-46) keys on EXCHANGE DISPLAY NAMES ('Nasdaq','NYSE','OTC Markets OTCPK','XETRA',...), none of which are the bucket strings. So REGION_TO_COUNTRY['US'] === undefined, never 'USA'; the proposed predicate REGION_TO_COUNTRY[region]==='USA' would be false for EVERY stock, silently collapsing the tie-break to pure mcap and DROPPING the US-preference entirely — a regression, not a fix. This is the exact schema mismatch already documented in-repo as F-ME-018 (meta.region holds buckets, display-name maps don't match). The same map is partly dead in renderCard l.356 too.

2) The dot-heuristic is a minor robustness gap, not a demonstrated correctness bug. The tie-break only fires on a name-collision (two snapshots normalizing to the same company key). For the common dual-listing case it behaves as intended: the foreign listing carries a dotted suffix (.DE/.SW/.MX) and loses to the dotless US/ADR ticker. The auditor's headline 'wrong for ADRs' case (dotless US ADR beats a dotted foreign ordinary) actually yields the DESIRED outcome — keep the US-tradeable listing. Remaining edge cases (two dotless tickers) fall through to mcap, a sane fallback. No evidence of wrong dedup output in production.

If anything were to be improved, the correct signal is the bucket compare (ev.stock.meta.region === 'US'), NOT REGION_TO_COUNTRY — but even that is a low-value cosmetic hardening with no shown impact, and needs human design (US ADR vs US primary still ties).

title: Status-strip 'Sektor-Exclude' count derived from HYPERGROWTH eligibility only, but eligibleForMode never applies mcapFloor
evidence: Line 591 `const sectorExcluded = totalStocks - eligibleByMode.HYPERGROWTH.length;` shown as 'Sektor-Exclude / Banks·REITs·Mining' (l.1011). But eligibleForMode (l.232-243) filters ONLY sector + dataGuards — not mcapFloor. Meanwhile evaluateMode (strategy-modes.js l.183-199) DOES reject on mcapFloor (QC has 5e9) returning a modeEval with no score. HYPERGROWTH has no mcapFloor, so the count is 'sector + failed-HG-dataguards', not pure sector exclusion.
why_it_matters: The headline 'Sektor-Exclude' figure actually folds in HYPERGROWTH dataguard failures (sloan, forecast-contamination, q-spike, revenue-volatility), so the number Karl reads as 'banks/REITs/mining removed' is inflated by earnings-quality rejects. Minor (a status badge, not a ranking), but it is a mislabeled metric on the front page and conflates two very different exclusion reasons.
fix: Compute sector exclusion explicitly: `totalStocks - evaluated.filter(ev => !SM.isExcludedBySector(ev.stock, SM.MODES.HYPERGROWTH)).length`, or relabel the cell to 'HG-ineligible'. Keep the dataguard count as a separate cell if useful.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed by source. generate-modes-report.js:591 `const sectorExcluded = totalStocks - eligibleByMode.HYPERGROWTH.length;` is rendered at line 1011 with label "Sektor-Exclude" + sub "Banks · REITs · Mining". But eligibleForMode (l.232-243) filters on TWO criteria: SM.isExcludedBySector (l.236) AND the HYPERGROWTH dataGuards (l.237-240) = ['sloan-ratio','forecast-contamination-guard','q-spike-dataguard','revenue-volatility-guard'] (strategy-modes.js:90). So the count = sector-excluded + HG-dataguard-failures, not pure sector exclusion as labeled. Genuine label-vs-value mismatch in a display cell.

Caveat on the auditor's framing: the TITLE blames mcapFloor, but that is a red herring for this count. HYPERGROWTH (strategy-modes.js:71-96) has NO mcapFloor key, so mcapFloor never enters the HYPERGROWTH-derived number. The QC mcapFloor=5e9 (strategy-modes.js:121) is real but irrelevant here since sectorExcluded derives solely from HYPERGROWTH. The actual inflation source is the dataGuards — which the auditor DOES correctly identify in the evidence body ("the count is 'sector + failed-HG-dataguards'"). So the bug is real; the headline mechanism is slightly misdiagnosed.

Severity low is correct: nothing downstream consumes sectorExcluded (only definition at l.591, only use at l.1011) — it is a cosmetic explanatory number in the HTML status strip, not a screening result. In practice the discrepancy is nonzero only when an HG dataGuard fires with computable===true && pass===false (q-spike/sloan/etc.), which does happen (e.g. IONQ per the l.88-89 comment), so the displayed number can overstate sector exclusions.

Proposed fix is valid: SM.MODES and SM.isExcludedBySector are both exported (strategy-modes.js:431-438) and SM is the require alias (l.19). The relabel alternative is also trivial. But fix_safe=false: the auditor offers two divergent options (recompute the count vs. relabel the cell) without choosing one, and the recompute option changes a user-visible reported number; this needs a human to decide intent rather than blind auto-apply, even though the risk is genuinely small.

title: Main HTML is written and announced BEFORE the failure-rate gate runs, so a 'failed' run still publishes a stale/degraded report
evidence: Line 1283 `writeFileAtomic(args.out, html);` and l.1284 logs 'Wrote ...' — this happens first. Only afterwards (l.1296-1311) is failure_rate computed and `process.exit(1)` thrown if >5%. The atomic write has already replaced modes-report.html on disk.
why_it_matters: When the gate trips, the intent is to fail the run and NOT promote a bad artifact. But modes-report.html is already overwritten at the target path before the gate fires; the daily-pull workflow copies modes-report.html to _site (daily-pull.yml l.666). Depending on step ordering and `|| true` guards in the deploy step, a report generated from a >5%-failed run can still be the file that gets deployed, defeating the gate's purpose.

title: Parent-directory fsync is skipped on Windows — the module's headline durability guarantee does NOT hold on Karl's actual deployment box
evidence: function _fsyncParentDirBestEffort(targetPath) { ... if (IS_WINDOWS) return; ... }  — and the Tag 230c-1 header claims '1. POSIX rename atomicity guarantees the DIRECTORY ENTRY swap is atomic, but the metadata write that records the new entry must itself be fsync'd on the PARENT DIRECTORY for the rename to survive a power loss'. The justification comment (line 107-111) asserts 'Windows neither requires nor supports fsync on a directory handle (NTFS journals metadata separately)'.
why_it_matters: Karl's primary box is Windows 11 (and snapshots/state live on a OneDrive-synced folder per the comment at lib/atomic-write.js:50). The whole point of this module (F-SM-015 alert-state baseline-wipe, ≥9 files) is crash-durability. On Windows the code does tmp-fsync + rename but never flushes the directory metadata, AND NTFS metadata journaling only guarantees consistency, not that the rename is durable at the moment writeFileAtomic returns — a power loss right after return can still lose the rename on NTFS without FlushFileBuffers on the volume/dir. The module advertises durability it does not deliver on the one OS that matters here. At minimum the claim is unverified folklore presented as fact.
fix: Either (a) on Windows open the target file after rename and fsync IT (FlushFileBuffers via fs.fsyncSync on an fd opened 'r+' flushes that file's metadata to the volume), or (b) soften the module header + the _fsyncParentDirBestEffort comment to state plainly that on Windows durability is best-effort and relies on NTFS journaling, so callers don't over-trust it. Do not silently claim POSIX-grade durability on NTFS.

_verdict.note:
Refuted as framed. Factual core is correct: _fsyncParentDirBestEffort early-returns on Windows (line 111), so the parent-directory-ENTRY fsync is skipped there. But the finding overstates this into a false "headline durability guarantee" and recommends a fix that doesn't fix anything.

1) No false headline claim. The module docstring (lib/atomic-write.js:2-23) claims only ATOMICITY-AGAINST-READERS, and for Windows explicitly scopes it: "on Windows the rename is also atomic against readers as long as no handle is open" (line 15). The power-loss/fsync reasoning lives entirely in the Tag 230c-1 IMPLEMENTATION comment (lines 35-58), which is explicitly framed around POSIX rename semantics. Callers are never promised POSIX-grade power-loss durability on Windows.

2) Data IS durable on Windows. The tmp file's bytes are fsync'd before rename on ALL platforms (line 152, fs.fsyncSync(fd)). The only thing skipped on Windows is durability of the directory ENTRY metadata, which on NTFS is covered by the metadata journal/log-file — exactly what the comment (lines 105-106) states. That assertion is substantially accurate, not a misread.

3) Deployment reality defuses severity. The pipeline that actually commits/pushes state files runs on ubuntu-latest (.github/workflows/daily-pull.yml:25), where the POSIX dir-fsync path is fully exercised. Windows is Karl's local dev box only; a local power loss costs at most a re-runnable local pull, never committed production state. The Tag 230c report itself states "no production impact (CI runs on Linux)" (audit-reports/2026-05-17-tag230c-infra-modules-2.md:73-75).

4) Proposed fix (a) is technically wrong: opening the renamed file and fsyncing its fd flushes that file's data/inode, NOT the containing directory's entry, on any platform — and the data was already fsync'd pre-rename. So (a) is a no-op for the cited gap and would add cost for nothing. Fix (b) (soften the comment) is a harmless wording tweak but the comment already says essentially this ("NTFS journals metadata separately").

Net: a doc-nuance / over-trust quibble at most, not a data-integrity defect. Real-world durability on Windows is best-effort-via-NTFS-journal as documented; on the production Linux runner the full guarantee holds.

title: writeJsonAtomic silently writes nothing/garbage when JSON.stringify returns undefined
evidence: const payload = JSON.stringify(value, opts.replacer || null, indent); writeFileAtomic(targetPath, payload, { encoding: 'utf8' });  — JSON.stringify returns undefined when value is undefined, a function, or a Symbol. writeFileAtomic then sees typeof data === 'undefined' (not 'string', not Buffer), falls to the else branch fs.writeFileSync(tmp, undefined, {encoding:'utf8'}) which writes the 9-byte literal string 'undefined' to the state file.
why_it_matters: A caller that passes an accidentally-undefined value (e.g. a function returning nothing, or a mistyped field) atomically overwrites a committed state file with the text 'undefined'. The next consumer's JSON.parse throws, OR — per the F-SM-015 pattern this very module exists to prevent — silently regenerates from scratch. The atomic-write helper turns a programmer slip into a durable corruption of exactly the files it was built to protect. NaN-bearing objects are silently coerced to null by stringify too (legitimate values 0/'' survive, but NaN→null can mask a compute bug).
fix: In writeJsonAtomic, guard: `if (payload === undefined) throw new TypeError('writeJsonAtomic: value serialized to undefined for ' + targetPath);`. Comment naming the failure mode it prevents: '// prevents F-SM-015-class corruption: JSON.stringify(undefined) -> writes literal "undefined" over committed state'.

_verdict.note: REFUTED. The finding's core failure chain is factually wrong. Premises check out — JSON.stringify(undefined|function|Symbol) returns undefined (verified), and undefined is neither string nor Buffer, so writeFileAtomic's line-147 guard fails and control reaches the line-157 else branch fs.writeFileSync(tmp, undefined, {encoding:'utf8'}). BUT the conclusion is false: fs.writeFileSync does NOT coerce undefined to the literal string 'undefined'. I tested both the raw call and the full writeJsonAtomic(path, undefined) path on the actual runtime (Node v24.15.0) against the actual file at C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/lib/atomic-write.js. Both THROW: `TypeError [ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE]: The "data" argument must be of type string or an instance of Buffer... Received undefined`. The auditor confused fs.writeFileSync's strict type-check with String()-style coercion (which is what console.log/template literals do). Because the throw happens on the TMP path before _renameWithRetry runs (line 159), the catch at line 161 unlinks the tmp and rethrows — the committed state file at targetPath is NEVER written or renamed over. No 9-byte 'undefined' file, no F-SM-015-class corruption. The actual behavior is already the safe outcome (loud throw, committed state untouched) that the proposed guard aims to produce. Only one caller exists in-repo (the doc example); it passes real objects. The proposed guard would merely produce a slightly clearer error message naming targetPath instead of Node's generic ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE — a diagnostic nicety, not a data-loss fix.

evidence: } else { fs.writeFileSync(tmp, data, options || undefined); }  — the explicit-fsync path (lines 147-155) only runs for strings and Buffers. Any other `data` (a TypedArray view that isn't a Buffer, a stream, an object accepted by some fs overloads) goes through plain fs.writeFileSync with NO fsync before the rename.

(aktienfinder-import:39, detect-changes:95/182, generate-screener:4316/4410, snapshot-picks:283/285/150/314, snapshot-methods-history:160/175, pull-prices-bulk:37, watchlist-cli:33, pull-sec-xbrl:181/188), HTML strings (generate-dashboard:601, generate-methods-report:1223, generate-modes-report:1283, generate-diff-report:38/120, generate-screener:4314), and writeJsonAtomic itself (atomic-write.js:173) always passes a JSON string. The module comment (atomic-write.js:142-144) is explicit and accurate that the fsync path 'covers strings and Buffers, which is what every caller in the repo passes today' — the fallback is a documented defensive net, not an oversight. title: _tmpPath monotonic counter is module-global and unbounded; comment overstates collision safety
evidence: _tmpPath._n = (_tmpPath._n || 0) + 1; return targetPath + '.tmp.' + process.pid + '.' + _tmpPath._n;  — comment: 'Including pid + a monotonic counter is enough to avoid collisions when the same process calls writeFileAtomic on the same path twice in flight'.
why_it_matters: writeFileAtomic is strictly synchronous (no await between tmp-create and rename), so there is never a second in-flight call within one process — the counter solves a problem that cannot occur, while a crashed run leaves orphan `<path>.tmp.<pid>.<n>` files that nothing cleans up (cleanup at line 164 only runs on the throwing call's own tmp). Over months on the OneDrive folder these accumulate and can themselves get synced. Minor but the comment is misleading and there is no orphan sweep.
fix: Either drop the counter (pid alone suffices for sync writes) or add a startup/best-effort sweep of stale `*.tmp.*` siblings older than N minutes in the target dir. Low priority; mainly correct the misleading comment.

_verdict.note: Refuted as a bug; at most a minor comment nitpick. Literal facts are correct (lib/atomic-write.js:31-32: `_tmpPath._n` is a module-global counter on the function object that increments forever and never resets), but the impact framing is wrong. The comment does NOT "overstate collision safety" — if anything the counter is unnecessary surplus. writeFileAtomic (line 132-167) is fully synchronous: openSync/writeSync/fsyncSync/closeSync/renameSync with no `await` anywhere. In single-threaded Node two invocations on the same path can never be "in flight" simultaneously — each runs to completion before the next JS executes — so the stated collision scenario cannot occur and pid alone would already suffice. The "worker pool" in pull-yahoo.js:2152 is async Promise concurrency, not worker_threads, and writes go to distinct per-ticker paths; manifest flushes (line 2161/2201) are sync. No collision path, no corruption path, no resource leak (unbounded JS number is harmless; would need ~9e15 writes). Stale tmp from a SIGKILL'd prior run under PID reuse is harmlessly truncate-overwritten by `openSync(tmp,'w')` (line 148), and every readdirSync consumer filters on `.endsWith('.json')` so `.tmp.<pid>.<n>` siblings are ignored; on-failure cleanup already exists (try/finally unlinkSync, line 164). The proposed stale-tmp sweep addresses a non-problem. Mislabeled category: this is informational/comment-only, not category=bug.

title: Retry budget is shared across 429/5xx/network so a 429 burst can exhaust attempts and drop the alert without honoring the last retry-after
evidence: for (let attempt = 0; attempt <= maxRetries; attempt++) { ... if (res.status === 429 && attempt < maxRetries) { ... continue; } ... }  with maxRetries default 2. The header comment (lines 33-37) says 'The pipeline-health flow can burst 3 alerts in quick succession; first two often 429.'
why_it_matters: With maxRetries=2 the loop makes at most 3 sends. On the final attempt (attempt===maxRetries) a 429 falls through all the `attempt < maxRetries` guards to the generic 4xx branch at line 119 ('Discord post failed: HTTP 429') and returns false — the alert is dropped even though Discord told us exactly how long to wait. Since the module's own comment says bursts 'often 429', the worst-case (every send 429) silently loses the alert this code exists to guarantee.
fix: Track 429 retries separately from a small fixed budget, or on the terminal 429 do one final honored sleep+send instead of treating it as permanent failure. Comment naming the failure mode: '// prevents dropped alert under sustained 429 — terminal rate-limit must still honor retry-after once'.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed against source. In postDiscord (lib/discord.js:79-122) with default maxRetries=2 the loop runs attempts 0,1,2. The 429 branch (line 97) and 5xx branch (line 112) are both gated on `attempt < maxRetries`, so on the terminal 3rd 429 (attempt==2) both guards are false; execution falls through to the generic 4xx terminal branch (line 119), logs "HTTP 429" and returns false WITHOUT performing a final honored retry-after sleep+resend. The budget is genuinely shared: two early 429s consume both retry slots, leaving none for a later network/5xx blip. So the described failure mode (sustained 429 burst drops the alert and the last retry-after is never honored) is real.

Severity correctly low, and the cited justification is partly misattributed: the header comment (lines 33-37) about "pipeline-health flow can burst 3 alerts; first two often 429" refers to scripts/pipeline-health-check.js, which does NOT use this shared helper — it has its own inline fetch (lines 82-94, no retry at all). The two actual callers, scripts/picks-regression-check.js (lines 150, 173) and scripts/check-pull-stats.js (line 151), each invoke postDiscord at most once or twice per run, sequentially with await, in separate CI processes. To actually drop an alert you need three consecutive 429s on the same route where the first two retry-after sleeps (each capped at 10s) fail to clear the limit — a narrow window. Real but low-impact.

fix_safe=false: the proposed fix is not behavior-preserving. Separating a 429 budget changes the semantics of the public `maxRetries` option, and adding "one final honored sleep+send" on the terminal 429 introduces an extra network round-trip plus up to 10s additional sleep on the failure path — the exact CI-time tradeoff the existing 10s-cap comment (lines 105-106) was guarding. It modifies retry/timing behavior in a shared module used by multiple scripts, so it needs human review.

title: Permanent failures are logged to console.log and swallowed (return false), not surfaced — a dead webhook URL fails silently forever
