The two ladders diverge: classifySubProfile (:79-82) routes `ind.includes('bank')`/`'mortgage finance'` to BANK and `'credit services'`/`'asset management'` to FINTECH BEFORE the `sec.includes('financial')` fallback, while classifySubProfileDetailed (:130,:133) has no BANK branch and folds bank into FINTECH, and its sector-financial check precedes its keyword checks. Delegating one to the other would silently reclassify banks (BANK -> FINTECH) and change ordering. That requires human review, so the finding as proposed (which couples to A-lib-08 delegation) is not safe to auto-apply.

title: Keyword precedence misclassifies multi-keyword industries; 'platform'/'media'/communication-sector overreach swallows SaaS and others
evidence: Line 96-98: `if (ind.includes('marketplace') || ind.includes('advertis') || ind.includes('e-commerce') || ind.includes('platform') || ind.includes('media') || sec.includes('communication')) return SUB_PROFILES.MARKETPLACE;`. This runs AFTER software (line 93-95) so 'Software—Infrastructure' is SAAS, but any industry string containing 'platform' that did not already hit software (e.g. 'Information Technology Platform', 'Gaming Platform', 'Media & Entertainment') is forced to MARKETPLACE. `sec.includes('communication')` sweeps the entire Communication Services sector (which includes telecoms, SaaS-like names, gaming) into MARKETPLACE.
why_it_matters: Sub-profile drives the anti-manipulation filters (SAAS carries NRR_CHECK/RPO_GROWTH; MARKETPLACE carries none) and the sector-relative peer group. A communication-sector SaaS name (e.g. a messaging-platform software vendor) loses its NRR/RPO manipulation guards and gets benchmarked against ad/marketplace peers — wrong peer medians AND a disabled fraud guard. First-substring-wins ordering is brittle for companies that legitimately match two buckets.
fix: Score all matching buckets and pick by an explicit priority weight, or at minimum move the broad `sec.includes('communication')` catch to the very end as a low-confidence fallback rather than ahead of the industrial/staples/energy checks. Each reorder needs a comment naming the failure mode (e.g. '// prevents comm-sector SaaS losing NRR_CHECK guard').

_verdict.note:
Central claim ("overreach swallows SaaS") is a misread of the ordering in lib/sub-profile.js. The software/saas/cloud/cybersec/it-services/analytics check is line 93-95, which runs BEFORE the marketplace/platform/media/communication check at line 96-98. Any industry string containing a SaaS keyword is captured as SAAS first and can never reach the communication/platform sweep — so no SaaS is "swallowed", and no NRR_CHECK guard is lost. The auditor's concrete examples are also not real Yahoo Finance taxonomy: "Information Technology Platform" is not a Yahoo industry — the real one is "Information Technology Services", which hits 'it services' (line 94) → SAAS correctly. Real fixtures (engine-fixtures.js) use strings like "Internet Content", "Software", "Semiconductors", "Drug Manufacturers". The headline tickers META/GOOGL are already pinned MARKETPLACE via TICKER_SUBPROFILE_MAP, so the heuristic never even runs for them.

Confirmed real impact path: classifySubProfile feeds (1) effectiveThreshold median-bucket selection (methods/_helpers.js:219-249) and (2) FILTERS_BY_PROFILE manipulation-filter selection (manipulation-filters.js:170-207, MARKETPLACE→_filter_marketplace_opinc_lag). So classification does matter. The only genuine residual is narrow and low-severity: a Communication-Services telecom (industry "Telecom Services") with no software keyword lands in MARKETPLACE rather than a more apt bucket — but there is no telecom sub-profile, this is intended design (Communication Services → MARKETPLACE is canonical for META/GOOGL), and the consequence is one INFO-severity filter plus a median-bucket choice. This is classification coarseness, not a medium-severity bug, and the "swallows SaaS / loses NRR_CHECK" framing is incorrect.

title: safeSnapshotFilename can map two distinct tickers to the same file — silent snapshot overwrite / survivorship loss
evidence: const sanitized = String(ticker).replace(/[^A-Z0-9.-]/gi, '_');  Every disallowed char collapses to '_'. So 'BRK/A' -> 'BRK_A.json' and a literal 'BRK_A' -> 'BRK_A.json' collide; 'RDS-A' vs 'RDS.A' stay distinct (both - and . are allowed) but 'A B' (space) and 'A_B' collide; any two foreign tickers differing only in an exotic separator collide.
why_it_matters: Snapshots are the single keyed store feeding methods/scoring/aggregator. A collision means the second ticker's pull silently overwrites the first's snapshot under the same filename — the first ticker disappears from the universe with no error (the JSON inside still names the wrong ticker, so a later read attributes the wrong fundamentals). This is exactly the asymmetric survivorship-attrition / silent-corruption class the audit targets, and it cannot be caught downstream because no error is raised. The header even brags this helper fixed an invisible-snapshot bug (CON -> _CON.json) while introducing a new invisible-collision bug.
fix: Make the mapping injective: when the sanitized stem differs from the raw ticker, append a short hash of the original ticker (e.g. `+ '.' + crypto.createHash('sha1').update(rawTicker).digest('hex').slice(0,6)`) so distinct tickers never share a file, OR assert no collision at write time by maintaining a ticker->filename index. Do NOT special-case individual tickers. Comment: '// prevents silent snapshot overwrite when two tickers sanitize to the same stem (survivorship loss)'.

_verdict.note:
Mechanism is technically correct but unreachable on real inputs; severity is overstated and the examples are mostly wrong. safeSnapshotFilename (lib/snapshot-fs.js:32-37) collapses every char outside [A-Za-z0-9.-] to '_', so it is not injective in the abstract. BUT it can only collide on tickers that differ solely in chars OUTSIDE that allowed set. In this codebase no such ticker exists: I scanned universe-list.txt (3176 real ticker lines) and watchlist.json (23748 'stocks' entries) — ZERO contain any char outside [A-Za-z0-9.-]. Tickers come only from those curated files plus Yahoo screener quote.symbol; Yahoo share-class/exchange forms use only '.' and '-' (RHM.DE, BRK-B), both of which are PRESERVED, so distinct tickers map to distinct stems.

The auditor's examples are flawed: 'BRK/A' and 'A B' (space) never occur — Yahoo never emits slashes or spaces; and the auditor itself concedes 'RDS-A' vs 'RDS.A' stay distinct (correct, no collision). Read and write paths in pull-yahoo.js / generate-screener.js / regional-oos-test.js all route through the SAME helper, so a ticker is always read from the exact file it wrote — no self-collision. This is a real but purely latent code smell, already independently logged by a prior audit as F-DP-007 (rated MEDIUM, 'latent today'). 'high' data-integrity / survivorship-loss framing is unjustified; downgraded to low.

fix_safe=false: the proposed fix (append sha1 suffix when sanitized stem != raw ticker) is NOT behavior-preserving. It changes the on-disk filename for every ticker that currently sanitizes — including the Windows-reserved '_'-prefixed names (CON->_CON.json) that already round-trip fine — orphaning all existing snapshots under their old names and forcing a full re-pull/migration of the snapshots dir. Needs human review + a migration step, not auto-apply. A safer low-risk alternative would be a write-time collision assertion (ticker->filename index that throws on stem clash), which preserves current filenames.

title: Case-insensitive sanitization preserves lowercase but no case-folding — same ticker in different case yields different filenames on case-insensitive FS, risking duplicate/overwrite on Windows
evidence: String(ticker).replace(/[^A-Z0-9.-]/gi, '_')  — the /i flag means a-z are KEPT (not replaced), so 'brk.b' -> 'brk.b.json' while 'BRK.B' -> 'BRK.B.json'. These are two different strings but the SAME file on NTFS/Windows (case-insensitive filesystem), Karl's deployment target.
why_it_matters: If any caller passes a ticker in lowercase (or mixed case) while another passes uppercase, on Windows they resolve to one file but the code believes they are two — readdir-based scans (e.g. sector-medians-compute.js:363 filtering f.endsWith('.json')) will see one filename, and writes race/overwrite. The JSON's internal ticker may then mismatch the de-facto filename casing. Tickers in this repo are conventionally uppercased by callers, but the helper makes no guarantee and the WINDOWS_RESERVED test already uses /i, signaling case is expected to vary.
fix: Normalize case explicitly and document it: either uppercase the stem before sanitizing (matching the uppercase convention used in sub-profile.js:67) or lowercase consistently, so the filename is deterministic regardless of input case. Comment: '// prevents two-files-believed, one-file-on-NTFS aliasing on Windows'.

_verdict.note: Regex claim is technically accurate — /[^A-Z0-9.-]/gi keeps a-z (the /i flag), so safeSnapshotFilename('brk.b')='brk.b.json' vs ('BRK.B')='BRK.B.json' collide on NTFS. But the overwrite/aliasing scenario is unreachable in this codebase, so it is a non-issue, not a medium bug. Every ticker-ingestion boundary uppercases before tickers reach the canonical watchlist: watchlist-cli.js:91/138/142/146, refresh-universe.js:205/220/279, discovery sources (sec-tickers.js:85, otc-markets.js:147, nasdaq-api.js:163, nasdaq-all.js:65/89, finnhub.js:55), history-cli.js:13. pullAll(watchlist,...) (pull-yahoo.js:1314) is the sole writer and reads stock.ticker straight from that already-uppercased store, so every produced stem is uppercase. Reader and writer both route through the same helper, so naming is at worst consistently-inconsistent (same input -> same file). The 'same security in two cases across runs' precondition for an overwrite never occurs; it requires hand-feeding a lowercase ticker directly to the helper, bypassing the pipeline. Latent hardening nicety at best. fix_safe=false: adding .toUpperCase() to the stem is a no-op for the real (uppercase) inputs but is NOT behavior-preserving for any pre-existing lowercase-named snapshot file — it would change the computed filename, orphan the on-disk file, and re-introduce exactly the phantom-ticker / silent-reprocessing class (F-218b-01 / regional-oos-test) this lib/snapshot-fs.js module was created to eliminate. Changing a filename-derivation function needs human review + a back-compat read or migration.

title: looksKeyedMap heuristic is duplicated verbatim in extractStocksArray and detectShape and can drift; a wrapped object missing its stocks array is misread as a ticker-keyed map
evidence: Identical block in both functions: `const looksKeyedMap = keys.some(k => /^[A-Z0-9.\-]{1,12}$/i.test(k) && raw[k] && typeof raw[k] === 'object');`. detectShape (line 61-69) and extractStocksArray (line 39-54) each re-derive it. If a wrapped file's `stocks` value is ever non-array (corruption, or an old `{stocks:{}}` shape), Array.isArray(raw.stocks) is false and the loader falls through to the keyed-map heuristic; a benign metadata key that happens to be <=12 chars of [A-Z0-9.-] with an object value (e.g. a future field) would be treated as a ticker.
why_it_matters: The module's stated purpose (header lines 11-16) is to be the single source of truth so 'future schema migrations need to land in exactly one file' — but the core discrimination logic lives in two places inside that very file, so they can silently disagree (one says shape='wrapped', the other extracts via the keyed-map branch). The downstream contract (size used by the drift gate in check-pull-stats.js:36) depends on these agreeing. A misclassified wrapped file yields a bogus synthetic stocks array and a wrong universeSize, which is the exact 'silently disabling the drift gate' failure the header warns about.
fix: Extract one private `_classify(raw)` returning {shape, stocks} and have both public functions call it, so the heuristic exists once. Tighten the keyed-map guard to require a MAJORITY of keys (not .some) to look like tickers, and explicitly exclude a present-but-non-array `stocks` key from being treated as keyed-map. Comment: '// prevents drift gate corruption from a wrapped file whose stocks field degraded to non-array'.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed against source. The verbatim duplication is real: the heuristic `keys.some(k => /^[A-Z0-9.\-]{1,12}$/i.test(k) && raw[k] && typeof raw[k] === 'object')` appears identically in extractStocksArray (watchlist-fs.js:48-49) and detectShape (watchlist-fs.js:65-66), re-derived in each. Because loadWatchlist (line 85-86) calls the two independently, divergence between the copies could yield an inconsistent {shape, stocks} (e.g. shape='invalid' with a non-empty stocks array). That is a genuine drift/maintainability smell.

The concrete misread is also reachable: for a degraded wrapped file like {_meta:{...}, stocks:{...}} where stocks is a non-array object, Array.isArray(raw.stocks) is false, so both functions fall through to the keyed-map branch. The literal key 'stocks' itself matches /^[A-Z0-9.\-]{1,12}$/i (6 chars, case-insensitive) with an object value, so looksKeyedMap becomes true and {_meta, stocks} are emitted as synthetic tickers — so the auditor's mechanism holds.

BUT the stated impact ("drift gate corruption") is overstated. The only caller is scripts/check-pull-stats.js:79-80, which sets stats.universeSize = wl.shape==='invalid' ? null : wl.size. universeSize is NOT in the watched drift-metric list (check-pull-stats.js:99: ['yahooOk','fxRatesCount','earningsWithDate','priceTickerCount','snapshotsCount']), so a miscounted universeSize from a corrupt file does not feed any drift comparison — it is a recorded-only stat. Other universeSize usages (court-score.js, picks-history, generate-dashboard.js, fitness/*) read from picks-history, not this loader. The trigger also requires an off-nominal corrupted watchlist (stocks degraded to non-array), which no current shape produces. Hence medium is too high; the real, present-day value of the finding is the duplication hygiene, so I revise to low.

fix_safe=false: the refactor half (extract a shared _classify) is behavior-preserving, but the proposed guard change — require a MAJORITY of keys to look like tickers instead of .some — is a behavior change to shape classification (a small keyed-map watchlist with even one metadata key could flip from 'object' to 'invalid'), and there are no tests pinning the loader's behavior to catch a regression. That part needs human review, so the fix is not safe to auto-apply as a unit.

title: loadWatchlist swallows parse/IO errors into {shape:'invalid', stocks:[]} — a corrupt watchlist looks identical to an empty universe to the drift gate
evidence: catch (e) { return { shape: 'invalid', stocks: [], size: 0, raw: null, error: e.message }; }  — and on unrecognized shape, returns size:0 with error set. check-pull-stats.js:36 uses loadWatchlist and (per the header) sets universeSize from it.
why_it_matters: The error string is returned but a caller that only reads .size/.stocks (the documented convenience fields, header lines 23-24) cannot distinguish 'watchlist is genuinely empty' from 'watchlist failed to parse'. The header itself cites check-pull-stats.js as 'the most visible casualty' of shape mishandling and says a bad shape 'silently disabl[es] the drift gate' — yet the new loader's contract makes that same silent-zero outcome easy to reproduce because error is an opt-in field. NaN/zero universe size should hard-fail the drift gate, not pass it.
fix: Keep the never-throw contract, but require consumers (or add a helper) to treat shape==='invalid' as fatal for gate purposes — e.g. export loadWatchlistOrThrow used by the drift gate, or have check-pull-stats.js assert wl.error==null && wl.size>0 before computing drift. Verify the consumer; this finding is about the contract inviting misuse, confirmed reachable via check-pull-stats.js:36/151.

_verdict.note: Refuted by the sole consumer. loadWatchlist is used in exactly one place: check-pull-stats.js:79 (confirmed via grep — only require + call site). At line 80 the consumer reads `stats.universeSize = wl.shape === 'invalid' ? null : wl.size;` — so a corrupt/missing/parse-failed watchlist yields universeSize=null while a genuinely empty universe yields 0. They are NOT identical, directly contradicting the finding's central premise ("looks identical to the drift gate"). Furthermore, universeSize is not even a gated metric: the drift watcher list at line 99 is ['yahooOk','fxRatesCount','earningsWithDate','priceTickerCount','snapshotsCount'] — universeSize is absent, so neither null nor 0 ever influences drift detection. And even if it were watched, line 102 `if (todayVal == null) continue;` skips null metrics, so a corrupt watchlist could never produce a false 'no drift'. The auditor's evidence quotes the loader's never-throw contract in isolation and the file header (which describes the OLD pre-fix behavior the shape-aware loader was built to eliminate), without checking that the consumer already branches on shape==='invalid'. The 'invalid' shape is handled, not swallowed. False positive based on the loader contract alone.

title: `generatedFromCacheAt: new Date && undefined` always serializes to nothing — provenance timestamp is silently dropped
evidence: Line 191: `fs.writeFileSync(OUT, JSON.stringify({ generatedFromCacheAt: new Date && undefined, filter: F, stats, count: candidates.length, candidates }, null, 2));`  `new Date && undefined` evaluates to `undefined` (truthy Date object short-circuits to the right operand), and JSON.stringify DROPS keys whose value is undefined. Verified: `node -e "console.log(JSON.stringify({generatedFromCacheAt: new Date && undefined}))"` prints `{}`.
why_it_matters: The candidate artefact carries NO generation timestamp — the field the author intended (a 'when was this cache snapshot scored' provenance marker) is invisible in every output. Anyone diffing or staleness-checking court-candidates.json has no as-of date. It also looks like a half-finished edit (likely was meant to be `new Date().toISOString()` then disabled to keep determinism). Note: a literal timestamp here WOULD break the byte-identical determinism test (court-score-tests.js:180-185), so the fix must be deliberate.
fix: If determinism across runs is required (it is — the gate hashes the full chain), drop the field entirely and stop pretending it exists, OR derive the timestamp from the newest cache file's mtime / an explicit COURT_ASOF env so it is stable within a snapshot. Do not emit a wall-clock `new Date()` — that re-breaks the determinism gate.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed at court-screen.js:191. `new Date && undefined` evaluates to `undefined` (truthy Date short-circuits && to RHS), and JSON.stringify drops undefined-valued keys. Reproduced: `node -e "console.log(JSON.stringify({generatedFromCacheAt: new Date && undefined, x:1}))"` prints `{"x":1}` — the field is silently dropped. Grep confirms `generatedFromCacheAt` appears ONLY at the write site; court-score.js reads court-candidates.json (via COURT_CAND_OUT) but never accesses this field, and nothing else reads it. So it is a genuine dead/no-op field — the provenance timestamp never exists in the artifact. This is real dead code.

BUT severity is overstated as medium. Functional impact is zero: no consumer reads the field, the field never propagates into court-results.json, and the determinism gate (court-score-tests.js:180-185, hashes court-results.json over a full court-screen + court-score chain) PASSES today precisely because the field serializes to nothing. So this is a cosmetic/confusing dead placeholder, not a behavioral bug. The `new Date &&` idiom looks like an intentional "parked" placeholder that deliberately serializes to nothing while preserving determinism. Downgrading to low.

The auditor's framing slightly misleads: removing the field does NOT risk the gate (output stays byte-identical), and the field was never breaking determinism — it was the opposite.

title: `F.degradedNote` referenced twice but never defined on any FORMULAS entry — degraded console output would print 'undefined'
evidence: Line 284: `degraded: F.degraded, degradedNote: F.degradedNote || null, a2Note: F.a2Note || null,` and line 301: `if (R.degraded) console.log(`⚠ DEGRADIERT: ${R.degradedNote}`);`. The FORMULAS objects (lines 62-104) define `degraded`, `dominantBlock`, `a2Note` — but no key named `degradedNote` anywhere. Grep confirms the only occurrences are the two consumers.
why_it_matters: Currently latent because both formulas ship `degraded: false`, so the branch never runs and the JSON field is always null. But the moment a bucket is flipped to degraded (e.g. A2 data drops out and the SaaS axis reverts to v1.0 degraded mode), operators get `⚠ DEGRADIERT: undefined` instead of the explanation the lamp 'A2-missing-degraded' (line 240) promises. It is a documentation/UX defect that will surface exactly when something is already going wrong.
fix: Either add a `degradedNote` string to each FORMULAS entry that can degrade (describing what is missing and how the score is affected), or change the consumers to fall back to a2Note / a static message. Carry a comment naming the failure mode: 'degradedNote absent -> operator sees "undefined" precisely when a bucket degrades'.

_verdict.note: Misread of data flow. The factual half is true: `degradedNote` is defined on NO FORMULAS entry (both `fabless_semi` line 79 and `system_app_software` line 101 lack it; only an unused baseline JSON `fitness/baselines/saas-v1.0-degraded-2026-06-16.json` has the key). But the predicted consequence — console prints 'undefined' — is wrong twice over. (1) The console.log at line 301 is guarded by `if (R.degraded)` and BOTH formulas hardcode `degraded: false`, so the branch is unreachable with current data; nothing is ever printed. (2) Even if `degraded` were flipped true, line 284 normalizes `degradedNote: F.degradedNote || null` into the result object BEFORE line 301 reads it — and line 301 reads `R.degradedNote` (the normalized value), not `F.degradedNote`. So the worst case is `⚠ DEGRADIERT: null`, never 'undefined'. The auditor assumed the consumer reads the raw `F.degradedNote`; it reads the `|| null`-guarded `R.degradedNote`. The missing key is a harmless latent gap, consistently defended by the `|| null` fallback and behind a dormant gate — not a defect that produces wrong output.

title: Dedupe fingerprint `${c.gm}|${c.scaleRevM}` can silently drop legitimately distinct companies (collision) and is order-dependent
evidence: Line 170-171: `const fp = \`${c.gm}|${c.scaleRevM}\`; if (seen.has(fp)) continue; seen.add(fp);`  gm is rounded to 4 decimals (court-screen.js:187 `round`) and scaleRevM is `Math.round(scaleRevM)` (integer $M, court-screen.js:178). Two genuinely different companies with the same rounded gross margin AND the same integer revenue-in-$M collide and the second is dropped.
why_it_matters: The intent (comment line 170) is to drop identical foreign-OTC double-listings of the SAME company. But the key is only (gm, revM) — not the issuer/CUSIP. At 4-dp gm and $1M revenue granularity, two distinct mid-caps colliding is plausible across a ~3200-name universe, and whichever the Map iteration reaches second is dropped with no lamp, no log, no record. This is asymmetric survivorship attrition driven by an accidental hash collision — a name vanishes from the rankable set for reasons unrelated to its merits, and it is invisible. Iteration order of `bucketOf` (a Map built from the classification list) determines which survives.
fix: Dedupe on a stable identity key (ticker root / CUSIP / SEC CIK) rather than (gm, revM). If only price-like fields are available, at minimum (a) require MORE fields to match before treating as a dup (e.g. gm AND revM AND growth AND fcfMargin), and (b) push a 'deduped-duplicate-listing' lamp / counter so dropped names are auditable. Comment must name the failure mode: 'fp collision on (gm,revM) silently drops a distinct issuer'.

_verdict.note:
Code claims verified in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening. court-score.js:170-171 builds fp=`${c.gm}|${c.scaleRevM}` and silently `continue`s on collision with no counter/lamp. court-screen.js:187 rounds gm to 4 decimals; court-screen.js:178 stores scaleRevM as Math.round (integer $M). So the dedupe key really is (gm@4dp, rev@integer-$M) and a second name with both equal is dropped with no audit trail; survivor depends on bucketOf insertion order (Map from cls, court-score.js:133) — both the collision-drop and order-dependence claims are factually correct.

BUT the realistic risk is small, so this is medium-overstated. (1) The drop is INTENTIONAL: line 169 comment says it collapses identical foreign-OTC dual listings of the SAME issuer (same gm+rev) — desired behavior. The bug is only the false-positive of two DISTINCT issuers colliding. (2) That conjunction is low-probability: gm to 4 decimals gives thousands of buckets, and identical integer-$M revenue is increasingly unlikely as revenue grows (true revenues differ by >>$0.5M). (3) The universe is narrow and bucket-relative (asset-light, GM>=0.30, growth>=0.12, rev>=$50M hypergrowth; the SaaS bucket is ~44 names per the ma-rpo comment), and gm>1.0 is already hard-rejected (line 168), so an intra-bucket distinct-issuer collision is improbable. Impact when it does fire: one name silently missing from a small cohort — a data-integrity/observability gap, not a correctness break of the scoring math. The strongest valid part of the finding is the missing audit counter for dropped names.

Real, but I revise severity medium -> low.

title: Membership gate calls logistic() on m.growth / m.gm with no isFinite guard; relies entirely on upstream prefilter invariant that is not enforced here
evidence: Line 200-202: `const mg = logistic(m.growth, ...); const mGM = logistic(m.gm, ...); const mSc = logistic(log10(Math.max(m.scaleRevM, 1)), ...);` with `logistic = (x,c,s) => 1/(1+Math.exp(-(x-c)/s))` (line 28). If m.growth or m.gm is null/NaN, `Math.exp(NaN)` -> NaN -> M=NaN -> membershipClass falls to 'Out' (NaN>=0.66 false, NaN>=0.20 false) and the name is silently excluded from ranking.
why_it_matters: court-score trusts that every candidate has finite growth/gm because court-screen's prefilter rejects nulls (court-screen.js:167-168). But the two files are coupled only by a JSON file on disk — a hand-edited or alternative candidate source (the COURT_CAND_OUT override exists precisely so external harnesses can supply candidates) with a null gm/growth produces a NaN membership that demotes the name to 'Out' with NO lamp explaining why. NaN propagation through a gate that fails closed = silent survivorship loss. The scaleRevM path is partially guarded (Math.max(...,1)) but growth/gm are not.
fix: Guard at the top of the per-member loop: if (m.growth == null || !isFinite(m.growth) || m.gm == null || !isFinite(m.gm)) { lamp 'membership-input-missing'; set membershipClass='Out'; continue; } so the exclusion is explicit and auditable instead of a NaN silently sorting to the bottom. Comment: 'prevents NaN-membership silent demotion when candidate source bypasses court-screen prefilter'.

_verdict.note:
Refuted as a live bug. The auditor's JS mechanics are correct in isolation (logistic(NaN)->NaN->M=NaN; NaN>=0.66 and NaN>=0.20 both false -> membershipClass='Out' -> filtered out at court-score.js:304), but the precondition (m.growth or m.gm null/NaN) is structurally unreachable. court-candidates.json is produced ONLY by court-screen.js, whose prefilter hard-drops any name with null growth/gm BEFORE pushing: court-screen.js:167 `if (growth == null || growth < F.minGrowth) continue;` and :168 `if (gm == null || gm < F.minGM) continue;`. Stored values are round(growth)/round(gm); round() (court-screen.js:187) returns null only for null/non-finite, which were already filtered, so the persisted fields are guaranteed finite numbers. court-score.js consumes them verbatim (byTicker at :130, m={...c} at :172) with no other ingest path. The "candidate source bypasses court-screen prefilter" scenario the fix's comment cites does not exist: the only override, COURT_CAND_OUT, merely redirects the file court-screen.js writes and court-score.js reads (test harness court-score-tests.js:29-39 still runs the full screen). The requested isFinite guard defends against an impossible input state, not a real defect.

fix_safe=false: the proposed `continue` is NOT behavior-preserving. Today a (hypothetical) NaN-membership name is still scored and surfaces in the printed Out-class (court-score.js:316-319); an early continue would remove it from `members` entirely, which also drives universeSize and the cross-sectional median/MAD anchors (stats computed over `members` at :185-195), shifting every other name's z-scores. It is a logic change inside the per-member loop, not a trivial auto-apply — needs human review.

title: Growth source can silently mix annual and quarterly YoY across the universe, and accel is annual-only — cross-sectional anchors compare apples to oranges
evidence: Line 99-101: `const gAnnual = (revA[0]..revA[1]>0) ? revA[0]/revA[1]-1 : null; const gQ = (revQ.length>=5 && revQ[4]>0) ? revQ[0]/revQ[4]-1 : null; const growth = gAnnual != null ? gAnnual : gQ;` — a name with no annual pair falls back to a 5-quarter (TTM-ish) YoY. Meanwhile accel (line 155) `gSeriesA[0] - gSeriesA[1]` is computed ONLY from the annual series gSeriesA, never from quarterly.
why_it_matters: court-score.js computes the cross-sectional Growth anchor (median/MAD) over `c.growth` mixing both definitions (court-score.js:185-188), so a quarterly-derived growth number is z-scored against annual-derived peers in the SAME bucket. Annual YoY and trailing-5Q YoY are not the same statistic (different smoothing, different as-of), so the pseudo-z is biased for the fallback names. Separately, accel is null for any name lacking >=2 annual YoY (young IPOs — exactly the high-growth targets), so the Accel axis is structurally absent for the most interesting cohort and they get neutral s=0 on a 15%-weighted axis (Fabless), depressing them relative to older names. Both are silent.
fix: Record which growth definition was used (e.g. a `growthSource: 'annual'|'quarterly'` field, already done for durSource) and either (a) compute anchors per-source or (b) prefer a single consistent quarterly-TTM YoY universe-wide. For accel, add a quarterly-YoY-acceleration fallback mirroring the durability source-selection so young names are not silently neutralised. Comment: 'prevents annual-vs-quarterly growth-definition mixing in cross-sectional z and accel-absence demotion of young names'.

_verdict.note: Confirmed real, but narrower/lower-impact than "medium" implies. (1) Growth-source mixing is real: court-screen.js:99-101 sets growth = gAnnual ?? gQ, where the fallback gQ = revQ[0]/revQ[4]-1 is a single-quarter YoY (latest Q vs same Q prior year), a different definition than the annual revA[0]/revA[1]. court-score.js:187-188,213 builds the bucket median/MAD anchor over the combined `growth` field and z-scores every name against it, and Growth is the highest-weight axis (0.35 fabless / 0.429 SaaS). So fallback names are compared against an anchor built mostly from annual-YoY — a genuine cross-sectional inconsistency on the top-weight axis. (2) The asymmetry vs durability is correct: durSource is recorded (court-screen.js:152, surfaced in lamps 235-236) but there is NO growthSource field/lamp; growth_annual & growth_q are stored (175) but nothing downstream knows which fed `growth`. (3) accel is annual-only: court-screen.js:155 accel = gSeriesA[0]-gSeriesA[1] needs >=3 annual revenue points; no quarterly-YoY-accel fallback, unlike durability which prefers SEC quarterly with annual fallback. A young name with <3 annual points gets accel=null -> sAxis returns 0 (court-score.js:32-33), contributing w*0.5 — neutral, NOT a penalty, but it denies a genuinely accelerating young name the positive accel credit a mature peer earns, so on a relative basis it is a mild demotion. Impact is bounded: only names lacking a clean annual pair are affected (young/recent-IPO), accel weight is just 0.15 (and SaaS has no accel axis at all), and the collapse-reweight can partially re-couple. Could not empirically quantify prevalence — no fundamentals-cache/ and no outputs/court-candidates.json in this worktree — so severity is judged from code alone.

title: INORGANIC_FALLBACK hardcodes 'AVGO' and 'GEN' as a name-level safety net — the kind of hardcoded exclusion/override the data-driven inorganicFlag was built to replace
evidence: Line 110: `const INORGANIC_FALLBACK = new Set(['GEN', 'AVGO']);  // hardcoded fallback: AVGO in fabless_semi has no snapshot row; GEN covered by data-driven rule but kept here for safety`. Line 234: `else if (_ioFlag === null && INORGANIC_FALLBACK.has(m.ticker)) L.push('M&A-growth(P_auth-blind,hardcoded-fallback)');`. The whole inorganicFlag() function (line 142-150) was explicitly written to 'replace the hardcoded INORGANIC set' (comment line 138).
why_it_matters: This is a lamp-only fallback (it doesn't alter score), so it is low-severity, but it re-introduces exactly the name-pinned logic the redesign removed: GEN is already covered data-driven (its snapshot row has paymentsToRev 0.206, rpoGrowth 0.013 -> 'inorganic'), so its presence here is redundant and will go stale if GEN's data changes; AVGO is pinned only because it lacks a snapshot row. Per the audit's binding constraint ('NO hardcoded ticker exclusions — fix the guard instead'), the guard, not the name list, should handle missing-snapshot coverage.
fix: Remove the GEN entry (data-driven rule already covers it). For AVGO/missing-snapshot names, replace the name set with a structural guard: when a fabless_semi member has a high headline growth but `maRpoByTicker.get(t)` is null (no M&A/RPO coverage), emit a generic 'M&A-coverage-missing(P_auth-blind)' lamp keyed on coverage absence, not on the ticker. This satisfies the no-hardcoded-ticker constraint and self-maintains as the snapshot universe grows.

_verdict.note: Confirmed against source + committed data. court-score.js:110 hardcodes `const INORGANIC_FALLBACK = new Set(['GEN', 'AVGO'])`, used at line 234. Line 138 explicitly says inorganicFlag() "replaces the hardcoded INORGANIC set", so re-adding a ticker-keyed set is the exact pattern the data-driven design retired — the architecture observation is accurate. Verified data (data/ma-rpo-snapshot.json, 44 rows): GEN HAS a row (pay 20.64%, rpoGrowthYoY 1.3%) so inorganicFlag('GEN') returns 'inorganic' and takes the line-232 branch; line 234 is gated on `_ioFlag === null`, which GEN can never satisfy — so the GEN entry is provably DEAD code (the code's own comment admits "GEN covered by data-driven rule but kept here for safety"). AVGO has NO snapshot row, so inorganicFlag('AVGO') returns null and line 234 fires only for AVGO — a genuine ticker-keyed hardcode. Severity 'low' is correct: line 234 only appends an informational disclosure lamp string; it does NOT affect score/rank (pAuth=0). Note the outputs/ artifacts aren't present in the worktree (runtime-generated), but the verdict rests on static logic + the committed snapshot, both confirmed.

title: members.sort uses b.score - a.score with no null/NaN guard; a null score sorts unpredictably and the ranked/out split re-sorts inconsistently
evidence: Line 282: `members.sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score);` — score is set at line 221-222 from `Math.max(0, 100*core - pDil - pAuth)` then rounded, so it is normally finite, BUT the collapse-reweight branch (line 268-276) only rewrites scores for `ranked = members.filter(m => m.score != null)` (line 252). If any member had a null score it is excluded from reweight yet still participates in the final sort, where `b.score - a.score` with a null operand yields NaN and V8 leaves comparator-NaN elements in arbitrary position. Line 304-305 then re-filter/re-sort by membershipClass independently.
why_it_matters: Score is finite on the happy path, so impact is low today, but the code itself hedges for `score != null` (line 252) while the sort (282) does not — an internal inconsistency that becomes a real ordering bug the moment a null/NaN score slips through (e.g. via the NaN-membership path in finding 06, or a future axis returning NaN). NaN in an Array.sort comparator gives engine-defined, non-deterministic order — which would also break the byte-identical determinism gate.
fix: Make scoring total: ensure m.score is always a finite number (coerce null->0 with a lamp, or filter null-score members out before the sort exactly as the reweight branch does). Use a NaN-safe comparator: `(a,b) => (b.score||0) - (a.score||0)` only AFTER guaranteeing finiteness, or `(a,b)=> (Number.isFinite(b.score)?b.score:-Infinity) - (Number.isFinite(a.score)?a.score:-Infinity)`. Comment: 'NaN/null score in sort comparator -> nondeterministic order, breaks determinism gate'.

_verdict.note: False positive — the null/NaN score state the finding depends on is unreachable. m.score is assigned for EVERY member in the single scoring loop (court-score.js:198-246) as `Math.round(Math.max(0, 100*core - pDil - pAuth) * 10)/10` (lines 221-222). core is provably finite: it sums `ax.w*(s+1)/2`, where s is either m._a2 (computeA2Forward returns 0 or a finite g+l) or sAxis(), which returns 0 on null/null-anchor and otherwise tanh(finite/k). Crucially the raw inputs come from candidate JSON, and court-screen.js's round() helper (line 187: `(x==null || !isFinite(x)) ? null : ...`) coerces every numeric field to null-or-finite — never NaN — so sAxis's `raw==null` guard catches the only non-finite case. pDil is also finite (clip of sbcPct-coerced-to-0 times a constant). Therefore m.score is always a finite number; it can never be null or NaN. Consequently `ranked = members.filter(m => m.score != null)` (line 252) is an always-true filter equal to all members, and the collapse-reweight branch (lines 264-276, which only exists for fabless_semi — the sole formula with a `durability` axis) rewrites score for every member in ranked. No member is "excluded from reweight yet still participates in the final sort" with a null operand. The sort at line 282 and the membershipClass split/re-sort at lines 304-305 always operate on finite scores. The finding's own antecedent ("If any member had a null score") never holds.

title: NVO fixture mixes DKK-scaled quarterly series with already-USD-converted marketCap and unconverted DKK annual series — a latent FX-normalization trap that the current CLI test never exercises
evidence: Line 138: `marketCap: m(450e9, 'USD'),  // already converted in input` while line 140 `revenueTTM: m(265e9, 'DKK')` and annual line 155 `annualRev: annual([265e9, ...], 'DKK')`. Quarterly (line 150) is built in DKK then multiplied: `tsRev([55,...], 'DKK').map(x => ({ ...x, value: x.value * 1e9 }))`. So within ONE fixture: marketCap is USD, revenue/annual are DKK, and the quarterly builder applies a 1e9 scale the annual builder does not (annual passes 265e9 literally). Mixed units, mixed scaling conventions inside a single canonical record.
why_it_matters: engine-cli-tests.js only calls classifySubProfile (which keys off sector/industry/margins, currency-agnostic) so this passes today. But the fixture is the canonical contract for ANY consumer that reads these fields — a scorer that does FX normalization (the live mode/tier scorer, per the header) would have to know that marketCap is pre-converted while revenue is not, and that quarterly is *1e9 while annual is literal. That asymmetry is precisely where FX/currency normalization bugs hide. The fixture encodes an inconsistent convention as 'realistic', so it will validate a buggy normalizer that happens to make the same wrong assumption, and reject a correct one.
fix: Make the fixture internally consistent: keep all monetary fields in reportingCurrency (DKK) at the same scale, and let the engine do the single documented FX step using fxRates.DKK_USD. If marketCap must be USD for a test, mark it with an explicit unit/flag the engine reads, and remove the per-builder *1e9 asymmetry (bake the scale into the literals so annual and quarterly use one convention). Add an FX-round-trip assertion to a test so the convention is enforced, not just commented.

_verdict.note:
Evidence is factually accurate but the impact assessment makes this a non-issue. Verified at C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/engine-fixtures.js: line 138 marketCap m(450e9,'USD') with the explicit comment "already converted in input"; line 140 revenueTTM m(265e9,'DKK'); lines 150-152 quarterly built `tsRev([55,...],'DKK').map(x => ({...x, value: x.value*1e9}))`; lines 155-159 annual `annual([265e9,...],'DKK')` with the 1e9 baked into literals. So yes: within one fixture marketCap is USD while revenue/annual are DKK, and quarterly applies a per-builder *1e9 that annual does not. The description is correct.

But this is latent-only in INERT data with no live behavioral defect, for three concrete reasons:
1) Sole code consumer: `engine-fixtures.js` is required by exactly ONE file, `engine-cli-tests.js` (verified by grep — only that one require). That test calls only `classifySubProfile(stock).id`, which (lib/sub-profile.js lines 58-112) reads ONLY stock.meta (ticker/sector/industry) and stock.manualSubProfile. It never touches marketCap, metrics, timeseries, or annual. So the mixed-unit fields are dead data the only test never reads — the finding itself concedes "the current CLI test never exercises" this.
2) The engine that WOULD have tripped on this is deleted. The prior tag220a audit (audit-reports/2026-05-17-tag220a-core-engine-audit.md, F-220a-03) already flagged exactly this NVO DKK-vs-USD mismatch, but in engine-v7.3.js:221-230 (isRevenueMaterial). Per the engine-cli-tests.js header and ADR-001 Phase 3 (2026-06-20), engine-v7.3.js and score-orchestrator.js were RETIRED AND DELETED — confirmed by glob: neither file exists. No current code normalizes these fields.
3) The USD marketCap is intentional and documented ("already converted in input"), not an accidental unit slip; fxRates is exported but no test wires it against these fixtures.

Net: accurate observation, but zero current data-integrity impact — it is a fixture-hygiene nit that only matters if someone resurrects a monetary-reading consumer over these fixtures. Already superseded by the deleted-engine F-220a-03. Not a real bug at the claimed medium severity.

title: Determinism test re-runs the chain into the SAME output path as run 1 — it proves run-2==run-2-of-itself, not that the canonical first run was reproducible from scratch
evidence: Line 40 `const r1 = fs.readFileSync(RESULTS, 'utf8');` captures the first run (from lines 38-39). The determinism test (line 182-184) re-runs court-screen+court-score into the SAME RESULTS path and reads r2, then asserts sha(r1)===sha(r2). Both runs read the SAME (untracked) outputs/court-buckets.json via the default BUCK path — neither run regenerates buckets — so the test cannot detect non-determinism that originates in the bucket input, and it conflates 'idempotent given a fixed buckets file' with 'reproducible'.
why_it_matters: The gate advertises 'VOLLE Kette byte-identisch' (full chain byte-identical) but the chain it tests excludes the classification step that produces the most variable input. Combined with finding 01 (buckets is an unreproducible artefact), the determinism guarantee is weaker than the test name claims: change the buckets file out-of-band and both runs change together, still passing. A future wall-clock/Date leak inside the classifier would not be caught here.
fix: Either bring bucket generation into the harness (generate a deterministic test buckets file into the isolated temp dir, see finding 01) and include it in the hashed chain, or rename/document the test as 'idempotent given fixed candidates+buckets' so its guarantee is not overstated. If a true cross-process determinism check is wanted, run into TWO distinct temp output paths and diff, to rule out same-path read-after-write artefacts.

_verdict.note:
False positive / mischaracterization. Data flow verified by reading all three files in C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening: court-screen.js reads fundamentals-cache/*.json and writes candidates (COURT_CAND_OUT, env-overridden to temp); court-score.js reads candidates + outputs/court-buckets.json (BUCK, fixed path, line 22) + data/ma-rpo-snapshot.json, writes results (COURT_OUT->RESULTS, env-overridden). The auditor's FACTUAL observations are correct: both runs write the same RESULTS path, and court-buckets.json is read via the non-overridable default BUCK path by both runs and regenerated by neither. But the INTERPRETIVE 'bug' is wrong on both counts.

(1) 'Same-path read-after-write artefact / proves run-2==run-2-of-itself': moot. r1 is captured into a JS string variable at line 40 immediately after run 1, BEFORE run 2 overwrites RESULTS (lines 182-184). The line-185 comparison uses that in-memory r1 vs the freshly-read r2. Run 1 and run 2 are two genuinely independent cross-process executions (separate execSync node processes for both court-screen AND court-score). It is a real cross-process reproducibility check of the screen+score chain, not a self-comparison; the shared output path cannot mask a difference because r1 lives in memory.

(2) 'Cannot detect non-determinism originating in the bucket input': vacuous. court-buckets.json is a STATIC INPUT file, not a chain stage. Identical bytes are read on both runs, so it cannot be a source of run-to-run variance by construction — fixing inputs constant is precisely what a reproducibility test does. Bucket *generation* is a separate upstream classification workflow (documented in court-score.js header, line 7), explicitly out of this script's scope. The test name 'VOLLE Kette (court-screen + court-score)' accurately scopes itself to exactly the two stages it re-runs; it never claims to cover bucket generation, so the 'overstated guarantee' charge does not hold.

Note: I could not execute the test in this worktree (fundamentals-cache/ dir is absent and outputs/court-buckets.json does not exist — outputs/ is gitignored except .gitkeep; court-screen.js crashes ENOENT on readdirSync). That is an environment/data-availability gap, separate from and not supporting the auditor's logical claim, which I evaluated on the source. No silent-corruption risk: court-screen.js line 191 deliberately omits a timestamp (`new Date && undefined`), so there is no obvious nondeterminism source the test would miss within its scope.

title: rankIC is computed over only the ~81 selected picks (all scores 56-100), measuring within-cohort discrimination, not selection power — the headline 'rank-IC' overstates what is being validated
evidence: `const rankingEntries = baseline.ranking.map(r => ({ ticker: r.ticker, score: r.score }));` (line 75) — ranking is the per-mode pick list (verified 81 entries, score range 56-100), NOT the 5657-name evaluatedTickers universe. rankIC(rankingEntries, returnByTicker) (line 147) therefore correlates score-vs-return only among already-selected winners. The full universe is used only to build the cohortSpread universe median, never to rank-correlate.
why_it_matters: Rank-IC across the full evaluated universe answers 'does my score separate future winners from losers?' — the question that matters for selection. Rank-IC across only the top 81 (a heavily truncated, range-restricted slice) answers a much weaker question and is severely attenuated by range restriction; near-zero IC here is expected even for a good model and is easy to misread as 'the score has no power'. The preRegistration honestLimitation (freeze-full-baseline.js:92) admits n<=100 but does not flag the range-restriction / selection-vs-discrimination confound, so a reader will over-trust a positive IC and under-trust the model on a null IC.
fix: Either (a) compute a second rank-IC over the full universe by carrying each evaluatedTicker's score into the baseline (requires baselines to store universe scores, not just the top picks' scores), labelling the two clearly as IC_selection (universe) and IC_discrimination (within-cohort); or (b) at minimum annotate the output that rankIC is within-cohort-only and range-restricted. No code in methods/ changes.

_verdict.note:
Mechanically the auditor is correct, but the issue is already explicitly documented as a known design limitation, so it is not an unaddressed defect.

Confirmed facts: measure.js:75 sets rankingEntries = baseline.ranking.map(...); rankIC (metrics.js:19-37) iterates only rankingEntries, so n is bounded by ranking.length. evaluatedTickers (the 5657-name universe) feeds only the survivorship classify loop (measure.js:123-135) and thus the cohortSpread/hitRate universe MEDIAN (metrics.js:83,109) — it is never carried into the rank-correlation. Baseline data verifies ranking is a truncated, range-restricted pick list: full-hypergrowth has ranking.length=81, scores 56-100, vs evaluatedTickers=5657 — matching the auditor's evidence exactly. So yes, this rank-IC measures within-cohort discrimination among selected names, not full-universe selection power.

Why not a real finding: this is deliberate and disclosed, not miswired. freeze-full-baseline.js:71-76 intentionally ranks WITHIN each mode's picks (per-mode rank-normalized scores; cross-mode pooling called 'degenerate', header lines 9-13). The freeze script's preRegistration.honestLimitation (lines 92-95) literally states: 'n<=100 per mode -> rank-IC has DIRECTIONAL power only (SE(IC) ~0.1 at n=100)' and frames survivorship quantification (naive-vs-conservative) as the primary value, with production rank-IC only 'once horizons mature.' The 'headline rank-IC overstates' is the auditor's framing: the output (measure.js:218) prints 'Rank-IC (naive): X (n=NN)' and the JSON carries n+dropped on every rankIC object, so a reader sees n=81, not n=5657. preRegistration.metric (line 89) lists both metrics. This is a labeling/interpretation nuance already covered by honestLimitation, not a data-integrity bug.

Fix feasibility: proposed fix (a) is NOT behavior-preserving and not auto-applicable — evaluatedTickers in the baseline is an array of bare ticker strings with no scores, so a universe-wide IC cannot be computed without re-architecting the freeze step to persist per-universe scores and re-freezing all baselines (the comment notes older vintages lack score entirely). Fix (b) (annotate output as within-cohort-only) is low-risk but cosmetic and edits human-facing metric semantics; should still be human-reviewed.

title: Output directory creation and atomic write are not coordinated; mkdir is non-atomic and the .tmp/rename can cross-device if outputs/ is a mount, leaving no fsync
evidence: atomicWriteJson (lines 36-40) does `fs.writeFileSync(tmp,...); fs.renameSync(tmp, filePath);` with no fs.fsync on the file or the directory, and the temp file is created in the same dir only because filePath is relative ('fitness/outputs/...'). main() builds outFile via path.join(outputDir,...) where outputDir='fitness/outputs' (relative, line 188). The whole run depends on process.cwd() being screener-data/ (documented at line 10 'Usage (from screener-data/)') — there is no resolution against __dirname.
why_it_matters: (1) No fsync means a crash/power-loss between rename and the OS flushing can still surface a zero-length or torn file on some filesystems; the comment 'Atomic write' overstates the guarantee. (2) The relative-path dependency on cwd is fragile: invoked from any other directory, measure.js reads prices/history.json and writes fitness/outputs relative to the wrong root, silently producing or overwriting files in the wrong place or FATAL-exiting on a missing baseline. walk-forward-perf.js by contrast anchors every path with path.join(__dirname, '..', ...).
fix: Anchor all paths against __dirname/ROOT like walk-forward-perf.js does, instead of relying on cwd. In atomicWriteJson, fsync the file descriptor before rename and (best-effort) fsync the directory after, or reuse the project's lib/atomic-write.js writeFileAtomic that walk-forward-perf.js already imports (consistency + single source of truth).

_verdict.note:
Factually confirmed in fitness/measure.js (C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/fitness/measure.js): atomicWriteJson (lines 36-40) does fs.writeFileSync(tmp,...) + fs.renameSync(tmp,filePath) with NO fsync on file or parent dir; outputDir='fitness/outputs' is relative (line 188) and outFile=path.join(outputDir,...) (line 191), so the run depends entirely on process.cwd()==screener-data/ (documented line 10), with no __dirname anchoring. The inconsistency claim also checks out: scripts/walk-forward-perf.js anchors every path against __dirname (lines 27-30) AND imports the hardened ../lib/atomic-write.js writeFileAtomic (line 25), which does fsync-file + Windows rename-retry + best-effort dir-fsync. measure.js reinvents a weaker writer while that single-source-of-truth helper already exists in the repo. So as a consistency/durability code-smell it is REAL.

BUT the auditor over-rates it as medium data-integrity. Blast radius is essentially nil: measure-*.json is consumed by NO other script (grep for 'measure-' hits only measure.js itself; freeze-full-baseline.js and CLAUDE.md only mention the path), it is in NO CI workflow (.github has zero 'fitness' refs), and fitness/outputs/ is gitignored (the 'outputs/' rule) — it is an ephemeral local report, not committed state read downstream. Compare walk-forward.json, whose own header (lines 21-24) justifies hardening precisely because methodology-report and snapshot-picks read it; measure.js has no such consumer, so the crash-durability case is academic. The cross-device claim is also speculative (tmp is a same-dir sibling, only crosses devices if outputs/ is itself a mount). The relative-cwd fragility is real but a documented usage contract whose only failure mode is a visible wrong-dir write/abort, not silent corruption. Realistic severity: low.

fix_safe=false: swapping atomicWriteJson -> writeFileAtomic/writeJsonAtomic alone is behavior-preserving and low-risk. But the proposed fix ALSO re-anchors all paths against __dirname/ROOT, which is a behavior change: baselinePath default, prices/history.json, and the output dir would resolve relative to the script location instead of cwd, and a relative baselinePath CLI arg (the documented 'node fitness/measure.js [baselinePath]' usage) would resolve against ROOT not cwd — that can change which inputs are read and where output lands. That portion needs human review, so the composite fix should not be auto-applied wholesale.

title: Human-summary loop assumes r.naive.rankIC / cohortSpread_top8 exist for any non-PENDING status, but a NOT_READY_COVERAGE horizon with all-null metrics can carry null sub-objects' fields — and r can be undefined if horizons array contains a value not computed
evidence: Lines 213-220: `const r = horizonResults[h];` then `if (r.status === 'PENDING_PRICES'){...} else { ... r.naive.rankIC.ic ... r.naive.cohortSpread_top8.spread ... }`. rankIC returns `{ic:null,...}` (metrics.js:36) when n<3, so r.naive.rankIC.ic.toFixed is guarded by the `!== null` check — OK. But there is no guard that r is defined: horizons comes from baseline.preRegistration.horizonsDays (line 85); the summary loop (line 212) re-reads the same horizons, so if a horizon value appeared twice or as a non-array it would throw on r.status. More concretely, status can be 'NOT_READY_COVERAGE' (line 140) which takes the else branch and dereferences r.naive.rankIC.ic — fine — but coverage<0.90 with zero ok names yields rankIC n=0 ic=null (printed 'null') which is correct yet mislabeled as a real measurement row rather than a suppressed one.
why_it_matters: The console summary is the operator's primary read of the run. A NOT_READY_COVERAGE horizon (coverage<90%) prints exactly like a healthy row except for the status token, and the IC line prints regardless — inviting the operator to read an IC computed on <90% coverage (heavy survivorship distortion) as if it were valid. The brittleness around r being defined is lower-probability but unguarded.
fix: In the summary, branch on coverageFlag too: for NOT_READY_COVERAGE print a 'metrics suppressed — coverage X% < 90%' line rather than the IC/spread numbers. Guard `if (!r) continue;`. This keeps low-coverage IC out of the operator's eye, matching the coverageFlag intent at line 140.

_verdict.note: False positive / cosmetic nitpick, no crash or data bug. (1) "r can be undefined": refuted. `horizons` is read once at measure.js:85 and BOTH the compute loop (line 88) and the summary loop (line 212) iterate the identical array. Every branch of the compute loop unconditionally assigns horizonResults[horizon] — PENDING (line 93), insufficient (line 106), and the full result (line 160). Duplicate horizon values merely overwrite the same key; a non-array horizonsDays would throw at line 88 long before the summary runs. So r is always defined; the proposed `if (!r) continue;` is dead code. (2) "r.naive.rankIC.ic.toFixed throws": self-refuted by the auditor — line 218 guards with `ic !== null` and line 219 guards spread the same way; rankIC returns {ic:null} for n<3 (metrics.js:35) and the code handles it. No crash. (3) The substantive claim ("NOT_READY_COVERAGE rows print IC/spread, mislabeled as real measurements"): not a bug. Line 217 already prints `${r.status}` = NOT_READY_COVERAGE plus the coverage%, so the operator DOES see the suppression flag; IC is annotated with n=. Any non-PENDING status is guaranteed to be the full result object carrying naive.rankIC and naive.cohortSpread_top8 (lines 160-184), so no missing-field deref. The machine-readable JSON output already carries status=coverageFlag and coverage. This is a presentation preference, not a correctness defect — the auditor's own evidence calls the values "fine"/"correct".

title: quintileMonotonicity defines monotoneScore as adjacent pairs where Q[i] >= Q[i+1], counting flat/tied quintiles as 'monotone' — a degenerate all-equal model scores a perfect 1.0
evidence: Lines 169-171: `for (let i = 0; i < 4; i++) { if (quintileMeans[i] >= quintileMeans[i + 1]) monotone++; }` using >= (not >). If every quintile mean is identical (e.g. all returns equal, or a model with no discriminative power that produces equal-mean quintiles by construction), all 4 comparisons pass and monotoneScore=1.0 — indistinguishable from a perfectly monotone, strongly predictive model.
why_it_matters: monotoneScore=1.0 is meant to certify 'top quintile reliably beats bottom quintile' — a strong fitness signal. A flat or near-flat model getting the same 1.0 makes the metric unable to separate a great model from a useless one in exactly the no-signal regime the harness is supposed to detect. Quietly inflates apparent model quality.
fix: Use strict > for the monotone count, OR additionally report the Q1-minus-Q5 spread and require it to exceed a threshold before treating monotoneScore as meaningful. Add a tie-rate field. Comment the failure mode: '// strict > so a flat (no-signal) quintile profile does not score as perfectly monotone'.

_verdict.note:
Code reading confirmed. metrics.js:169-171 uses `>=` (not `>`): `for (let i=0;i<4;i++){ if (quintileMeans[i] >= quintileMeans[i+1]) monotone++; }` with monotoneScore = monotone/4. A degenerate model with all-equal quintile means scores monotoneScore=1.0, identical to a perfectly monotone, strongly-predictive model — the auditor's math is correct. This is also the *documented* behavior (docstring line 134 explicitly says ">= lower quintile mean"), so it is a metric-design weakness, not a typo. Tied quintile means are plausible in practice (e.g. the conservative variant pins all delisted names to -1.0, and discrete/clamped returns can tie quintile means), so the failure mode is reachable, not purely theoretical.

MATERIALITY (why I revise severity down to low): monotoneScore never gates any decision. It is computed in metrics.js, copied verbatim into the output JSON by measure.js (lines 175, 182), but is NOT printed in the human summary (only rankIC and cohortSpread are, measure.js:218-219) and there is no GO/NO-GO or NOT_READY flag derived from it anywhere. I grepped the whole worktree (incl. scripts/_tag225d_effectiveness_probe.js) — no consumer reads monotoneScore back for any decision. So the misleading 1.0 is a diagnostic value in a JSON dump that no logic acts on; it cannot currently cause a wrong screener result. Real but cosmetic/diagnostic, hence low rather than medium.

FIX_SAFE=false: switching `>=`→`>` is NOT behavior-preserving — it changes monotoneScore for any legitimately-tied quintiles, alters emitted JSON values, and directly contradicts the documented contract at metrics.js:134 (docstring would also need updating). It is a semantic change to a metric and needs human sign-off on the intended definition. (The existing 'perfect ordering' test at measure.test.js:418 uses strictly decreasing means so it would still pass, but that does not make the change safe — it just means tests don't catch the semantic shift.) The additive parts of the proposed fix (Q1-Q5 spread, tie-rate field, threshold gating) change the output schema and introduce a new threshold policy, also requiring review.

title: isGood() only checks picks[0].score on the FIRST pick of SOME mode; the oldest-good-vintage scan JSON.parses every vintage with no try/catch, so one corrupt picks-history file aborts the whole freeze
evidence: isGood (line 42): `MODES.some(md => { const p = modePicks(vintage, md); return p && p[0] && p[0].score != null; })` — only the first pick of one mode needs a numeric score; later picks with null scores still flow into ranking (where they're filtered at measure-time line 74, OK) but isGood gives false assurance. More importantly the auto-select loop (lines 56-58) does `JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(...))` for every file with NO try/catch, unlike loadJson in walk-forward-perf.js (line 80-82) which swallows parse errors. A single malformed YYYY-MM-DD.json throws and crashes the freeze.
why_it_matters: The freeze is the deterministic entrypoint for the whole fitness pipeline. A partially-written or corrupt vintage (the snapshot pipeline can produce these on cron failure — walk-forward-perf.js explicitly defends coverage gaps at F-BT-012) will hard-crash freeze-full-baseline.js with an unhandled SyntaxError rather than skipping to the next-oldest good vintage. The isGood weakness is minor (first-pick-only) but means a vintage with a scored first pick and null-scored remainder passes the 'good' gate with a misleadingly sparse ranking.
fix: Wrap the per-file parse in try/catch and skip-with-warn on failure (mirror loadJson). Strengthen isGood to require that a mode has at least N picks with numeric scores, or that the median pick carries a score, not just p[0]. No constraint impact.

_verdict.note:
Partially confirmed. The CRASH sub-claim is REAL and reproducible: C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/fitness/freeze-full-baseline.js does `JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(...))` with NO try/catch at line 52 (explicit-arg branch) and line 57 (auto-select loop over every YYYY-MM-DD.json). I simulated the loop semantics with one malformed file ahead of a valid vintage and it threw SyntaxError, aborting before reaching the good vintage. The contrast is accurate: the sibling scripts/walk-forward-perf.js loadJson (lines 80-82) wraps the same parse in try/catch returning null, proving the defensive pattern exists in-repo.

The isGood() sub-claim is WEAK/speculative, not a real bug. I inspected actual data: the oldest vintages (e.g. 2026-05-08.json) correctly fail isGood (no evaluatedTickers, all scores null). In the first good vintage (2026-05-14.json) every mode that carries scores carries them on ALL picks (HYPERGROWTH 81/81, QUALITY_COMPOUNDER 23/23, TURNAROUND 59/59) — there is no real mix of scored+null picks within a mode for p[0] to give "false assurance" about. Even hypothetically, null-score picks are correctly filtered at measure-time (line 74), which the auditor concedes is OK. So the isGood weakness is theoretical only.

Severity LOW is correct: this is a READ-ONLY measurement/analysis tool (not the production pipeline), run manually; picks-history files are machine-written so corruption is unlikely; and a crash here is LOUD and non-silent (stack trace names the file) — no data corruption or wrong results.

fix_safe=false: the try/catch-skip-with-warn half is safe and behavior-preserving, BUT the proposed fix bundles it with strengthening isGood (require N numeric-score picks / median pick scored). That second part changes t0-vintage selection logic, which directly determines the produced baselines — not behavior-preserving, and unnecessary per the data above. Also, applying skip-with-warn to the explicit-CLI-arg branch (line 52) would wrongly downgrade an explicitly-requested-but-corrupt file from a hard error to a silent skip. The try/catch hardening should be applied only to the auto-select loop (lines 56-58); keep the explicit-arg branch erroring; drop the isGood change. Because the bundled fix is not behavior-preserving as written, it needs human review.

title: Universe median in cohortSpread/hitRate is taken over Object.values(returnByTicker), so the conservative variant's universe silently includes every -1.0 delisting while the naive universe excludes them — the two variants' universe medians are not a clean apples-to-apples baseline shift
evidence: cohortSpread line 83: `const universeReturns = Object.values(returnByTicker).filter(r => Number.isFinite(r));`. In measure.js the conservative map adds delisted→-1.0 for EVERY delisted evaluated ticker (lines 130-132), so the conservative universe median is dragged down by potentially hundreds of -1.0 entries, while the naive universe simply omits them. The spread = cohortMean - universeMedian then mixes two effects (cohort change AND universe-baseline change) between variants.
why_it_matters: The naive-vs-conservative comparison is sold as isolating survivorship impact on the COHORT. But because the universe median also shifts (often dramatically, since delistings are universe-wide), the reported spread delta between variants conflates 'how delisting hurt my picks' with 'how delisting moved the whole-universe baseline'. Combined with A-fitness-02's over-counting of delistings, the conservative spread can swing sign for reasons unrelated to pick quality, undermining the headline survivorship-bias number.
fix: Report cohortMean and universeMedian separately for each variant (they already are returned) and have the dashboard read the cohortMean delta, not just spread. Better: define one fixed universe baseline (e.g. naive universe median) and measure both naive and conservative cohorts against it, so only the cohort side changes between variants. Document which universe each spread uses.

_verdict.note: Mechanism is accurately described but it is intended, documented, and explicitly unit-tested behavior — not a bug. Confirmed: metrics.js:83 (cohortSpread) and :109 (hitRate) take the universe baseline from Object.values(returnByTicker); measure.js:127-133 adds delisted->-1.0 only to returnByTickerConservative. So the conservative universe median is indeed dragged down by -1.0 delistings while naive omits them. BUT this is by design: the conservative variant models survivorship bias by treating delistings as -100%, and including those losses in its own universe baseline is internally self-consistent (each variant is apples-to-apples WITHIN itself). measure.test.js:350-393 (test #7) hand-derives exactly this dual effect — it asserts conservative universeMedian shifts from 0.05 to 0.035 precisely because of the -1.0 entry, and that the two variants' spreads MUST differ. The auditor's harm claim assumes a consumer compares spread_naive vs spread_conservative cross-variant; no such consumer exists in the worktree. cohortSpread output is only written to fitness/outputs/measure-<baselineId>.json, and generate-dashboard.js does not read the fitness output at all (grep for measure/fitness/spread/naive/conservative in it returns nothing). cohortMean and universeMedian are already returned separately (metrics.js:96), so no decomposed data is lost. The 'hundreds of -1.0 entries' is hyperbole — delisting count is bounded by survivorshipCounts.delisted. Net: a low-value interpretability/design opinion, not a correctness defect.

title: A currency that has NEVER succeeded is treated as fresh by pull-yahoo's staleness gate
evidence: refresh-fx sets `currencyMeta[c].lastAttemptAt = nowIso` unconditionally (line 105) but `lastSuccessAt` only on success (line 109). So a currency that fails on its very first appearance ends up with {lastAttemptAt} and NO lastSuccessAt. Cross-file: pull-yahoo.js:196 does `const lastSuccess = meta && meta.lastSuccessAt ? new Date(meta.lastSuccessAt) : fetchedAt;` — falling back to the fresh top-level fetchedAt. Because the rate key may still exist in `rates` (seeded from a prior file or fallback), perCurAgeDays is computed against fetchedAt (fresh) and the currency is marked FX_PROVENANCE='live'.
why_it_matters: The whole point of F-DP-010 / F-DP-051 per-currency staleness is to stop silently applying a rate that hasn't been confirmed live. A never-confirmed currency slips through the gate as 'live' as long as ANY currency succeeded that run (which keeps fetchedAt fresh). New EM currencies added to the list, or one that breaks on day one, get the worst-case treatment — a possibly-stale carried-over rate trusted as fresh — exactly the silent EM-mispricing this machinery was built to prevent.
fix: In refresh-fx, when a currency fails AND has no prior lastSuccessAt, write an explicit marker (e.g. currencyMeta[c].neverSucceeded = true) so pull-yahoo can treat absent lastSuccessAt as Infinity age rather than inheriting fetchedAt. Add comment: 'prevents a never-confirmed currency being scored fresh via top-level fetchedAt fallback (pull-yahoo loadFx line ~196)'.

_verdict.note:
False positive based on a misread of how `rates` keys are populated. The finding requires a currency that "has NEVER succeeded" to nonetheless have its key present in `raw.rates` so pull-yahoo's gate (pull-yahoo.js:193, which iterates `Object.keys(raw.rates)`) visits it and hits the `fetchedAt` fallback at line 196. That premise is self-contradictory in refresh-fx:

1. refresh-fx writes `rates[c]` ONLY on success — refresh-fx.js:108 is the sole `rates[` assignment, inside the `rate != null && rate > 0` branch. A never-succeeded currency therefore has NO key in `rates`, so pull-yahoo's loop never visits it and never reads its (lastSuccessAt-less) meta. It stays FX_PROVENANCE='fallback-hardcoded' (set at pull-yahoo.js:158, only flipped to 'live' at :215 for currencies present in raw.rates). The claimed 'live' outcome is unreachable.
2. The rate and lastSuccessAt are co-written in the same success branch (refresh-fx.js:108-109) and both carry forward via existing/existingMeta (lines 71-72, 96-97). So "key in rates" implies "lastSuccessAt present" — meaning line 196's fetchedAt fallback is NOT taken for it; the gate uses the true last-success age.

The auditor's two escape hatches both fail: (a) "seeded from a prior file" — a prior-file rate implies a prior success implies a carried-over lastSuccessAt, contradicting "never succeeded"; (b) "or fallback" — refresh-fx never seeds `rates` from any fallback table (only seed is {USD:1.0}+prior rates); FX_FALLBACK exists only in pull-yahoo and is applied to FX_TO_USD, not to raw.rates which the loop iterates.

Empirically confirmed against the live fx-rates.json: 33 rate keys, the only one with no meta is USD (identity 1.0, harmless), and zero rate keys have meta without lastSuccessAt. The line-196 fetchedAt fallback realistically only ever fires for USD=1.0, which is harmless. No data-integrity exposure.

The no-snapshot grace branch (line 171) and isInvalidSymbol (line 60, guarded) both acknowledge non-string is possible; this one call does not.

Therefore entry.ticker.padEnd(10) at line 171 is guaranteed to be called on a non-empty string and cannot crash. The auditor's premise is backwards: line 157 uses String() because it sits INSIDE the invalid-symbol branch — the one branch that deliberately handles non-string tickers (the ones isInvalidSymbol just rejected). title: isInvalidSymbol length>12 heuristic can false-positive-prune legitimate long symbols
evidence: `if (ticker.length > 12 && !/[.\-:^]/.test(ticker)) return 'looks-like-company-name';` (line 65). The rationale targets literal company-name entries like 'STMicroelectronics' (15 chars). But the rule prunes ANY separator-free symbol over 12 chars, with no requirement that it be alphabetic — and prune is destructive (rewrites watchlist.json via writeFileAtomic).
why_it_matters: Some legitimate Yahoo symbols (certain mutual-fund classes, structured products, and crypto pairs) exceed 12 chars without dot/dash/caret. Such an entry would be silently evicted as 'looks-like-company-name' and, once removed from the committed watchlist, only recoverable from git history. Currently 0 live entries trip it, so it's latent — but it's a hardcoded-shape heuristic doing irreversible deletion.

This still catches 'STMicroelectronics' but spares all-caps long symbols. Comment the precise failure mode it prevents.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed real (low severity), with the caveat that no current data triggers it. Code at C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/scripts/prune-watchlist.js:65 reads `if (ticker.length > 12 && !/[.\-:^]/.test(ticker)) return 'looks-like-company-name';`. The $-preferred-share case is already handled separately at line 62, so this length rule is purely the company-name backstop.

title: list/info assume wrapped {stocks:[...]} shape — crash on the legacy array/object shapes the rest of the pipeline tolerates

There is a shared schema-aware loader for exactly this (lib/watchlist-fs.js loadWatchlist, which handles array/wrapped/object shapes), and prune-watchlist.js:135-142 + daily-pull.yml:146 both go out of their way to handle all three shapes. why_it_matters: The codebase explicitly treats the three historical watchlist shapes as a live hazard (lib/watchlist-fs.js header; Tag 207a CI fix). watchlist-cli.js is the human-facing editor for that same file but is the one consumer that ignores the contract — a rollback or hand-edit to the legacy shape makes every CLI command crash with a cryptic TypeError instead of degrading. Low severity because current file is wrapped.
fix: Replace the hand-rolled load() with `const { loadWatchlist } = require('./lib/watchlist-fs.js')` and operate on the normalized `.stocks` array; on save, write back through the existing wrapped path. Single source of truth, no duplicated shape logic.

_verdict.note:
Confirmed real. watchlist-cli.js:23-24 load() returns raw JSON.parse with no shape normalization. cmdList (line 38: wl.stocks.length, line 39: for..of wl.stocks) and cmdInfo (line 75: wl.stocks.find) — plus cmdAdd/cmdRemove/cmdImport/cmdExport — all dereference wl.stocks unconditionally. On a bare-array or bare-object (ticker-keyed) watchlist, wl.stocks is undefined → TypeError. Evidence the rest of the pipeline tolerates all three shapes is solid: lib/watchlist-fs.js provides loadWatchlist/extractStocksArray handling array/wrapped/object (header explicitly documents the three historical shapes), and scripts/prune-watchlist.js:135-142 hand-rolls the same array-vs-wrapped-vs-other branching with an explicit comment that it previously crashed (TypeError on undefined.length) on the non-wrapped shapes. The current watchlist.json is the wrapped shape ({_meta, stocks, lastUniverseRefresh,...}), so the crash only fires on a legacy/rolled-back file, not in normal operation. Severity low is correct: operator-facing maintenance CLI, not pipeline-critical, and the failure is a loud crash rather than silent data corruption. revised_severity stays low.

fix_safe=false. The proposed swap is not behavior-preserving as written. The CLI's write path save(wl) mutates the loaded object in place (sets wl._meta.updated_at) and writes the ENTIRE object back, preserving _meta and sibling keys. loadWatchlist returns a normalized .stocks that for the bare-object shape is a brand-new synthetic array (Object.assign({ticker:k}, raw[k])) distinct from .raw, and for the bare-array shape has no _meta to carry. 'Operate on .stocks and save through the wrapped path' would (1) silently convert a legacy array/object file into the wrapped shape on first write — a schema migration, not a no-op — and (2) risk losing the in-place _meta-preservation unless explicitly wired through .raw per shape. Adopting the shared loader is the right direction (single source of truth), but the read+mutate+write round-trip needs human review to define save semantics for each shape. Mutating add/remove/import without that is risky to auto-apply.

title: normScore fallback in pickStockForMode is dead code — ev.normScore never exists

In methods/strategy-modes.js evaluateMode's return object (lines 279-300) emits `score: scoreResult ? scoreResult.score : null` but NEVER a `normScore` key. The real consequence is silent: whenever the score-aggregator is unavailable (methods/strategy-modes.js line 5 wraps `require('./score-aggregator.js')` in try/catch, so scoreResult can be null → ev.score === null), the pick is written with score:null and falls to the bottom of the sort (lines 250-260) and into the primaryMetric tiebreak. There is no normScore safety net at all — the comment claims one exists. picks-history is the walk-forward backtest's source of truth, so a missing aggregator silently nulls every pick.score for that vintage rather than degrading gracefully.

Do NOT leave a comment asserting a fallback that the data path never produces. (Does not touch methods/index.js.)

(1) methods/score-aggregator.js computeScore() returns keys score/baseScore/tier/redFlags/softGuardPenalty/breakdown/mode/dataQualityGrade/dataQualityCapped (lines 446-456) — NO normScore key; normScore at line 296 is only an internal local var. (2) methods/strategy-modes.js evaluateMode() return object (lines 278-298) emits `score: scoreResult ? scoreResult.score : null` and never a normScore key; all early-return failure objects (lines 179-211) also lack it. (3) In snapshot-picks.js pickStockForMode, ev is always evaluateMode's full return object (guarded by `if (!ev || !ev.passed) return null;` at line 89), so ev.normScore is always undefined. The middle ternary branch (line 103 `ev.normScore != null`) is therefore unreachable dead code, and the multi-line Tag 232c-22 / F-BT-009 / F-BT-010 comments (lines 81, 97-101) assert a normalized-fallback scale-alignment behavior the data path can never trigger.
