Severity medium is slightly high for pure dead code with a misleading comment — it produces no wrong output, only maintenance/comprehension hazard — but the misleading comment that documents non-existent behavior justifies keeping it at low-to-medium; setting medium->low.

title: firstSeenAt defaults to today for any ticker missing from the first-seen cache → weeksOnList look-ahead/under-count for backtests
evidence: const seen = modeFirstSeen[p.ticker]; p.firstSeenAt = seen || today; p.weeksOnList = _weeksBetween(p.firstSeenAt, today);  — combined with the cache trust at lines 156-159: `if (cached && modes.every(m => typeof cached[m] === 'object')) return { map: cached, fromCache: true };` (cache is accepted whole; never reconciled against the actual vintage files once it exists).
why_it_matters: weeksOnList feeds 'how long has this name been a pick' analytics. Two failure modes: (1) If _first-seen.json is ever truncated/partial (the very thing Tag 189 atomic-write tries to prevent but cannot guarantee against logic gaps) or a ticker legitimately reappears after falling off, the ticker is stamped firstSeenAt=today and weeksOnList=0 even though it was a pick months ago — a survivorship/recency artifact. (2) The cache is trusted permanently after first build (fromCache short-circuits the full rebuild) so a ticker that was dropped from the cache map is never re-derived from the vintage JSONs that still contain it. This is the asymmetric-attrition / look-ahead class the audit targets: the metric silently resets history rather than failing loudly.
fix: On cache hit, still cross-check today's picks against the newest vintage file(s) and, for any pick whose firstSeenAt would default to today, scan existing vintages before stamping today. Alternatively add a cheap integrity check (cache ticker count vs newest vintage) and force a full rebuild on mismatch. Keep FTS_CACHE_VERSION untouched (this is picks-history, not the FTS cache).

_verdict.note:
REFUTED on two independent grounds.

(1) Wrong impact model — no backtest look-ahead. firstSeenAt/weeksOnList are NOT consumed by the walk-forward backtest. I grepped every .js consumer: walk-forward-perf.js anchors all entry/exit dates to each vintage's `asOf` (evaluateVintage line 417 getEntryDate(asOfRaw); canonical dates via computeBenchmarkReturn on entryDate), never reading firstSeenAt. pick-diff.js, picks-regression-check.js, compute-picks-lookback.js, generate-dashboard.js: zero references. The ONLY reader is elliott-export.js (lines 92/124-125), which emits them as descriptive CSV columns weeks_on_list / first_seen_at. So even a wrong firstSeenAt cannot bias forward returns — the auditor's stated mechanism ("weeksOnList look-ahead/under-count for backtests") does not exist.

(2) The premise "ticker missing from the first-seen cache" cannot occur for tickers that appear in vintage files. The cache is incrementally maintained as a superset of all vintage tickers: each run's persisted picks (result.modes[modeId] = top100, lines 262-270) are exactly the set added to the cache afterward (lines 289-297). By induction the cache contains every ticker ever written to any vintage. The bootstrap case (cache introduced after vintages already existed — true here; vintages go back to 2026-05-14) is handled: cache absent -> full rebuild scans all vintages (lines 160-179) and seeds the true earliest date. Cache corruption is also handled: parse failure returns null (line 142 -> rebuild) and the structural gate `modes.every(m => typeof cached[m] === 'object')` (line 157) forces rebuild on a malformed cache. F-SM-027 makes the write atomic, so no partial-loss path. Thus the only way a vintage ticker is absent from the cache is manual external tampering, which the gates already convert into a full rebuild.

(3) `seen || today` is correct by construction: a genuinely first-time ticker's first-seen date IS today. The default is the right value, not a bug.

The cited lines (265-268) and the cache-trust line (157) are working as designed.

title: dedupePicksByCompany tiebreak uses `|| 0` — a legitimate score of 0 loses to a null-scored duplicate
evidence: else if (pIsUS === exIsUS && (p.score || 0) > (existing.score || 0)) byKey.set(key, p);
why_it_matters: Targeted '|| 0 falsy' class. score can legitimately be 0 (0-100 scale) and can be null (aggregator unavailable, see finding 01). `(p.score || 0)` collapses both null and 0 to 0, so a real score of 0 never wins the tiebreak and the comparison can't distinguish 'scored 0' from 'unscored'. For two same-listing-status duplicates this picks an arbitrary survivor. Low impact today (ties at exactly 0 are rare) but it is the exact operator-precedence/falsy footgun the audit flags, and it compounds finding 01 (null scores are common when aggregator is missing).
fix: Compare with explicit null handling: const ps = p.score == null ? -Infinity : p.score; const es = existing.score == null ? -Infinity : existing.score; if (ps > es) ... — so a scored 0 beats an unscored null and 0-vs-0 is a true tie.

_verdict.note: Confirmed real but minor. At snapshot-picks.js:128 the dedup tiebreak `(p.score || 0) > (existing.score || 0)` does conflate a legitimate score of 0 with null. score CAN legitimately be exactly 0: score-aggregator.js:320 `score = Math.max(0, baseScore - softGuardPenalty)` and :388 `Math.max(0, Math.round(score * auditMultiplier))` clamp at 0, and a pick reaches dedup only after `ev.passed` (snapshot-picks.js:89), so a passed-but-penalized stock can carry score 0; null arises only if the aggregator is absent/threw (fallback at :102-104). In the corner where p.score===0 and existing.score===null (same company key, same US-ness class), `0 > 0` is false so the null-scored duplicate is retained over the legitimately-scored-0 pick. However materiality is tiny: this only decides WHICH of two same-company duplicates survives (both already passing picks), cross-listings differing in US-ness are handled earlier by the pIsUS branch, and the intersection (same normalized company + same US-class + one exactly-0 + one null) is a near-unreachable edge. Severity low is correct.

title: getMcap lacks the Number.isFinite guard that strategy-modes uses — NaN marketCap propagates into pick output
evidence: function getMcap(stock){ const m = stock.marketCap || (stock.meta && stock.meta.marketCap); if (typeof m === 'number') return m; if (m && typeof m === 'object' && 'value' in m) return m.value; return null; }  — contrast methods/strategy-modes.js line 192-194 which does `if (mcUnwrapped == null || !Number.isFinite(mcUnwrapped)) return mcap_missing`.
why_it_matters: If marketCap.value is NaN or Infinity, getMcap returns it verbatim into the pick. JSON.stringify(NaN) serializes as null so the on-disk vintage is not corrupted, but the value flows through in-memory consumers and the asymmetry with strategy-modes (which treats NaN mcap as 'missing') means the same stock can be mcap_missing for gating yet carry a non-null in-memory mcap here. Minor NaN-propagation / no-isFinite-guard instance the audit asks for.
fix: Mirror strategy-modes: `const v = (typeof m === 'number') ? m : (m && typeof m === 'object' && 'value' in m ? m.value : null); return Number.isFinite(v) ? v : null;`

_verdict.note:
Verified the behavioral difference is real. snapshot-picks.js:61-66 getMcap unwraps {value} and returns it with no finiteness check, while methods/strategy-modes.js:191-194 guards `if (mcUnwrapped == null || !Number.isFinite(mcUnwrapped))`. So a NaN marketCap.value would be returned by getMcap unguarded. The title's claim of a real inconsistency is accurate.

HOWEVER the impact is overstated and the severity is correctly LOW (arguably borderline cosmetic):
- getMcap has exactly ONE caller (snapshot-picks.js:105) and its return value goes only into the `marketCap` OUTPUT field of a pick. It is NOT used for sorting (picks.sort uses score/primaryMetric.value, lines 250-260), filtering, the mcap floor, or any selection logic. So a NaN cannot change which stocks are picked or their order.
- The pick object is written via JSON.stringify (lines 283/285). JSON.stringify(NaN) === "null", so even an unguarded NaN serializes to `"marketCap": null` in the output file — identical to what the proposed fix emits explicitly. The observable JSON is the same with or without the guard.
- NaN reaching the snapshot at all is a narrow edge case: pull-yahoo.js wraps marketCap via _metric() and applies a floor filter (lines 2007-2018) that skips null/out-of-range mcap. NaN would slip past the floor (NaN comparisons are false, and NaN != null) only in the rare event Yahoo returns NaN or the price-only path computes q.marketCap*tradingFactor === NaN.

Net: genuine defensive-consistency gap worth closing to match the sibling function, but no functional corruption of picks and no different output bytes in practice. LOW is right.

Relevant files: C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/snapshot-picks.js (getMcap 61-66, sole caller 105); C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/methods/strategy-modes.js (contrast guard 191-194); C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/pull-yahoo.js (upstream wrap/filter 890, 1592-1594, 2007-2018).

title: generatedAt uses wall-clock new Date() while `date`/vintage uses frozen RUN_DATE_UTC — re-introduces the cross-UTC-midnight skew the freeze was meant to kill
evidence: Line 53: const today = process.env.RUN_DATE_UTC || new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10);  Line 54: outFile = path.join(args.out, `${today}.json`);  Line 148: data.generatedAt = new Date().toISOString();  (Tag 232c-16 comment claims this 'aligns with walk-forward's anchor'.)
why_it_matters: The whole RUN_DATE_UTC mechanism (workflow 'Freeze Run Date', daily-pull.yml lines 51-55) exists so every snapshot-* script agrees on TODAY even when the ~3h pull crosses UTC midnight. The vintage filename and data.date honor the frozen date, but data.generatedAt is raw wall-clock. If the methods-history step runs after 00:00 UTC (common — it is near the end of a 165-min pull that may start at 22:00 UTC), generatedAt's date can be TODAY+1 while the filename is TODAY. method-effectiveness.js's fallback `(asOf + 'T00:00:00Z')` is avoided by having generatedAt, but generatedAt now disagrees with the vintage date by a full day in exactly the midnight-crossing scenario the freeze targets — the opposite of the comment's claim. Reintroduces the F-219b-01 skew through a side channel.
fix: Anchor generatedAt to the frozen date when present: `data.generatedAt = process.env.RUN_DATE_UTC ? process.env.RUN_DATE_UTC + 'T00:00:00.000Z' : new Date().toISOString();` matching snapshot-picks.js line 220's asOf handling.

_verdict.note:
False positive based on a misread of which field feeds what. Two fields serve deliberately different purposes: `date`/vintage (line 53/67, frozen to RUN_DATE_UTC) is the vintage IDENTITY/cohort label and IS correctly frozen — no cross-midnight skew exists there. `generatedAt` (line 148) is the actual production WALL-CLOCK timestamp, and it is intentionally wall-clock.

The sole consumer of generatedAt is method-effectiveness.js line 262-263: `const asOfTs = file.generatedAt || (asOf + 'T00:00:00Z'); const realEntryAsOf = WF.getEntryDate(asOfTs);`. WF.getEntryDate (walk-forward-perf.js line 164-184) inspects the TIME-OF-DAY: if hours < 21:00 UTC (pre-close) it shifts entry to T+1, else same day. This is the F-BT-001 look-ahead-bias guard. The field exists precisely to carry the real run time so the backtest knows whether the snapshot was produced pre- or post-market-close.

The proposed fix (`RUN_DATE_UTC + 'T00:00:00.000Z'`) would be a REGRESSION: it pins the hour to 0, so getEntryDate always classifies every methods-history vintage as pre-close and always shifts entry to T+1 — discarding the very information generatedAt exists to provide and breaking the post-close distinction. It directly contradicts the documented Tag 232c-16 intent (lines 141-147: 'the timestamp reflects when the script actually ran ... which aligns with walk-forward's anchor').

The 'matching snapshot-picks.js line 220' comparison is also wrong: line 220 anchors `asOf` (the vintage IDENTITY field, analog of snapshot-methods-history's `date`/`today` at line 53 — which is ALREADY frozen to RUN_DATE_UTC). There is no `generatedAt` in the picks file; walk-forward reads picksFile.asOf via getEntryDate (line 417), and that asOf retains time-of-day from the same `new Date().toISOString()` fallback. So the cited pattern is already followed for the corresponding field, and the picks path itself relies on wall-clock time-of-day for the entry-shift logic, confirming the design is intentional and consistent.

No data-integrity bug. The freeze was meant to make vintage labels deterministic (done), not to strip time-of-day from the run timestamp that the look-ahead guard depends on.

title: Health failure_rate denominator (fileList.length) excludes files that failed to read, double-discounting I/O failures
evidence: loadFilesAsync returns {file,data,error} for every file; read errors push to _pipelineFailures (line 100). But n_total = fileList.length (line 165) and that list already excludes '_*' files. A file that fails JSON.parse is counted in fileList AND in _pipelineFailures, which is correct. However a file that disappears between readdir and readFile yields an error entry counted in n_failed while still in fileList — fine. The subtle issue: parse-error tickers use file.replace(/\.json$/,'') as the ticker id (lines 99,103) so a corrupt 'AAPL.json' is attributed to ticker 'AAPL', but a corrupt '_manifest-full.json' is excluded from fileList by the startsWith('_') filter (line 66) and never reaches the loop, so manifest corruption is invisible to the health gate.
why_it_matters: Lower-severity than the picks denominator bug, but the methods-history 5% gate (line 177) is the guard for the 14 MB backtest source of truth. Underscore-prefixed pollution is correctly excluded for ticker safety, yet that means a pull that produces only manifests and zero real snapshots reports n_total=0 → failure_rate=0 (line 168 `n_total > 0 ? ... : 0`) → gate passes on an empty run. The empty-universe case silently passes the health threshold.
fix: Add an explicit floor: if fileList.length is below a minimum (e.g. share the workflow's 2500 floor or a fraction of watchlist size) emit ::error before the 5% check, so a near-empty snapshots/ dir cannot pass via the n_total>0?...:0 short-circuit.

_verdict.note:
Refuted on its stated bug; the residual concern is real-but-already-gated, not a live defect.

TITLE CLAIM ("failure_rate denominator double-discounts I/O failures") is FALSE and contradicted by the auditor's own evidence. At lines 165-168: n_total=fileList.length, n_failed=_pipelineFailures.length, failure_rate=n_failed/n_total. A file failing JSON.parse is counted exactly once in the denominator (it's in fileList) and once in the numerator (pushed to _pipelineFailures at line 100) — that is correct 1-of-N accounting, not double-discounting. The evidence paragraph itself says "which is correct" and "fine" twice, never demonstrating any double-count.

EVIDENCE PIVOT ("manifest corruption invisible to health gate") is true but BY DESIGN, not a bug. Line 66 excludes all '_*' files (startsWith('_')) deliberately — Tag 227c-1 / audit F-227c-01 HIGH (lines 56-65) added this exclusion precisely because letting _manifest-full.json through caused Runner.evaluateStock to write a fake "_manifest-full" ghost ticker into every methods-history vintage since 2026-05-14, polluting the backtest base. Re-including manifests in the health denominator would reintroduce the very HIGH bug they fixed. Manifest integrity is the upstream pull-yahoo concern (see manifest partial/n_ok logic in daily-pull.yml lines 302-360), not this snapshot script's.

PROPOSED FIX (add a min-file-count floor before the 5% check) targets a third scenario — a near-empty snapshots/ passing via the n_total>0?...:0 short-circuit (failure_rate=0 when there are few-but-valid files). That hole is real in isolation, BUT it is already gated upstream in the same job: daily-pull.yml lines 355-360 hard-fail (exit 1) the run when ok < max(2500, total*0.13) BEFORE the Snapshot Methods-History step (line 452) ever runs. Additionally this script runs with continue-on-error:true (line 454), so its own process.exit(1) wouldn't fail the job regardless — only the dedicated Pipeline Health Check step gates. So a near-empty dir cannot reach this step in CI. The proposed floor is defense-in-depth, not a fix for a live exposure.

Net: the named bug doesn't exist, the cited mechanism is an intentional hardening, and the fix addresses an already-covered scenario. Not a real finding.

File: C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/snapshot-methods-history.js (lines 66, 97-102, 165-168); upstream gate: C:/Users/Karlr/screener-wt/audit-hardening/.github/workflows/daily-pull.yml (lines 355-360, 452-454).

title: Per-filter catch swallows the error into a details entry but the caller only appends `codes` — filter crashes vanish from reasonCodes
evidence: catch (e) { details.push({ code: 'MANIPULATION_FILTER_ERROR', error: e.message }); }  — the MANIPULATION_FILTER_ERROR code is pushed to `details` but NOT to `codes` (contrast the success path lines 198-199 which push to both). A systematically-crashing filter would therefore be completely invisible in production output — no flag, no code, no health signal — exactly the 'catch → return null/empty' silent-failure pattern the audit targets.

title: history-cli keys method rows by data.date (file content) but the column header uses filenames — a vintage whose internal date disagrees with its filename misaligns the table
evidence: Header columns: `const allDates = files.map(f => f.replace('.json', ''));` (line 29) and printed at line 43. Cell lookup: `methodValues[mid][data.date] = r;` (line 38, keyed by the file's INTERNAL data.date) and rendered via `byDate[d]` where d iterates allDates (filenames) at line 45-46.

The CLI would silently show a gap where real data exists. Low severity (read-only diagnostic) but it is a real filename-vs-content key mismatch.

title: history-cli assumes r.value is numeric (.toFixed) — a non-numeric method value would crash the row render
evidence: return `${v.value.toFixed(1).padStart(5)}${passSym}`;  guarded only by `if (!v || v.value == null) return '   —  ';` (line 47).

But there is no Number type/Number.isFinite check, so the moment any method emits a string/bool value (or a future schema change) this throws TypeError mid-table and aborts the whole listing. Line 26: `(stock.marketCap.value / 1e9).toFixed(0)` guarded only by the truthiness of `stock.marketCap` (`stock.marketCap ? ... : '?'`), not by .value being present/finite.
why_it_matters: Manual diagnostic CLI (not in workflow), so low severity, but: (1) one corrupt/partial snapshot among the requested tickers aborts the entire diagnostic rather than SKIP-ing that ticker like the missing-file path does (line 20). (2) If stock.marketCap is a wrapper present but with value:null/NaN, `null/1e9` → 0, `NaN/1e9` → NaN, and `.toFixed(0)` yields '0B' or 'NaNB' silently instead of '?'. Inconsistent with the careful '?' fallback the same line uses for missing marketCap.
fix: Wrap the parse in try/catch and `continue` with a SKIP message on failure (mirror line 20). For mcap, check Number.isFinite(stock.marketCap && stock.marketCap.value) before dividing; else print '?'.

title: earnings-cli silently drops calendar entries with unparseable dates (new Date('garbage') → Invalid Date comparisons are always false)
evidence: for (const [ticker, info] of Object.entries(cal)) { if (!info.date) continue; const d = new Date(info.date); if (d >= today && d <= cutoff) { ... } }  — no Number.isNaN(d.getTime()) check.
why_it_matters: If info.date is present but malformed (e.g. a Yahoo format change), `new Date(info.date)` is an Invalid Date; every comparison with it is false, so the entry is silently omitted from 'upcoming' with no warning. The --days validation (lines 18-21) was hardened against NaN exactly to avoid Invalid-Date silent-empty output, but the per-entry date is not similarly validated — same NaN/Invalid-Date class, one layer down. A whole-calendar format drift would render an empty list that looks like 'no upcoming earnings' rather than a parse problem.
fix: After `const d = new Date(info.date);` add `if (Number.isNaN(d.getTime())) { /* optionally count + warn */ continue; }` and emit a summary count of skipped-unparseable entries so silent drift is visible.

title: tag22 updateHistory window test relies on insertion order of zero-padded-less date strings and an off-by-context assertion comment
evidence: for (let i=0;i<16;i++){ h = FC.updateHistory(h,{date:'2026-05-'+i, coverage:{}}); }  assertEq(h.length, FC.HISTORY_WINDOW) // 14;  assertEq(h[0].date, '2026-05-2'); // 'oldest still in (pushed 0-15, keep latest 14 = 2-15)'.
why_it_matters: The dates are built as '2026-05-0' .. '2026-05-15' (not zero-padded, not valid ISO for single digits). updateHistory (field-coverage.js line 130) slices the last 14 by ARRAY position, which happens to make the test pass, but the test's date strings are malformed ('2026-05-0', '2026-05-2') and only work because the assertion checks array slicing, not date semantics. If anyone later changes updateHistory to sort/dedupe by parsed date (a plausible hardening), this test would break for the wrong reason and the malformed-date fixtures would mask it. The test also encodes HISTORY_WINDOW=14 as a literal comment that must be hand-synced with field-coverage.js line 70.
fix: Use valid zero-padded ISO dates (or explicit ordinal markers) in the fixture and assert on a value that survives a date-aware refactor; keep referencing FC.HISTORY_WINDOW (already done) but drop the brittle '// 14' literal in favor of computing expected boundary from FC.HISTORY_WINDOW.

title: evaluateStock result indexed as flat map r[m.id] but exported evaluateStock returns {} keyed by id — fragile to the runner's dual API
evidence: Line 36-41: `const r = Runner.evaluateStock(stock); ... const res = r[m.id];` runner.js line 90 exports `evaluateStock: evaluateStockLegacy`, and evaluateStockLegacy (line 83-86) returns `out.results` (flat `{id: {computable,value,pass}}`), so `r[m.id]` is correct TODAY. But evaluateStockExtended (the non-legacy) returns `{results, disqualified, ...}` where `r[m.id]` would be undefined. analyze-correlation, tune-threshold, and both backtests all silently depend on getting the LEGACY export.
why_it_matters: The two exported shapes differ and a future caller (or a refactor that swaps which export is default) would make `r[m.id]` undefined for every method, and `(res && res.computable)` would push null for all → every correlation pair has <5 points → script prints 'Keine starke Korrelation' (a false all-clear) instead of crashing. The F-GC-011 null-guard (line 38-40) masks the failure as 'no data' rather than surfacing a contract break. This is an architectural fragility shared across all the analysis scripts.
fix: Have these scripts call the explicitly-named `Runner.evaluateStockExtended(stock).results` (or add a stable `Runner.evaluateFlat`) so the contract is explicit and a shape change fails loudly instead of degrading to a false 'no correlation' / 'no computable values' result.

title: Short-history rejection compares hist[0].date to requested period1 using monthly bars with only 45d slack — drops legitimate full-window stocks on alignment jitter
evidence: Line 55-56: `const firstDate = ...; if (Math.abs(firstDate.getTime() - past.getTime()) > 45 * 86400 * 1000) return null;` with `interval:'1mo'` (line 49). Monthly bars are stamped at month start; `past` is computed as exactly `now - N years` (line 46-47, an arbitrary day-of-month). For a stock that genuinely traded the full window, the first monthly bar can legitimately be up to ~31 days after `period1` plus Yahoo's month-boundary placement, and the 5Y window amplifies any offset — borderline cases get nulled out.
why_it_matters: This is the survivorship/horizon-integrity guard (F-BT-016a). Too-tight slack on monthly bars rejects stocks that DID trade the full horizon, shrinking the cohort and biasing the median toward the survivors that happen to align cleanly to month boundaries. Combined with the documented survivorship caveat, the reported outperformance-vs-benchmark is computed on a self-selected subset.
fix: Widen the slack to ~40-50 days only relative to the bar interval, or better: compare against the SECOND bar / use the count of bars vs expected (`hist.length >= years*12 - 1`) instead of date-distance, which is robust to month-boundary placement. Document the chosen tolerance.

title: No-arg JSON.parse of huge state files + no fs.existsSync guards → uncaught crash with no diagnostic on missing/oversized inputs
evidence: Line 9 `const wl = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync('./watchlist.json'));` and line 10 `const prices = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync('./prices/history.json'));` — no encoding arg (returns Buffer; JSON.parse coerces but is slower and unguarded), no existence check, no try/catch. watchlist.json is 5.7 MB and prices/history.json holds 17,183 tickers (probed). Unlike its siblings (backtest-pass-vs-fail.js guards with fs.existsSync at lines 41-43; compute-picks-lookback wraps main in .catch), this file does neither.
why_it_matters: If either file is missing or partially written (the workflow runs pull-historical-prices.js with continue-on-error, so a truncated prices/history.json is a real outcome), the script dies with a raw SyntaxError/ENOENT stack and no actionable message, and re-parsing the full 17k-ticker prices map into memory on every invocation is wasteful for an ad-hoc CLI. It is also the only one of the three backtests with no _bias-style guardrails on input validity.
fix: Add `fs.existsSync` guards with clear errors (mirror backtest-pass-vs-fail.js lines 41-43), pass `'utf8'` to readFileSync, and wrap in try/catch that names the offending file. Consider streaming/keying only the needed tickers rather than parsing all 17k series.

file: backtest-10-weeks.js, backtest-from-history.js, backtest-pass-vs-fail.js, compute-picks-lookback.js, analyze-correlation.js, tune-threshold.js, sector-trends.js
title: All seven analysis scripts are orphaned CLI tools — referenced by no workflow step, no package.json script, and no require() in code
evidence: daily-pull.yml invokes only detect-changes.js (line 365) of the eight target files. package.json scripts (pull/pull:fast/pull:single) reference only pull-yahoo.js. Grep for the seven script basenames across all non-JSON files returns hits ONLY in docs (README.md, CONTEXT.md, ROADMAP, audit-reports/*) and the scripts' own headers — zero `require(...)` of any of them and zero workflow `node X.js` lines. monthly-sec-xbrl.yml does not call them either.
why_it_matters: These are hand-run research tools, not pipeline steps. That is legitimate, but it means: (a) their bugs (findings 02/03/07/08/10/11 above) are invisible to CI — nothing exercises them, so regressions accumulate silently; (b) they all depend on snapshot files (./snapshots/TICKER.json) that the audited worktree does not actually contain (only _manifest.json present), so they currently produce empty cohorts / 'No computable values' on this checkout without erroring. They cap the screener's analytical value precisely because the backtest/validation layer is unrun and partly broken.
fix: Either (a) wire the deterministic ones (analyze-correlation, sector-trends, tune-threshold, backtest-pass-vs-fail — the ones needing no live Yahoo pull) into a lightweight scheduled 'analysis' job or a smoke-test that runs them against committed methods-history/prices fixtures so their bugs surface in CI; or (b) move them under a scripts/research/ folder and document them as manual tools. Do not delete without Karl's OK (binding rule).

title: Cron weekday range '2-6' (Tue–Sat UTC) pulls Saturday with no fresh US market data and never refreshes on Monday morning, creating an asymmetric staleness pattern across the week
evidence: Line 5: `cron: '17 2 * * 2-6'` = 02:17 UTC Tue–Sat. US markets close 21:00 UTC (Mon-Fri). So: Tue 02:17 captures Mon close, ..., Fri 02:17 captures Thu close, Sat 02:17 captures Fri close. There is NO Sun and NO Mon run. The Saturday run (capturing Friday's close) is fine, but the next run is Tuesday capturing Monday's close — meaning Monday's intraday/close data is first reflected ~25h later and there is a 3-day gap (Sat 02:17 → Tue 02:17) over the weekend during which the committed snapshots/dashboard show Friday's close as 'latest'.
why_it_matters: Downstream freshness gates use a 36h window (line 255). The Sat→Tue gap is ~72h, so on Monday the dashboard data is up to 3 days stale yet the freshness gate (which only runs inside a pull) never evaluates on Mon. A user opening the dashboard Monday sees Friday data with no staleness indicator driven by a fresh run. If the intent was 'capture each trading day's close once', the correct range is the day AFTER each trading day: Tue–Sat already does that, so this may be intentional — but the Saturday run capturing Friday and then nothing until Tuesday is the asymmetry worth confirming.
fix: If the goal is freshest-possible weekday data, this is acceptable; document it explicitly in the cron comment. If Monday-morning freshness matters, add a Monday run (range '1-6' minus Sun, i.e. capture is already Tue-Sat; consider '2-6' is Tue-Sat — to also refresh Monday AM add Mon: use '1-6' won't help since Mon pre-market has Fri close). Simplest: keep as-is but surface 'data as of <asOf>, N days stale' prominently on the dashboard so the weekend gap is visible to the reader.

title: Commit step uses `git add -A` which stages ANY runner-side file change (e.g. a newly written gitignored-miss, _manifest-full.json, or a tool-generated temp), risking accidental commit of large/ephemeral artifacts to main
evidence: Line 584: `git add -A` stages the entire worktree. pull-yahoo.js writes _manifest-full.json (line 2202) described as 'gitignored' and screener-detail.json (~44MB/day, line 671) described as gitignored. .gitignore covers node_modules/, external-data/sec-xbrl/*.json, _site, screener-detail.json — but `git add -A` relies entirely on .gitignore being exhaustive. Any new artifact a future script writes (or a path the ignore misses, e.g. a tmp from lib/atomic-write's `_tmpPath`) gets force-staged and committed to main with the chore commit.
why_it_matters: monthly-sec-xbrl.yml:120 deliberately stages ONLY `git add external-data/sec-xbrl/_manifest.json` — a tight allowlist. daily-pull.yml uses the opposite, blanket `git add -A`. The atomic-write tmp files (lib/atomic-write.js:27 _tmpPath) are written next to the target; if a crash leaves a `.tmp` file and it is not gitignored, `git add -A` commits a partial-write temp into main, which the next run's parser may pick up. Repo bloat from a 44MB artifact slipping the ignore is permanent in history.
fix: Replace `git add -A` with an explicit allowlist of the directories/files this workflow is meant to publish (snapshots/, picks-history/, methods-history/, alert-state.json, *-report.html, *.json data files), mirroring the monthly workflow's tight `git add <path>`. Add `*.tmp` and the atomic-write tmp suffix to .gitignore as defense-in-depth.

title: Universe refresh and prune both run continue-on-error and BOTH write watchlist.json; the only guard is a size>=200 floor, so a partial-corruption that leaves >200 but wrong entries (e.g. truncated/duplicated) passes the sanity check
evidence: Refresh Universe (line 122, continue-on-error) and Prune Watchlist (line 127, continue-on-error) both mutate watchlist.json. Verify Watchlist Sanity (line 134-151) only checks existence and `size >= 200` (line 148). The comment (line 130-133) acknowledges 'a failure leaves a stale or degenerate watchlist that silently propagates' but the floor is a single absolute count. A refresh that half-completes and writes 8000 garbage/duplicate tickers, or a prune that mangles structure but keeps >200 stocks, sails through. There is no upper-bound or delta check against the prior watchlist size, despite MAX_UNIVERSE=25000 (line 115) being a 92% jump from the prior 13000 cap (line 94-105).
why_it_matters: The watchlist is the universe denominator for the coverage gate (line 315) and the input set for the entire pull. A silently-degenerate-but-large watchlist (e.g. refresh duplicated entries to inflate to 25000, or pruned to a biased subset) introduces survivorship/selection bias into every downstream pick and backtest, while passing the >=200 floor. The 200 floor only catches catastrophic emptying, not the more dangerous quiet corruption.
fix: Add a delta guard: compare new watchlist size against the committed prior size and fail (or require ALLOW_UNIVERSE_DRIFT, mirroring ALLOW_PICKS_DRIFT at line 437) if it moved more than ~±30%. Add a duplicate-ticker check and a schema-shape assertion (every entry has ticker+required keys). Do NOT hardcode ticker exclusions — fix the guard, per the binding constraint.

title: Snapshot-freshness gate parses only the first 800 bytes for asOf/fetchedAt; a snapshot whose timestamp falls beyond byte 800 (large meta header) is silently counted as unparseable, biasing the fresh-fraction downward toward the 50% abort
evidence: Line 259: `readFileSync(...).slice(0, 800)` then line 264 regex-matches asOf|fetchedAt within those 800 bytes. pull-yahoo.js writes the canonical object with fetchedAt (line 831) and asOf (line 840) AFTER potentially large preceding fields — the mapper builds marketCap/annual/quarterly metrics. If the JSON serialization places asOf/fetchedAt after 800 bytes of leading content (field ordering depends on object construction order in mapYahooToCanonical, lines 831-896 show fetchedAt/asOf set inside a large object), the regex misses and `unparseable++` (line 268). The gate's denominator is `files.length` (line 270/272), so unparseable counts AGAINST the fresh fraction.
why_it_matters: The gate aborts the whole pipeline if `fresh/files.length < 0.5` (line 272). Miscounting fresh snapshots as unparseable purely due to byte-offset of the timestamp can push a healthy pull below 50% and kill a run that actually succeeded — discarding ~4h of work. The 800-byte cap is an optimization that assumes timestamp position; it is fragile to any mapper field-ordering change.
fix: Parse the full file (these snapshots are small per-ticker JSON, not the 14MB methods-history) or, better, JSON.parse and read meta.asOf directly instead of a byte-window regex. If perf matters, read meta first by structuring snapshots with meta/asOf as the leading key, and assert that invariant in a test. Treating unparseable as a hard-down vote (line 268 + denominator) should at minimum be logged per-file so the operator can see WHY freshness dropped.

title: Canary couples to a single anchor (NVDA) and a duplicated, drift-prone MODULES copy
evidence: ANCHOR='NVDA' (single ticker). MODULES is a hand-maintained copy of pull-yahoo's list with the comment 'Keep in sync with MODULES in pull-yahoo.js line ~77' — but the real array is at pull-yahoo.js:104, and the only thing forcing sync is a human reading a comment. Verified the two lists currently match (13 modules, same order), so no live bug today.
why_it_matters: Two failure modes. (1) Single-anchor: NVDA happens to populate every module; a field that regresses only for ADRs/financials/small-caps (e.g. financialCurrency, which the canary exists for, is ALWAYS USD for NVDA so the canary can never observe the ADR bug it was built to catch). (2) Duplicated MODULES drifts: if pull-yahoo adds a module the canary doesn't, the new field's schema is never guarded. The canary's value is capped by its narrowest assumption.
fix: Import MODULES directly from pull-yahoo (export it) instead of copying, so the canary always tests what's pulled. Add a second anchor that is an ADR or non-USD reporter (e.g. TSM or BABA) so financialCurrency!=USD is actually exercised — that is the only way this canary can ever catch the bug class named in its own header. Keep network calls cheap by limiting to 2 anchors.
